experiment_title: Induction of Bystander Effects by High LET Radiation In Cells and in Tissue Models
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The mission of NASA’s space radiation biology program is to provide knowledge on the effects of high energy charged particles on biological systems at the molecular, cellular, tissue, and organism levels in order to enable better prediction of risks of carcinogenesis and damage to normal tissues from exposures of astronauts to the ionizing radiation in space. With charged particles such as alpha-particles and low energy protons, significant differences from direct DNA damage-mediated responses have been demonstrated in a number of biological systems. Occurrence of these effects, including bystander effects and genomic instability, calls into question the use of a simple linear extrapolation of cancer risks from high dose data to low doses. This is of particular relevance to NASA because the occurrence of bystander effects in cells exposed to heavy ions or energetic protons, as found in space, has not been evaluated to date. The overall goals of this study are to test the hypothesis that heavy ions and energetic protons efficiently cause bystander effects in neighboring cells not directly traversed by the radiation and to study the mechanisms involved. There were four specific aims:

1. Determine induction of bystander effects by heavy ions compared to X-rays and protons in cultured human diploid fibroblasts and keratinocytes using endpoints specific for each cell type and including production of micronuclei, apoptosis, clonogenicity and increased gene expression.
2. Test the hypothesis that heavy ion-induced bystander effects can be modified by exposure of cells to reactive oxygen species (ROS), an overlying oxidative stress.
3. Test the hypothesis that exposure to low LET radiation alters the heavy ion-induced bystander effects.
4. Begin development of 3-D tissue models for assessment of bystander effects from heavy ions and energetic protons.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The investigators have developed a novel transwell insert co-culture system in which irradiated and unirradiated cells share medium, but are physically separated, and used this approach to demonstrate medium-mediated bystander responses in AG01522 normal human fibroblasts after X-ray exposure. At the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory they have used this co-culture system, as well as irradiating cells at low particle fluences, to study bystander responses induced by heavy ions (1 GeV/n Fe, 1 GeV/n Ti and 290 MeV/n C) and protons (1 GeV/n). They have used iron, titanium, carbon and protons because they represent particles found in space that span a range of LET values from 0.24 to about 150 keV/micrometer, thus allowing us to test the LET dependence of various bystander responses. Investigators found substantial effects in directly irradiated AG01522 fibroblasts and h-TERT immortalized human keratinocytes using endpoints including clonogenic survival, micronuclei (MN) formation and p21 expression. For example, with the clonogenic survival assay in the AG01522 cells, we have found relative biological effect (RBE) values at 10% survival are 2.5, 2.3, 1.0 and 1.2 for 1 GeV/amu Fe, 1 GeV/amu Ti, 290 MeV/amu C and 1 GeV/amu protons, respectively, compared to 250 kVp X-rays, indicating the greater effectiveness of Fe and Ti for inducing cell killing. Fe and Ti are also very effective inducers of MN in these cells, although C ions are less effective, similar to protons.

Using their insert system,investigators have demonstrated that irradiation with 1 GeV/amu Fe ions induces a 2-3 fold increase in MN formation in unirradiated bystander AG0 cells, which is similar in magnitude to that seen with X-rays. The increase in damage in bystander cells is independent of the dose to the hit cells between 0.1 and 2 Gy Fe ions, although it is somewhat lower at 0.05 Gy. The insert system allows investigators to study the timing of bystander signaling by altering the time at which the co-culture of irradiated and unirradiated cells is started or how long the two cell populations are together. Using this approach, they have shown that when irradiated and unirradiated bystander cells are combined in shared medium immediately, one hour or three hours after irradiation, a full bystander MN formation effect is observed. However, when combining the irradiated and unirradiated cells is delayed six hours after irradiation, the bystander effect is lost. Furthermore, bystander micronuclei formation is observed even when the bystander cells are co-cultured with irradiated cells for only one hour if they are combined immediately after irradiation. This suggests that the signal transduction to bystander cells from irradiated cells occurs at a short time after irradiation, and these early stage signals sent by irradiated cells are crucial to the induction of bystander effects. The results with iron ions are similar to those with X-rays, suggesting that the bystander MN formation in this system is independent of LET. Protons also induce a medium-mediated bystander effect in terms of MN production, although the magnitude is less than seen with Fe ions or X-rays.

In addition to X-irradiation, the investigators have now shown gamma-H2AX foci formation in unirradiated bystander cells that shared medium with Fe ion-irradiated cells at different time points after co-culture. The data indicate that a 2-3-fold increase in percentage of bystander cells with gamma-H2AX foci occurs as early as one hour after irradiation, and lasts at least 24 hours. Compared to the directly irradiated cells, which have a high yield of gamma-H2AX foci at early times after irradiation and return to control levels by 24 hours, bystander cells have slower kinetics of disappearance of gamma-H2AX foci. Fe ions and X-rays induce a similar pattern of gamma-H2AX foci in unirradiated bystander cells, suggesting gamma-H2AX foci induction in bystander cells is independent of LET of the radiation.

The investigators were interested in studying the effects of very low fluences of particles where only one to two percent or less of the cells would be traversed by particles. Dr. Rusek and his team of NSRL physicists have developed procedures for obtaining these very low fluences, and, most importantly, being able to accurately quantify the particle fluences, determine the beam uniformity and determine the purity of the beam. They have now demonstrated that very low fluences of energetic protons and iron ions induce bystander MN formation and 53BP1 foci (another surrogate for DNA DSBs) in non-irradiated bystander fibroblasts that share medium with irradiated cells. Results show that while there is no significant increase in MN formation in cells directly irradiated with low fluences (2e3 to 5e6 particles/cm2 for protons and 2e3 to 2.25e5 particles/cm2 for iron ions) of protons and iron ions, there is 1.5-2-fold increase in MN formation in bystander cells in the insert system. On the other hand, 53BP1 forms foci in both directly irradiated and bystander cells with low fluences of protons and iron ion, with the percentage of irradiated cells with 53BP1 foci being a little higher than that of bystander cells. It is noteworthy that within the range of low fluences used, 53BP1 foci formation is independent of dose. This suggests that the linear no-threshold hypothesis for relationship of radiation-induced damage to dose may not hold at very low doses. Furthermore, although the the typical dose response plateau pattern of irradiation-induced bystander effects, the fluence at which the threshold occurs is still unclear. At 2e3 particles/cm2, which equals 0.4 mGy of iron ions or 0.57 microGy of protons, there is bystander MN formation with iron ion irradiation but not with protons. The lowest proton fluence that induces the bystander effect is 2e5 particles/cm2, which equals 57 microGy. These data suggest that there might be a threshold for irradiation-induced bystander effects at about 60 microGy for protons and somewhere below 400 microGy for Fe ions.

With regard to aim 2 the investigators have reported previously that ROS play a significant role in transmission of signals from irradiated to bystander cells after exposure to X-rays or Fe ions. They have now begun studies to determine the effect of low levels of oxidative stress on responses of irradiated and bystander cells to subsequent irradiation. Their preliminary data show that if bystander AG0 cells are exposed to a low, non-toxic level of hydrogen peroxide before co-culturing with irradiated cells, there does not appear to be any radiation-induced bystander MN formation, but if bystander cells are oxidatively stressed after the start of co-culturing with irradiated cells, the radiation-induced bystander MN formation is not changed compared to the sham control. Further studies are needed to confirm those results.

Relevant to aim 3, the investigators have been among the pioneering groups at NSRL to investigate the effects of “mixed,”, actually sequential, irradiations with iron ions and protons. Their preliminary data suggest that in irradiated cells the induction of micronuclei is greater when the two particle exposures are separated by three or 24 hours compared to when given within five minutes. However, depending on the time between irradiations, bystander cells appear to “adapt” to the second signal, i.e., a smaller bystander response was seen when irradiated cells were “hit” twice with 3-24 hours between the hits, than when the same dose was given in a single irradiation. Clearly, these data need repeated, but the results are intriguing.

Previously, the investigators reported progress on aim 4 showing significant signaling from X-irradiated fibroblasts to unirradiated keratinocytes and vice versa (endpoints of MN formation and p21 expression). However, interestingly, after Fe exposure their data suggest that with some endpoints there is no signaling from irradiated keratinocytes to unirradiated fibroblasts or keratinocytes, and the effect is delayed from irradiated fibroblasts to unirradiated keratinocytes. Additional investigation is still underway, and they have made progress developing a 3D tissue model using these two cell types that will allow them to test the importance of microenvironment to cell-cell signaling.

experiment_title: Monitoring of Bone Loss Bio-Markers in Human Sweat: A Non-Invasive, Time Efficient Means of Monitoring Bone Resorption Markers under Micro and Partial Gravity Loading Conditions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Loss of bone mass, density and structural integrity is a significant health risk in a variety of populations such as the elderly, post-menopausal women, young female athletes and astronauts. Such changes in overall bone quality lead to a greater risk of bone fracture and potentially a reduced rate of bone healing after injury. The ability to monitor biomarkers of bone remodeling (e.g. ionized calcium, collagen cross links) using sweat as an analytical sample provides an attractive alternative to the more invasive and costly measures presently employed, such as a bone density scans by DXA, 24-hour urine collection protocols or whole blood analyses.

The development of a non-invasive, skin-mounted monitoring device which allows the quantitation of ionized calcium and/or collagen cross links in sweat will allow bone loss to be monitored in a wide variety of terrestrial populations that to date have not easily been monitored outside of a clinical setting. This particular project focuses on validating the concept that sweat analysis can be used as a non-invasive means of monitoring bone loss in crew members during periods of mechanical unloading under altered gravitational conditions. In addition, this project is also investigating the best technical approach to collecting a sweat sample, specifically applicable to the space-flight environment, while utilizing well-accepted, clinically validated analytical methods. Development of a technology capable of real-time monitoring of biomarkers of bone loss that satisfies the criteria required for use in the space-flight environment (i.e. non-invasive/non-intrusive, passive, small, light-weight, low power) has many direct applications in various populations here on Earth.

APPROACH:
The team was tasked with validating that the rate and extent of unloading-induced bone loss in humans can be assessed by monitoring the levels of two bone resorption markers in sweat, namely ionized calcium and collagen break-down products. Initial testing was carried out in a young healthy population (at rest and during activity) and then in a clinical population undergoing active bone loss, namely spinal cord injury patients. All groups included both male and female participants. Biomarker concentration was determined in contemporaneous samples of sweat, blood, and urine collected during both short (24 hour) and long-term studies (multiple sessions over a period of months) to define the relationship between biomarker levels in the respective biological samples. Several different sweat collection techniques were investigated to determine the most appropriate and efficient means of sample collection suitable for deployment during a space flight mission. These experiments also included investigation of the most appropriate biomarker analysis techniques that allow for future deployment in micro- or partial gravity environments. This near-real-time monitoring approach also provided the information required to justify modifying an ineffective bone loss countermeasure prescription during a mission. One of the approaches tested was a novel, micro-fabricated fluid collection capillary array, known as the micro-fabricated sweat patch (MSP) device, specifically developed for use in microgravity. The MSP technology was initially developed because of its potential to become an autonomous, solid-state collection/analysis device worn on the skin of an astronaut requiring little or no crew interaction to perform its monitoring function.

RESULTS:
Initial studies indicate significant individual variation in the amount and rate of sweating observed between subjects based on: 1) the anatomical site sampled (i.e. forehead, shoulder, forearm); 2) level of activity (i.e. "active" sweating during exercise; and 3) the concentration of biomarkers relative to the onset of "active" sweating. In addition, the existing sweat collection technology previously employed to collect sweat (i.e. commercial absorptive pad) exhibited significant analytical issues based on sub-optimal analyte retention and analyte extraction efficiency. To overcome these difficulties investigators developed a standardized sweat collection protocol in which subjects performed a defined exercise protocol at a fixed level of intensity (i.e. 30 minutes of aerobic exercise at an intensity of 40 percent of their age-predicted VO2max) under similar environmental conditions and hydration status. Sweat samples were collected at the forehead using micro-fabricated polymer capillary arrays which collect sweat as an unadulterated liquid sample. This approach allows both determination of the volume of sweat produced and has the advantage of minimal residual analyte retention within the array due to its polymer construction, unlike the commercially available absorptive sweat collection technology.

Sweat samples were initially collected at discrete time intervals to determine when during exercise-induced sweating did biomarker concentration reach "steady-state" levels. These experiments indicated that biomarker concentrations (i.e. Ca2+ and T-CCL) in "active" sweat reached a "steady state" after 15 minutes of exercise regardless of the volume of sweat produced by a particular individual. In addition, analyte concentration (i.e. T-CCL) in actively produced sweat was found to be highly correlated (R = 0.92) with plasma levels of the same analyte during the period sweat was being collected. However, comparison of analyte concentration produced during actively produced sweat and 24 hour urine voids in the same individual indicated, indicated that although related in a linear fashion (R = 0.61), sweat analyte excretion during the 15 min period of exercise was not predictive of total 24hr urine analyte excretion. As 24 hour urine void collection provides an integrated value for whole body biomarker excretion rates, comparison of the amount of biomarker excreted during a 15 minute period of “active” sweating from 7.5cm of skin surface at the fore-head appears inappropriate as a means of predicting total calcium and T-CCL excreted in a 24 hour urine void.

The team investigated the accuracy of the existing commercially available absorptive patch sweat collection technology with regard to analyte concentration relative to unadulterated liquid sweat samples collected in a contemporaneous fashion at the same anatomical site. These data indicated that the cellulose matrix of the commercially available absorptive patch posed significant analytical problems. These issues were that the cellulose matrix: 1) contained significant amounts of endogenous calcium signal; 2) resulted in significant retention of sweat-derived T-CCL that could not be extracted from the matrix using the standard method (i.e. extraction in ddH2O); and 3) that extraction efficiency from the matrix was variable between identical samples. To address these analytical issues during Year 2 of these projects, investigators studied the use of two new absorptive materials, a glass fiber material and a polypropylene woven material, for the collection of sweat over a 24 hour period. Their initial experiments focused on the extraction efficiency of four bone loss biomarkers of interest, namely calcium, T-CCL, NTx and osteocalcin (OST). They also modified the extraction protocol to utilize acidified ddH2O (pH 5.0) or a Tris buffer (pH 5.0) to enhance the solubility of these biomarkers in the extraction buffer and reduce ionic interactions within the matrix of the absorptive material. Unlike the original commercially available cellulose absorptive pad technology, efficient recovery of known amounts of all analytes was achieved using our modified extraction method from both the glass fiber and woven polypropylene materials.

Glass fiber absorptive pads (7.5cm2 in area) and the modified extraction protocol were used to collect sweat samples from a total of 18 normal healthy subjects over a period of 24 hours at three separate anatomical locations: shoulder, hip and forearm. 24 hour urine voids were also collected from these subjects during the same 24 hour period. When the total amount of calcium excreted in sweat over a 24 hour period into a 7.5cm2 glass fiber absorptive pad was compared to the total amount of calcium excreted in a 24 hour urine void obtained from the same individual, results indicated that there is a near linear correlation between the two values in sweat collected from the shoulder (R = 0.90) and forearm (R=0.86) and contemporaneous 24 hour urine voids. A similar relationship between 24 hour sweat T-CCL and 24 hour urine void T-CCL levels was observed at the shoulder (R = 0.99) in a subset of these subjects (N=6) for which this analysis has been completed. Data indicate that calcium and T-CCL levels detected in 24 hour sweat samples are highly correlated with levels detected in 24 hour urine voids from healthy individuals, suggesting that bone loss biomarker concentration in the criterion sample (i.e. 24 hour urine void) can be accurately predicted from that found in a sweat sample collected over the same 24 hour period using an absorptive pad technology.

The project then focused on validating this approach to monitoring bone loss biomarkers in a terrestrial population undergoing active bone loss (a clinical population of spinal cord injured patients). In addition, the team also developed a new protocol suitable for deployment on-orbit for the extraction and collection of analytes from the absorptive sweat patch based on the Salivette technology previously validated for use on-orbit.

experiment_title: Hepatic Function in Rats After Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Among the changes that have been observed during and after space flight are elevated adrenal steroid secretion and altered concentrations of various lipids and carbohydrates in blood and other tissues. Since the liver is an important site of nutrient and xenobiotic metabolism, further study of the effects of space flight on this organ appear warranted. Based on previous findings, it was proposed that several aspects of hepatic function are altered by space flight. In particular, these include key enzymes of cholesterol and sphingolipid biosynthesis and drug metabolism (e.g. cytochrome P-450). This study was to provide additional data from analyses of liver and serum samples from space-flown rats that support this hypothesis.

Approach:

To determine the possible biochemical consequences of prolonged weightlessness on liver function, tissue samples from flight and control rat were analyzed for hepatic protein, glycogen, and lipids as well as the activities of a number of key enzymes involved in metabolism of these compounds and xenobiotics.

Results:

Among the parameters measured, the major differences were elevations in the hepatic glycogen content and HMG-CoA reductase activities of the flight rats, and a decrease in the amount of microsomal cytochrome P-450 and the activity of aniline hydroxylase, a cytochrome P-450-dependent enzyme. Decreases in these two indices of the microsomal mixed-function oxidase system indicate that space flight may compromise the ability of liver to metabolize drugs and toxins. The higher HMG-CoA reductase correlated with elevated levels of serum cholesterol. Other changes included somewhat higher blood glucose, creatinine, SGOT, and much greater alkaline phosphatase and BUN. These results generally support the earlier observation of changes in these parameters. The importance of these alterations is not known; however, they have the potential to complicate long-term space flight.

experiment_title: Morphologic and Histochemical Studies of Bone Cells from SL-3 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Non-weight bearing or hypogravity conditions are known to result in skeletal loss in the long bones. The mechanism is unknown but one hypothesis suggests that the lack of mechanical force or stress on the bone results in reduced osteoblastic activity and thus reduced new bone formation. The objectives here were to investigate the cellular activity of the bone forming cells, the osteoblast, in animals exposed to seven days of microgravity.

Approach:

The osteoblasts from tibias of adult flight and control rats were studied using cytochemical methods for alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and dipeptidyl peptidase II. In addition, electron microscopy was used in combination with morphometric techniques to measure numbers of secretory granules containing procollagen, to count lysosomes and to measure cytoplasmic areas of osteoblasts.

Results:

Measurements of alkaline and acid phosphatase, Golgi activity, secretory granule size, and lysosomal activity, all indicated very little difference between flight and flight-simulated controls. However, there was a tendency for osteoblasts in compact bone of flight animals to show a smaller cytoplasmic volume compared to non-flight controls. Thus the "processing" of protein (including procollagen) in these osteoblasts, especially the dipeptidase cleavage activity, may be operating normally but within a smaller cytoplasmic volume, and this normal proteolytic activity within a smaller volume could result in more rapid intracellular protein degradation, including procollagen, and thus less collagen secretion. This, in effect would result in less new bone formation. An alternative explanation concerns the twelve-hour postflight delay before animal sacrifice. As collagen synthesis is stimulated during cell growth, the osteoblasts could have begun to return to normal function in this period. With a longer recovery time one presumes that a return to normal cell size would also have occurred.

experiment_title: HZE-induced Skin Carcinoma: An in-vivo-like Multicellular Epithelial Model System for Analysis of Radiation Quality Effects and DSB Repair Processes
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Skin as a model system to study radiation-induced human epithelial cancers: Skin is one of the most complex organs of the body, consisting of multiple cell types, including epithelial keratinocytes and connective tissue (i.e. fibroblasts). Keratinocytes form a stratified squamous epithelium and are composed of one basal cell layer and several differentiated cell layers. Proliferation is limited to the basal layer, whereas differentiating cells withdraw from the cell cycle and express various differentiation markers, dependent on the stage of their differentiation. Because radiation-induced neoplasms in skin derive primarily from epithelial cells, radiobiological studies on keratinocyte monolayers (2D) provide a good first approximation for assessing cancer development processes triggered by ionizing radiation, but also by other environmental mutagens.

APPROACH:
There is considerable evidence that ionizing radiation causes non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), and the risk for NMSC in astronauts is increased. To further assess the cancer risk for humans from space radiation, an in-vivo-like multicellular skin model system was used. Multiple different endpoints as surrogate markers for skin cancer were assessed. Persistent chromosomal damage, altered cell proliferation, and evasion from apoptosis were studied in 2D monolayer cultures of normal primary and of initiated human keratinocytes exposed to a variety of charged nuclei (Aim 1). In addition, to more realistically recapitulate the complex architecture of a tissue, an in-vivo-like skin model system, composed of fibroblasts and keratinocytes, was used to ascertain the risk of space radiation-induced cancer development processes in 3D (i.e. persistent chromosomal damage, altered cell proliferation, evasion from apoptosis, and differentiation) (Aim 2). Lastly, a surface transplantation assay of exposed 3D reconstructed human epithelia onto immunodeficient mice was carried out to test for intermediate and late events in cancer progression (cell invasion and metastasis, respectively) (Aim 3). Investigators hypothesized that, in basal cells, unfaithful DNA DSB repair will lead to persistent chromosomal damage, promoting altered cell growth and escape from tissue homeostasis. They believe that the proposed approach is highly relevant for assessing the risk of skin cancer in astronauts and for modeling space radiation-induced tumor development in other epithelial tissues.

RESULTS:
The cytokinesis-block micronucleus (MN) assay was used to assess the genotoxicity of low doses of different types of space radiation. Normal human primary keratinocytes and immortalized keratinocytes grown in 2D monolayers each were exposed to graded doses of 0.3 or 1.0 GeV/n silicon ions or similar energies of iron ions. The frequencies of induced MN were determined and compared to gamma-ray data. RBEmax values ranged from 2.0 to 3.9 for primary keratinocytes and from 2.4 to 6.3 for immortalized keratinocytes. At low radiation doses = 0.4 Gy, 0.3 GeV/n iron ions were the most effective at inducing MN in normal keratinocytes. An “over-kill effect” was observed for 0.3 GeV/n iron ions at higher doses, wherein 1.0 GeV/n iron ions were most efficient in inducing MN. In immortalized keratinocytes, 0.3 GeV/n iron ions produced MN with greater frequency than 1.0 GeV/n iron ions, except at the highest dose tested. MN formation was higher in immortalized keratinocytes than in normal keratinocytes for all doses and radiation qualities investigated.

MN induction was also assessed in human keratinocytes cultured in 3D to simulate the complex architecture of human skin. RBE values for MN formation in 3D were reduced for normal keratinocytes exposed to iron ions, but were elevated for immortalized keratinocytes. Overall, MN induction was significantly lower in keratinocytes cultured in 3D than in 2D. Together, the results suggest that tissue architecture and immortalization status modulate the genotoxic response to space radiation, perhaps via alterations in DNA repair fidelity.

Investigators also established a surface transplantation assay, which allowed them to extend their studies of the biological responses of human skin equivalents up to several months post radiation exposure. To do so, male NOD.SCID mice (obtained from Jackson Laboratory) were subjected to the skin grafting procedure at approximately 8 weeks of age and sent to BNL 4 weeks post-surgery. Cohorts of 6 mice each were exposed to 1 Gy of 300 or 1000 MeV/n Fe ions, or to 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-rays for comparison purposes. Six mice were sham irradiated. All mice remained at BNL until necropsy at 8 weeks post radiation exposure. Tissue sections of the human skin grafts and of the undisturbed mouse skin were fixed in 10% buffered formaldehyde for 48 hours, followed by transfer and storage in 70% ethanol until processed and embedded in paraffin. Sections of 3 µm each were assessed by H&E staining for tissue architecture, by FISH using mouse and human COT1 DNA for tissue origin, and by IHC for markers of radiation exposure (53BP1 (i.e. genomic instability), Ki-67 (i.e. cell proliferation), and involucrin (i.e. keratinocyte differentiation).

Preliminary results show that 53BP1 foci are elevated and persistent in basal keratinocytes of human skin equivalents after radiation exposure. Keratinocytes with locally accumulated nuclear staining for 53BP1 are negative for Ki-67, indicative of a reinforced irreversible growth arrest of cells with persistent genomic instability. Investigators speculate that cellular senescence is accelerated in human basal cells following high LET radiation exposure to limit the proliferation of damaged cells that are at risk for neoplastic transformation, similar to the observations reported by others using low LET IR.

experiment_title: Effect of Sex on Orthostatic Intolerance and Cardiovascular Responses during Lunar Descent and Ascent
experiment_description:
Objectives
The Artemis missions to the Moon have initiated the development of the Human Landing System (HLS) to transport astronauts to and from the lunar surface. The risk of orthostatic intolerance (OI) and the cardiovascular responses experienced during lunar descent and ascent are important considerations in the development of the HLS. OI is characterized by a group of signs and symptoms that occur after assuming an upright posture, including lightheadedness, dizziness, visual changes, increased heart rate, sudden drops in systolic or diastolic blood pressure, and significant cardiac arrhythmias. Given that OI is a concern during re-exposure to normal gravity (1-G) even after short duration exposures to weightlessness and that crew may be in a standing posture in the vehicle during decent to and accent from the lunar surface, G-loads during the dynamic phases of the Artemis mission may be problematic for some individuals. OI when standing is apparent after just days of exposure to weightlessness and spaceflight analogs, and thus it is expected that OI may be a concern even during lunar descent. Furthermore, it is unlikely that the partial gravity exposure during stays on the lunar surface will be protective against OI during ascent from the surface.

There were no reports of symptoms consistent with OI during the Apollo missions. However, all the Apollo crewmembers were male with a history high performance aircraft experience, and almost all the commanders demonstrated high heart rates during sustained G-levels ranging from 0.4- to 0.6-G over ~9 min during lunar descent and ascent. The G-levels to which the Artemis astronauts will be exposed have not been defined, but it is likely that the G-levels will be greater and/or the exposures will be longer than those experienced by Apollo astronauts based upon the flight plan required to reach Gateway, which will be at a higher orbit than the Apollo Command and Service Module. Further, the proportion of women in the astronaut corps has been increasing and it has been publicly stated that the first Artemis mission to the lunar surface will include at least one woman; thus the effect of sex on the cardiovascular responses to acceleration should be considered with regard to lunar descent and ascent. In general, women have lower orthostatic tolerance and are more susceptible to post-spaceflight orthostatic intolerance when re-exposed to 1-G. However, it is unclear whether women also would be less able to the tolerate lower levels of acceleration that likely will be experienced during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.

Lower body compression garments are one of the countermeasures that have been used to protect against OI after exposure to weightlessness. Specifically, NASA has developed the Orion Orthostatic Intolerance Garment (OIG) for the Artemis missions, but the suit's efficacy has not been demonstrated in women and men during long exposures (20 minutes) to simulated G-levels (0.5-, 0.75, 1.0-G) that astronauts may experience during lunar descent and ascent during the Artemis missions.

This study has the following aims

1. To determine whether there are differences between hypovolemic men and women in orthostatic tolerance (assessed by tilt time) and cardiovascular responses during 20 minutes of exposure to a range of gravity levels (0.50-, 0.75-, and 1.00-G) simulated by different angles of head-up tilt that Artemis astronauts might experience during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.
2. To determine whether the Orion Orthostatic Intolerance Garment (OIG) will protect men and women against orthostatic intolerance (assessed by tilt time) and reduce the cardiovascular responses caused by exposure to the range gravity levels (0.50-, 0.75-, and 1.00-G) simulated by different angles of head-up tilt that Artemis astronauts might experience during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.

Approach
19 men and 19 women will be recruited to complete this study. The participants will be similar to the astronaut population along important characteristics such as age, body mass index, and physical fitness. To complete the study, subjects will participate in two phases of testing.

Phase I will evaluate differences in OI between the sexes (Aim 1). During the first of two laboratory visits (1A), test operators will obtain anthropometric measurements to be used in the design and construction of an individualized Orion OIG, familiarize the subjects to the tilt test procedures, and measure the subject’s baseline plasma volume (carbon monoxide rebreathing method) and tolerance to 80° head-up tilt (1.00-G). During the second of two laboratory visits (2A), plasma volume will be measured prior to inducing hypovolemia through administration of a furosemide infusion (20 mg). Once hypovolemia is achieved, participants will be exposed to three 20-minute sessions of head-up tilt tests at 30° (0.50-G), 50° (0.75-G), and 80° (1-G) in a randomized order counterbalanced across subjects. During each tilt test, measurements that will be obtained while supine and during head-up tilt include brachial blood pressure, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and heart rate (ECG) and ultrasound parameters required to calculate stroke volume, cardiac output and total peripheral resistance. Hematocrit, hemoglobin, and carboxyhemoglobin will be measured from blood samples and used to calculate red blood cell volume, total blood volume, and plasma volume. Blood samples will be collected prior to each tilt test to calculate changes in plasma volume across the test day.

Phase II also will consist of two laboratory visits. During the first visit (2A), subjects will don the OIG constructed from the anthropometric measures obtained in visit 1A to ensure correct sizing. During the second visit (2B), plasma volume will be measured using the same carbon monoxide rebreathing method prior to inducing hypovolemia through administration of furosemide infusion. After hypovolemia is achieved, subjects will don the OIG, and will be assessed for orthostatic tolerance with compression garments using the same tilt test protocol as in phase I, with G-levels presented in the same order in which they were in visit 1B to avoid any potential confounding effects of order when comparing tilt results within subjects.

Results
It is expected that females will be more susceptible to OI and demonstrate a greater heart rate response when hypovolemic than males at 1-G (Phase I) and that differences between sexes (tolerance time and cardiovascular responses) will be less as simulated G-levels decrease. The findings from this phase of the study will provide additional detail to the HLS acceleration limits during the dynamic flight phases when astronauts are standing but not wearing compression garments. However, it is expected that all subjects will be able to tolerate the entire tilt duration when hypovolemic and using lower body compression garments (Phase II). The findings from this phase of the study will provide additional detail to the HLS acceleration limits during the dynamic flight phases when astronauts are standing, but wearing compression garments, particularly with regard to the duration of tolerance.

experiment_title: Improving Cardiovascular Risk Prediction - Biomarkers and Beyond; Implications for Astronaut Selection and Monitoring During Prolonged Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The most likely cause of a non-traumatic life- or mission-threatening medical events in astronauts are from acute cardiovascular disease (CVD). Current risk prediction models utilize only traditional atherosclerosis risk factors and focus narrowly on coronary heart disease events rather than global cardiovascular risk, ignoring outcomes such as heart failure or atrial fibrillation that could also be potentially mission-threatening. Numerous studies have evaluated novel risk markers in an attempt to improve CVD risk prediction, with several promising imaging and blood-based biomarkers identified. Most of these studies have investigated the incremental predictive value of a single biomarker added to a traditional risk factor model, with a few reporting combinations of biomarkers. Moreover, few studies have evaluated strategies for risk prediction that cross testing modalities. Such a multi-modality approach has the potential to markedly improve CVD risk prediction among potential and existing astronauts, and would have direct relevance to the general population.

The primary objective of this study was to develop a consortium of biomarker and aerospace medicine leaders, with expertise in multiple different testing modalities, and with access to robust existing databases, to identify and validate novel strategies to enhance global CVD risk prediction over two time windows: 1) 10-20 years, representing the full career of the astronaut and 2) 2-5 years, representing the planning and operational phase of a manned mission to Mars. The Biomarker Consortium aimed to provide “real time” advice to NASA on the design of existing screening programs, the status of new biomarkers, and the interpretation of test results.

APPROACH:
The team of collaborative investigators pooled data from multiple existing cohort studies to develop two distinct multi-modality risk prediction tools, one based on 10-year global CVD risk and one based on 3-year CVD risk. These models sequentially evaluated novel testing modalities on top of standard risk factors, including coronary calcium (a measure of the extent of coronary atherosclerosis), multiple blood based protein biomarkers that reflect inflammation, cardiac injury and cardiac stress, as well as imaging-based assessments of cardiac function. Finally, investigators worked directly with NASA researchers in the Human Research Program to explore the feasibility of transforming the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health into a prospective state-of-the-art cohort study of the astronaut corps. They utilized the expertise of the Biomarker Consortium to design a novel program for study of the effects of training and space flight on astronaut health.

RESULTS:
The investigators derived a multimodality risk prediction tool that led to marked improvement over traditional risk prediction algorithms both for predicting 10 year atherosclerotic risk as well as global and cause-specific CVD risk. Five screening tests - coronary calcium screening by CT, left ventricular hypertrophy by ECG, and elevated levels of N-terminal pro b-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitive cardiac troponin (Ths-cTnT), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) markedly improved global CVD risk prediction compared with standard risk assessment strategies. Investigators created a simple score, consisting of the number of abnormal CVD screening tests. In both MESA and DHS a > 25-fold gradient of risk for CVD was seen across the range of scores. Of particular relevance for NASA, participants with zero abnormal tests results have an extremely low risk for any CVD outcome over 10 years of follow-up. The findings replicate extremely well across the two distinct cohort studies.

experiment_title: Solid Tumor Risk Estimation: Incorporating Intercellular Interaction Effects
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Under this NSCOR grant, investigators made a number of findings that help provide a mechanistic framework for biologically-based risk models. Investigators requested and received a cost extension to finish off experimental characterization of proton and iron irradiation studies to address angiogenesis processes that are important in radiation carcinogenesis and can be viewed as bottlenecks to carcinogenesis advancement. The significance of this in the carcinogenesis risk context lies in the challenge it presents to the standard radiogenic cancer paradigm. This paradigm holds that cancer may be understood as an autonomous expansion of an initiated cell clone, followed by the chance genetic creation of a cancer cell in that clone that then inevitably expands to become a diagnosed cancer. At the basis of these events is thought to be the DNA lesion. Investigators argue that essential population-level and tumor-environmental dynamics can alter this picture dramatically, either promoting cancer development or slowing the course of existing cancers. Their basis extends beyond DNA damage to include the familiar “hallmarks” of cancer that constitute “bottlenecks” to tumor advancement – population-level logistic growth effects, acquisition of angiogenic potential, and competency for invasion, to name three. Investigators have shown that radiation can progress or limit cancers by modifying these bottlenecks. Because these bottlenecks may be significant enough to increase the likelihood of transforming an initiated cell, or to change the likelihood an existing cancer advances to clinical detection over a lifetime, they must be included in the overall assessment of radiogenic cancer risk. It follows that existing models that fail to include such bottleneck effects are inherently flawed in that they do not include all radiation actions bearing on the development of manifest cancer disease.

APPROACH:
Proton-induced gene regulation was investigated in a number of human cell types that actively contribute to carcinogenesis progression, including not only cancer cells but also primary non- transformed stromal and microvascular endothelial cells. A baseline was obtained by analysis of the proton-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0Gy and 2Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated six hours after proton exposure.

RESULTS:
Investigations to this end show that cancer-progression-modifying tumor-host interactions indeed occur at a number of levels, including: 1) reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma); 2) reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures; in contrast with 3) augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions; 4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation; effects opposite to 5) the stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma). In addition, 6) mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression. Lastly, investigating the potential influence of intercellular interactions within the tumor on radiation modulation of cancer progression, investigators found that 7) cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course.

1) Reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma):
Using pan-genomic arrays, expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found generally to be downregulated by protons (1GeV). RT-PCR reconfirmed this down-regulatory trend for a number of specific angiogenesis-regulating genes, including VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, and IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1, in human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC), normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHCF), and A549 lung carcinoma 6 hours after receiving doses of sizes 0.5, 1 and 2Gy. In contrast, when the fibroblast, endothelial and tumor cells were gamma-irradiated at the same doses, the expressions of VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A and IL-6, were upregulated in a dose-dependent manner relative to control (0Gy) 6hr post-irradiation.

Having established the proton-induced downregulation of these angiogenic genes (6 hours post-irradiation), regulation of the corresponding proteins was examined. ELISA assays specific for VEGF and IL-8 were performed after irradiation of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cultures. At 24h hours post-irradiation, levels of secreted IL-8 in the culture supernatants were reduced by 31% and 50% in endothelium and tumor cells respectively. Secreted VEGF was also significantly reduced in proton-irradiated fibroblast (17%) and tumor cells (34%) versus sham-irradiated controls (although results with endothelial cells were indeterminate). These findings indicate a dose-dependent downregulation of important angiogenic genes and, for the most part, a significant reduction in protein levels following proton irradiation.

For comparison, 56Fe-induced gene regulation was investigated in the same cell types as for protons. Again, a baseline was obtained by analysis of the iron ion-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0, 0.2, 0.4, and 1Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated 6 hours after radiation (or sham) exposure. Expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including, VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found to be upregulated. The expression patterns of a number of the angiogenesis-regulating genes, including: VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1 were again investigated using quantitative RT-PCR. Results from the quantitative assessment of a number of these genes are shown. Significant upregulation of expression was observed for these genes in both the irradiated HLMVEC and NHDF cells, compared to sham-irradiated controls (p<0.05). To further investigate the ability of 56Fe ion irradiation to upregulate specific pro-angiogenic genes, expression levels were also investigated in human lung adenocarcinoma (A549). Just as for primary human fibroblast and endothelial cells, these cancer cells also showed upregulation of VEGF, IL-8, IL-6 and HIF-1A, at 6hr post-irradiation.

2) Reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures:
Beyond the suppression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that proton irradiation could also suppress the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. The invasion of the proton-irradiated endothelial, fibroblast, and tumor cells was investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, proton-irradiated cells (2Gy) showed significantly reduced invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix. Quantification of the results demonstrated that following proton irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549, NHDF and HLMVEC cells was reduced, by 46, 15 and 14% respectively.

Next, the invasion/migration of endothelial (HLMVEC) in response to soluble factors produced by either proton-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) or proton-irradiated tumor cells (A549) was analyzed. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk that occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and microvascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor or fibroblast cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated endothelial cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that chemoattract endothelial cells, investigators studied how proton irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. Compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 2-Gy proton-irradiated fibroblasts and tumor cells were less effective (19% and 16% respectively) at inducing endothelial cells to invade and traverse to the underside of the membrane. They propose that the reduced invasion of endothelial cells was, in part, a direct consequence of the demonstrated reduced secretion of angiogenic factors from the proton-irradiated cells. Indeed, addition of either recombinant VEGF or IL-8 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the anti-migratory effect of proton irradiation.

3) Augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions:
Extending the finding of increased expression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that iron ion irradiation could also augment the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. Thus far, the invasion of the iron ion-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cells has been investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, iron ion-irradiated cells (0.2Gy) showed significantly increased invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix; even more so than 1Gy. Quantification of the results demonstrated that, following 0.2Gy iron ion irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549 and NHDF cells was increased by 47% and 18% respectively.

Investigators next analyzed the invasion/migration of HLMVEC in response to soluble factors produced by either iron ion-irradiated A549 or iron ion-irradiated NHDF cells. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk which occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and micro-vascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 or NHDF cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated HLMVEC cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that are chemoattractant to endothelial cells, investigators studied how iron-ion irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. They found that, compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 0.2-Gy iron-irradiated fibroblast and tumor cells were more effective at inducing endothelial cells to traverse to the underside of the membrane.

Investigators hypothesized in this case that increased secretion of angiogenic factors from the iron ion-irradiated cells was responsible for the increased invasion of endothelial cells. Addition of small molecule inhibitor of VEGF, SU11248 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the pro-migratory effect of iron ion irradiation.

Invasion of tumor (A549), fibroblast (NHDF) and human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLVMEC) towards conditioned media from 56Fe-exposed cells was also analyzed. A dose-dependent upregulation in invasion was observed. Interestingly, breaking this trend was a dramatic upregulation of invasion of fibroblast cells towards CM from tumor cells irradiated at 0.2Gy, and a downregulation of tumor cells towards CM from LMEC cells irradiated at 0.2Gy. As a matter deserving further investigation, an upward deviation in the vicinity of 0.2Gy from linearity has been consistently noted for the pro-progression effect of 56Fe radiation.

4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation:
To investigate the modulation of additional aspects of tumor progression by proton radiation, the ability of endothelial (HLMVEC) cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with proton-irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor (A549) or fibroblast (NHDF) cells. Cancer cells are already known to secrete pro-angiogenic factors e.g. VEGF and IL-8 that can recruit endothelial cells and stimulate their proliferation. Decreased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with proton-irradiated fibroblasts or proton-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls. In contrast, when this same assay was conducted using photon-irradiated fibroblast or tumor cells, an increased, rather than a decreased, proliferation of endothelial cells was observed.

Next examined was the degree to which proton-irradiated cells (cancer, fibroblast, or endothelial), plated in the upper chambers of transwell plates modulates the proliferation of fibroblast or endothelial cells in the lower chambers. A measurable reduction in proliferation of both fibroblasts and endothelial cells associated with proton-irradiated cancer cells was detected compared to that of controls. Investigators further investigated whether addition of the angiogenic factors VEGF or IL-8 could restore the original proliferation capacity. The proton radiation-induced reduction in responding cell proliferation was partially ameliorated by the addition of VEGF (20ng/ml) or IL-8 (20ng/ml) to the irradiated cell compartment (normalized to sham-irradiated controls). The data suggests that proton-induced suppression of these specific angiogenic factors may well play a direct role in inhibiting adjacent cell proliferation. Such proton-induced suppression of cell proliferation could well have ramifications for treatment optimization. The reduction in proliferation/survival was most pronounced for the NHDF stromal fibroblasts that shared media with 2Gy-irradiated tumor cells. Proliferation levels of the fibroblast cells that shared media through transwells with proton-irradiated tumor cells were less than 50% of their matched fibroblast controls that shared media with sham-irradiated tumor cells. In line with other growth factor rescue experiments, addition of recombinant VEGF or IL-8 partially restored the proliferation levels to 71% and 90% respectively. Similar results were observed for the other cell combinations.

To ascertain the dose dependence of survival of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF), or tumor (A549) cells, and whether proton-irradiation induced inhibition of IL-8 might actually contribute to the radiation sensitivity of these cells, clonogenic assays were performed with or without the addition of recombinant human IL-8 (20ng/ml). Cells were irradiated at 1, 2 and 4Gy of protons. It was found that treatment of cells with recombinant IL-8 significantly spared the 2-Gy proton irradiated cells from clonogenic inhibition. The SF2 (survival fraction after 2Gy) of proton and photon/gamma (results not shown) was found to be 0.68 and 0.78 respectively, with the cell killing effect of proton being slightly higher than that of photon radiation.

5) Stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma):
The ability of the HLMVEC cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with iron ion irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 tumor (or NHDF fibroblast) cells. Contrary to protons, increased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with iron ion-irradiated fibroblasts or iron ion-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls.

6) Mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, and was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression:
Tumor progression dynamics for young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice, with or without iron irradiation at 1GeV/u, were studied for LLC implanted in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice with and without 5x0.2Gy of iron irradiation. Progression was gauged in terms of two quantities: tumor growth rates after approximately exponential growth starts, and “effective” initial tumor volumes, which is proposed to account for differential tumor/stromal “reorganization” times following injection and before growth of the tumor mass.

To do this, the two quantitative aspects of tumor development just mentioned were taken to be the growth rate c and the “effective initial tumor volume” b, obtained by extrapolating the fitted exponential curve backwards to time zero and interpreted as mainly a measure of either stromal incorporation into the tumor, or how supportive the microenvironment was prior to the near exponential growth phase. Growth data were fitted to V = b*exp(ct), with b the geometric mean of the b’s for individual mouse fits, and c the arithmetic mean of the c’s for individual mouse fits.

The data show generally that tumor growth rates are dependent on host age, and that there was a statistically significant decrease in average growth rates c for the unirradiated middle age (MA) as compared to the unirradiated young (Y) hosts, with only a modest increase in the effective initial volume. As regards perturbation by irradiation, the following results were found: i) the effective initial volume b was very significantly decreased by irradiation in both young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice; ii) the overall progression decrease by irradiation in the young (Y) mice was due exclusively to a dramatic decrease in effective initial volume; while iii) the more modest decrease in progression by irradiation in middle-aged (MA) mice was due to a slight increase in growth rate compensating for a substantial decrease in effective initial volume; and iv) modest decreases in both average growth rates and effective initial volumes were noted for irradiated middle-aged (MA) mice compared to irradiated young (Y) mice.

To gain some molecular-level understanding, protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed from the gene array data. Demonstrated were highly regulated protein interactions for tumors of the young (Y) iron-irradiated mice compared with those of the unirradiated groups and of the middle-aged (MA) iron-irradiated compared with those of the unirradiated groups. Overall, the network based on data from tumors growing in irradiated versus unirradiated young (Y) mice demonstrated more regulation of activity than did the network based on data from tumors growing in the irradiated versus unirradiated middle-aged (MA) mice. The general directions of the significantly regulated proteins due to irradiation also coincided with the direction of regulations of genes; mostly down in young (Y) hosts, and a slight bias upward in the middle-aged (MA) hosts. As was also true for the gene regulations, iron irradiation induced a greater genetic response overall in young (Y) compared to middle-aged (MA) hosts.

Interestingly, two central network hubs, FASN (fatty acid synthase) and AKT1 genes, were found to be downregulated within the tumors of young (Y) mice in response to iron-irradiation. FASN is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for lipogenesis and it plays a central role in energy homeostasis. It has been shown that FASN can be highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic tumors. AKT1 is one of three homologous isoforms of the AKT (PKB) protein kinase family that control a wide variety of cellular functions including proliferation, survival, and metabolism. Given the wide range of pro-growth cellular functions AKT1 modulates, it is not surprising it is also implicated in tumor progression and metastases.

Using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) software, specific pathways were constructed around FASN and AKT1 that included those genes directly or indirectly up or down regulated for tumor samples from young (Y) or middle-age (MA) mice with and without iron irradiation. Comparisons between groups were done by calculating the log2-fold change, with increasing levels of up- (red) or down- (green) regulation indicated by the darker shades of the respective color and with grey indicating genes present in the network without a 2-fold change under the perturbation studied. In the case of young (Y) unirradiated versus irradiated mice, FASN is seen to be downregulated. By contrast, no FASN regulation was detected between the tumors from the middle-aged (MA) irradiated and unirradiated groups, consistent with the reduced degree of suppression of progression by irradiation noted for these hosts.

7) Cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course:
In recent years cancer stem cells (CSCs) have been hypothesized to comprise only a minor subpopulation in solid tumors that drives tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; the so-called "cancer stem cell hypothesis." While a seemingly trivial statement about numbers, much is put at stake. If true, the conclusions of many studies of cancer cell populations could be challenged, as the bulk assay methods upon which they depend have, by, and large, taken for granted the notion that a "typical" cell of the population possesses the attributes of a cell capable of perpetuating the cancer, i.e., a CSC. In support of the CSC hypothesis, populations enriched for so-called "tumor-initiating" cells have demonstrated a corresponding increase in tumorigenicity as measured by dilution assay, although estimates have varied widely as to what the fractional contribution of tumor-initiating cells is in any given population. Some have taken this variability to suggest the CSC fraction may be nearly 100% after all, countering the CSC hypothesis, and that there are simply assay-dependent error rates in the ability to "reconfirm" CSC status at the cell level. To explore this controversy more quantitatively, investigators developed a simple cellular automaton model of CSC-driven tumor growth dynamics. Assuming CSC and non-stem cancer cells (CC) subpopulations coexist to some degree, we evaluated the impact of an environmentally dependent CSC symmetric division probability and a CC proliferation capacity on tumor progression and morphology. Their model predicts, as expected, that the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric highly influences the frequency of CSCs in the population, but goes on to predict the two frequencies can be widely divergent, and that spatial constraints will tend to increase the CSC fraction over time. Further, tumor progression times show a marked dependence on both the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric and on the proliferation capacities of CC. Together, these findings can explain, within the CSC hypothesis, the widely varying measures of stem cell fractions observed. In particular, although the CSC fraction is influenced by the (environmentally modifiable) CSC symmetric division probability, with the former converging to unity as the latter nears 100%, the CSC fraction becomes quite small even for symmetric division probabilities modestly lower than 100%. In the latter case, the tumor exhibits a clustered morphology and the CSC fraction steadily increases with time; more so on both counts when the death rate of CCs is higher. Such variations in CSC fraction and morphology are not only consistent with the CSC hypothesis, but lend support to it as one expected byproduct of the dynamical interactions that are predicted to take place among a relatively small CSC population, its CC counterpart, and the host compartment over time.

Overall conclusions:
Cell-cell interactions between the tumor and host, and between tumor cell subcompartments, affect radiation-induced cancer progression, and thus cancer risk, in a highly radiation-quality-dependent fashion. Investigators focused on two radiation types, 56Fe and protons, and found them to generally encourage and discourage, respectively, a number of molecular and functional indicators of progression. This fact must be considered alongside the risks of cancer cell creation when making conclusions as to astronaut safety during long-term space flight. Closer to home, the favorable tumor-host dynamical effects noted for proton radiation in space may work to supplement its well-established physical attributes as a therapeutic modality.

experiment_title: Regulation of Blood Volume During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Human adaptation to space flight is accompanied by a loss of red blood cell mass (RBCM), a loss of plasma volume (PV), and a decrease in total blood volume. This leads to a decrease in gravity-dependent space below the heart. In this study, rats were examined to determine whether similar hemodynamic changes occur, making them a suitable subject for study. SLS-1 marked the first time PV and RBCM were measured before and after flight. SLS-2 allowed for repeat determinations and the first opportunity for inflight assessment of erythropoiesis. An additional inflight experiment tested the ability of the rat bone marrow to respond to a bolus of erythropoietin, the major hormone controlling erythropoiesis in animals and humans.

Approach:

Seven days prior to launch PV and RBCM were determined by isotopic dilution of 125I labeled albumin and 51Cr labeled red blood cells respectively. On flight day 6, five rats (group A) were given 125I labeled albumin and 59Fe injections. Samples were taken ten minutes later to determine PV. Samples to determine 59Fe incorporation into RBCs were taken 24 hours later and on landing day (9 days later). The remaining 10 rats (groups B and C) were given 59Fe injections on flight day 9. Group B was also given a 200-U injection of erythropoietin at this time. Upon landing, RBCM and PV were measured for all flight rats and ground controls. 59Fe incorporation into red blood cells was also determined.

Results:

RBCM showed an increase in both the spaceflight animals and ground control animals, but less of an increase in flight animals. When this increase was normalized for growth (flight animals had a lower growth rate than ground controls), a decrease was seen in the flight animals' RBCM. Plasma volume increased in both flight and ground control animals. The PV increase was greater in ground control animals although not statistically different. 59Fe incorporation was lower in flight animals but again not statistically different. Animals that received erythropoietin injections had higher levels of iron incorporation. Incorporation was not statistically significant, indicating erythropoiesis is stimulated normally under conditions of microgravity.

experiment_title: Study of the Digestive Transportation Function of the Small Intestine
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous experiments have revealed an increase in the acidic-peptic potential of the stomach and a decline of the functional capability of the pancreas. This experiment was to conduct a morphological and biochemical investigation of changes in the mucous membrane of the small intestine after spaceflight.

Approach:

The duodenum, jejunum, and ileum sections of the small intestine were removed from flight and control animals, and the mucosa was examined with an electron microscope. Enzymes involved in cavity and membrane digestion (carbohydrases, peptidases, monoglyceride lipase, alkaline phosphatase) were investigated biochemically.

Results:

The investigation of the functional status of the small intestine revealed complex changes of enzyme activities. In the system of protein membrane hydrolysis there was a shift of proximodistal gradient dipeptidase activity indicating the compensatory nature of the changes. Analysis of processes of lipid digestion revealed a number of alterations in their digestive pattern manifested as a significant decrease of nonglyceridelipase activity, and an increase of alkaline phosphatase activity in the proximal segment of the small intestine, again, reflecting the compensatory and adaptational nature of the alterations. In the carbohydrase enzymatic change no significant alterations were found. Changes of digestive/transport hydrolysis of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates were reversible and functional in nature. The adaptive nature of the rearrangements of membrane digestion is demonstrated by a self-regulatory activity of the digestive system in the distribution of enzyme activities.

experiment_title: The Effect of Spaceflight on Osteogenesis and Dentinogenesis in the Mandible of Rats: Supplement 1: The Effects of Spaceflight on Alveolar Bone Remodeling in the Rat Mandible
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Under space flight conditions, and assuming animals are eating normally, alveolar bone should be subjected to only slightly different mechanical conditions, which should not induce marked changes in bone remodeling if all other metabolic conditions are unchanged. On the other hand, if the changes observed in the long bone are due totally or in part to systemic changes, alveolar bone remodeling should also be affected, and even more markedly considering its high normal turnover rate.

Approach:

The molar area was dissected from the right lower jaw and embedded without decalcification. Horizontal sections (4 µm) from the cervix to the apex of the root were prepared with a microtome. Sections from middle part of the buccal root of the first molar were stained for examination, one section out of every five of these was prepared for fluorescent microscopic analysis. A technique of dynamic histomorphometry was used to determine the extent and duration of each phase in the bone remodeling sequence, the mean calcification rate, and the amount of bone mineralized per day.

Results:

The results obtained showed the absence of effects of space flight upon the balance between bone formation and resorption. There was, however, a slight but constant decrease in the alveolar bone turnover rate. This decreased remodeling activity, although present in the synchronous animals, was significantly lower in the flight animals, even after a three-week recovery period. In terms of bone remodeling activity, results indicated a decrease in the birth rate of new Basic Multicellular Units (BMU) at the tissue level rather than an abnormal activity at the BMU or the cellular levels. The most dramatic effect of space flight was observed along the periosteal surface, and especially in areas not contiguous with (covered with) masticatory muscles, where bone formation almost stopped completely during the flight period. As this bone was submitted to the same mechanical forces in the flight animals and controls, it was concluded that factors other than mechanical loading might be involved in the decreased bone formation during space flight.
