experiment_title: Protein Turnover During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this experiment was to investigate the effects of space flight on whole-body protein metabolism by simultaneously assessing protein turnover and hormonal concentrations. Results from this experiment would provide crucial information for the establishment of a viable ground-based model for protein metabolism. Such a model would provide researchers the capability to test potential countermeasures and determine nutritional requirements for future extended-duration missions, as well as conferring benefits to healthy and metabolically stressed individuals on Earth.

APPROACH:
Whole-body protein turnover, including muscle protein breakdown, was assessed in two subjects before, during and after flight. Blood and urine samples were collected during all phases of the study. Hormonal and biochemical concentrations were measured to better understand neuroendocrine indices of protein metabolism during space flight. Food, fluid, drug intake, and amount and type of exercise were monitored. Body composition was assessed before and after flight. Preflight data were compared with inflight data to determine the effect of microgravity on each subject. Postflight data were used to monitor the readaptation process.

Blood: Blood samples were collected preflight, inflight and postflight during several 72-hour periods. These collection periods began 60 days before launch (L-60), L-35, on flight day 3 (FD3), FD6, 5 days after flight (R+5), and R+14. The protocol was similar for all collection sessions. Baseline specimens were drawn as soon as possible after awakening and before the first meal. Five milliliters (ml) of blood were drawn via butterfly into a serum separator (SST) VacutainerTM tube. An additional 2.7 ml blood sample was collected via monovette syringe for fasting glucose and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) determination with a commercial portable clinical blood analyzer (PCBA). After the fasting blood draw, each subject ingested 15N-alanine (approximately 333 micromole/kg) in capsule form.

Twelve hours after 15N-alanine ingestion, a second butterfly was inserted into the opposite arm from the initial blood draw. The subject was infused with 3-methyl-d3-histidine (1.3 micromole/kg to measure muscle protein breakdown. This was followed by a 5 ml flush of sterile saline to insure that all the tracer was delivered into the subject's circulatory system. Ten minutes later, a third butterfly was inserted in the contralateral arm and 5 ml of blood were drawn into a SST VacutainerTM. Additional blood draws (5 ml into SST) were collected 24, 48, and 72 hours after 15N-alanine ingestion. During these times, an additional 2.7 ml blood sample was collected via monovette syringe for fasting glucose and BUN determination by PCBA.

In flight, blood samples were centrifuged and stored frozen until returned for analysis. The time of inflight blood draws was recorded using a bar-code reader; relative time of day was also known (i.e., hours after awakening). After flight, specimens were analyzed for the 15N enrichments of urea and ammonia by gas chromatography / mass spectrometry. Muscle protein breakdown was determined by computer modeling of the concentration of 3-methyl-d3-histidine circulating in the blood. Serum cortisol and insulin were measured by radioimmunoassay to assess the endocrine regulation of protein metabolism and turnover.

Urine: Urine samples were collected as separate voids. Subjects were provided with small coolers and ice packs to store samples. Sample bottles were collected by the research team at least twice a day. Samples were logged and void volumes measured. Each sample was analyzed to determine protein turnover. Aliquots were removed from each sample and frozen. These frozen aliquots were used to construct 24-hour pools to determine total nitrogen excretion and nitrogen balance. Data collection took place over several 24-hour periods beginning with the first void prior to the 15N-alanine ingestion at L-60, L-35, R+5, and R+14.

During flight, urine voids were collected for 24-hour periods beginning on FD3 and on FD6 in specially configured urine collection bags. Each collection bag contained a known amount of lithium chloride (LiCl) as a volume marker. One aliquot was obtained from each void and stored frozen for processing after return to Earth. All urine aliquots were logged using a bar code reader. After flight, the urine volume per void was calculated via the LiCl marker and all samples were analyzed individually to determine protein turnover. The aliquots from FD3 and FD6 were used to construct separate 24-hour pools to determine total nitrogen excretion and nitrogen balance.

Urea and ammonia 15N enrichments were determined in all specimens by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry after flight. Although ammonia analysis depended on the ability to maintain frozen samples until return to Earth, it provided the added advantage of calculating protein turnover by averaging a rapid and smaller pool (ammonia) with a larger and slower (urea) pool. Total nitrogen (needed to determine body nitrogen balance) was determined from 24-hour urine pools by the Kjeldahl method.

Dietary Intake: Prepared and weighed meals were provided by certified dietitians during the 72 hour periods at L-60 to L-58, L-35 to L-33, R+5 to R+7, and R+14 to R+16 following the 15N-alanine ingestion. Three-day monitoring allowed any abrupt dietary changes that might affect protein turnover to be identified. In addition, subjects were asked to record any medications or supplements taken, duration and type of exercise, and phase of the menstrual cycle (if applicable).

During space flight, food/fluid/drug/exercise intakes were recorded and monitored by means of a bar-code reader during two 3-day periods: from awakening on FD3 to FD5 (inclusive) and, similarly, from FD6 to FD8 (inclusive). The bar code device had an integrated laser that allowed the user to scan items using only one hand. The bar-code reader logged the following information: subject ID, Mission Elapsed Time (MET), and food item (and lot number). This information was stored in the bar-code reader's internal memory to be retrieved after return to Earth.

Body Composition: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) was used to determine body composition (lean body mass) preflight and postflight. Whole-body scans were obtained on L-60 and L-35 and again on R+2, R+5, and R+14. Leg scans were subdivided at the knee into upper and lower regions to allow preflight-to-postflight comparisons of locomotor muscles.

RESULTS:
Space flight results in a down regulation of protein turnover; however, protein breakdown exceeds protein synthesis. In addition, hormonal changes which accompany space flight are conducive to a net loss of muscle and body protein. Nutritional, exercise or pharmacological interventions which promote net protein synthesis must be considered.

experiment_title: Using Cyanobacterial Hemoglobins to Sustain Human Life on Mars
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Human exploration of and inhabitation of other terrestrial planets is limited by the need for continuous supplies from Earth. The establishment of a permanent habit on Mars would be greatly simplified if the natural resources of the planet could be harvested, thereby eliminating the need for constant supply or perfect recycling. U.S. Patent # 4,343,715 describes a system for sequestering O2 from seawater using a polymer matrix made of foam or gel which contains immobilized hemoglobin molecules. This idea could be used to design an O2 extraction device for use on Mars. The most important component of this device would be the O2 extraction molecule. The hemoglobin from the cyanobacterium Synechococcus sp. PCC 7002 (S7002 Hb) has certain desirable properties for this purpose. These properties include a high O2 affinity for extraction from the low partial pressure of the Martian atmosphere and a high stability to withstand possible stresses from the extraction device and Martian environment. The current study will examine methods for improving S7002 Hb stability along with determining what reducing agents may be used to facilitate bound O2 release. Also, an examination of the structural and electronic changes that occur upon small molecule binding will be conducted. In the second year of funding, the focus of this project include included studies to modulate the affinity of the protein for oxygen and carbon monoxide. In its current state, S7002 trHb most likely binds carbon monoxide with a higher affinity than oxygen. This problem will have to be overcome because the Martian atmosphere has about half as much CO as O2, which is not a large enough threshold. In addition to the CO discrimination, examination of factors that contribute to the protein stability was extended. These goals were accomplished through detailed phylogenetic analysis, characterization of novel proteins, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange NMR to explore the strength of hydrogen bonding interactions.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Specific aim 1: Phylogenetic analysis of the truncated globin family
An original phylogenetic study on the truncated globin family showed that these proteins were split into three distinct phylogenetic subgroups (N, O, and P) (1). Since the time of this study, a few members of two of the three subgroups have been biophysically and structurally characterized. Of these proteins, the truncated globin from Mycobacterium tuberculosis of the O subgroup was found to have a higher oxygen affinity than carbon dioxide affinity (2). If this characteristic could be implanted into S7002, both the advantage of added stability due to the cross-link and the CO discrimination could be instituted into one molecule. In order to assess what changes would need to be made to the S7002 primary structure, detailed sequence alignments are needed to find the corresponding positions between the proteins. The trHbs from all three subgroups have potential to reveal unique ways of stabilizing and discriminating ligands along with novel ways to improve protein stability or modulate redox potential. Discoveries are being made at a rapid rate in the trHb field and it would be beneficial to take advantage of any desirable characteristics as quickly as possible. In order to do this, a detailed phylogenetic analysis of all the current trHb sequences needs to be completed. Accurate sequence alignments will allow for direct comparison between positions in all the proteins so decisions about what residues to vary will be easy to make when a particular protein trait is desired. The phylogenetic analysis will also reveal which residues are highly conserved and therefore presumed to be important for ligand binding and structural stabilization. This study will serve as a basis for all future decisions involving variation of the S7002 protein to obtain a desired trait of another trHb.

The first aim, a phylogenetic analysis of the 2-on-2 globin family, found that these proteins split into three groups of orthologs and that each of the groups was paralogous to one another. This analysis lead to the conclusion that each group should be examined separately to look for conserved features that potentially detail some functional aspect. This was completed, and various conservation patterns were discovered that likely determine the ligand binding characteristics within each group. Some of these characteristics involved ligand stabilization and discrimination, both of which are important to the design of an oxygen scavenging system for the Martian atmosphere. It seems very possible that aspects of any of the proteins in this family could be combined unto the S7002 Hb scaffold, which would provide a very stable oxygen binder that discriminates between oxygen and carbon monoxide. In addition, much was learned about the history of the 2-on-2 globin history, which serves to aid the overall history of the globin gene.

Specific Aim 2: Characterization of a trHb P Globin
Of the trHb family, only the N and O globins have been studied to any extent. These trHbs all have unique ligand binding characteristics and other properties such as cooperative oxygen binding that could be useful in an oxygen extraction system. Therefore, it seems necessary to examine the P globin subgroup as initial inspection of primary structure indicates a unique and highly regulated heme pocket. Thus, the goal of the second specific aim will be to clone and express a P globin gene from Helicobacter hepaticus and complete the initial NMR and EPR studies of the heme pocket. Ligand binding studies will also be completed. Any desirable characteristics could then be identified on a residue basis, and the phylogenetic analysis will be able to determine what changes would need to be made in S7002 to obtain those characteristics. By having at least one member of each subgroup well studied, all the positive attributes for successful Martian oxygen extraction can be exploited in the most structurally sound framework.

Specific aim 2 was not completed due to problems with the preparation of the protein. These problems are being addressed and solved.

Specific Aim 3: Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange in S7002
It is known that the formation of the heme-protein covalent-link in S7002 increases the melting temperature of the protein by about 20 degrees C (3). This is an extremely desirable feature for this system because added stability will help in the harsh Martian climate to prevent unfolding of the protein and heme loss. Understanding the factors that increase protein stability is important if optimal stability is to be obtained. One characterization method consists in monitoring exchangeable hydrogens, i.e., those that can be replaced by solvent hydrogens on a practical time scale. The amide hydrogens of the protein backbone are used as probes in experiments exposing the protein to heavy (2H) water. In its most efficient form, the study requires 15N labeled protein so both the amide proton and nitrogen can be examined using NMR spectroscopy. The protein is first put in a solution of 1H2O so all the amides are the regular NMR active nuclei. Then the sample is dried and resuspended in 2H2O. As the amide 1H’s are replaced by 2H’s, the corresponding 1H NMR signals decrease and eventually reach the isotopic composition of the solvent. It is generally observed that the hydrogen exchange rate is retarded in relation to the stability of hydrogen bonds and ultimately the structure of the protein. A comparison of exchange rates in the non-cross-linked form and the cross-linked form of the protein will provide insight into the region of the structure that are affected by the cross-link, and therefore reveal where additional changes should be made to increase the stability further.

The hydrogen-deuterium exchange experiments showed that the stabilization of S7002 through cross-linking was not a general feature of every amide in the protein. Particular regions were either stabilized or destabilized. Of the regions that were stabilized, the most important was the proximal side of the heme. In addition, the distal, or ligand binding side, was destabilized. Due to the endogenously hexacoordinate nature of the protein, this result would imply more rapid ligand binding in the non-crosslinked protein if hexacoordination is a factor in the exogenous binding. This result was reported for an ortholog of S7002 Hb that is also hexacoordinate and can crosslink the heme. The nonuniform nature of stabilized also implied that the can in stability from crosslinking is most likely an entropic effect. This means that a crosslink engineered into any heme protein could result in increased stability.

experiment_title: Effects of Spaceflight on Plasma and Glandular Concentrations of Pituitary Hormones
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The important role played by hormones in regulation of metabolic parameters affected by space flight suggests that altered endocrine function may have contributed to other observed metabolic changes. The aims of the present study were to clarify the effects of space flight on pituitary function by measuring plasma and glandular concentrations of pituitary hormones and, where feasible, evaluating the status of the appropriate target tissue.

Approach:

At the conclusion of the flight all rats were weighed and inspected. Anterior and posterior-intermediate lobes were collected, weighed, and individually frozen for assays. Plasma and pituitary growth hormone (GH), and prolactin were immunoassayed using GH and prolactin purified in-house as standards. Thyrotropin was assayed by a double antibody method, and luteinizing and follicle stimulating hormones by procedures employing NIAMDD (National Institute of
Arthritis, Metabolism and Digestive Diseases) rat standards. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was immunoassayed using the 3rd International Standard (porcine). Vasopressin was measured by a radioimmunoassay procedure and melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH) by the bioassay method.

Results:

Although of modest extent, some perturbations of endocrine function were found in this investigation. The low plasma GH titers of flight animals either reflects the unusual sampling conditions at recovery or the effects of weightlessness. The larger adrenals of flight rats suggests they were secreting increased quantities of corticosterone over a significant part of the flight, which may have contributed to the smaller flight body weights by its protein catabolic effect. The adrenal hypertrophy of flight rats suggests these animals were secreting more ACTH and corticosterone during flight. There were no changes in either pituitary or plasma MSH suggesting that either the type or degree of stress was not adequate to stimulate MSH secretion.

experiment_title: Boron-Doped Microcrystalline and Nanocrystalline Diamond Thin-Films: New Materials for Electrochemical Detection in Microfluidic Systems and Electrolytic Water Purification
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Research during fiscal year (FY) 2002 was directed toward developing electrochemical-based water quality monitoring methods for Advanced Environment Monitoring and Control (AEMC) using electrically conducting diamond thin film. Diamond is a new electrode material that outperforms other common electrodes (e.g., glassy carbon)by providing significantly improved analytical figures of merit (e.g., linear dynamic range, limit of detection, response precision and response stability)and, in some cases, enabling the detection of analytes that cannot be easily monitored with other electrodes. Our goal is to create assays that are easy to use, function in a microgravity environment, small in scale, reliable, sensitive and stable.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
In one task, investigators used the diamond electrodes for the detection of trace metal ions (e.g., Ag(I), Cu(II), Cd(II), Pb(II),and Zn(II)) via anodic stripping voltammetry (ASV). ASV involves a two-step measurement: (i) electroreducing the metal ions at a negative potential to form metal deposits on the electrode surface, thereby preconcentrating the analytes, and (ii) selectively electrooxidizing each metal during a slow potential scan in toward positive potentials. Hg and Hg-coated electrodes are often used for ASV; however, there is a need to develop alternate electrodes that possess the same attractive properties as Hg, because of toxicity and volatility issues. Diamond possesses many of the same attributes as Hg and, therefore, appears to be a viable material for this electroanalytical measurement. Diamond exhibits superb properties for the detection of metal ions at low ppb levels. The investigators demonstrated that the electrode could be used to accurately determine the concentrations of metal ions in city drinking water, waste treatment sludge, and contaminated soil. Work in FY2003 focused on implementing pulsed electrodeposition for the preconcentration step, miniaturizing the electrochemical cell and standardizing the steps in the analysis, and applying the method to the analysis of water samples from the International Space Station (ISS).

In a second task, diamond electrodes were combined with electrophoretic separation in a microchip format (so-called laboratory-on-a-chip) for the separation and detection of chemical contaminants in water supplies. Plastic microchips were used (e.g., PDMS and PMMA). Diamond is unique in the carbon electrode family in that is possesses the requisite properties to support anodic oxygen transfer reactions. Important biological and environmental analytes that undergo oxidation via anodic oxygen transfer include amino acids, indoles, alkylhydrazines, chlorinated phenols and alkanolamines. The investigators focused on the electrophoretic separation and amperometric detection of alkanolamines. These compounds are used extensively by the chemical and pharmaceutical industries as lubricants, corrosion inhibitors, and ingredients in various pharmaceutical preparations. They have been identified as pollutants and there is a strong need to quantify alkanolamines with high sensitivity and accuracy, and without extensive sample manipulation. This class of analytes is useful for developing the diamond/microchip analytical methodology and, more importantly, is a reasonable mimic for antibiotics in water - an emerging issue in water quality monitoring. They constructed an appropriate cell holder and sample reservoirs for the diamond/microchip assembly, constructed and tested a multichannel power supply for controlling the sample injection and separation voltages, and demonstrated that the chips can be effectively sealed and that diamond microelectrodes can be reproducibly positioned at the end of the separation channel for electrochemical detection. In addition, they completed a preliminary cyclic voltammetric investigation of the electrooxidation of three model alkanolamines (3-aminopropanol, 4-aminobutanol and 5-aminopentanol) in an alkaline electrolyte solution, as a function of the potential scan rate, scan number and analyte concentration. They also established the appropriate conditions for electrophoretically separating these analytes in a fused silica capillary column. Work in FY2003 focused on electrophoretically separating these analytes on the microchip and amperometrically detecting them with diamond microelectrodes. A complete set of analytical figures of merit were obtained.

In a third task, investigators explored the use of diamond anodes for the electrochemical treatment of wastewater. Diamond functions as a dimensionally stable anode and is extremely stable at high current densities and in harsh chemical environments, exhibits a large overpotential for oxygen evolution in aqueous media, and supports anodic oxygen transfer reactions. This new electrode material appears to be quite useful for the remediation of organic and inorganic waste. They demonstrated the use of a diamond anode for the oxidative remediation of atrazine. Work in FY2003 focused on testing the effectiveness of the electrode at remediating simulated wastewater from a space crew.

experiment_title: Inflight Study of Cardiovascular Deconditioning
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Orthostatic intolerance, a manifestation of cardiovascular deconditioning, constitutes a significant problem for astronauts on their return to normal gravity. Adaptation presumably occurs while subjects are freed from the need to enhance venous return from dependent parts of the body. The changes become undesirable when the cardiovascular system once again includes a hydrostatic column and plasma volume is reduced. The problem, therefore, can be broken down into two separate questions, namely, what happens during microgravity exposure and what happens when gravitational acceleration is experienced again.

Conditions under which the normal gravitational pull of blood to the legs and abdomen is reduced or counterbalanced have been supposed to mimic the effects of microgravity. Extended periods of bed rest, head-down tilt (HDT), or thermoneutral water immersion are commonly used, resulting in the well-documented initial dilation of central blood vessels and increases in stroke volume (SV) and cardiac output (Q). Adaptations occur in a matter of hours, with cardiovascular variables generally returning to erect control levels unless rehydration is forced.

The investigators studied resting and exercising subjects before, during, and after two space flights, Spacelab Life Sciences (SLS)-1 and SLS-2. Thus, they were able to make the first measurements of exercise Q during space flight. Their results and the interesting discrepancies with ground-based simulations are best explained by taking into account the results of other measurements from the same subjects made by different research teams before and during these flights.

The primary objectives of this study were: 1) determination of the time course of changes in resting cardiovascular/cardiopulmonary variables resulting from a prolonged exposure to zero-G followed by a return to one-G, and 2) determination of the manner in which acute and prolonged exposure to zero-G affects the cardiovascular/cardiopulmonary response to stress induced by exercise.

APPROACH:
Data were obtained preflight, inflight and postflight, both at rest and at various levels of exercise. Non-invasive measurements made on members of the crew yielded: metabolic values (oxygen uptake, carbon dioxide output, gas exchange ratio), circulatory values (cardiac output, heart rate, stroke volume, arterial blood pressure, approximate total peripheral resistance), and pulmonary values (functional residual capacity, lung tissue volume, expired and alveolar gas pressures, arterial-alveolar CO2 difference).

Cardiac output (Q), heart rate (HR), blood pressure, and oxygen consumption (Vo2) were measured repeatedly both at rest and at two levels of exercise in six subjects during microgravity exposure. Exercise was at 30 and 60% of the workload producing the individual's maximal Vo2 in 1 G. Three of the subjects were on a 9-day flight, Spacelab Life Sciences-1, and three were on a 15-day flight, Spacelab Life Sciences-2.

At the beginning of each session, a three-lead ECG was connected, and a blood pressure cuff was wrapped around one arm. The subject then rested on the cycle ergometer. Feet were secured to the pedals with cleated bicycle shoes, and shoulder restraints were adjusted when appropriate. For steady-state measurements, the subject breathed room or cabin air until the computer-generated graphs of breath-by-breath oxygen consumption (V02), carbon dioxide production, and respiratory quotient showed at least 10 consistent breaths. After this, the subject pushed a button that initiated rebreathing by causing the computer to connect the subject to the rebreathing bag at the end of the subsequent expiration. The rebreathing bag volume, which the subject inhaled and exhaled completely on every breath, was 1,590 ml at rest and was increased with exercise so as to remain higher than the subject's tidal volume. The duration of the rebreathing was 25 seconds at rest and 4 seconds shorter for each 100-W increment of exercise. Before beginning measurements on the first exercise runs, the subject warmed up by pedaling for three minutes at 30% exercise and for two minutes at 60% exercise.

Steady-state measurements of Vo2 and carbon dioxide production were made by integrating the flow-gas fraction product over 30-60 seconds of the steady-state period. The total volume of nitrogen inhaled during the period was assumed to equal the total volume exhaled, and expiratory flows were corrected accordingly. The rebreathing method used is based on the mass balance for carbon dioxide and is a modification of the original single-step technique. All carbon dioxide entering the gas in the lungs in a time interval leaves the blood in that interval. That amount can be expressed as the product of Q, arteriovenous carbon dioxide content difference, and time interval.

Results:
There were no significant differences in cardiovascular variables among flight days (FDs) for the measured durations of the missions, from FD2 to FDS on SLS-1 and from FD2 to FD14 on SLS-2. We therefore averaged in-flight data across sessions. This not only reduced the scatter of our in-flight data but also allowed for easier combination of the data from the two flights.

Resting values are tabulated by subject. In-flight Q at rest was an average of 1.5 l/minutes greater than erect preflight values but was not different from supine preflight values. In-flight resting heart rate was an average of 15 beats/minute lower than the erect control value and five beats/minutes lower than the supine control value. The calculated in-flight resting SV was elevated on average by 47 ml relative to the erect control value and 11 ml relative to the supine control value.

In-flight resting mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) was an average of 6 mmHg less than the erect control MAP, although not different from the supine control MAP. In microgravity, systolic pressure at rest was not different from preflight (an average of 4 mmHg greater in flight than erect and 2 mmHg greater in-flight then supine). In flight diastolic pressure at rest was an average of 11 mmHg less than that erect and not different from that supine. Resting pulse pressure in flight was increased by an average of 15 mmHg relative to the erect control value and 7 mmHg relative to the supine control value.

Different subjects exercised at different absolute workloads. Furthermore, workloads for preflight erect exercise and in-flight exercise were different from those for preflight supine exercise. This makes direct-statistical comparison difficult. However, comparisons of linear relationships with V02 are possible. The slopes of MAP, respiratory quotient, minute ventilation, and tidal volume were not different among conditions.

experiment_title: Structural and Metabolic Plasticity of Leg Muscle
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Changes in the structure and metabolism of the skeletal muscles of the leg have been observed in both humans and animals after space flight. Some examples of the effects of microgravity on skeletal muscle are changes in the cross-sectional area of slow- and fast-twitch muscle fibers, decreases in fiber size (muscle atrophy), and decreases in oxidative potential and number of capillaries. Although most investigators believe that the major factor affecting these changes in the extensor muscles is the gravitational unloading experienced in space, others believe that factors such as physical exercise or dehydration may also have an impact. Rhesus monkeys can be used effectively in studies of the musculoskeletal system in microgravity, as their physiology is similar to humans, and monkey experiments can be performed under controlled conditions to exclude the masking effect of countermeasures used by human subjects. This experiment examined the effect of microgravity and diminished motor activity (restraint) on the structure and metabolism of the m. vastus lateralis and m. soleus muscles of the Rhesus monkey.

Approach:

Muscle biopsies were taken from flight, capsule control, and vivarium control monkeys approximately 100 days before launch and at R+1. Samples were frozen, and cut into serial cross-sections 10 _m thick. Sections were pre-incubated at pH 4.2 and stained for succinate dehydrogenase (both muscles) or myofibrillar ATPase (m. soleus only). Cross-sectional areas (CSA) of types I and type II fibers were measured from each biopsy. Morphometric measurements were made in a minimum of 50 fibers of each type. In the m. vastus lateralis, total protein, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial creatine kinase, oxygen uptake, and mitochondrial respiration were measured. After measurements were made, muscle fibers were dried and weighed. In the m. soleus, capillary/fiber ratio, capillary density, and total protein were measured.

Results:

In the m. vastus lateralis postflight, both monkeys showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type I fibers. One of the monkeys also showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type II fibers. In R+17 capsule controls, significant decrease in the CSA of type I fibers was seen in only one monkey, and no change was seen in the CSA of type II fibers. In the vivarium controls, CSA of both fiber types increased. Total protein content remained essentially unchanged in the three groups of monkeys. Maximum oxygen uptake was lower in the flight animals than in the controls. SDH activity in the flight and capsule controls was unchanged in type I fibers, and lower in type II fibers. SDH activity in the vivarium controls remained essentially unchanged. In the m. soleus, flight monkeys showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type I fibers. One of the monkeys also showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type II fibers. The R+17 control monkeys showed mixed effects. In vivarium controls, three monkeys showed an increase in the CSA of type I fibers and one monkey showed a decrease. The CSA of type II fibers diminished in all vivarium animals. Total protein in type I fibers decreased in both flight animals, and the CSA of type II fibers decreased in one flight animal. In the vivarium controls, total protein remained essentially unchanged. The number of capillaries per fiber decreased in the m. soleus of both flight monkeys, but the capillary density varied differentially. The muscle atrophy observed in this experiment agrees with earlier studies on monkeys, rats, and humans.

experiment_title: Metabolic and Morphologic Properties of Muscle Fibers and Motor Neurons after Spaceflight: I. Muscle Fibers
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The present study allowed several issues raised by Cosmos 1887 to be addressed. These include the difference in atrophy suggested by wet muscle and fiber size data (40%), and the adaptability of selected metabolic enzymes to space flight. Also, a question not addressed in previous studies of tail-suspension or space flight is whether myosin ATPase activities of single fibers changes in parallel with the changes in expression of fast myosin.

Approach:

Serial sections (10 µm) were cut. Qualitative staining of ATPase was performed at pH 8.7; quantitative staining for myofibrillar ATPase activity at pH 8.6. Triplicate sections were stained at 37°C with ATP in the substrate medium, and two sections were stained without ATP. The difference in optical density between the with and without substrate was used to calculate activity (optical density/min.). Additional serial sections were stained with monoclonal antibody against fast or slow myosin heavy chain. Fibers were identified as having reacted positively for the slow, fast, or both antibodies.

Results:

Significant atrophy was found in both dark and light myosin ATPase fibers following space flight and tail suspension. In suspension, dark and light (Type II and Type I) were 40% and 38% smaller than controls, respectively, while flight fibers were 28% and 38% smaller. The distribution of fibers which were positive to a monoclonal antibody for fast myosin heavy chain increased from 9.6% in controls to 24.1% after space flight; however, the percent responding positively to slow myosin antibody did not change. The ATPase activity in light ATPase fibers was less in flight than control muscle. Those fibers that stained intermediately with ATPase had intermediate quantitative ATPase, SDH, and GPD enzyme activities suggesting that these fibers were in a transitional state.

experiment_title: Urine Monitoring Investigation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This investigation was designed to evaluate the Urine Monitoring System (UMS) and to monitor the fluid balance and urine biochemistry of the crew. The primary objectives of the Urine Monitoring Investigation were (1) to verify the operation of the UMS in the collection and sampling of urine in a zero gravity environment, (2) to perform an inflight calibration of the UMS, (3) to estimate the crewmembers’ ratio of fluid intake to urine output, and (4) to study the effects of microgravity on various biochemical constituents of urine. The data from the volume measurements and biochemical analysis of inflight samples will help extend the present understanding of the adaptive changes which affect the fluid, electrolyte, renal, and circulatory status of humans exposed to microgravity during space flight. Subsequent dedicated life sciences missions will incorporate the UMS in support of a number of experiments directed at studying the fluid redistribution hypothesis. This hypothesis focuses on the idea that three primary organ systems, namely, the circulatory system, the renal system, and the endocrine system are involved with the sudden loss of fluids and electrolytes that occurs during the immediate inflight period.

APPROACH:
The experiment protocol included preflight, inflight, and postflight procedures involving calibration and sampling activities. The preflight procedures included functional and calibration testing of the UMS in addition to several measurements of residual flush water. Preflight collection of urine samples started two days prior to launch and continued through the launch date. The inflight protocol consisted of the following activities: Calibration, Residual Volume Determination, Urine Volumetric and Sampling Measurements and Urine Volumetric Measurements. Premeasured aliquots of water and a dilute lithium chloride solution were used for the calibration and residual volume measurements, respectively. The calibration aliquots were divided into six groups which ranged in size from 60 to 720 grams. The residual volume (residual volume of flush water) determination used 180 gram aliquots and was essentially a cross-contamination check between sampling operations. Postflight analysis was performed on two samples taken from each of the residual volume measurements to determine the amount of dilution caused by rinse operations. The protocol for the urine volumetric measurements required crew members to record all water and food consumption in order to monitor their total water intake. The samples obtained from inflight urinations were preserved in a refrigerator/freezer and returned for postflight biochemical analysis. The postflight protocol called for volumetric measurements and sampling operations to be performed immediately after landing and for 3 days thereafter for comparison to preflight and inflight samples.

RESULTS:
The primary objectives involving the verification of operation, inflight calibration, and residual volume determinations were completed for this investigation. Twenty-four usable data points were obtained from the inflight calibration procedures. These points were used to establish a calibration curve which could be used to convert the UMS readout to mass (grams) for an unknown quantity of fluid introduced into the device. The confidence limits on the masses estimated by this procedure of inverse prediction were established by standard statistical methods. The 95 percent confidence interval averages ± 8 percent of the estimated mass while the 50 percent confidence interval averages ± 2 percent of the estimated mass. The mean residual volume estimated from the eight residual volume determinations was 25.9 ml with a standard error of 1.8 ml. This indicated that more time is necessary to flush the fluid lines in the UMS prior to taking a sample. Values for the physiological parameters of the urine samples were corrected to account for the residual volume dilution factor. Urine samples were collected for three days preflight and for four days postflight, however, the inflight protocol was limited to eight samples collected by a single crewmember over a 25-hour period. Operational difficulties involving insufficient air flow through the UMS prevented the inflight collection/sampling portion of the protocol from being completed. All samples were subjected to biochemical analysis. Biochemical analyses investigated changes in osmolality and differences in levels of creatinine, sodium, potassium, and chloride. Endocrine measurements investigated changes in levels of aldosterone and cortisol.

experiment_title: Cardiovascular Imaging and Strategies to Mitigate the Risk for Cardiac Events in Astronauts during Prolonged Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project from the Cardiovascular Alterations Team was designed to enhance current NASA cardiovascular disease risk reduction strategies by partnering with investigators for the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study (ACLS) and the Dallas Heart Study (DHS) to determine how to minimize the risk of a catastrophic cardiovascular event in asymptomatic astronauts. During an exploration class space mission, such as a mission to Mars, astronauts will not have access to comprehensive health care services for periods of two years, and possibly longer. Since the majority of experienced astronauts are middle aged (average age 46, range 33-58 years), they are at risk for developing serious cardiovascular events which are life-threatening for the astronaut, and mission threatening for NASA. The ability to identify 'at risk' individuals who are currently asymptomatic is a topic of intense research within the cardiovascular community that is relevant both for NASA and public health. The primary objective of this application was to determine the risk of coronary events associated with changes in coronary artery calcium (CAC) scores over time, and to determine whether this risk can be mitigated by increases in physical fitness, or use of lipid lowering therapy.

Hypothesis 1: A change in coronary calcium score over time from <10 to >10, is associated with an increase in risk for coronary events; this risk is most prominent when the CAC score increases above a threshold level of 100. Hypothesis 2: The increased risk associated with increasing CAC scores is mitigated by increasing levels of physical fitness and/or the use of lipid lowering therapy (statins). To test these hypotheses, investigators sought to accomplish the following specific aims:
Specific Aim 1: To identify all clinical events in the ACLS data base. Investigators will identify and verify all myocardial infarctions, new onset angina, and revascularization procedures in ACLS patients who fit the astronaut demographics and who have had more than one CAC measurement. Specific Aim 2: To update the ACLS data base to include information about timing and dose of statin medications. This information will be linked with treadmill time and the clinical events from aim 1 to developed robust risk prediction models. After completion of these specific aims investigators will acquire information that is essential to inform decisions regarding astronaut selection for space exploration and will allow the flight surgeons to minimize the risk for catastrophic cardiovascular events. The project will have wide spread implications for public health and cardiovascular risk reduction in the population at large, especially for the asymptomatic individual.

experiment_title: The Effects of Weightlessness on Human Single Muscle Fiber Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigations on previous space flights have documented that microgravity produces significant muscle atrophy, particularly in the anti-gravity muscles, such as those in the calf. However, a comprehensive description of microgravity-induced changes in human skeletal muscle structure and function and the underlying cellular mechanisms contributing to the altered function have not been established. Consequently, the overall objective of this project was to study the effects of microgravity on skeletal muscle function and to establish the cellular causes of the reduced functional capacity of skeletal muscle.

Specific objectives were the following:
1. To determine the extent to which microgravity alters human performance and skeletal muscle function.
2. To study the effects of microgravity on single fiber function, including the physiological and biochemical properties of the individual slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibers of human skeletal muscles.
3. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms of the observed microgravity-induced alterations in single fiber function.
4. To assess the role of an altered cellular capacity in eliciting the microgravity-induced reduction in both skeletal muscle and whole body performance and physical work capacity.

APPROACH:
To determine the effects of microgravity on maximal aerobic work capacity (VO2 max), maximal heart rate, VO2 max, calf muscle functions, and calf muscle performance were monitored during different tests. In addition, a muscle biopsy sample was obtained from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles of the calf, both preflight and immediately postflight.
Test for maximal oxygen consumption (VO2 max): The subject exercised on a bicycle ergometer with gradually increasing workloads. During the test the subject rode with a mouthpiece and noseclip in place for measurement and analysis of the expired oxygen and carbon dioxide. Preflight and most postflight tests were performed up to a 100% volitional maximum. Inflight and immediately postflight, tests were performed at 85% of this level.
Calf muscle testing: The Torque-Velocity Dynamometer (TVD) was used to evaluate functional capacity of the calf muscle group. During the tests, the astronaut was supine with the right leg secured to the TVD. Three different protocols were tested: isometric, isokinetic and fatigue test. They are described as follows:
1. Isometric: The test subject was asked to apply the maximal force onto the TVD, while the footplate was in a fixed position. The test was repeated three times with different angles of the footplate: 80 degrees, 90 degrees, and 100 degrees.
2. Isokinetic: This test was employed at six different velocities (30, 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees per second), starting with the slow speed. The footplate was moving and the subject was asked to apply as much force as possible onto the moving surface.
3. Fatigue test: Thirty contractions were completed at 180 degrees per second. The subject was asked to perform with maximal effort and then attempt to maintain that effort.
4. Muscle biopsy: A small section of muscle (about 50 mg) was taken from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles with a special biopsy needle. The sample was taken from the left leg preflight and right leg postflight. Muscle samples were analyzed by single fiber physiology to look at their contractile characteristics and biochemistry, by histochemistry to look at the fiber composition and size and the capillary density, and by electron microscopy to look at fiber microtrauma.

In addition to the above tests, VO2 max was tested three times during the flight; on Flight Days 3/4, 8/9 and 13/14. VO2 max tests were preceded and followed by a pulmonary function test (Experiment 284030). Calf muscle function testing was performed on Flight Days 2/3, 7/8 and 12/13 following the motor control tests of Experiment 284036 on the right leg. The fatigue test portion of the test was only performed during the Flight Day 2/3 and 12/13 sessions. Postflight testing included another muscle biopsy sample on landing day, calf muscle function testing on R+2, 4, 8, 15 and 30, and VO2 max testing on R+1, 5, 9, 16 and 31 (R is the day of landing).

RESULTS:
The 17 day LMS space flight resulted in significant decline in the whole body aerobic capacity of the crew, and in the functional performance of individual slow- and fast-twitch fibers. The fiber atrophy and decline in function (force and power) was greatest in the slow type I fibers of the antigravity soleus muscle. Considerable subject variability occurred for example, subject 0 showed a 40% decline in peak power of the soleus type I fiber, while this parameter was reduced by only 12% in subject A. The reason for the different responsiveness of the crew to microgravity is unknown, but could relate to the degree of exercise countermeasure performed.

Cell atrophy was the primary cause of the decline in fiber force and power as the force per cross-sectional area showed only minimal changes. In the slow type I fibers of the soleus, 2 of the 4 crew members showed a significant drop in peak power. All 4 subjects showed an increased shortening speed, and this partially protected against the loss of power. The increased velocity appears to have resulted from a selective loss of filamentous actin. This increased the actin-myosin filament spacing which in turn allowed a faster cross-bridge cycling rate and increased fiber speed. The structural rearrangement of the filaments represents an important adaptation to preserve cell power. One expects that this strategy is considerable more efficient than switching the myosin phenotype from the slow to the fast isozyme. The latter strategy occurs in rats flown in space, and results in a faster but less efficient muscle.

The reduced force and power of the individual fibers of the soleus and gastrocnemius did not result in a compromised calf muscle function. This suggests that the cellular changes were either too small to be detected by the TVD or that the crew compensated for the decline in cell function by altering their motor unit recruitment pattern.

experiment_title: Hematology, Cytological Composition of Bone Marrow and Standard Blood Parameters
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Exposure to microgravity has numerous effects upon human physiology. The effects of the space flight environment upon blood are not well understood. The extent of the hematological analysis of cosmonauts has been blood tests during flight, or for the most part, after their return to Earth. Only one postflight bone marrow draw has ever been performed on a human subject. Other bone marrow studies have been limited to myelograms of rats sacrificed after the Cosmos biosatellite missions. Rhesus monkeys have the same hemopoietic type (myeloid) as humans, and therefore are useful in the study of cytological components of bone marrow after microgravity exposure. This experiment measured hematological parameters in Rhesus monkeys after a 14 day space flight.

Approach:

Under ketamine anesthesia, bone marrow samples were drawn from the proximal metaphysis of the humerus twice before flight and several times after landing. Bone marrow hemopoiesis was measured as cell counts and cytological composition in 1 ml of marrow. A minimum of 500 cells were counted in the myelogram. Blood tests were performed to measure erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hematocrit, hemoglobin, erythrocytes, reticulocytes, and total and differential leukocytes. Proliferative, maturing, and mature pools of neutrophils, and early and mature erythrokaryocytes were measured. The ratio of early erythroblasts to total erythrokaryocytes was used to determine the rate of erythropoiesis. After the postflight ground control studies at R+17 and R+45, hematological tests were performed according to the flight protocols.

Results:

Data were collected from three Bion missions: Bion 9, 10, and 11. Preflight, animals received antibiotic treatment following bioimplantation. This may have impacted preflight blood data. Postflight data were compared with data collected at the last stage of preparation before flight. After both the flight and the R+45 control study, stress reactions were manifested through increased neutrophils and decreased lymphocyte and eosinophils in the blood. These stress reactions are due to such factors as decreased motor activity (restraint) and examinations, as well as microgravity exposure. Space flight led to diminished erythropoiesis and granulocytopoiesis in the bone marrow, indicated by a reduced reticulocyte count in the blood and a reduced population of early erythroid elements and proliferative neutrophils in the bone marrow, observed at R+1. Upon return to 1G, stimulated erythropoiesis and granulocytopoiesis were indicated by a greater number of dividing neutrophils, eosinophils, early generations of erythrokaryocytes, and a higher reticulocyte count in the blood. Decreased lymphoid population in the bone marrow was only observed after space flight, not after the ground control studies.

experiment_title: Portable Quantitative Ultrasound with DXA/QCT and FEA Integration for Human Longitudinal Critical Bone Quality Assessment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Skeletal complications, i.e., osteoporosis, induced by microgravity during extended space mission, represent a key astronaut health problem. Lack of on-board diagnosis has increased significant risk in astronauts' bone loss during long-term space flight. Early diagnosis of such disorders can lead to prompt and optimized treatment that will dramatically reduce the risk of fracture and longitudinal monitoring microgravity and countermeasure effects. Advents in quantitative ultrasound (QUS) techniques provide a method for characterizing the material properties of bone in a manner for predicting both bone mineral density (BMD) and mechanical strength. Investigators have developed a scanning confocal acoustic navigation (SCAN) system capable of generating noninvasive ultrasound images at the site of interest. Both animal and human tests indicated strong correlations between SCAN determined data and microCT determined BMD, and bone strength, as well as monitoring fracture healing with guided ultrasound. experiment_title: Hyperosmotic Fluid Countermeasure
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a resultant decrease in body fluid. Hypovolemia may be one cause of the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. Drinking a salt-water solution (or ingesting an equivalent combination of salt tablets and water) may help to restore plasma volume, but the effectiveness of such a countermeasure may depend upon whether the ingested solution is isotonic (its concentration is the same as the concentration of substances dissolved in the blood) or hypertonic (its concentration is higher than that of the blood). The objective of this study was to test the ingestion of 3 salt and water combinations during flight, comparing the efficacy of isotonic and hypertonic combinations for maintaining orthostatic function after space flight.

APPROACH:
Twenty-three astronauts on 5 Shuttle flights were assigned to consume one of the following 1 to 2 hours before landing: a hypertonic combination of salt tablets and water, isotonic saline, or an isotonic combination of salt tablets and water. Each astronaut performed stand tests before the flight, on landing day and 3 days after landing.

RESULTS:
The ingested volumes of the test solutions and of other fluids were too variable for any conclusions to be made. Evaluation of the relative efficacy of the different candidate fluid loading solutions was difficult due to the existence of several factors that compromised data quality. These factors were: (1) a flight rule requiring crew members to repeat half of the fluid load protocol in the event of a one revolution wave-off of landing, (2) variations in the amount of solution ingested, (3) subsequent uncontrolled fluid ingestion after completion of the fluid loading protocol, which, in effect, diluted the prescribed solutions,and (4) use of fluids other than water, as prescribed, which altered not only the conditions of the investigation but also the efficacy of the countermeasure.

Evaluation of the candidate fluid loading countermeasure solutions and their ability to maintain orthostatic function after spaceflight was terminated without providing a conclusive answer to the question of the efficacy of a hypertonic solution as an end-of-mission rehydration countermeasure.

experiment_title: Erythroid Colony Formation In-Vitro and Erythropoietin Determinations
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In a continuing investigation of the pathogenesis of "space anemia", three red blood cell studies were performed on five flight rats and compared to controls. The bone marrow cell differentials, clonal bone marrow studies of red blood cell colony formation, and plasma erythropoietin determinations were performed, and compared to previous studies of these three parameters.

Approach:

Bone marrow smears were made at the landing site; received slides were stained, and bone marrow cells were counted (500 cell differential counts were performed) and classified. For erythroid clonal studies, tibial bone marrow plugs were cultured in Petri dishes; colonies were scored by the ability of hemoglobin-containing cells to reduce 2,7-diaminofluorene. Frozen plasma (0.2 ml) was used for erythropoietin determinations, utilizing a commercial kit.

Results:

While some minor variations were found, there were no essential differences in bone marrow differential counts or erythropoietin levels of flight or tail-suspended animals as compared to controls. In studies of colony formation there was a marked increase in the number of CFU-e colonies in frozen flight bone marrow, while no such increase was noted in the "fresh" cultures prepared in Moscow. As with previous studies, no pattern of erythropoiesis has emerged, and the rat may or may not be a valid model to study the decrease in red blood cell mass that occurs in humans exposed to microgravity.

experiment_title: Emergence of Wheat Seedlings in Zero Gravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment was to determine whether seeds would produce normal seedlings when germinated in the absence of a significant gravitational force. As the negative geotropism of the coleoptile and the positive geotropism of the roots would be eliminated during flight, seedling organs could be expected to show alterations similar to those produced through a clinostat. Even after only three days growth, measurable differences in coleoptile and primary root orientation should appear in the absence of the even distribution of auxin in these organs by reason of the downward transport of, and equalizing action on, auxin by the force of gravity.

Approach:

Seventy-eight wheat seedlings (38-39 mg) were surface sterilized in a 0.05% Hg Cl2 and soaked for three hours at 95 °F. The seedlings were then placed in polycarbonate stalks containing wet vermiculite. Gas samples were taken and lids were sealed. All growth took place in the dark. Photography was done rapidly at recovery by means of special camera rack systems which included a 45° mirror that reflects the side view of each seedling in the row that is set to face the camera. The orientation of the seedlings was described in quantitative terms by the combination of face-view and side-view angles that are made by the intersection of a line from the tip to the base of a root or coleoptile with a vertical line through the axis of the seedling.

Results:

Growth physiology of wheat seed germination and the development of wheat seedlings in their early stages were not disturbed sufficiently by the absence of gravity as reflected in growth rates or external morphology. The stresses of launch acceleration and vibration had no measurable effects on ungerminated wheat seeds. The basic metabolic processes, which supply the energy for normal growth, were apparently undisturbed. This indicates the independence from gravitational force of certain organelles which carry key enzymes to the sites of energy release and use. Weightlessness had no measurable effects on the endogenous mechanisms for production and distribution of the growth hormone, auxin. The wheat seedling proved to be an excellent choice of a small test plant for a space flight experiment in the growth and orientation of plant organs known to be geosensitive. The development and performance of this study led to the discovery of root epinasty, previously unknown to plant physiologists, as a factor in the orientation of plagiotropic roots.

experiment_title: Cytogenetic Study of Heavy Ion-Induced Chromosomal Damage in Human Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Energetic heavy ions pose a great health risk to astronauts during extended International Space Station (ISS) and future Mars missions. High-LET heavy ions are particularly effective in causing various biological effects, including cell inactivation, genetic mutations and cancer induction. Most of these biological endpoints are closely related to chromosomal damage, which can be an indicator of health risks.

The major objectives were to: 1) comparatively assess the frequencies of complex and simple, as well as interchromosomal and intrachromosomal, aberrations induced by low- and high-LET radiation, and 2) evaluate the pattern and types of heavy-ion induced chromosomal aberrations between human 2-D epithelia cells, 3-D epithelia cells, and lymphocytes.

Experimental results of this investigation may provide the knowledge for identifying the complexity of chromosomal aberrations due to space-like radiation and for assessing the radiation risks from such end-points observed in differential cell systems. The differential radiation environment encountered in space may cause deleterious effects in humans, and these effects are of special concern for prolonged space missions beyond the protective terrestrial magnetosphere. Before such missions can be undertaken, a much more detailed understanding of these effects is required to allow planning and implementation of protective countermeasures.

APPROACH:
In this study, investigators quantitatively analyzed chromosomal damage induced by energetic heavy ions in human epithelia and lymphocyte cells, by using advanced cytogenetic techniques including the multi-color fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) and mBAND techniques, which allowed the analysis of chromosomal exchanges involving all human chromosomes and intrachromosomal aberrations, respectively. Human epithelia cells were cultured in both the conventional two-dimensional (2-D) and tissue-equivalent three-dimensional (3-D) platforms. The exposure of human cells to energetic heavy ions was conducted at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at the Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL), and a gamma radiation source at the Baylor College of Medicine was used for low-LET exposures.

RESULTS:
Results of this study validated the observation of a higher incidence of inversions for high-LET radiation. However, detailed analysis of the inversion type revealed that both iron ions and gamma rays induced a low incidence of simple inversions. Half of the inversions observed in the low-LET-irradiated samples were accompanied by other types of intrachromosome aberrations, but few inversions were accompanied by interchromosome aberrations. In contrast, iron ions induced a significant fraction of inversions that involved complex rearrangements of both inter- and intrachromosome exchanges.

experiment_title: 6 Degree Headdown Tilt with Balance Traction to Emulate Spinal Lengthening Experienced by Astronauts during Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of ARCbedrest117 was to develop a balanced traction to elongate the spine to the degree experienced by astronauts. The effects of traction on the spine exposed to the 6o head down tilt (HDT) model is compared to effects on the spine with traction and horizontal bed rest (HBR).  The second part of this study (ARCbedrest129) was designed to determine the electrical activity and intramuscular pressures of the muscles along the lumbar spine while upright and while in 6o HDT or HBR position.

APPROACH:
Healthy volunteers were tested in the MRI before and after 3 days exposure to a balanced traction device that placed a load on the spine by suspending a load corresponding to 5% of the body weight from each leg with a cable-pulley system.  The volunteer was at bed rest in the 6 degree HDT or in HBR position.  Activity was not restricted.  HDT with traction was compared with HBR with traction. The second part of the study conducted a few days after #117 estimated the electrical activity of lumbar spine muscle through surface electrodes for specified hours of normal activity.  Through a catheter inserted into the muscle on either side of the lumbar spine, the pressures were recorded during upright and then at three time intervals during of HDT or HBR.  Electrical activity was recorded concurrent with intramuscular pressure.  Subjects were randomized into 2 groups of three.  Group 1 underwent HBR followed by HDT in balanced traction.  Group II underwent HDT in balanced traction followed by HBR.  There was a two-week recovery period between the two forms of 3d-bed rest.
 


RESULTS:
Repeated measures ANOVA indicated that total body length increased more (mean±SE) during HDT with balanced traction (22±8 mm) than during HBR (16±4 mm).  Spine length between L5 and C7 also increased more during HDT with traction  (25±8 and 14±9 mm).  Ultrasonography showed increases in lumbar disc height during HDT and HBR (2.9±0.8 mm vs. 3.3±0.6 mm), but there were no differences among groups.  Seventy percent of the increase in disc height occurred during the first 5 hours of bed rest.  Within the first hour of standing, there was a 10 mm decrease in body height, about 80% of the normal diurnal variation in our subjects.  The intensity of pain in the back, abdomen and head was greater during HDT with traction than during HBR with traction.  Reflexes were normal in both groups.  Intramuscular pressure in erector spinae muscles that averaged 8.4±0.7 mm Hg did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT.  Ankle joint torque during plantar- and dorsi-flexion did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT with balanced traction.

Conclusions: Results suggest that HDT with balanced traction may combine the advantages of both models to simulate total body and spinal lengthening, as well as back pain associated with microgravity. 

Note: Both studies were carried out on the same group of subjects.  The measurements of intra muscular pressure in ARCbedrest129 were reported separately, but the protocols for each study were the same.  Therefore, it is more complete to have both ARCbedrest117  and ARCbedrest129  reported together as the first part and the second part of the study as described.

experiment_title: Contribution of the Vestibular and Sympathetic Nervous Systems to Space-Induced Bone Loss - Postdoctoral Fellowship
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Research has shown that genetic and pharmacologic approaches to sympathetic nerves contribute to the regulation of bone homeostasis. Osteoblasts express the beta-2 adrenergic receptor (ß2AR) and respond to catecholamines or pharmacological ßAR agonists with decreased proliferation and induction of RANKL expression, which leads to enhanced osteoclast formation and bone resorption. Propranolol, a ß1/ß2AR non-selective antagonist, inhibits these effects of sympathetic activation and protects from ovariectomy and unloading-induced bone loss in mice and rats. External factors also influence bone remodeling. In particular, gravity and inertial accelerations exert a range of mechanical stimulations on the skeleton that have an osteogenic effect demonstrated in birds, mice, rats, pigs, sheep and humans. In contrast, mechanical unloading as a consequence of bed-rest or microgravity conditions causes bone loss in humans and rodents, which is associated with suppressed bone formation and a mild increase in resorption.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine if vestibular lesion causes bone loss by activation of the sympathetic nervous system.
  2. Analyze the bone phenotype of mice devoid of vestibular gravity sensor.

APPROACH:
Investigators evaluated the effects of a bilateral vestibular lesion (VBX) on femoral bone mass using micro-CT analyses on two-month old mice. In addition, they used three-month old mice lacking otoliths (gravity sensors), in order to mimic the decrease in vestibular stimulation in space.

RESULTS:
The first step of this study consisted in evaluating the effect of a VBX on femoral bone mass. Using micro-CT analyses on two-month old mice, investigators demonstrated that VBX induces a significant decrease in femoral bone mass one month after the lesions. Histomorphometric analyses revealed that this bone loss was associated with a decrease in bone formation whereas bone resorption was not affected. The second step was to determine whether the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) mediates this VBX-induced bone loss. Using two-month old beta-2 adrenergic receptors Knockout (KO) mice, investigators detected no bone change in bone volume over total volume (BV/TV) one month after VBX. Moreover, daily propranolol treatment had no effect on WT-sham mice but completely blunted VBX-induced bone loss in WT-VBX mice. Finally the SNS involvement in the VBX-induced bone loss was further supported by the increase in Ucp1 gene expression in brown adipose tissue (a marker of the SNS activity). No change in BV/TV was observed one month after VBX in two-month old beta-2 adrenergic receptors osteoblasts-specific KO mice. These results suggest that VBX-induced sympathetic outflow to bone triggers bone loss via its effect on beta-2 adrenergic receptors expressing osteoblasts.

experiment_title: Prevention of Renal Stone Complications in Space Exploration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this proposal is to refine and validate ultrasound to reposition kidney stones to prevent medical complications on space exploration missions. The objective will be met by adding a probe and software to the Flexible Ultrasound System (FUS). The probe will send ultrasound through the skin to create real time images of the stone and kidney and also to move or fragment the stone within the kidney.

Specific Aims:

  1. Refine ultrasound probes to detect, reposition, and fragment kidney stones.
  2. Validate probes to visualize, reposition, and fragment stones.
  3. Refine and validate imaging to guide therapy.

APPROACH:
In Aim 1, the probe(s) will be refined. The capability to image and reposition stones will be added to 1) the kidney imaging probe of the FUS manufacturer and 2) a clinical 3D probe. A third plug-and-play probe will also be developed to fragment kidney stones as a last resort. In Aim 2, the first probe will be validated as a countermeasure for the contingency of stone formation. The five tasks in Aim 2 are to refine and validate the capability 1) to displace a large blocking stone from occluding the exit of the kidney to delay treatment and complications, 2 and 3) to detect and displace a medium-sized stone in the ureter to alleviate complications, 4) to expel a small stone from the kidney to avoid complications, and 5) to measure the size of kidney stones to inform decision making.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. However preliminary results are available.

Two patients reported skin discomfort and sensation at depth with a few pushes. Otherwise, there was no pain or adverse effects associated with the treatment. Stones were localized with the system and repositioned in 14 of 15 subjects. In total, the system targeted and repositioned stones from all parts of the kidney and ureteropelvic juncture (UPJ), including the lower pole (20 targets), midpole (10 targets), upper pole (6 targets), and renal pelvis/UPJ (7 targets). Stones were imaged and repositioned at depths as great as 11 cm. Stones were repositioned to a new location in all 6 post-lithotripsy patients, while four of the six passed over 30 stone fragments within a few days of treatment. One passed two 2 mm fragments immediately after the completion of treatment. De novo stones and stones as large as 8 mm were repositioned in awake patients and during URS, although movement was not as great as seen with residual fragments. In four of the 15 subjects, what was noted in clinical imaging as a single, potentially unpassable stone was shown to be several passable stones upon repositioning with ultrasound. One subject with a potentially obstructing UPJ stone felt relief. The FDA has granted 15 more subjects for the next clinical trial. Investigators have developed and tested new probes and systems to continue to improve and validate performance of ultrasonic propulsion. They have participated in several meetings with General Electric (GE) and ExMC about NASA's FUS, and have recently received the GE probe used on the FUS. Investigators have started integrating their ultrasonic propulsion onto the GE probe. A new stone specific imaging mode was developed and reported, and a patent application was submitted. In the first step the system automatically identifies the location of stones in the image and highlights them with color during real-time scanning. In the second step, the system automatically determines the size of the kidney stone.
