experiment_title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Plasma Volume
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this test was to measure plasma volume to aid in the proper assessment of hemodynamic parameters, vascular responses, and cardiac size and function. The investigators hypothesized that plasma volume losses will be similar to those following space flight. They expected to see changes in blood volume for subjects following extended periods of bed rest.
APPROACH:
Plasma volume was measured by the carboxyhemoglobin rebreathing method. The test subject breathed into a mouthpiece into which 60 cc of carbon monoxide (CO) was injected. In addition, blood draws were completed before and 10 minutes after CO administration.
RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded. Tabular results are available for the public..
Interim results were published from Campaign 3 using thirteen subjects which were studied before and during bed rest. Statistical analysis was limited to the first 49-60 days of bed rest and compared to pre-bed rest data. Ultrasound data were collected on vascular and cardiac structure and function. Tilt testing was conducted for 30 minutes or until presyncopal symptoms intervened. Plasma volume was significantly reduced by day seven of bed rest. Flow-mediated dilation in the leg was significantly increased at bed rest day 49. Arterial responses to nitroglycerin differed in the arm and leg, but did not change as a result of bed rest. Anterior tibial artery intimal-medial thickness markedly decreased at bed rest days 21, 35, and 49. Several cardiac functional parameters, including isovolumic relaxation time (73 ms to 85 ms at day 7) and myocardial performance index, were significantly increased during bed rest. There was a trend for decreased orthostatic tolerance following 60 day of bed rest. Over all the data suggest that bed rest altered cardiovascular structure and function in a pattern similar to short-duration spaceflight. Additionally, the vascular alterations were primarily seen in the lower body, while vessels of the upper body were unaffected.
During the artificial gravity (AG) pilot study it was concluded that AG can mitigate some aspects of bed rest-induced cardiovascular deconditioning, including orthostatic intolerance and aerobic power. Mechanisms of improvement were not cardiac-mediated, but likely through improved sympathetic responsiveness to orthostatic stress.

experiment_title: Starch Metabolism in Space-Grown Soybean Seedlings
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

This was the second flight of this experiment, in which the hypothesis that starch concentration in plant tissue decreases due to the effects of the space/microgravity environment was tested and possible mechanistic causes for the changes in starch concentration were investigated. Measurements were made of starch and soluble sugar concentrations, critical biosynthetic and degradative enzyme activities, localization and visualization of the starch grains, structural and ultra structural make-up of different tissues within soybean (Glycine max) seedlings, along with growth and biomass partitioning, and canister atmospheric components.

APPROACH:

The BRIC-03 experiment flew on STS-63 in February 1995. This was an 8-day mission. Two canisters of twenty-six soybeans (Glycine max) each were flown. One was frozen in space after 5 days and the other returned unfrozen for postflight harvesting. Analyses for these experiments included measurements of growth, biomass partitioning, gas concentrations in the canisters, carbohydrate concentrations and related enzyme activity measurements in the cotyledons and ultrastructural analysis of cotyledon, hypocotyl and root tissue sections.

RESULTS:

While overall biomass accumulation by the growing seedling was diminished as a result of space flight, the mobilization of reserves for the cotyledons was not affected, suggesting an increase in respiration in the space-grown plants. Analysis of the cotyledons frozen in flight revealed lower starch concentration, lower activity of the starch synthetic enzyme adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-glucose pyrophosphorylase and higher activity of the sucrose synthetic enzyme sucrose phosphate synthase relative to the ground controls. Other starch and sucrose metabolic enzymes were unaffected by space flight. In seedlings returned to earth unfrozen, starch concentrations in the flight cotyledons were not significantly different from those in the ground controls. However, ultrastrucutural analysis revealed that both the number and total area of the starch grains were significantly greater in the cotyledons from the space-grown plants, suggesting a reduction in starch grain density. Ethylene concentrations were twice as high in the headspace of the space-flight canisters relative to the ground controls. Ethylene, often produced under conditions of plant stress, may play a role in the observed space-flight effects on growth and carbohydrate metabolism.

experiment_title: Quantitative CT and MRI-based Modeling Assessment of Dynamic Vertebral Strength and Injury Risk Following Long-Duration Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts exposed to microgravity for extended periods have incurred damage to their musculoskeletal systems. There is concern that the changes observed may lead to reduced performance and an increased risk of injury, including fractures, when dynamic loads are experienced. This experiment is a flight definition investigation in which the investigators hypothesize that crewmembers exposed to long-duration microgravity will exhibit profound degradation in cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae and spinal musculature. It is further hypothesized that spaceflight-induced changes to crewmember vertebrae and spinal musculature will result in reduced vertebral strength and increased fracture risk from dynamic loading.
The central objective of this investigation is to quantify the dynamic strength changes in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae incurred following long-duration microgravity exposure. Specific objectives are to:
  1. Quantify vertebral geometry, volume, cortical thickness, and volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) changes and spinal muscle volume changes in pre- and postflight medical images of crewmembers on long-duration ISS missions.
  2. Quantify vertebral strength and assess injury risk in dynamic simulations with a human body model (HBM) altered to represent long-duration ISS crewmembers’ pre- and postflight vertebrae and spinal musculature.
APPROACH:
In this study, a unique engineering approach will be used for determining musculoskeletal strength and injury risk under dynamic loading conditions. Quantitative computed tomography (qCT) scans will be used to measure bone morphology, vBMD, and cortical thickness of the spine. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) will be used to measure the volume of spinal musculature. Results derived from pre- and postflight scans will be integrated and applied in dynamic simulations.
Subjects for this study will be ISS crewmembers who have previously flown as well as nine crewmembers who have yet to fly.
Retrospective data will include pre- and postflight qCT scans and MRI scans archived with NASA’s Life Sciences Data Archive. The lumbar spine (L1 and L2) were the focus of the qCT scans. MRIs focused on the cervical and lumbar areas.
Data collection from prospective subjects is planned to occur once preflight between L-180 and L-45 days and once postflight between R+0 and R+14 days. Each data collection will include a qCT scan of the C3, T3, and L1 vertebrae. Each data collection will also include MRI scans of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine regions. qCT scanning and MRI scanning need not occur on the same day, but must occur within 30 days of each other. There will be no inflight data collection.
Tissue degradation will be measured from retrospective and prospective qCT and MRI pre- and postflight scans. Image segmentation, registration, cortical thickness, and vBMD analysis techniques will be applied to quantify morphological and material property changes that occur in the vertebrae (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar) and spinal musculature when exposed to long-duration microgravity.
Geometric, volumetric, cortical thickness, and vBMD data will be used to morph and scale a finite element (FE) HBM to represent the pre- versus postflight spinal anatomy of individual crewmembers. Dynamic loads representing launch, pad or launch abort, and landing will be simulated with each altered HBM to assess individual and group strength decrement and injury risk with stress, strain, force, moment, and acceleration-based metrics.
RESULTS:
This investigation is in progress and results are not yet available. However, this study is expected to provide a greater understanding of spaceflight-induced bone and muscle degradation of the vertebral column and the resulting risk of vertebral fracture. Knowledge gained will inform the development and evaluation of countermeasures to prevent or reduce the effects of microgravity.

Investigators aim to study changes in blood proteins of astronauts before and after space flight by using the latest proteome analysis technique, and identify the causal protein of osteopenia. Blood will be drawn three times during preflight, four times inflight, and five times postflight. experiment_title: Cancer Induction by Repeated Doses of High-LET Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Past research has shown that radiation is a strong carcinogen. Vitamin A, a retinoid, can reduce the cancers caused by radiation in rat skin. This ground-based study focused on identifying genes whose expression is either induced or blocked by radiation and on the counteraction of retinyl acetate on those changes in gene expression.

Although retinoids, which are chemical derivatives of vitamin A, have been shown to counteract carcinogenic effects in several animal models, the molecular mechanisms behind the retinoid inhibition of radiation-induced cancer are not established. To better understand the mechanisms, this project focused on how a non-toxic naturally occurring retinoid in the diet called retinyl acetate, or vitamin A acetate, alters gene expression upon exposure of rat skin to radiation. This study may apply to the identification of genes involved in the broad mechanism of the retinoid role in skin cancer, such as its influence on cell proliferation, cell differentiation and apoptosis, which is also known as programmed cell death. Although these and other cellular responses to ionizing radiation are protective, if the responses are insufficient or overwhelmed, genetic errors may accumulate in cells. Those cells then divide, and cancer could eventually occur.

Preliminary findings with low Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation showed that dietary retinyl acetate counteracts radiation-induced expression in hundreds of genes. The most prominently affected genes were markers of cell proliferation in keratinocytes suggesting that the retinoid prevented radiation-induced increases of cell proliferation genes. No information is available on the effect of high LET radiation such as ƒ56/ƒFe on gene expression in skin keratinocytes. It is of interest to obtain information on gene expression patterns following skin exposure to the ƒ56/ƒFe beam in rats on normal diet and diet with retinyl acetate supplement. Similarities and differences between high and low LET radiation could then be analyzed. Earlier results suggested that the vitamin A retinoid is almost as effective against induction of skin tumors induced by ƒ56/ƒFe as by those induced by low LET electron radiation, thus gene expression studies are of interest.

One approach to study genes of interest is to find the genes that are altered by radiation and vitamin A in opposite ways. The expression of such genes may change in response to radiation exposure. These same genes may be expressed in the opposite manner upon vitamin A exposure without the radiation. In addition, some genes may not be affected by the vitamin A treatment without the radiation, but, if radiation is given and it causes changes, the vitamin A may be able to reverse those changes even though an effect of vitamin A alone is not observed. Organization of the genes into groups with similar functions in the cell can enable researchers to glean insight on whether certain functions of the cell are affected by radiation and, possibly, the counteraction of vitamin A.

APPROACH:
Eight rats that were 23 days old were divided into two dietary groups of four rats each. One dietary group was fed the regular food while the second group received the same food mixed with 250 ppm vitamin A acetate supplement. After one week, all of the rats received nine Gray and eighteen Gray of low LET electron radiation on two different dorsal skin patches about the size of 1.5 cm by 2 cm. A separate dorsal patch that was not exposed to the radiation was analyzed as a control. Each rat then had three patches of skin that were evaluated. One patch received zero radiation, one received nine Gray and the other received eighteen Gray. Twenty-four hours or seven days after the irradiation, the rats were euthanized, and the irradiated skin and non-irradiated skin sections were excised and pooled according to the radiation dose and vitamin A condition.

Total ribonucleic acid (RNA) was extracted from the skin samples and reverse transcribed to synthesize a special type of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). This particular DNA, called cDNA, was comprised only of the genes that were expressed at the time of analysis. The reverse transcription utilized a primer, a short segment of nucleic acid, which hybridized adjacent to the RNA polymerase promoter region. Double stranded cDNAs were then transcribed into a cRNA probe that was labeled with biotin through in vitro transcription as suggested by the gene chip manufacturer.

The cRNAs were differentially displayed using a rat genome gene chip. Each chip contained 8740 specific probes for rat genes. They represented every known functional category of genes. With this chip, expression all 8740 genes and gene groups were examined in one hybridization. The function of the chip was to recognize the genes that were expressed under the radiation and retinyl acid conditions. The gene chip identified by name those genes that were expressed and recognized. Northern blotting and reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) confirmed the genes that were differentially displayed, those that were identified when the probe bound to the specific genes on the rat genome gene chip. Finally, the patterns of the gene expression alterations from the radiation and vitamin A were categorized. Affected genes were grouped by their cellular functions to focus on pathways that are involved in the process of carcinogenesis by radiation and its reversal by retinyl acetate.

The gene chip analysis was not used for the eighteen Gray plus vitamin A treatment. Thus, five skin samples were analyzed for gene expression under low LET radiation. The five samples were from rats with normal diet and zero Gray radiation, normal diet with nine Gray radiation, normal diet with eighteen Gray radiation, vitamin A diet with zero Gray radiation and vitamin A diet with nine Gray radiation exposure.

For a study of carcinogenesis, the skin of approximately 200 rats was exposed to high LET radiation, a ƒ56/ƒFe beam. The rats were observed weekly for four weeks, then at six-week intervals thereafter. All skin abnormalities were noted, photographed and identified for histological diagnosis. The effects of multiple doses of high-LET ƒ56/ƒFe radiation in comparison to single doses of argon ion radiation were examined.

A different experiment utilizing the high LET radiation was to obtain information on gene expression patterns in a manner similar to that of the low LET electron radiation experiment. Rats were grouped into groups of three, with only twelve rats irradiated. One group of rats, the control group, received no treatment. Another group received vitamin A dietary retinoid and no radiation. Of the twelve irradiated rats, one group received vitamin A and three Gray of ƒ56/ƒFe high LET radiation. Another group received vitamin A plus 1.5 Gy ƒ56/ƒFe. Two groups of irradiated rats had no vitamin A supplement; one of these received three Gray of ƒ56/ƒFe and the other 1.5 Gy. At 24 hours or seven days after radiation exposure, the rats were euthanized, and the irradiated tissue was excised and frozen in liquid nitrogen for future analysis of RNA expression patterns with the gene chip technology.

RESULTS:
Retinol concentration in the skin was measured in rats with both diets. By seven days after the retinyl acid diet was begun, the retinol had accumulated in the skin but not in the blood of the rats that were given the supplement. The skin concentration of retinol in rats on that diet was 4.5-fold higher than in the rats that did not consume the retinyl acid diet. Plasma retinol levels were steady with or without the retinyl acid diet.

Gene expression signals ranged from zero to 278,710, with an average of 4217. Signal strength above 1000 was considered significant. For the five experimental groups, normal diet at zero, nine and eighteen Gray and vitamin A diet at zero and nine Gray, 50.4% of the genes were considered positive in at least one of the groups and the remaining 49.6% were considered as not significantly expressed in any of the five gene chips. Thus, 4402 of the 8740 genes were altered in expression for at least one of the five conditions, and 4338 of the genes did not show an alteration in expression in any of the five conditions.

Genes with induction or inhibition were compared among experimental conditions. Normal diet with nine Gray radiation versus normal diet with no radiation showed 188 altered genes. Eighteen Gray radiation versus normal diet with no radiation gave 92 altered genes, with 54 of those genes also altered under the nine Gray of radiation versus zero Gray, showing a radiation response dependent on dose. Eighteen Gray versus nine Gray of radiation with a normal diet showed 77 altered genes. For vitamin A supplemented diet, the vitamin A with no radiation compared to normal diet with no radiation showed 231 altered genes. Nine Gray of radiation on normal diet versus nine Gray of radiation with the vitamin A diet showed 58 altered genes.

There were 56 genes that showed at least 2.5 fold change between nine Gray and nine Gray with the vitamin A diet gene chips, and also had consistency in the other chips. In one group, genes were repressed by vitamin A alone and were induced by radiation, and the radiation induction was reduced by the vitamin A retinoid. In a different group, vitamin A alone did not change the expression in comparison to control but the combination of vitamin A and radiation reverted the radiation back to control levels. Other genes were inhibited by radiation, but were reversed to control level by vitamin A. The genes that showed the greatest reversal of radiation effects by vitamin A were a keratin gene, ornithine decarboxylase, an intracellular calcium-binding protein and a gene that is similar to an intracellular calcium-binding protein.

Genes that share similar functions were grouped together to learn if any groups were more susceptible to the radiation or the mitigating effects of vitamin A. The genes were checked to see if a significant change of greater than two-fold in expression levels were observed. Several functional groups did not show any genes with significant changes after radiation with or without vitamin A treatments. Tumor suppressor genes and genes related to apoptosis were two of the functional gene groups of interest that showed no changes in expression. The gene chips contained 16 cytokines and only one, Cyclin G, showed a greater than two-fold change between nine Gray with normal diet and nine Gray with vitamin A supplement.

The top one hundred genes with the greatest alteration in expression between nine Gray versus zero Gray normal diet and between vitamin A with no radiation versus zero Gray normal diet were grouped into one category. As a control, one hundred random genes from the expressed control sample were assigned into different functional categories. The genes affected most by the radiation or the vitamin A belonged to the categories of differentiation, stress response, inflammation or immune related and nucleic acid metabolism.

Northern blots, which analyzed RNA, showed a similar trend of expression as the gene chip for the keratin gene, a putative marker of proliferating basal cells. Although the Northern blot supports the gene chip results, the expression ratios differed between the two techniques for expression analysis. On the gene chip, the keratin gene showed 11.7-fold increase in expression with radiation versus the zero radiation. The vitamin A treatment (vitamin A with radiation) reversed the expression back to the control level. On the Northern blot, the increase in the radiation over control was only 4.9-fold rather than 11.7-fold, and the vitamin A reduced the expression to 2.2-fold above the control level rather than control level. The increase in gene expression from radiation that was reversible by vitamin A suggested that the vitamin A may have inhibited the dedifferentiating effects of radiation, and restored the normal differentiation status of the rat skin. Another laboratory technique, PCR, was also used to confirm gene chip results, and the gene chip expression pattern of the involucrin gene was confirmed by RT-PCR.

For the carcinogenesis study in which rat skin was exposed to radiation and the rats observed for tumors, a strong tendency was observed for the tumors to be inhibited by the presence of 250 ppm retinyl acetate in the food. Multiple doses of high LET ƒ56/ƒFe ion radiation in comparison to single doses of argon ion radiation were examined and indications were that multiple exposures produced more carcinomas than expected from the summation of single dose responses. Cancer induced by high LET radiation was indicated to be possibly as preventable by retinyl acetate in the diet as low LET radiation was in previous experiments.

Most tumors found in rats that had been irradiated with the ƒ56/ƒFe beam appeared to be fibromas. Single doses of ƒ56/ƒFe ions were somewhat more effective than argon in producing tumors at 4.5 Gy but not at three Gray or nine Gray. The 250 ppm of dietary retinyl acetate reduced the incidence of tumors to approximately 30% of the incidence found in groups that did not have the supplement in the diet.

Beneficial effects of vitamin A have been observed upon exposure to both high LET radiation and low LET electron radiation. Vitamin A reduced tumor incidence in rats exposed to high LET radiation. Under low LET radiation exposure, vitamin A blocked the expression of genes associated with increased proliferation and inflammation, and accelerated the expression of genes associated with epidermal differentiation. Some fibroblast or macrophage migration or invasion responses may have been inhibited as well. Vitamin A promoted epidermal differentiation on top of the abnormal differentiation from the radiation. Thus, it possibly protected the skin from cancer by preventing damaged cells from producing more cells and by promoting their death. Inhibition of epidermal cell proliferation and stimulation of differentiation limited the number of irradiated cells that could pass the genetic damage to future cells.

experiment_title: Non-Invasive Assessment of Intracranial Pressure for Space Flight and Related Visual Impairment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this study is to non-invasively estimate the changes in intracranial pressure and cerebral circulation induced by long-duration spaceflights by analyzing the arterial blood pressure (ABP) and the cerebral blood flow velocity (CBFV) waveforms before and after long-duration spaceflight. In addition, it will be confirmed that abnormal visual function and/or ocular structure (e.g. optic disc edema) occurs among the subjects whose intracranial pressure has increased.

Currently, this is the only study that relates to optic disc edema looking at “intracranial pressure”, by using non-invasively obtained multiple indexes. It is expected that the non-invasive methods developed and validated during space flight of six months will be found appropriate for the monitoring of space-related intracranial alterations. This study method may also lead to development of a screening examination.

APPROACH:
The Principal Investigator and Co-Investigator have reported changes in cerebral auto-regulation by analyzing ABP and CBFV in middle cerebral artery by non-invasive ABP monitor and transcranial Doppler sonography during variety of environment including spaceflight. Recently, an analysis method has been developed which uses high resolution waveforms with increased sampling frequency to estimate intracranial pressure. Intracranial pressure can be estimated non-invasively by this method.

Before and after flight, ABP and CBFV waveforms will be recorded simultaneously in a supine/sitting position at rest, and/or while doing a 15 sec Valsalva maneuver. Two preflight data collections are planned. The first will be at Launch - 3 months (L-3 months) and the second at L-2 months. Postflight data collections will take place at Return to Earth + 0 (R+0) and R+1.5 months. During flight, 4 months after launch, facial photographs will be taken to document facial edema. The analysis of changes in intracranial pressure and cerebral circulation will be performed offline.

experiment_title: Cell and Molecular Biomechanics: Cardiac and Skeletal Muscle
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this study was to produce a muscle cell model that will: explain biomechanical adaptations that occur with alterations in muscle protein isoforms due to changes in activity level, as in prolonged space travel; predict bioenergetic changes associated with changes in activity level; be integrated into computational models of human limb and heart. It was a collaborative project between Florida State University and the University of Washington. The original Aims of the project are: a. Identify contractile protein composition of skeletal and cardiac muscles from high-activity and low-activity rats. b. Characterize contractile properties (phenotype) of selected muscles containing unique mixtures of protein isoforms. c. Develop a “digital” cell biomechanical model.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Key Findings during the study period: a. Nano-mechanical model of the muscle sarcomere (a component of the Digital Astronaut): Presence of filament compliance could modulate the dependence of steady state isometric force and the rate of tension development on thin filament activation level that is determined by calcium in the living cell. Tuning of biomechanics through compliance at the protein level as demonstrated in the investigators’ studies may be as significant as biomechanical tuning at higher levels of organization as demonstrated by Professor Tom McMahon and colleagues’ ability to improve human runners’ performance through altering the characteristics of the track surface. The influence of compliance (or its inverse, elasticity) thus needs to be considered in biomechanical components at all levels of organization in physiological models to describe changes in muscle associated with exercise and microgravity. b. Signaling pathways in muscle plasticity: The immunosuppressant drug rapamycin has little or no effect on maximum calcium-activated force, but (at some concentrations) increases calcium-sensitivity of isometric force and inhibits the kinetics of tension redevelopment; this indicates that rapamycin affects calcium-regulatory proteins (troponin/tropomyosin) more than actomyosin. Attenuation of cardiac hypertrophy by rapamycin is not due to direct effects of rapamycin on myofilament contractility.

experiment_title: Advanced Diamond Electrodes for Electrochemical Based Monitoring of Spacecraft Water
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This research was focused on developing advanced water quality monitoring methods for the potable and technical water supplies onboard the International Space Station (ISS). The methods being developed could also have broad application on other long-duration space flight and habitation projects. Electrochemical methods were developed for water quality monitoring with two contaminant types targeted: (i) heavy metal ions including Ag(I), Cu(II), Cd(II), Pb(II) and Zn(II) and (ii) iodine and iodide as well as phenol and iodinated phenols. The key enabling material is the boron-doped diamond electrode, which provides a sensitive, reproducible and stable response for these analytes.

APPROACH:
Investigators completed studies of the electrode and method for a series of laboratory-prepared standard solutions. They also redesigned a small flow cell that could be used in microgravity environments for water quality assessment. They devised and tested a multiple step analysis protocol that involved sampling the water from the galley, mixing with a prepackaged supporting electrolyte (in a sealed syringe), adding the solution to the cell, making the anodic stripping voltammetric measurements of the metal ion content and analyzing the data. The focus was on Ag(I).

RESULTS:
Investigators demonstrated that a Au-coated, boron-doped, diamond thin-film electrode provides a sensitive, reproducible, and stable response for total inorganic arsenic (As(III) and As(V)) using differential pulse anodic stripping voltammetry (DPASV). As is pre-concentrated with Au on the diamond surface during the deposition step and detected oxidatively during the stripping step. Au deposition was uniform over the electrode surface with a nominal particle size of 23 +/- 5 nm and a particle density of 109 cm-2.

experiment_title: Pilot Studies of Radiation Damage in Organ Tissues of Mice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Low doses of radiation have been shown to protect against the biological effects of later exposure to toxic levels of radiation, a phenomenon known as the radioadaptive response. High dose whole body radiation is a common strategy in biomedical research to reduce or destroy bone marrow cells as an introduction to stem cell transplantation. Radiation treatments for cancer in humans or in biomedical research causes damage to other areas of the body, including the skeletal tissue.

APPROACH:
The pilot study involved a preliminary experiment with 12 mice and a comprehensive experiment with 36 mice. In the preliminary experiment, the mice were exposed to a low dose of 0.05 Gy, followed by a high dose of 6 Gy 24 hours later. The mice were sacrificed three days after the high dose exposure. The bone analysis included bone histomorphometry and microCT of tibia and lumbar vertebrae (L1 and L2) to evaluate the effects of bone marrow transplantation in mitigating whole body y-radiation-induced adverse skeletal effects.

RESULTS:
Radiation-induced death of marrow cells is associated with 1) a transient increase in bone formation due, at least in part, to activation of bone lining cells, and 2) an increase in bone resorption due to increased osteoclast perimeter. Bone marrow transplantation is effective in mitigating the detrimental effects of acute exposure to high dose whole body radiation on bone turnover. High dose whole-body gamma radiation results in a dramatic bone turnover response in which both formation and resorption are increased. The increased turnover is temporally associated with bone marrow failure and may result from disturbed regulation of osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation by hematopoietic cells. Bone marrow transplantation, by restoring normal bone marrow function, is effective in restoring normal bone turnover following lethal irradiation.

experiment_title: Noninvasive Biosensor Algorithms for Continuous Metabolic Rate Determination--SMS01302
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is designing new spacesuits to meet the needs of future space exploration. Real-time measurement of metabolic rate during astronaut activity is a key function of the biosensor suite which is planned for the new spacesuit. This project developed novel near infrared spectroscopic (NIRS) algorithms and sensors for real-time assessment of metabolic rate (measured as the rate of oxygen consumption, VO2). This capability was intended to be incorporated into a smart system advising astronauts on their use of consumables during Extravehicular Activity (EVA). The specific aims of this project include the development of algorithms to calculate VO2 from NIRS spectra and validation of the algorithms during exercise in ground-based protocols which simulate plasma volume reduction during spaceflight. An additional aim of this project is to support the EVA suit testing program by developing small, lightweight, and robust sensors which can be used within the spacesuit to evaluate metabolic cost of the suit itself, on individual muscles.

APPROACH:
Data collection in the first year of this study was shown to provide an early indication of patients who had significant plasma leakage and were at risk for shock. The company formed to commercialize the sensor, Reflectance Medical, has received substantial funding from the US Army Medical Research and Materiel Command. The company received clearance from the FDA to sell the CareGuide Oximeter 1100, a hospital-based system to noninvasively and continuously determine SmO2. The company has submitted its second 510(k) application for the mobile CareGuide 2100 Oximeter, which is a battery powered SmO2 sensor that displays results on an Android tablet or the Sotera ViSi mobile wrist worn vital sign monitor. The CareGuide 3100 development is complete. The 3100 updates the CareGuide 2100 software to calculate pHm and hematocrit (Hct) from the same spectra.

RESULTS:
Investigators completed the development of an algorithm for calculating VO2 during cycling using data from the Near Infrared Spectroscopic Sensor to determine muscle oxygen saturation (SmO2) and heart rate. This algorithm was demonstrated to be accurate for 11 subjects who completed a cycling protocol in both a normovolemic and hypovolemic state. Reflectance Medical, with synergistic funding from the US Army Medical Research and Materiel Command, completed the development of a wearable, lightweight solid state NIRS sensor which is small and lightweight enough to be worn under the spacesuit. The system has been shown to reliably determine SmO2, pH, and blood hematocrit for both light and dark skin individuals with a range of fat thicknesses over the muscle. Reflectance Medical has received clearance from the FDA to market the SmO2 sensor, and will soon submit an application to add pH and hematocrit capability to the sensor. This sensor is slated to be included in a newly approved NASA flight study to examine the effects of fluid shifts in space.

experiment_title: Hypogravity's Effect on the Life Cycle of Japanese Quail
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To determine if quail embryos exposed to microgravity use minerals from the egg shell in the same manner as embryos on Earth.

Approach:

This experiment was performed twice, once during Mir 18 (returning on STS-71) and once during Mir 19 (returning on STS-74). Fertilized eggs were carried to the Mir space station aboard a Russian Progress (227) supply vessel, and placed in an incubator supplied by the Institute for Biomedical Problems. On days 7, 10, 14 and 16, eight eggs were fixed and stored for return to Earth.

Results:

During both runs of the experiment, internal incubator temperature was higher than nominal throughout the experiment, and most of the quail embryos failed to develop as expected, resulting in low science return. During Mir 19, ten embryos developed past 7 days and four embryos developed to an appropriate age. No viable results were obtained.

experiment_title: Effects of Exposure to Heavy Particles
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Future missions in space may involve long-term travel beyond the magnetic field of the earth, subjecting astronauts to radiation hazards posed by solar flares and galactic cosmic rays. The objectives of this research project were to describe and characterize heavy particle-induced behavioral and neurochemical deficits, determine their underlying causes, and develop approaches to minimize such deficits. To achieve these objectives, behavioral and neurochemical models were used that have been previously shown to be sensitive to radiation exposure, and which may provide a basis for defining the risks of exposure to heavy particles on brain functioning and related behavior. An understanding of this risk may be vital to the effective performance and possibly the survival of astronauts during future missions in space.

Project Aims
The general objectives of the experiments reviewed in this report were to determine the effects of exposure to heavy particles on dopaminergic neurons in the brain, the neurochemical processes that mediate the effects of exposure, and on the behaviors that depend upon the integrity of the dopaminergic system.

More specifically, the aims of the research program were to:
1. Further characterize the neurochemical effects and the mechanisms that mediate the effects of exposure to 56Fe particles.
2. Further characterize both acute and late behavioral/cognitive effects of exposure to 56Fe and other particles.
3. Characterize organismic variables, such as age, as mediators of the effects of exposure to HZE particles.
4. Further characterize the effects of exposure to high-energy protons on neurochemical and behavioral functioning.
5. Evaluate the effects of diet on the neurochemical and behavioral effects of exposure to 56Fe particles.

APPROACH:
Behavioral Measures
Measurement of behaviors within 3-7 days following exposure to heavy particles or protons utilized the facilities available at the site of irradiation. For the measurement of behaviors that require specialized equipment, or which can take repeated trials for the acquisition (e.g., conditioned place preference, water maze performance or operant conditioning procedures) the animals were shipped to University of Maryland Baltimore County (UMBC) or Human Nutrition Research Center on Aging at Tufts University (HNRCA) for testing. In each case, both irradiated and non-irradiated controls were shipped to provide a control for any possible effects of the shipping. The basis for the selection of the behavioral tests is: (a) the behaviors are dopamine mediated (CPP, amphetamine-induced CTA, variable interval operant responding, upper body strength); and (b) they are behaviors that show deterioration as a function of age (water maze, radial arm maze).

Conditioned Taste Aversions:
The conditioned taste aversion (CTA) is a procedure by which rats are placed on a 23.5-hr water deprivation schedule for 7 days. On the conditioning day, they are presented with a calibrated drinking tube containing 10% sucrose solution instead of water, and intake recorded. Immediately following the drinking period, the rats are presented with the unconditioned stimulus (amphetamine, 3 mg/kg, ip). On the test day the rats are again given the 10% sucrose solution for 30 min. The acquisition of a CTA is shown by reduced sucrose intake on the test day compared to the conditioning day.

Conditioned Place Preference:
This procedure, which is used to evaluate the reinforcing qualities of a specific stimulus, utilizes an apparatus with three distinct compartments (black and white compartments which are separated by a gray compartment). The rat is given a reinforcing stimulus (e.g., amphetamine, 2 mg/kg) in one compartment and, on alternate days, a neutral stimulus (e.g., saline) in the other. An “unbiased” procedure is used, in which the compartment associated with injection of amphetamine is randomly assigned - some rats are given the amphetamine in the black compartment and some in the white compartment. After three pairings of each compound with a specific compartment, the rat is allowed to move freely about the apparatus and the amount of time spent in each compartment is measured. A Conditioned Place Preference (CPP) is shown when the organism spends significantly more time in the compartment paired with the presumptive reinforcing stimulus (amphetamine) than in the compartment paired with the neutral stimulus.

Operant Conditioning: The proposed procedure is a standard one in which rats are rewarded for making an instrumental response on a fixed ratio schedule. In a fixed-ratio design, the animal is rewarded after n number of responses, such that on an FR-5 schedule, the rat is rewarded after 5 responses (bar presses) and on an FR-10 schedule, after 10 responses. Rats are first trained to press a lever using an FR1 schedule by placing them in an operant chamber for 12 hrs. After the response has been learned, the rats are trained to respond on a fixed-ratio schedule by providing several trials using an FR-5 schedule. During testing the rats are then given 30-min sessions in which they are rewarded using FR-1, FR-5, FR-10, FR-15, FR-20, FR- 25, FR-30 and FR-35 reinforcement schedules. If exposure to 56Fe particles disrupts operant performance, then the irradiated animals should make fewer responses than the sham-irradiated controls and the discrepancy between the irradiated and control rats should increase as the number of responses required for the delivery of a food pellet increases.

Water Maze and Radial-Arm Maze:
These procedures are the standard ones used to evaluate changes in spatial learning and memory. Performance on these tasks were sensitive to hippocampal damage and show decreased performance in aged organisms.

Morris water maze: The Morris water maze consists of a circular black fiberglass pool (134 cm in diameter x 50 cm in height), filled to a depth of 30 cm with water maintained at 23oC. The pool is divided into four equal-size quadrants. A circular escape platform (10 cm in diameter) is colored black and therefore hidden from sight. The platform is submerged 2 cm below the surface of the water in the center of one of the quadrants; its location is changed to a different quadrant for each session of testing. The maze is placed in a room with the lights dimmed, and there are numerous extramaze cues on the walls. Performance on each test is videotaped and analyzed with image tracking software (HVS Image, Hampton, England). The task requires an animal to use spatial learning and memory to find a hidden platform just below the surface of the water, and to remember its location from the previous trial. The rat must acquire a cognitive representation of location in space and have the ability to effectively navigate the environment; therefore, the animal must use distal cues to effectively locate the hidden platform. Accurate navigation is rewarded by escape from the pool. Several dependent measures are used to estimate the efficiency of the rat's performance: directionality, latency of finding the hidden platform on each trial, length of swim path as well as the distribution of swimming time and swim path in the four quadrants of the pool during transfer or probe trials (in which the platform is removed from the pool) or during reversal trials (in which the platform is moved to another quadrant of the pool), number of crossings and latency to cross a previous platform location, and swim speed. Several experimental procedures have been developed to measure different aspects of cognitive performance, including reference (long-term) and working (short-term) memory.

Radial Arm Maze: The radial arm maze consists of eight equally spaced plexiglass arms (70 cm long, 12 cm wide) radiating from an octagonal central area 30 cm in diameter. Various extra-maze cues are present in the testing room. Each maze arm contains a small dish at its end that can be baited with 0.25 ml of 0.30% saccharine solution or a small food pellet (45 mg pellet). The task involves the successive selection of arms, radiating from the center of the maze, in order to obtain a water or food reward. Rats are water or food deprived to 85% of their body weight to ensure motivation. An optimal strategy involves using spatial memory to visit each arm only once, since the arms are not rebaited. Working memory is required while the rat is selecting the next arm to visit, apparently "keeping track of" which arms were previously selected. Various control experiments strongly suggest that the rat performs the radial arm maze test by utilizing extra-maze cues. One possibility is that the rat builds a cognitive map of the environment to learn the maze, and utilizes its working memory to monitor which arms have been visited.

Motor Behavior
Motor behavior is assessed using a wire suspension task. Each rat's forepaws are placed on a taut horizontal wire placed 10 cm above a foam cushion. The length of time that the animal can remain suspended is measured. This test measures muscle strength and prehensile reflex of the forepaws. Each animal serves as its control, with suspension time measured before, and following irradiation.

Neurochemical Measures

Dopamine Release:
Dopamine release was determined by preparing 300: m slices of striata using a McIlwain tissue chopper. Slices of one caudate nucleus from each animal were placed in glass vials containing a modified Krebs-Ringer buffer that has been bubbled for 30 min with 95% O2/5% CO2. The buffer consists of 21 mM NaHCO3, 3.4 mM glucose, 1.3 mM NaH2PO4, 1 mM EGTA, 0.93 mM MgCl2, 127 mM NaCl and 2.5 mM KCl (pH 7.4). The slices were washed in this medium and 150: l aliquots are placed into two chambers of a superfusion apparatus containing 16 chambers, the perfusion of the slices from eight animals in the same experimental "run". The tissue and buffer media are maintained at 37oC throughout the course of the experiment. The tissue is then allowed to equilibrate for 30 min while being perfused with the oxygenated basal release medium at the rate of 124: l/min. After equilibration, a 5 min baseline fraction is collected and the medium is switched to one containing (in mM) KCl 30, CaCl2.H2O 1.26, (in place of EGTA) and NaCl 57, as well as the other components listed above. Following the switch, 5-min fractions continue to be collected for 30 min into vials containing 0.4 perchloric acid (to prevent the autoxidation of the dopamine). To assess cholinergic effects on dopamine release, oxotremorine (500: M) is added to the release medium perfusing alternate chambers. Dopamine release is assessed by HPLC coupled to electrochemical detection.

Oxidative Stress
Aliquots of tissue were prepared the same as the dopamine release. To evaluate oxidative stress the aliquots of tissue were loaded with 2',7'-dichlorofluorescin diacetate which oxidizes to 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein in the presence of reactive oxygen species. The level of brain-associated fluorescence was monitored using a Cyto Fluor Multi-Well Plate Reader (perSeptive Biosystem, Framingham, MA).

Neurogenesis
Assessment of neurogenesis in the rat brains is determined by bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation into the nuclei of dividing cells. BrdU is a thymidine analog used as a mutagen in genetic research, which is selectively incorporated into cellular DNA during the S-phase of cell division. Each rat receives 1 daily intraperitoneal injection of BrdU (50mg/kg) for 6 consecutive days. Rats are sacrificed and perfused one day after the last BrdU injection in order to study the proliferation of newly divided cells. Additional rats are sacrificed 28 days following the last injection to study the differentiation into cell types. Every sixth section of a series through the hippocampus (approx. 240um apart) will be selected and BrdU-positive cells were counted using a modified version of the optical fractionator method. Stereological estimates are made of the total number of BrdUpositive cells located throughout the entire extent of the granular cell layer, subgranular zone and the hilus.

RESULTS:
Neurochemical Mechanisms
Oxidative Stress: Different brain regions (striatum, hippocampus, frontal cortex) were evaluated for oxidative stress using 2',7'- dichlorofluorescin diacetate 1-2 months following exposure to 1.5 Gy 56Fe particles. In the presence of reactive oxygen species, the compound oxidizes and becomes highly fluorescent. Results indicated that there were significant increases in reactive oxygen species in the hippocampus and frontal cortex, but not in the striatum of rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles. These results suggest that exposure to 56Fe particles cause oxidative stress, although irradiation may not produce equivalent effects throughout the entire brain.

Cellular Signaling in the Brain: Calcium homeostasis and calcium-dependent signaling (e.g. calcium dependent protein kinases (PKs) and calcium-mediated neurotransmitter release) are essential for memory formation, particularly spatial memory. Changes in calcium-dependent PKC, PKA, were observed during the experiment, suggesting altered cellular signaling. Furthermore, these changes in brain responses significantly correlated with reference and working memory errors in the radial arm maze. These results show differential brain-region-specific sensitivity induced by exposure to 56Fe particles.

Neurogenesis: Recent research has indicated that, neurogenesis occurs in mature, as well as developing organisms. One way of determining whether or not neurogenesis is occurring is to evaluate cells in specific brain regions for bromo-deoxy-uridine (BrdU) staining. Preliminary combined counts of the subgranular zone and granular cell layer of the hippocampus suggest that the subjects irradiated with 2.5Gy of 56Fe radiation have significantly less BrDU-stained cells in this region than do control subjects.

Behavioral Studies of Exposure to 56Fe and Other HZE Particles
Conditioned Taste Aversion Learning: Previous research had shown that the motor deficits in dopaminergic function were still observed up to 180 days following exposure to 1 Gy of 600 MeV/n 56Fe particles. The amphetamine-induced CTA, which depends upon the integrity of the dopaminergic system was utilized to evaluate whether or not there is recovery of behavioral function 4 months following exposure to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles (1 GeV/n). These results compared to the control animals revealed that radiated animals showed a significantly greater decrease in sucrose intake, indicating an enhanced aversion to the normally preferred sucrose solution. Although more research is needed to evaluate the mechanisms that may have been responsible for this change in behavior, it is possible that the loss of dopamine may have resulted in the up regulation of these receptors.

Morris Water Maze: The effects of exposure to 56Fe particles on cognitive performance were analyzed by using the Morris water maze to evaluate possible heavy particle induced deficits in spatial learning and memory. Rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe particles demonstrated cognitive impairment compared to a control group, as shown by increased latency to find the hidden platform, particularly when the location of the platform was moved 180° from its previous location or when the platform was removed from the pool to test for the use of spatial strategies. These results provided the first indication that exposure to non-lethal levels of 56Fe particles could affect the cognitive ability of an organism.

Radial Arm Maze: The radial arm maze consists of 8 arms radiating from a central area. The arms can be baited with food and the rat enters each arm to obtain food. The most efficient procedure is to enter each arm once, and only once, to obtain the food. When all arms are baited, rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles show somewhat better performance than control rats by entering each arm in turn. However, when only half the arms contain food, the performance of the radiated rats is poorer than that of controls. It appears that under these conditions, the radiated rats are not able to use spatial cues to guide their behavior, so they repeatedly enter the unbaited arms or arms which they have previously entered. These results support previous research, which indicates deficits in spatial learning and memory following exposure to 56Fe particles.

Operant Responding: Groups of rats were exposed to 0, 1.0, 1.5, or 2.0 Gy of 56Fe particles and trained to press a lever in order to obtain food reinforcement. Once the response was acquired the rats were placed on an ascending fixed-ratio (FR) schedule starting with FR-1 (every lever press rewarded with a food pellet) and extending to FR-35 (35 lever presses are required to produce 1 food pellet). In general, as the ratio increases, rats increase their rate of responding. However, the results showed that at ratios greater than FR-20, rats exposed to 2.0 Gy failed to increase their rate responding. These results indicate that rats exposed to 2.0 Gy of 56Fe particles cannot respond appropriately to increasing work requirements.

The rats that had been trained on the operant response tested on the ascending fixed ratio reinforcement schedule at 7, 10 and 15 months following irradiation. The results showed that the rats exposed to 1.0 or 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles and which showed no differences from control animals (0 Gy) when tested at 3 months post-irradiation, showed significant decreases in performance compared to the control rats when tested at these later time intervals. In addition, the rats exposed to 2.0 Gy continued to show a significant reduction in performance. These results indicate that, not only is there no recovery of function over time following exposure to heavy particles, there is a further decrease in performance which may be related to the increased age of the rats at the time of testing.

Conditioned Place Preference (CPP): CPP, a standard procedure for evaluating the capacity of a stimulus to reinforce behavior, is produced by pairing a rewarding stimulus (e.g., amphetamine) with specific environmental cues. The first experiment in this series showed that 2-4 weeks following exposure to 1.0 Gy of 56Fe particles, radiated rats fail to acquire an amphetamine-induced place preference. This indicates a disruption of the dopaminergic mechanisms that mediate reinforcement. Follow-up experiments evaluated place preference learning 2 months and 4 months following irradiation to determine if there was any recovery of function. The results showed that the irradiated rats failed to acquire an amphetamine-induced place preference when trained 2 or 4 months following exposure to 56Fe particles. These results indicate that the effects of irradiation on reinforcement show no recovery as a function of time following exposure to 1.0 Gy of 56Fe particles.

Because the results of the initial experiment showed a high degree of variability in terms of the amount of time spent in the amphetamine-paired compartment, it was decided to use a higher dose of 56Fe particles (1.5 Gy) to determine if the higher dose could eliminate the variability in the behavioral effects of exposure. Although the higher dose did eliminate the variability, it also eliminated the effect of irradiation on behavior: there was no effect of exposure on the acquisition of an amphetamine-induced place preference. Currently available data do not permit a determination of the factors that might be responsible for the dose-dependent effects of exposure to 56Fe particles on behavior.

Environmental Responsiveness: As shown with operant responding, rats exposed to 56Fe particles have difficulty in responding to changes in environmental contingencies, including adjusting work requirements to reinforcement contingencies. An alternate approach determining the effects of irradiation on the responsiveness of the organism to the environment is to evaluate the open field activity of irradiated rats and their reaction to spatial and non-spatial changes. Animals irradiated with 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles took longer to enter, visited less and spent significantly less time in the middle and the center portions of the open-field than did controls independently of total frequency and duration of activity of both groups. Likewise, irradiated subjects reacted significantly more to novel objects placed in the open-field than did controls. However, irradiated subjects did not vary from controls in their exploration patterns when objects in the open-field were spatially rearranged. Thus, irradiation with a dose of 1.5 Gy of 56Fe high-energy particle radiation elicited age-like effects during the spatial and non-spatial rearrangement tasks.

Taste Aversion Learning 28Si: Because astronauts will be exposed to other types of heavy particles in addition to 56Fe on long-duration missions outside the magnetosphere, it is necessary to evaluate the neurochemical and behavioral toxicity of other types of heavy particles. The initial experiments evaluated the effects of exposure to 28Si particles on amphetamine-induced CTA learning. This endpoint was selected because it has been shown to be very sensitive to irradiation with 56Fe particles and because there is a significant amount of data from 56Fe experiments to provide comparisons. Rats were exposed to 2.0, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of silicon particles. These doses were selected to take into account the lower LET of 600 MeV 28Si compared to that of 1GeV and 600 MeV 56Fe particles which have thresholds for behavioral and neurochemical effects of .8 and .1 Gy, respectively. Doses of 28Si particles produced an enhanced aversion compared to the non-irradiated controls. Because similar results have been observed following exposure to higher doses of 56Fe particles, these results suggest that the tested doses were too high, despite the lower LET of 600 MeV/n 28Si particles.

Operant Responding Following Exposure to 5 GeV/n 56Fe: Most of the research reviewed in this report has utilized 1 GeV/n 56Fe, which has an LET = 148keV/?m. For one run we had access to 5 GeV/n 56Fe, which has an LET = 142keV/?m. Rats were exposed to doses ranging between 1.5 to 2.5 Gy. When tested on an ascending fixed-ratio task 3 months following exposure, there were no significant differences between any irradiated group and the non-irradiated controls.

Organismic Variables (Aging)
Two approaches have been utilized to evaluate the effects of age on neurochemical and behavioral endpoints following exposure to HZE particles. First, rats have been maintained up to 1 year post irradiation and performance on specific tasks measured at intervals during the is time period. This approach using operant responding on a fixed-ratio reinforcement schedule shows that performance decreases as age increases: doses of 56Fe particles that were ineffective in altering performance in young animals had deleterious effects on aged animals.

The second approach studied the effects of exposure to HZE particles in older organisms. Exposure to HZE particles produces a series of neurochemical changes and motor deficits that are similar, but not identical, to those seen in older animals. To begin an evaluation of the possibility of an interaction between age and heavy particle irradiation, a preliminary experiment was run to determine oxotremorine-enhanced dopamine release in young and middle-aged F-344 rats following exposure to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles. The results showed a greater deficit in dopaminergic function in the older animals than in the younger animals. Statistical analysis of the results showed that there was a significant decrease in dopamine released in the aged, non-irradaiated rats. The difference between the middle-aged control rats and the irradiated young animals was not significant. These results suggest that dopamine release in a young rat exposed to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles is similar to that in old rats that have not been irradiated.

Neurochemistry: Exposing rats to 1.5, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of 250 MeV protons produced no significant alterations in dopamine release. Comparted to control animals, all groups of irradiated animals, particularly those exposed to 1.5 and 3.0 Gy, showed a slight increase in dopamine release, but this was not significant. These results indicate that exposure to up to 4.0 Gy of high energy protons does not affect the functioning of the dopaminergic system.

Conditioned Place Preference: Rats were tested for the acquisition of a CPP following exposure to 4 Gy of protons or following control procedures. Both the irradiated and the control rats showed a similar preference for the amphetamine-paired compartment. The amount of time spent in each compartment was not significantly different for the proton-exposed and control rats.

Spatial Learning and Memory: Exposing rats to protons produced no consistent alteration in water maze performance. Rats irradiated with 4.0 Gy showed increase latency to find the hidden platform on Day 1, but by Day 2 were identical to controls. Rats irradiated with 1.5 Gy demonstrated impairments in re-learning compared to the control group as shown by increased latencies on the reversal day (Day 4), when the platform was moved to the opposite quadrant. However, spatial memory and learning were not disrupted as all groups performed equally well on the probe trials, showing that all groups utilized spatial strategies to find the platform.

CTA Learning: Two sets of experiments were conducted. In the first experiment, rats were exposed to 1.5, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of protons. There were no significant differences between the irradiated or the control rats; both groups of rats showed equivalent test day sucrose intakes following injection of amphetamine. In contrast to the results obtained with rats exposed to 56Fe particles, exposing rats to up to 4.0 Gy of 250 MeV protons did not disrupt the acquisition of the dopamine-mediated CTA produced by injection of amphetamine.

In the second experiment, the rats were placed behind 6 gm/cm2 aluminum to see whether the fragmentation characteristics produced by protons passing through aluminum shielding would affect the behavioral response to administration of a dopamine agonist. The acquisition of a CTA following exposure to 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of protons was not affected by shielding. There were no differences in the intensity of the amphetamine-induced CTA between the control rats and the radiated rats.

Operant Responding: Proton-irradiated and control animals were trained to press a lever for food reinforcement using a fixed-ratio schedule. In contrast to the results obtained following exposure to 56Fe particles exposure to 4 Gy of high-energy protons had no effect on fixed-ratio responding for food reinforcement. Both irradiated and control animals showed increased levels of responding as the ratio was increased from FR-1 to FR-35. Exposing rats to high-energy protons does not affect the capacity of the organism to respond appropriately to changes in reinforcement contingencies.

Effects of Antioxidant Diets
Dopamine Release: Previous research had shown that exposing rats to 1.5 Gy 56Fe particles produces a significant decrease in potassium-enhanced striatal dopamine release. Because similar effects are observed in aged animals, and because diets rich in antioxidant phytochemicals can prevent the neurochemical change, the first experiment in this series was designed to evaluate whether or not these diets are equally effective in preventing heavy particle-induced neurochemical changes. Rats maintained on the control diet continued to show a 56Fe-induced reduction in dopamine release. In contrast, the rats maintained on either the strawberry or blueberry diets did not show the radiation-induced reduction in dopamine release. Compared to their respective controls, the radiated animals maintained on the antioxidant diets apparently showed an enhanced dopamine release.

Dopamine-Mediated Taste Aversion Learning: Rats were maintained on the control diet or on the diets containing 2% blueberry of strawberry extract. Two days following irradiation with 1.5 Gy of articles failed to develop a CTA to amphetamine. The rats fed either the blueberry or strawberry diet did show an amphetamine-induced CTA. These results indicate that antioxidant diets that have been shown to ameliorate the effects of normal aging are equally effective in preventing the disruption of amphetamine-induced CTA learning by exposure to 6Fe particles.

Tumorigenesis: Among other effects on the health and functioning of the organism, oxidative stress and the production of reactive oxygen species have been linked to carcinogenesis. As part of another study, rats that had been given either antioxidant or control diets prior to 56Fe exposure were evaluated for tumor development for 1 year after irradiation. Rats were sacrificed when a tumor developed or when there was some obvious health problem. The rats that were maintained on the blueberry or strawberry diets prior to irradiation with 56Fe particles showed a significantly greater survival time and developed significantly fewer tumors than rats maintained on the control diet.

Effects of Diet on Operant Responding: Rats were maintained on control or antioxidant diets for 2 months prior to exposure to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles. When tested on an ascending fixed-ratio schedule 7 months post-irradiation, there were no significant differences in response rate as a function of irradiation status or diet. When tested 12 months post-irradiation, the irradiated rats fed control or blueberry diets showed significantly poorer performance than the non-irradiated rats or the radiated rats fed the strawberry diet.

experiment_title: Adaptations of Motor Control in Response to Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Although past experiments have proven that some muscles weaken and atrophy during space flight, the exact mechanism behind this is unknown. Three hypotheses help explain the phenomenon: 1) Some "normal" level of activity, which is lacking in microgravity, is needed to maintain normal muscle properties, 2) Force generated by a muscle is directly related to muscle fiber size, loss of which occurs in space, and 3) Hormonal deficiencies, such as those seen during microgravity exposure, contribute to a loss in muscle mass. This experiment will help to quantify the response of muscle to space flight.

Approach:

Muscle biopsies were taken from the soleus (Sol), medial gastrocnemius (MG), tibialis anterior (TA), and vastus lateralis (VL), before and after a 14 day space flight. Samples were used to determine myosin heavy chain (MHC) composition, fiber type distribution, and fiber size. Single fibers from the soleus muscle were analyzed for cross-sectional area (CSA), myonuclear number/mm and myonuclear domain.

Results:

Percentage of pure type I fibers was decreased in the Sol postflight, in both the flight and the flight simulation groups. The number of hybrid fibers increased in both groups, and the MHC composition changed in a similar direction. In the MG or TA, no consistent changes in MHC, fiber type composition, or size of type II fibers were observed. However, pure type I fibers were smaller postflight in both the MG and the TA. In the single soleus fibers, mean CSAs of type I MHC fibers were smaller postflight. Mean myonuclear number/mm was similar between pre- and post-flight in all groups, but the mean myonuclear domains of the type I MHC fibers were decreased postflight. The Sol, a slow antigravity muscle, was affected the most by the 14 day space flight.

experiment_title: Morphofunctional Characteristic of Blood Cells and the Intensity of Erythropoiesis in Humans by the Influence of Factors of Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Deriving new data on the space flight factors impact on the human blood system to extend diagnostic and prognostic capabilities of detecting mechanisms of arising shifts in hematologic indices ("space anemia" and lymphocytosis).

APPROACH:
Collecting samples of venous and capillary blood with the aim:
1. To study erythrocyte forms.
2. To investigate metabolism of erythrocytes, cell membrane conditions, indices of ferrum metabolism and erythropoetin content in blood.

RESULTS:
Erythropoiesis is the production of new red blood cells and removal of old ones. This investigation examined that process to determine the ideal level of red blood cells astronauts need to readapt to terrestrial gravity. Results confirmed that the anemia astronauts often experience in space is caused by many factors in addition to decreased red blood cell production. Those factors may include ineffective erythropoiesis, cell metabolism changes, and premature removal of red blood cells from the bloodstream. The data will support future diagnosis and treatment of space anemia and related conditions in space flight and blood system conditions on Earth.

The findings will allow to detect mechanisms of the blood system adaptation to space flight factors, to extend the system of diagnostic and prognostic criteria for assessment of human physical state under extreme effects, as well as they can be used to develop prophylactic and pharmacologic preparations to treat disturbances in the blood system in these conditions.

experiment_title: A Low-Intensity Mechanical Countermeasure to Prohibit Osteoporosis in Astronauts During Long-Term Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The osteoporosis which develops in microgravity, is one of the greatest hurdles to an extended human presence in space. Earth-based animal and human studies have demonstrated that extremely low magnitude mechanical loading, if imposed at a high frequency, is strongly anabolic to the skeleton, and can serve to inhibit the bone loss, which typically parallels disuse. This experiment is designed to evaluate the efficacy of this unique biomechanical countermeasure to inhibit the microgravity-induced osteoporosis. To achieve this in a non-invasive, non-pharmacologic means would have tremendous impact not only in space, but would also address the bone loss which plagues over 20 million people world wide each year on Earth.

The specific objectives of this experiment are:
1. To establish the efficacy of a 10-minute daily in-flight dose of high frequency (30Hz), low magnitude (0.3-G, or 3m s-2) mechanical acceleration to inhibit the loss of bone density in the lower appendicular and axial skeleton.
2. To establish the efficacy of this same stimulus to inhibit the loss of muscle strength and postural stability in the lower appendicular skeleton.

APPROACH:
During extended missions International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers will receive ten-minute daily doses of high frequency (30Hz), low magnitude (0.3-G, or 3m s-2) mechanical accelerations. The subject will be secured to an oscillating plate by a shoulder harness, at 60% of their pre-launch body mass thus imparting sufficient force to allow the vibration of the platform to induce 0.3-G accelerations to the lower appendicular and axial skeleton. The experimental equipment is designed such that it will not transmit vibration to the vehicular structure. To determine efficacy, crewmembers not participating in the VIBE protocol will serve as prospective controls, as well as reference to previously collected Quantitative Computer Tomography (QCT) and Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) data from the astronaut corps. Comparison between control and treated crewmembers will allow for the efficacy of the treatment to be assessed in a dose dependent manner.

Following flight durations of at least three months, the bone quantity and quality will be evaluated by comparing postflight DXA, QCT and ultrasound measurements to baseline (preflight measurements). The principal areas of interest will be R&L femora, tibia, calcaneus, the spine (L1-4), and non-dominant radius. Assays will evaluate bone density, trabecular and cortical bone density, cortical thickness, apparent bone quality, and bone mineral density. Muscle strength and postural stability will also be evaluated, again comparing pre and post-launch data.

Differences from the baseline will be examined in terms of the ability of extremely low-level mechanical stimulation to inhibit the loss of bone quality and quantity. The preservation of muscle strength and postural stability, as based on these mechanical signals will provide a key to the regulatory stimulus in the maintenance of the musculoskeletal system.

Efficacy will be determined as based on the ability of the signal to inhibit bone loss, prevent loss of muscle power and loss of postural stability as compared to controls. Given the ground-based evidence, we anticipate that treated crewmembers will retain bone density and muscle strength regardless of the deleterious consequences of the absence of gravity. Further, it is anticipated that bone loss in the axial skeleton (spine) will be reduced through exposure to the low-level mechanical signal.

RESULTS:
Three clinical studies have been completed (post-menopausal women, children with cerebral palsy, young women w/ osteoporosis), each which supports the hypothesis that low-level mechanical signals can benefit the mass and morphology of the musculoskeletal system.

This investigation has been demanifested; therefore, there are no results available from this experiment.

experiment_title: Bone Tissue and Cell Effects of Spaceflight in Young Rhesus Monkey
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous space flight experiments utilizing the rat have shown that bone loss during microgravity exposure is primarily due to diminished bone formation. Few histological studies have been done on non-human primates flown in space, and delays between reentry and surgery in those experiments prevented early post-flight cell activity studies. This experiment was the first to investigate bone cell activities in space-flown primates using histological and cell culture methods.

Approach:

Two flight monkeys and eight ground control monkeys were used in the experiment. Iliac bone biopsies were taken 4-5 months preflight and at recovery. The samples were processed for histological and cell culture analysis.

Results:

A loss of bone mass was observed postflight in the iliac cancellous area. The bone volume to total volume ratio (BV/TV) was 35% lower postflight in the flight animals, while control animals did not show significant changes in this area. The osteoblast surface as a function of bone surface and osteoid thickness, indicators of osteoblast activity, were 40% and 18% lower, respectively, in flight monkeys postflight. Mineral apposition rate and mineral surface as a function of bone surface, mineralizing parameters, were 33% and 32% lower, respectively, in flight monkeys postflight. Osteoclast surface, referenced to bone surface, was unchanged in both flight and control animals. Overall, data suggests that space flight alters iliac bone formation in young rhesus monkeys.
