experiment_title: Packaged Food Mass Reduction Technology Development
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Advanced Food Technology (AFT) project seeks to define a safe, palatable, and nutritious food system to support long-duration space missions beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO). Balancing resources such as water, food preparation time, stowage volume, launch mass, and power requirements is central to defining a functioning food system solution for these missions. Prior AFT work has addressed the need to decrease the mass of the food system, and has recommended means such as reducing the moisture of the food system, increasing the nutrient density of the food system, and streamlining food packaging systems to accomplish this. Building on these recommendations, the objective of this project was to identify technologies required to formulate meal replacement options that would decrease the mass and volume of the food system, as well as decrease the crew time associated with meal preparation. As commercially available meal replacement products are not adequate for NASA needs, this project proceeded by formulating new products that meet the unique requirements of spaceflight beyond LEO. The development of meal replacement options for the packaged space food system were achieved by:
1. Aligning previous studies on nutrition and mass savings to compile the nutritional requirements and consumption guidelines for meal replacement beverages and bars.
2. Developing meal replacement bar(s) meeting nutrition, sensory, and shelf life requirements for space food systems.
3. Developing meal replacement beverage(s) meeting nutrition, sensory, and shelf life requirements for space food systems.
4. Assessing the meal replacement system and creating an implementation plan for the meal replacement options.

APPROACH:
Some accommodations have been made in the product development design to ensure that the project is completed within budget and on schedule. The recipe development of the bars and beverages were baselined from existing commercial bars and beverages rather than starting from new formulas even though significant changes are likely required to meet nutritional needs. Researchers leveraged flavor concepts from existing commercial bar and beverage products. Accelerated shelf life testing was done to assess stability as the project duration is shorter than the desired shelf life. While the ideal sensory evaluation would be a repeated exposure test to ensure acceptability levels were sustained over multiple experiences, the product amounts and the availability of panelists required a one-time sensory evaluation for each product. Upon the completion of this study, an assessment of representative formulated meal replacement options will be provided to stakeholders, in order to offer an understanding of meal replacement technology and associated mass savings.

RESULTS:
The task work began by meal replacement bar and beverage prototypes being developed to meet macronutrient requirements for breakfast and lunch meals, based on current consumption guidelines. Additional food categories were identified as having low nutrient density and commercial food products and new formulations were proposed as replacements. Accelerated shelf life testing was conducted for all products to determine acceptability and general stability. Bars were confirmed to have a 48 to 72 week shelf life while beverages and most category replacements remained stable for 96 weeks. A variety of menus implementing these substitutions in the ISS Standard Menu were proposed and estimated mass savings ranged from 11%-25%, and packaging savings of 16% - 18% when one meal was replaced each day.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) was a unique space flight in which spacecrafts from America and the Soviet Union docked together in space. This presented an opportunity to study cross-contamination of one crew with the medically important microorganisms carried by the other crew. Accordingly, the objectives of this study were to identify and trace all microorganisms of potential medical importance. Medical microbiological analysis of U.S. crewmembers was performed as a part of a larger study, the Microbial Exchange Experiment (AR-002), conducted during the historic ASTP space flight.

APPROACH:
Microbial samples were collected from the three Apollo crewmembers and two Soyuz crewmembers on L-45 days, L-30, L-15, L-7, L-0 (launch day), once during flight, and on recovery days R+0, R+15 and R+30. Backup crewmembers served as experimental controls. Sample collection sites included:

1) A 20 square centimeters area of hair (and scalp) on the top of the head
2) Right and left external auditory canals
3) 20 square centimeters area below hairline at base of neck
4) Internal area of both nostrils
5) The tonsils and posterior pharyngeal vault
6) 20 square centimeters area on right and left palms
7) 20 square centimeters area below the hairline of each axilla
8) 5 centimeter strip from rear to front on right and left inguinal area between legs
9) Area between the two smallest toes of each foot
10) The throat and mouth

Preflight and post flight, microbial specimens were collected from each crewmember using calcium alginate swabs wet with 0.3 millimolar phosphate buffer. Dry calcium alginate swabs were used to sample the tonsils and pharyngeal vault prior to the collection of the gargle specimen.

In-flight samples, consisting of the first six areas outlined above, were obtained from all five flight crewmembers on flight day 3. A specially developed microbial sample collection device was used to collect in-flight samples. This device consisted of a cotton-tipped Teflon swab on a capillary tube containing a conservative fluid, which kept the microorganisms alive. Each swab was housed within an airtight case to prevent desiccation.

Each sample was serially diluted under aseptic conditions and inoculated onto nutrient media. The variety of media, number of plates inoculated and dilution range were selected on the basis of what was required to isolate and quantitate the autoflora present in each sample area. Sabauraud's Dextrose Agar (SAB) plates were incubated at 30 degrees Celsius for five days. Cornmeal, malt-extract, yeast extract (CMMY) agar plates were incubated at 25 degrees Celsius for 7 days and all others were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 48 hours. Following incubation, the resulting aerobic bacterial colonies were categorized and counted with one sample of each morphologically different colony type transferred to nutrient media and stained with Gram's stain. Apollo sample analysis was conducted at the NASA Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, Texas.

RESULTS:
Gram-negative Rods:
Escherichia coli, Enterobacter aerogenes and Proteus mirabilis, members of the enteric bacilli group, were found on the ASTP crewmembers at sites other than the lower intestinal tract. Bacilli species are generally considered of potential medical importance when they are recovered repeatedly, or in large numbers, from sites other than the lower digestive tract.

Escherichia coli is generally accepted as the most reliable evidence of fecal contamination. Outside the intestinal tract it can cause urinary tract infections, peritonitis, gall bladder infections, wound infections, septicemia and enteritis. E. coli was repeatedly recovered from the groin of ASTP subject B and occasionally from the upper respiratory tract of the other two prime crewmembers. In all cases, no medical significance was indicated by the occurrence or quantities of E. coli.

Enterobacter aerogenes is found in the large intestine of man. Its pathogenic significance is similar to that of E. coli. This species was always carried in the nasal and buccal cavities of ASTP subjects B and C and was frequently isolated from two backup crewmembers. E. aerogenes was not spread to ASTP subject A or to other sites on the carrier subject during the flight. In addition, E. aerogenes quantities were not increased postflight.

Proteus mirabilis can cause urinary tract infections, abscesses and gastroenteritis. More often, they cause secondary infections of the middle ear, mastoid process, meninges and urinary tract, as well as in existing wounds. P. mirabilis was carried in low numbers in the nasal passage of ASTP subject A. This species and E. aerogenes provided a good model system for analyzing the response of Gram negative rods to space flight conditions. It has previously been reported that the Gram-negative rod component of the autoflora could change during or following confinement in a closed environment and that this change could result in "dysobacteriosis," such as flooding of an area with a particular species. The ASTP mission had no such effect on the qualitative or quantitative presence of these microorganisms.

Moraxella species are parasites found in the mucous membranes of man that can cause diseases such as conjunctivitis. Although carried in the mouth of ASTP subject C for 45 days preflight, no discernible microbial alteration was demonstrated following the mission.

Acinetobacter calcoaceticus, of minor medical importance, was isolated from multiple sites on ASTP subject B. It did not contribute significantly to the microbial load of Gram-negative rods recovered from ASTP crewmembers.

Four species of Haemophilus were isolated from the oral cavity of each ASTP astronaut. These were H. influenzae, H. haemolyticus, H. parahaemolyticus and H. parainfluenzae. Although each of these species is a common inhabitant of the human mouth, each is a strict parasite, requiring certain growth factors present in blood. H. influenzae is found in lesions and in the upper respiratory tract of carriers. It may be either a primary or a secondary invader. This microorganism is responsible for meningitis, septicemia, conjunctivitis and upper respiratory tract infections, and as a secondary invader in influenza and pertussis cases. H. influenzae was isolated from each crewmember preflight in quantities from 10,000 to 600,000 viable cells/ml of gargle. The post flight loss from two crewmembers and quantitative reduction in contamination of ASTP subject A was contraindicative of a space flight mediated increase in infective potential.

H. haemolyticus and H. parahaemolyticus are often associated with acute pharyngitis when present in high numbers. As with the H. influenzae, the overall incidence and quantitation of H. haemolyticus and H. parahaemolyticus decreased following the ASTP flight. H. parainfluenzae is the least harmful of the four species recovered and is used largely as a marker organism due to its universal appearance.

Candida albicans
Candida albicans has been recovered from astronauts throughout the Apollo and Skylab missions. Because this species can cause serious oral cavity diseases, its presence was carefully monitored. C. albicans was isolated from ASTP subjects B and C at all sampling periods. Data analysis indicates the inflight transfer of C. albicans to ASTP subject A. No such transfer occurred in the backup crew, although C. albicans was carried by one crewman. All of these events demonstrate the importance of this species in space flight. The importance could increase during the in-flight use of antibiotics, because this could cause a loss of competing bacterial species and eventual overgrowth of C. albicans.

Staphylococcus aureus
Although Staphylococcus aureus is a common skin and nasal contaminant, all strains are potential pathogens. S. aureus can cause boils, abscesses, meningitis, furunculosis, pyemia, osteomyelitis, suppuration of wounds and food poisoning. Several studies have indicated increases in the toxigenic activity, virulence and pathogenicity of this species with stressful confinement of the human host. Lesions caused by S. aureus in space flight were important because of their interference with close contact surfaces, such as the tight fitting and abrasive pressure suits. Accordingly, the presence and activity of this species was monitored before and after each space flight. Data from Apollo 13, 14 and 15 missions, and from the Skylab missions confirm in-flight cross contamination with S. aureus.

Data show that each crewmember (flight and backup) carried a different strain of S. aureus. Different strains are expressed as bacteriophage types. One type (52,52A,80,81), carried by ASTP subject C, was transferred to ASTP subject A during flight. Apparently colonization did not ensue, as this strain was not recovered from subject A post flight.

During the ASTP mission, a post flight increase of S. aureus did not occur among the astronaut population, as reported during previous missions, and disease events did not result from its presence.

Total Load of Potential Pathogens
One idea that resulted from previous space flight microbial studies was that crewmembers could suffer "microbial shock" upon return to Earth, and therefore, respond negatively to renewed contact with the potentially pathogenic microorganisms absent in the space flight environment. This was based on the assumption that contact with potential pathogens during space flight would be very limited, resulting in a reduction of immunocompetence. However, there was no demonstrable decrease in the incidence of medically important microorganisms recovered from the astronauts on R+0, a finding which supports earlier results. Therefore, if a reduction in total immunocompetence occurred during the ASTP mission, it was not in response to decreased contact with medically important components of the resident microflora.

Although several potential pathogens were recovered from each of the flight and backup crewmembers before and after flight, no disease events were reported. C. albicans and S. aureus were transferred from one crewmember to another in-flight, but no other medically significant changes in the microbial population were observed.

experiment_title: CNS Control of Rhythms and Homeostasis During Space Flight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Research has shown that the static gravitational field of the Earth and the dynamic cyclic changes caused by the Earthï¿½s rotation are two important selective pressures that shaped the evolution of biological organisms. Many features of an animalï¿½s physiology and behavior are a consequence of both static and dynamic geophysical influences. The circadian timing system (CTS) is one important temporal organizer controlling both physiology and behavior. Animals (including humans) exposed to microgravity exhibit alterations in both CTS function and homeostasis. These experiments examined the effects of space flight on the physiology of the CTS and the homeostatic control system of animals, specifically: 1) circadian rhythms; 2) neural responses of the circadian pacemaker and the sensory pathway for light information from the retina to the CTS; 3) adaptations in homeostatic regulation; and 4) neural changes in hypothalamic nuclei that regulate specific homeostatic functions.

Approach:

Six flight rats and ground control rats (six flight simulated and six vivarium controls) were utilized in one set of experiments. Twelve flight rats and two sets of ground control rats (12 simulated and 12 vivarium) were used in another set of experiments. The rodents were implanted with biotelemetry units to monitor circadian rhythms of body temperature, heart rate, and activity. In addition, eating and drinking was monitored for all rats. To examine the space flight effect on circadian and homeostatic regulation of physiological and behavioral functions, rats were exposed to 24-hour light/dark cycles (LD) consisting of 12 hours of light (approximately 30 lux) followed by 12 hours of darkness. The circadian rhythms and daily mean of rat body temperature, heart rate, feeding, drinking and activity (as a measure of homeostasis) were compared. To examine the space flight effect on free-running circadian rhythm characteristics, a subset of rats was maintained in a constant light condition (LL). Data were analyzed to determine circadian rhythms and results were compared to those of rats exposed to 24 -hour light/dark cycles. To examine the space flight effect on the pattern of c-Fos synthesis in hypothalamic nuclei, and whether it alters the effect of light pulses to induce c-Fos expression in the central nervous system, one group of rats received a one-hour pulse of light during the dark cycle. Another group was not exposed to a pulse of light. The brains and eyes from both groups were then removed and sections of the hypothalamus were histochemically stained for c-Fos reactive neurons.

Results:

The LL flight rats exhibited an increase (p<0.001) in free-running period of body temperature and heart rate relative to controls. The periods returned to preflight values after landing. The LL flight animals maintained internal phase angle relationships between rhythms compared with controls. The LD flight rats remained entrained to the LD cycle; however, they evidenced a pronounced phase delay in body temperature, suggesting an increase in period, compared to controls. The LD flight rats also demonstrated a decrease in body temperature and a change in the daily waveform compared to controls. Both the LD and LL flight rats and controls exhibited an increase in heart rate, suggesting a possible caging effect. Finally, the Flight Day 2 flight animals demonstrated a reduced sensitivity to light as evidenced by highly attenuated c-Fos immunoreactivity in the SCN compared to controls. The sensitivity to light of the flight animals returned to preflight and control levels by Flight Day 14. These findings demonstrate that microgravity affects the circadian clock, including the clockï¿½s ability to maintain temporal organization and to properly entrain to an external LD cycle.

experiment_title: Total System Approach
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA has established the goal of returning human expeditions to the moon and extending exploration to Mars. Extended manned missions of these types require massive quantities of food to be flown into space. This presents two challenges when dealing with a food system. These challenges are maintaining the quality of the food throughout its shelf life which may be in excess of five years, and to assure the mass and volume of the food system are minimized.

A Total System Approach is an operating system that considers each parameter of an overall process and seeks to optimize each of these parameters to maximize the output. In the case of the NASA food system, the output would be a food system with low mass packaging using high barrier packaging materials.

The purpose of this project was to evaluate the processes related to the packaging of the current NASA food system being used for the International Space Station (ISS) and the Shuttle (STS). The evaluation will define the current processing parameters and identify ways to improve the processes. These parameters include those related to sealing, internal atmosphere of the package, and materials. Parallel to this evaluation, a literature review will be conducted in an effort to identify available materials with high potential for long-duration missions, possible packaging defects, and ways to prevent them in the future, ways to improve oxygen elimination, and the impact of these on product shelf life.

Even though the current packaging system processing parameters have been documented, these parameters have not been evaluated from the perspective of improving packaging integrity and mass reduction. This is due largely to the success of the current packaging system using the current high payload vehicles such as the STS and Russian Progress vehicle. Payload for long-duration missions of years rather than months, like ISS missions, will require a greater quantity of food in proportion to other supplies than do the missions of today. Thus, the need for reduced packaging mass becomes critical in order to execute future missions.

APPROACH:
The outline below describes specific processing points that were evaluated. These processing points are parts of the Total Packaging System. Any improvements that can be made in each of these areas may benefit the overall packaging system.

1. Literature review - Identify high potential materials, minimize pinholes and critical defects, optimize Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) flushing , and improve shelf life.
2. Define existing packaging system - food processing
3. Effects of Temperature on Materials - heat seal
4. Effects of temperature variation
5. Seal Width (possible area of mass reduction)
6. Quality - defects , seal Integrity, vacuum
7. Oxygen quantities - MAP flushing quality
8. Using current system
9. Modified system
10. Gases other than nitrogen - Material quality, film, septum, gases (i.e. ppm 02), Packaging design/configuration

RESULTS:
Optimal sealing parameters for each type of material currently being used by the space food system have already been incorporated into the packaging procedures. As new materials are added to the system, it is recommended that the procedure used in the heat seal evaluation be used to determine the optimal seal setting for each material.

Although the seal reduction evaluation showed considerable mass saving, it is not recommend that the seals be reduced below the 3/8” standard. The safety and health of the crew is more important than minimal mass savings when it comes to a mission’s success. Reducing the seals would increase the potential for package failure from contaminants in the seal leading to food spoilage and food borne illness.

The data that was gathered during the Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) evaluation shows that the current methods used in the space food packaging system is inefficient and seals in a significant amount of air in some cases. It is highly recommended that the optimal equipment setting determined during the evaluation be incorporated as soon as possible to improve the quality of food in the space food system.

The gusseted pouch design yielded very good results in making the rehydratable packages easier to produce while minimizing mass, volume, and waste. It reduced the production process from using three pieces of packaging equipment to one. It reduced the packaging from two pouches to one and decreased the total amount of packaging mass by approximately 63%.

The literature review and MAP gas research stated that argon is a viable gas with great potential. Argon gas is more efficient, does not require a vacuum cycle, and can be used with liquid products, like the thermostabilized foods which currently have residual air in the headspace. More research and development is required for the use of argon gas for MAP applications because it is not widely used and requires equipment modifications. Also, it would need to be determined whether the levels of argon released from opened packages in an in enclosed environment would be hazardous to crew health.

experiment_title: Meal Replacement Mass Reduction and Integration Acceptability Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Meal replacement bars have been postulated as a means to decrease mass and volume of the food system. Bars have previously been used to supplement a meal every three days in the Skylab food system, indicating that regular consumption of bars will be acceptable, but commercially available products do not meet the requirements for a meal replacement in the space flight food system. The bar and instant beverage prototypes produced in a preceding validation study demonstrated that a full meal may be replaced and mass may be conserved with the strategy of implementing palatable, nutrient dense, nutritionally balanced, single meal items. However, the frequency with which meals can be replaced by these items, and the resulting amount of mass that may be conserved, is dependent on acceptability to crew and associated physical and psychosocial impacts.

The purpose of this study was to complete the development of a limited variety of true meal replacement options that meet space flight and nutritional requirements and to assess the frequency with which actual meal replacements may be implemented based on impact to satiety and psychosocial subjective ratings of hunger, cravings, mood, and stress pre-meal, post-meal, and pre-sleep daily throughout NASA's Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) mission for all meals, including the standard International Space Station (ISS) diet and the meal replacement bars. The microbiological, nutritional, and acceptable sensory shelf life stability of these meal replacement options stored at ambient temperature over two years will be analyzed.

APPROACH:
Data was collected from four HERA 30 day campaigns, each with four subjects participating in this experiment, totaling n=16 subjects. All subjects filled out various questionnaires. Future exploration missions are mass constrained and as a result the mass of the food system must be reduced by 10%, at the same time maintaining safety, nutrition, and acceptability.

RESULTS:
The purpose of this task was to develop a variety of nutritionally balanced breakfast replacement bars, which meet space flight nutritional, microbiological, sensorial, and shelf-life requirements, while enabling a 10% food mass savings. Seven nutrient-dense meal replacement bars containing approximately 700 kcal per serving have been developed. Bars were evaluated in the HERA to assess the frequency with which actual meal replacement options may be implemented. Feedback from HERA crews show that the bars are generally acceptable but additional flavor development is required to combat the effects of food monotony and aversion. The data suggest that meal replacement on an interrupted schedule (every three days) may be acceptable on a mission up to 30 days, but meal replacement every day may result in reduced food intake, greater body mass loss, and increasingly negative changes in mood, affect, and somatic complaints in some individuals.

experiment_title: Food Fortification Stability Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA has established the goal of traveling beyond low-Earth orbit and extending manned exploration to Mars. The length of proposed Mars missions and the lack of resupply missions increases the importance of nutritional content in the food system, which will need a five year shelf life. The purpose of this research was to assess the stability of vitamin supplementation in traditionally processed space flight foods. It is expected that commercially available fortification nutrients will remain stable through a long-duration exploration mission at sufficient levels if compatible formulation, processing, and storage temperatures are achieved.

APPROACH:
Five vitamins (vitamin E, vitamin K, pantothenic acid, folic acid, and thiamin) were blended into a vitamin premix such that the vitamin concentration per serving equaled 25% of the recommended daily intake after two years of ambient storage. Four freeze-dried foods (Scrambled Eggs, Italian Vegetables, Potatoes Au Gratin, Noodles and Chicken) and four thermostabilized foods (Curry Sauce with Vegetables, Chicken Noodle Soup, Grilled Pork Chop, Rice with Butter) were produced, with and without the vitamin premix, to assess the impact of the added fortification on color and taste and to determine the stability of supplemental vitamins in spaceflight foods.


RESULTS:

The addition of fortification to space flight foods appears to be a plausible mitigation step to inadequate nutrition concerns when considering the ease of adding vitamin premix to the formulations for provisions and the sustainability of the vitamins through the initial processing steps. Vitamin fortification with this premix did not have immediate impact to sensory and color of the food. At this stage, the caveat to introduction is the preciseness to which vitamins can be added. The total amount of vitamin premix required for the largest space production run equates to 10 - 20 grams, a tiny percentage of the formulation. As demonstrated by Italian Vegetables and Grilled Pork Chop, the homogeneity may be difficult to achieve with such small amounts so pouch-to-pouch variability, over-fortification, and under-fortification may ensue. Future analysis should reveal the extent to which this issue should be a concern.

No data sets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Integration of Product, Package, Process, and Environment: A Food System Optimization
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is working to achieve manned space flights beyond low-Earth orbit within the next 25 years. Specifically, the vision includes a manned mission to Mars, which demands that astronauts survive extra-terrestrially for a minimum of three years. The space foods themselves must maintain quality for up to five years so that the food can be prepositioned on the Martian surface prior to crew arrival if necessary. This product life requirement is beyond the capability of the current stabilized food system used on the International Space Station (ISS). Thus, the food system optimization is vital for the viability of all extended duration missions.

Optimizing the food system to achieve a five-year shelf life mitigates the risk of inadequate food system during extended missions. Two causes of an inadequate food system are inadequate nutritional content within the food and inadequate acceptability of the food leading to insufficient intake. This study directly addresses those nutrition and acceptability concerns. Nutritional content and food quality, particularly as products age, are indicative of the food matrix, history, and storage environment. For example, a high availability of oxygen in a food package can be detrimental to product shelf life. The oxidative reactions that cause rancidity also lead to the degradation of vitamin C, vitamin A, folic acid, and thiamin. Likewise, a product subjected to high heat in processing may undergo nonenzymatic browning, but broad vitamin degradation should also be expected after thermal processing. By establishing the proper recipe, process, package, and storage condition, the product is better positioned to sustain nutrition and acceptability over the product life. The chances of performance decrement or illness due to insufficient nutrition or poor food intake decreases with implementation of this integrated food system.

The objective of this experiment is to optimize food product shelf life for the space food system through product recipe adjustments, application of new packiagin and processing technologies, and modified storage conditions. The aims are to:

  1. Summarize the available packaged food technologies that would offer significant barrier or antioxidant property improvements over current space packaging.
  2. Complete a risk-benefit analysis on the usage of the space environment for cold food storage.
  3. Provide recommendations as to the formulation changes, processes, packages, and environments for each space food product that would result in a five-year shelf life for that product.
  4. Identify the technology needs associated with implementing any of the aforementioned integration recommendations.

At the study conclusion, a course to shift the space food products to a five-year shelf life will be proposed. Overall system or category changes will be clearly identified, and products with little chance of meeting the five-year shelf life hurdle will be delineated for replacement or removal from long-duration menus. The required future work to deliver this postulated integration for the food system will be identified.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn't available.

RESULTS:
In this study the space food system was divided into five food category modules – thermostabilized fruits, thermostabilized vegetables, thermostabilized entrees, freeze-dried foods, and baked goods. Through hypothesis-driven experimentation alternative storage, processing, and packaging technologies were evaluated to achieve better sensory, color, texture, and nutrient quality. None of the experiments singularly resulted in five-year shelf life, but important evaluation of the technologies was achieved as indicated in the following key results. Thermostabilized fruits have significant quality issues when stored at ambient temperatures, but colder temperatures alone did not drive enough stabilization in the assessed products to reasonably achieve a five-year shelf life through storage modifications. Pressure-assisted thermostabilization (PATS) resulted in better color and texture of the fruit, but not vitamin stability, as compared to traditional retort. The greatest challenges with thermostabilized vegetables, nutrient degradation and textural softening, were not alleviated by microwave-assisted thermal stabilization (MATS) of the Carrot Coins. The MATS process did produce carrots with brighter color and better texture initially, but due to inadequate packaging barrier, improvements were not sustained over the shelf life of the product. Similarly, the MATS process did not provide a significant, sustained improvement for the evaluated entree, Sweet and Sour Pork. In the freeze-dried food module, the rehydration of freeze-dried items appeared to be most affected by the moisture content of the food. Even slight changes in moisture resulted in noticeable shifts in the amount of water absorbed. Finally, in the baked goods module the evaluation of Butter Cookies demonstrated that the initial development of off-flavors in baked goods may not be the direct result of fat reacting with residual oxygen but the rancidity and chemical activity that comes with higher moisture.

Because the five-year shelf life was not fully achieved, future research will focus on a hurdle approach, a likely stability solution for most of the foods. Cold storage has the capability to slow the chemical reactions that cause color darkening and vitamin degradation as well as slow the enzymatic reactions that lead to textural degradation. Hence, alternative processing technologies, along with colder storage, improve the probability of getting a five-year shelf life for thermostabilized space foods. Opportunities exist to alter freeze-dried product quality by optimizing process parameters and tightening end product specifications. Processing the food precisely and protecting the food against moisture ingress should result in five years of shelf life in freeze-dried items. Moisture control should be the focus area of future baked goods work. Refrigeration or freezing should be considered for baked goods as the colder temperatures slowed moisture and oxygen ingress. Encapsulated vitamins should be considered for all food items.

experiment_title: Case Report Form
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During bed rest studies, the Case Report Form (CRF) provided a mechanism by which nursing and dietary staff, and other subject monitors, could record subject monitoring data. The information was then shared with each of the experiment teams as necessary.
APPROACH:
The CRF was comprised of the following forms:
  • Medical Status and Vitals: a daily record of the subject's vital signs, including blood pressure, respiration rate, pulse, body temperature, and weight. The temperature and ambient humidity of the subject's room were also recorded daily. Height was measured once at the beginning of the pre-test, in-test, and post-test periods.
  • Daily Meal Status: a daily record of the times that breakfast, lunch, and dinner meals were started and completed. Any deviation from the dietary protocol was noted.
  • Stretching Session I and II: a daily record indicating whether two separate stretching sessions were completed during the 24-hour period.
  • Medication Log: a record of all medication given during the campaign, including the dosage, time of administration, medical indication, and outcome.
  • Protocol Deviation Summary: a record of any protocol deviations that might have occurred during the campaign.
  • Symptom Complaint Log: a record of all complaints reported by the subject during the campaign, the measures taken address the issue, and the resolution of the complaint.
  • Urine Collection Log: a record of all urine specimens collected during the campaign, including the weight and specific gravity of each specimen.
  • Water Intake Log: a daily record of water intake by the subject.
  • Fecal Collection Log: a record of the date, time, and weight of each bowel movement.
  • Emesis Log: a record of each emesis episode (if any), for the Artificial Gravity Pilot Study, including the measured weight of the emesis.

experiment_title: Development of Spaceflight Foods with High Microbial Concentrations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Strict microbiological standards have been established for the thermostabilized, freeze dried, low moisture, and intermediate moisture foods that make up the current space flight food system. However, for long-duration missions, it may be prudent to consider space food items with higher microbial counts. The feasibility of including shelf-stable probiotics and establishing appropriate handling procedures for extraterrestrially grown and processed foods needs to be determined in order to re-evaluate microbiological guidelines for the space flight food system.

A space habitat food system that involves growing and processing fresh produce in situ (bioregenerative foods) and launching payloads of unprocessed grain, legumes, and seeds (bulk foods) is being explored as an avenue to longer shelf life. However, these foods could contain a high concentration of microorganisms with respect to current microbiological standards for microbial load of space flight foods. With mounting evidence of a link between the consumption of probiotic microorganisms and health benefits, including increased immune function and cancer prevention, the inclusion of probiotics in the space flight food system is also being considered. The potential to impact crew member health through functional foods is yet unexplored but highly relevant to risks associated with space travel. As with extraterrestrial food processing, probiotic foods and supplements fall outside of the current microbiological standards for space flight.

The purpose of this study was to perform a review of relevant information to assess the feasibility of developing a microbially-safe, space flight food system that includes extraterrestrial processing and/or probiotics. If deemed feasible, guidance for standards of microbial acceptability and appropriate testing methods for foods/supplements will be recommended. The study proceeded as follows:
1. Determine the potential of microbial load from bioregenerative produce.
2. Determine the current microbial strains and uses of live cultures in shelf stable foods.
3. Compare levels of microbial load in these foods/supplements to current requirements and assess the level of additional risk.
4. Investigate current literature and commercial operations to provide guidance in establishing microbiological requirements and testing methods for foods with high and diversified microbial concentrations.

APPROACH:
Current space flight food requirements are inadequate for microbial monitoring associated with crop production, the use of bulk foods, and subsequent processing and handling, as well as foods with inherently high microbial concentrations, such as probiotics, which may be beneficial for crew health. This review provided an initial investigation into (a) the potential of microbial load from bioregenerative produce, (b) the current microbial strains and uses of live cultures in shelf stable foods, (c) a comparison of levels of microbial load in these foods/supplements to current requirements and an assessment of additional risk, and (d) an investigation of current literature and commercial operations to provide guidance in establishing microbiological requirements and testing methods for foods with high and diversified microbial concentrations.

RESULTS:
The evidence from this review indicates a need for further research to determine the procedures necessary for growing and processing regenerative produce and development of specific cleaning methods to mitigate microbiological risks. In addition, data mining performed during this review identified potential benefits for the use of food products with high microbial concentrations. Specifically, this review has performed an extensive market survey to generate a comprehensive list of potential probiotic products, which should be evaluated in future research to determine preferred probiotic formulations for space flight. Future research would also determine the specific microbial testing procedures for those formulations and assess the risk of adding the formulation to the food system.

experiment_title: Stabilized Foods for Use in Extended Spaceflight: Preservation of Shelf-Life, Nutrient Content and Acceptability
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to develop shelf stable and highly acceptable food with increased nutrient (vitamins) stability for extended space missions utilizing innovative processing and packaging technologies. The design of feeding and nutritional strategies for multi-year, non-resupplied flights is an undertaking requiring substantial research and development. This investigation aimed to yield strategies for the development of extremely stable, nutrient-dense foods, and the development of packaging materials compatible with new quality-preserving sterilization techniques.

APPROACH:
There were two research areas. For the first area, investigators formulated, tested, and optimized the quality and nutrient content of a range of fortified shelf-stable foods. The focus was on extruded/pressed low-water activity bar-type products. Advances in innovative pre-treatment technologies (encapsulation) for vitamins was assessed, as well as synergy with matrix chemical character.

For the second area, different packaging technologies was investigated with research focused on the interaction of packaging material with various innovative sterilization processes such as microwave heating, irradiation, and high pressure treatment. The availability of highly nutritious and health-promoting food is a factor that is a significant prerequisite for prolonged space travel.

RESULTS:
Vitamin levels in relatively low and high fat content compressed bars and dispersed drink mixes, fortified with twice the Space Flight Requirement for vitamins A, B1, B9, C, and E, were analyzed after three years storage at 70F. Vitamins in relatively low fat products had been encapsulated in a lipophilic coating; vitamins in relatively high fat products had been encapsulated in a starch-based coating. Vitamin contents were measured by Covance Co., with n=6.

Losses for the vitamins after three years storage at 70F are as follows.

  1. Vitamin A: low and high fat bars= 15 % (both); low and high fat beverage bases= 17% and 16%, respectively.
  2. Vitamin B1: low and high fat bars= 23% and 8.5%, respectively; low and high fat beverage bases= 4.8 and 23%, respectively.
  3. Vitamin B9: low and high fat bars= 26% and 21%, respectively; low and high fat beverage bases= 30% and 26%, respectively.
  4. Vitamin C: low and high fat bars= 11% and 5.7%, respectively; low and high fat beverage bases= 4.8% and 7.4%, respectively.
  5. Vitamin E: low and high fat bars= 4.9% and 3.7%, respectively; low and high fat beverage bases= 4.6% and 8.4%, respectively.
Results show that vitamin loss susceptibility after three years storage, on average, followed the sequence, B9 > A > B1 > C > E.

experiment_title: Countermeasures for Neurobehavioral Vulnerabilities to Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Risk assessment of the biological consequences of living in the space radiation environment represents one of the highest priority areas of NASA radiation research. Astronauts will be spending more time in space and ultimately will venture to the Moon, Mars, and other destinations outside of the protection of Earth’s magnetosphere. It is essential that methods are developed to detect behavioral changes induced by radiation exposures and that potential strategies and countermeasures are developed for ameliorating radiation damage, with the long-term goal being the prevention of those sequelae that impact astronaut health and mission success.

To this end, the proposed research will focus on determining the effectiveness of biomedical countermeasures for mitigating the effects of space radiation on the human central nervous system (CNS) function. The proposed studies will assess the effectiveness of a number of pharmacologic compounds in ameliorating the deleterious effects of radiation exposure on neurobehavioral function. This work will provide animal performance data obtained with an animal analog of the human Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) that is employed on the International Space Station (ISS) and in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) for human risk assessments via quantification of sustained attention (e.g., ‘vigilance’ or ‘readiness to perform’ tasks). The proposed research will thus use an animal model that employs neurobehavioral tests identical or homologous to those currently in use in human models of risk assessment.

APPROACH:
Within this framework, the first aim of this research will be to assess the degree to which likely biomedical countermeasures can mitigate the known effects of space radiation on cognitive neurobehavioral functions relevant to astronaut mission performance. Rodents will be trained in tests analogous to human neurobehavioral tests (e.g., a rodent version of the human PVT). Performance measures will include assessments of general motor function and speed, inhibitory control (“impulsivity”), attention, motivation, and basic sensory function. Separate groups of rats will be trained until stable performances are obtained, following which they will be transferred to NASA’s Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) for radiation exposure to protons (25 and 100 cGy, 150 MeV/n) encountered in the space radiation environment, and then returned to Johns Hopkins for extended post-exposure testing to 1) identify neurobehavioral performance deficits over durations similar to a long-term exploratory mission, and 2) assess the effectiveness of a number of pharmacologic compounds to mitigate the deficits.

The second aim will be to assess the mechanisms of action of effective radioprotective countermeasures on the CNS by employing different types of potential mitigating and protective compounds. These will include compounds that directly alter dopaminergic (DA) signaling by binding to the dopamine transporter protein (DAT; e.g., amphetamine), compounds that directly alter dopaminergic signaling by binding to one or more receptors from the D2 receptor family (e.g., aripiprazole), and compounds that indirectly alter dopamine levels through another mechanism (e.g., norepinephrine reuptake inhibition, atomoxetine). Two FDA-approved radioprotective compounds that have mechanisms of action not specifically DA-related will also be employed (the putative DNA repair targeting drug cholorquine, and the hemopoietic growth factor erythropoietin) to provide assessments of alternative mechanisms of action.

RESULTS:
The results for this experiment are currently not available.

experiment_title: Simulated Space Radiation and Weightlessness: Vascular-Bone Coupling Mechanisms to Preserve Skeletal Health
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts may develop bone loss in space as a result of environmental challenges such as exposure to weightlessness and ionizing radiation. Oxidative stress results from an imbalance between production of free radicals and the ability of cells to counteract their harmful effects at the molecular level. To date, little is known about the combined effects of weightlessness and space radiation on the musculoskeletal system, the cardiovascular system, and how these two systems interact in maintaining bone health. The overall objectives of this study were to define mechanisms and risks of bone loss in space, to explore the relationship between microvessel function and bone loss due to weightlessness and radiation exposure, and to help develop effective ways to prevent bone loss.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the functional and structural consequences of prolonged weightlessness and space radiation (simulated spaceflight) for bone and skeletal vasculature in the context of bone cell function and oxidative stress.
  2. Determine the extent to which an anti-oxidant protects against weightlessness and space radiation-induced bone loss and vascular dysfunction.
  3. Determine how low dose space radiation influences later skeletal recovery from prolonged weightlessness.
  4. Determine if transient treatment with countermeasures protects from bone loss caused by weightlessness and radiation during subsequent aging.

APPROACH:
16-weeks old, male mice were exposed to low linear-energy-transfer (LET) protons or high-LET 56Fe ions using either low or high doses of radiation at NASA’s Space Radiation Lab. Five weeks or one year after irradiation, tissues were harvested and analyzed by microcomputed tomography for cancellous microarchitecture and cortical geometry. Marrow-derived, adherent cells were grown under osteoblastogenic culture conditions.

RESULTS:
Investigators discovered that simulated weightlessness causes decrements in both slow-turnover cortical bone tissue and high turnover cancellous tissue, whereas ionization radiation (0.5-2Gy) causes decrements only in cancellous tissue. Whereas the radiation-induced deficits in skeletal microarchitecture diminish over a period of six to seven months due to age-related bone loss in control animals, dysfunction in cell populations persists. HZE but not protons or gamma cause defects in osteoblastogenesis from bone marrow derived stem cells and progenitors. This defect can be attributed to persistent deficits in progenitor cell proliferation and colony growth, whereas the capacity to differentiate into osteoblast-like cells and mineralize an extracellular matrix (the hallmark of osteoblasts) is retained.

In addition, bones from HZE-irradiated animals can respond later to anabolic loading stimulus with improved bone formation, although there is some evidence from analyses by dynamic histomorphometry and gene expression that there may be persistent defects in osteoprogenitor cell populations localized to regions adjacent to the periosteal surfaces of bone tissue. Together, these findings on marrow-derived progenitors and periosteal cell behavior lead investigators to predict that fracture healing and perhaps other wound healing processes that depend mesenchymal stem cells derived from the marrow and/or periosteal bone surfaces are deficient after exposure to HZE at space relevant doses. This prediction is both consistent with a few reports in the scientific literature and may have relevance to regenerative medicine in space, thus represents a potentially important area for future study. With respect to prevention, either mechanical stimulation (resembling vigorous exercise) or feeding a diet containing dried plum, can improve bone structure despite prior exposure to HZE. In contrast, treatment with antioxidants that have displayed at least some radioprotective properties (lipoic acid injections, anti-oxidant cocktail, or treatment with an anti-inflammatory (Ibuprofen)) failed to prevent radiation-induced bone loss. These findings imply treatment with antioxidants alone are unlikely to prove fully protective to the skeleton exposed to ionizing radiation.

experiment_title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) after Exposure to Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In microgravity, bones and muscles are not used as they are on Earth. As many studies have shown, this altered use results in calcium loss, degeneration of the skeleton, lengthening of the spine by expansion of the intervertebral discs, change in spinal bone marrow composition and muscle atrophy. Bedrest patients on earth show this same musculo-skeletal response with the exception of bone marrow alterations.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is one method that can be used to measure the resulting muscular and skeletal changes. MRI is a safe, non-invasive scanning technique that uses a large magnet and low frequency radio waves to form an image by reading the amount of hydrogen in an area of the body. These images can be used to examine soft tissues in the body, as well as determine muscle volume, spinal bone marrow mass and cross-sectional area of intervertebral discs.

The objectives of this investigation were to use MRI procedures (1) to measure the muscle volumes of the calf, thigh, back and neck of the Mir astronauts and cosmonauts before and after flight; (2) to determine and compare muscle volume changes on the day of landing and four days after landing; (3) to determine the change in intervertebral disc size in the lumbar spine after flight, and determine the rate of recovery after return to gravity; and (4) to determine the bone marrow cellularity of the third lumbar vertebra (L3) before and after flight.

Findings from this investigation will lead to improved therapies that will facilitate the recovery of patients on Earth who have been bedridden for extended periods and will aid in the development of countermeasures allowing longer duration space flights.

APPROACH:
All crewmembers of the NASA 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 missions, as well as the Mir 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25 missions participated as subjects in this study. MRI scans were performed 30 and 60 days before launch, on the day of landing (U.S. crewmembers only), and 4, 14 and 30 days after landing on all crewmembers.

Imaging was performed using a 1.5 Tesla Siemens Magnetom MRI system (1.5 Tesla denotes the strength of the magnet used for the test) with various coils, including spine, Helmholz neck and whole body coils. These coils are the antenna of the MRI system that broadcast the radio frequency signal to the patient and/or receive the return signal to form an image. Specific coils are used to image different parts of the body; for example, Helmholz coils are used to image the cervical spine and muscles in the neck.

To begin the test, crewmembers were to lie down on a padded table, which would enter the magnet. Crewmembers were recumbent for approximately 10-15 minutes before beginning the test to minimize the effects of fluid shifts caused by lying down after standing. The order in which the measurements were made was kept the same for each crewmember from one imaging session to the next. The normal order was L3 spectroscopy, and then imaging of the intervertebral discs, then differential muscle volume measurements of the back muscles, neck muscles, thigh muscles and calf muscles.

A number of variables are used to acquire MRI images, including echo time, echo sequence, repetition time and matrix size. The echo time is the amount of time between magnetic pulses. Echo sequences are the number of magnetic pulses used to create an image. The repetition time is the amount of time between repetitions of the echo sequence, and the matrix size determines the resolution quality, or clearness, of the image.

Muscle volume of calf, thigh, lower back and neck:
For imaging of the calf and thigh muscles, the feet of the subject were positioned in a holder during the test to minimize movement and insure repositioning. The portion of the leg being imaged was suspended, while the non-imaged portion was supported with foam supports. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portion of the leg to remove artifacts in the image, which arise from parts of the body outside the imaging region but near the edge of the gradient coils.

For the thigh and calf muscles of NASA 2, 3, 4 and 7 and Mir 21, 22, and 23 crewmembers, 32, 1 centimeter slices (0.8 centimeter slices for NASA 5, NASA 6, Mir 24, and Mir 25) with a 0.2 millimeter gap between slices were obtained using an echo time equal to 10 milliseconds (msec), a repetition time of 800 msec and a 256 x 512 matrix.

Every tissue in the human body has its own spin-spin relaxation time (T2) value. Therefore, it can be used to differentiate between different tissue types (e.g. fat and muscle) and changes due to tissue changes (e.g. edema in sore muscles). Calf muscle spin-spin relaxation time (T2) was measured by rescanning the calf region using the same receiver gain at an echo time of 50 msec. Spin-spin relaxation times for each muscle pixel were calculated by comparing the image intensity between the echo times of 10 msec and 50 msec. T2 for a particular muscle was obtained by averaging the T2 for all pixels within that muscle.

For the back muscles, 20, 0.5 centimeter slices centered on the third lumbar vertebra were obtained using a spine coil and a 10 msec echo time, an 800 msec repetition time and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the neck muscles, a similar protocol was used with 32, 3 millimeter thick slices, and a Helmholtz neck coil in place of the spine coil.

Lumbar spine disc size and lumbar spine length:
To measure lumbar spine intervertebral disc size and lumbar spine length, subjects were positioned within the MRI machine so that the imaging area was centered within the third lumbar vertebra, determined from a sagittal scout view. A coronal scout image was used to position a 1 centimeter slice of interest down the center of the spinal column.

Imaging sequences of the lumbar spine varied between missions. During NASA 2 and 3 and Mir 21 and 22, two acquisitions of a four echo, spin echo sequence were obtained using echo times of 20, 45, 72 and 106 msec and a repetition time of 1 second.

For NASA 4, 5, 6 and 7 and Mir 23, 24 and 25, two different sequences were performed. First, one gradient echo sequence was obtained with an echo time of 7 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. Second, two single echo, spin echo sequences were obtained using echo times of 10 and 25 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. The matrix size for spinal images of all NASA-Mir crewmembers was 256 x 256.

Disc area was obtained for intervertebral discs in the lower back (T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4 and L4-5) from the number of pixels in each image. A phantom was also imaged during each imaging session to correct for any changes in pixel size.

To measure spine length, templates (small sub-images) were taken from the first preflight images, each containing a spinal disc. Each of these was registered (a mathematical best fit of position) for each subsequent measurement. The change in separation from the preflight positions to postflight positions was the change in spine length.

Bone marrow content (L3 spectroscopy):
To measure the fat to water ratio in vertebral bone marrow, volume selective proton spectroscopy was performed on a 15mm x 15mm cubic volume of interest in the third lumbar vertebra (L3) using a surface receive coil. Spectroscopy uses absorption, emission or scattering of electromagnetic radiation by atoms or molecules to qualitatively or quantitatively study the atoms or molecules. The Gradient Inversion Spectroscopy (GIS) technique was used to acquire spectra at echo times equal to 12, 18, 24 and 30 msec with a repetition time of 2 sec. Images were corrected for T2 weighting by exponential extrapolation of the spectra obtained at various echo times. Non-linear peak fitting was performed on the final spectrum to separate the water peak and different fat peaks from the background and to calculate their relative intensities. Bone marrow cellularity was determined from the fat to water ratio. T2 of the fat and water component was determined by fitting the decay of fat and water peaks with an exponential function.

Back pain questionnaire:
The crew also filled out questionnaires to document the frequency, severity and location of back pain or discomfort during the first 10 days of flight and the first 10 days after flight.

RESULTS:
Muscle volume:
The muscle volume changes as a percentage of the mean baseline volume in 16 crewmembers after long-duration flight were determined. To calculate percent change from baseline, the first postflight measurement at 0 to 4 days after landing was used. These flights ranged from 115 to197 days in duration. Paired t-tests of the average preflight volume to the first postflight measurement showed significant decreases for all regions except the neck muscles. The values, expressed as a percent of baseline (%±SD), for the 16 subjects were: anterior leg, 85.5±2.9%; gastrocnemius, 83.1±4.4%; soleus, 83.2±4.4%; quadriceps, 89.9±4.4%; hamstrings, 87.3±3.4%; intrinsic back, 84.1±5.8%; psoas, 95.6±6.1%; neck, 100.9±8.3%. A linear regression of the percent loss against flight duration showed no significant slope for any of the regions suggesting that the volume changes reached a new steady state by or before about four months of flight.

After landing, each of the flight crew were measured at multiple time points. Results indicate that muscle volume recovers at variable rates depending on the region, but generally have returned to baseline by 30-60 days postflight.

A comparison of percent change in muscle volume versus the size of the muscle before flight showed poor or no correlation for any of the muscle groups except the hamstrings, r=0.71. This was also true for when change in muscle volume was correlated with total weight or total body lean mass. This indicates that the suggestion that the percentage loss might be greater in those individuals with greatest mass before flight is not supported by the results in this study.

There was no significant correlation between the percentage loss in spinal bone mineral content and intrinsic back muscle volume during flight (n=12). However, when 12 bed rest subjects, half who performed an exercise countermeasure and the remaining who served as controls, were added to the flight data, the correlation was significant (r=0.61, p<0.0009). This may indicate that muscle atrophy might provide an early indicator for the extent of bone loss.

Comparison of flight results with bed rest data shows that the changes in the leg muscles during flight were generally less than bed rest. This is likely a consequence of the exercise countermeasure employed during flight since the bed rest data did not include exercise. The back muscles, however, showed greater loss during flight compared to bed rest, which may be reasonable, considering that the back muscles are active to a substantial degree in bed rest.

Muscle T2:
No muscle T2 measurements were possible on landing day. Therefore, the initial postflight measurements were obtained several days after landing which would obviously include significant ambulation prior to the first T2 measurement. The general pattern, however, is that T2 tends to be increased relative to baseline at the first postflight measurement and was almost always elevated at R+14 compared to the initial postflight measurement or baseline. By 30-70 days postflight the T2 decreased toward baseline in all cases where these measurements were available. The general response pattern is consistent with postflight muscle swelling associated with muscle damage.

Muscle Swelling:
Results show that muscle swelling can occur during the early reambulation period after landing. A similar pattern is seen following reambulation after bed rest. The largest changes were in the calf, particularly the gastrocnemius. The explanation for this swelling could represent rehydration of the muscle following dehydration of the muscle in microgravity. However, the muscle T2 postflight were invariably elevated above baseline, increased further for several weeks after flight and then returned toward the original baseline. These changes along with the reported sore muscles postflight would suggest muscle damage. The large change in the intrinsic back muscles of one crewmember has not been seen previously and may represent postflight swelling.

Intervertebral Disc:
Data indicate only minor spine lengthening and disc expansion by the time measurements were obtained on landing day. Measurements were made within 2-4 hours after landing with some walking and sitting up on a stretcher by the crewmember before testing. By 2-4 days postflight, slight residual expansion remained which by 2 weeks was back to baseline. Importantly, no long-term residual changes in disc size were found following these flights.

Proton Spectroscopy:
Comparison of NASA-Mir data to the LMS 17-day mission suggests that although the postflight T2 tends to increase as in the shorter LMS flight followed by a gradual return to baseline levels, there appears to be some differences. The first postflight T2 values were significantly reduced relative to preflight values; this was not detected after the shorter LMS flight. There is some evidence that the degree of decrease in the cellular bone marrow T2 is correlated with the percent change in spinal bone mineral density. Two distinct patterns exist. Postflight, some individuals begin below baseline and simply return to values close to baseline, while others like the LMS crew increase above baseline and gradually return to baseline over a period of several months.

Back Pain:
Out of 17 crewmembers (including one German guest cosmonaut on the Mir 97 mission), 9 (53%) indicated that they experienced back pain or discomfort during the flight. Generally, this occurred in the lower lumbar region during the first week or two of flight. The pain was typically described as "can be ignored," lasted a few hours to several days in duration and was most noticeable during or after resting. In one crewmember, it was most noticeable during exercise or applying bungies. Some crewmembers indicated that bending or application of massage seemed to relieve the pain. Postflight 8 of 17 (47%) crewmembers reported significant discomfort for some or all 10 days that monitoring was reported following flight. There were a number of cases where written reports were not available or were not filled out. Whenever possible, the crew were asked about their experience during and after flight. When no information was available these were treated as being negative reports and therefore, the incidence rates above may underestimate actual rates.

Conclusion:
There are measurable decreases in muscle volume during flight, which presumably represents muscle atrophy. These changes appear to be maximized within the first 4 months of flight. This degree of atrophy may indicate that bone loss may also reach a maximum probably at or around this same point, i.e., the rates of loss are different, but it seems reasonable that the degree of loss may be similar at the equilibrium point. If this turns out to be the case, muscle atrophy might be used as an early indicator of bone loss. Compared to bed rest without exercise, the inflight muscle changes are less, except in the back muscles. Recovery in all muscle groups is complete within the first 30-60 days after return to Earth, similar to recovery after bed rest. There are muscle volume and T2 changes during the first days and weeks after return from space flight compatible with muscle damage. We did observe small, but no long-term changes in disc size following these flights. There was a significant decrease in the T2 of the cellular component of the bone marrow of L3 which either increases to baseline during the first few weeks after landing or increases above baseline and subsequently returns to baseline over several months. No significant changes in the T2 of the lipid fraction of the same bone marrow or in the cellular to lipid fraction was seen. About 50% of the crewmembers reported some back pain during flight, however, the duration and magnitude of this problem seems not to be of major concern for long-duration flight. A more important consideration may be the potential for significant injury/pain after flight since about 47% reported significant postflight discomfort lasting for a number of days to weeks. This may be an important consideration after lengthy flights in microgravity followed by a visit to a planet that has significant gravity.

experiment_title: 3D Tissue Models for Study of Intercellular Signaling Stimulated by High Energy Particles
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex, unique radiation environment including energetic protons and charged particles from galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events. Although these radiations can result in significant cumulative doses to astronauts during long-duration space flights, most exposures occur at low fluences, so that particle traversals through an astronaut's body are well separated in tissue location and time. Under such conditions, bystander effects, where unirradiated cells express biological changes in response to signals from irradiated cells, have increased significance. The overall hypothesis of this investigation is that increased oxidative stress caused by charged particle-stimulated intercellular signaling-- bystander effects-- in cells and tissues creates a microenvironment conducive to altered carcinogenic processes; responses can be triggered at very low doses, with the lowest effective dose depending on radiation type, but the magnitude of the response being radiation quality-independent. Previous studies showed that bystander responses can be induced in unirradiated cells in a 3D skin model, including after low fluences of protons or iron ions, and that in 3D both irradiated and bystander cells are more resistant to induction of DNA damage than cells in monolayer. Different epithelial tissues can differ in their 3D architecture and, therefore, might be expected to have different radiation and bystander responses. This project proposes to compare bystander signaling in 3D models of colon with previous data for the skin epithelial model. The specific aims for this study are:
  1. Develop a 3D model of colonic epithelium for testing effects of low fluences of charged particles in comparison with the responses in our previously developed 3D skin model.
  2. Quantify DNA damage, apoptosis, differentiation and proliferation in the 3D model of colonic epithelium exposed to low fluences of charged-particles
  3. Determine whether the bystander response in the colon model has the same radiation dose and LET dependence as the skin model, and whether reactive oxygen species (ROS) play a role in the intercellular signaling. <\li>

APPROACH:
The Caco2 colon cancer cell line was chosen for initial studies since this line has been used as a model for colon epithelium in published literature, including one radiation study. The 3D colon model was established with the CaCo2 cells as the epithelium and AG01522 normal human fibroblasts as the stromal cells embedded in collagen. Cells were irradiated with X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With the cells in monolayer, a transwell insert co-culture system was used to assess DNA damage in both irradiated cells and unirradiated bystander cells sharing medium with the irradiated cells.

RESULTS:
Data show induction of micronuclei (MN; surrogate for chromosome aberrations) in Caco2 cells 72 h after irradiation with X-rays, 1 GeV protons or 1 GeV/n silicon or iron ions. In all cases, there is a large, radiation dose-dependent increase in MN in irradiated cells, but importantly, there is up to a 3-fold increase in the fraction of unirradiated bystander cells having MN after co-culture with irradiated cells. Additional studies using induction of foci of the DNA repair-related protein 53BP1, a surrogate for DNA double-strand breaks, as an endpoint have been done in irradiated and bystander Caco2 cells after exposure to X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With all radiation types, in the irradiated population, the fraction of cells with foci is substantially increased at 1 h, is maximum 5 h after irradiation, then decreases substantially by 24 h. In the bystander cell population, the increase in fraction of cells with foci is slower, not being maximal until 12 h after irradiation and the start of co-culture, and still being elevated at 24 h. The maximum fraction of bystander cells with increased level of foci is about 3-fold higher than in untreated cells, similar to the magnitude of bystander effect seen using MN as endpoint. This delayed development and removal of damage in bystander cells compared to irradiated cells is similar to the responses seen in the 3D skin model.

Comparing the 2D and 3D data in the CaCo2 cells suggests several findings: First, in 3D there are fewer foci per cell, including in untreated samples, so a cut-off of only 1 focus per cell for analysis was used in 3D compared to 5 foci per cell minimum for scoring in 2D. If the 5 foci per cell cut-off had been used in the 3D samples, the fraction of cells with damage would be much lower in 3D, consistent with the finding with the skin model. Second, the time courses for development and disappearance of foci in 3D are similar to those in 2D, with cells in both architectures showing the delay in bystander responses compared to responses in irradiated cells. The model has been extended to use normal human colon epithelial cells (FHC cells) in both 2D and 3D studies. The early data had some scatter, but the trends show that in monolayer, 53BP1 foci appear to be maximal at 5 h after irradiation in both irradiated and bystander FHC cells, but replicate experiments are needed to confirm this finding. Furthermore, although these cells grow very slowly, 3D constructs in which the FHC cells form a single epithelial layer on the basement material containing fibroblasts, consistent with the single-layered colon epithelium have been successfully produced.

experiment_title: International Space Station (ISS) Urine Monitoring System (UMS) Test Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Science teams using the International Space Station (ISS) Human Research Facility (HRF) identified a need for an automated void volume measurement and sample acquisition system for long-term ISS science applications. A similar system has been used on Shuttle and, prior to installation on ISS, the design of the ISS UMS) was required to first undergo integrated test operations in microgravity on a Shuttle flight.

The ISS UMS is an upgrade to the previous Shuttle UMS that is capable of:

  1. collecting and accurately measuring void volume,
  2. separating urine from air, and
  3. allowing acquisition of individual, uncontaminated urine samples.

Although ISS UMS is a design upgrade, all existing Shuttle and ISS Waste Collector Subsystem (WCS) interfaces remain unchanged. ISS UMS was designed to operate in conjunction with the airflow of the WCS of both the Shuttle and ISS. The hardware consisted of two modules, the Avionics Module (AM) and the Mechanical Module (MM). The AM includes electrical components and the primary crew interfaces, a color-coded keypad and Liquid Crystal Diode (LCD) screen. The MM contains a liquid/air separator, a motor, solenoid valves, fluid plumbing and the sample acquisition port. While deployed for the Shuttle test flight, the MM was targeted to reside in the Orbiter Side hatch, next to the Waste Management Compartment (WMC). The AM was capable of being temp-stowed in any location convenient to the WMC. Similarly, the eventual location on ISS was targeted to be the Node 3 Waste & Hygiene Compartment (WHC).

It was expected that the innovative design features within the ISS UMS would result in very accurate and repeatable micturition measurements suited for science applications on ISS. The objectives were to:

  1. Functionally test the effectiveness of the ISS UMS hardware in solving the following operational issues of the previous shuttle UMS; liquid carry-over between cycles, inaccurate void volume measurements, and cross-contamination in void samples
  2. Obtain crew insight as to the effectiveness and ease of use of the new design
  3. Validate extensive 1g development testing and provide a basis for the development of future urine analysis capability upgrades

APPROACH:
Inflight the crew de-stowed and set up the hardware and performed an initial air purge, followed by a validation sequence. The crew utilized the UMS for nominal use and performed void collections and sampling. After testing, the hardware was disassembled and stowed.

RESULTS:
Successful verification of ISS UMS hardware will result in eventual installation on ISS for science applications. A safe, very accurate and reliable means of obtaining representative urine samples and total void volume measurements from ISS crewmembers is essential to human research. The ISS UMS measurements are a vital component in calculating bone calcium loss and other metabolic changes that occur as a function of microgravity exposure duration and microgravity countermeasure evaluations.
