experiment_title: Inner Ear Otoconia Response in Mice to Micro- and Hyper-gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Does exposure to long-duration spaceflight lead to neural structural alterations and does this remodeling impact cognitive and functional performance? This knowledge gap (SM26) recognizes an inherent risk to crew health and performance due to neural structural plasticity associated with space flight. Otoconia crystals of the mammalian inner ear otolith sensory organs are critical for spatial orientation and balance. Because of their normal biomineralization and their density is related to neural sensitivity, exposure to long-duration spaceflight puts them at risk to structural remodeling. A widely considered mechanism by which the nervous system responds to a change in gravity load is a change in the weight-lending otoconia. When subjected to weightlessness, it is argued the organism counters the loss of gravity load by increasing calcium carbonate production, thereby seen as a means to increase the "system gain". It is hypothesized that weightlessness over a significant period of time triggers a compensatory mechanism that leads to a constructive process of ion deposition and an increase of otoconia mass. Upon entry to a novel gravity environment and later return to Earth, this response is maladaptive and will have a severely negative impact on cognitive and functional performance of the crew during the mission and on health and wellness at home. Although not mutually exclusive, it is also hypothesized that long-duration hypergravity exposure leads to an ablative process and loss of otoconia mass. On Earth the clinical syndrome of canalithiasis, the most common single cause of vertigo, is now clearly biomechanical in origin and occurs when otoconia or fragments from them are displaced from their normal location. Despite this significant morbidity, the potential exists for structural remodeling of otoconia by the intensity and duration of gravity loading to which the animal is exposed.

APPROACH:
To address this risk there is one specific aim, namely to specify the structural integrity of otoconia as a result of short- and long-duration exposures to altered gravity conditions. Until recently, mammalian studies were confined to space missions and ground-based centrifugation studies of relatively short duration, and as a result studies have reached mixed conclusions. The Mouse Drawer System (MDS) housed mice on the International Space Station (ISS) for 91 days, roughly 20% of the lifespan of a mouse in the wild. Preliminary results of inner ears of MDS flight mice showed a dramatic alteration of symmetry and topographical surface features of otoconia; controls were normal in appearance. Subsequent studies have acquired otoconia samples from: 1) equivalent mouse models of MDS mission to 2G centrifugation and hindlimb unloading for 91 days in two separate series; and 2) inner ear samples of mice flown on the 13-day STS-133 and -135 missions. Preliminary results of inner ears of 2G mice also showed a dramatic alteration in topographical features of otoconia, but in the opposite sense in support of this experiment’s hypothesis. The proposed research is a one year ground-based study from existing tissues and addresses fundamental mechanisms of neural compensation that directly effect crew health and performance during the exploration missions and on return to Earth. We will apply scanning and transmission electron microscopy and microstructural-crystallographic techniques to evaluate the possible mechanisms of otoconia restructuring in response to gravity loading. This experiment seeks to answer the following questions: are there structural changes in otoconia as a result of experimental altered gravity conditions? If so, is the change due to a constructive or destructive process? And, is the process dependent on length of exposure to altered gravity loading? It is anticipated that the study will produce both a path toward quantification of a crew health and performance risk and provide the basis for valid ground-based studies for countermeasure development.

RESULTS:
The overall findings of this study provide a more comprehensive understanding of the structural integrity of otoconia in response to adverse consequences of weightlessness, provide a time frame in which structural changes are expected, and identify possible fundamental mechanism(s) of plasticity used by the nervous system. We are still pursuing other techniques in the short term to enhance our imaging of the otoconia in the different mice. Together with existing data our current findings indicate that the initial response to weightlessness is likely a change in synaptic organization due to unweighting of the otoconia mass and a change in mechanical linkage between otoconia and hair cell stereocilia, and the influence on otoconia integrity is relatively minor. The initial responses to microgravity are rapid and are likely confined to the hair cells as evident by an increase in synaptic bodies and a hypersensitivity of the supplying vestibular nerve afferents. However, in response to prolonged missions a compensatory structural change in otoconia is induced through a constructive process of CaCO3 deposition; in gravity altered environments in the opposite sense, namely gravity loading via centrifugation, a compensatory structural change in otoconia is induced through a destructive process of CaCO3 ablation. The electrophysiological results of a current study in the laboratory support the present findings. In animals exposed to variable duration hypergravity (3G centrifugation) vestibular nerve afferents show a biphasic response: initially over the first 3-4 days the afferent are hypersensitivity to head accelerations suggesting a rapid change in synaptic organization, followed by a severe hyposensitivity when the 3G centrifugation continues to extended durations suggesting a possible remodeling of the otoconia. If structural changes do indeed occur, as our results suggest, these data will establish the basis of crew monitoring protocols, quantitative diagnostic tests of inner ear health and biomechanical function during flight and, more importantly, within a gravity environment on the mission and at home for early detection of pathology, and development of countermeasures to mitigate long-term health risks. However, caution is still needed in the final interpretation, because the samples were collected in tissue sharing programs. Defining the mechanisms underlying these observed structural changes of the otoconia in altered gravity environments requires more experimental manipulations of parameters that were not possible in the present confines of the programs, such as simply having detailed blood chemistry profiles in the different mice.

experiment_title: Plant Growth at Sub-Ambient Atmospheric Pressures with Control of the Partial Pressures of Constituent Gases
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The development of an Advanced Life Support System for Lunar/Mars bases, and space-flight, including orbital-based missions, will incorporate the use of physicochemical and biological components, in which there will be a role for plant growth systems for air and water revitalization and food production. Some environmental conditions to which plants will be exposed are certain to differ from those on Earth (NASA, Advanced Life Support Program: Advanced Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions), and such conditions have not been extensively tested before with higher plants. A central goal of this research is for the targeted crop species to successfully complete their life cycles at sub-ambient pressure. The objectives of the proposed research are: 1. To characterize plant growth, gas exchange (respiration and photosynthesis), constituent gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene and other trace gases), and water reclamation (transpirate) under environmental conditions that may apply to an Advanced Life Support System.
Investigators will determine the effectiveness of plant performance at low total gas pressures. In some experiments low pressure will be combined with high partial pressures of CO2, with or without O2 enrichment. They will test the hypothesis that at low gas pressure, the detrimental effects on cellular respiration of a low partial pressure of O2 will be offset by increased gaseous diffusion, and also by the beneficial effects of high CO2. With newer, leak-tight design, low-pressure plant growth system — ethylene (C2H4), a plant hormone, and water vapor, a byproduct of transpiration — can reach unacceptable levels and need to be controlled.

2. To model the dynamics of carbon dioxide exchange in a closed microecosystem such as an Advanced Life Support System. Investigators will utilize modeling principles to determine the steady state and transient control parameters of carbon dioxide exchange by plants in an Advanced Life Support System. Modeling will include release of CO2 by plants in dark respiration, and transient changes in CO2 concentration as a result of increased metabolic activity by plants (in response to light or temperature) or by crew during exercise.

The growth and gas exchange of plants in long-term experiments at different concentrations of O2, CO2, N2, and trace gasses, as well as total gas pressure, have not been extensively characterized. Such data is extremely useful in determining the overall design requirements for Advanced Life Support Systems. This information is also relevant to nutrient cycling, sustainability and closed-system microenvironments on Earth. 1. To characterize plant growth, gas exchange (respiration and photosynthesis), constituent gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene and other trace gases, and water reclamation (transpirate) under environmental conditions that may apply to an Advanced Life Support System.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
Engineering Developments for the Texas A&M Low Pressure Plant Growth System
The Low Pressure Plant Growth (LPPG) system at Texas A&M University was upgraded to improve performance and enhance data collection. The GCX gas chromatograph was replaced with individual gas sensors for O2 and CO2 in each chamber. Although functional, the GCX had several disadvantages when incorporated with the LPPG:
The sampling time is five minutes per chamber so that a complete sampling circuit of the six chambers took thirty minutes. This limited the ability to control gas concentrations to tight specifications and limited the accuracy of in situ gas exchange measurements. The GCX removed a small amount of gas (140 mL) for each sample and violated the design goal of maintaining a closed system. The sampling subsystem of the GCX was limited by design to six chambers. The GCX had ongoing maintenance issues and reliability concerns. Much of the work done by the factory field installer had to be reworked by the engineering staff to function as intended. Unfortunately, when the GCX is not functioning correctly the entire LPPG system is shutdown. When one or more of the four columns in the GCX failed and required replacement, the engineering team decided to accelerate incorporation of new gas sensors rather than spend $5,000 per column to repair the GCX, which we wanted to eliminate from the LPPG system anyway. Thus, the engineering focus for the second half of the year was to incorporate the sensors identified under the previous grant into the LPPG system at Texas A&M University. This new system is currently designated as the Generation IV Low Pressure Plant Growth (LPPG) system.

Generation IV LPPG Hardware Development
The Generation IV LPPG utilizes individual PIC16F877 microcontrollers (Microchip Technologies, Scottsdale, AZ) for pressure and gas composition control and data acquisition for each growth chamber. This is the same MCU that was used in the Generation III LPPG and it has proven to be highly serviceable. A newer MCU from Microchip, the 18F452, shares the same pin configuration with the 16F877 and could be used to upgrade if additional program memory was needed.

The selected O2 sensor is a motion stable, weak acid electrolyte oxygen sensor (MAX-250, Maxtec Inc, Salt Lake City, Utah). This sensor provides a stable signal over an oxygen concentration range of 0 – 100% (0 – 101 kPa partial pressure of O2), will operate for 900,000 hours, utilizes a non-caustic electrolyte, and is unaffected by acid gases including CO, CO2, and NOx. Testing of these sensors in two LPPG chambers has shown them to be reliable over the range of total pressure and O2 partial pressures used in our plant growth experiments. The sensor output is approximately 10 mV DC at ambient O2 partial pressure (20.9 kPa) and must be amplified prior to sending it to an available analog to digital conversion (ADC) channel on the MCU. A similar sensor from a different manufacturer (P8R-11-37-D7, Analytical Industries, Pomona, CA) is under evaluation as a replacement for the Maxtec sensor. The Analytical Industries sensor provides an output of about 20 mV at ambient O2 pressures and may improve the resolution on the O2 measurements.

The CO2 sensor selected utilizes a silicon based non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) technology to optically determine the CO2 concentration (model GMM222, Vaisala). The sensor response is converted to a 1 – 5 VDC signal, which is proportional to the CO2 concentration, and sent to another of the available ADC channels on the MCU. An additional vacuum rated instrumentation conductor fitting was needed for each chamber to incorporate the new sensors. Temperature and relative humidity (RH) will be measured with a HT-761 transmitter from Ohmic Instruments, Co. (Easton, MD). This instrument provides two 0 to 1 VDC outputs, proportional to temperature over the range 0 to 100oC and 0 to 100% RH, respectively. Temperature measurement is to a precision of ± 0.3oC and RH is measured to a precision of ± 2%. The conditions in the LPPG chambers are typically between 25 and 35oC and 60 to 80% RH.

An additional hardware upgrade between the Generation III LPPG and the Generation IV system was the addition of nine mass flow controllers (MFCs) so that each chamber has a dedicated set for O2, N2, and CO2. With the dedicated MFCs, the response is greatly improved and O2 and CO2 levels are held much closer to the setpoint. Also, the CO2 flow meters were calibrated to a much lower maximum flow (7 mL per minute) which greatly reduced the amount of overshoot in the gas addition. The improved control of the Generation IV system and ability of each chamber to be fully independent has greatly expanded our capabilities. New printed circuit boards (PCBs) were designed to provide access to the MCU analog input pins to read the new sensors and to provide the appropriate power to the RH/Temperature sensor.

Generation IV LPPG Software Development
There were only minor software modifications needed from the Generation III LPPG program to accommodate the Generation IV LPPG hardware. The MCU program is written in C and programmed into the MCU using Microchip development tools. In preparation for incorporation of the new sensors, the microcontroller (MCU) program was modified to access the additional analog inputs and to set up a secondary timing circuit to control when the sensors are read. Both the O2 and CO2 sensors have a reported response time to of about 30 seconds to reach 97% of the final reading. The only other significant modification of the program was relocation of the calibration equations from the MCU to the LabVIEW interface program. That allows investigators to recalibrate without having to reprogram the MCUs. The research team has determined to work exclusively in units of partial pressure for CO2 and O2. These units are equivalent to mass by the ideal gas law (PV=nRT) and eliminate any confusion about the environmental conditions surrounding the plants. Partial pressure is also the driving force in gas exchange in the plants.

Plant Biology Studies at the Texas A&M Low Pressure Plant Growth System
There are advantages in growing plants under hypobaric (reduced atmospheric pressure) conditions in biomass production for extraterrestrial base or space flight environments. Elevated levels of the plant hormone, ethylene, occur in enclosed crop production systems and in space-flight environments leading to adverse plant growth and sterility. Objectives of this research were to characterize the influence of hypobaria on growth and ethylene evolution of lettuce (Lactuca sativa L. cv. Buttercrunch).

As reported in the Engineering Section, considerable time was spent on reconfiguring the LPPG system from its reliance on the process GCX gas chromatograph to direct sensor monitoring of the partial pressures of CO2 and O2. Because of the difficulty in changing over the system from the GCX, investigators have been limited to shorter 7-8 day duration studies. They plan on doing longer-term studies under low pressure (25 kPa) and ambient (101 kPa) total pressure.

Investigators are finding that plants can be grown under low pressure and that dark respiration and ethylene levels are much higher under ambient than low total pressure with lettuce production. The night (dark respiration) levels were greater under ambient than low pressure. The O2 levels increased under both ambient and low pressure. There was a faster draw-down, which had a higher dark respiration and subsequent CO2 substrate level. This suggests a higher net assimilation rate of the ambient pressure plants. A minimum CO2 of 100 Pa was maintained during the light cycle. The dark respiration of 101 kPa (ambient) is greater (larger slope) than low pressure plants.

Growth was comparable in lettuce grown under low (25 kPa) and ambient (101 kPa) total gas pressures. However, tip burn occurred under ambient, but not low pressure, in part because of adverse ethylene levels (He et al., 2005). Under ambient pressure, there were higher CO2 assimilation rates and dark respiration rates (higher night consumption of metabolites) compared to low pressure. This could lead to greater growth (biomass production) of low pressure plants during longer crop production cycles.

experiment_title: The Effects of Spaceflight on Some Liver Enzymes Concerned with Carbohydrate and Lipid Metabolism in the Rat
experiment_description:
Objectives:

During early manned space flights, a specific physiological enigma concerning caloric requirements was noted. While theoretically in the absence of gravitational force less energy should be required for life-sustaining functions, on the initial flights where caloric intake was restricted, a marked inflight loss in body weight resulted. It is important to study a key organ like the liver in order to determine whether any regulative enzymes of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism might have been affected; that is, whether the capabilities of the organ to produce these cellular constituents is, in fact, altered in space flight.

Approach:

In the rat liver, the activities of about thirty enzymes concerned with carbohydrate and lipid metabolism were examined according to well-established methods or modifications of currently used techniques. In addition, the levels of glycogen and of the individual fatty acids in hepatic lipids were determined. The livers from rats subjected to near weightlessness space flight and rats subjected to a 1 g force via an onboard centrifuge were compared to appropriate ground-based controls. Several key enzymes of lipid biosynthesis, many of which are known to be regulative, were studied in this experiment, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthetase, palmitoyl-CoA synthetase, and stearoyl-CoA desaturase.

Results:

In rats sacrificed at recovery, statistically significant decreases in the activity levels of a-glycerol-phosphate acyltransferase, diglyceride acyltransferase, aconitase, and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase were noted in the flight-weightless group versus flight-centrifuged animals. The flight-weightless group also contained, on average, more than twice the amount of glycogen than did flight- centrifuged livers, and a remarkable shift in the ratio of palmitate to palmitoleate was noted. As a possible explanation, it was observed that although glycogen synthetase activity was about the same in all groups, its glycogen phosphorylase activity was significantly less. The observed alterations, particularly those that involved increased glycogen levels and decreased activities of the acyl transferases concerned with lipid synthesis, appear unique to the weightless condition. Most of the enzyme activities, though, did not show any significant differences between weightless and centrifuged rats, and all parameters had returned to normal by 25 days postflight.

experiment_title: Graviperception in Starch-Deficient Plants in Biorack
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Understanding the effects of spaceflight upon plant growth and reproduction is necessary for developing life support systems for long duration missions. This study utilized wild-type (WT) and three starch deficient strains of Arabidopsis thaliana to investigate the validity of the starch-stratolith model of plant gravity perception. Specifically, this study focused on the threshold level of stimulus necessary to initiate a gravitropic response in roots and hypocotyls, the effect of microgravity on starch structure, and if microgravity affects integrin localization in plant cells grown in space.

Approach:

Prior to launch, Arabidopsis seeds were sown in 28 mini-containers, which were, contained in 14 Type I/O containers. Arabidopsis Growth Medium (AGM) was used to hydrate the seeds which were then placed in the Biorack Incubator A at 22 degrees Celsius. This was performed at Mission Elapsed Time (MET) 2/01:45 for Plastid containers 1-4, at MET 1/01:25 for containers 5-8, and at MET 3/01:30 for containers 9-14. Twenty-four hours after hydration, the seeds were placed in the Biorack Glovebox and stimulated by light for 14 hours. Fifty hours after illumination, 2 I/O containers were transferred to the 1-g centrifuge for 5 minutes. This was repeated with different sets of 2 I/O containers for 10, 20, and 60 minutes. The remaining 6 containers were left in constant microgravity. Seedlings were videotaped at either 60 minute or 120 minute intervals for 240 minutes. At the end of the experiment, 18 of the containers were fixed with 4% (by volume) glutaraldehyde in 100 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.2) while the other 8 mini-containers were allowed to remain at ambient temperature.

Results:

Hypocotyls of the WT Arabidopsis seedlings exhibited the greatest magnitude of curvature by the 90-minute 1-G stimulus, with the starchless mutant showing the smallest curvature. The two reduced-starch mutant strain seedlings had an intermediate magnitude of curvature. These data, in which increasing amounts of starch correlated positively with increasing sensitivity to gravity, are consistent with a starch-statolith model of gravity perception in plants. In addition, space-grown plants showed a greater number of root hairs, an anomalous hypocotyl hook structure, and a decreased starch content compared with 1-G ground controls. However, these structural changes were attributed to the effects of elevated ethylene levels reported in the spacecraft atmosphere.

experiment_title: Biochemical and Morphological Evaluation of the Effects of Space Flight on Rat Salivary Glands
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Studying salivary gland biochemistry and morphology in experimental animals can yield information regarding general hormonal and environmental responses, specific reactions affecting the oral cavity, and comparative aspects of exocrine gland function. Environmental stimuli such as the action of catecholamines are known to result in altered cell morphology and in changes of cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase (cA-PK) activity and cellular localization. In this experiment, the biochemical and morphological changes in salivary glands of space-flown rats were examined.

Approach:

Tissues were fixed and processed for electron microscopy. Salivary glands were trimmed, homogenized, and separated into a soluble and particulate fraction by centrifugation. The fractions were assayed for protein kinase activity, and photoaffinity labeled to determine the distribution of protein kinase. A photoaffinity probe (32P-labeled azido analog of cAMP) was used to determine the compartmental distribution of the R subunits in salivary gland cells.

Results:

Several aspects of phosphorylative protein modification in rat salivary glands are apparently influenced by space flight conditions. Endogenous protein phosphorylation was increased in the parotid and in the sublingual glands of flight animals, while measurements of cA-PK activity using an exogenous substrate showed no significant difference in the flight animals. An increase in photoaffinity labeling of regulatory subunits in the parotid cell particulate fractions from flight animals was noted when compared to controls. Changes in cA-PK holoenzyme association and subcellular subunit distribution suggest alterations in reactions which are mediated via cyclic AMP, observations which are consistent with the reported decrease in circulating catecholamines during simulated weightlessness. Testing human saliva or salivary glands after space flight may yield useful indices of cellular reactions related to catecholamine metabolism and thus afford some insight into possible stress-associated responses.

experiment_title: Clinical Trial of the Efficacy of Melatonin as a Countermeasure for Entrainment to the Sleep/Wake Schedules Required during Shuttle Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Shuttle astronauts are typically exposed to "sleep cycle shifting" due to mission-dependent orbital mechanics and mission requirements. This is equivalent to imposition of a non-24 hour 'day' and is likely to result in misalignment of the endogenous circadian timing system with respect to the desired sleep-wake cycle, even among crewmembers who begin the mission with their sleep-wake cycle well synchronized to mission elapsed time (MET) on the day of launch. Such misalignment is known to produce sleep disturbances, daytime sleepiness, reduced attention, negative mood, slower reaction times, gastrointestinal disorders and impaired daytime alertness. Although appropriately scheduled exposure to bright light has been shown to be capable of resetting the phase of the human circadian pacemaker, existing Shuttle technology precludes use of such bright light delivery systems aboard the Shuttle. Several lines of evidence, including the discovery of melatonin receptors on the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the human hypothalamus and the results of animal and human studies, indicate that melatonin administration may be effective in generating phase shifts of the circadian pacemaker. The current study evaluated the ability of melatonin to entrain the human circadian pacemaker in sighted humans to a shorter-than-24-hour day length.

The current research was designed to test the following hypotheses:

  1. the human circadian pacemaker will be unable to maintain synchronization with a sleep-wake cycle of 23.5 hours, typical of that required on Shuttle missions;
  2. that such loss of synchronization will result in sleep-onset insomnia, decreased sleep efficiency, and decreased daytime alertness and performance resulting from imposition of the 23.5-hour day; and
  3. that a daily dose of melatonin (5 mg), administered one hour before bedtime, will be sufficient to entrain the circadian pacemaker to a 23.5-hour scheduled sleep-wake cycle.

To test the hypotheses, researchers conducted long-term (50-day) inpatient trials utilizing methodologies that allowed direct measurement of endogenous circadian phase and amplitude before, during and after extended duration exposure to a shorter-than-24-hour day length (i.e., similar to that occurring on many space shuttle flights). Each trial took place in an environment with low light intensities similar to that measured aboard the space shuttle on STS-90. It was anticipated that when subjects were scheduled to a 23.5-hour day and room lighting conditions were maintained to 8 lux maximum, that the endogenous circadian pacemaker would oscillate with a period that was different (24.1 to 24.2 hours) from the period of the imposed sleep-wake/work cycle. Failure to entrain the human circadian pacemaker to the 23.5-hour day was expected to be associated with disturbed sleep, and impaired waking alertness and performance. It was also expected that a daily dose of 5 mg of melatonin, one hour prior to scheduled sleep, would entrain the human circadian pacemaker to the 23.5-hour day. The melatonin countermeasure was expected to maintain normal sleep and circadian patterns, and normal waking alertness and performance.

APPROACH:
Five healthy male subjects (age: mean ± SD, 34 ± 7.25; range, 26-44) were studied. All subjects were required to pass a rigorous health screening including medical history, physical and psychological exams, blood and urine chemistries and an electrocardiogram. Toxicology screens for drug use, including alcohol and caffeine verified that participants were drug-free upon admission to the laboratory.

Blood was sampled for melatonin and cortisol during circadian phase estimations (constant routines) and 28-hour sampling windows throughout the intervening study days between constant routines. (In general, during a constant routine protocol, subjects remain under constant conditions, awake, engaged in light, mainly sedentary activity, and consume identical food and fluid every hour.) Core body temperature, waking electroencephalogram (EEG) and polysomnography were recorded throughout most of the protocol. Subject's performance, alertness and mood were assessed every 2 hours during wakefulness using valid, reliable standardized measures, which are sensitive to circadian misalignment and homeostatic sleep drive.

Ceiling-mounted fluorescent lamps with a 4100 K color temperature produced a spectrum of white light. Clear polycarbonate lenses filtered 99.9% of the light in the UV range. Light-dark cycles during the 23.5-hour day were of very dim light (< 8 lux maximum at ~183 cm with the sensor aimed toward the light fixtures) during scheduled wakefulness and darkness during scheduled sleep. Light intensity was measured with a photometer. The < 8 lux maximum light intensity was very similar to the light intensity measured on the middeck of the Space Shuttle during research on the Neurolab STS-90 mission.

Subjects were assigned to one of two cells: A or B. The protocol was divided into 9 segments:

CELL A

Segment A1 (Ambulatory Baseline) consisted of a minimum of 7 days, during which wrist activity and light levels were recorded using ambulatory-recording devices while the subjects were at home on a normal routine maintaining a sleep log.

Segment A2 (Adaptation) began with admission to the Intensive Physiologic Monitoring (IPM) Unit of the Brigham & Women's Hospital on Experimental Day 1 and ended on the morning of Experimental Day 4. Physiologic and neurobehavioral monitoring commenced upon admission on Experimental Day 1 and continued throughout the duration of the study. Subjects continued to sleep and wake at their regularly scheduled times for three normal scheduled nights. A placebo, was administered (single blind) one hour prior to lights out on nights 2-3 to determine if .

Segment A3 (Endogenous Circadian Phase Assessment-ECPA) began on the morning of Experimental Day 4 and ended on the evening of Experimental Day 5. Upon waking on Experimental Day 4, the subjects were placed on a constant routine protocol for 40 hours after which time subjects underwent an 8-hour recovery sleep. The constant routine protocol, as is true with the rest of the protocol from this point forward, was conducted in dim room light. Blood was sampled for melatonin and cortisol until the morning of Experimental Day 5. The constant routine was used to assess the phase and amplitude of the endogenous circadian pacemaker under strictly controlled conditions.

Segment A4 consisted of eighteen successive 23.5-hour days, which began on the morning of Experimental Day 6 and ended on the evening of Experimental Day 23. Each day consisted of 15.67 hours of scheduled wakefulness and 7.83 hours of scheduled sleep. Melatonin (5.0 mg) was administered orally, double blind, one hour prior to lights out each night. Light exposure was maintained at < 8 lux maximum during scheduled wakefulness. In addition to the blood sampled during the constant routines, one 28-hour window of blood sampling took place during Experimental Days 14-15. During this window, blood was sampled for melatonin and for cortisol.

Segment A5 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A3.

Segment A6 (Adaptation) consisted of a repetition of the adaptation that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A2.

Segment A7 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segments A3 and A5. In addition, this segment was used to reestablish a normal phase relationship between sleep and the phase of the endogenous circadian pacemaker.

Segment A8 consisted of a repetition of the eighteen 23.5-hour-day segment that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A4. Placebo was administered, double blind, one hour prior to lights out each night.

Segment A9 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A3, A5 and A7.

CELL B

The procedures for this cell were identical to that of Cell A except that in Segment B4 subjects received placebo instead of melatonin one hour prior to each sleep episode and in Segment B8 subjects received melatonin instead of a placebo one hour prior to each sleep episode.

In order to determine whether assessment of endogenous melatonin levels provided a method to assess the status of circadian phase and period, researchers assessed the potential impact of the sleep-wake cycle and associated light-dark cycle on the endogenous circadian rhythm of plasma melatonin. Researchers performed a detailed analysis of the melatonin phase during a 20-hour forced desynchrony protocol.

In this protocol, twelve young healthy subjects (5F, 7M) aged 24.1 ± 3.70 years (mean ± SD) were studied in an environment free of time cues for 18-27 days. Following three 24-hour baseline days (16 hour wake / 8 hour sleep), the subjects were scheduled to 24 cycles of a 20-hour flight day (FD) protocol (13.33 hour wake/6.67 hour sleep). Ambient light intensities were <15 lux during all scheduled wake times and <0.03 lux during all scheduled sleep episodes. Melatonin data were fitted with a non-orthogonal spectral analysis (NOSA) program, which simultaneously fit the imposed (20-hour, 2 harmonics) and endogenous (near 24-hour, 6 harmonics) components (and their interactions) of melatonin in order to calculate the subjects' intrinsic circadian periods t (tau). Each subject's melatonin data were then folded by their fitted t. For each circadian day researchers calculated: 1) duration of melatonin peak (DMP, time between upward and downward crossings of the mean); 2) circadian phase of melatonin peak (MIDPT, midpoint of upward and downward crossings of the mean); and 3) area under melatonin curve (AUC, estimated using the trapezoidal rule, z-scored for each subject). Linear regressions were fitted to the AUC and DMP data from the entire FD protocol to assess any overall change in the mean levels of melatonin secretion during the experiment. To determine whether the timing of the 20-hour sleep/wake schedule systematically modulated the phase or amount of melatonin secretion, each subject's AUC, DMP and MIDPT data were folded by the beat period (mean ± SD = 117.27 ± 0.13 hour) of their &964; (mean ± SD = 24.12 ± 3.10 hour) and the 20-hour FD protocol. For each variable, sine curves were then fitted to the data from all 10 subjects, and a Student's t-test was used to determine whether the fitted amplitude of the sinusoid was significantly different from 0.0.

RESULTS:
Hypothesis 1: Entrainment Studies of the Human Circadian Pacemaker to a 23.5 hour day.
Most subjects who received the placebo treatment failed to entrain to the scheduled 23.5-hour day, whereas most subjects given 5.0 mg of melatonin one hour prior to each bedtime maintained normal phase relationships between the timing of their core body temperature rhythms and the timing of the scheduled sleep-wake cycle. Two of three subjects in the melatonin condition maintained phase angles in the normal range with low levels during sleep suggesting that they entrained to the 23.5-hour day.

Hypothesis 2: Impaired Neurobehavioral Performance During Circadian Misalignment.
The neurobehavioral function during the entrainment studies to the 23.5-hour day with and without melatonin (n=3) was also examined. Daily performance averages were computed for subjects who completed both melatonin and placebo conditions. Researchers assessed vigilance performance every two hours during wakefulness using the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). The primary outcome measures analyzed were median reaction time and lapses (response times > 500 ms). Results of these analyses showed that reaction time performance and lapses in attention were similar in the melatonin and placebo conditions. Researchers also assessed working memory, cognitive speed and accuracy trade-offs using the Addition Performance Task and the Digit Symbol Substitution Test. Both tasks showed significant interaction effects (P < 0.05) between Drug Condition and Day such that performance continued to improve (i.e., learning occurred) in the melatonin but not the placebo condition. Subjective Sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale was significantly lower (less sleepiness) near the end of the protocol for the melatonin compared to the placebo condition (P < 0.05).

Hypothesis 3: Progress on the relationship between melatonin and circadian entrainment.
The AUC (p<0.20) and the DMP (p<0.15) did not show any significant changes in their mean levels over the course of the FD protocol. The DMP also showed no systematic alteration in relation to the 20-hour FD regimen. However, the AUC (p<0.0001) and the MIDPT (p<0.0001) manifested systematic modulations in relation to the 20-hour FD protocol. When sleep episodes were scheduled near circadian phase 240°, MIDPTs occurred approximately one hour later in the circadian day than when sleep was scheduled to occur near circadian phase 60°. When sleep episodes were scheduled near circadian phase 180°, the AUC was approximately 1.5 standard deviation larger than when sleep was scheduled to occur near circadian phase 0°.

These data demonstrated that the quantity of melatonin secreted and the phase of the midpoint of the melatonin curve are significantly affected by the timing of the sleep/wake, light/dark, upright/supine conditions during a 20-hour FD protocol. The data also demonstrated that the endogenous melatonin rhythm was robust and provided an accurate estimate of the period of the pacemaker under the current space-flight conditions of dim light.

The current results suggest that:

  1. additional research is necessary to evaluate the impact of non-24-hour sleep-wake/work schedules on circadian entrainment, sleep and performance during ground-based simulations and space-flight conditions;
  2. a dose of 5.0 mg of melatonin taken daily one hour prior to bedtime appears to be well tolerated and may be able to entrain the human circadian pacemaker to a shorter-than-24-hour day in some but not all individuals. Thus, additional research is needed to determine the effective dose necessary to entrain all individuals to non-24-hour day lengths. A flight-based test of daily administration of a larger dose of melatonin (=5.0 mg per day) as a countermeasure to circadian misalignment during space flight is warranted since melatonin appears to hold promise as an entraining agent at this higher dose;
  3. individual differences, likely due to differences in the intrinsic circadian period, make some individuals more vulnerable to circadian misalignment. These individual differences in vulnerability to circadian misalignment suggest that robust countermeasures need to be developed to ensure entrainment of all astronauts to a variety of imposed sleep-wake schedules during space flight.
  4. some sleep disturbances in space are likely related to a failure to maintain entrainment of the human circadian pacemaker to the imposed schedule, especially for missions with schedules that deviate from the 24-hour day; and
  5. measurement of the endogenous melatonin rhythm can be used to assess the status of the circadian time keeping system in humans under the current dim lighting conditions of space flight.

experiment_title: Hypogravity Induces Vascular Atrophy Leading to Bone Loss
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Hypogravity leads to a loss of ground reaction forces transmitted through the lower appendicular and axial skeleton. Loss of weight bearing (WB) loads leads to a state of progressive osteopenia in these skeletal sites. Hypogravity mediated unloading reduces mechanical compression forces resulting in decreased local bone strains and reductions in hydrodynamic forces within bone tissue. In addition to this mechanism, investigators hypothesized hypogravity mediates reductions in the vascular supply serving these bone sites that contribute to hypogravity induced osteopenia and may help explain the prolonged time to recover bone mineral density (BMD) and bone strength upon return to Earth.

This proposal frames a novel hypothesis that could contribute new knowledge impacting on both NASA's Risk of Accelerated Osteoporosis and its risk of Impaired Fracture Healing. If hypogravity unloading leads to an atrophy of bone-associated vasculature, then a negative impact could result contributing to the progressive osteopenia observed during space flight. A reduced bone vascular supply will hamper nutrient and waste product exchange rates in cortical bone thereby stressing osteocytes metabolically, and quite possibly leading to some osteocyte death and localized osteonecrosis. Given the slow remodeling rate of cortical bone, such a possibility could manifest in long term skeletal health complications. First, the presence of any localized osteonecrosis within cortical bone may elevate the risk of fracture upon return to Earth after a long space mission. Second, the remodeling and revascularization of cortical bone in skeletally mature adults takes a long time, and this slow process may help explain why the recovery rates for BMD and bone strength are slow in astronauts returning from long-duration space missions. A slow recovery of bone-associated vascular supply may also compound into long term health effects to astronauts in their later years of life (e.g., peripheral artery disease).

A cause and effect relationship between blood supply and osteopenia will need to be investigated in a future study by directly modulating blood supply to the hind limbs of rats. The blood supply to the hind limbs of WB rats could be reduced using unilateral femoral artery ligation and treatment with a VEGF inhibitor. The blood supply to the hind limbs of HLU rats could be enhanced using a hydrogel-based timed release of VEGF in proximity to the tibia and fibula. In addtion, a loss of bone-associated blood supply could hamper a proper angiogenic response thereby delaying fracture healing. In this case, after HLU exposure, fibulae would be fractured and the extent of repair would be monitored by micro-CT imaging, followed by vascular volume assessments at the fracture callus site using 3D micro-angiography. Vascular volume, bone volume, BMD and vascular morphology within the fracture callus would be compared between HLU and WB rats.

APPROACH:
Vasculature associated with bone tissue was assessed using 3D micro-angiography imaging, which uses contrast agents to fill blood vessels including those in bone followed by micro-CT imaging and histomorphometry. Using micro-angiography, they have developed the tissue and image processing means to assess the bone-associated vascular volumes in the hind limbs of rats. Using the hind limb unloaded (HLU) analog, a time-dependent loss of vascular volume in the lower legs was monitored and compared to the temporal pattern of progressive bone loss at these skeletal sites. Blood flow and vascular volumes were assessed in these rat groups and a subsequent effect of these treatments on bone volume, BMD, and vascular morphology in the tibiae and fibulae were determined.

RESULTS:
This progress report represents the final year of funding for the study. In the year since the last progress report much has been completed as the project approaches its final phase. This progress report will include an update on the mouse specimens flown aboard the STS-135 space shuttle mission (CBTM-03 payload), which was a supplement to NNX10AE40G. The relatedness of this space flight study compared with the ground-based rat study should allow the two to be analyzed similarly and compared to one another. In section A the original grant’s ground based rat study will have its task progress reported. Section B will cover the progress with the STS-135 samples and section C will cover the tasks that will be completed in the final months of project funding under an approved no-cost extension (NCE).

A. Ground based studies

1) All animal based work has been completed, including all vascular profusions and tissue retrieval from specimens.
2) The tissue sections that were previously being used for immunohistochemical analysis have been shown to be just as efficiently imaged using light microscopy. Barium-perfused vessels show enough contrast with the tissue to be easily identified and scored. As such, tissue sections of perfused animals were imaged using light microscopy and full tissue section images were compiled. These tissue sections are still imaged for alpha-Smooth Muscle Actin (aSMA) antibody detection under fluorescent microscopy. The aSMA staining acts to verify the presence of vessels ensuring a minimal number of false positive vessels. These tissue sections are awaiting analysis using ImagePro software. Analysis of 2D histomorphometry will allow for vessel metrics to be quantified, these include vessel size and vessel number.
3) The micro-CT imaging of perfused rat specimens was completed and the raw data is currently undergoing 3D morphometric analysis. These analyses are currently being validated for consistency and calibration in order to produce valid results that could be compared with existing vascular literature.
4) 3D volumes of perfused rats were aligned to each animal’s baseline scan due to each animal’s anatomically unique characteristics. 3D volumes of perfused hind limbs were cropped to cover a 5-mm vertical region of interest (ROI) within the middle of the lower hind limb. These crops were then divided into 3 additional regions of interest classified as anterior, central, and posterior based on the anatomical position in the hind limb. Once the vessels and bone had been aligned and cropped, the bones were masked out of the image this prevents the bone from interfering with the analysis of vasculature.

B. Space Flight Study

1) The genetic analysis of all STS-135 (CBTM-03) spaceflight and synchronous ground-based control samples was completed. These specimens represent a similar mid-calf ROI as the prior mentioned rat HLU study but only for the left hind limb of untreated control mice in this study. These quantitative gene expression analyses were accomplished using a Qiagen qRT-PCR arrays interrogating the activity of 88 genes related to endothelial cell function. The genetic data obtained from these arrays was analyzed using 7500 systems software and Qiagen supplied analysis software.
2) Additional specimens for an HLU ground control study were obtained from Dr. Bouxseim’s group at Harvard University. These samples included both HLU and WB control C57Bl/6 female mice (identical to those flown on STS-135). Specimens in the HLU group were exposed to HLU for the same duration as the space flight duration of the STS-135 mission (12.5 days). The control mice in this study were the same age as the HLU experimental mice and all animals were treated similarly to those from the STS-135 mission. The mid-calf ROI of each animal’s left hind limb was utilized for this control study and (given the small size of the C57Bl/6 female mice used) the bone and skeletal muscle were not separated. The proximal end was placed in RNAlater at 4° C to preserve RNA for genetic analysis of factors associated with endothelial cell alterations. The distal end was placed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin and stored at 4°C. The same analysis of gene expression was done using Qiagen gene arrays. This genetic data was also analyzed statistically using 7500 system software and Qiagen supplied analysis software. The distal ends were decalcified and embedded in tissue freezing medium and were cryo-sectioned for immunohistochemical analysis.
3) The genetic analysis of the spaceflight and Harvard studies was divided into 4 unique groups; spaceflight ground control, spaceflight, Harvard ground control, and Harvard HLU. These groups were designated to allow for comparison of control groups as well as comparison of the spaceflight animals with the HLU mice. These findings are of great importance as hind limb unloading is a NASA approved model for spaceflight studies.
4) It was determined that the von Willebrand factor (vWF) staining was too variable to be of use in the histomorphometric analysis of vasculature. As such it was found that isolectin B4 (IB4) gave much more consistent and useful staining, especially of microvasculature (vessel diameters less than 50 microns).
5) The immunohistochemical staining done on the tissue sections utilized fluorescently tagged primary antibodies alpha-Smooth Muscle Actin (aSMA) and Isolectin B4 (IB4). The tissue sections were stained along with DAPI which fluorescently labeled the nuclei. The tissue sections were then imaged on a fluorescent microscope and full-sized tissue section images were compiled. These immunohistochemical sections are undergoing visual validation and morphometric analysis using ImagePro software. Analysis of vasculature will quantify vessel size and vessel number in several regions of interest throughout the tissue.

experiment_title: Investigation of Host-Pathogen Interactions, Conserved Cellular Responses, and Countermeasure Efficacy During Spaceflight using the Human Surrogate Model Caenorhabditis elegans
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Changes that occur to both the host immune system and pathogenesis of microbes during spaceflight represent a formidable challenge to the successful transition from short-to-long-duration spaceflight. While spaceflight has been shown to induce changes that can independently affect the host or the pathogen in a manner that is directly relevant to the development of infectious disease during spaceflight – no studies have been reported when both the host and pathogen are simultaneously exposed to the spaceflight environment. We propose to challenge the human surrogate model Caenorhabditis elegans with S. typhimurium during spaceflight to study the role of the intestine in host-pathogen interactions in real-time, define virulence mechanisms, identify evolutionarily conserved responses, and test novel therapeutic strategies to prevent infectious disease. We hypothesize that the combination of a spaceflight-induced increase in virulence of the pathogen coupled with a blunted immune response of the host will result in a synergistic effect on the host-pathogen interaction such that the risk of infectious disease during spaceflight is exacerbated. We further propose that these responses represent evolutionarily conserved mechanisms at the level of both host and pathogen that are dependent on media ion composition, specifically the local concentration of phosphate.

APPROACH:
The Micro-5 experiment infects the human surrogate model C. elegans with S. typhimurium during space flight and follows the survival of the C. elegans roundworms on orbit, compared to controls on Earth. Inflight infection of the whole C. elegans organisms will be accomplished by injecting bacterial growth on orbit. The use of phosphate as a nutritional countermeasure to protect C. elegans against infection with a foodborne pathogen will also be evaluated. Physiological data will be collected by video and RNA analysis.

RESULTS:
Completed RNA-Seq gene expression profiles for C. elegans spaceflight and ground control cultures infected with Salmonella cultured in either Lennox Broth (LB) or LBM9 media (as well as flight and ground non-pathogenic E. coli controls cultured in the same media). RNA-Seq analysis was successfully performed (for both host and microbe) using high integrity RNA extracted from samples. Our findings indicate significant differences in gene expression between flight and ground samples.
Omics data is available from GeneLab's Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/genelab/

experiment_title: Apoptosis in Microgravity-Sensitive Cells After Space Flight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The regulation of the intracellular level of Ca2+ is very crucial for a number of biological functions such as gene expression, muscle contraction, bone remodeling, glucose metabolism, and apoptosis. Calbindins are Ca2+-binding proteins that have among their known functions in cells the buffering of intracellular Ca2+ and thus, inter alia, potentially modulate Ca2+-dependent biological functions in living organisms. In order to better understand the mechanism of action of calbindins including their role in the (1) active absorption of Ca2+ in the kidney, (2) the regulation of insulin producing cells (beta-cells) and (3) glucagon producing cells (alpha-cells) of the pancreas we have used microgravity as a perturbent and have analysed the in situ levels of calbindins in kidney and intestine and levels of insulin and glucagon in the pancreas. The rats were flown aboard the Space Shuttle (STS-40, STS-58, and STS-90) to expose them to microgravity. The in situ levels of calbindins, insulin and glucagons were then determined by quantitative immunocytochemistry coupled to digital video imaging. The study provides microgravity as an important perturbent for understanding signaling mechanisms in living systems.

Approach:

Quantitative immunocytochemistry (QICC) experiments were carried out in conjunction with the digital video image analysis in order to measure the in situ expression of calbindins, insulin and glucagons from 10% formalin-fixed tissues of flight rats and their controls. Cellular localization of calbindin-D28k was carried out with a monoclonal antibody directed against chicken intestinal calbindin-D28k (clone CL-300, Sigma), which specifically and strongly cross reacts with calbindin-D28k in higher vertebrates, including rats, and an indirect peroxidase method. Cellular localization of calbindin-D9k was carried out with a rabbit anti-rat intestinal calbindin-D9k. Monoclonal antibodies were used to localize insulin and glucagon. Using the quantitative in situ immunocytochemical analysis, differences in percentages of reactive cells and in intensity of the reaction product in specific cells indicate differences in gene expression for the proteins under some microgravity-associated conditions.

In situ levels of calbindins, insulin and glucagon were quantified on the basis of the intensity of the oxidized diaminobenzidine reaction product present in individual cells, using a MetaMorph image acquisition, processing, and integrated morphometric analysis system (Universal Imaging Corp., PA). Labeling intensities were measured on digitized images in arbitrary average gray level units based on a 256 tone gray scale, where a 0 value indicates completely black and 255 indicates completely white (transparent). The intensity value included both the labeled cells and their individual brightness values, and was obtained by defining the outline of cell clusters using an inclusive thresholding procedure and determining the average gray values over the thresholded areas. The brightness of the background was determined on the entire image by using the exclusive thresholding protocol in which the objects were excluded and specifically the average gray level of the background was counted. Data is expressed as relative labeling intensity and is defined as the inverse of (average gray level of the area of interest/average gray level of the background) x 100, so that the higher numbers correspond to the higher levels of calbindins and pancreatic hormones. QICC was performed blindly, i.e., without knowing initially the protocol for the groups from which the tissue was derived.

The insulin and glucagons content in pancreas was also determined by using standard biochemical Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) protocol.

Results:

A summary of the results for the three experiments are listed below. For a complete discussion and tables see the final report "Calbindins and Apoptosis After Short-term Spaceflight".

TASK 1: To quantify in situ levels of calbindins in the small intestine, hypothalmic nuclei, kidney, and pancreas.

Kidney: analysis by QUICC revealed a significantly higher f (by one way analysis of variance) level of calbindin-D28k in animals in space for 16 days on STS-90 plus 1-day at Earth gravity (R+1) (Figure 1) compared to asynchronous ground control rats ((48 hour delay from experimental group, vivarium, R+3 (P=0.008); 96 hour delay from experimental group, simulation, R+5 (P<0.001)), flight animals plus 14-days at Earth gravity (R+14) (P<0.001), and asynchronous ground controls: 15 days delay, vivarium (R+15) (P=0.004); 17 days delay, simulation (R+17) (P=0.008).

Only the flight animals at 1 day following return from on orbit exhibited statistically significant differences from the other groups, including flight animals after 14 days at Earth gravity.

Duodenum: levels of calbindin-D28k determined by QUICC were rather consistent across groups, flight and controls. No statistically significant differences were found (P>0.06).

Hypothalmus: sections of hypothalami from STS-56 showed little or no reactivity for calbindin-D28k. This was an unexpected result since calbindin-D28k has previously been described as present in neurons of the ventromedial nucleus, supraoptic nucleus and medial mammillary nucleus of the rat. Because there was weak immunoreactivity for positive control peptides (neuropeptide Y and neurophysin), it is believed that the lengthy storage time in fixative contributed to the diminished immunoreactivity for calbindin-D28k and the control neuropeptides in the hypothalamus. The flight controls as a group showed weaker neurophysin II immunoreactivity than flight animals, however, the flight group exhibited considerable variability in the density of reaction product. Due to weak or absent immunoreactivity in the available tissue specimens, no conclusion can be reached regarding the effect of mg on hypothalamic levels of calbindin-D28k.

Pancreas
Our results confirmed that there is little or no expression of calbindin-D28k in Beta-cells of normal pancreatic islets of the rat. There were no observed differences in calbindin-D28k levels in the pancreatic islets of flight and control animals.

TASK 2: To evaluate apoptosis in the small intestine, hypothalmic nuclei, kidney and pancreas.

Duodenum: Apoptosis in the duodenum ranged from five to about 11 apoptotic nuclei per three microvillous profiles over all experimental and control groups. There was no statistically significant difference by ANOVA in apoptotic rates between any groups (P=0.2).

Pancreas: For the pancreas, apoptosis was expressed as the number of FITC-positive (apoptotic) Beta-cell nuclei per pancreatic islet. The apoptotic rate based upon TUNEL staining and morphological criteria was low for all islets examined (0-3). There was no statistically significant difference by ANOVA in apoptotic rates between any groups.

Hypothalmus: Apoptotic nuclei were only infrequently observed in nerve cells of the hypothalmus in flight and control specimens. There was no statistically significant difference by ANOVA in apoptotic rates between any groups.

Kidney: Distal convoluted tubules exhibited few apoptotic nuclei and there was no statistically significant difference in apoptotic rates between any groups.

TASK 3: To determine if levels of renal calbindin-D28k depleted by microgravity are restored to normal after nine- and 14-days at Earth gravity.

The results of this study with ELISA of calbindin-D28k did not confirm the reduction in calbindin-D28k found in our earlier study (Sergeev, et al. 1996). Calbindin-D28k levels in kidneys of SLS-1 flight animals after just returning to Earth (R+0), 2.24 ± 0.17 ï¿½g/mg protein, were significantly greater than those of basal controls (L+0), 0.89 ± 0.06 ï¿½g/mg, but not ground controls (GC), 1.97 ± 0.03 ï¿½g/mg. Levels of calbindin-D28k measured by ELISA were equivalent in flight animals immediately following flight (R+0) and after nine days at Earth gravity (R+ML), 1.94 ± 0.12 ï¿½g/mg protein (P=0.5). In SLS-2 animals, renal calbindin-D28k in flight animals after just returning to Earth (R+0), 2.22 ± 0.27 ï¿½g/mg protein, was significantly greater that basal controls (L+0), 1.08 ± 0.13, (P<0.001) and ground controls, 0.62 ± 0.04 (P<0.001). Calbindin-D28k in kidneys of flight animals after 14 days of Earth gravity (R+ML), 2.03 ± 0.31 (P=0.06). Thus, the results of this study indicate an incrrease in calbindin-D28k levels in microgravity. Differences in the results of this and our previous study (Sergeev, et al., 1996) suggest that other factors the animals are exposed to during flight regulate in a substantial way calbindin-D28k. Among these factors may be environmental stresses, such as elevated temperatures (from about 24.5 to 28.5 degrees C in SLS-2) and reduced humidity (slightly more than 30 percent to over 100 percent for SLS-2). Temperature extremes were even greater for SLS-1 (27-32 degrees C).

TASK 4: To determine pancreatic levels of insulin.

Head of pancreas
Insulin content of the head of the pancreas from rats flown on STS-58 (SLS-2) was significantly higher (P>0.001) immediately following recovery (R+0 F) 364.7 ± 52.0 ng/mg (n=6), than all of the appropriate controls: R+0 FC (flight control), 160.1 ± 17.8 ng/mg (n=6), R+0 GC (ground control), 104.4 ± 14.0 ng/mg; BC (basal control), 71.2 ± 4.1 ng/mg (n=6).

The elevated insulin content of flight animals following recovery was also significantly greater (P<0.001) than the content of flight animals held for mission-length following recovery (F, R+ML), 141.7 ± 28.6 ng/mg (n=6), and their controls ((FC, R+ML, 94.1 ± 19.2 ng/mg (n=6); GC, R+ML, 92.4 ± 17.8 ng/mg (n=5)). After 14-days at Earth-gravity; the insulin content of flight rats (F, R+ML) was similar to control levels (FC R+0; GC, R+0). There was no significant difference between flight animals held on the ground for the length of the mission after recovery (F, R+ML) and mission-length and recovery flight controls (FC: R+ML and R+0) and ground controls (GC: R+ML and R+0). There also was no statistically significant difference between mission-length controls (FC, R+0; GC, R+0) and recovery plus mission-length animals. No other significant differences were present by ANOVA.

The concentration of insulin in the head of the pancreas from rats flown on STS-40 (SLS-1) tended to be lower than that of STS-58. The insulin concentration for flight animals from STS-40 "immediately" following recovery (F, R+0) was 103.9 ± 11.9 ng/mg (n=10), which was significantly greater (P<0.02) that flight controls (C, R+0), 58.2 ± 11.0 ng/mg (n=5). The insulin content of flight animals (F, R+0) was not significantly different from vivarium controls (CV, R+0), 84.9 ± 9.4 ng/mg (n=5) or basal controls (L+0), 83.4 ± 12.1 ng/mg (n=5). As with rats from the STS-58 flight, there was no difference between flight animals held for mission-length after recovery (F, R+ML), 97.9 ± 14.2 ng/mg (n=9) and recovery plus mission-length control animals (C, R+ML: 67.4 ± 16.3 ng/mg; CV, R+ML: 131.3 ± 9.3 ng/mg).

Tail
Sample of the tail of the pancreas for insulin extraction were only available for STS-58. In contrast to the findings with the head of the pancreas, the insulin content of the tail of the pancreas from flight animals following landing (R+0), 19.4 ± 47.7 ng/mg of protein (n=6) did not differ significantly from any of its controls: FC, R+0, 202.1 ± 30.0 ng/mg (n=5) (P=0.81); GC. R+0, 235.0 ± 31.2 ng/mg (n=6) (P<0.05); L+0. 153.7 ± 35.8 ng/mg (n=6) (P<0.05).

In summary, the concentration of insulin in the head of the pancreas is increased following nine and 14 days of exposure to microgravity. Additional experiments are necessary to evaluate the functional significance of increased insulin levels in the pancreas following return to earth after exposure to microgravity.

experiment_title: Veggie Hardware Validation Test (VEG-01)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:

The VEG-01 hardware validation test investigation utilizes the Veggie facility on ISS. This investigation will assess on-orbit function and performance of the Veggie, and focus on the growth and development of ‘Outredgeous’ Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) seedlings in the spaceflight environment and the effects of the spaceflight environment on composition of microbial flora on the Veggie-grown plants and the Veggie facility. Lettuce plants are harvested on-orbit, frozen at <-80oC and returned to the ground for post-flight evaluation. Microbial sampling swabs will be taken of the Veggie facility and plant material, frozen and returned to the ground for environmental microbiological examination. Rooting pillows and water sample syringes will also be returned for microbial sampling and root analysis.

APPROACH:
The overall goal of VEG-01 is to demonstrate proof-of concept for the Veggie plant growth chamber and the planting pillows. This research builds upon hardware development via an SBIR grant to ORBITEC for the initial prototype Veggie units with subsequent hardware development for next-generation units. Both ORBITEC and KSC have been involved in plant growth optimization of the Veggie hardware and testing and collaboration have resulted in the development of the pillow planting concept to interface with the Veggie hardware. Through numerous tests the VEG-01 science team has refined the pillow concept and selected growth media and fertilizers, plant species, materials, and protocols for using the pillow concept in Veggie to grow healthy plants that can provide crew with food and recreation. The pillow concept is designed to be low mass, modular, require no additional energy and be very low maintenance. Pillows of different sizes have been designed to accommodate a wide variety of plant types and different types of growing media.

The primary goal of the VEG-01 testing will be to demonstrate plant growth in the Veggie hardware using lettuce as a test species. Plants will be grown in two different sizes of arcillite, a calcined clay media. This test will help us compare root zones of the two media sizes to determine water and root distribution in the different sized-particles to provide recommendations for future Veggie investigations. Shoot samples will also provide information on any growth anomalies when compared with ground controls and will provide information on microbial growth and food safety. Photographs will be used to assess plant growth rates and plant health. A data logger will record the environment within the Veggie hardware. Crew questionnaires will provide insight into the appropriateness and thoroughness of the crew procedures for Veggie hardware and plant growth operations.   

Pillows are single use and thus reduce the chances of microbial contamination of the Veggie hardware and produce. A major aspect of the proof of concept flight, VEG-01, is to collect baseline microbial data from plants and pillows grown on ISS. Ground testing has demonstrated very low microbial levels on lettuce plants grown in Veggie-relevant conditions. Discussions with space microbiologists, flight surgeons, and space food technologists at JSC indicate that if microbial levels are sufficiently low the crew could consume the fresh produce without sanitizing. For crops that naturally have higher levels of microorganisms (e.g. radishes, which grow in contact with water and nutrients) a space-rated produce sanitation method must be developed and tested.   

The baseline data collected from the VEG-01 flight will be a resource for future Veggie investigations. This information will provide data on necessary procedural changes, hardware upgrades or horticultural options as Veggie becomes an integral part of ISS expeditions in the future.  


RESULTS:
Veggie is considered one of the most advanced salad-machine precursors available, and passed the Phase II NASA flight safety review as the hardware is developed for flight to the ISS.

Nutritional and horticultural evaluation results have been analyzed. Comparison of flight and ground tissues showed some differences in total counts for bacteria and yeast/molds (2.14 – 4.86 log10 CFU/g), while screening for select human pathogens yielded negative results. Bacterial and fungal isolate identification and community characterization indicated variation in the diversity of genera between leaf and root tissue with diversity being higher in root tissue, and included differences in the dominant genera. The only difference between ground and flight experiments was seen in the third experiment, VEG-03A, with significant differences in the genera from leaf tissue. Flight and ground tissue showed differences in Fe, K, Na, P, S, and Zn content and total phenolic levels, but no differences in anthocyanin and ORAC levels. This study indicated that leafy vegetable crops can produce safe, edible, fresh food to supplement to the astronauts’ diet, and provide baseline data for continual operation of the Veggie plant growth units on ISS (Massa et al. 2020).

experiment_title: Changes in Endocrine Regulation of Orthostatic Tolerance Following Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In response to a drop in blood pressure, catecholamines (norepinephrine and epinephrine) are released from the sympathetic nerves and the adrenal gland to adjust the heart rate and peripheral resistance and thereby maintain normal blood pressure. Disruption of this response may be responsible, at least in part, for the orthostatic intolerance that astronauts frequently experience after space flight. The objective of this study was to evaluate orthostatic changes in plasma catecholamine levels and total peripheral resistance before and after space flight.

APPROACH:
Twenty-four astronauts who flew on missions of 5 to 14 days' duration participated in this study. Blood samples were drawn at the end of a 20-minute supine rest period, and after 5 minutes of standing, for measurement of plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels. The blood pressure and heart rate were recorded while the astronauts were lying supine and then standing. These assessments were done 10 days before launch, on landing day and 3 days after landing.

RESULTS:
Catecholamine levels were higher when the astronauts were standing than when they were lying supine, both before and after flight. Postflight catecholamine levels were higher than preflight levels in both the supine and the standing positions. From before the flight to landing day, supine plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels and standing norepinephrine and epinephrine levels increased by 34%, 65%, 65% and 91%, respectively. Standing catecholamine levels were reported for only 16 astronauts. Epinephrine levels had returned to preflight levels 3 days after landing, but norepinephrine levels remained elevated. Supine heart rate, supine systolic blood pressure, standing heart rate and standing diastolic blood pressure also increased between the preflight period and landing day. However, increases in peripheral vascular resistance per unit increase in circulating norepinephrine were reduced; sympathetic nervous system activity and peripheral resistance apparently became uncoupled.
