experiment_title: Microbiological Investigations of the Mir Space Station and Flight Crew (Phase 1A)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microorganisms are ubiquitous in spacecraft environments, as they are on Earth. Microbes pose several risks to humans in space including: infectious diseases, allergies, degradation of air quality (e.g., release of volatiles), release of toxins, degradation of critical materials, and systems failure (e.g., water reclamation system). Maintaining the health and performance of humans in closed microgravity environments while reusing reclaimed air and water is a daunting task. Determining medical and technological risks that are dependent on microbiological factors during long-term space flight is a vital problem in theory, as well as practice. In such a closed environment, humans will be a major source of microbes released into the spacecraft. Animals and plants, when present, will also be significant contributors to the overall bioburden, and suitable containment and purification technologies are essential. Studies of microbial ecology in spacecraft have been mostly limited to short (<30 days) duration missions in the US program. Similar studies have been conducted during long-duration missions in the Russian program. The Mir space station provided an opportunity for a relatively comprehensive US-Russian joint study of the crewmembers and the environment of the Mir.

The success of long-duration space missions will depend on our ability to mitigate the adverse effects of microorganisms. This will require a much better understanding of the microbiology of closed environments and the human-microbe-environment interactions than are currently available. This joint US-Russian investigation was an important first step in gaining this understanding.

The investigators hypothesized that during long-term space flight (>30 days) human microbiota and the microbial ecology of the Mir station will undergo quantitative and qualitative changes. The objectives of this study were to 1) characterize microbiota of crewmembers, air, surface, and water before, during, and after a long-duration mission aboard the Mir Space Station, 2) determine the exchange and distribution of microbes among crewmembers, and 3) assess the distribution and dynamics of crew microbiota throughout the Mir Space Station.

APPROACH:
Protocols for the collection and analysis of specimens from the crew, air, surface, and water were designed to provide the data necessary for a thorough characterization of their microbial populations. The protocols and sample collection schedules for the first Shuttle-Mir mission were developed to obtain the maximum possible data despite the limitations of space flight.

Crew Microbiology
Microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, axilla, scapula, groin, and urine, were collected, before and after flight, and examined for bacteria and fungi. Stool samples were also collected before and after flight and examined for bacteria, fungi, ova and parasites. Samples from the Mir 18 crew were collected on L-149 (149 days before launch), L-117, L-79, L-44, R+0 (landing day), R+9 (9 days after landing), R+14, and R+19. Samples from the Mir-19 crew were collected on L-254, L-221, L-148, L-112, L-14, R+0, R+7, R+14, and R+22. Each throat, nasal, ear and skin site was sampled using Culturette devices moistened with phosphate buffer. Throat samples were collected by swabbing the surfaces of the tonsils and posterior pharyngeal vault of the crewmember. Nasal samples were collected by swabbing the nares. Ear swabs were collected by swabbing the external ear canal. Skin surface samples from the hand, axilla and groin regions were collected by swabbing the skin surface of the area. Clean-catch midstream urine samples were collected in 4-ounce sterile specimen containers. Stool specimens were collected in commode collection kits and transferred to bacterial transport medium for culture and to SAF fixative for ova and parasite examination.

Throat cultures were examined for the presence of pneumococci, beta-hemolytic streptococci, staphylococci, yeast, filamentous fungi and other microbes of medical significance. Fecal examination was performed to establish the obligate and facultatively aerobic microbes, including yeast and molds and anaerobic microbes, including bacteriods, bifidobacteria, lactobacilli and sporiferous bacilli (Clostridium). Enterobacteriaciae, pseudomonads, enterococci, staphylococci, hemolytic streptococci, yeast, molds and other microbes of medical significance were identified to the species level. Quantitative estimates were made in terms of Colony Forming Units (CFU). Species identification was conducted using either a Vitek Automated Identification System or a Biolog Automated Identification System. Species that were not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification by fatty acid analysis, or by other means of microbial classification as needed.

Air Microbiology
Air samples were collected inflight using a Russian supplied impaction air sampler (SAS), in which a small fan unit draws a known volume of air through the sampler and airborne particles are impacted onto growth media. Trypticase soy agar (TSA) and rose bengal agar (RB) were used for collection of bacteria and fungi, respectively. Mir samples were collected in the area of the Control Panel Post #1 in the Core Module (CM), the dining table, the Captain's cabin, and the Kristall module. Mir 18 samples were collected on FD 98 (Flight Day 98) and FD 107 (while docked with STS-71). Upon arrival of the Shuttle (STS-71), all inflight samples were transferred to refrigerated storage space aboard the Shuttle until landing. Mir 19 samples were collected on FD 19 and FD 55. Pre-, in- and postflight samples were also collected from the STS-71 middeck and Spacelab using the US supplied microbial air sampler (MAS) on L-57, L-1, launch day and FD 3.

The number of colonies found on the surface of the collection media was used to determine the total bacteria and fungi present in the volume of air sampled. Airborne microorganisms were measured in CFU per cubic meter of air. Identification of isolated colonies was performed as described in the crew microbiology section.

Surface Microbiology
Surface samples were collected inflight using the Surface Sampler Kit (SSK) that contained Biotest Hycon Contact Slides. The slides consisted of a flexible plastic tray containing a microbial growth medium. The medium was pressed into contact with the surface area being sampled. The slides provided a nutrient surface on which microorganisms could adhere and grow. Bacterial and fungal samples were collected using trypticase soy agar and rose bengal agar, respectively. Microbial samples were collected from the Mir spacecraft surfaces on the control panel #1, the dining table, the mission commander's cabin wall, the treadmill trainer handles and the Kristall Module Hatch. Mir 18 samples were collected on FD 97 and FD 107. Upon arrival of the STS-71, all inflight samples were transferred to refrigerated storage space aboard the Shuttle until landing. Mir-19 samples were collected on FD 23 and FD 55. Pre- and postflight samples were collected from the STS-71 half-moon vent near the toilet, the Left-most Air Return in Crawl through between Middeck and Flight Deck, and the Spacelab Workbench Handle on L-77, L-57, L-1, FD 0, FD 3 and R+0.

Total bacterial and fungal counts were determined by the number of colonies found on the surface of the collection media. Surface microorganisms were measured in CFU per squared centimeter. Identification of isolated colonies were performed as described in the crew microbiology section.

Water Microbiology
Water samples were collected and processed using the Water Microbiology Kit (WMK). The kit contained a microbial capture device through which a water sample volume was processed. An ampoule containing R2A medium was introduced into the microbial capture device to cultivate any microorganisms trapped on the filter. A preflight sample was collected from the ground water source of Mitischi, Moscow, that was supplied on a Progress resupply ship. Mir-18 samples were collected from the Rodnick tank and the galley hot water tap. The Rodnick tank, which holds water transferred from the Progress and Shuttle supplied stored water, was sampled on FD 107. The Mir galley hot water tap, which consisted of recycled potable water, was sampled on FD 13, 97, and 107. Upon arrival of STS-71, all inflight samples were transferred to refrigerated storage space aboard the Shuttle. STS-71 water samples were collected from the galley water tap on L-1 and R+2. Mir 19 samples were collected on FD 23, FD 42 and FD 55. Unprocessed water samples were collected using the water sampler/archiver. These archived samples and the processed water sample filters were returned for ground based examination.

Total bacterial counts were determined by the number of colonies found on the surface of the collection media. Water microorganisms were measured in CFU per 100 milliliters. Identification of isolated colonies was performed as described in the crew microbiology section.

RESULTS:
Crew Microbiology
Mir 18: Staphylococcus aureus was chosen as the bacterial species to follow microbial dissemination from crewmember to crewmember and throughout the Mir environment. S. aureus was recovered from the throat swab of crewmember #1 three months before flight. It was also recovered from the hand of crewmember #2 eight days before flight and in substantial numbers in six of nine samples collected on landing day. S. aureus was recovered from crewmember #3 in six of nine samples collected at most sampling sessions. S. aureus was not recovered from backup crewmembers #4 and #6 but was recovered from backup crewmember #5 in seven of the nine samples during most of the preflight sampling periods (backup crewmembers did not participate in postflight sampling). Fungi were very rarely isolated from the crew. Fungal isolates, when present, represented common environmental contaminants, such as Aspergillus niger.

Aerobic bacteria recovered from the fecal specimens were consistent with that of healthy individuals. Significant changes were not apparent in the aerobic bacteria isolated from the various specimens before and after flight. The anaerobic bacteria recovered from the feces included bacteroides, bifidobacterium, clostridium, and lactobacillus. No ova or parasites were seen from any crewmember.

Although not a part of this experiment, Russian microbiological specialists used the data to assess flight readiness of the crew. The specialist identified a dysbacteriosis in all three crewmembers at 45 days prior to launch. This resulted in a course of bacteriotherapy to normalize and stabilize the crew's microflora prior to the mission. Re-examination at 7 days prior to launch showed marked improvement. Dysbacteriosis was again observed in one crewmember on landing day; again, bacteriotherapy was administered to normalize his microflora.

Mir 19: Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from the throat, ear and hand of crewmember #1 before flight, and from his nasal, scapula and groin at pre- and postflight. It was also recovered from the throat of crewmember #2 pre- and postflight. Enterobacter aerogenes was isolated from the nasal swab of crewmember #2 at all sampling periods except L-254 but was isolated from his ear at L-254. Fungi were rarely isolated from crewmember #1, but were frequently isolated from crewmember #2. Aspergillus niger, a common environmental fungus, was not found on crewmember #2 preflight, but was found on his scapula, nose and throat postflight. Candida albicans, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from crewmember #2 fecal samples preflight. The yeast was also recovered from the postflight throat swab of crewmember #2. Urine samples were received in unsterile containers and all data was lost, which impacted science objectives. Fecal samples were collected improperly postflight.

Air Microbiology
STS-71: Air samples were collected from the middeck of the Space Shuttle and in the Spacelab. The bacterial levels were low in both locations on launch day and flight day 3. The levels were 38 CFU per cubic meter or less. However, the fungi tended to be much higher than usual. Levels reached a high of 930 CFU per cubic meter on the middeck and were over 100 for three of the four sampling periods. Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Cladosporium, common environmental taxa, were the frequently isolated fungi. Fungi were not detected on the Shuttle middeck during two preflight sampling sessions.

Mir 18: Air samples were collected on flight days 98 and 107 from four locations in the Mir. Bacteria were not recovered in four of the eight bacterial samples. The levels in the other four samples never exceeded 22 CFU per cubic meter. These levels were exceptionally low and comparable with the levels found on the Shuttle. Fungi were not recovered from five of the eight samples. Fungal levels were generally low, but reached 220 CFU per cubic meter in the Kristall module on FD 97. Aspergillus and Penicillium were the predominant fungal genera isolated. The levels of both fungi and bacteria were clearly below the 1000 CFU per cubic meter acceptability limit for the International Space Station (ISS).

Mir 19: Air samples were collected on flight days 19 and 55 from four locations in the Mir. Bacteria were not recovered from any of the sampling sites. Aspergillus niger was found in all four sampling sites. It was isolated in low levels in two sampling sites and in high levels in the two other sites. Control panel #1 revealed the highest counts of 1290 CFU/cubic meter on day 55, which is above the acceptability limit (1000 CFU/cubic meter) for the ISS.

Surface Microbiology
STS-71 and Mir 18: Surface data were collected from two areas in the Shuttle and one site in the Spacelab before, during and after the mission. The levels and species of bacteria and fungi were comparable to previous Shuttle data. Surface data were collected from five locations inside the Mir on FD 97 and 107. The level of bacteria and fungi were low and generally less than found in the Shuttle. The exception was the Kristall module, in which the highest bacterial levels of >300 CFU/cubic meter were found on FD 97. Unlike the air samples, surface fungal levels in the Kristall were low when detected.

Mir 19: Surface data were collected from five locations inside the Mir on FD 23, 28 and 55. This data is from both contact slides and archived swabs. The levels of bacteria and fungi on the contact slides were low and generally less than found in the Shuttle. The microorganisms isolated are similar to those isolated from the Shuttle, with the exception of a larger number of Bacillus species recovered. Aspergillus niger was found on four of the five surfaces sampled. Only qualitative data was obtained from the archived swabs because the tubes were not maintained in a frozen state.

Water Microbiology
STS-71, Mir 18 and Mir 19: The only bacterial contaminant found in the Shuttle potable water system was Burkholderia cepacia. This common contaminant was recovered at L-1 (23 CFU/100 ml) and at R+2 (1 CFU per 100 ml). The Mir recycled potable water supply (galley hot water) was analyzed three times during the Mir-18 and Mir-19 missions. During Mir-18, there were problems associated with water collection. The bags leaked causing a decrease in the amount of water received postflight. The impact of this was minor. The cold water sample that was to be collected from Mir and archived was not collected. The total bacterial count for Mir-18 was: 60 CFU/100 ml on FD 13; 5 CFU/100 ml on FD 97, and 23 CFU/100 ml on FD 107. The total bacterial count for Mir-19 was: 3 CFU/100 ml on FD 23; 6 CFU/100 ml on FD 42; and 6 CFU/100 ml on FD 55. All of these values are within the International Space Station acceptability limits of 100 CFU/100 ml. The microbes recovered from the Mir recycled water was much different from those recovered from the Shuttle water system. The rigorous filter treatment and final heat step of the Mir system appeared to have eliminated many of the more fragile organisms. Bacillus and Staphylococcus, two robust gram positive bacteria, were the only organisms recovered from this source. Technical difficulties during Mir 18 made analysis and interpretation of the archived water samples difficult. Due to contamination, there were no quantitative results from the Mir 19 archived water samples.

In conclusion, the aerobic microbiota of the three Mir 18 crewmembers was characteristic of healthy individuals and medically significant changes were not found after return to Earth. One crewmember was clearly a carrier of S. aureus and dissemination of this species in the environment and colonization of other crewmembers was probable. Levels of bacteria and fungi from the air, surface and water samples were within the ISS acceptability limits. The species recovered from the air and surfaces were similar to those found on the Shuttle. However, conclusions are difficult until the database for long-duration flight is expanded. Detection of Aspergillus and Penicillium fungal isolates from selected air and surface samples is a basis for further observations of their quantitative dynamics and distribution in the orbital station, as it is evident that these microorganisms are growing on different polymeric materials, causing biological harm and destruction. Microbial water analysis was successfully performed for the first time aboard a spacecraft. The bacterial content of the Mir water supply was much different from bacterial species isolated from the Shuttle water system.

The aerobic microbiota of the two Mir 19 crewmembers was characteristic of healthy individuals. Remarkable change in the body-bioburden was not apparent upon return to earth with the exception of the presence of A. niger on the skin and throat swabs of crewmember #2. This fungus is commonly present in the terrestrial environment and was also isolated, in rather large numbers, from Mir surfaces and air samples. It is obvious, therefore, that the fungus was a "carry over" from Mir; no undesirable health effects were noticed. One crewmember was clearly a carrier of S. aureus, and completion of DNA fingerprinting will verify the suspected colonization of the other crew member. The surface and water borne bacterial and fungal loads were mostly within the limits set for the ISS. However, the fungal counts in the air tended to be higher. In general, the microbiological profile of the Mir was comparable to that of the Shuttle and Spacelab.

experiment_title: The Response of Articular Cartilage to Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this experiment was to determine if the reduced biomechanical forces due to microgravity impair the ability of chondrocytes to maintain healthy articular cartilage, leading to increased cartilage breakdown; specifically whether the reduced mechanical forces associated with microgravity lead to osteoarthritis. Although the effects of microgravity on bone are well known and appear to be reversible, the effects of reduced mechanical forces on the cartilage surfaces of articulating joints are less well understood. Studies in humans and animals clearly demonstrate that osteoarthritis results from abnormal (both increased and decreased) mechanical forces on cartilage. Based on these findings, the hypothesis is that appropriate mechanical forces are critical for the health of articular cartilage. Following on from this, a further hypothesis is that the absence of significant biomechanical forces affects that ability of the chondrocyte to maintain healthy functioning cartilage. This may lead to accelerated cartilage breakdown and osteoarthritis.

APPROACH:
For the STS-131 mission, animals were subjected to 15 days of microgravity and the joints harvested three hours following landing. Femoro-tibial joints from four flight and four ground control animals were paraffin-embedded, sectioned and stained for proteoglycan using toluidine blue. Proteoglycan degradation is a key indicator of cartilage breakdown and one of the first stages in osteoarthritis. Stained sections were scored using a modified Mankin histological semi-quantitative grading system (see Research Plan for description of scoring system).

For RNA expression analyses, joint articular cartilage total RNA from the four flight and ground control samples were isolated. Since the function of microRNAs (miRNAs) in cartilage has received substantial research attention and several appear essential to normal development and homeostasis each of the eight samples were subjected to miRNA microarray analysis using the Affymetrix Genechip miRNA array. Samples were also hybridized to the Affymetrix Murine Gene 1.0 ST GeneChip microarray for mRNA expression.

RESULTS:
miRNA data: Bioinformatic analysis of the miRNA data demonstrated that 10 miRNA were upregluated (p>0.001) and 26 were downregulated in flight compared to control mice. Interestingly, miR-35, which was downregulated 1.4-fold, is a known mechanoresponsive microRNA in chondrocytes. It has been reported that miR-35 was upregluated following cyclical loading of chick sternal chondrocytes and that it plays a role in chondrocytee proliferation and differentiation. Furthermore, miR365 binds to and inhibits HDAC4, a negative regulator of chondrocyte hypertrophy. Our finding that miR-365 is downregulated in the reduced biomechanical unloading of spaceflight is consistent with a role in mechano-sensing. Reduced levels of miR-365 would be expected to reduce chondrocyte proliferation thereby contributing to an OA phenotype.

Thirteen mRNA were upregulated>1.5-fold in flight compared to the ground control animals and one downgraded>1.5 fold. Of the 13 upregulated genes, 7 have been implicated in either osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or both. There are Vdr, Nfkbia, Cited2, Traf6, Mtl, Txnip, and Cdknla. The highest upregulated gene was Vdr which encodes the vitamin D receptor. Vdr is a key genetic and biochemical marker of osteoarthritis (OA). Several genetic association studies on large populations of OA patients have linked the Vdr gene locus with knee OA. The link between Vdr and OA is further highlighted by the finding that Vdr mRNA ius upregulated in severe osteoarthritis. Consistent with this is the finding that, vitamin D, the Vdr ligand, upregulates matrix metalloprteinase (MMP) production. MMPs are the major class of matrix-degrading enzymes in cartilage.

experiment_title: Effects of Alphalipoic Acid on Irradiation Induced Cognitive Deficits (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Radiation exposure of the brain occurs during space missions. The space radiation environment contains high-energy charged particles including protons and fully ionized atomic nuclei, such as iron-56 (56Fe), and may be a hazard to space flight crews during their mission. Major adverse effects of radiation exposure are impairments in hippocampus-dependent learning and memory and hippocampal plasticity. Since the hippocampus is involved in complex learning that requires the ability to learn about multiple relationships among stimuli, disturbances in hippocampal functioning reduce spatial learning and memory and the ability to explore the environment adequately.

Preliminary data support that radiation exposure impairs hippocampus-dependent cognitive function and that female mice might be more susceptible than male mice to Cesium-137 and 56Fe radiation-induced hippocampus-dependent cognitive impairments three months following irradiation. The potential effects of 56Fe radiation on cognition one-to-two weeks after irradiation are not known. Irradiation increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels that may contribute to these cognitive impairments. Preliminary data show that in male and female mice irradiated with 56Fe (3Gy) at six-to-nine months of age and fed a diet containing the antioxidant lipoic acid (LA), or a regular diet starting two-weeks prior to irradiation and throughout cognitive testing, LA prevented radiation-induced impairments in spatial memory retention in the water maze probe trials three months following irradiation. However, LA treatment caused cognitive impairments in sham-irradiated mice. This study had the following specific aims:

  1. To determine the short-term effects of 56Fe radiation irradiation on hippocampal function and assess whether these effects are sex-dependent.
  2. To determine whether the severity of the cognitive effects are associated with reduced choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) immunoreactive cell bodies in the medial septum and nucleus basalis and ChAT immunoreactive fibers in the hippocampus and cortex.
  3. To determine the ability of the dietary supplement LA to antagonize the effects of 56Fe irradiation on hippocampus-dependent cognitive function, measures of ROS, and ChAT immunoreactive cell bodies in the medial septum and nucleus basalis and ChAT immunoreactive fibers in the hippocampus and cortex.

APPROACH:
Investigators studied whether apolipoprotein E (APOE) isoform modulates hippocampus-dependent cognitive performance in mice two weeks after (56)Fe irradiation. Changes in ROS can affect cognition and are induced by irradiation. Therefore, after cognitive testing, they evaluated hippocampal ROS levels in ex vivo brain slices, using the ROS-sensitive fluorescent probe, dihydroethidium (DHE).

RESULTS:
Investigators first determined short-term effects of 56Fe irradiation on spatial learning and memory, novel object recognition, and fear conditioning in C57Bl6J male and female mice. 56Fe irradiation had differential effects on cognitive performance in a dose, but not sex, dependent manner. Moreover, these deficits were associated with sex-dependent changes in the ROS marker 3-nitrotyrosine (3NT) and in the acetylcholine marker ChAT.

experiment_title: Microgravity Effects during Fertilization, Cell Division, Development, and Calcium Metabolism in Sea Urchins
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

This investigation explored the effects of microgravity on cytoskeletal organization and calcium metabolism during fertilization and early development in the sea urchin model system. Emphasis was placed upon calcium-dependent sperm incorporation, calcium-triggered cortical granule exocytosis, membrane fusion, and cytoskeletal organization within eggs and embryos fertilized and cultured in space.

APPROACH:

Sea urchin (Lytechinus pictus) eggs and embryos were maintained and cultured in the Aquatic Research Facility (ARF) on board the Space Shuttle Endeavour in May 1996 (STS-77). The ARF controlled temperature and illumination, and recorded video images of embryo behavior at programmed intervals during flight. It held two centrifuges, with one providing a 1-g environment in space and the other being a microgravity (10 minutes per revolution) centrifuge. This permitted a direct comparison of embryos grown in microgravity with those grown at 1 g in space. A third set of samples (the ground control) was cultured on earth with a 24 hour lag interval.

ARF utilized 33 mL volume aquaria called Standard Container Assemblies (SCAs). Each SCA was equipped with a fixative block assembly that was actuated by computer control at preset time points to release fixative into the SCAs and achieve a final (embryo stage-dependent) concentration of either 0.5% or 2% glutaraldehyde. 8 SCAs were situated on each of the 4 centrifuges (spaceflight mg, spaceflight 1 g, ground control mg, ground control 1 g). Two SCAs from each set were fertilized pre-flight on the ground and fixed at 6 and 24 hours into the flight, while cultures in the six other SCA chambers were fertilized in-flight 6 hrs after launch using the Fertilization Syringe Unit (FSU). The FSU stored the sperm inactive at 4-6 degrees C until fertilization operations. These cultures were fixed at 3 hours, 7 hours, 24 hours, and 8 days after fertilization.

The in-flight fixed specimens were processed at recovery for analysis with SEM, TEM, fluorescence and immunofluorescence microscopy. High resolution electron microscopy was used to examine the molecular components of cytoskeletal structures. Fluorescent-labeled anti-tubulin antibodies were used to identify microtubules. Fluorescent-labeled anti-centrosomal antibodies were used to detect the microtubule-organizing centers and the fluorescent compound Hoechst 22358 was used to observe chromosomes.

RESULTS:

Postflight analysis indicated that fertilization took place in microgravity, and embryos were obtained at the 2-cell, 16-cell, blastula, gastrula and early pluteus stages. However, the processes of cortical granule exocytosis, fusion of cortical granule membranes with the plasma membrane, elongation of microvilli, and degree of elevation of the fertilization coat were reduced in comparison with embryos cultured at 1 g in space and under normal conditions on earth. These results indicated that calcium and secretion processes are affected by microgravity during fertilization and early development in sea urchin eggs and embryos. Also, 4% of all cells undergoing early cell divisions in microgravity showed abnormalities in the centrosome-centriole complex. These abnormalities were not observed within the 1-g flight and ground control specimens. These findings indicate that the centrosome-centriole complex may be gravity-sensitive.

experiment_title: Role of Corticosteroids in Bone Loss During Space Flight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies have shown that stress-induced corticosteroid hormones increase during spaceflight. Negative effects on bone, such as decreased bone formation, are also associated with these hormones. The objective of this study was to determine whether corticosteroid excesses contribute to the bone loss that occur during spaceflight.

Approach:

Prior to the flight, male Sprague Dawley rats were anesthetized and subjected to bilateral adrenalectomy. Pellets made of cholesterol with dissolved corticosterone and aldosterone were implanted in each adrenalectomized rat. All rats had been injected with a label to mark the bone forming surfaces. After the flight, serum samples of corticosterone and aldosterone concentrations were measured by radioimmunoassay techniques. The left tibia was frozen and subsequently used to measure dry and ash bone weights. Bone samples were sectioned, stained, and counterstained for measurements of cancellous bone volume (%), osteoclast surface (%), an index of cancellous bone resorption, and osteoblast surface (%), an index of cancellous bone formation. The right tibia underwent a polymerization process and was cut into cross-sections. From the cross-sections, cortical bone area, cortical width, and marrow area were measured.

Results:

From the data in this study, it was found that rats in both the experiment and control populations had increased in body weight. This result indicated that the rats went through the flight well and were healthy. The flight group that did not undergo adrenalectomy showed significant increased adrenal gland weights. Thus, it suggests that the rats had corticosteroid excess during spaceflight. It was determined that the intact flight rats had normal bone mass, thus the objective of this experiment was not met.

experiment_title: Skeletal Responses to Long-Duration Simulated Microgravity in Male and Female Rats
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Long duration spaceflight can cause severe bone loss, particularly at the lumbar spine and hip. The rate of bone loss in crewmembers while on the space station can be profound, and a significant increase in estimated fracture risk remains even one year after returning to Earth. In addition to microgravity, the natural aging process leads to declines in bone mass and also increases in fracture risk, which suggests that the combination of the two could have compounding effects on bone structure and integrity. Changes in bone structure and strength have unknown consequences and important implications for the skeletal health of crewmembers. In recent ISS missions, crewmembers have maintained bone mass better, presumably due to improved resistance exercise protocols coupled with adequate energy intake and vitamin D; however, no predictors of bone geometry or strength were evaluated. As NASA is preparing to send astronauts to the ISS and beyond for missions exceeding one year, it is critical to characterize and understand bone loss and recovery for longer duration spaceflight.

The proposed project will take advantage of the unique tissue sharing opportunity for obtaining frozen specimens from a UC Davis experiment that entails 90-day rat unloading and reloading studies. Specifically, the aims of this project are: 1) Determine structural and gene expression changes in cortical and cancellous bone in growing rats (3 month old) during long-duration simulated microgravity exposure and recovery. 2) Determine whether skeletal responses to long-duration simulated microgravity differ in males compared to females (3 month old). 3) Determine age effects (9 mo old) on temporal changes in skeletal structure and gene expression during extended simulated microgravity followed by recovery. We predict that osteoclastogenic and oxidative stress-related factors relates directly to the extent of bone decrements.

APPROACH:
To accomplish our Aims, we will determine how responses to simulated weightlessness vary in young (3 month old) versus adult (9 month old) male rats as a function of time, using 3D imaging (microcomputed tomography), mechanical testing, and molecular gene expression analyses. We also will determine if bone loss and recovery differ between male and female rats.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Gene Expression in the Brain
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The mammalian brain exposed to space flight experiences profound changes in neuronal activity. Immediate early genes (IEGs), such as c-fos and Fos-Related Antigens (FRA), are useful indicators of changes in neuronal activity and plasticity. Within minutes of exposure to neural stimulation, the mRNA levels of these genes increase. The corresponding proteins can be detected for hours (Fos) or days (FRA) afterwards. These proteins may act as messengers to regulate the transcription of target genes involved in the physiological responses and adaptation to mG or readaptation to 1 G. This experiment investigated whether changes in IEG expression, occurring during space flight, affect brain structures involved in the control of: a) somatic (postural and motor) functions; b) vegetative (cardiovascular, respiratory and gastrointestinal) functions; and c) the regulation of the sleep-waking cycle. These changes were investigated to see if they depend on alterations in neuronal activity induced by macular gravity signals and, if so, whether they could be related to or modified during different phases of the sleep-waking cycle.

Approach:

Flight rats used in this study were part of the integrated adult rat dissections performed on FD 2 and FD 14. Postflight, remaining animals were sacrificed at different days after landing (R+1 and R+13, respectively). Simulated Caged Control (SIM) and vivarium animals were sacrificed on a 48-hour and 96-hour delayed basis. All brain tissue, excepting the cerebellum, was used in this experiment. Adjacent sections of the same brain tissues were alternatively stained with either a Fos or a FRA antibody, to mark both short- and long-lived responses to changes in gravity stimulus. These were characterized by hypergravity followed by exposure to mG at FD 2 after launch, stabilization to mG at FD14, hypergravity followed by exposure to 1 G at R+1 after landing, stabilization to 1 G at R+13. Tissue was removed from the fixative, cryoprotected in 30% sucrose solutions in phosphate buffer (PB) at 4 °C, frozen, and sectioned into 40 micrometer sections with a cryostat. Immunocytochemistry was used to detect Fos and FRA proteins in the forebrain and brainstem. The distribution of labeled cells in each brain region was examined and quantified. The number of labeled cells was compared between flight and SIM groups.

Results:

Variable numbers of Fos- and FRA-positive cells were found during different space flight conditions in Medial (MVe) and Spinal Vestibular nuclei (SpVe), which contribute to the vestibulo-ocular and the vestibulo-collic reflex, and in Group F nuclei, which projects to the vestibulocerebellum. In particular, all these structures showed a small increase in Fos and FRA expression at FD2, due to exposure to hypergravity partially compensated by exposure to mG, while a prominent increase of this expression occurred at R+1, due to hypergravity followed by exposure to 1 G. Similar changes in Fos and FRA expression occurred in the Area Postrema, which appears to be involved in the development of motion sickness, in the Nucleus of the Solitary Tract (NST) and the related ventrolateral reticular structures, which intervene in the central and reflex regulation of cardiovascular and respiratory activities, and finally in the Central nucleus of the Amygdala.

An increased level of Fos expression occurred in the noradrenergic Locus Coeruleus nucleus (LC) of flight rats with respect to ground controls, without variations at different time points of the space flight. However, the number of FRA-positive cells selectively increased in the LC of flight animals sacrificed at FD 2 and more prominently at R+1. These differences were attributed to the fact that, while the Fos protein induced by the gravity force returns to basal levels within hours after stimulation, thus being undetected 24 h after launch or the reentry, FRAs persist for days after induction. Since activity of noradrenergic LC neurons has been shown to produce gene expression in several target structures, it is likely that the long-lasting induction of FRAs in the LC at FD 2 and more prominently at R+1 contributes to the molecular changes occurring in the vestibular and the related structures indicated above.

An increase in Fos expression was also observed in the spinal areas of both the Inferior Olive (IO) and the Lateral Reticular nucleus (LRt) at FD 2 and FD 14, i.e., during and after the launch. However, only few labeled cells were observed in these precerebellar nuclei at R+1 and R+13. This last finding was partly attributed to reduced somatosensory and motor activities occurring at these specific time points of the space flight.

In addition, the increase in gravity force at R+1 selectively increased the number of FRA-positive cells in the dorsomedial cell column of the IO (which corresponds to the vestibular area of this structure), while no such changes affected the Fos expression. This increase in gene expression could then be detected by using only a long-lasting (FRA) and not a short-lasting (Fos) marker of neuronal plasticity.

The results of this experiment indicate that the gravity force acts on specific vestibular nuclei and related structures controlling somatic and vegetative functions, and that the noradrenergic LC neurons, driven by the gravity force, may contribute to long-term molecular changes occurring in the brain during adaptation to mG and readaptation to 1 G. Changes in gene expression in forebrain structures, such as the cerebral cortex, were finally used to identify the different phases of the sleep-waking cycle and relate the molecular changes occurring during different time points of the space flight to the animal state.

experiment_title: HZE Radiation: Modulation Of Genetic Effects By RNA Interference Of NHEJ--NAG9-1516
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
For extended missions in space, astronauts will be exposed to a radiation environment unlike any on the earth's surface. Galactic cosmic rays include a particularly worrisome component of energetic iron nuclei which are high atomic number, high energy (HZE) charged particles with linear energy transfer (LET) similar to alpha particles but with very different track structures. While the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of a particular radiation roughly depends on the LET, the very different track structures for these two radiations may well modulate this RBE even if they have identical average LETs. Further, this "radiation quality" for the exposures actually relevant for astronauts will be modified by interactions with materials in the spacecraft, including their own bodies.

Basic to virtually all relevant biological effects of ionizing radiation is the underlying damage produced in DNA, and the subsequent cellular processing of such damage. The damage can be qualitatively different for different kinds of radiations, and the genetics of the biological systems exposed can greatly affect damage processing and ultimate outcome the biological effect of concern. The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosome rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. It is important, therefore, to understand cellular responses to DNA damage and to elucidate the mechanisms and phenotypic consequences of DSB misrepair.

APPROACH:
The general aim in this proposal is to examine connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis, namely chromosome aberration formation, mutagenesis and telomere fusions, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining system, using RNA interference to systematically knockdown gene products known to be involved, either singly or in combination.

RESULTS:
In 2002, it proposed to utilize the relatively new technique of RNA interference (RNAi) to deplete levels of various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) double-strand break (DSB) repair system, and to study the effects on HZE radiation-induced chromosomal rearrangements and gene mutation. This was supported with a one-year of awarded support. The suggestion from reviewers and NASA program officers was that before the project could be considered for further funding, it would be necessary to demonstrate that the proposed studies involving siRNA knockdown of various proteins would be feasible. During this year (June 1, 2003 - May 31, 2004) considerable additional data has been collectedsupporting the ability to conduct theses studies.

The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosomal rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. Focus has been on the consequent phenotypic effects of faulty repair by examining connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis after exposure to IR, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) system. Deficiencies of individual components of the DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) holoenzyme (Ku86 and the catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs) were produced, both singly and in combination, using RNA interference (RNAi) in human lymphoblastoid cell lines. Exposure of cells exhibiting reduced protein expression to either gamma-rays or 1GeV/nu Fe particles demonstrated differential effects on telomere dysfunction and mutation frequency, as well as differential effects between radiation qualities. The initial results are reported in the article "Suppression of DNA-PK by RNAi has different quantitative effects on telomere dysfunction and mutagenesis in human lymphoblasts treated with gamma-rays or HZE particles" by Qinming Zhang, Eli S. Williams, Kristin F. Askin, Yuanlin Peng, Joel S. Bedford, Howard L. Liber and Susan M. Bailey, currently in press (2005) in Radiation Research (NASA supplement).

experiment_title: Microcirculatory Adjustments to Simulated Microgravity Exposure in Humans
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure of an individual to microgravity activates a series of compensatory alterations. Reduced tolerance to orthostatic stress is a primary concern when the individual returns to a 1-G environment, whereas reduced thermoregulatory capability could affect performance in space, as well as following the flight. This investigation included a series of experiments that addressed both issues by assessing the effects of simulated microgravity on the control of the cutaneous vasculature at the level of the microcirculation. These studies were performed using non- and minimally invasive techniques to assess skin blood flow simultaneously with administration of vasoactive substances primarily via intradermal microdialysis. Dose-response relationships were constructed with this information.

It is recognized that the cutaneous circulation may not be significantly involved in the maintenance of blood pressure during orthostasis in normothermia. To this regard, two important points should be made, a) information regarding the effects of simulated microgravity on the cutaneous microcirculation may be valuable in identifying mechanisms associated with altered control of the microvasculature in regions more important to the regulation of blood pressure, but less easily studied; b) in hyperthermia 50-60 percent of cardiac output is directed towards the skin. In this environment the skin represents the largest fraction of total vascular conductance, and its control is, therefore, critical in the maintenance of blood pressure.

The following five hypotheses were tested. In each case microgravity exposure was simulated via 14 days of 6 degree head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest, and a subset of these subjects exercised throughout HDT exposure to see if impaired responses could be improved by aerobic exercise training.

  1. Prolonged HDT exposure decreases cutaneous adrenergic vasoconstrictor responsiveness.
  2. Prolonged HDT exposure reduces cutaneous vasoconstriction associated with the venoarteriolar response.
  3. Prolonged HDT exposure reduces maximal cutaneous vasodilator responsiveness.
  4. Prolonged HDT exposure impairs sweat gland function.
  5. Impaired thermoregulatory responses due to HDT bed rest will be preserved in subjects exercising through bed rest exposure.

APPROACH:
Twenty-two subjects (19 male and three female) were exposed to 14 days of strict 6 degree HDT bed rest. Fourteen of these subjects were randomly assigned to an exercise group (including two females), while eight subjects served as control subjects and thus did not exercise during HDT bed rest. This study was a component of an 18-day HDT bed rest study. However, the reported data were obtained from subjects after 14 days of HDT bed rest. On the final day of HDT bed rest (i.e., day 18) subjects in the exercise group were further subdivided to investigate questions unrelated to the present findings. Thus, for the reported data there are an unequal number of subjects in the control and exercise groups. The subjects' average age was 34 ± 2 years and all were of normal height (180 ± 2 cm), weight, (82 ± 4 kg), and health. A written informed consent from each subject was obtained prior to participating in the institutionally approved study.

Bed Rest & Exercise
Strict bed rest was maintained in the 6 degree HDT position for 14 days. Subjects remained in this position at all times, except they were allowed to elevate on one elbow for meals and were horizontal for exercise, transport, and bathing. Subjects were housed in a hospital-based general clinical research center and given a controlled diet, while fluids were allowed ad libitum. Pre-bed rest data were obtained within a week of the onset of bed rest. Post-bed rest data were collected on day 14 of bed rest. For the exercise group, exercise was performed at 75 percent of pre-bed rest heart rate maximum for 90 minutes per day using a supine cycle ergometer. Subjects chose to exercise for this duration either in two sessions of 45 minutes or three sessions of 30 minutes per day.

Hypothesis #1: Two intradermal microdialysis membranes were placed in dorsal forearm skin. This technique involved placing a small (200 µm outer diameter, 10 mm length) sterile, semipermeable membrane intradermally using a 25-gauge needle. The microdialysis membranes were perfused with Ringer's solution at a rate of 2 µl/min via an infusion pump. The protocol commenced once skin blood flow (SkBF) returned to normal levels after needle insertion trauma (~60-120 minutes). Local temperature was controlled at 34 degrees Celsius via a local heating element that housed a laser-Doppler flow probe centered directly above the microdialysis membranes. Once SkBF stabilized, eight doses of norepinephrine (NE) were delivered (in 10 fold increments) at a flow rate of 2 µl/min for 5 minutes per dose. Data are presented from doses of 1x10-9 to 1x10-2 M, which represent both threshold and saturation for the subjects. Microdialysis membranes were placed at similar regions of the forearm between pre- and post-HDT bed rest trials. However, it is recognized that slight variations in probe placement likely occurred between these periods. For each period (i.e., pre- and post-HDBT), responses between the two sites for each dose were averaged.

Hypothesis #2: With the subject in the supine position and the arms and legs at heart level, the forearm venoarteriolar response was assessed by inflating a cuff placed around the upper arm to 45 mmHg. The same procedure was performed to assess the venoarteriolar response of the lower leg except the cuff was placed around the thigh. The cuff remained inflated at this pressure for a minimum of two minutes. SkBF, assessed via laser-Doppler flowmetry, was measured at two sites on the dorsal forearm for the forearm assessment. For the lower leg assessment, laser-Doppler measures were obtained from nonglabrous skin over the tibialis anterior 39 ± 1 cm from the bottom of the foot. When SkBF from two sites were measured, the laser-Doppler signals were averaged between those sites. Anatomical measurements were obtained to place the laser-Doppler flow probes in the same region between pre- and post-bed rest trials. However, as indicated above, given the small sampling area of the laser-Doppler flow probes, it is doubtful that the probes were placed at the exact location between trials.

Hypothesis #3: Assessment of maximal cutaneous vasodilation was accomplished by exposing the subject's left forearm to 42 degrees Celsius for 45 minutes using a cylindrical water spray device that encircled the subject's forearm. A thermocouple was attached to forearm skin within the cylindrical water spray device to verify skin temperature was held at 42 degrees Celsius. Prior to and following the 45-minute heating protocol, the average of six forearm blood flow measurements was obtained using venous occlusion plethysmography. Arterial blood pressure was obtained under both conditions via R-wave triggered auscultation of the brachial artery, and forearm vascular conductance (FVC) was calculated from the ratio of forearm blood flow and mean arterial blood pressure. The units for FVC are ml/100ml tissue/min/100 mmHg, however for clarity these units will be reported as FVC units. Since local heating of the forearm does not alter muscle blood flow, elevations in total forearm blood flow and FVC were due solely to elevations in forearm skin blood flow and forearm cutaneous vascular conductance, respectively.

Hypothesis #4: Two intradermal microdialysis membranes were placed in dorsal forearm skin. Probes were placed a minimum of 3 cm apart and at the same location for both pre- and post-HDT trials. This technique involved placing a small (200 µm outer diameter, 10 mm length) sterile, semi-permeable membrane intradermally using a 25-gauge needle. Both microdialysis membranes were perfused with Ringer's solution at a rate of 2 µl/min via an infusion pump. The protocol commenced once skin blood flow returned to normal levels after needle insertion trauma (~60-120 minutes). Chambers having a small window (10 x 5 mm, i.e., surface area of 0.5 cm2) were positioned over each membrane to measure sweat rate by the ventilated capsule method using compressed nitrogen as the perfusion gas. The gas was delivered at a rate of 150 ml/min. Location of capsule placement was aided through the use of markings on the tubing that indicated the center of the membrane portion of the microdialysis probe. Humidity of the effluent gas was measured via a humidity/temperature probe that was positioned one meter from the capsule on the skin. The humidity/temperature probe connected to a humidity data processor that calculated absolute humidity from the measurement of relative humidity and temperature. Local skin temperature around the microdialysis membranes was maintained at 40 degrees Celsius through the use of a lamp and a thermocouple. Sweat gland function was assessed by perfusing nine doses (1x10-6 to 2 M) of acetylcholine through the microdialysis membranes. Each dose of acetylcholine was administered for 5 minutes, while sweat rate over the microdialysis membranes was continuously recorded. Sweat rate during the final minute of each 5-minute period was averaged and used for the statistical analysis. Sweat rates from both sites were averaged and are reported as a single value for each dose of acetylcholine. Following the acetylcholine challenge, with the sites continuing to be perfused with the highest dose of acetylcholine, the number of activated sweat glands was assessed in triplicate over the microdialysis membranes using the starch-iodine technique.

Hypothesis #5: For this component ten subjects (nine male and one female) participated in the study. Throughout HDT bed rest subjects exercised at 75 percent of pre-bed rest heart rate maximum for 90 minutes per day on a supine cycle ergometer. Heart rate was monitored during these exercise sessions. Immediately prior to beginning HDT bed rest and on the 13th day of bed rest, thermoregulatory responses were assessed throughout 25 minutes of supine cycle ergometry exercise tested in a room held at 28 degrees Celsius. The same absolute workload was performed during both the pre- and post-HDT testing. Upon entering the laboratory, each subject was instrumented with six thermocouples placed on the skin. The weighted average of the six thermocouples was used for the measurement of mean skin temperature (Tsk). Internal temperature (Tcore) was measured by thermister or telemetry pill. A thermister probe measured esophageal temperature and was inserted through the nose to a distance equal to one-quarter of the subject's height. A telemetry pill was used in a subject who refused to insert esophageal temperature probe, and was swallowed two hours before the thermoregulatory response test. Heart rate (HR) was monitored using the ECG. Arterial blood pressure was obtained under both conditions via R-wave triggered auscultation of the brachial artery. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was calculated as one-third of pulse pressure plus diastolic pressure. Skin blood flow (SkBF) on the chest and forearm was measured by laser-Doppler flowmetry, and sweat rate (SR) on the forearm by the ventilated capsule method using compressed nitrogen as the perfusion gas delivered at a rate of 500 ml/min. Cutaneous vascular conductance (CVC) was indexed from the ratio of SkBF to MAP. CVC was normalized relative to maximum CVC obtained via local heating of the skin to 42 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes. Humidity of the effluent gas was measured via a humidity-temperature probe that was positioned one meter from the capsule on the skin. The absolute humidity was calculated from the measurement of relative humidity and room temperature.

RESULTS:
These data were obtained to identify the effects of 14 days HDT bed rest on the control of the microcirculation and sweating. Moreover, the effects of aerobic exercise training during bed rest on the hypothesized impaired responses, as well as on thermoregulatory responses during exercise, were assessed. The primary findings were as follows: a) HDT bed rest does not alter cutaneous post-synaptic vasoconstrictor responsiveness; b) vasoconstriction associated with the venoarteriolar response is impaired following HDT bed rest regardless of whether the subject exercises during bed rest; c) maximal cutaneous vasodilator and sweating responses are impaired following HDT bed rest, however these responses are preserved if the subject exercises during bed rest; and d) aerobic exercise during bed rest preserves thermoregulatory responses previously shown to be attenuated after HDT bed rest.

Hypothesis #1: The mean goodness of fit (R2) of the dose-response model was high both pre- (exercise: 0.94 ± 0.02 and non-exercise: 0.95 ± 0.03) and post- (exercise: 0.93 ± 0.02 and non-exercise: 0.95 ± 0.03) HDT bed rest. Neither HDT bed rest alone nor exercise during HDT bed rest had an effect on the concentration of norepinephrine (NE) that caused 50% of maximal cutaneous vasoconstriction (i.e., EC50, HDT bed rest: P > 0.30; exercise during HDT bed rest: P > 0.15). Similarly, maximal and minimal responses from the dose-response model were not altered by HDT bed rest (maximal: P > 0.30 and minimal: P > 0.40) or exercise during HDT bed rest (maximal: P > 0.50 and minimal: P > 0.15). Finally, no interactions were observed between main factors of the ANOVA for any of the dose-response variables.

Hypothesis #2: The magnitude of forearm vasoconstriction associated with the venoarteriolar response was not affected by HDT bed rest regardless of the group (pre- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 53.1 ± 4.2 percent; post- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 52.2 ± 4.5%; pre- HDT bed rest exercise: 56.6 ± 2.1 percent; post- HDT bed rest exercise: 52.7 ± 3.0 percent). Probability values from the ANOVA were P > 0.30 for HDT bed rest, P > 0.70 for exercise during HDT bed rest, and P > 0.50 for the interaction found between pre/post- HDT bed rest and the exercise/non-exercise main factors. In contrast, cutaneous vasoconstriction of the lower leg due to the venoarteriolar response was significantly attenuated following HDT bed rest in both groups (pre- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 51.0 ± 5.0 percent; post- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 43.0 ± 6.6 percent; pre- HDT bed rest exercise: 48.4 ± 7.4 percent; post- HDT bed rest exercise: 36.4 ± 8.5 percent). Probability values from the ANOVA were P < 0.03 for HDT bed rest, P > 0.50 for exercise during HDT bed rest, and P > 0.60 for the interaction between pre/post- HDT bed rest and the exercise/non-exercise main factors.

Hypothesis #3: In the non-exercise group both maximal FVC (21.5 ± 1.3 to 18.7 ± 1.7 FVC units; P=0.01) and the change in FVC with local heating (i.e., ”FVC; 18.1 ± 1.2 to 15.9 ± 1.7; P=0.01) were significantly attenuated following HDT bed rest. In contrast, in the exercise group, these responses were not significantly different between pre- and post-HDT trials when reported either as maximal FVC (21.8 ± 2.0 to 21.4 ± 2.5 FVC units; P=0.39) or as the increase in FVC due to local heating (17.7 ± 1.9 to 18.4 ± 2.4; P=0.32).

Hypothesis #4: In both the exercise and non-exercise groups the EC50 of the sweating response was unaffected by HDT bed rest. However, maximal stimulated sweat rate for the non-exercise group was significantly attenuated following HDT bed rest (0.63 ± 0.06 to 0.42 ± 0.03 mg/cm2/min; P=0.001), while no significant difference was observed for the exercise group (0.81 ± 0.15 to 0.77 ± 0.10; P=0.31). Regardless of the group, HDT bed rest did not significantly change the number of activated sweat glands during administration of the highest dose of acetylcholine.

Hypothesis #5: Exercise during HDT exposure preserved VO2 max, blood volume, and plasma volume relative to pre-HDT bed rest levels. Internal temperature prior to exercise and at the end of exercise was not different between pre- and post-HDT trial. The onset of sweating and maximal sweat rate during exercise were no different between pre- and post- HDT trials. Moreover, cutaneous vascular responses were also preserved by exercise throughout HDT. Taken together, these data indicate that 90 minutes of exercise throughout HDT bed rest preserves thermoregulatory responses.

experiment_title: Mechanisms for Induction of Bystander Effects by High Energy Particles in Cells and Tissues
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex and unique radiation environment composed of trapped proton and electron radiation, galactic cosmic rays (GCR; energetic protons and heavy charged ions, HZE), and solar particle events (SPE), primarily protons. Although these radiations can result in appreciable cumulative doses to astronauts during long-duration missions, the exposures occur at low fluences and fluence rates, such that particle traversals through individual cells in an astronaut’s body may be well separated in tissue location and time. Under such conditions, so-called non-targeted effects such as bystander responses may have increased significance. The radiation-induced bystander effect is the occurrence of biological responses in unirradiated cells near to or sharing medium with cells actually traversed by radiation. It is hypothesized that at the low fluences of protons and HZE particles to which astronauts are exposed in space, a significant fraction of the cellular changes may be due to bystander responses, in addition to the damages caused in cells directly traversed by ionizing particles or their associated delta rays.

The specific aims for this study are:

  1. Test the hypothesis that bystander effects occur at particle fluences so low that only 1-2 % of cells in a culture dish are traversed by an energetic proton or HZE particle.
  2. Test the hypothesis that cells that have survived an initial traversal and sent a bystander signal, can again send a signal when traversed once again by a particle or can subsequently respond as bystanders to a hit in a neighboring cell by extending low fluence work to studies using repeated exposures of cells to low fluences and mixed (actually sequential) beams of more than one particle type.
  3. Test the hypothesis that non-nuclear damage-initiated, metabolically produced reactive oxygen species (ROS) in hit cells are involved in the early steps of bystander signaling. Chemical countermeasures to reduce the bystander responses based on removal of ROS or prevention of their formation will also be studied. Previous studies have indicated that ROS are at least partially involved in transmittal of the Fe ion-induced bystander signal from hit to unirradiated cells.
  4. Test the hypothesis that radiation-induced bystander signals can be sent between differing cell types, but the characteristics of the responses depend on the cell types and the types of radiation.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
At very low iron ion (1 GeV/n) fluences, i.e., 2-50% of cells traversed by an ion, or very low proton (1 GeV) fluences, i.e., 2-200 protons/cell, there was increased damage in cells in both irradiated and bystander populations. That finding--that about 100-fold lower particle fluence is needed to produce DNA damage in irradiated or bystander populations with Fe ions than with protons of the same energy--suggests that linear energy transfer (LET) or particle track structure, including delta-rays, is a determinant of the minimum dose needed for the effect. Studies with 300 MeV/n Fe ions (higher LET) show a shift to even lower minimum particle fluence for induction of the effect, consistent with LET being important. Ongoing analysis of samples irradiated with silicon and carbon, of intermediate LET, appear to yield consistent data.

The studies with mixed cell types (fibroblasts and keratinocytes) in 2D and with the same cells in a 3D model of epithelial tissue (aim 4) have been completed. The data in monolayers show that with either X-rays or protons (low LET radiations), there is a 1.5-2-fold increase in micronuclei (MN) formation in bystander fibroblasts or keratinocytes after either cell type is irradiated, but there is no significant increase in MN in bystander fibroblasts in co-culture with irradiated keratinocytes.

In the 3D studies, the data in irradiated cells show that the fraction of fibroblasts with DNA damage when irradiated in the 3D constructs is significantly less (4-fold at the shortest time of 1 h) than in cells irradiated in 2D monolayers. With time after irradiation, the fraction of damaged cells decreases such that at 24 h it is back to background in cells in 3D, but remains elevated out to 72 h in cells in 2D. In contrast to the irradiated cells in 3D, the level of damage in the bystander portion of the 3D model is low at 1 h, but increases to a peak at 12 h after protons and a maximum at 24-48 h after Fe ion exposure. The data further show that bystander signals can travel considerable distances (mm) and that, although scavengers have no effect on DNA damage in irradiated cells in 3D, the level of DNA damage in bystander cells in 3D is reduced nearly to control, unirradiated, levels by scavenging hydrogen peroxide, superoxide and nitric oxide in the medium shared by the construct halves, findings similar to those in 2D.

In studies to assess intercellular signaling between normal fibroblasts and tumor cells, this study has shown that there is no bystander signaling with a human chrondrosarcoma cell line (HTB94) irradiated with X-rays, protons or iron ions. However, irradiated HTB94 cells can send signals to bystander fibroblasts, to elicit DNA damage, although the tumor cells do not respond to signals from the fibroblasts.

experiment_title: Effects of Micro-G on Gene Expression in Higher Plants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Although various effects of microgravity at the whole plant, organ, tissue, and cellular levels have been observed, little is known about the molecular mechanisms involved. This experiment studied the effects of microgravity on the expression of auxin-regulated genes in transgenic tomato and tobacco seedlings that express the auxin-inducible GH3 gene promoter-GUS and SAUR gene promoter-GUS fusion genes.

The objective of this experiment was to use transgenic plants that express GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS fusion genes to study the effects of microgravity on expression of auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes, GH3 and SAUR, at the organ and tissue levels.

This experiment provided information about how expression of the auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes is altered in microgravity as compared to the ground controls. It also provided some insights into the effects of microgravity on auxin transport/distribution and/or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in higher plants.

APPROACH:

The BRIC-09 experiment flew on the STS-80 mission that lasted approximately 18 days. The experiment was placed in five BRIC-60 canisters, each containing eleven 60 mm petri plates. Transgenic tomato and tobacco seedlings were grown on the petri plates, which contained five layers of filter paper and one layer of nylon membrane to support seedlings and nutrient media. No inflight manipulation was performed. Ground controls were conducted on a 24-hour delay in the Orbiter Environment Simulator at environmental conditions (temperature, % relative humidity, and CO2) similar to those experienced by the samples during flight.

Upon recovery, three to four representative seedlings from each petri dish were photographed with a camera coupled with a microscope. Forty seedlings from each petri dish were incubated in x-gluc solution for histochemical staining of the GUS activity at 37 degrees C for 12 to 24 hours, and after staining, the seedlings were photographed. All seedlings stained with x-gluc solution were stored in water with sodium azide for further analysis at the investigator's lab. Thirty seedlings from each petri dish were fixed in 5% glutaraldehyde solution for microscopic analysis. One hundred and fifty seedlings (50 seedlings per assay, 3 replicates) from each petri dish were frozen at minus 70 degree C for quantitative assay of GUS activity.

RESULTS:

The results of this study indicate that the expression of both the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS fusion genes was significantly enhanced (2 to 3-fold increases) in space-grown seedlings when compared with the ground control seedlings. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS fusion gene in tobacco plants was dependent on the developmental stage, initially with an activation in cotyledons, followed by an activation in elongating regions of hypocotyls and roots of the space-grown seedlings. As seedlings developed, the expression of the gene was reduced in cotyledons but further enhanced in root elongating regions. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene was relatively higher in vascular tissues and much lower in other tissue types. The expression of the SAUR promoter-GUS gene in the elongating region of hypocotyls in the space-grown seedlings was also significantly higher than in the ground controls. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS genes in space-grown plants strongly suggests that micro-gravity affects auxin transport/distribution or tissue's sensitivity to auxin.

The space-grown seedlings from the BRIC-9 experiment had shorter roots and more and longer root hairs. Increased auxin concentration or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in elongating regions of roots, as indicated by activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene, suggests that auxin is involved in the microgravity mediated reduction in root growth and increases in root hair elongation.

experiment_title: Spaceflight-Induced Changes in Non-Shivering Thermogenesis and Effects on Bone in Mice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this project is to test the hypothesis that spaceflight will compromise the ability of mice to employ huddling and postural strategies to slow heat loss. To maintain body heat, flight animals will become more dependent on a mechanism, non-shivering thermogenesis, which is associated with bone loss. We anticipate that fat metabolism will be increased during spaceflight in response to increased sympathetic outflow (a negative regulator of bone formation). The proposed research will address the mechanism(s) by which the spaceflight environment impacts energy balance. At the completion of this study we expect to show that spaceflight results in increased non-shivering thermogenesis and increased fat oxidation in white adipose tissue. We have obtained and analyzed interscapular brown adipose tissue (BAT) from RR1. The results to date demonstrate upregulation of genes related to energy metabolism, supporting our hypothesis.

APPROACH:
Intraperitoneal white adipose tissue (WAT) is requested from mice flown on the International Space Station and their respective ground controls. We will isolate total cellular RNA from WAT and then measure mRNA levels for enzymes involved in fat metabolism. The results will establish whether the increased thermogenesis associated with activation of BAT has a functional outcome, specifically whether fat oxidation is increased in WAT.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.
