experiment_title: Gravitational Effects on Biofilm Formation During Spaceflight (Micro-2A)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Micro 2A is a follow-on flight to Micro-2 that flew on STS-132. There is an urgent need to understand the effects of microgravity on the growth, cellular physiology, and cell-cell interactions in microbial biofilms. This information can then be used to curtail harmful activities of microbial consortia thriving as biofilms on the International Space Station and for the long-term success of human space exploration. The Micro 2A experiment will study how gravity alters microbial biofilm formation with the goal of developing new strategies to reduce their impact on the operation of spacecrafts and the health of their crew.

APPROACH:

The experiment will compare microbial biofilms formed on membranes in normal gravity and during spaceflight, and examine the influence of mutations affecting bacterial motility on biofilm formation and structure. Assess the effects of newly developed, non-leaching, nanotechnology-based antimicrobial surfaces on biofilm formation during spaceflight and assess their potential to reduce the impact of biofilms in future spacecraft designs. Identify changes in gene expression related to biofilm formation and virulence that occur when cells are cultured during spaceflight.

RESULTS:

Biofilm formation is significantly increased during space flight. Further, we have found that biofilms formed during spaceflight exhibit a novel structure that has not been previously observed and that would be unlikely to form under normal gravity conditions. Our recent experiments included P. aeruginosa motility mutants and replicates with varied nutrient availability. We have observed that changes in motility, carbon source and phosphate availability all modulate biofilm formation and the extent to which P. aeruginosa responds to space flight. Results from these experiments are providing insight into the mechanisms underlying the observed differences between biofilms formed in normal gravity and space flight.

experiment_title: Crew Health
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of the Apollo Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) Crew Health program was to ensure the health and safety of the crewmembers. To achieve this goal, U.S. and USSR medical specialists met on several occasions, from 1972 to 1975, to discuss inflight crew safety, crew transfers, and inflight medical support systems. Representatives from both sides exchanged information about pre-, in- and postflight medical evaluations; a Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program; inflight bioinstrumentation; possible drug kit exchange; drug testing; protocols for inflight crew transfers; and schedules.

APPROACH:
Previous space missions, such as Apollo and Skylab, elucidated four areas of importance in health preventive maintenance:

1) The flight medicine support system and drug (tolerance) testing
2) The work/rest cycle
3) Inflight exercise and bioinstrumentation
4) Food and nutrition

Three months prior to flight, individual drug tolerance testing was conducted to determine the response of the crewmembers to each item in the medical kit. This was done to preclude any allergic reactions or other undesirable side effects inflight.

A series of physical examinations were conducted in order to determine the preflight physical status for the mission and for postflight comparison and to detect any medical problems during the preflight period that would require remedial or preventive intervention. Comprehensive examinations were conducted on all three crewmembers 30, 15 and 5 days prior to launch (L-30, 15, and 5). Abbreviated examinations were scheduled for L-4 to L-1.

A comprehensive examination was also scheduled for recovery day (R+0), with follow-up examinations scheduled for R+1, R+3, and at 48-hour intervals thereafter, until the crewmen's measurements returned to preflight baseline values.

On L-4, each crewman was switched to a low-residue diet and on L-1, each crewman used a Travid enema and two Pericolace tablets to further reduce the fecal content in his bowels. Flight menus were designed to meet individual energy requirements under normal gravity conditions. Total caloric intake requirement was computed before flight from lean body mass measurements.

A modified Apollo Inflight Medical Support System (IMSS), which provided the tools and medications for inflight diagnosis and treatment of possible illness, was utilized for the ASTP mission. Two cardiovascular drugs, quinidine sulfate and dipyridamole, were added to the IMSS medication list in deference to the medical history of one crewmember. In addition to the IMSS, data from the flight bioinstrumentation system would also be used as a diagnostic aid to assist in the recommendation for treatment. Subject B received a 2-hour training session which covered proper use of the available drugs.

During the 21-day preflight crew health stabilization program, the crew was maintained on a nominal work/rest schedule. This schedule allowed for daily exercise periods and at least 7 hours of sleep per night. Each crewman attempted to establish a more operationally desirable sleep/work cycle by going to sleep at approximately 11 p.m. EDT and waking at 9 a.m. EDT.

The health status of the three crewmembers was monitored during flight. Electrocardiographic and respiratory rate data were obtained through the bioinstrumentation data system during launch and on mission days 2, 7, and 8 in conjunction with the exercise periods. Additional data were obtained during the entry phase of the mission. Subject A was not subjected to studies involving radiation procedures because of a history of exposure to high radiation levels.

During reentry, the crew was exposed to toxic gases (mostly nitrogen tetroxide) from inadvertent reaction control system (RCS) firings. In the Mobile Laboratories (MOLAB) aboard the primary recovery ship, oxygen was administered to all three crewmembers for approximately 10 minutes. Because of time constraints, the medical team proceeded with recovery day protocols while the history of exposure to toxic fumes was being reconstructed. Subject A had a short blood draw and went on to the Lower Body Negative Pressure protocol (this protocol was terminated 3 minutes early during the negative 50 mm Hg period because of a drop in the subject's systolic blood pressure).

Once the history of the toxic gas (nitrogen tetroxide) exposure was completed, the MCC flight surgeons decided that all of the planned medical experiments, with the exception of the clinical examinations needed to assess crew health, would be stopped. Daily physical examinations were still conducted on all crewmembers as well as chest X-rays, EKG, and pulmonary function tests. Blood samples were drawn for analysis and microbiological samples were obtained. Follow-up medical evaluations were conducted four weeks after the initial exposure to nitrogen tetroxide (N2O4) vapors to determine if there were any lasting ill effects from the gas exposure.

RESULTS:
Inflight Crew Health Status
Biomedical Instrumentation and Physiological Data - All three crewmembers experienced fullness-of-the-head sensation immediately after entering Earth's orbit. This symptom was mild and did not interfere with crew performance. There were no reports of nasal stuffiness or sinus congestion. Head movements did not provoke symptoms of motion sickness nor were there any instances of nausea, vomiting, disorientation or loss of appetite.

All physiological measurements remained within the expected limits. No medically significant arrhythmias were detected during this mission. Isolated premature heartbeats were observed in all three crewmembers. The fact that the frequency and character of these prematurities remained consistent with data obtained previously during ground-based studies indicated that they were not related to space flight.

On mission day 2, Subject C's exercise harness interfered with his bioinstrumentation electrodes; this resulted in poor quality data which was not suitable for analysis. On mission day 6, because of ground-support technical difficulties, no biomedical data were received in the Mission Control Center (MCC).

Medications - On mission day 3, Subject A notified MCC that he took 3 Lomotil tablets prophylactically in an attempt to decrease the frequency of inflight bowel movements. He took another 2 tablets on mission day 4 because of a loose bowel movement and again took 2 more Lomotil tablets prophylactically on mission day 8 before docking module jettison. Subject B took one scopolamine-dextroamphetamine sulfate tablet (anti-motion-sickness medication) prophylactically immediately after orbital insertion and repeated the dose approximately 5 hours later.

On entry, approximately one hour after the sleep period, Subject A took 2 Actifed tablets prophylactically to prevent possible ear blockage during the entry phase. No medications for sleep were taken at any time during the inflight period.

Postflight Crew Health Status
Recovery - The crew was exposed to toxic gases (mostly N2O4) from inadvertent reaction control system (RCS) firings during the descent phase. During the postflight medical debriefing, Subject A reported that there was a yellowish-brown colored smoke which "smelled like RCS." Once the crew disabled the RCS, and after initial peak exposure, uncontaminated air was drawn into the cabin until landing occurred. Simultaneously, the lithium hydroxide (LiOH) scrubbers continued to absorb the N2O4 mixture.

After the spacecraft landed and while it remained in the inverted position, Subject A unstrapped himself (he fell into the command module tunnel, hurting his right shoulder and elbow), unstowed oxygen masks, and proceeded to provide oxygen to the other crewmembers. Not until the spacecraft had assumed an upright position did Subject A notice that Subject B's mask was hanging on the side of his face and that he was unconscious (it was estimated that he was unconscious for approximately 50 seconds). This loss of consciousness was thought to be due to the combination of exposure to the toxic fumes and the feet being lower than the head. Subject B recovered promptly when the face mask was positioned properly and oxygen flow increased. The total time of crew exposure was 4 minutes 40 seconds, from the closure of the RCS isolation valves until the crew donned oxygen masks after landing.

Initial Recovery Day Physical Findings - In general, the crew complained of burning of the eyes with profuse tearing, burning sensation and itching of the exposed skin surfaces (which subsided shortly after entering the MOLAB), tightness of the chest, retrosternal burning sensation, and an inability to inhale deeply ( which led to a nonproductive and nonspasmodic cough). The 3 astronauts were in no acute distress and were oriented to times, persons, and place. The results of examinations of the skin and mucosa were within normal limits. Detailed neurological examination showed only slight fine tremors of the fingers. Slight hyperreflexia of the deep tendon reflexes was noted. Physical examination of the endocrine system was normal and the peripheral vascular system was in good condition. Generally, the musculoskeletal system was within normal limits, as well. Chest x-rays of all 3 crewmen failed to reveal any signs of pulmonary involvement. Electrocardiographic tracings were within normal limits and identical with baseline data.

Subject A's right shoulder and elbow showed slight tenderness on palpation; there was no bruising or limitation of motion. Subject C experienced some limitation of motion in the lumbar region of the spine and a straightening of the lordosis. This was caused by a strain sustained during inflight exercise. Subject C also had a minor bruise over the right temporal region and the right patella. During the physical examination, following five minutes in the standing position, Subject B experienced a drop in systolic blood pressure to 50 mm Hg with no audible readouts for the diastolic blood pressure. He complained of generalized weakness. The test was halted and he was returned to the supine position where he recovered from the orthostatic episode after about 3 minutes.

For the remainder of the evening, the crewmembers did not exhibit any significant changes in general symptomatology. Following showers and dinner, the crewmen were transferred to sick bay for rest and further observation. There they spent a relatively quiet evening with only occasional interruptions due to coughing.

Subsequent Course of Events - The astronauts again underwent physical examinations on the day after landing (R+1); examination results were unremarkable. However, all crewmembers reported a slight tightness of the chest and a more pronounced inability to breathe deeply without coughing. In fact, they were unable to hold their breaths and to perform the forced expiratory maneuvers required for repeat pulmonary function tests.

Shortly after chest X-rays were taken, and while brushing his teeth, Subject C experienced slight shortness of breath, developed giddiness, and fainted; he was unconscious for about one minute. There was a slight twitching of the eyelids without evidence of seizure activity. He recovered quickly when placed in the supine position. The episode was attributed to orthostatic intolerance.

The repeat chest exams revealed the presence of diffuse, nodular-type infiltrates throughout both lung fields. A rosette-type pattern with occasional confluence of the infiltrates was present. Both costodiaphragmatic angles were clear with no evidence of pleural effusion, Kerley B lines, or increased pulmonary vasculature. There was no prominence of the pulmonary artery and no signs indicative of the left or right heart involvement. These findings were suggestive of alveolar exudative fillings, characteristic of a diffuse chemical pneumonitis. Each astronaut was given 16 mg of dexamethasone intravenously and then transferred to the Tripler Army Medical Center in Honolulu, Hawaii, for further medical care.

Additional chest x-rays revealed an increase of the infiltrates (which was more pronounced on Subject C's x-ray). Blood gas study results indicated mild respiratory alkalosis with hyperventilation and hypoxemia. A decision was made to switch to oral steroid therapy, which consisted of daily doses of 80 mg of Prednisone. Because of the lack of symptomatology and the absence of cyanosis and/ or signs of severe anoxia, oxygen was not administered. Vital signs remained stable, and there was no evidence of cardiac rhythm disturbances. Throughout their stay in the hospital, the crewmen remained afebrile and vital signs remained normal.

The crewmembers continued to experience discomfort with deep inspiration, but this gradually decreased. By R+3, these symptoms had subsided. By R+5, chest x-rays had returned to normal and the crew was released from the hospital on R+6. Corticosteroid administration was gradually tapered then discontinued on R+9. A period of rest, reconditioning and observation followed. Daily medical evaluations remained within normal limits. All crewmembers participated in mild exercise under medical supervision and eventually improved their physical endurance. They returned to regular duties by R+14.

The follow-up medical evaluations performed 4 weeks after the initial exposure established that there were no obvious residual aftereffects from the exposure to the toxic fumes.

experiment_title: Microbiological Investigations of the Mir Space Station and Flight Crew
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microorganisms are ubiquitous in spacecraft environments, as they are on Earth. Microbes pose several risks to humans in space including: infectious diseases, allergies, degradation of air quality (e.g., release of volatiles), release of toxins, degradation of critical materials, and systems failure (e.g., water reclamation system). Maintaining the health and performance of humans in closed microgravity environments while reusing reclaimed air and water is a daunting task. Determining medical and technological risks that are dependent on microbiological factors during long-term space flight is a vital problem in theory, as well as practice. In such a closed environment, humans will be a major source of microbes released into the spacecraft. Animals and plants, when present, will also be significant contributors to the overall bioburden. Suitable containment and purification technologies are essential. Studies of microbial ecology in spacecraft have been mostly limited to short (<30 days) duration missions in the US program. Similar studies have been conducted during long-duration missions in the Russian program. The Mir space station provided an opportunity for a relatively comprehensive US-Russian joint study of the crewmembers and the environment of the Mir.

The success of long-duration space missions will depend on our ability to mitigate the adverse effects of microorganisms. This will require a much better understanding of the microbiology of closed environments and the human-microbe-environment interactions than are currently available. This joint US-Russian investigation was an important first step in gaining this understanding.

The investigators hypothesized that during long-term space flight (>30 days) human microbiota and the microbial ecology of the Mir station will undergo quantitative and qualitative changes. The objectives of this study were to 1) characterize microbiota of crewmembers, air, surface, and water before, during, and after a long-duration mission aboard the Mir Space Station, 2) determine the exchange and distribution of microbes among crewmembers, and 3) assess the distribution and dynamics of crew microbiota throughout the Mir Space Station.

APPROACH:
Crew microbiology
Pre and postflight, microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, scapula, axilla, groin, feces, and urine were collected and examined for bacteria and fungi. Feces were also examined for ova and parasites. In-flight microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, scapula, axilla, and groin were collected with the Crew Microbiology Kit (CMK). Quantification and isolation of organisms was performed by, preparing serial dilutions of each sample and spread-plating those samples onto selective media. Any aerobic bacteria or fungi isolated were identified using a Vitek Automated Identification System, Biolog Automated Identification System, or classical means. Species that were not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification.

Air microbiology
Air samples were collected from the Shuttle middeck and flightdeck, pre, in, and postflight using the Microbial Air Sampler (MAS). In-flight air samples were also collected from and Mir with the MAS. Mir sampling locations included the area of the Commander's seat (Core Module), area of the dining table (Core Module), in the Commander's cabin (Core Module), and in the Kristall Module hatch. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

Surface microbiology
Surface samples were collected from the Shuttle pre, in, and post flight. Shuttle sample areas included the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System in the middeck, the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through, and the half-moon shaped air vent for the Commander's chair in the flight deck. In-flight surface samples were collected from the Shuttle and Mir with the Surface Sampler Kit (SSK). Mir sampling locations included the Commander's seat post #1 (Core Module), the dining table (Core Module), the Commander's cabin wall (Core Module), the right handle of the treadmill (Core Module), and the wall above the hatch in the Kristall Module. Once during the NASA 3 mission, a sample from the galley water dispenser needle was collected. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

Water microbiology
Water samples were collected from the Shuttle pre and postflight. Tank A was sampled preflight, and tanks A and B were sampled postflight. In-flight water samples from the Mir were collected and processed with the Water Experiment Kit (WEK). Mir sampling locations included the galley hot and coldwater ports, and the SVO-VZ port. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

Food packet microbiology
During the NASA 4 mission, a food packet was contaminated due to a puncture in the packaging material. A sample was obtained and processed similar to the procedure used for the shuttle surface sample.

'Free' surface sample
During NASA 6 and 7, crewmembers came in contact with 'free' surface condensate in various locations during housekeeping procedures. Representative samples were collected for evaluation of any potential risks that the crewmembers might be exposed to. The samples were collected using the Contingency Water Quality Kit (CWQK), this being assembled from hardware components contained within the Water Experiment Kit (WEK). The condensates were aspirated into a 60cc syringe, and then expelled into a 300 ml sample bag. These samples were returned to ground for complete analyses. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.

RESULTS:
CREW MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3/Mir 22
6 subjects were sampled pre and post flight, three of which were also sampled in-flight. No significant changes were apparent in the aerobic bacteria isolated from the pre-, in-, and postflight specimens. Staphylococcus aureus was the bacterial species used to follow microbial dissemination from crewmember to crewmember and throughout the Mir environment. Crewmembers 1 and 2 were the prime crewmembers that were replaced one week before flight; S. aureus was recovered only once from the nose on each of these crewmembers. Candida albicans was also recovered once from the throat of Crewmember 2. S. aureus was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 3 twice preflight and once postflight. This bacterium was also recovered from the nose of this crewmember at all preflight sampling sessions, three of four in-flight sessions, and two of three postflight sessions; the organism was occasionally isolated from this person's skin, urine, and feces samples. Candida albicans, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the feces of Crewmember 3 once postflight. S. aureus was recovered from the throat, nose, hand, and axilla of Crewmember 4 at L-2 days. Enterobacter cloacae, Aeromonas hydrophila, and Enterobacter hormaechei were isolated from the throat of Crewmember 4 at L-2 days; E. cloacae were also isolated from the nose at this sampling time. Yeast was present in 5 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 4 at R+0; Serratia liquefaciens was isolated from the hand at this collection period. Specimens from Crewmember 5 frequently had S. aureus isolated; is was present in the nose at 6 of 11 sampling periods. Once during flight, the organism was present in 4 of 7 samples. At R+0, it was recovered from 4 of 9 specimens, from 5 of 9 at R+7, and from 5 of 9 at R+11. At L-59, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 5; Pseudomonas aeruginosa was isolated from the throat at L-2. S. aureus was not recovered from Crewmember 6.

NASA 4
One crewmember was sampled pre, in, and postflight. Opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from the throat at several sampling times: Panteola agglomerans on FD19, Pastuerella multicoida, Serratia odifera, Serratia species, Enterobacter gergoviae on FD117, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa on landing day. Candida albicans, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the throat 143 days before flight. Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from the nose at landing. Organisms recovered from the hand included Acinetobacter haemolyticus on L-9 and Enterococcus faecalis and Serratia marcescens on FD117. Candida albicans was recovered from the groin on FD117, and was present in the feces before and after flight. Enterococcus faecalis was present in low numbers in the urine on landing day and 5 days thereafter.

NASA 5/Mir 24
3 crewmembers were scheduled to be sampled pre, in, and postflight. The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on all crewmembers on FD15, FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135, was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. A number of opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from 5 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 1 at the L-10 sampling period. Staphylococcus aureus, a potential pathogen, was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 1 at all postflight sampling periods; this organism was also recovered from the throat at R+0.
Several opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from 4 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 2 at the L-11 day sampling period. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 2 at all sampling periods; this organism was also recovered from the throat and groin at R+0. Candida species, an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the throat at all three postflight sampling periods.
Opportunistic gram negative rods were only occasional recovered from Crewmember 3. Klebsiella pnuemoniae was isolated from the groin at R+0 and from the nose at R+14 days. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 3 at L-28 days; this organism was recovered from the throat and hand at R+14 days. Candida species, was isolated from the throat and feces during both preflight and postflight sampling periods.

NASA 6/Mir 25
3 subjects were sampled pre and postflight. The opportunistic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus as well as Candida albicans (a yeast) were recovered from the throat of Crewmember 1 during both of the preflight sampling times. Staphylococcus aureus was also recovered from the nose of this crewmember at all three sampling times. Enterobacter cloacae were isolated from the throat of Crewmember 1 at L-21; at L-14, Candida albicans was recovered from the feces. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 2 on landing day and from the nose at the L-9 and R+0 sampling times; Candida albicans was isolated from the feces on L-9 and was too numerous to count in the throat at R+0. On landing day, Crewmember 2 exhibited a colony count of too numerous to count from the urine; the organism recover from this specimen was Staphylococcus species and was probably a contaminant. Enterobacter aerogenes was isolated from the throat and nose of Crewmember 3 on landing day. Candida albicans was recovered from this crewmember's throat at L-9 and R+0 (too numerous to count), and from the urine at R+0. Penicillium species (too numerous to count) and Candida parapsilosis were also present in the nose of Crewmember 3 on landing day. Staphylococcus aureus is frequently a resident of the nasal passages; Candida species are ubiquitous yeasts, being found as normal flora of the alimentary tract and mucocutaneous membranes.

NASA 7
One crewmember was sampled pre and postflight. The opportunistic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose at all three sampling times. No clinical symptoms were experienced by the crewmember as a result of the presence of this organism. Staphylococcus aureus is frequently a resident of the nasal passages.

AIR MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3 and STS-79
Fungal levels were often above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Enterococcus faecalis was isolated from the area of the dining table and in the Commander's cabin on FD52. On FD80, both bacterial and fungal levels in three of four Mir sampling locations greatly exceeded the US standard of 1000 CFU/m3 proposed for the International Space Station (ISS).
The highest bacterial level observed during any of the Shuttle sampling sessions was 319 CFU/m3, found in the middeck of STS-79 at R+0. The highest fungal level observed on the Shuttle was 550 CFU/m3 in the flight deck of STS-79 at R+0.

NASA 4 and STS-81
On board the Mir in the area near the commander's chair, the bacteria Aeromonas hydrophila and Comamonas testosteroni were recovered on FD53. Bacteria recovered from the area of the dining table included Staphylococcus aureus on FD80 and Pseudomonas putida on FD117; fungi isolated from this same area included Aspergillus niger and two species of the yeast Candida. The bacterium Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was isolated from the commander's cabin on FD19 and FD80; Sphingobacterium spiritovorum and Chryseobacterium meningosepticum were also recovered on FD80. Candida guilliermondii was recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD117; Sphingomonas paucimobilis and Candida fumata were isolated during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3 in all sampling locations at all sampling times. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only occasionally exceeded, e.g. in the area of the commander's seat on FD80, in the area of the dining table on FD117, and in the Kristall Module hatch on FD80 and FD117. Onboard the Shuttle, the fungal levels increased during the docked phases of STS-81.

NASA 5 and STS-84
The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135, was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. The in-flight recording of data from Mir samples collected on FD19 was received.
On board the Mir, Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the area of the dining table during the docked phase of STS-84; Sphingomonas paucimobilis and Candida famata were isolated from the area of the Kristall module during this same sampling session. On FD19, Mir bacterial levels slightly exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3 in 3 of the four sampling sites. Fungal levels were above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3 in all sampling locations at all sampling times. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only occasionally exceeded, e.g. in the area of the commander's seat and in the Commander's cabin on FD19. Onboard the Shuttle, the fungal levels increased during the docked phase of STS-84.
 

NASA 6 and STS-86
On board the Mir, in the area of the dining table, the fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated on FD29. Bacillus cereus was recovered from this location of FD 54 and FD100; Staphylococcus aureus recovered on FD100. Fungi recovered from the area of the commander's cabin included Aspergillus niger on FD54. This same fungi was also recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD54. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were always above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only exceeded once in the area of the Commander's seat on FD54 and once in the area of the dining table on FD29.
Onboard the Shuttle, the bacterial and fungal levels exceeded acceptability limits in the Middeck on FD5 of STS-86 during the docked phase. Aspergillus niger was recovered in low numbers from the Flight Deck during the pre-docked phase of STS-86.
 

NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91
On board the Mir in the area near the commander's chair, the fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated; yeast recovered from this location included Rhodotorula rubra on FD43, Candida guilliermondii on FD 119, and an unidentified yeast on FD 135. Bacteria recovered from the area of the dining table included Pseudomonas fluorescens on FD119. Bacteria isolated from the commander's cabin included Serratia marcescens on FD78, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia on FD119, and Pasteurella haemolytica on FD135. Aspergillus niger was recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD135; The bacterium Serratia liquefaciens was recovered from all of the locations during multiple sampling periods; these included site 4 on FD 43, sites 1,2, and 4 on FD78, and from all sampling sites on FD 119. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were frequently above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3. This amount was only exceeded once in the Kristall Module hatch on FD43.
Onboard the shuttle, the fungus Aspergillus niger was isolated during the pre-docked phase of STS-89 in the Flight Deck. The yeast Candida guilliermondii was isolated during the docked phase of STS-91 in the Middeck; however, the bacterial and fungal levels never exceeded acceptability limits.

SURFACE MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3 and STS-79
Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded both US and Russian standards; fungal levels exceeded the standards only once during the mission. S. aureus was isolated from the Commander's seat (post #1) on FD24. Yeasts were isolated from the dining table on FD24, FD52, and FD80 of the NASA 3 mission, as well as during the docked phase of STS-81. During the docked phase with STS-79 and on FD52, yeast was recovered from the wall in the Commander's cabin. In the Kristall Module hatch, yeast was isolated on FD109; Serratia liquefaciens was found during the docked phase of STS-81.
Both bacterial and fungal levels during all of the sampling sessions for STS-79 were within the US limits proposed for ISS. The yeast Cryptococcus albidus was isolated from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System in the middeck at both preflight sampling periods of STS-79; an unidentified yeast was isolated from the same location during the docked phase with Mir. No yeast was recovered from any location after landing.

NASA 4 and STS-81
Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2, but exceeded the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS only once. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 included Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD19, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria, Pseudomonas putida, and an unidentified gram negative rod on FD53, as well as an unidentified gram negative rod on FD80. Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was isolated at 4 of the 6 sampling periods from the dining table; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Rhodotorula rubra (a yeast) during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-81, Aspergillus niger on FD19, Aeromonas hydrophila on FD53, Candida parapsilosis on FD117, and Sphingomonas paucimobilis during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. From the commander's cabin wall, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was again isolated at 4 of the 6 sampling periods; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Aeromonas caviae, Sphingomonas paucimobilis, and Vibrio alganolyticus on FD19, Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD80, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and an unidentified gram negative rod on FD117, and Aspergillus niger during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Bacteria isolated from the handle of the treadmill included Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria on FD53 and Chryseomonas luteola on FD80. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the Kristall Module hatch on FD117 and during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Bacterium also recovered from this location were Serratia liquefaciens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia during the during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-81, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria on FD19, Aeromonas caviae on FD53, and Sphingomonas paucimobilis during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. On STS-81, both bacterial and fungal levels exceeded US limits at R+0 at the same air vent.

The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. The in-flight recording of data from Mir samples collected on FD19 was received. Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2, but never exceeded the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. On FD5, Sphingomonas paucimobilis was recovered from the dining table and Kristall module hatch; Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was recovered from the dining table and the commander's cabin wall. Staphylococcus aureus was also isolated on FD5 from the dining table and Kristall module hatch.

NASA 6 and STS-86
Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2 as well as above the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS once. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 (site 1) included Vibrio alginolyticus on FD54. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was isolated from the dining table (site 2) on FD28; an unidentified Gram negative rod was recovered from this location was on FD54. Rhodotorula glutinis, a yeast, was isolated from the handle of the treadmill (site 4) on FD100. The bacterium Pasteurella haemolytica was recovered from the Kristall Module hatch (site 5) on FD54.

NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91
Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 included Serratia marcescens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia on FD78, and Pasteurella haemolytica on FD135. The fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated from this site on FD43; yeast recovered from this location included Candida parapsilosis on FD78 and an unidentified yeast on FD135. Pseudomonas stutzeri and Serratia marcescens were isolated from the dining table on FD43; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Klebsiella pneumoniae and Rhodotorula rubra on FD78, and Serratia fonticola on FD119. From the commander's cabin wall, Serratia liquefaciens was recovered on FD43 and Aspergillus niger on FD78. Bacteria isolated from the handle of the treadmill included Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD43; Aspergillus niger was recovered on FD43. Serratia liquefaciens and Aspergillus niger were recovered again from the Kristall Module hatch on FD43.
Onboard the Shuttle, Aspergillus niger, Candida parapsilosis, and Candida guilliermondii were recovered from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System during the docked phase of STS-89. Yeast recovered from the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through included Candida guilliermondii during the docked phase of the STS-89. Acinetobacter lwofii was recovered from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System during the sampling session performed 26 days before the launch of STS-91. Yeast recovered from the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through included Candida guilliermondii and Candida parapsilosis during the docked phase of STS-91. Acinetobacter lwofii was recovered from the half-moon shaped vent for the Commander's chair in the Flight Deck one day before the launch of STS-91.

WATER MICROBIOLOGY
NASA 3 and STS-79
All but one of the Mir hot water samples had no bacterial growth, indicating that the rigorous treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is well able to maintain the quality of water from this source at standards well below the US and Russian maximum limits. Burkholderia cepacia was the only bacterial contaminant recovered from the Shuttle potable water system; this organism is frequently recovered from this system. Tank B represents pre-treated water, and predictably contained many bacteria.

NASA 4 and STS-81
All Mir hot water samples were within the US acceptability limits set for the International Space Station. All but one of the Mir hot water samples had no bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria.

NASA 5 and STS-84
The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD15, FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135 was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. Pre and postflight samples from STS-84 were analyzed.
All Mir hot water samples were within the US acceptability limits set for the International Space Station. The one Mir hot water sample had a bacterial level of only 20 CFU/100 ml, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria.

NASA 6 and STS-86
None of the Mir hot water samples had bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. SVO-ZV samples predictably contained a moderate number of bacteria.

NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91
None of the Mir hot water samples had bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria.
During the first water sampling session of the mission, the NASA 7 crewmember reported the presence of "brown specks" in the unprocessed sample. The crewmember was instructed to proceed with the sample processing and retain the sample collection bag for return to ground. All of the samples that were collected during the mission were returned to Earth. Analysis was based on the descriptions given by the crewmember during debrief, by visual inspection of the sample collection bags which were returned to ground, and by chemical analysis of the discolored water. Upon inspection of the bags, laboratory personnel did not observe any type of particulate present. However, in four of five bags that were returned, there was a small amount of discolored water in one of the two valve stems present on the bags. Chemical analysis showed that the water was found to contain sodium thiosulfate. Each sample bag contains a small amount of sodium thiosulfate, a chemical that is added to the bags before flight to neutralize the biocide (silver) used in the Russian water reclamation system. The cause of this observation noted by the crewmember has not been conclusively determined. One possible cause could have been inadequate temperature control of the Water Experiment Kit. It is known that elevated temperatures will cause a yellowish-brown discoloration of this compound.

FOOD PACKET
The microorganisms present seem to be of environmental origin, rather than contamination of the food.

'FREE' SURFACE CONDENSATE
NASA 6
A sample of 'free' surface condensate was collected on FD113 and returned to ground on STS-89 for complete analyses. Upon visual examination of the sample, the following observations were noted: the sample was cloudy with a brown particulate matter present. A wet mount preparation resulted in the rare observation of amoeba (Figure 1) and ciliated protozoa (Figure 2). Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed the presence of rod- and spirochete-form bacteria (Figure 3). Selected staining techniques resulted in no ova or parasites being observed. Culturing was performed using selective media for the detection of aerobes and fungi. A wide variety of bacteria were present in the samples. The bacteria isolated were of types that will grow in different environmental conditions and can tolerate a wide temperature range. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family (organisms of enteric origin) that were isolated, such as the genera Serratia and Yersinia, can colonize sites in healthy hosts. The presence of these organisms is noteworthy in that they are opportunistic pathogens and can cause disease in immuno-compromised hosts. Other bacteria that were isolated, such as Flavobacterium meningosepticum, are rarely of clinical significance but may occasionally cause wound infections.

NASA 7
Two samples of 'free' surface condensate were collected on FD127 and returned to ground on STS-91 for complete analyses. Upon visual examination of each sample, the following observations were noted: the "slimy" sample was cloudy with a brown particulate matter present; the "fresh" sample was slightly cloudy with a white particulate matter present. A wet mount preparation resulted in the rare observation of dust mites and showed the presence of a few ciliated protozoa. Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed the presence of rod- and spirochete-form bacteria. Selected staining techniques resulted in no ova or parasites being observed. Culturing was performed using selective media for the detection of aerobes, anaerobes, fungi, Legionella spp., and mycobacteria. A wide variety of bacteria were present in both samples. The bacteria isolated were of types that will grow in different environmental conditions and can tolerate a wide temperature range. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family (organisms of enteric origin) that were isolated, such as the genera Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia and Yersinia, can colonize sites in healthy hosts. The presence of these organisms is noteworthy in that they are opportunistic pathogens and can cause disease in immuno-compromised hosts. Although a presumptive identification of Legionella spp. was reported, final pneumophila species identification was not confirmed. Other bacteria that were isolated, such as Comamonas spp., Flavobacterium meningosepticus and Pseudomonas fluorescens, are rarely of clinical significance but may occasionally cause wound infections.

CONCLUSIONS:
Overall, the microbiota of all crewmembers sampled was characteristic of healthy individuals. When present the fungal isolates recovered from specimens generally represented common environmental contaminants. No significant changes were found during spaceflight or upon return to earth relative to preflight results.

Amounts of microorganisms observed in the air and on surfaces of the Shuttle and Mir station were mostly within the acceptability limits set by the US for the ISS. The types of organisms recovered were consistent with previous findings from both Shuttle and Mir missions. Fungal levels of the air samples collected on the Mir were often above the limits set for this station; however, no major adverse health effects were seen in the crewmembers. The temporal fluctuations in levels of organisms probably reflect changes in environmental characteristics, such as temperature and humidity, at the time of sample collection.

The bacterial load of the Shuttle water samples were consistent with those seen on previous missions. All Mir galley hot water samples were within the standards set for both the Mir and the ISS. All isolates were consistent with findings from previous Shuttle and Mir missions.

The hardware designed for in-flight microbial monitoring performed nominally.

Collection and examination of 'free' surface condensate can prove to be a valuable tool in assessing the overall condition of the health of a closed environmental system such as a space station.

Although many potential pathogens were isolated from the surfaces, air and "free" surface condensate, it is interesting to note that the microbial flora of the crewmembers remained that of healthy individuals and that these microorganisms imposed no adverse health effects.

experiment_title: Commercial Biomedical Testing Module (CBTM)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Commercial Biomedical Testing Module: Effects of Osteoprotegerin on Bone Maintenance in Microgravity (CBTM) provides the capability to use the microgravity environment for evaluation of new pharmaceutical candidates in small mammals. Results may expedite the review of new pharmaceuticals for allowing immediate access to new disease treatments.

Osteoporosis is a debilitating disease that afflicts millions of people worldwide. One of the physiological changes experienced by astronauts during spaceflight is the accelerated loss of bone mass due to the lack of gravitational loading on the skeleton. This bone loss experienced by astronauts is similar to osteoporosis in the elderly population. Osteoprotegerin (OPG), a bone metabolism regulator, is being considered by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a new treatment for osteoporosis.

APPROACH

Laboratory mice were treated with either OPG or a placebo before launch. The mice were housed in an Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) designed specifically for spaceflight. This experiment provided a preclinical trial model to determine the effectiveness of OPG in treating bone loss.

RESULTS:

Mice exposed to microgravity exhibited a 15 - 20 percent decline in femur elastic strength and a 40 - 60 percent decrease in bone formation when compared to the controls. The femur elastic strength decline was caused by three mechanisms: reduced bone formation, increased bone resorption, and inhibition of mineralization. OPG treatment in mice exposed to microgravity nearly reversed the decline in strength and the increase in bone resorption found in untreated mice.

Gene expression data is available in the NASA GeneLab Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/ (accession number GLDS-21, Effects of spaceflight on murine skeletal muscle gene expression).

experiment_title: Patterns of Energy Deposition by HZE Particles in Cellular Targets
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
HZE particles are part of the Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) which exist in deep space and cannot be shielded completely inside spacecraft. However, little is known about the interaction of HZE particles with the human body. This study will focus on leukemia, i.e., on the bone/bone-marrow interface from realistic mouse or human dimensions down to single cells. The latency time of leukemia is 2-3 years which coincides more or less with the mission time for the planned expedition to Mars.

The interpretation of data from mechanistic studies on radiation biology requires detailed descriptions of the local patterns of energy deposition in the appropriate cellular or sub-cellular sites to explore the effects of radiation quality on biological response.

The objective of this project is to provide Monte Carlo (MC) simulations on the local patterns of energy deposition by HZE particles in the appropriate cellular environment including effects of micro-, and macro-geometrical considerations. More specifically, this investigation aims to:

1. Determine the frequency of energy deposition in the target regions of importance to the initiation of leukemia in laboratory animals. Volumes appropriate to chromosomal damage in cell nuclei (micrometer dimensions) and local damage to DNA (nanometer dimensions) will be explored for HZE ions, including iron, silicon, and protons. Calculations will be made for similar volumes for low-LET radiation such as 250 kVp x-rays and 60Co gamma rays for comparison of RBE effects.

2. Determine the relative probability of damage cluster formation in volumes comparable to DNA strand break formation. Determination of the relative probability of event size clusters from a few to many events per nanometer can provide the quantitative information necessary to correlate radiation quality with reparability of lesion damage

3. Determine the effects of bone and bone marrow geometry on the frequency of energy deposition events in hematopoietic tissue structures, such as the cell nuclei and DNA. This information is particularly important in efforts to scale biological response from animals to human bone structures.

4. Determine the effects of experimental structures on the dose to blood forming organs. The supporting experimental structures required to position animals, tissues, and cells for irradiation in the HZE beam line can influence the local patterns of energy deposition in the targets of interest. Because of the energetic secondary particles that can be produced when HZE particles interact with tissue and support structures, effects of charged particle equilibrium, or the lack thereof, might have profound effects on local energy deposition

APPROACH:
Calculations focused on interpretation of microscopic “event” or “dose” distributions appropriate to studies of HZE radiation induced leukemia in animal and cellular models [NSCOR Program, Colorado State University, R. Ulrich, PI] and those encountered in the production of clustered damage in DNA [e.g., Brookhaven National Laboratory, B Sutherland, PI].

Progenitor cells for leukemia are haematopoietic stem cells that are located in clusters within marrow cavities having dimensions on the order of a few hundred microns. These cavities are surrounded by trabecular bone matrix, which forms a wall of several hundred microns thickness around the marrow. The dimensions and geometry of the bone marrow are too irregular for direct dosimetry measurements and dose-averaging methods are inappropriate for chronic low dose-rate (single particle) exposures.

Detailed Monte Carlo charged particle track structure simulation provided quantitative information on spatial patterns of energy deposition in cellular targets of dimensions as small as a few nanometers on a particle-by-particle basis; these distributions were the starting point to characterize the detailed nature of radiation-induced damage produced by high-LET radiation.

The modeling approach combined the capabilities of full event-by-event Monte Carlo track simulation codes with codes employing condensed history capabilities; the latter was more appropriate for the description of high-energy secondary electrons. The event-by-event ion code PROTRAC (which is part of the biophysical simulation tool PARTRAC) developed at GSF Neuherberg for protons and alpha particles will be extended for heavy charged particle (HZE) interactions using appropriate relativistic theory. Generated secondary electrons that traverse specific regions of interest, e.g., bone marrow cells or their nuclei, were followed also event-by-event using ETRAC (the electron transport code of PARTRAC) whereas electron transport in adjoining tissues and the surrounding structural material will be followed by the more computer efficient condensed history general purpose MC transport code PENELOPE developed at the University of Barcelona. Appropriate interaction cross sections for a wide range of target materials will be added to the ETRAC and PROTRAC codes, specifically to explore the effects of bone-tissue interfaces on energy deposition in bone marrow cells. Comparison of the spatial pattern of energy deposited in volumes of interest obtained from models of the HZE particles with that obtained from low-LET radiation will provide a firm basis to interpret radiation quality effects on biological response and the mathematical structure developed is amenable to scaling to volumes appropriate to human dimensions for considerations of risk assessment.

RESULTS:
A simple, non-bone-site-specific, non-species specific, and computationally-efficient geometrical model for trabecular spongiosa was developed using the general purpose Monte Carlo code PENELOPE.

Internal dimensions for human models were obtained from path-length distributions as measured in different human bones. The murine model, referred to as the scaled mouse model, consists of the human model scaled by a factor of 0.1. Internal dimensions of murine bones published in the literature strongly suggest that simple scaling of the human model suffice.

The track structure transport code PARTRAC has been extended to transport HZE particles (bare heavy ions) through liquid water to energies up to 1 GeV/u.

The optical constants of metallic calcium were determined and the dielectric response function was modeled in a suitable way to use it for cross section calculations at relativistic energies. Total and energy differential interaction cross sections were calculated as well as stopping powers, straggling parameter and mean free paths for calcium. The cross sections and a transport model for calcium remain to be implemented into PARTRAC.

In combining the geometry with electron and HZE transport in a simple, but not too efficient, way, a hybrid transport code was created. Simulations of an external pencil beam of heavy ions (4He, 16O, 28Si, and 56Fe) in the energy range from 10 to 300 MeV/u were performed.

Microdosimetric concepts were used to characterize the energy deposition within the bone/bone-marrow geometry. In particular, the spongiosa deposition factor (SDF) was used as the dosimetric quantity for interspecies comparisons. The SDF is defined as the ratio of energy deposited in the marrow to the energy deposited in the spongiosa. It also serves for comparisons between different ions used in irradiation of a single species. There is a substantial difference in SDF values between human and mice models for incident energies below 50 MeV/u. This can be attributed to the attenuation of the incident particles, charge particle equilibrium (or the lack of), and the Bragg-peak location. However, for incident energies above 50 MeV/u the same SDF values (except for alpha particles) were seen for both the human and murine models. This strongly suggests that scaling or extrapolating from mouse model findings to human risks should be possible, at least for sufficient fast HZE particles.

experiment_title: Defining the Relationship Between Biomarkers of Oxidative and Inflammatory Stress and the Risk for Atherosclerosis in Astronauts During and After Long-duration Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Future human space travel will primarily consist of long-duration missions onboard the International Space Station (ISS) or exploration class missions to Mars, its moons, or nearby asteroids. These types of missions will put astronauts at risk of increased oxidative and inflammatory damage primarily from radiation, but also from psychological stress, reduced physical activity, diminished nutritional standards and, in the case of extravehicular activity, hyperoxic exposure. There is evidence that increased oxidative damage and inflammation can accelerate the development of atherosclerosis. The purpose of this experiment is to identify biomarkers of oxidative and inflammatory stress and to correlate them to indices of atherosclerosis risk before, during, and after long-duration space flight. The team will measure a number of blood and urine biomarkers, some of which have previously shown to be elevated with space flight. Furthermore, arterial structure and function via ultrasound measures of carotid intima-media thickness, arterial stiffness, and brachial artery flow-mediated dilation will be measured before, during, and after flight. Carotid intima-medial thickness has been shown to be an indicator for prediction of atherosclerosis. Measures of both pulse wave velocity and artery longitudinal displacement are established echocardiographic indices of vascular stiffness. Brachial artery flow-mediated dilation is an index of endothelium-dependent vasodilatation, which is a sensitive predictor of atherosclerotic risk. The investigators hypothesize that these biomarkers of oxidative and inflammatory stress will be increased with space flight and will correlate with decreased flow-mediated dilation, increased carotid intima-medial thickness, and increased vascular stiffness. Furthermore, they hypothesize that measures of oxidative stress will return to baseline after flight, but that biomarkers of inflammatory stress and vascular indices of atherosclerosis risk will remain elevated. This is the first study to propose assessing atherosclerotic risk using biochemical, structural and functional measures during, immediately after, and for up to five years after landing.

The objectives of this experiment are:

  1. To determine the effects of long-duration space flight on measures of inflammatory and oxidative stress.
  2. To determine the effects of long-duration space flight on measures of arterial structure and function through R+3.
  3. To determine how alterations in vascular function and structure correlate with changes in circulating biomarkers of oxidative and inflammatory stress.
  4. To monitor oxidative, inflammatory, and vascular status of astronauts for up to five years after the completion of their long-duration space flight mission (surveillance).

APPROACH:
Ultrasound scans of carotid and brachial arteries with ECG recording will be performed on L-180, L-45, R+3 days, R+1 year, R+3 years and R+5 years. Each scan includes baseline carotid and brachial measures, measures of flow-mediated (endothelium-dependent) dilation (reactive hyperemia), and assessment of endothelium-independent (sublingual nitroglycerine-induced) dilation (0.4 mg tablet of nitroglycerine will be administered sublingually). Blood pressure and stroke volume (ultrasound) also will be measured. Urine collections (48-hr void-by-void) and fasting blood draw will be performed on L-180, L-45, R+3 days.

Ultrasound scans (carotid/brachial) with ECG recording will be performed on flight days (FDs) 15, 60 and R-15 using real-time remote guidance. Each ultrasound session will be preceded or followed by a blood draw and 24-hr void-by-void urine collection.

experiment_title: Telemedicine During Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project Phase III
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is the potential for accumulation of toxic levels of many substances within the confines of a closed-loop isolated chamber such as that used in the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). These noxious or possibly harmful substances may be components of the habitat structure that become volatile with pressure changes or over time, or they may be produced by the recycling/reclamation process itself. It is the responsibility of the space medical team to ensure that the environment is routinely monitored for levels of possible harmful agents and that the crewmembers are monitored for signs of toxicity. The medical team also conducts routine health evaluations of the crew to maximize human performance in the extreme environments of planetary exploration.

In the LMLSTP Phase III test, the medical operations team used improved methods to monitor, evaluate, and treat the isolated crew, and provided support for several planned medical experiments. The Telemedicine Instrumentation Pack (TIP) was utilized in this study to provide real-time medical care, medical monitoring, and science evaluation during the LMLSTP Phase III 90-day study. The goal of the medical operations participation in the LMLSTP Phase III project included the evaluation of training and use of the TIP by the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) and NASA flight surgeons for isolated long-duration crews. Another aim for this study included the use of the TIP to support medical and life science research evaluations requiring serial crew physical examinations during isolated chamber stays.

The objectives of the TIP telemedicine evaluations by CMOs to flight surgeons were: 1. To evaluate the CMO training plan for TIP use in an isolated environment.
2. To evaluate the quality of the TIP physical examination imaging capabilities performed by nonphysician CMOs, as a preparation to DSO 334 which was scheduled to fly aboard STS-89 (January 1998).
3. To understand the flight surgeon interaction requirements with the CMO, in order to obtain diagnostic or high-clinical utility images.
4. To test the limit of diagnostic accuracy of the TIP hardware by screening for signs of airborne mucous membrane irritation, injuries, and other clinical events.
5. To evaluate the use of the TIP in evaluating and following contingency medical condition (such as skin wounds) during periods of chamber isolation.

The objectives of the use of the TIP in supporting medical research in isolated crew chamber studies were:
1. To assess the TIP's utility in accurately assessing skin responses for immune function testing, as a prelude to a follow-on study of immune status proposed for long-duration space flight.
2. To assess common indications of external physical signs of nutritional status using the TIP.

APPROACH:
A two-hour session with the crew and trainers was conducted to review the immune response study design and rationale, procedures for subcutaneous application of antigens, and response measurement technique. No time was scheduled to provide the nonmedical CMOs with training for recognition of pathological conditions of the human body or even for normal immune responses to antigenic challenge in the integument. Therefore, the CMOs were trained in observation techniques and were instructed how to visualize and palpate expected findings on the skin and mark the findings with a supplied nonpermanent marker.

A two-hour session was conducted with CMOs to train on deployment, configuration, operation, and stowage of the TIP and techniques for utilizing the various lenses, ophthalmoscope, and otoscope attachments. The CMOs were shown the techniques for:

  • acquisition and verification of the nature of images of: the skin, the exterior eye and conjunctiva, the interior eye (lens and retina), the external ear canal and tympanic membrane, the nasal mucosa, the buccal mucosa, palate, and uvula
  • placement of electrocardiogram (ECG) electrodes and activation of the tracing acquisition software
  • placement of pulse oximeter for obtaining O2 saturation readings
  • placement of the electronic stethoscope in appropriate anatomic locations for acquiring physiologic heart and lung sounds
  • basic first aid provision

Examinations of the crewmembers were conducted on two occasions, chamber days 30 and 60, for general health assessment and to evaluate the possible effects of the atmospheric environment. The skin examinations for immune function were also performed simultaneously with the general health examinations.

Evaluations of the TIP hardware performance, the video image quality, and the utilization protocols were conducted concurrently with the examinations. The CMOs performed the TIP examinations on one another on chamber day 30 in the wardroom area.

Contingency examinations were to be conducted as needed but, in this study, were performed concurrently with the general examinations. Flight surgeons and technical support personnel set up a telemedicine workstation in Building 7 at JSC, external to the LMLSTP chamber, and monitored the examinations with direct video monitors from both the mounted internal chamber cameras and the video images generated by the TIP camera chip. Audio connections provided real-time feedback between the flight surgeons and CMOs.

RESULTS:
Due to the user-friendly nature of the hardware and the well-formulated protocols for utilization, the CMOs rapidly acquired the skills required for effective deployment and operation of the TIP, thus resulting in brief training sessions. Queries of the CMOs revealed that they felt well prepared for conducting examinations utilizing the TIP. They also felt well prepared to perform the periodic immune system study evaluations and were at no time uncomfortable with the procedures or observation techniques that they learned.

Image quality - The images obtained during the hardware evaluation and while performing the immunologic examinations in general were very good and were considered by the flight surgeons to be of diagnostic quality. There were several incidents of interference lines, generated by simultaneously operating electronic equipment, obscuring the video images. Interference suppression was felt to be important in preventing future obscurity.

Flight Surgeon/Crew Medical Officer interaction - A key to the ability of the crew to provide the flight surgeons with quality imaging, with the limited CMO training, was real-time feedback of transmitted images and data to the CMO performing the examinations. The flight surgeons had no delay in communication in this evaluation and, therefore, were able to provide instant feedback for position of camera lenses, otoscopes and ophthalmoscopes, and TIP instrument settings. The flight surgeons' feedback to the CMO allowed acquisition of images that were of maximal diagnostic value, without the need for later review and reacquisition of images that may have been suboptimal.

Mucous membrane assessment - The flight surgeons felt that they were able to adequately view the crewmembers' mucous membranes for signs of injury or toxic effect using the video images provided by the CMO via the TIP. In the Phase III test, no signs of adverse effects from off-gassed agents were detected by the medical surveillance. However, several superficial linear lesions were noted in the nasal mucosa of one examined crewmember. These lesions were felt as a result of the chamber's reduced relative humidity during the period preceding the examination.

Contingency medical management - A superficial laceration in the middle of the shin was sustained in one crewmember as a result of striking the lower leg on the metal stairs between levels in the chamber. The wound was evaluated by the macrolens of the TIP and found by flight surgeons not to require suturing. It was treated with steristrips, topical antibiotic ointment, and dressing. The wound was observed on a subsequent exam and found to be healing well, with no evidence of infection. The TIP provided excellent images for inspection, assessment, and treatment recommendations for this minor medical contingency situation.

Immune function evaluation - The flight surgeons were easily able to visualize the sites of antigen application on the ventral forearm of all four crewmembers in the study. Erythema, when present, was easily discernable. The flight surgeons relied on the palpation skills taught to the CMOs for assessment of induration, but they were able to give real-time feedback on the measurements of both erythema and induration through the video and audio connections at the flight surgeon's external workstation.

Nutritional assessment - Views of triceps skinfold measurements, as well as inferior conjunctiva for signs of anemia, were easily accomplished with the aid of the CMO-operated TIP.

Accurate skin response measurement data was obtained with high confidence by the investigator because the TIP was used to guide the measurements real-time from a remote flight surgeon workstation. The CMOs performed above expectations in operating the TIP hardware, especially considering the limited training, and were able to provide the flight surgeons with quality physical exam information. Real-time or near real-time audio exchange capability was invaluable in directing the CMO performing the examination in order to obtain the desired images. The images obtained were adequate to make real-time diagnostic decisions based on visual appearance of the mucous membranes. For example, an intranasal hemorrhage lesion was identified following a night of low-humidity sleep. Also, tympanic membrane motility could be observed during a Valsalva maneuver, etc.

experiment_title: Effects of Micro-G on Gene Expression in Higher Plants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Although various effects of microgravity at the whole plant, organ, tissue, and cellular levels have been observed, little is known about the molecular mechanisms involved. This experiment studied the effects of microgravity on the expression of auxin-regulated GH3 and SAUR genes in transgenic tomato, tobacco and Arabidopsis seedlings that express the auxin-inducible GH3 gene promoter-GUS and SAUR gene promoter-GUS fusion genes.

This was the second flight of this experiment and there were four objectives. The first objective was to determine how the expression of the auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes (e.g. GH3 and SAUR genes) is altered under the microgravity environment. The second objective was to identify the effects of microgravity on auxin transport/distribution and/or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in higher plants. Identification of the genes whose expression is significantly altered in microgravity grown plants (in addition to the auxin inducible genes) was the third objective. The fourth was to determine the functions of the genes whose expression is altered in plants grown in microgravity.

This experiment provided information about how expression of the auxin- and gravistimulation-inducible genes is altered at microgravity as compared to the ground controls. It also provided some insights into the effects of microgravity on auxin transport/distribution and/or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in higher plants. Molecular cloning and characterization of gravity-regulated genes is a crucial step to elucidate the mechanisms of gravity effects on growth, development, and metabolic processes in higher plants.

APPROACH:

The BRIC-10 experiment flew on the STS-85 mission which lasted approximately 12 days. It was launched aboard Discovery on August 19, 1997. The experiment was placed in two BRIC-60 canisters, each containing eleven 60 mm petri plates. Transgenic tomato, tobacco and Arabidopsis seedlings were grown on the petri plates, which contained five layers of filter paper and one layer of nylon membrane to support seedlings and nutrient media. At 5 dayts into the flight (MET 5/02:10) one of the BRIC-60 canisters was frozen in the LSLE GN2 Freezer. Ground controls were conducted on a 24-hour delay in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator at environmental conditions (temperature, % relative humidity, and CO2) similar to those experienced by the flight samples.

Upon recovery, the flight samples frozen in space were treated in the following fashion: forty representative seedlings were fixed in a solution containing 5% formaldehyde for microscopic analysis; ten seedlings were photographed; and the remainder were returned to the investigator's lab on dry ice for RNA isolation and screening for the genes of interest.

The flight samples which were not frozen in space were treated in the following fashion: three to four representative seedlings from each petri dish were photographed with a camera coupled to a microscope; forty seedlings from each petri dish were incubated in x-gluc solution for histochemical staining of the GUS activity at 37C for 12 to 24 hours, and after staining, the seedlings were photographed. All seedlings stained with x-gluc solution were stored in water with sodium azide for further analysis at the investigator's lab. Thirty seedlings from each petri dish were fixed in 5% formaldehyde solution for microscopic analysis. Between sixty and one hundred and fifty seedlings (50 seedlings per assay, 3 replicates) from each petri dish were frozen at -70C for quantitative assay of GUS activity.

RESULTS:

The results of this study indicate that the expression of both the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS fusion genes was significantly enhanced (2 to 3-fold increases) in space-grown seedlings when compared with the ground control seedlings. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS fusion gene in tobacco plants was dependent on the developmental stage, initially with an activation in cotyledons, followed by activation in elongating regions of hypocotyls and roots of the space-grown seedlings. As seedlings developed, the expression of the gene was reduced in cotyledons but further enhanced in root elongating regions. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene was relatively higher in vascular tissues and much lower in other tissue types. The expression of the SAUR promoter-GUS gene in the elongating region of hypocotyls in the space-grown seedlings was also significantly higher than in the ground controls. The activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS and SAUR promoter-GUS genes in space-grown plants strongly suggests that micro-gravity affects auxin transport/distribution or tissue's sensitivity to auxin.

The space-grown seedlings from the BRIC-9 experiment had shorter roots and more and longer root hairs. Increased auxin concentration or tissue's sensitivity to auxin in elongating regions of roots as indicated by activation of the GH3 promoter-GUS gene, suggests that auxin is involved in the micro-gravity mediated reduction in root growth and increases in root hair elongation.

We have isolated mRNA from both the space-grown and ground control seedlings of Arabidopsis. A cDNA library has been constructed and we are currently in the process of screening genes whose expression is altered in space-grown seedlings. Once the genes of interest are recovered, the investigators will perform sequence analysis, Northern blot analysis and other analysis.
