experiment_title: In-flight LBNP Test of Countermeasures and End-of-Mission Countermeasure Trial
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and results in a decrease in body fluid. Hypovolemia may be one cause of the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. Countermeasures such as fluid loading and the use of a g-suit, have not completely prevented this problem. It’s possible that postflight orthostatic intolerance could be prevented by the ingestion of isotonic saline while negative pressure is applied to the legs and abdomen to allow the plasma volume to increase. The purpose of this study was to conduct a controlled trial of performing this lower body negative pressure (LBNP) and fluid loading countermeasure once, 24 hours before landing.

APPROACH:
Twelve astronauts participated in the study. Four months and three months before launch, their tolerance of LBNP was assessed by applying LBNP in steps of 10 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) until they showed signs of presyncope (fainting). Three months and one month before launch, their orthostatic tolerance was assessed independently of gravity in LBNP ramp tests, in which the astronauts spent five minutes at each 10-mm Hg drop of pressure down to -60 mm Hg while heart rate, blood pressure, and electrocardiogram were monitored. Ultrasound echocardiography was used to measure heart dimensions and aortic blood flow in two of the astronauts for correlation with later in-flight measurements. Orthostatic tolerance was assessed in stand tests preflight.

The LBNP chamber that could be collapsed and stowed was used aboard the Shuttle. Negative pressure was provided by connecting it to a vacuum source (the Waste Collection System or the Spacelab Vacuum Vent). The countermeasure treatment, called a "soak," included a stepwise decompression to -50 mm Hg followed by 3.5 hours at 30 mm Hg below ambient pressure. During the first hour at -30 mm Hg, the astronauts ingested one liter of water or artificially sweetened fruit drink and eight grams of sodium chloride to provide isotonic saline. The soak was performed one day before the intended landing day by five of the astronauts, while seven others from the same missions served as controls. Heart rate, diastolic and systolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure, and pulse pressure were determined at each stage of decompression. In-flight ramp tests were performed by the five test astronauts as well as by one of the controls. Stand tests were repeated shortly after landing, with g-suits inflated.

Several LBNP tests were conducted on each subject before flight and during the mission. Two "ramps," a test consisting of a 10-rain rest period, followed by five 5-min stages at each level of decompression (-10, -20, -30, -40, and -50 mmHg), and then completed with a 5- min recovery period after recompression to ambient pressure, were performed preflight, as well as 4 in flight. One countermeasure session ("soak") was performed on the flight day before the nominal landing day. This soak session consists of a standard "ramp" test followed by 3.5 h of continuous decompression at a level of 30 mmHg below ambient cabin pressure, ending with a 5-min recovery period. During the time spent at -30 mmHg, the crew member ingested the standard landing day fluid load of salt tablets and water. No postflight LBNP sessions were performed, however, orthostatic tolerance was assessed using stand tests on landing day and 3 days postflight. Blood pressure, heart rate (HR) and Echocardiographic (2-D and Doppler blood flow) measurements were made during each LBNP session. These data were collected approximately every minute throughout the various stages of the tests, except that the Doppler measurements were collected every 30 min during the soak test. Blood pressure (auscultatory technique) was measured using a commercially available automatic blood pressure monitor (ABPM) modified for space flight. A set of ECG leads (three) were also attached to the subject via the ABPM to determine HR and document electrocardiographic activity. These data were telemetered to the ground in real-time to monitor the crew's responses to the LBNP tests. Echocardiography was performed using the American Echocardiographic Research Imaging System (AERIS), a commercial Ultrasound unit modified for flight at the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC). These data were recorded onboard and returned to JSC for postflight analysis, specifically cardiac dimensions, stroke volume (SV), cardiac output (CO), and total peripheral resistance (TPR). dimensions, stroke volume (SV), cardiac output (CO), and total peripheral resistance (TPR). Preflight testing was performed with flight-like hardware and techniques for consistency.

RESULTS:
The soak treatments occurred one or two days before landing for two astronauts. Shortly after landing, diastolic blood pressure and heart rate were lower in the treated astronauts than in the controls, whether they were seated or standing. The controls were more likely than the treated astronauts to have a decrease in systolic pressure after standing. No differences were found between treated astronauts and controls in heart rate and blood pressure during stand tests one to three hours after landing. These results show that the combination of LBNP with ingestion of isotonic saline one or two days before landing may be an effective countermeasure against postflight orthostatic intolerance. However, the countermeasure is impractical for use during Shuttle missions because treatment of one astronaut takes approximately five hours.

experiment_title: Bioavailability of Scopolamine Dosage Forms and of a Combination Dosage Form with Dextroamphetamine after Oral Administration to Human Subjects
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness (SMS) is one of the most common ailments experienced in space by astronauts. Although on ground, motion sickness is regarded as a nuisance or a discomfort, SMS occurs during mission-critical times in space and is suspected to hinder crew performance during launch and reentry. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Bioastronautics Critical Path document states that "the most overt change affecting an astronaut in space flight is the immediate response of the neurovestibular system to changes in gravity. Astronauts experience orientation illusions, posture and locomotion disturbances, vestibulo-occular function and gaze changes, space motion sickness, and possible structural changes affecting sensory-motor behavior and reorganization". SMS occurs most severely during gravity shifts (launch and reentry) and also during the first few days of (orbital) missions. Nearly 40% of in-flight medication use by US astronauts has been for the treatment of SMS. SMS symptoms include nausea and vomiting, both of which negatively affect drug concentration after oral administration and reaction time. Reaction time is a marker of cognitive performance.

Scopolamine (SCOP) is an alkaloid which has been used historically for many years as an anti-emetic, a medicine that prevents or controls nausea and vomiting, and a sedative. It is a muscarinic (a type of receptor in the parasympathetic nervous system that releases acetylcholine as its neurotransmitter) anticholinergic (a substance that opposes or blocks the action of acetylcholine) agent with anti-emetic and anti-vertigo activity resulting from suppression of vestibular labyrinthine input to the central nervous system (CNS). Earlier reports indicate that SCOP is efficacious for countering space motion sickness symptoms. Several sources report SCOP as being the most effective drug for suppressing nausea and vomiting caused by motion sickness. Many motion sickness drugs, including SCOP, have been reported to negatively affect concentration, cognition, and other cognitive behavioral measures. SCOP has a shorter half-life compared to other SMS medications used at the present time and therefore, side effects caused by the drug may resolve more rapidly.

Therapeutic effect of a drug is governed by its intrinsic activity and concentration at the site of action. Pharmacokinetics is the mathematical description of drug concentrations in the body (usually in blood or plasma) as a function of time after administration and the physiological variables that govern pharmacokinetic processes, absorption from the site of administration, distribution to the site of action and elimination from the body by metabolism and excretion. Pharmacodynamics, on the other hand, deals with the mathematical description of the onset, magnitude and duration of pharmacologic effect in relation to circulating drug concentration as a function of time. The therapeutic efficiency of a drug, therefore, is determined by the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of a dosage form. Earlier reports on SCOP pharmacokinetics indicate that the drug is rapidly eliminated from the body after administration with a systemic clearance of 65 ± 5.2 L/h and a moderate volume of distribution of 1.4 ± 0.3 L/kg. Oral and intranasal bioavailability of the drug is 10.7-48.2% and 83% after oral and intranasal administration, respectively.

There are no reports on the bioavailability or pharmacokinetics of the custom-dispensed combination dosage form of SCOP and dextroamphetamine (DEX), commonly referred to as SCOP-DEX. The KC-135 and currently the DC-9, affectionately referred to as the "vomit comet," are, or have been, operated by NASA's Reduced Gravity Office (RGO) as the primary simulation method of microgravity. They are flown in a series of parabolic maneuvers which cause brief periods of microgravity onboard and they are usually used for both astronaut reduced gravity training and equipment testing. Both the parabolic microgravity simulations of the KC-135/DC-9 and longer-term microgravity exposure, such as shuttle and International Space Station missions, induce SMS. Recent studies of SMS suppression on the KC-135 using SCOP-DEX have demonstrated an unexpected lack of efficacy prompting this investigation into the relative bioavailability of dosage forms of SCOP currently used by the NASA health care program. Further, KC-135 passengers who elect to take scopolamine to suppress or prevent motion sickness often have visual deficits which impede their performance.

A recent study comparing the efficacy of existing motion sickness medications indicated that SCOP was the most efficacious treatment for suppression of both nausea and the vomit reflex. Of the medications tested in the study, only SCOP was able to affect a prolongation in mean duration of rotation time in a vertical rotation chair. Additionally, accuracy of Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS) test, a short term memory and attention test, was found to be unaffected by SCOP whereas other medications negatively affected DMTS; this finding illustrates SCOP's lesser negative impact on cognitive performance when compared to other motion sickness medications.

Scopolamine pharmacokinetics
Bioavailability of 0.4 mg SCOP tablets in normal, nonsmoking male volunteers was reported to be 26.8 ± 5.1%. Plasma and renal clearance estimates in this study were 65.3 ± 5.2 L/h and 4.2 ± 1.4 L/h. Approximately 6% of intravenous and 1% of oral dose was reported to be eliminated unchanged in the urine.

SCOP is known to cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta and to be reversibly bound to plasma proteins. SCOP is known to be metabolized in the liver mainly to conjugated forms. Oral bioavailability of SCOP has been shown to be increased by pretreatment with grapefruit juice due most likely to inhibition of gut metabolism and/or inhibition of gut transporter proteins caused by flavanoid-like compounds in grapefruit. No significant effect of grapefruit juice on elimination of SCOP was detected.

Dextroamphetamine pharmacokinetics
Dextroamphetamine is readily absorbed from the GI tract following oral administration with an onset of action generally within an hour of administration. Biological half-life of the drug was reported to be 11 h in adults with a systemic clearance of 0.31 L/h/kg. It is distributed throughout the body with high concentrations in the CNS. Elimination of the drug is affected by urinary pH: alkalinization of urine increases half-life and decreases clearance (18 h and 1.5 L/h/kg); acidification of urine decreases half-life and increases clearance (to 4 h and 2.6 L/h/kg).

Significance
Scopolamine is regularly used in the space program as a custom dispensed formulation, both by itself and in combination with dextroamphetamine, as a countermeasure for motion sickness; however, adequate pharmacotherapeutic evaluation of these formulations has not been conducted. It is important to characterize interactions between currently used countermeasures in order to optimize pharmacotherapeutics in space and on the ground. This study examines the pharmacotherapeutics of operational countermeasure formulations and interaction potential of two currently used medications for SMS; this study was conceived based on anecdotal reports of treatment failure by NASA RGO physicians. The results presented herein are also useful for the Space Medicine and Health Care Systems Office in selecting or optimizing treatment of SMS.

APPROACH:
Study design overview
The overall design consisted of 4 treatments administered separately in a randomized fashion to 12 healthy subjects. Treatments were separated by a minimum four-day washout period between doses. Serial biological samples were collected for 24 h post dose along with administration of the ANAM Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) test battery. ARES is a selection of Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) tasks presented on a handheld computer.

Subjects
Twelve healthy, non-smoking subjects of normal weight for body size between the ages of 21 and 48 years participated in the study. All subjects were screened and selected through the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) Human Test Subject facility. Subjects were excluded if they reported: drug allergies to scopolamine or amphetamines, use of prescription or over-the-counter medications within 3 days of starting the study, use of antibiotics (especially furazolidone) or mono-amine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors within 14 days of starting the study, use of an investigational drug within 30 days of starting the study, tobacco smoking within the past year, blood donation or significant blood loss within 30 days of starting the study, significant gastrointestinal disorder, asthma, seizure disorders, glaucoma, history of urinary retention, history of alcohol or other drug abuse, pregnancy or suspected pregnancy, or lactation, or packed cell volume (Hematocrit®) values less than 41% for males and 37% for females.

Scopolamine dosage forms
All formulations were supplied by the flight medicine clinic at the JSC. The tablet manufacturers were Hope Pharmaceuticals & Eli Lilly & Company.

Treatments
A 0.8 mg dose of SCOP and a combination dose with 0.8 mg SCOP and 10 mg DEX were administered as tablets or in a gel cap on the morning of the study day after 8-10 h of overnight fasting. Subject numbers were assigned randomly.

Visual examination
Visual testing was administered by a nurse or laboratory personnel. All vision measurements were taken in the same windowless briefing room after having no less than five minutes of accommodation to the ambient lighting. Subjects identified their dominant eye after being taught a simple cover-uncover test. All vision measurements were taken on subjects' dominant eye, with the non-dominant eye covered by an eye patch. Visual acuity was measured using a Snellen chart held 38 cm from the dominant eye. Visual accommodation was determined using a Prince Rule, consisting of text of known font size on a card mounted on a slide rule. Subjects were instructed to hold the Prince Rule to their dominant eye with the text card adjacent to the eye, and to slowly slide the card out until the text is legible, but not yet clear. All three tests were administered immediately prior to dosing and immediately after ARES had been completed by the subject at 0.5, 1, 2, 8, and 24 hours post dose.

Sample collection
Blood and saliva samples were collected at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24h post dose. Urine samples were collected pre-dose and as PRN (pro re nata, a Latin term used in medicine that means "as necessary") voids for 24h post dose. Blood samples (7 ml) were collected into heparinized VacutainerTM tubes from an indwelling catheter (Intracath®, Becton and Dickinson) placed in the antecubital vein of the arm. Stimulated mixed saliva samples were collected using Salivettes® (Sarstedt Inc.). Blood and saliva samples were centrifuged at 3000 rpm, samples transferred to cryotubes and stored frozen at -70°C until analyzed. Urine samples were collected into labeled polycarbonate bottles, volumes measured, aliquots (10 ml) stored frozen at -70°C for future analysis, and the remainder discarded.

Sample analysis
SCOP and DEX concentrations were quantitated using a modified liquid chromatography quadrupole mass spectrometry (LC-MSMS) method. Plasma and saliva samples were processed by solid phase extraction followed by analysis by positive ion electrospray LC-MSMS; urine samples were diluted 1/100 fold before solid phase extraction.

Pharmacokinetic Analyses
Plasma and saliva concentration versus time profiles were plotted and PK parameters were calculated by area moment estimation using WinNonlin (software for pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and noncompartmental analysis). Relevant parameters were compared using both paired t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine differences in PK parameters as a function of treatment.

RESULTS:
Significant differences were noticed between SCOP administration as a tablet and other formulations included in this study; most significant differences were observed with coadministration of SCOP and DEX.

SCOP Tablets (ST)
The pharmacokinetic parameter estimates of SCOP given orally are similar to those reported in the literature. Maximum concentration was 0.26 ± 0.04 ng/mL with time for maximum concentration at 0.71 ± 0.02 h after dosing; these data indicate a fairly rapid absorption rate after oral administration. Volume of distribution and clearance after oral administration are 47.6 ± 4.72 L/kg and 23.0 ± 4.58 L/h/kg, respectively, both of which were lower than those from earlier reports.

SCOP Gelcaps (SG)
Time to maximum SCOP concentration was significantly longer when given as gelcap formulation (1.04 h) than when given as a tablet; however, maximum concentrations for both formulations were not statistically different. No other pharmacokinetic parameter estimates were different from ST.

SCOP-DEX Tablets (SDT)
The area under the (concentration vs. time) curve (AUC) of SCOP was significantly lower when given with DEX than when given as SCOP tablet; bioavailability of SCOP from SDT was 75% of that from ST. In addition, both SCOP volume of distribution and clearance were higher with SDT (60.9 L/kg and 25.5 L/h/kg, respectively) than with ST (47.6 L/kg and 23.0 L/h/kg, respectively); however, this could be a result of lower bioavailability from SDT which leads to overestimation of clearance and volume of distribution parameters. This decrease in relative oral bioavailability may indicate a drug-drug interaction at absorption site.

SCOP-DEX in gelcap (SDG)
A trend similar to that with SDT was noticed after SDG administration. The AUC of SCOP was significantly lower with SDG; bioavailability of SCOP from SDG was only 78% of ST. The decreased relative oral bioavailability indicates the possibility of drug interaction between SCOP and DEX. Differences in clearance and volume of distribution of SCOP with SDG and ST were similar to those with SDT and ST. These results indicate that the effects of DEX on SCOP (SDT, SDG) pharmacokinetics and bioavailability are greater than those from gelcap (SG) formulation.

For pharmacodynamic analysis, linear regression analysis was performed between scores from ARES tests and circulating SCOP concentrations using both pooled data from all subjects and individual subject data. Simple reaction time throughput, a parameter that incorporates both accuracy and reaction time, was significantly (p<0.05) affected by SCOP concentrations from pooled data analysis. When the data were analyzed subject by subject, performance indices for several tests (reaction time and accuracy for simple reaction and memory related tasks) were found to be significantly affected by scopolamine concentrations. No uniform trend was observed in performance decrements; however, SCOP-related performance decrements were different among different subjects. Although DEX has been reported to enhance performance in humans, in this study, no significant differences in performance scores were observed between SCOP and SCOP-DEX treatments (p=0.69).

Visual acuity for some individuals, but not for all, was significantly affected by SCOP. Visual acuity for sensitive individuals was affected by even the lowest concentrations of SCOP. The relationship was sigmoidal, meaning that the effect of SCOP on visual acuity is linear, and therefore concentration dependent. In lower concentration ranges there is a minimal response, and in higher concentration ranges there is a maximum response.

experiment_title: The Effect of Daily Activity and Age on Bone Density in Women

OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between daily physical activity and bone density in young and elderly women. It is known that the rate of bone loss in the calcaneus (heel bone) is 0.2-0.3% per year beginning at age 35-40 years. The hypothesis of his study is that declining physical activity is a contributor to age-related bone loss. We have developed a device (in-sole sensor) that quantifies the activity level in an objective manner so that we can determine the loading history of a bone through the daily exposure to ground reaction forces. This data is then applied to mathematical models for bone adaptation in response to loading histories.

APPROACH: Forty-two female subjects, ranging in age from 25 to 74 years were placed into two self-selected activity groups (18 runners and 24 non-loading type of activities, i.e. swimming, cycling or no sport). Our ground reaction force monitor was fitted to the right foot of each subject and worn for five consecutive days. The monitor measured average daily loading histories (GRFz). The density of the right heel was measured as close to the monitoring of activity as possible. A bone density index (BDI) was estimated from the average daily loading history and correlated with the heel density in each subject. The BDI was determine from [ ni ( GRFzi ) m ]1/(2m) where activity is determined from i loading conditions with n cycles of load per day, is a subject specific scale factor to account for differences in body weight (BW) and GRF is the ith ground reaction force cycle peak load magnitude normalized to BW.

RESULTS:
The observed number of gait related steps (>0.8 or 0.95 BW) was similar to data obtained by others with stepmeters or pedometers. Histograms of cycles of activity (load vs. frequency) could be made in terms of the subjects actual BW (‘relative’ load) or in terms of a BW scaled factor (absolute load). ‘Relative’ loading history is used when the intensity of the activity is compared among groups or individuals whereas ‘absolute’ loading histories are used to describe the actual force history. The histograms of higher body weight subjects showed a shift to higher GRFz loads when expressed in terms of , the scaled factor, a more accurate description of actual applied forces. One goal of this study was to determine a value for m, a stress exponent relating GRFz history to Calcaneal Bone Mineral Density. The Bone Density Index was significantly correlated with the Calcaneal bone density (r = 0.437, p = 0.004). Through least squares fitting, for all subjects, a stress component of 6.07 was determined as a value for m. Female volunteers were divided into high loaders (HL) and low loaders (LL) based on self-reported activity. There were 18 HL with an average age of 42 yrs, height of 1.66 m, BW of 61.5 kg and BMI of 22.3. There were 24 LL with an average age of 48, height of 1.63, BW of 73 and BMI of 27.3. Both BW and BMI were greater in the LL than in the HL in both the young and elderly age groups. The number of cycles of activity for more than 0.8 BW or 0.95 BW were higher in both elderly and young HL. However, for most activity parameters, elderly and young did not differ. Nevertheless, we did find a significance to activity grouping when the BW is accounted for in the bone density measurement. experiment_title: Spaceflight Effects on Bacterial Antibiotic Resistance and Its Genetic Basis “AntimicrobialSat”
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Effective treatment of bacterial infections has required therapy customized for the space environment, as evidence has accumulated that microbes respond differently to antimicrobials in the space environment (1). The EcAMSat experiment focuses on directly documenting alterations in antibiotic resistance in the space environment using a well-defined microbial system - the bacterium, E. coli, and a widely-used antibiotic, gentamicin, against a uropathogenic strain of this bacterium. Fully autonomous microsystems like EcAMSat reduce the cost and obviate other limitations of human-tended space biological experiments, while expanding significantly the number of launch opportunities. 

The rationale of the project is based on the fact that there is convincing evidence that microgravity (MG) increases bacterial resistance and weakens the human immune response, which necessitates careful examination of bacterial threat to astronauts in spaceflight. We previously discovered, using simulated microgravity [called low shear simulated microgravity (LSMMG)], using the high aspect to volume (HARV) bioreactors, that the resistance of uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) to the antibiotic gentamicin (Gm) increases under these conditions, and this increase is dependent on a gene called rpoS. This bacterium causes cystitis, incidence of which has been reported in astronauts; Gm is used to treat this disease.

APPROACH:
EcAMSat’s “2U” payload will support wild-type UPEC and its isogenic rpoS mutant (lacking s, which is encoded by the rpoS gene) in four independent banks of 12 100-µL wells (6 wells each for wild-type and mutant) in a microfluidic card that delivers nutrient, confines cells using integral 0.2-µm-pore filters, and maintains temperature (37°C). Each microwell (pathlength: 8 mm) has a dedicated 3-color LED and photodetector to track growth of the organisms via light scattering (470 nm). Cellular metabolism is tracked using Alamar Blue indicator dye (615 nm) and its reduced form (525 nm), generated by bacterial metabolism.

Growth and metabolism of E. coli are measured versus the concentration of the antibiotic gentamicin (four well banks provide three concentrations and a control). Following orbital stabilization, bacteria in stasis are given nutrients and grown to stationary phase, the phase most important in disease causation. The bacteria are then rinsed with nutrient-free buffer and starved for 24 hr (to firm up the innate resistance of stationary phase cells). Finally, they are treated with gentamicin for 24 hours, followed by tracking survival dynamically via Alamar Blue. We have performed detailed baseline and feasibility experiments, showing that Alamar Blue measurements reliably indicate the increased sensitivity of the mutant to gentamicin. 

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Graviperception in Starch-Deficient Plants in Biorack
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this experiment was to provide preliminary data to optimize the larger "PLASTID" experiment in Biorack on Shuttle to Mir Mission 06 (S/MM-06). In PREPLASTID, the growth characteristics of wild-type and three starch-deficient mutant strains of A. thaliana are assessed. In addition, the effect of a short unilateral gravitational stimulus, created by the onboard 1-g centrifuge, on these seedlings is studied. Based on the PREPLASTID results, the optimal developmental and stimulation times for the seedlings will be selected for the PLASTID experiments on S/MM-06.

Approach:

One week prior to flight, Arabidopsis seeds were sown in sterile Biorack minicontainers. The experiment was activated inflight by the addition of Arabidopsis growth medium and incubated at 22 °C for 24 hours (in darkness). Minicontainers were then illuminated for 14 hours in the glovebox before a further 48 hours incubation at 22 °C. Seedlings were placed on a 1-G centrifuge in the 22 °C incubator for 60 minutes before being fixed in 4% (v/v) gluteraldehyde in 100mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.2) to terminate the experiment. Non-centrifuged seedlings served as inflight controls. An identical ground control experiment and a supplementary ground control in which seedlings were grown on a 1-rpm rotating clinostat were also performed. Video data was collected throughout the experiment.

Results:

In comparison to the ground controls (stationary and rotating clinostat), the flight seedlings were found to be smaller. Two morphological features that distinguished the flight seedlings from the controls were greater root hair density and abnormal hypocotyl hook structure. While the starch-deficient seedlings did not respond to a unilateral one hour long stimulus by a 1-g centrifuge, the hypocotyls of WT seedlings were discovered to respond. Although the hypocotyls of flight seedlings were less sensitive to gravity than the controls, the seedling strain with the most starch responded to the in-flight stimulus.

experiment_title: The Effects of Space Radiation on Stem Cells and Vascular and Cardiac Disease
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The integrity of organs and tissues is maintained through continued cell production to replace damaged or senescent cells. In particular, stem cells are pivotal to this process providing the primary source for production of functional cells. In the heart, cardiac stem cells (CSCs) reside in close proximity to stromal cells or mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) that produce proteins that control the growth and development. Stem cells are quiescent cells that cycle through self replication very slowly. This decreases the ability of these cells to repair damage to DNA and may lead to increased risks of vascular and heart disease. In this study, investigators aimed to evaluate the effects of exposure of stem cells to space flight-relevant radiation.

APPROACH:
To determine the effect of space flight relevant radiation on stem cells, stem cell populations were exposed to radiation in vitro. Two types of stem cell populations were used for these experiments including:
a) Human Fetal Heart (HFH) derived plastic adherent CSCs: The heart tissue was digested with collagenase and cells cultured in standard plastic culture flasks in media supplemented with recombinant human stem cell factor (rhSCF). Over 1 to 2 weeks, adherent cells were grown from the tissue as CSCs. These CSCs were passaged using trypsin treatment.
b) Bone Marrow (BM) Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs): The human MSCs were isolated from BM from normal donors and expanded using standard culture conditions and stored frozen in liquid nitrogen. The MSCs have a standard phenotype expressing CD105, CD90 and CD73 but negative for CD45. Early passage (P3 to P5) cells were thawed and cultured in T162 cm2 culture flasks and were finally grown in T75 flasks, T25 flasks, chamber slides, e-plates, and six well plates for irradiation at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) for irradiation.

RESULTS:
To study the effects of radiation on activation of repair genes and induction of DNA damage, cells were analyzed for gamma-H2AX staining by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Gamma-H2AX marks sites of double-strand breaks. CSCs or MSCs grown either in 6 well plates or in 2 well chamber slides were exposed to radiation at BNL. For immunofluorescence, 15 minutes, 1, 2, 6, 12, 18, and 24 hours after, cells were fixed in cold acetone: methanol (1:1). Media was collected at each time for cytokine analysis later. The fixed cells were analyzed for DAPI (red-nucleus) and immunofluorescence staining with gamma-H2AX antibody (green). For flow cytometry, cells were trypsinized and stained with FITC conjugated gamma-H2AX antibody and propidium iodide (PI) at 15 minutes, 1, 2, 6, 12, and 18 hours after radiation and analyzed. HFH74 cells showed a 2-4 fold increase in the staining up to 2 hours following 100 cGy of proton irradiation. At later time points, this increase was lost. Following HZE ion irradiation however, an increase in gamma-H2AX was observed at 6 hours or 18 hours. Significant induction of gamma-H2AX was not observed in NHMSC cells following proton irradiation; however, an increase in gamma-H2AX was observed at 6 hours or 18 hours following Iron irradiation. In the case of Iron irradiation, a significant increase in cell death was observed up to two hours following 20 cGy exposure in both the cell lines. However, it appears that cells were able to recover from this initial damage. Since flow cytometry provides an average number of positive events in a cell population, investigators are currently analyzing gamma-H2AX staining using immunofluorescence.

One potential effect of space flight-relevant radiation may be to induce aging of stem cells and therefore investigators compared the CFU-F formation potential of cells after radiation exposure. In NHMSC cells following Iron irradiation (10cGy), a surviving fraction (SF) of 0.43 ± 0.0 was observed. Following continuous gamma irradiation for 12 hours, a SF of 0.91 ± 0.1 at 50mR/h and 0.8 ± 0.1at 100mR/h was observed. HFH74 cells showed a plating efficiency of only 7% even in matrigel coated plates, therefore the growth of the cells with and without radiation was followed in real time using cell electronic sensing system (ACEA Biosciences). As expected, with all types of irradiation in HFH74 cells increased growth delay was observed with increasing radiation dose. However, in NHMSC cells, except following proton irradiation, significant differences in growth were not observed with the increasing doses of radiation.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: A Phantom and Test Bed to Enhance Kidney Stone Comminution by Therapeutic Ultrasound
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Kidney stones are common on Earth, and space travel only exacerbates the risk. Over 15 years of National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) funded research have developed burst wave lithotripsy (BWL), which comminutes stones faster and more completely than shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) in a bench top water bath. The University of Washington licensed the technology to a commercial partner, and NSBRI funded the BWL development for integration into NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC)’s Flexible Ultrasound (FUS) system. However, neither SWL nor BWL comminutes stones as well in a confined space, such as the kidney, and both perform even less well when the stone is obstructing and surrounded by tissue. In addition, cavitation is acutely sensitive to carbon dioxide, which is 30 times more soluble than oxygen in water, and carbon dioxide levels can be elevated 20 times in NASA vehicles. Carbon dioxide dissolves bubble nuclei and quenches cavitation collapse, has been associated with visual impairment and intracranial pressure (VIIP), and suppresses kidney stone detection. This study sought to discover effective BWL exposures to counteract the effects of confinement and carbon dioxide.

APPROACH:
Five farm-bred pigs were implanted with ex vivo human calcium oxalate monohydrate kidney stones (approximately 4-mm diameter) that had been stored in water for at least a week and known to display the twinkling artifact in vitro via retrograde ureteroscopy. A baseline twinkling was collected at least 15 minutes before the anesthetic gas carrier was changed in four of the pigs from oxygen to elevated carbon dioxide in compressed air; the fifth pig was maintained on oxygen for more than one hour to serve as a control. The four treated pigs continued to breathe the increased carbon dioxide levels for two hours or until the oxygen saturation levels dropped below 45%, at which point the anesthetic gas carrier was switched back to oxygen. After about thirty minutes on oxygen, the pigs were again exposed to the elevated carbon dioxide levels until the oxygen saturation levels dropped below 45% at which time the pigs were once again returned to oxygen. Blood and urine samples were collected every thirty minutes and immediately before changing the anesthetic carrier gas.

RESULTS:
A mannequin phantom was developed for testing and as a continued training and research tool. Outputs were developed and measured to effectively comminute human kidney stones in the confinement of the kidney and ureter phantoms and in animal models breathing elevated carbon dioxide. Investigators developed and tested an ultrasound phantom and surrogate testing capabilities in the ground analog environment of an elevated CO2 atmosphere to enhance the utility of therapeutic ultrasound for kidney stone comminution. These validated outputs have been added to the BWL system integrated with NASA's flexible ultrasound system (FUS).

experiment_title: Receptor Countermeasures to Bone Loss in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The prevention of bone loss due to skeletal unloading is a complex problem whose reasons for this loss have not been fully elucidated. The overall goal is to develop countermeasures that will not only prevent quantitative loss of bone, but also maintain bone strength. Measures that simply prevent resorption may maintain mass, but may block the necessary remodeling that ensures adequate bone strength.

Studies to date suggest that good nutrition and exercise regimens will be insufficient to achieve this goal so pharmacological alternatives must be considered. The biological actions mediated by the estrogen receptor (ER) and vitamin D receptor (VDR) play key roles in the normal control of bone growth and skeletal turnover that are necessary for skeletal health. These receptors act by controlling the differentiation and/or function of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, and other cell types within the bone and bone marrow microenvironment, as well as play a role in calcium absorption (VDR). It is hypothesized that the appropriate combination of an agent that will improve calcium absorption and encourage bone formation (VDR agonist) along with an agent that will reduce bone resorption (selective estrogen receptor modulators SERM) will achieve the goal of maintaining bone mass and bone strength. To test this, studies have been designed to:

  1. Assess the ability of novel receptor agonists of the ER and VDR, alone or in combination, to modulate osteoblastogenesis, mature osteoblast function and osteoclastogenesis in vitro and in vivo, and
  2. Assess the ability of novel receptor agonists of the ER and VDR, alone or in combination, to prevent bone loss in the hindlimb suspension model of skeletal unloading.
The effects of unloading and of the countermeasures are being assessed by:
  1. Measuring changes in bone mineral density, histomorphometry, mechanical strength testing and biochemical markers of bone metabolism;
  2. Determining the effects of these treatments on osteoblastogenesis and osteoclastogenesis and function, and
  3. Characterizing gene expression profiles in bone resulting from skeletal unloading and administration of the countermeasures.

With these specific aims, the role of these agonists will be examined in both male and female animals. This is important since astronaut crews are composed of both genders and previous unloading studies have revealed gender differences in unloading-induced bone loss. This will lead to a better understanding of the causes of skeletal unloading and the means to prevent bone loss. In addition, the results of these studies will provide a foundation for future experiments that will examine the ability of the most promising pharmacological countermeasure(s) to maintain bone mineral density and strength in established models of unloading-induced osteopenia in humans and/or during space flight.

APPROACH:
This research outlines studies designed to investigate the physiological, cellular and molecular alterations that occur in the hindlimb suspension (HLS) rat model of skeletal unloading and to evaluate the ability of ER and VDR agonists to counteract the deleterious effects of mechanical unloading on the mature rat, with respect to parameters associated with the skeleton and its associated soft tissues, endocrine system and calcium homeostasis. In so doing, molecular, cellular and tissue data that will be obtained to provide information on the ability of our countermeasures to prevent unloading-induced bone loss, as well as information on the mechanisms that contribute to this undesired consequence of microgravity.

RESULTS:
Results indicate that ligands of both the ER and VDR possess the ability to attenuate bone loss in the rat hindlimb suspension model of skeletal unloading. Collectively, these studies will lead to a better understanding of the changes associated with skeletal unloading and will test the utility of VDR agonists and SERMS as countermeasures.

experiment_title: Signaling at the Vestibular Calyx Synapse (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The vestibular system is responsible for our sense of balance. Precisely how mechanical signals generated by head movements are detected and transformed into electrical signals by hair cells and their afferent nerve fibers is poorly understood. Signals are altered during space flight, changing the perception of body orientation and movement. Astronauts experience dizziness and disorientation during the first few days in microgravity and again on return to Earth. Temporary disorientation on leaving and on returning suggests that there is plasticity in the system. Investigators aimed to better understand the transfer of information between hair cells and afferents as well as the mechanisms underlying plasticity. This is important in understanding alteration of vestibular perception in space. Mammalian vestibular epithelia can be divided into central and peripheral zones which differ in hair cell morphology, ribbon synapse number, afferent innervation, and firing pattern. Calyx-only afferents contact type I hair cells in central regions, whereas dimorphic afferents form bouton and calyx endings and supply peripheral and central hair cells. Action potential firing is irregular in calyx-only afferents and varies from regular to irregular in dimorphic afferents. The investigators were interested in how mechanisms on either side of the type I hair cell/calyx synapse shape transmission in central and peripheral zones. The first aim was to use whole cell patch clamp to record postsynaptic responses from semicircular canal calyx afferents while their second aim was to investigate efferent modulation of calyx responses.

APPROACH:
To elucidate the roles of ion channels in the processing of signals in the vestibular periphery investigators developed slice preparations of rodent crista and utricle which allowed electrophysiological comparisons between central zones (CZ) and peripheral zones (PZ).

RESULTS:
To study the hypothesis that zonal variations in calyceal ion channels play a role in shaping postsynaptic events, the investigators developed a slice preparation of the gerbil crista to record spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents, action potentials, and voltage-dependent conductances from CZ and PZ calyx terminals. Spontaneous firing was regular or irregular and frequency ranged from 1.3 to 63 Hz. Firing persisted when transduction channels in hair cell stereocilia were blocked by streptomycin and when postsynaptic receptors were blocked by NBQX, suggesting that calyceal ion channels play a role in generating action potentials. The investigators further hypothesized that zonal variations in ion channel expression underlie the variation in inactivation of potassium currents previously seen in isolated calyces. They discovered that inactivation, expressed as percent reduction of peak current, had a median value of 9.4% in PZ calyces, which was significantly different from the value of 4.2% in CZ calyces. The greater inactivation of potassium currents in PZ calyces could contribute to tonic activity of regular afferents, which may be better suited to signaling long duration stimuli.

The investigator team studied the contribution of diverse potassium channels to whole cell outward current. XE991 dihydrochloride (20 µM), a KCNQ channel antagonist, reduced outward currents in both CZ and PZ calyces. XE991 also reduced the frequency of spontaneous action potentials. 4-aminopyridine (10-50 uM) blocked rapidly activating and moderately inactivating currents more prevalent in PZ calyces. Dendrotoxins, which block Kv1.1, 1.2, and 1.6 channels, reduced a non-inactivating current in CZ calyces and dampened excitability. Dendrotoxin-sensitive currents may allow detection of high-frequency signals and may therefore be important in generating rapid vestibular-driven reflexes. Margatoxin, a Kv1.3 and 1.6 channel antagonist, blocked a slowly inactivating current more prevalent in PZ calyces.

experiment_title: Global Transcriptome Profiling to Identify Cellular Stress Mechanisms Responsible for Spaceflight-Induced Antibiotic Resistance
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Responses of various microorganisms to the spaceflight environment have been examined by numerous studies conducted either in space or on the ground in clinostats. The results clearly show that several microbial behaviors differ in space, but not in a consistent way. The underlying mechanism(s) involved are not explainable by a single model. Exposure to the spaceflight environment (e.g., microgravity, radiation) alters a microbial cell's immediate surroundings, lowering convective mass and heat transfer or reducing mechanical shear forces. Changes in such fundamental physical forces affect the rates at which gases, nutrients, signaling molecules, and waste products are exchanged between microbes and their surroundings. Microbes perceive these alterations as environmental stress (i.e., the "spaceflight syndrome") and mount a complex set of stress responses. One consequence of the spaceflight stress response is alteration in their susceptibility to antibiotics. This could be due to mechanisms such as: production of biofilms, alteration of cell surfaces, up-regulation of drug efflux systems, or an increased rate of mutation in genes encoding drug targets. All of these mechanisms have been well documented as outputs of global microbial stress responses. Of particular interest is oxidative stress, which has been shown both to trigger maladaptive responses in higher organisms including astronauts, and to increase bacterial resistance to antibiotics. Central Hypothesis: Microorganisms subjected to the integrated spaceflight environment invoke a spectrum of stress responses, some leading to alterations in their antibiotic susceptibility. The underlying mechanisms can be identified using transcriptome profiling of model organisms.

APPROACH:
Specific Aims: We postulate that spaceflight stress responses vary depending on the organism studied because each species of microbe is endowed with its own unique collection of stress response systems. In order to probe the underlying mechanism(s) involved it will be necessary to study spaceflight stress response at the genomic level using model organisms. Specifically we plan to: A. Expose the model bacteria Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus epidermidis to: (i) simulated microgravity in the laboratory and (ii) actual spaceflight in 2 parallel BRIC canisters (BRIC-A and BRIC-B) aboard the International Space Station (ISS), with appropriate ground controls. Cells cultivated in BRIC-A will be fixed rapidly with RNA Later and cells in BRIC-B will be frozen in a viable state for return to Earth. B. Total RNA will be extracted from cells in BRIC-A and subjected to transcriptome analysis using Whole Transcriptome Shotgun Sequencing (a.k.a. RNA sequencing or "RNA-Seq") at the University of Florida Interdisciplinary Center for Biotechnology Research (UF-ICBR), to identify the suite of stress responses induced by exposure to spaceflight or simulated microgravity. Cells in BRIC-B will be thawed and immediately assayed for (i) viability, (ii) resistance levels to a battery of antibiotics in the Omnilog system, and (iii) rates of spontaneous mutation to antibiotic resistance.

RESULTS: Post-experiment sample processing: Frozen cell samples were transferred to the benchtop and partially thawed. The partially frozen cell slurry was transferred using a sterile disposable rubber spatulas into sterile 50-mL conical centrifuge tubes and placed immediately on ice. The culture volume recovered was recorded for later calculations. Samples were further processed for (i) viable counts; (ii) isolation of rifampicin-resistant (RFM^R) mutants; (iii) total RNA isolation; or (iv) Omnilog phenotype microarray profiling. (i) For viable counts, cultures were diluted serially tenfold in TSY medium, dilutions plated on TSY, and colonies counted after incubation at 37°C for 24 hours. (ii) To select for RFM^R mutants, cultures were concentrated by centrifugation, plated without dilution onto TSY+RFM (5 µg/mL) plates, and colonies counted after incubation at 37°C for 24 hours. The frequency of mutation to RFM^R was calculated by dividing the total number of RFM^R mutants by the total number of viable cells from each culture. Individual RFM^R mutants were streak-purified and saved as frozen -70°C glycerol stocks for further characterization by DNA sequencing. (iii) For total RNA isolation, cells were recovered by centrifugation (10,000 rpm, 20 min, 4°C) in a benchtop centrifuge. Supernatants were discarded and cell pellets immediately processed on ice for total RNA extraction. (iv) For Omnilog phenotype microarray experiments, frozen samples were thawed, washed once in Phosphate-Buffered Saline, diluted to the appropriate cell concentration in Inoculating Fluid, and inoculated into PM-11, PM-12, and PM-13 plates containing various concentrations of 72 different antibiotics. Plates were incubated at 37°C in the Omnilog instrument (Biolog, Inc.) and plate images recorded at 15-min intervals for 24 hours. Antibiotic resistance profiles were compared between FL and GC samples for significant differences.

experiment_title: The Use of Aspirin and Other NSAIDs to Ameliorate Muscle Atropy Due to Simulated Weightlessness (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overall objective of this study was to test the ability of aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) to inhibit skeletal muscle atrophy, weakness, and changes in gene expression due to simulated weightlessness in rats using the hind limb suspension model. The specific aims for this study were to: 1) determine if high dose aspirin treatment inhibits: soleus and plantaris fiber atrophy, deficits in maximum force, and the activation of NF-kappa B seen after seven days of hindlimb unloading. The inhibition of cyclooxygenase activity by NSAID treatment will also be assessed in muscles; 2) determine if curcumin or naproxen treatment inhibits: soleus and plantaris fiber atrophy, deficits in maximum force, and NF-kappa B or cyclooxygenase activity due to seven days of unloading; and 3) determine if the expression of genes known to be upregulated with seven days of unloading are “normalized” by treatment with any of the NSAIDs. To gain further insight into other components of the NF-kappa B pathway that are necessary for unloading-induced atrophy a fourth and fifth aim were added using genetic approaches to focus on the I kappa B alpha protein (which is downstream of I kappa B kinase) and the c-rel gene. By determining the involvement of particular proteins and genes in the atrophy process, specific pharmacological countermeasures may be tested in subsequent studies.

APPROACH:
To determine if curcumin inhibits NF-kappa B activity, C2C12 mouse myotubes were treated with 10 ngrams/ml TNF-alpha (a potent activator of NF-kappa B) for three hours either in the presence or absence of 200 mM curcumin. While TNF-alpha caused a 9-fold increase in NF-kappa B activity, curcumin completely abolished this increase. These results suggest that curcumin may be an effective countermeasure. However, in hind limb unloaded animals injection of curcumin did not attenuate the increase in NF-kapp B activity, nor did it attenuate the unloading-induced muscle atrophy. While disappointing, this is in agreement with a very recent study showing dietary curcumin does not attenuate unloading-induced NF-kappa B activity in skeletal muscle or unloading-induced skeletal muscle dysfunction or atrophy.

To determine if aspirin inhibits NF-kappa B activity, C2C12 mouse myotubes were treated with 10 ngrams/ml TNF-alpha for three hours either in the presence or absence of 20mM aspirin. TNF-alpha caused an 11-fold increase in NF-kappa B activity and aspirin abolished this increase. In unloaded animals, injection of aspirin did not attenuate the increase in NF-kappa B activity, but it did attenuate the unloading-induced muscle atrophy. Therefore, this dose of aspirin may be working by the inhibition of other molecules, which investigators have yet to test.

To determine if naproxen inhibits muscle atrophy and NF-kappa B activity investigators injected 10 mg/kg naproxen twice daily, beginning one day prior to hind limb unloading and for the duration of the unloading period. The results showed that this dose of naproxen did not inhibit NF-kappa B activity or muscle atrophy, due to hind limb unloading.

Aim 4: To determine if I kappa B alpha is required for unloading-induced NF-kappa B activity, muscle atrophy, and upregulation of atrophy-related genes. For this aim an I kappa B alpha dominant negative plasmid (known as a “superrepressor”) was injected into the soleus muscle of rats. This superrepressor is resistant to phosphorylation by I kappa B kinase and therefore resistant to ubiquitination and subsequent degradation.

NF-kappa B activity was increased 5-fold with hind limb unloading, but completely abolished in the unloaded muscles injected with the superrepressor. Furthermore, soleus muscle fiber cross sectional area was decreased by 40% following seven days unloading but was attenuated by 40% in the unloaded muscles injected with the superrepressor. In addition, the increase in gene expression of atrogin-1/MAFbx, Cathepsin L, Nedd4, IEX-1, 4E-BP1 and FOXO3a with unloading was significantly attenuated in the unloaded muscles injected with the superrepressor.

Aim 5: To determine if c-rel is required for unloading-induced NF-kappa B activity and muscle atrophy. For this aim investigators unloaded wild type (WT) and c-rel knockout (-/-) mice. NF-kappa B activity was increased 8-fold, with unloading, in the soleus muscle of WT mice, and remained equally elevated with unloading in the c-rel -/- mice. Moreover, muscle atrophy was the same in WT unloaded and c-rel -/- unloaded. This eliminates c-rel as a contributor to the atrophy process and, therefore, as a therapeutic target.

In this study investigators demonstrated that p50 is necessary for unloading-induced muscle atrophy and NF-kappaB activation. Based on this data they chose to add one further countermeasure - andrographolide - that has been shown to inhibit p50-DNA binding. To determine if andrographolide inhibits NF-kappa B activity in hands, investigators treated C2C12 mouse myotube with 10 ngrams/ml TNF-alpha for three hours either in the presence or absence of 50µM andrographolide. TNF-alpha caused an ~17 fold increase in NF-kappa B activity, which was abolished with andrographolide. Since andrographolide is only soluble in DMSO, the investigators chose to supplement the rat chow with 20 mg/kg/day andrographolide, instead of injecting the countermeasure. Andrographolide supplementation inhibited NF-kappa B activation by 28% and muscle atrophy by 27%, following seven days of unloading, suggesting that andrographolide could be a suitable countermeasure. However, further investigation is clearly necessary.

experiment_title: The Effect of Microgravity on Mycobacteria
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The aim of this work is to determine whether mycobacteria have enhanced virulence during space travel and what mechanisms they use to adapt to microgravity. We will use M. marinum as a model mycobacterium species, as its optimal growth is at 30-33°C and it is less problematic in terms of causing serious human infections. M. marinum also infects fish, and this provides a future small animal model for both ground-based studies and possible experiments on the International Space Station. We therefore hypothesize that M. marinum grown under conditions of microgravity will be more infectious in terms of entry and survival inside macrophage cells, and that this will be achieved by altering gene expression to promote survival under stressful conditions. Oxygen has been found to play a role in altering gene expression in Pseudomonas aeruginosa grown during space flight, and Salmonella enterica are more resistance to oxidative stress when grown under microgravity. We hypothesize that genes involved in surviving oxidative stress will be induced in M. marinum grown under microgravity. M. marinum grown under microgravity and normal gravity will be tested for their ability to infect and survive in macrophage, for resistance to hydrogen peroxide and for gene expression changes stimulated by microgravity. Specific mutant strains defective in detoxification processes, damage repair or biofilm formation will also be generated and if time allows will also be tested for survival in macrophage after growth under microgravity. This will further extend our understanding of mycobacteria pathogenicity during space travel and potentially reveal mechanisms to target mycobacterium infections in space and on Earth.

APPROACH:
The liquid culture medium for M. marinum was Middlebrook 7H9 liquid medium supplemented with 0.2% tween 80, 100 µg/ ml cycloheximide, 0.5% glycerol and 10 % ADS (albumin, dextrose, saline solution). M. marinum were grown from colonies until the optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was 0.8-1 in 3-5 mls of liquid medium in a bacterial incubator at 30°C and 120 rpm. This takes between 4-6 days. The culture was then diluted either to OD600= 0.002 for early gene expression and growth studies or OD600= 0.0005 for long term gene expression studiesand cytotoxicity studies. The diluted culture was then put into two 10 ml or 50 ml high aspect ratio vessels (HARV) and attached to a rotary cell culture system (RCCS) in a water-jacketed humidified incubator at 30°C. One disk was orientated to be subjected to normal gravity and one disk was subjected to low shear simulated microgravity. The disks were rotated at 25 rpm in all the experiments. All methods are described in Abshire et al NPJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi: 10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38.

1. Growth analysis – Two types of M. marinum were used for this study: the parental 1218R strain and a derivative of this strain (LHM4) carrying a plasmid integrated into the genome that expresses resistance to kanamycin and encodes for expression of red fluorescent protein (RFP).

2. Gene expression – The M. marinum 1218R strain were used for these studies. The effect of growth in the HARV subjected to normal or simulated microgravity on gene expression was studied.

3. Resistance to hydrogen peroxide, acid and gamma radiation - These studies used M. marinum LHM4 grown and treated as described in Abshire et al NPJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi: 10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38..

RESULTS:
The objective of this proposal was to determine whether waterborne pathogenic mycobacteria alter gene expression, become resistant to stress, and hence could be more infectious when grown under low shear simulated microgravity (MG). Mycobacterium marinum was the model organism used in this study. This is a bacterium that naturally infects fish and amphibians to produce a tuberculosis-like disease in a variety of organs. In humans, M. marinum can cause a disease known as swimming pool granuloma, which is restricted to the skin due to the lower temperature of body extremities. The pathology is similar to dermal Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and the infection route is through cuts or abrasions. Infection is usually limited to the skin in humans since M. marinum grows at 28-35°C. M. marinum infects and survives inside immune cells called macrophage by the same mechanisms as M. tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium. M. tuberculosis and M. avium cause serious lung infections in humans. M. marinum is therefore a good model to understand how these pathogenic mycobacteria survive and adapt to the hostile environment inside macrophage. Since M. marinum and M. avium exist in the environment on Earth and can form biofilms in water systems, it is important to understand the effect of microgravity on these pathogenic mycobacteria as they could exist in the water systems on space vehicles.

M. marinum strain 1218R and LHM4 (a derivative of M. marinum carrying a plasmid encoding kanamycin resistance and red fluorescent protein) were grown in high aspect ratio vessels (HARV) in a rotary cell culture system (RCCS) under normal gravity (NG) or MG. By following the optical density of the culture as well as the colony forming units per milliliter we determined that the growth of both strains was altered by growth under MG once the culture was in exponential phase. There was no difference in the growth for ~40 hrs (early exponential phase) but the growth of the MG culture was significantly slower after 40 hrs. The doubling time during early exponential was ~6 hrs and after 40 hrs this increased to ~10-11 hrs for the NG cultures and to ~15.5-16 hrs for the MG cultures. We hypothesized that the slowing of growth may have been due to an oxidative stress in the bacteria. Hydrogen peroxide can cross membranes and so we repeated the growth studies adding catalase to the culture. Any hydrogen peroxide exiting the bacteria and existing in the medium would be detoxified by the catalase. This did not however improve the growth of the M. marinum under MG.

To determine the effect of MG on the stress responses activated by the growth conditions, we used RNAseq to examine what genes were expressed. For RNAseq, the bacteria were harvested, RNA isolated and converted DNA (cDNA), and the cDNA sequenced using the MiSeq benchtop sequencer. Using bioinformatics, the amount of expression of the different M. marinum genes were compared between the NG and MG samples. To make sure that we were examining only gene expression changes due to MG, only bacteria in early exponential growth were used in the RNAseq studies. Triplicate NG and MG cultures were used to generate samples of bacteria grown for ~40 hrs. We also grew triplicate cultures for 4 days and then diluted them again and grew them for another ~40 hrs so we could examine gene expression from bacteria exposed for a longer time. From these studies it was obvious that stress response pathways were activated in the MG cultures and the stress responses were at a higher expression level the longer they were exposed to MG. Expression seemed to change to be similar to responses of M. tuberculosis inside macrophage. This suggests that the MG stress was similar to that of mycobacteria inside immune cells. Using the MG growth conditions may be useful in the future to test drugs designed to kill mycobacteria during infection. We are in the process of identifying regulator proteins that may be involved in aiding mycobacteria survival under MG.

Published studies indicate that other species of bacteria show altered resistance to hydrogen peroxide and acid (pH 3.5) once grown under MG. We tested our LHM4 strain and determined that as found for other bacteria M. marinum were more sensitive to killing by hydrogen peroxide but did not alter their resistance to acid conditions once grown under MG. M. marinum sensitivity to gamma radiation did not change also. This type of study may aid in designing disinfection techniques for future space travel.

In summary, growth of M. marinum under MG results in changes in growth, gene expression and sensitivity to stress conditions. SigH is a stress response protein that increases transcription at specific operons and this work suggests SigH may be involved in the response to growth under MG. We are in the process of generating an M. marinum sigH mutant that can be used in future studies to determine whether SigH is an important factor in the adaptation of M. marinum to the stress of growth under MG.

experiment_title: Histologic Examination of Lung Tissue
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Limited information is available regarding the effect of microgravity on the lung, though several functional aspects of the respiratory system have been shown to be extremely sensitive to microgravity exposure. Human studies have showed a headward fluid shift during weightlessness. Pulmonary blood flow and alveolar ventilation become more uniform. It is hypothesized that exposure to changes in gravitational forces could potentially induce pathological changes in the lung related to abnormal lung fluid balance, altered pulmonary capillary hemodynamics and possible pulmonary hypertension. The objective of this experiment is to examine the effects of microgravity exposure on lung ultrastructure and relate the changes in lung histology, if any, to alterations in lung physiology.

APPROACH:
Lungs were removed from the animals within 10 minutes of decapitation. One lung from each animal was fixed in a glutaraldehyde fixative. Samples for electron microscopy were taken from the most ventral and dorsal aspects of a tissue slab cut perpendicular to the cranio-caudal axis of the lung. Tissue samples were rinsed overnight in 0.1M phosphate buffer adjusted to 350 Osm, then dehydrated, rinsed and embedded in Araldite. Sections were also cut from two tissue blocks selected randomly from each lung site (dorsal/ventral), stained, and examined by light microscopy. Ultrathin sections were examined with an electron microscope. Samples were examined for peribronchial cuffing of smaller pulmonary vessels, the presence of alveolar edema, and general appearance of the pulmonary capillaries and lung parenchyma. The ultrastructure of the blood-gas barrier was also examined by electron microscopy.

RESULTS:
Only minor changes were noted in any of the lung tissues examined. Six of the animals had very rare intraalveolar fragments of debris. In all cases, these were limited to one to three total fragments in the section examined. In two of the animals (animals 2 and 7) a single hair fragment was noted within an alveolus. In the remaining animals, the debris was limited to rare, tiny, sharp, somewhat crystalline shards that were not identifiable as to specific type of material due to the very small size and limited amount of material present. Congestive changes consistent with decapitation were most prominently noted in animals 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10, while rare to mild peribronchiolar accumulations of small numbers of lymphocytes and rare plasma cells were noted in animals 4, 5, 6, 7 and 10.

In summary, there were no distinctive features separating any one group of animals clearly from another group.

experiment_title: Hybrid Training - A Sensory Stimulation Countermeasure for Long Duration Space Exploration Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study concentrated on assessing the efficacy of physical exercise while using a cycle ergometer combined with an interactive virtual environment, i.e. Hybrid Training, as a countermeasure for augmenting sensory stimulation during long-duration space missions. This countermeasure combined validated tools and virtual reality (VR) technologies in a new way to reveal the full potential of Hybrid Training, and took into account (a) key needs that fulfill sensory stimulation, (b) “hedonic adaptation”, i.e. a reduced affective response to stimuli with continued or repeated exposure, (c) delivery schedule, and (d) size, mass and volume requirements, and (e) reasonable cost. The system basically consisted of a cycle ergometer, a human computer interaction (HCI) interface, and a visual display. The ergometer was linked via Bluetooth to the HCI and the visual display consisting of a touchpad or alternatively a head-mounted VR system plus a personal computer (PC). In addition, the ergometer was equipped with contact electrodes for logging heart rate as an additional indicator of exercise intensity (as well as haptic feedback). Due to its web-based interface, the system also promoted real-time monitoring of comprehensive metrics for each training session, and provided an easy reporting tool for individuals (feedback to crewmembers including training history). The research had the specific aims of investigating the effect of Hybrid Training on:
  1. Brain structure and function,
  2. Cognitive performance,
  3. Biochemical markers of stress and neuroplasticity,
  4. Mood, depression, and subjective assessments of workload, stress, sleep quality, tiredness, sickness, and conflicts,
  5. Sleep duration and sleep-wake rhythms using continuously wrist-worn actigraphy,
  6. Heart rate, heart rate variability, and sleep structure using monthly 24-hour electrocardiogram (ECG) measurements, and
  7. Crew cohesion and team structure (pending crew consent).
The main aim of the study was to assess the effect of Hybrid Training on changes in brain structure and function as well as cognitive performance in subjects during two 1-year Antarctic winter-over missions at Neumayer station and compare these data to data collected in previous Neumayer crews, other Antarctic stations, space analog environments, and the International Space Station (ISS)
APPROACH:
Investigators planned to study a crew in Antarctic winter-over missions in Neumayer station. Both immediate and long-term benefits of Hybrid Training were investigated. Each Neumayer winter-over crew consisted of nine subjects. Investigators intended to investigate two consecutive winter-overs (2017 and 2018), and sampled data in a maximum of 18 subjects. Structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) were performed on Neumayer crewmembers about three months before the winter-over during a crew briefing at the Center for Space Medicine Berlin at Charité, about two months after the winter-over, and again about six months after the winter-over. During the winter-over mission, investigators continuously recorded wrist-actigraphy and proximity (the latter only if the crew consents) information to monitor changes in sleep-wake behavior and crew cohesion with time-in-mission. Data was downloaded from the actigraphs every other week. On a monthly basis, crewmembers performed cognitive testing via the Cognition test battery, the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B), and a virtual maze. In addition they recorded a 24-hour ECG as an objective measure of workload and sleep continuity, and filled out four longer surveys. Investigators also assessed biochemical markers of stress and neuroplasticity via blood and saliva samples.
RESULTS:
This study addressed the risk of Adverse Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders, and the need to identify and validate countermeasures and effective methods for modifying the habitat/vehicle environment that promote individual behavioral health and performance during exploration class missions (BMed1, BMed7). The efficacy of physical exercise was investigated, combined with an interactive virtual environment as a countermeasure for augmenting sensory stimulation during long duration space missions. Both, immediate and long-term, benefits of Hybrid Training were examined, and the primary outcomes focused on neurostructural/neurofunctional and cognitive changes. The results showed that crewmembers who exercised a lot were able to improve both accuracy and speed with increasing time in mission, while those with low levels of exercise mostly showed a pattern of higher speed at the expense of lower accuracy. The overall results hinted at the benefits of Hybrid Training (HT) for maintaining high levels of cognitive performance during prolonged delays in ICE environments.
Biochemical markers of stress and neuroplasticity, along with objective measures of sleep-wake rhythmicity and sleep structure were also assessed. These provided insights into mechanisms and consequences of the observed structural and functional brain changes, and their reversibility by HT. Neurotrophic factors and neuroprotective cytokines, Vitamin D, and cortisol did not change during the mission in the Hybrid Training group. The Hybrid Training group was characterized by significantly higher BDNF and VEGF levels relative to the controls. The crew reported average levels of sleep quality, workload, sleepiness, physical exhaustion, mental fatigue, freshness; high levels of happiness and health; and low levels of stress, depression, boredom, depression, and crew conflicts. The only significant change with increasing time in mission was observed for increased mental fatigue in the Control group only.
Several differences were observed in the brain function and structure that suggest a neuroprotective effect of Hybrid Training. High-resolution hippocampal imaging revealed some considerable effects of HT on hippocampal subfields. Hippocampal changes strongly predicted tasks assessing working memory. Widespread decreases in gray matter were noticed in the Control group relative to the Hybrid Training group, the right medial prefrontal cortex, the left precuneus and left supramarginal gyrus, bilaterally in the Para hippocampus, lingual gyrus, the calcarine cortex and the posterior cingulate cortex. Functional connectivity analyses showed hyperconnectivity in the Control group, characterized by increases in connectivity of the bilateral precuneus in the default mode network (DMN), and between the bilateral hippocampus and areas of the posterior cingulate gyrus and right precuneus.

experiment_title: Nanoscale Test Strips for Multiplexed Blood Analysis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of the nanoscale test strips, or nanostrips, is to provide rapid, low-cost, powerful multiplexed analyses in a diminutive form so that whole body health checks can be performed on a single drop of blood. The approach is conceptually similar to pH or urinalysis test strips which allow multiplexed measurements in a linear format. The main difference is that we are proposing test strips at the nanoscale, shrunk in size over a billion-fold in volume, allowing multiple sensing elements to be included in a tiny area. In Phase I, we fabricated, tested, and demonstrated functional parathyroid hormone and vitamin D nanostrips for bone metabolism. Furthermore, we developed thrombin aptamer and immune IgG antibody nanostrips. For Phase II, we will develop a breadth of nanostrips designed to address key space-flight medical needs. These will be for assessment of bone metabolism, immune response, cardiac status, liver metabolism, and lipid profiles. We plan to enhance our technology capabilities by developing a Rapid Nanostrip Assay Capability, mix-and-run assay capability, in-house aptamer production, advanced lyophilization technology, and nanostrip accelerated stability tests. The nanostrips will be read out in a time-of-flight flow-based manner utilizing our rHEALTH sensor.
