experiment_title: Radiation, Endothelial Cell Senescence, Accelerated Aging, and Atherosclerosis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to ionizing radiation represents one of the most significant health risks to astronauts during both short, but particularly long,-duration space flight. Vascular endothelial cells (ECs), the most radiosensitive vascular cell type, remain the major regulating interface between the blood and vessel wall. There, they act as a paracrine organ releasing signaling molecules that regulate vessels tone, permeability and cell and platelet adhesion. Dysfunction of the endothelium may result from both an increase in endothelial cell damage (oxidative stress with nitroso-redox imbalance), an impairment of the endothelial repair mechanisms (decrease in the number and function of endothelial progenitor cells) or an acceleration of endothelial cell senescence. Radiation is known to induce cellular oxidative stress, as well as suppress bone marrow proliferation. Data from the investigators’ lab suggests that gamma and heavy iron ion radiation results in the activation of the ROS producing enzyme xanthine oxidase (XO). Activation of enzymes such as arginase results in a decrease in endothelial protective nitric oxide (NO) with altered nitroso-redox balance and endothelial damage. Investigators hypothesized that radiation will result in activation of ROS producing enzymes that will result in increased oxidative stress, nitroso-redox imbalance and endothelial cell damage. Thy also hypothesized that radiation will decrease endothelial repair mechanism by reducing bone marrow derived endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs). Additionally, they hypothesized that radiation will accelerate endothelial cell senescence by decreasing telomerase activity and increasing the rate of telomere attrition. This will ultimately result in significant endothelial dysfunction, mimic the aging phenotype and accelerate the development of atherosclerosis. They tested the countermeasure hypothesis that the XO inhibitor (oxypurinol) will reduce radiation related endothelial dysfunction, that arginase inhibition (which reciprocally regulates nitric oxide synthase) will restore nitroso-redox balance and promote endothelial cell protection. They also tested the hypothesis that statins (endothelial cell protectants through a number of pleotropic effects independent of their lipid lowering effects) will prevent oxidative stress, improve nitroso-redox imbalance, enhance endothelial progenitor cell production, and prevent telomere decay. In this way, the adverse effects of radiation on the endothelial cell will be attenuated.

APPROACH:
Sprague-Dawley 4-month-old male rats (Harlan) were exposed to a single cesium-137 gamma irradiation at either 0 or 5 Gy. The animals were whole body irradiated while being held in a bowl-like container without anesthesia. For inhibition of XO, animals were randomized to receive 1 mM oxypurinol in their drinking water. Treatment began one week before irradiation and continued until death, at two weeks after irradiation. Rats were housed at Johns Hopkins Medical Institution with controlled light and temperature conditions and ad libitum feeding and watering. Consumption of normal water and Oxp water per pair of rats was tracked, and no noticeable differences were detected. All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Johns Hopkins University.

RESULTS:
Investigators measured XOR protein abundance and activity to verify that 5 Gy gamma radiation upregulates XO in rat aorta and to determine the effect of 1 mM Oxp treatment. In aortas from irradiated rats, normalized XDH protein band intensity was greater than that of aortas from sham irradiated rats; however, this increase was not statistically significant. Rats receiving Oxp diet and control rats demonstrated nearly identical aortic XDH expression. To measure XO and XDH activity, they used the pterine-based fluorescence assay. The aortas of 5 Gy gamma-irradiated rats demonstrated a significantly elevated XO activity compared with controls. Remarkably, this activation was abolished by Oxp dietary inhibition (P < 0.001). Total XO + XDH activity was not significantly affected by radiation; however, a slight increase was noted. Aortas from 5 Gy irradiated rats on Oxp diet demonstrated significantly lower XO + XDH activity compared with untreated 5 Gy aortas (P < 0.05). Acute XO + XDH inhibition with allopurinol significantly reduced the activities of the 0 Gy, 5 Gy, and 5 Gy + Oxp groups (P < 0.001 vs. respective XO + XDH activity). Endothelium removal in irradiated rat aortas significantly reduced the XO and XO + XDH activities, indicating that a substantial portion of XO and XDH activity is confined to the aortic endothelium. Furthermore, the aortic XO:XDH activity ratio was increased by 5 Gy irradiation (P < 0.05), whereas Oxp treatment significantly reduced the ratio (P <0.001) compared with control. These data, when coupled with the XDH immunoblots, imply that radiation-induced XO activation derives from XDH-XO conversion and, potentially, an increased expression of total XOR.

OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between daily physical activity and bone density in young and elderly women. It is known that the rate of bone loss in the calcaneus (heel bone) is 0.2-0.3% per year beginning at age 35-40 years. The hypothesis of his study is that declining physical activity is a contributor to age-related bone loss. We have developed a device (in-sole sensor) that quantifies the activity level in an objective manner so that we can determine the loading history of a bone through the daily exposure to ground reaction forces. This data is then applied to mathematical models for bone adaptation in response to loading histories.

Our ground reaction force monitor was fitted to the right foot of each subject and worn for five consecutive days. The monitor measured average daily loading histories (GRFz). experiment_title: Use of a Molecular Marker of Learning and Memory to Assess Effects of 56Fe Irradiation on Hippocampus-dependent Cognition and Neurogenesis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Particulate irradiation in the space environment may pose a significant risk to space flight crews during a mission or upon return to Earth. This may involve the central nervous system, where low radiation doses can induce cognitive or behavioral impairments. Understanding the cellular and molecular basis of cognitive injury will facilitate the establishment of risk estimates and may provide a foundation for the establishment of effective countermeasures or treatments for such injury. Using an animal model, we will determine the extent to which low doses of 56Fe irradiation affect cognitive function and will determine if such changes are associated with the alteration of a gene that is associated with learning and memory, or with the production and maturation of newly born neurons.

APPROACH:
The overall goals of this project were to determine: (1) how low doses of 56Fe ions affected behavioral performance; (2) if specific cellular (e.g. neurogenesis) and molecular factors (immediate early gene Arc) might play a role in cognition; and (3) if those endpoints were affected by inflammatory changes. The experimental methods chosen to accomplish these goals provided a means by which the effects of low radiation doses could be quantified both in terms of behavioral performance as well as specific cellular and molecular endpoints that are associated with learning and memory.

The proposed measures of behavioral performance, which were also used to induce Arc expression, involved a fear conditioning paradigm with 2 versions: one that required the hippocampus (context version) and one that did not require the hippocampus (cued version). The version that required the hippocampus consisted of two types of behavioral paradigms. The first involved no tone shock pairing (-/-) and represented the ability of an animal to recognize an environment previously encountered. Animals that recognized that environment would explore it less, a behavior that is referred to as spatial habituation learning. The second paradigm involved tone shock pairing (+/+) and represented a Pavlovian type of response; that is, animals received a mild shock the first day, and when subsequently placed in the same environment, they would freeze more if they remembered having received an adverse stimulus in that environment the day before. For each version used, thirty minutes after the end of the final testing session on day 2, tissues were collected and prepared for microscopic analyses.

RESULTS:
Investigators completed all analyses related to behavior, neurogenesis, Arc protein expression, and measures of the endogenous inflammatory cells in the brain, the microglia. These endpoints were assessed after whole body irradiation with either 0, 0.25 Gy, 0.5 Gy or 1.0 Gy of 56Fe. All animals underwent cognitive testing 3 months after irradiation using a fear conditioning training- and testing-paradigm. The three-month time point was selected because that time has been previously used to show cognitive deficits after photon or HZE irradiation, as well as changes in Arc expression. Investigators quantified the effects of whole body 56Fe irradiation (600 MeV, 0.5 or 1 Gy) on hippocampus-dependent and hippocampus-independent cognitive performance and determined if those effects were associated with changes in Arc expression in the enclosed and free blades of the dentate gyrus. Whole body 56Fe irradiation impacted contextual but not cued fear freezing and the percentage of Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In mice tested for contextual freezing, there was a correlation between Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In addition, in mice irradiated with 0.5 Gy, contextual freezing in the absence of aversive stimuli correlated with the percentage of Arc-positive cells in the enclosed blade. In mice tested for cued freezing, there was no correlation between Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In contrast, cued freezing in the presence or absence of aversive stimuli correlated with Arc-positive cells in the free blade. These data indicate that there are blade dependent effects after particulate irradiation. More studies are required to address the physiologic significance of such findings.

One of the microenvironmental factors that may influence how irradiation affects cognition is inflammation. Investigators addressed this issue by irradiating animals deficient in a specific chemokine receptor: chemokine receptor-2 (CCR2). CCR2 mediates the recruitment of infiltrating and resident microglia to sites of CNS inflammation, and is upregulated by 56Fe irradiation. CCR2 knock out (KO) and wild-type mice were used to compare effects of 56Fe radiation (600 MeV, 0, 0.25 Gy) on hippocampal function using contextual fear conditioning involving tone shock pairing during training (+/+) and exposure to the same environment without tone shock pairings (-/-). In the -/- condition, irradiation increased freezing and hippocampal Arc protein levels in WT but not CCR2 KO mice, suggesting that a lack of CCR2 was associated with a poorer outcome. In contrast, in the +/+ condition, irradiation reduced freezing but there was no genotype difference. There were no significant correlations between the number of Arc-positive cells in the dentate gyrus and freezing in either genotype but in CCR2 KO mice, there was a trend towards a negative correlation between freezing and Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In the +/+ condition, BrdU alone and BrdU/NeuN were reduced in the free blade but not the enclosed blade of CCR2 KO. CCR2 status had no influence on total numbers of newly born activated microglia before or after irradiation, indicating that other mechanisms are involved in the genotype-dependent radiation response.

The investigators’ standard markers of neurogenesis, microglia, and the immediate early gene Arc have been shown to be good predictors of radiation response after relatively high doses of photons or heavy ions. However, in their current studies they were not particularly responsive to low dose irradiation with iron ions. Given those findings they wanted to look for other markers that might track with cognition and provide predictive value after low dose exposures. The formation of long-term memory relies on modulation of synaptic connections in response to neuronal input. This plasticity requires coordinated activity-dependent synthesis of specific mRNAs and proteins that facilitate molecular and structural changes at the synapse. Dendritic spines are bulbous membrane projections of mixed morphology, that form the postsynaptic specializations of the vast majority of excitatory synapses in the central nervous system (CNS) and their structure and density are important factors in synaptic function. Spine morphology can predict both spine stability and synaptic strength, and changes in dendritic spine density or structural reorganization of spines is thought to be important for cognitive processes such as learning and memory.

In their new study of dendritic spines, investigators irradiated young adult male C57BL6 mice with 0 or 0.5 Gy (whole body) of 56Fe ions. Within each radiation treatment group, animals were randomly assigned into cohorts that received cognitive testing using a no shock/no tone paradigm or no cognitive testing, i.e. caged controls. Half of the mice from each specific treatment group were used for the determination of dendritic spine density/morphology and the other half were used for measurement of Arc and other cellular markers. Dendritic spines were visualized using a well-established Golgi staining paradigm. In the CA1 and dentate gyrus of sham-irradiated mice, the behavioral testing enhanced the spine density as compared to behaviorally naïve mice. In contrast, behavioral testing did not affect spine density in irradiated mice. These intriguing data indicate that irradiated mice did not benefit from the environmental enrichment (i.e. behavioral testing) as sham-irradiated mice did.

Finally, investigators initiated and completed a mixed beam study to determine how the brain responds when it is confronted by two different types of irradiation. Mice either received a single whole body exposure of 1.0 Gy protons (n = 24), a single whole body dose of 0.05 Gy 56Fe (n = 24), a single whole body exposure of 1.0 Gy protons immediately before a single whole body dose of 0.5 Gy 56Fe (n = 24) or no irradiation (n =24). Two months following irradiation, all animals receives a daily i.p. injection of bromodeoxyuridine (100 mg/kg) for 7 days, and 1 month later mice were either cognitively tested for novel object recognition or acted as caged controls. Thirty minutes after the onset of the last session of the cognitive testing, animals were sacrificed and their brains bisected into the two hemispheres and then frozen. Tissues were either analyzed for cellular markers of neurogenesis, the immediate early gene Arc, or for molecular/biochemical assays for markers of inflammation/oxidative stress. No cellular, molecular, or biochemical changes were observed after either of the single doses or the combined treatment. This suggests either that the low doses used did not induce any significant alterations, or the specific endpoints chosen for study were not sensitive to minor changes induced by the relatively low doses used.

The data highlights the complexity of assessing how low doses of 56Fe affect hippocampal function. Those data suggest that even a relatively low dose of 56Fe can induce behavioral changes that involve the hippocampus, but the cellular/molecular/biochemical mechanisms responsible are still not yet known.

experiment_title: Growth Hormone Regulation, Synthesis, and Secretion in Microgravity: I. Somatotroph Physiology
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Since the pituitary growth hormone (GH) controls the activity of both muscle and bone, effects of space flight on GH cell function have received some attention. Taken together, results suggested that GH cells from flight animals had experienced a partial shutdown in hormone secretion. The overall objective of this experiment was to determine if results from the SL-3 experiment were repeatable. Additionally, this study was to extend the earlier findings in light of the longer duration of flight. Finally, the design of the methodology was modified to permit statistical analysis of the GH secretion data.

Approach:

The design of this study was dictated by the following considerations: five pituitary glands were available for study; ~2 x 1,000,000 cells could be prepared from each gland; and a number of structure function tests, each requiring different numbers of cells, was possible. In order to accomplish experimental goals, some cells from each gland were cultured individually while the remaining cells from each gland were then pooled with others from the same treatment groups for subsequent morphological analyses and transplantation study.

Results:

The percentages of GH cells prepared from glands in the different groups, based on counts of 50,000 cells/treatment group, did not differ. However, the staining intensity of the GH cells in the flight group was two times greater than that of cells in the synchronous group. The increased intensity of specific cytoplasmic GH fluorescence was also documented by the morphological appearance of cells. These results suggest, but do not prove, that there was more GH/cell in the flight group. Cell culture data revealed that: 1) levels of secreted GH were, in the case of serumless medium, ~70% of those in serum-containing medium; 2) relative to the first three-day culture period, levels of hormone in the synchronous group were two to three times greater during the second three-day culture period; and 3) flight cells did not show the same corresponding increase in iGH during the second three-day period. Results support the contention that there is a secretory lesion in pituitary GH cells of flight animals.

experiment_title: (NSCORT) for Advanced Life Support at Purdue/Howard/AAMU - Solid Waste Resource Recovery
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A significant fraction of waste material (plant residue, greywater and human waste) generated during space missions and on the earth, contains recoverable energy. The specific objective of the project was to optimize an approach that will demonstrate a Plant-based Anaerobic-aerobic Bioreactor Linked Operation (PABLO) that efficiently converts plant residuals and greywater into fuel grade methane (CH4), electricity, and biosolids that will be suitable for plant and fungal culture. This effort will optimize the potential for CH4 production by aerobically treating anaerobically recalcitrant waste materials - biosolids before they are used as a plant growth material. These steps will breakdown the resistant materials, freeing soluble carbon and stabilizing the materials. In a second part of the project we modified the PABLO system to a system concerned with converting human waste in to CH4 and biosolids. The Waste-ABLO (WABLO) approach is for the conversion of human waste into CH4 and biosolid residuals that are condensed but not used in the production of food.

In both the space based and Earth-based systems the starting point was waste materials. The major difference is in the space-based system we dealt primarily with dried residues that will be rewetted with greywater. In the earth-based system, the residues were wet or dry. Outputs from the system include: CH4, CO2 and solids. In this system, the residuals were treated with an aerobic process to and returned to the anaerobic system. The residuals that settle in the system were removed and land applied (earth) or used in confined growth systems (Mars).

The project was divided into three tasks:
Task 1: The objective was to use an anaerobic-aerobic bioreactor system to optimize production of methane from plant-based waste materials and for the recovery of high-quality biosolids.
Task 2: Methods for the optimization of the PABLO biosolids for use in fungal and plant cultivation were investigated. This required an evaluation of the makeup the aerobic reactor’s microbial population to maximize the formation of soluble carbon for use in the anaerobic portion of PABLO.
Task 3: The objective was to use a bioreactor system to optimize production of methane from human waste materials

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
For the first set of biological methane production (BMP) experiments, corn residue was milled and added to a phosphate buffer. Anaerobic digester sludge was used as an inoculum. Digesters were incubated at 23oC and periodically checked for gas and acid production over a period of time.

Corn residue in a phosphate buffer showed poor methane production over a 45 day time period. The maximum amount of methane produced was 0.09mLs after 32 days. Investigators also found this trend of low methane production to be true for several other crop residues that were tested. Low methane production resulted from the lignin matrix surrounding cellulose carbon sources, preventing the anaerobic bacteria from accesses these sources. Because of these findings, an efficient and simple pretreatment method should be used on crop residues to reduce the lignin content. There are several methods of pretreatment that could be employed to break down lignin including gamma-ray irradiation, alkali treatment, or aerobic composting. All of these methods would either require hauling large amounts of chemicals or supplies, or consume valuable resources such as oxygen.

Lignin degrading fungi appear to be a promising method of pretreatment for space missions. The mushroom species Pleurotus ostreatus, or Oyster mushroom, is edible, easy to grow, and is able to selectively degrade lignin, leaving the more soluble forms of carbon available for digestion by anaerobic microorganisms. This species also grows well in a high carbon dioxide environment during its longest growth stage, so oxygen consumption could be minimized with careful planning. The oyster mushroom requires a lot of water to sustain good growth; however, investigators have found that this mushroom species is able to grow well when using a mimicked hygiene graywater solution in place of regular water.

The process of growing the Oyster mushroom is quite simple. The mycelium is first grown on a grain, such as wheat or rye, to establish the fungi. Plant materials to be degraded are then pasteurized. Once cooled, the grain grown mycelium are then transferred and mixed with the pasteurized plant materials and grown under high humidity conditions. While the mycelium is being established, they grow best under a higher carbon dioxide concentration. Oyster mushrooms will begin to appear after about 18 days and grow to fruition in just 3-5 days. Graywater can be used throughout the mushroom growing process to conserve drinking water.

After one harvest of mushrooms grown on pasteurized corn residue, graywater was leached through the remaining residue and collected for methane production studies. This time, only the leached graywater and anaerobic sludge was used. No buffer was added. The digesters were incubated at 35oC. Methane production was greatly increased over digested corn residue in buffer, with a maximum production value of 8.3mLs after 35 days.

Milled plant residue alone will not produce enough methane to use a fuel source. A pretreatment method should be used to break down the lignin. The Oyster mushroom is an efficient and simple pretreatment method for degrading the lignin found in plants. This method opens up useable forms of carbon to the anaerobic bacteria and greatly increases the amount of methane produced. Using graywater throughout the methane production process will conserve valuable drinking quality water while recycling another waste material created by the crew on space missions. Degrading plant materials anaerobically is showing great promise for both long-term space missions and here on Earth.

Of the three residues tested, miscanthus produced the least amount of methane during all stages. More methane was produced after pasteurization and at the pinhead stage, but there was little difference between post-pasteurization and the pinhead stage. Corn residue produced more methane after pasteurization and after the pinhead stage, reaching a maximum methane production of 8.6mL and 8.3mL respectively. Tomato residue reached maximum methane production of all treatments at 9.5mL at the pinhead stage. Uninoculated controls were used for all treatments and consistently showed less methane production than inoculated treatments. This suggests that fungi are an effective method of pretreatment for production of methane from crop residues. Further research is needed to optimize this system. Greater methane production may be possible by extending the amount of time the bottles are incubated for. The bottles used for the experiments were small and only held a limited amount of gas. A different gas collection system should be developed so that pressure does not build up in the bottles.

experiment_title: Morphometric Studies of Atrial Granules and Hepatocytes: II. Atrial Granular Accumulations
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Since electrolyte imbalance and fluid shifts have been experienced by humans (and animals) during space flight, it seemed appropriate to examine the atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) granulated regions in the atria of rats from the Cosmos 1887 flight, and to ascertain, by means of morphometric and stereological methods, if quantitative changes occurred in flight animals.

Approach:

Light microscopic computer assisted morphometry of the atria was performed with an image analysis system. To make measurements for the area and perimeter, an editing function was used to outline the granular regions projected on the image monitor; because the reference area did not always fill the monitored field, the same method was used to delineate the pertinent reference regions when necessary. From values for object (granular accumulation) area, object perimeter, and reference field area, the stereology program calculated volume density and mean volume of the objects. Numerical density was calculated as the number of objects per unit reference area x103.

Results:

Those of the flight group had a significantly greater volume density than the synchronous or vivarium control groups, while the controls did not differ in this respect. The number of granular accumulations per unit reference area was also increased in flight animals. Mean volume on the individual granulated regions did not differ among the three groups. The increase in the flight group was there fore due to an increase in the number of granular regions rather than their size. No differences were seen between right and left atria of any groups. Likely causes for the increase in volume density of the granular regions in the flight group include reduced blood volume and/or body water content, but an exhaustive attempt to interpret these findings in terms of physiological importance would be speculative, especially because no chemical determinations of ANF were made.

experiment_title: The Role of the Bone Marrow Microenvironment in Space Radiation-Induced Leukemogenesis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) comprise less than 0.1% of the bone marrow (BM) of adults, yet they produce all blood cells that are responsible for constant maintenance and immune protection of the body. In addition to the requirement for high cell output, the concentration of the different blood cell lineages produced are precisely controlled to allow not only preservation of normal homeostasis, but also the prompt response to specific stimuli and demands. Previous studies have suggested that exposure to galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) and solar particle event (SPE) radiation that occur or may potentially occur during space flight may increase the likelihood of carcinogenesis, with leukemia being one of the most frequent radiogenic cancers, and the ones with the smallest latency period. The investigators hypothesize that GCR and SPE radiation can have a deleterious impact not only at the level of the mature immune cells and their committed progenitors, as is currently thought, but at the earlier developmental stage of the HSC. Genetic lesions induced by this exposure can lead directly to leukemic transformation, and may also cause these cells to generate a functionally compromised immune system lacking the ability to effectively fight challenges such as pre-leukemic transformations and viral/bacterial infections. As such, investigators hypothesize that astronauts would be doubly at risk, due to both the potential for induction of leukemia by SPE/GCR radiation, and the reduced ability of the astronauts’ immune systems to identify and eliminate malignant cells or pathogens in the body.

APPROACH:
In ground-based studies performed at NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) and Wake Forest, investigators spent four years assessing the risk of leukemogenesis from space radiation by examining the effects of simulated SPE/GCR exposures on human hematopoiesis, testing the hypothesis that the quality and quantity of cells being produced can be altered not only from direct exposure of HSC themselves, but also via indirect, biological bystander effects arising from exposure of MSC within the critical hematopoietic niche. Human HSC and MSC were immunomagnetically-sorted with antibodies to CD34 and Stro-1 respectively and exposed to: A) sham irradiation; B) 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-irradiation (LET = 0.91 keV/µm); C) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons (primary SPE energy; LET = 1.26 keV/µm); D) 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions (model GCR radiation; LET = 151 keV/µm); or E) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons followed 15 minutes later by 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions at NSRL. Immediately following irradiation, aliquots of HSC and MSC were cultured for chromosomal aberration (CA) analyses and DNA/RNA isolations, one aliquot of HSC was immediately assessed for functionality/ differentiative potential using the highly sensitive and quantitative, luminescence-based Hemogenix HALO® assay, and the remainder of the cells were placed in an MSC-based HSC maintenance/expansion culture system, testing four different combinations: 1) unirradiated HSC plated over unirradiated MSC; 2) unirradiated HSC plated over irradiated MSC; 3) irradiated HSC plated over unirradiated MSC; and 4) irradiated HSC plated over irradiated MSC. Hematopoietic cells were then collected after seven days, and methylcellulose or HALO® assays were used to assess the impact of irradiation of the HSC, the MSC, or both cell types on hematopoietic colony-forming potential.

RESULTS:
Direct Effects on Human HSC: Methylcellulose and HALO® assay data showed that gamma-rays and 50 MeV protons exerted fairly similar effects on HSC function, both reducing by 50–80% the ability of HSC to form both more primitive (HPP-CFC and CFU-GEMM) colonies, as well as more differentiated myeloid (CFU-GM), erythroid (BFU-E), megakaryo-cyte/platelet (CFC-Mk), and lymphoid (CFC-T and CFC-B) colony types. The marked deleterious effect of protons on the ability of human HSC to give rise to cells of the T and B lymphoid lineages is of particular note, given the body of published work showing that astronauts, even on fairly short missions, exhibit pronounced immune alterations. In contrast to the result seen with gamma-rays and 50 MeV protons, 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions had much less pronounced effect on HSC colony-forming potential, exerting no significant effect on their ability to give rise to the most primitive HPP-CFC colonies, but reducing the colony-forming potential in the remaining lineages by 20–40%, depending upon the specific colony type. Exposing sequentially to protons then iron ions, however, proved to be highly deleterious to HSC function, reducing the ability of HSC to produce all colony types by 80–90%. This decrease was, in all cases statistically different than the effects seen with either iron ions alone or protons alone.

Indirect/Biological Bystander Effects on Hematopoiesis following Exposure of the Niche to SPE/GCR: Irradiation of MSC with gamma-rays or protons produced similar effects on the most primitive HSC, reducing HPP-CFC output 30–40%. Importantly, irradiation of both HSC and MSC produced a negative additive effect on the most primitive HSC, reducing HPP-CFC output ~75%. The results with 56Fe ions were far more unexpected, as irradiation of MSC alone reduced HPP-CFC output 30%, yet co-culture of both irradiated HSC and MSC somehow restored the HPP-CFC potential.

Additive Negative Effects on Hematopoiesis Following Sequential Exposure to SPE then GCR Radiation: Perhaps the most remarkable results came from the sequential treatment with protons and iron ions. While sequential treatment reduced HPP-CFC output 70%, treating the MSC with this sequential dosing regimen actually increased HPP-CFC output of the co-culture roughly 20%. Unexpectedly, however, co-culturing HSC and MSC that had both been sequentially exposed to both ions resulted in an 80% reduction in HPP-CFC output. Very similar results were obtained when the investigators examined the next most primitive colony type, CFU-GEMM, and more differentiated myeloid CFU-GM. Striking results were also obtained when they examined the effect proton and iron ion irradiation of the MSC had upon co-cultured HSC’s ability to generate megakaryocyte and lymphoid (CFC-T and CFC-B) colonies.

Alterations to Human Hematopoiesis Assessed in vivo: The investigators conditioned NOD/SCID/IL-2rgamma null (NSG) mice by administering 2 sequential doses of busulfan spaced 24 hours apart. Conditioned NSG mice were then transplanted with 2x10(5) human HSC that had been exposed to one of the following irradiation schemes (n=9 per group) at the NSRL: 1) sham irradiation; 2) 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-irradiation; 3) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons; 4) 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions; or 5) 1Gy of 50 MeV protons followed immediately by 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions. Mice were then sacrificed at 4–6 months post-transplant, their spleen and bone marrow harvested, and analyzed by multicolor flow cytometry to ascertain the levels of human hematopoietic engraftment and assess whether exposure to SPE/GCR altered the engraftment potential and/or differentiative capacity of the HSC. In addition to affecting overall levels of engraftment, treatment with protons, 56Fe ions, or sequential exposures also led to pronounced skewing of the differentiative potential of the human HSC, as shown by the relative lineage distribution of the engrafted human cells in the bone marrow and spleens of the transplanted mice. Commitment to the erythroid lineage was significantly impaired following exposure of human HSC to all radiation types tested, and there was a significant expansion of both the T and B lineages. In addition to this lineage skewing, 5 of the 14 recipients of 56Fe ion-irradiated human HSC (obtained from 2 different healthy donors) exhibited dramatic splenomegaly, with one mouse’s spleen reaching ~30X the normal size. To ascertain the cause of splenomegaly, spleens were analyzed by histopathology and immunophenotyping. The spleen exhibited an abnormal morphology, populated largely by cells with a rounded, highly monotonous appearance consistent with lymphoid cells. Immuno-histochemistry with human-specific anti-bodies confirmed that the vast majority of the cells populating the spleen were human, and they expressed CD3 and CD7. Many of these cells also expressed terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), a marker frequently associated clinically with human lymphocytic leukemias. The absence of any staining in an untransplanted NSG mouse spleen stained with the same panel of antibodies verified their specificity. The observed histopathology and immunophenotyping led a team of clinical hematopathologists to concur that human T-ALL developed in these mice.

experiment_title: A Methods Validation Protocol for Estimating Gastroinestinal Motility and Drug-Induced Motility Changes
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bioavailability and effectiveness of drugs and nutrients given by mouth are governed by gastrointestinal (GI) function; key physiologic factors that affect GI function are GI motility and transit, microflora and secretions, and splanchnic (belonging to the internal organs of the body) blood flow. One or all of these factors are influenced by fluid intake, body position, gravity, food and drug constituents, physical activity, and illness. Microgravity associated with space flight has been shown to induce in addition to space motion sickness (SMS), loss of appetite, constipation and indigestion, all of which can be attributed to changes in GI function.

Investigators at Johnson Space Center (JSC) examined GI motility, microbial proliferation and absorption of a marker drug, acetaminophen, in astronauts before, during, and after space flight. In addition, they studied healthy subjects during ambulation and during antiorthostatic (non-standing) bed rest (ABR). The test battery consisted of four independent noninvasive tests, lactulose (Lac) breath hydrogen test (LBH) to measure GI transit time, glucose breath hydrogen and 13C urea breath tests to examine microbial proliferation including H. pylori incidence and proliferation, and acetaminophen absorption.

Promethazine (PMZ) is often used in space to treat SMS early in flight while the laxative bisacodyl (Dulcolax®) is used during later flight days. We propose caffeine as an alternative for the treatment of space-flight associated pathophysiology of the GI tract. Caffeine has been shown to have limited anti-motion sickness properties as well as the ability to stimulate GI motility. It also has cognitive stimulant and anti-somatic activity that may enhance performance and feeling of well-being in astronauts during flight.

In clinical settings, diagnostic procedures for GI pathology are invasive and require extensive laboratory facilities and technical support. The PillCam™, an endoscopy camera embedded in a capsule, is a new technology that is utilized to diagnose diseases of the small intestine including Crohn's Disease, Celiac disease and other malabsorption disorders, benign and malignant tumors of the small intestine, vascular disorders, and medication-related small bowel ulcers and injury. Capsule endoscopy is designed to replace the current, more invasive procedure as well as extend its diagnostic capabilities beyond the stomach or the colon. The PillCam™ is designed to record images from the esophagus all the way through to the colon. The images can then be scanned for GI pathologies. We intend to investigate the usefulness of this technology for estimating GI motility decrements and for assessing efficacy of proposed interventions in GI function restoration. Once validated, this innocuous test can then be administered as a standard diagnostic and treatment efficacy assessment test for space flights.

The investigators proposed to evaluate the usefulness of PillCam™ as a minimally invasive and unobtrusive alternative for estimating GI motility in comparison with lactulose breath hydrogen test. In addition, they evaluated the effects of PMZ and caffeine on GI motility to evaluate the usefulness of the device to estimate changes in GI motility as a function of ingested medications.

This study is uniquely designed such that validation of a diagnostic technology and intervention methods can be achieved in one protocol. The objectives were:

  • Determine the applicability of PillCam™ to estimate GI transit by comparing with the lactulose breath hydrogen test.
  • Examine the effects of promethazine and caffeine on several parameters of GI function.
  • Establish the usefulness of caffeine as a pro-peristaltic agent to enhance GI function in a microgravity environment.

APPROACH:
Twelve healthy non-smoking volunteer subjects between ages 21-49 were recruited for this study. There were 4 oral treatments administered on separate days and data was collected 8 hours post administration of the designated test compound and/or PillCam™.

Treatments

  1. PillCam™ SB (small bowel) Capsule
  2. Lactulose 10 g liquid + PillCam ™ SB Capsule
  3. Caffeine 200 mg tablet + PillCam™ SB Capsule
  4. PMZ 50 mg tablet + PillCam™ SB Capsule

Study Design Overview
The protocol was implemented in two phases. In phase I, 6 subjects completed treatments 1 and 2 on two days with at least 6 days washout in between. On treatment day 1, subjects were treated with only the PillCam™. On treatment day 2, subjects were treated with lactulose and the PillCam™. A separate group of 6 subjects completed treatments 3 and 4 in week 1 and 2, respectively, first with caffeine and then with PMZ, also with a 6 day washout period. Phase II began a week after completion of Phase I with the two groups (6+6). Treatments were swapped between the two groups. In all cases, the PillCam™ capsule was administered to the subject after the drug dose.

Subjects were instructed to be on a clear liquid diet from 3 pm the prior day and fast for the last 10 hours (overnight fasting) prior to administration of each treatment. On the morning of testing, each subject was equipped with a recording device and ingested the designated test dose and a PillCam™ capsule. Serial breath samples were collected for 6 hours post dose and analyzed for hydrogen concentrations. GI recordings were collected for 8 hours (480 minutes).

Data Analysis

  1. PillCam™ - PillCam™ captured gastric images were processed using software provided by Given Imaging; transit times were recorded in a spreadsheet, and appropriate statistics were used to determine changes in transit time. Transit time was determined as the time the PillCam™ enters the bowel to its entrance into the cecum.
  2. Lactulose - Gastrointestinal transit time (GITT) was calculated as a time point of first sustained increase of >10 ppm H2 over baseline level. Sustained increase is defined as an increase lasting over 3 or more samples. Bacterial overgrowth was assessed by observing a spike of >5 ppm H2 over baseline 15-30 minutes prior to sustained elevation.

RESULTS:
The PillCam™ capsule reached the colon prior to termination of recordings during all sessions for all subjects, with overall GITT ranging from 84 to 452 minutes. Maximal recording period is dependent on the capsules' battery-life and has been found to be approximately 480 and 540 minutes.

No difference was found between PillCam™ alone and PillCam™+Lac groups when means are collapsed across sex, indicating that at this low dose of Lac does not alter GI motility after fasting. An overall significant increase in GITT was noticed after administration of PMZ when compared to PillCam™ alone or PillCam™+Lac. However, the increase in GITT 2 hours after the administration of caffeine was not significant. Further, no overall significant differences were found between any of the groups with regards to GTT or ITT.

Sex Differences
No significant effect of sex was detected when means were collapsed across treatments for each subject then compared. GTT, ITT, and GITT means for males were 53, 209, and 263 min respectively and 55, 213 and 268 min for females.

Within treatment, sex differences were found in the PMZ+PillCam™ group. Mean GITT was significantly (p <0.05) higher in males (350 min) than females (255 min). Although mean GTT and ITT were also higher in males than in females during this treatment, the differences were not significant. A difference approaching significance (p=0.055) in GTT was found during the PillCam™+Lac treatment, with mean GTT for males 36 minutes and females 81 minutes. ITT and GITT were not significantly different for this treatment. In the control group, PillCam™ alone, no differences were found for the three dependent variables GTT, ITT and GITT.

Between treatments in males, GITT was found to be reduced 2 hours after the administration of PMZ as compared to both control treatments, the PillCam™ alone and PillCam™+PMZ (p< 0.03). This was not the case in females, where no differences between treatments were found. No other differences were detected.

Order Effect
This analysis was done to determine the effect of repeated fasting periods on GI motility. Order effect was determined by comparing GTT, ITT and GITT in the PillCam™ alone group, which is designated as the control group. For six of the subjects this was the first treatment received and for the other six this was the 3rd treatment. No order effect was detected, indicating that repeated sessions of 18 hour fastings do not alter GI motility when measured with PillCam™ endoscopy. Because pharmacological treatment can confound the results, whereby repeated fasting may alter drug effects, no further analysis was conducted.

Lactulose Breath Hydrogen Test (LBHT)
GITT can be assessed accurately using 10g of lactulose. The concentrations of H2 produced are sufficiently high to differentiate between steady state production and Lac fermentation in the cecum. The results indicate normal GITT in all subjects with results ranging between 45 and 135 minutes as compared with the literature. No correlation was found between GITT using PillCam™ and LBHT.

In conclusion, the PillCam™ capsule endoscope is effective at recording GITT of a solid material. It can be used repeatedly and along with other substances. When administered alone the capsule reached the colon in less than 5 hours in all subjects. Since recording capabilities have been extended to 10+ hours it should be tested in bed rest subjects to determine the extent of GI motility reduction.

experiment_title: Microgravity Plant Nutrient Experiment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Among the investigations that have grown plants in space, none have claimed to have achieved optimal conditions for plant growth. It is believed the most crucial components holding back major advancements in this research are providing adequate levels of water and oxygen to the root zone. Previous studies utilizing other hardware designs have found that the surface tension of water under microgravity conditions has often been found to lead to either severe water-logging or excessive drying in the root zone. Consequently, differences in plant growth responses between space flight experiments and their ground controls occur based merely upon differences in moisture distribution patterns between the two conditions. Until a better means of controlling these critical aspects of plant culture are developed, results of all investigations will be called into question. The Microgravity Plant Nutrient Experiment (MPNE) hardware was designed to address these concerns.

The primary objective of this test was to demonstrate the potential use of porous tubes to provide water and essential minerals to higher plants grown in microgravity. This was accomplished by: (1) assessing whether the Water Availability Sensors and Water Delivery System could work in concert to maintain a predetermined volume of nutrient solution at the root zone, (2) collecting and archiving system performance data from various sensors for post-flight analysis of system operation, and (3) automatically imbibing and germinating seeds on-orbit.

APPROACH:

A Hardware Verification Test (HVT) of MPNE was conducted on STS-89 in the Space Shuttles Middeck. As a biological indicator of hardware performance, wheat (Triticum aestivum cv Yecora rojo) seeds were flown. The seeds were loaded dry three days prior to Orbiter lift-off. Environmental conditions were set to 80-100% relative humidity and 15-35 degrees C. The system was initiated by the crew after three days on-orbit.

RESULTS:

Several hours after the system was initiated a failure of the Water Availability Sensor (WAS) resulted in the inability of the fluid circuit to adequately manage the plant nutrient solution for the plant tubes. MPNE requires that the delivery of water to roots grown in microgravity be done in a precisely controlled fashion. This involves the non-invasive detection and monitoring of a thin-film of the nutrient solution on the surface of the porous tubes by the WAS and the subsequent active control of this "wetness level" via a "fuzzy-logic" feedback system. When the WAS failed to perform this function early in the mission, the system switched to the back-up operational mode where the calculated reservoir volume was divided into time specific delivery volumes required to last for the missions duration, and these amounts (ca 65 microliters) were delivered once a minute. Ground tests have shown that when this back-up mode was implemented (even at the start of an experiment), plant germination and subsequent growth proceeds nominally. However, during the MPNE space flight test, without gravity pulling downward on any excess nutrient solution being provided to the tubes, the seed cylinders became flooded at the time of system initiation and consequently germination failed to proceed. Hence, our water delivery rate in the fixed-feed mode was incorrect for the pattern of water distribution as it occurred in microgravity. Despite most of the MPNE subsystems functioning nominally, the failure of the WAS (although followed by a successful automatic switch to the back-up, fixed-feed, mode of operation) coupled with this excessive water delivery characteristic (in microgravity) of the back-up control method, resulted in the flooding of the seeds.

experiment_title: Space Radiation and Bone Loss: Lunar Outpost Mission Critical Scenarios and Countermeasures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Crews on exploratory missions will face complex radiation from cosmic and solar sources with components ranging from protons to iron. Investigators have identified trabecular bone loss in mice after exposure to multiple radiation types with doses of 50 cGy and lower, suggesting space radiation can increase bone loss from reduced gravity during exploratory missions. They have identified that bone loss is rapid and initiated by an early activation of osteoclasts.

The impact of radiation on bone quality in reduced gravity is unknown, and must be studied to understand effects of space radiation on bone health. The long-term objective of the proposed research is the development of countermeasures to prevent bone loss during missions and thus reduce fracture risk. To define the risks associated with space radiation-induced bone loss, the following aims were studied to examine the effects of modeled space radiation using scenarios applicable for Lunar Outpost missions:

Specific Aim 1: Examine the combined effects of a modeled solar particle event and unloading on bone, and subsequent recovery during reloading. Hypothesis: Proton radiation with unloading will induce a more severe bone loss than unloading alone.

Specific Aim 2: Examine the cellular and molecular mechanisms for initiating bone loss following exposure to several types of modeled space radiation, including acute proton exposure, low-dose-rate proton exposure, and mixed radiation types (proton and HZE). Understanding underlying molecular causes is critical to developing countermeasures for radiation-induced bone loss. Hypothesis: The initiating mechanism of bone loss is initiated by osteoclast activation caused by a radiation-induced inflammatory response.

Specific Aim 3: Test the efficacy of three countermeasures for bone loss caused by proton exposure: 1) the bisphosphonate risedronate; 2) the RANKL blocking protein osteoprotegerin, and 3) an antioxidant agent, alpha-lipoic acid. Hypothesis: Potent inhibitors of bone resorption, both zoledronate and osteoprotegerin will prevent the bone loss caused by radiation. Antioxidants will address multiple radiation-induced problems; alpha-lipoic acid decreases osteoclast differentiation and activity.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Summary of Aim 1 Findings: Mice that were exposed to a 1 Gy dose of protons and 28-days of hindlimb suspension experienced damage that was additive. Irradiation caused a 15% decline in trabecular bone mass in normally loaded mice and a 17% decline in skeletally unloaded mice. A long-term suppression of bone formation inhibits recovery of bone mass.

Aim 1 Future Direction: The effects of mixed radiation, modeling solar particle events and cosmic radiation, needs to be modeled with fractionated exposure during skeletal disuse. It is important to understand if skeletal disuse modifies the threshold dose at which bone loss from radiation is observable. The degree to which animal models predict the human response to space radiation (astronauts) needs to be better understood by studying cancer patients receiving radiation therapy, particularly at the periphery of the radiation field where doses are lower.

Summary of Aim 2 Findings: The acute response to 50 cGy dose of protons or heavy ions is the activation of osteoclastic bone resorption. Serum markers for bone resorption increase 24 hours after exposure and osteoclast numbers and eroded surface are greater at 3-days. Osteoclast activation is temporary, reducing to baseline levels approximately 10-days after irradiation. Investigators identified that this bone loss is preceded by death of bone marrow cells, followed by greater expression then levels of inflammatory cytokines IL-1, IL-6 and TNFalpha. This osteoclast-mediated acute response is not mitigated by low-dose-rate exposure to protons. Acute, osteoclast-mediated bone loss from 50 cGy proton exposure is approximately 50% that of a 2 Gy exposure. The acute bone loss caused by heavy ions (oxygen, silicon, neon, iron) is approximately 30% - 50% greater than that caused by protons.

Aim 2 Future Direction: A more detailed description of acute relative biological effectiveness (RBE), both at the functional and cellular level, needs to be characterized. The association of acute marrow death and osteoclast activation needs to be studied at the causation level with cell culture models.

Summary of Aim 3 Findings: The osteoclast inhibiting bisphosphonate risedronate fully prevented bone loss from a 2 Gy whole body dose of X-rays. Because of intellectual property concerns with a patent application filing, the RANKL-inhibiting protein osteoprotegerin was not able to be tested. As a substitute for OPG, two additional bisphosphonates, pamidronate and zoledronate, were tested. Zoledronate was more effective than pamidronate. Neither of the antioxidant compounds alpha-lipoic acid nor n-acetal cystine (NAC) reduced bone loss from radiation exposure. The IL-1 and TNFalpha blocking compounds, IL-1ra (Kineret) and TNFbp (Enbrel), were tested as potential countermeasures. Neither protein, independently or in combination, mitigated bone loss from radiation exposure.

Aim 3 Future Directions: As an antiresorptive agent that suppresses osteoclast activity through a different mechanism than bisphosphonates, osteoprotegerin should be studied as a countermeasure (intellectual property concerns are currently being addressed). The most effective dosing regimen for risedronate and zoledronate needs to be further refined. Additionally, a myostatin inhibitor should be studied as a countermeasure that may have positive effects on both bone and muscle. Finally, countermeasures should be tested in models that combine both skeletal challenges astronauts will be exposed to microgravity and space radiation.

experiment_title: In-Flight LBNP: Countermeasure to Reduce Post-Space Flight Orthostatic Intolerance
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a resultant decrease in body fluid. Hypovolemia might contribute to the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. However, countermeasures like oral fluid and salt loading or the use of an anti-gravity suit have not succeeded in preventing postflight orthostatic intolerance. It may be that orthostatic intolerance could be counteracted by the ingestion of isotonic saline while negative pressure is applied to the legs and abdomen to allow the plasma volume to increase. The objective of this study was to evaluate this lower body negative pressure (LBNP) and fluid loading countermeasure for use in flight.

APPROACH:
Thirteen astronauts were studied before and during space flights of 7 to 14 days. Two months or more before a flight, the astronauts' tolerance of LBNP was checked by applying LBNP in steps of 10 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) until the astronaut showed signs of presyncope (impending fainting). Orthostatic tolerance was assessed independently of gravity in LBNP ramp tests, in which blood pressure and heart rate were monitored while the astronauts spent five minutes at each 10-mm Hg drop of pressure down to -40 to -60 mm Hg. Ramp tests were carried out before the flight as well as during the flight at three-day intervals before, and one or two days after, the LBNP countermeasure protocol, which was called a "soak." A stepwise decompression (ramp) to -50 mm Hg was followed by 3.5 hours at 30 mm Hg below ambient pressure. During the first hour at -30 mm Hg, the astronauts ingested one liter of water or artificially sweetened fruit drink and eight grams of sodium chloride to provide isotonic saline. The effect of the soak treatment was evaluated by comparing heart rate and blood pressure responses to ramp tests before and after the treatment. A LBNP chamber that could be collapsed and stowed was used aboard the Shuttle. Negative pressure was provided by connecting it to a vacuum source (the Waste Collection System or the Spacelab Vacuum Vent).

RESULTS:
Evaluable data were obtained from only four astronauts. The heart rate at maximum LBNP increased significantly between preflight and early in-flight ramp tests. Decreased heart rate responses to LBNP one day after the in-flight soak indicated that it provided a protective effect. The systolic and diastolic blood pressures during maximum LBNP were not significantly different from preflight levels during any of the ramp tests or soaks. These results showed that the combination of LBNP with ingestion of isotonic saline may be an effective countermeasure against postflight orthostatic intolerance. Results also suggested that orthostatic tolerance was lost after only 10 days or less in space, and that treatments may be beneficial even during flights of short-duration. However, the countermeasure is impractical for use during Shuttle missions because one treatment of one astronaut takes approximately five hours.

experiment_title: Ultrastructural Changes in Choroid Plexus of Rats Maintained in Microgravity During a Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The aim of the experiment was to evaluate the effects of microgravity on fine structure and protein organization of choroidal cells after a space flight. The functional consequences of spaceflight and hindlimb-suspension were evaluated by immunocytochemistry and by molecular biology by detecting changes in the expression of cytoskeletal and membrane proteins in choroidal cells which produce cerebrospinal fluid. Moreover, qualitative changes in the biosynthesis and storage of natriuretic peptides (using electron microscopy, immunocytochemistry) in hypothalamus and heart were evaluated under microgravity conditions.

Approach:

Rat brains were removed after decapitation and choroid plexuses from 5 brains dissected and fixed inflight and 3 others dissected 5-8 hours after landing were carefully isolated, briefly rinsed in PBS, and fixed by immersion in 2.5 percent glutaraldehyde in cacodylate buffer 0.1M, pH 7.4, post-fixed in 1 percent osmium tetroxide in sodium barbital-acetate buffer 0.05M, pH 7.4 and embedded in LX-112 epoxy resin. Those from 2 other animals dissected 5-8 hours after landing were fixed in the same conditions in 3% paraformaldehyde in PBS. Hypothalamus and the remaining brain with brainstem from these same brains were removed and directly frozen on dry ice, before storage at -80 degrees C. and shipping on dry ice to the lab, where they were stored at -80 degrees C until sectioning. Whole brains from 2 animals in each group were immersed in Bouinï¿½s fixative for 16 h, washed and dehydrated in ethanol, before embedding in Paraplast. Four other whole brains were directly frozen on dry ice, and stored at -80 degrees C. Hearts were similarly processed for electron microscopy, immunocytochemistry. Atrial and ventricle samples were frozen for radioimmunoassay and northern blot.

Results:

Ultrastructural observations of choroidal cells dissected inflight or 5-8 h postflight from adult rats showed a loss of cell polarity (altered kinocilia, loss of microvilli, decreases in apical ezrin) and a reduced choroidal secretion (accumulation of apical vesicles, loss of apical membrane and cytoplasmic molecules, involved in water and ionic transports, such as aquaporin 1, Na/K ATPase, carbonic anhydrase II). Similar effects were observed in hindlimb-suspended rats, whereas control rats displayed typical choroidal features. Those results suggested that, after 2 weeks in weightlessness, choroidal functions were altered, indicating a reduction in the secretory processes. As cerebrospinal fluid is mainly produced by these cells, we concluded that spaceflight and head-down suspension probably induce a reduced CSF production. Analyses of natriuretic peptides in hypothalamus and heart are still in progress.

experiment_title: Rodent Research 9 (RR9)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Rodent Research 9 (RR-9) science investigation was conducted by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Space Life and Physical Sciences program. The mission consisted of three experiments led by principal investigators Michael Delp, Xiao Wen Mao, and Jeffrey Wiley. Delp's investigation was designed to study the effects of long duration spaceflight on fluid shifts and increased fluid pressures in the head, Mao's was to examine the impact of spaceflight on the vessels that supply blood to the eyes, and Wiley's was designed to study the extent of knee and hip joint degradation caused by prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Specific aims of each experiment are summarized below.

Michael Delp's experiment had four aims:
1. To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS alters rodent basilar artery spontaneous tone, myogenic and KCl (Potassium Chloride)-evoked vasoconstriction, mechanical stiffness and gross structure.
2. To estimate whether spaceflight on the ISS alters the blood-brain barrier in rodents, as indicated by ultrastructural examination of the junctional complex of the cerebral capillary endothelium.
3. To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS alters rodent basal vein (inside cranium) and jugular vein (outside cranium) spontaneous tone, myogenic and KCl-evoked constriction, distension, and gross structure.
4. To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS alters the ability of the cervical lymphatics to modulate lymph flow, and thus, regulate cerebral fluid homeostasis.

Xiao Wen Mao's investigation had two aims:
1. Define the relationships between spaceflight condition-induced oxidative stress in reactive oxygen species (ROS) expression and retinal vascular remodeling and BRB function in mice return to Earth alive.
2. Determine whether spaceflight condition-induced oxidative damage in retina is mediated through photoreceptor mitochondrial ROS production.

Jeffrey Willey's investigation had two aims:
1. Determine the extent of knee and hip joint degradation in mice after 30 days of spaceflight on the ISS.
2. Use the DigiGait System to assess gait patterns before and after returning from the ISS.

experiment_title: Complex Study of Micro and Macro Structure and Mineral Composition of Spongy Bone
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Exposure to microgravity leads to many changes in bone formation and growth. Diminished osteoblast production, osteoporotic signs, bone mass density loss, and reduced strength can occur. Though these effects can prove especially dangerous on long-term missions, little is known about the actual mechanisms by which bone loss occurs. The differentiation of osteoblasts and alteration of bone matrix in microgravity is not well understood. This study utilizes electron microscopy to examine bone changes in Bion 11 monkeys exposed to microgravity.

Approach:

Flight and control animals were anesthetized using isofluorethane and iliac crest samples were taken. Samples were fixed for 24 hours in 2% glutaraldehyde adjusted to pH 7.2 with paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffer. Fixed samples were rinsed three times with 70% ethanol, then postfixed in 1% OsO4, dehydrated, and embedded in araldite. Ultrathin sections were cut, contrasted, and examined using transmission electron microscopy. Other samples were fixed in 2% glutaraldehyde, dried, gold plated, and examined using scanning electron microscopy. Observed osteoblasts were classified into four categories. Type I osteoblasts predominantly synthesize and secrete proteoglycans and alkaline phosphatase, and also accumulate and secrete Ca and P. Type 2 osteoblasts predominantly synthesize collagen proteins. Type 3 osteoblasts secrete accumulated protein and glycosaminoglycans. Type 4 osteoblasts are inactive.

Results:

Bone structure in samples taken from the vivarium and flight control animals were similar. Osteogenesis was slow in the monkeys, compared to rats observed in previous studies. The flight monkeys' osteoblast synthetic rates were lower than the control monkeys. A small number of Type 2 and Type 3 osteoblasts versus a large number of Type 4 osteoblasts was observed, indicating a lower rate of collagen synthesis and secretion. Signs of asynchronicity of synthetic processes were not seen, which are typically observed in the norm. Signs of adaptive changes were seen in osteoblasts in several zones. These changes may be associated with osteoblast transformation into fibroblasts. The osteoblast changes observed in this experiment are consistent with the changes found by histomorphometric analysis of monkeys on the Cosmos 2044 flight. Osteocyte structure in flight animals was normal, but some osteocytes developed increased osteolysis. These changes were interpreted as bone adaptation to microgravity.

experiment_title: Gastrointestinal Function During Extended Duration Space Flights
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The combined effects of fluid shifts, fluid loss, decreased fluid consumption, and postural changes in microgravity are postulated to decrease splanchnic blood flow, decrease gastrointestinal (GI) motility, and thereby decrease absorption and availability of pharmaceutical countermeasures and nutrients. Decreases in gastric emptying rate are suspected of causing variability in the absorption of oral acetaminophen during short-duration flights of up to 5 days (Cintron et al., 1987). We hypothesize that GI function in microgravity will be altered as a result of decreased GI motility. Therefore, the overall objective of this ongoing inflight investigation is to determine, using two well characterized noninvasive probe compounds, the effect of space flight on GI motility, as measured by changes in the rates of gastric emptying and intestinal transit time. This information will be useful for designing and delivering safe and effective pharmacologic treatment during space flight.

Assessment of GI function, physiology and availability of oral medications during space flight will help identifying effective pharmaceutical and nutritional countermeasures to enhance health and performance of crewmembers during extended durations of space missions.

APPROACH:
During each testing session, astronauts ingested 650 mg acetaminophen and 20 mg lactulose with a proscribed breakfast. Serial saliva and breath samples, as well as void by void urines, were collected for 24 hours. Concentrations of acetaminophen and its metabolites were assayed in saliva and urine to determine acetaminophen pharmacokinetics. Breath hydrogen levels were analyzed to determine gastrointestinal transit time.

RESULTS:
The clinical portion of this study has been completed with a total of 7 astronauts. Of these 7 participants, four completed testing procedures pre-, in-, and post-flight and three completed testing pre- and post-flight.

Maximum acetaminophen concentrations were reduced in spaceflight by 69% compared to pre-flight. Acetaminophen bioavailability was also reduced in spaceflight, by 36% compared to preflight. Absorption rate of acetaminophen, an indicator of gastric emptying time, and time to maximum concentration were not affected by spaceflight. Gastrointestinal transit time was increased by 29% compared to preflight.

experiment_title: Quantitative Analysis of Selected Bone Parameters: Supplemental Report 1: Effects of Weightlessness on Osteoblast
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Marked depression or arrest of bone formation has been associated with space flight and simulated weightlessness. The mechanism of this suppression of osteogenesis is unclear, but probably involves altered induction. Data indicate that nuclear volume frequency distributions are an effective means of assaying preosteoblast differentiation in a population of connective tissue cells. Thus, the objective of this experiment was to determine whether space flight would alter cellular induction in the fibroblast-like cells in the rat periodontal ligament (PDL).

Approach:

PDL, the osteogenic interface between tooth and bone, was morphometrically analyzed. The region studied was a 300 µm length of midroot PDL on the medial aspect of the medial root of the maxillary first molars. Volumes for 100 nuclei from throughout the width of the PDL were determined, and frequency distributions of nuclear volume for each group were calculated. Studies were conducted on rats sacrificed at recovery and six and 29 days postflight.

Results:

Immediately postflight, PDL width and total cell number were decreased. Frequency distributions of nuclear volume revealed that presumptive preosteoblasts (nuclei >= 130 µm-3) were particularly depressed. Compared to vivarium controls, frequency distributions of nuclear volume revealed a relative increase in smaller nuclei (<=80 µm-3) at the expense of these larger nuclei. No significant differences in interzone mean nuclear volumes were observed for the groups sacrificed at six and twenty-nine days postflight. This study suggests that depleted numbers of preosteoblasts may be an important factor in the arrest of bone formation during weightlessness. Data are consistent with either a defect in proliferation and/or differentiation. Additional cell kinetic studies utilizing 3H-thymidine are needed to define the mechanism of this important aerospace problem.

experiment_title: Long Term Effects of Weightlessness on a Biological System-Isoenzyme Analysis: Supplemental Report
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The main objective of the gel electrophoresis study was to determine if weightlessness or other gravity treatments altered the isoenzyme profile of crown gall tumors. This objective was extended to include nontumored cortex and stele tissue. Although tumor growth in weightlessness was minimal, and the amount of material available for study was limited, it was decided to proceed with electrophoretic analysis where a sufficient amount of tumor tissue was available.

Approach:

A system involving the generation of crown gall tumors induced by Agrobacterium tumefaciens Conn. on root disks of carrot was developed, which was responsive to gravity treatments. Lyophilized carrot disk samples and frozen tumor samples were weighed and ground; the homogenate was centrifuged; and the supernatant served as the sample for electrophoresis. Protein concentrations were estimated by spectrophotometric protein assay. Isoenzyme patterns were examined after isoelectric focusing of samples in polyacrylamide gel cylinders. Gels were then stained for general proteins, esterase, acid phosphatase, and peroxidase.

Results:

Several repeated electrophoretic trials failed to yield consistent results with general protein stains. Similarly, peroxidase isoenzyme patterns were difficult to assay because of a high degree of background interference in the gels. Six major bands of esterase activity were found in all tissues. When the approximate pH values were determined from 1 mm sliced gels, a linear regression was apparent as the pH value for each band changed slightly, with values ranging from 5.36 to 4.38. Although the disk tissue was separated into cortex and stele, the esterase pattern was unchanged. The gravity treatments did not appear to affect the esterase enzyme pattern. No other conclusions could be made from the protein, peroxidase and acid phosphate data because of a lack of sufficient material for complete analysis, non-uniform condition of the material, and inconsistent results.

experiment_title: The Influence of Space Flight on the Rat Soleus
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Results from previous Cosmos experiments have shown that several biochemical and physiological properties of rat skeletal muscle are altered after space flight. These studies have been based primarily on analysis of whole muscle properties. Since there is a potential difference in the response of muscle fibers differing in size and alkaline adenosinetriphosphatase (ATPase) type, this study focused on the adaptation to space flight of single muscle fibers. The purposes of the study were: 1) to define the size and metabolic responses to space flight and 2) to determine the specificity of these responses to the muscle and the ATPase type and size of its fibers.

Approach:

The left soleus (SOL), adductor longus (AL), plantaris (PL), extensor digitorum longus (EDL), and medial gastrocnemius (MG) muscles were removed. Frozen serial sections (10 µm) were prepared for determination of alkaline (pH 8.8) myofibrillar ATPase staining density, and SDH and GPD activity. Fiber cross-sectional areas were also determined from ATPase stained sections. A computer- assisted image analysis system was used to quantify the rate of change of optical density (OD) for each fiber, and the rate of staining (OD/min) was directly proportional to the enzyme activity. Remaining SOL and EDL tissue was powdered and lypholized for biochemistry. Myofibrillar ATPase, the release of inorganic phosphate in the reaction, and protein content were determined from 1 mg samples.

Results:

Wet weight of each of the flight muscles was significantly reduced compared to controls; loss varied from 36% in the SOL to 15% in the EDL. Cross-sectional areas of fibers in flight muscles were also reduced, except for the dark ATPase in the MG. The greatest relative fiber atrophy occurred in the muscles with the highest proportion of light ATPase fibers. An increase in the percentage of dark ATPase fibers was also observed in flight muscles with a predominance of light ATPase fibers. There was an increase in the biochemically determined myofibrillar ATPase activity of tissue sections of the flight SOL. No changes in histochemical or biochemical measures of ATPase activity were observed in the EDL. In general, the SDH activity of the flight muscles was maintained, whereas GPD activity either was maintained or increased. This suggests an increase in the proportion of fast oxidative-glycolytic fibers in some muscles, apparently at the expense of slow oxidative fibers.

experiment_title: Single Fiber Muscle Function
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies examining the soleus (SOL) and extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles of the rat hindlimb indicate that muscles exposed to microgravity undergo atrophy and a change of fiber composition from slow to fast twitch types. These changes can vary depending upon the muscle participation in antigravitational activity (i.e. posture) and on the functional profile of the muscle (slow or fast twitch). In order to corroborate these earlier findings, this study will examine the functional (activated tension characteristics) and structural (myofibril composition) changes caused by microgravity in the tibialis anterior (TA), vastus intermedius (VI), as well as the soleus (SOL), and extensor digitorum (EDL) muscles of the rat hindlimb.

Approach:

Fiber bundles were removed, isolated and skinned from selected rat hindlimb muscles (SOL, VI, TA, EDL). In order to quantify the atrophy of the fiber, mass, cross-sectional area and maximal tension were measured. Then, each fiber underwent force measurements to establish tension/pCa and tension/pSr, and to determine the functional properties of the muscle. Additional calculations and measurements were performed in order to determine Ca and Sr affinity. After the completion of these physiological measurements, the muscle fibers underwent analysis with sodium dodecyl sulphate polyacrimide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) in order to determine myosin heavy and light chain composition. The results were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).

Results:

Tension analysis revealed that SOL fibers exposed to microgravity showed a significant increase in the proportion of fast fibers when compared to control fibers. In contrast, VI fibers, which have a similar proportion of fiber as normal SOL fibers, did not show a significant increase in fast twitch fiber composition when exposed to microgravity. The change in fiber composition for TA and EDL fiber was insignificant, since these muscle contain exclusively fast type fibers. Electrophoretic analysis corroborated these results. After flight, SOL fibers showed a decrease in fast myosin proteins, while in VI fibers, the proportion of proteins did not change.
