experiment_title: Spaceflight effects on the mouse retina: Histological, gene expression and epigenetic changes after flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Visual function and neuroanatomical ocular changes have been observed in some long-duration crewmembers. These alterations seem to be related to microgravity-induced fluid shifts and ensued ICP increase. The mechanisms by which these factors cause eye damage are not understood. Damage may extend beyond anatomical alterations of the eye. The hypothesis that these two pilot studies will test is that pathophysiological pathways at the molecular and cellular levels in the retina may also contribute to microgravity-induced vision risks. These pathways may be triggered by oxygenation perturbations and mechanical and oxidative stress associated to the fluid shifts in microgravity. In Part I, a mouse experiment aboard two shuttle missions, STS-133 and STS-135, will allow us to test the hypothesis that mouse eyes in microgravity (together with confounding space environment factors) exhibit alterations in the histological and gene expression profile that may be indicative of cellular stress pathways. To date, there have been limited flight animal studies aimed at studying the effects of microgravity on the retina (Tombran-Tink, Adv Exp Med Biol, 2006; Grigoryan, Adv Space Res, 2002). In Part II, a ground animal analog, the rat hindlimb suspension model (HS), will be used to test the same hypothesis using a model of simulated microgravity. A second hypothesis within Part II will test the efficacy of nutritional countermeasures. Resveratrol, a potent antioxidant and activator of the cellular stress response pathway, has been shown to ameliorate bone loss (Habold et al, J Bone Min Res 2010) and muscle atrophy in hindlimb suspended animals (Jackson et al, Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 2010). Likewise, resveratrol has been shown to prevent and ameliorate oxidative damage and retinal neurodegeneration in several experimentally induced ocular conditions in animals (Liu et al, IOVS 2007; Shindler et al, IOVS 2007; Kubota et al, IOVS 2009). This study will examine whether resveratrol has a cytoprotective effect in the retinas of rats subjected to the stress caused by cephalad fluid shifts. In addition, the protective effects of resveratrol will be compared to those of another reactive oxygen species scavenger, epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) found in green tea extract.

APPROACH:
This project aims at testing the overall hypothesis that cephalad fluid shifts elicited by either microgravity or hindlimb suspension (HS) represent a stress factor that induces optic disc neuroanatomical changes, as well as retinal cell deterioration and loss via oxidative stress. The first specific aim of this pilot project is to perform histological and gene expression analysis of retinas collected from mice flown in STS-133 and STS-135 and from their ground control counterparts. The second specific aim is to perform similar analysis in retinas from hindlimb suspended rats, focusing on pathways consistent with cellular and oxidative stress, thus validating this ground analog animal model for the study of retinal stress in microgravity. The third specific aim will explore the potential efficacy of reversatrol and EGCG as a nutritional countermeasures to mitigate the risks or retinal oxidative stress and degeneration in conditions of simulated microgravity.

RESULTS:
Upon completion of this task, we have expanded the immunohistopathologic analysis of the rodent retina as far as the effects of and responses to spaceflight observed in the eyes of mice aboard shuttle mission STS-133 and STS-135, focusing, for the first time, on molecular and cellular processes. While the results reported here represent pilot data due to the small sample size, these data provide for the first time, direct evidence suggesting that oxidative stress, neuronal damage, and mechanical injury take place in the retina and optic nerve of rodents flown in low-Earth orbit for a period under 2 weeks. Our work gives a first insight into the impact of space-associated factors on biological processes like cell death, oxidative stress, and probable mechanical injury in the rodent eye.

Moreover, comparative results obtained with two different mouse strains (albino versus pigmented mice) suggest that susceptibility to stress factors is determinant of the extent of the stressors effects. While individual variability is not regularly encountered with genetically homogenous mouse strains, we observed some individual susceptibility variation, which may be ascribed to a particular stress impact in spaceflight, part of which is stochastic in nature (radiation).

The present work also investigated the contribution of cephalad fluid shift alone in the rat retina by using the well-characterized hindlimb suspension (HS) model, and identified, for the first time, a gene expression response suggestive of mechanical stress imposed by cephalad fluid shift on the eye. In addition, an antioxidant nutritional countermeasure based on a green-tea enriched diet resulted in a decreased stress response, suggesting an association between the possible mechanical stress and oxidative stress genetic circuits.

experiment_title: Epigenetic and Protein Expression Pattern Profiling of Caenorhabditis elegans Exposed to Time-Varying Gravitational Fields: a Multi-Generational Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
We hypothesize that long term temporal changes in the gravity vector will result in animal adaptation via epigenetic mechanisms that are passed onto subsequent generations. We further hypothesize that the gravity-influenced epigenetic profile can be restored to the consensus wild-type (i.e., Earth born) upon introduction to stable 1x g conditions. We propose to utilize C. elegans as a model organism to address this hypothesis by performing the following experiments. 1) Determine C. elegans behavioral responses (i.e., changes in migration dynamics, animal body posture, metabolism, etc.) due to temporal changes in the gravity vector. The gravity vector will be controlled by placing the animals inside a rotating CubeSat microscope developed by our group. The frequency, direction and duration of rotation will be varied to elicit the most dramatic behavioral responses. Habituation time will be evaluated, and also changes in lifespan. 2) Identify gravity responsive genes by utilizing the vast collection of fluorescent strains of C. elegans available to researchers. We will monitor gene expression by fluorescence microscopy from the embryonic stage through adulthood during changes in the gravity vector. Genes of interest include those associated with muscle development, cell apoptosis, and neuronal development. 3) Profile the epigenetic marks on C. elegans exposed to long periods of continuous gravity vector changes that range from 1/4 of an animal's lifespan to three generations. We will examine the epigenetic consequence of restoring constant 1xg conditions over successive generations. The three Specific Aims can be conducted with the same animal strains, and thus allows the opportunity to correlate the findings across different experiments.

APPROACH:
For simulated microgravity experiments, we designed and constructed a clinorotation device with integrated microscope, and a fluidic sample system. As clinorotation necessarily involves a fluid environment, C. elegans were maintained in liquid CeMM (C. elegans Maintenance Media); control animals were maintained on agar plates with a bacterial food source (OP50 strain). Stock cultures were maintained on agar plates at 16C.

Five histone modifications were targeted, based on previous publications: H3K4Me3, H3K27Me3, H3K9Me3, H3K36Me and H4K20Me. ChIP was performed in duplicate, in varying environmental conditions (i.e., agar, liquid, clinorotation settings or generational). Bioinformatics software packages such as: MACS, Homer, IGV, DiffBind and SICER were utilized to identify changes in gene expression, as well mine public genome/protein databases. RNA sequencing was used to validate epigenomic data.

We used the method of Chromatin ImmunoPrecipitation (ChIP) followed by high throughput Next Generation Sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 to identify DNA sequences enriched in specific histone modifications. C. elegans embryos were harvested from stock cultures by bleaching and centrifugation. Embryos were transferred to different environment and grown up to roughly synchronized late L4-young adult stage of development (6 days for CeMM cultures). Animals were also maintained for multiple generations, estimated by the amount of time (days).

RESULTS:
This project provided insight to the major Decadal Identifier AH16: Studies on transmission across generations of structural and functional changes induced by exposure to space during development. Our initial hypothesis that exposure to simulated microgravity will change gene expression levels, and that these changes will persist through multiple generations was confirmed primarily by RNA sequencing. We find that C. elegans embryos raised during clinorotation (F1 generation) elicits the transcription of new genes that were are not expressed in the parent (P0, ground control), and many of these genes are non-coding (nc)RNAs with unknown function. These new genes are still expressed in generations F2 through F4 raised in ground conditions, demonstrating a powerful epigenetic memory of the microgravity environment. It is important to note that these ncRNAs are not typically included in “standard” gene hybridization arrays (e.g., Affymetrix), but are identified using next-generation sequencing (NGS) methods. Future flight experiments should favor NGS over hybridization arrays because this will enable a complete representation of the transcriptome. Our RNA expression profiles show that upon return to ground conditions, about 1500 genes are differentially expressed for two generations; by the third generation on ground this number drops sharply to 104 genes. Thus, for the case of C. elegans and clinorotation, the exposure to altered gravity persists for about three generations.

We compared our simulated microgravity results with similar flight experiments involving C. elegans in the NASA GeneLab database (four flight experiments + our clinorotation). The largest differentially expressed gene overlap between all the experiments was with the CERISE 4 spaceflight experiment and our clinorotation data. These results support the use of clinorotation as a ground- based analog that captures some aspects of true space microgravity, quantitated through gene expression profiling. It might be expected that CERISE 4 and CERISE 8 should be the most similar, but the experiments differed in that 9,000 animals were used in CERISE 4, while only 30-50 were used for CERISE 8. A low number of animals will produce highly variable DNA microarray results, which may have been the case for the CERISE experiments.

Additional results will be made available by NASA's GeneLab.

experiment_title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Latent Virus Reactivation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prolonged exposure to reduced gravity, physiological stress or other factors associated with space flight may result in immune system dysregulation. Latent herpesvirus reactivation, a measurable result of dysregulated immunity, has been detected in crewmembers during and immediately following space missions.
A panel of assays was designed to monitor immune system dysregulation, viral reactivation, and physiological stress has been developed and validated at the Johnson Space Center (JSC). These assays will be applied to a future ISS/Shuttle Supplemental Medical Objective (SMO). This assay panel is also appropriate to monitor the status and function of the immune system, viral reactivation, and physiological stress during ground-based analog studies. These assays will be included on all future bed rest campaigns for the purpose of monitoring the immune status of the participants. While bed rest is not the most appropriate model for space flight-associated immune dysregulation, it is possible that the various countermeasures proposed for evaluation during bed rest may affect immune function. For this reason, the immune function of the participants will be monitored.
APPROACH:
There have been comparatively few flight studies investigating the effect of space flight on the human immune system. Those studies that have been performed may be subdivided into the following categories: (A) in flight culture of immune cells; (B) postflight assessments of crewmembers; (C) in flight crewmember immune assessments. These data were recently reviewed by Dr. Gerald Sonnenfeld (Sonnenfeld 2002, Sonnenfeld 2003) and are summarized as follows:
A. In flight culture of immune cells
Human studies have indicated that space flight changes human cell culture activities such as leukocyte blastogenesis, production of cytokines, and signal transduction of leukocytes. Studies on animal cell cultures have also shown altered cytokine production and macrophage hematopoesis and function.
B. Postflight assessments of crewmembers
Most human space flight immunologic studies have explored the effects of space flight on cell-mediated immunity. Inhibited mitogen-induced blastogenesis of leukocytes has been observed in cells obtained from astronauts and cosmonauts after the Apollo-Soyuz test project, Skylab, Space Shuttle and Soyuz flights. Altered leukocyte subset distribution, altered cytokine production and altered natural killer (NK) cell activity have also been found to be altered immediately postflight.
C. In flight assessments of crewmembers
Precious few studies have been performed using astronaut subjects during space flight. Delayed hypersensitivity skin tests to common recall antigens were inhibited during short term and long term space flights. On Space Shuttle mission STS-71 a novel device for staining whole blood samples with fluorescent antibodies was flight tested using three MIR-18 crewmembers as subjects. Blood was collected and stained at a single timepoint late in the mission. Only the bulk leukocyte and lymphocyte subsets were evaluated and no change was found in these crewmembers. Recently, an in flight assessment of latent viral reactivation was performed using flight-collected saliva samples. Latent viral reactivation is thought to directly correlate with diminished immune function. The data showed that latent herpesviruses reactivate during flight to high levels. This is important since persistent viruses have been associated with non-Hodkins lymphoma tumors. A short term space flight study on Shuttle assessed total antibody levels and found no change in total immunoglobulin levels, whereas a long-duration Soviet mission indicated small increases in total immunoglobulin levels.
In the investigator's previous studies of astronauts, investigators found altered peripheral leukocyte distribution, altered cytokine production profiles, elevated levels of latent viral reactivation and elevated levels of cortisol during or immediately following long and short duration space flight. In addition, significant increases in stress hormones (i.e., cortisol, catecholamines) were found after landing. Notably, investigators found increased shedding of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV), two medically important herpesviruses, during space flight along with evidence of decreased cellular immunity. These increases in stress hormones directly correlated with CMV and EBV reactivation. Thus, latent herpesvirus reactivation in these astronauts may have resulted from both direct (i.e., stress hormones) and indirect (i.e., decreased immune function) mechanisms stemming from launch and landing acceleration. These results underscore the need to determine the causes underlying immune suppression in space in order to develop countermeasures.
RESULTS:
In general, subjects did not display altered peripheral leukocyte subsets, constitutive immune activation, altered T cell function, or significant latent viral reactivation (EBV, VZV). Levels of constitutively activated T cells (CD8+/CD69+) and virus-specific T cells (CMV and EBV) decreased during the study. Cortisol levels (plasma and saliva) did not vary significantly during 90-day bed rest.
Conclusions: These data demonstrate the absence of significant immune system alteration and physiological stress during 90-day bed rest, and establish control data against which future studies (including countermeasures) may be compared.

experiment_title: Genotypic and phenotypic responses of Candida albicans to spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Modeling the microgravity environment, using rotating suspension culture bioreactors, has allowed investigation of eukaryotic cellular responses in a ground-based model and has provided insights into the impact of spaceflight on cellular physiology. Extrapolation of results from modeled systems to that expected in space is useful and informative, but evaluating the impact of actual space exposure strengthens the validity and interpretation of data from both environments. Using the Candida albicans (C. albicans) yeast system, it is demonstrated that simulated microgravity affects differential expression of several groups of genes, including those related to morphogenic transformation, environmental sensing and ergosterol biosynthesis; induces morphologic changes such as filamentation, biofilm formation and colony morphology; and results in an increased resistance to the antimicrobial agent Amphotericin B. The constellation of these physiological responses is consistent with a potential increase in the virulence of this opportunistic yeast pathogen. The focus of the current proposal is to characterize physiological outcome measures of C. albicans following exposure to flight on the International Space Station (ISS). The overall objective of this experiment is to evaluate the response of C. albicans to spaceflight in order to 1) predict the potential health risk posed by this opportunistic pathogen in the spaceflight environment, and 2) to further characterize the phenotypic and genotypic response of a eukaryotic system to conditions of microgravity.

APPROACH:
The Micro-6 experiment will provide new insights into better management and treatment of Candida infections. Candida albicans was chosen since extensive studies have provided a broad set of benchmarks, including the sequence of the entire genome, against which results can be compared. By comparing the cells grown in microgravity to cells grown in normal gravity, the susceptibility of the yeast to an antimicrobial agent will be examined. The equipment consists of BioServe's flight certified hardware: Group Activation Packs (GAPs) stored in a Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (CGBA), an incubator capable of controlling the temperature between 8ºC and 37ºC. Each GAP contains eight Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) inserts designed to meet the unique requirement of mixing fluids in microgravity. Each FPA contains an isolated amount of the microbial culture of Candida, a growth medium, and a termination reagent or fixative. The experiment will be initiated by increasing the incubator temperature to 30ºC and activating the FPAs by mixing the Candida with a growth medium. After 24 or 50 hours, depending on the sample, the experiment will be terminated by combining a fixative agent to effectively stop the growth of the yeast cultures. After the yeast return from the three-week flight aboard the space station, changes to the genetics within the organism will be examined.

RESULTS:
A primary concern was the survival of the yeast stored in water until experimental processing and then, for the appropriate experiments, survival during return to Earth. As predicted based on our ground-based assessment, the yeast survived the pre-experimental-processing storage in water as well as the post-experiment storage during the trip back to Earth. The next basic analysis was to assess whether yeast grow more quickly when exposed to the microgravity environment, as has been documented for some prokaryotes. Our data would suggest that there is not a significant difference in growth between ground and flight samples (data not shown) although design of appropriate ground control conditions is difficult due to sedimentation or employing a rotation device. Perhaps more interesting is the suggestive, but not significant data, that the longer cells are exposed to flight, the slower they are likely to grow relative to ground.

Our preliminary LSMMG studies demonstrated that cells acquired a complex and highly convoluted colony morphology following growth in the HARV. In the Micro-6 study, colonies with similar morphology as was observed during LSMMG where not observed in the live samples when plated upon return to the Montana laboratory. Actually, the colonies derived from flight cells were more normal than those derived from ground based samples. Either exposure to microgravity was not long enough to induce similar changes (phenotype takes 5-8 days of continuous culture in HARV to observe, whereas cells in flight only grew 1.5-2 days), the phenotype reverted during the 4 days of gravity exposure before the analysis could be performed (although the phenotype was relatively irreversible when induced by LSMMG), or the response to microgravity is different than the response to LSMMG.

Our ground-based studies demonstrated that yeast grown under LSMMG conditions were more resistant to the effects of the antifungal agent Amphotericin B. For this reason, we evaluated the ability of cells to grow in the presence of the antifungal agent while on the ISS. Cells were then fixed on station and cell growth was quantified upon sample return. In addition, viable cells were exposed to AB upon sample return and cell viability was analyzed by flow cytometry. Flight samples were significantly more resistant to the highest dose (2.4 mg/L) of drug, similar to the results obtained in our LSMMG studies. Although less conclusive, both in-flight and post-flight samples showed a trend toward increased resistance at lower concentrations of drug (1.2 mg/L) as compared to ground controls.

Please see results in related experiment Micro-8 (NNX12AH29G).

experiment_title: Microgravity Vestibular Investigations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Microgravity Vestibular Investigations (MVI) studied the underlying perceptual and physiological mechanisms associated with sensori-motor adaptations to space flight. Human perception of orientation in space depends on the interaction of virtually every sensory system. Changes in the environment and the interaction with the new stimuli result in a different interpretation by the central nervous system (CNS) of the incoming sensory information. Because the human orientation system is adaptable and complex, it is difficult to trace a change in behavior to any one sensori-motor unit in the synergistic orientation system. In this investigation, the effects of different stimuli on the human sense of orientation was determined; thereby an interactive model for orientation was used.

APPROACH:
The MVI experiment used a rotator chair, which provided angular rotation stimuli about a single axis (subject’s yaw, pitch or roll). The drive rotators were computer controlled and provided three types of velocity profiles: pseudorandom, step, and sinusoid. The rotator axis was oriented for earth-vertical rotation for the ground tests, and perpendicular to the Spacelab floor for inflight testing. The chair utilized straps and padding to stabilize the subject and minimize pressure points. A helmet with inflatable bladders was used to fix the head in respect to the chair. The helmet also blocked any external light sources and integrated earphones masked any noises from other ongoing Spacelab activities. The helmet-mounted optokinetic stimulus (OKS) module provided visual stimuli, including targets for eye calibrations. The OKS module was mounted over the subjects right eye and a camera module was mounted over the left eye. The visual scene, visible for the subject when wearing the helmet was a black-red checkerboard pattern and illuminated by red Light Emission Diodes (LEDs). The speed, direction and pattern of the LED display were computer controlled.

Eye measurements were recorded with both electro-oculographic (EOG) and video techniques. For EOG recordings, surface electrodes were placed at the outer canthi of both eyes to record horizontal eye movements, and above and below the right eye to record vertical eye movements. Video was used to analyze roll rotation of the eyeball. To record nystagmus, the subject wore a contact lens with reference markings in the left eye.

The MVI experiments were integrated into eight different functional objectives to address: (1) semicircular canal dynamics, (2) vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression, (3) visual-vestibular interaction, (4) VOR responses to velocity steps, (5) optokinetic nystagmus, (6) sensory perception and motion sickness reports, (7) positional and spontaneous nystagmus and (8) changes in dynamic posture. The objectives (1) through (6) were performed pre-, post- and inflight, while objectives (7) and (8) were only tested pre- and postflight.

(1) Semicircular canal dynamics. The vestibular system provides information of angular acceleration (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration (otoliths) to the central nervous system (CNS). There is evidence that under some circumstances one set of receptors can modulate the input of the other system. It was hypothesized that in the microgravity environment, which is defined by the absence of the gravity vector, the semicircular canals would continue to supply input about the direction and magnitude of any rotation, while the otoliths would not provide the expected information regarding linear acceleration. Thus, this sensory conflict would cause a change in the VOR.

Sinusoidal and pseudorandom rotational stimuli, provided by the rotator chair, were used to study the dynamic response characteristics of the VOR. The selected frequencies covered a broad range to observe any changes in the interactions between the VOR and other visual tracking reflexes caused by different frequencies. Four single frequencies were tested during pitch rotation, including 0.05 Hertz (Hz) (for 100 seconds), 0.2 Hz (for 25 seconds), 0.8 Hz (for 20 seconds) and 1.25 Hz (for 20 seconds). The peak angular velocities of these profiles were maintained constant at 60 degrees per second (except for 1.25 Hz which was limited to 40 degrees per second). The test subjects had their vision occluded and were asked to fixate an imaginary wall target approximately 1 meter (1.1 yards) away. To evaluate the horizontal VOR, a pseudorandom (sum-of-sine) stimulus was used, and corresponding single sine measurements were obtained during 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz yaw rotations. The pseudorandom stimulus was comprised of seven frequencies ranging from 0.02 to 1.39 Hz.

(2) Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression. Turning the head produces a vestibular stimulus which activates the VOR and generates a compensatory eye movement in the opposite direction to hold the gaze stationary. When humans use head and eye movement to track a (moving) target the VOR is suppressed at low frequencies and diminishes slowly with increasing frequencies. During the MVI experiment, the vertical VOR was tested during pitch sinusoidal chair rotations at frequencies of 0.05 Hz (low frequency) and 1.25 Hz (high frequency). During the tests, the subjects were asked to fixate on the stationary checkerboard pattern displayed inside the OKS module. Yaw VOR suppression was tested by pseudorandom stimulus profiles utilizing the rotator chair.

(3) Visual-vestibular interaction. The vestibular motion sensors detect transient head rotation, but during sustained rotation their signal becomes progressively less accurate. During head rotation in light, the optokinetic system compensates for the fading vestibular response, which leads to the conclusion that during light both systems are stimulated and the eye movement response, called the visual-vestibular nystagmic response (VVR), is the result of the combined response of both systems. The objective of this part of the experiment was to evaluate the relative role the vestibular and optokinetic systems encounter during adaptation to microgravity.

The subjects were sinusoidally oscillated at 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz with the rotator chair while viewing a constant velocity optokinetic stimulation at + 35 degrees per second inside the OKS module. This procedure caused a nystagmic response of different quality when both stimuli were of same or opposite directions. The visual-vestibular interactions were tested both in the horizontal plane (rotation of subject in yaw combined with horizontal optokinetic stimulation), and in the vertical plane (rotation in pitch combined with vertical optokinetic stimulation).

(4) VOR responses to velocity steps. When a human subject is rotated in the earth vertical axis and in darkness for an extended period of time, the nystagmus decays and after several minutes of rotation the nystagmus disappears and the subject is no longer aware of the rotation. If the rotation is suddenly stopped, the subject indicates rotation in the opposite direction. This phenomenon is called post-rotatory nystagmus. Previous experiments demonstrated that the duration and magnitude of post-rotary nystagmus is gravity dependent. During the MVI investigation, post-rotatory VOR was studied after chair rotations of one minute at a speed of 120 degrees/second clockwise with fast accelerations and an abrupt stop. During the test, the subject was instructed to gaze straight ahead. The eye movements were recorded for 1 minute after the chair was stopped. After a brief pause, the procedure was repeated with counter-clockwise rotation.

(5) Optokinetic nystagmus. The objective of this experiment was to detect any changes in optokinetic nystagmus, which was induced by a rotating image inside the binocular OKS module. Horizontal and vertical optokinetic responses were recorded while the subjects were restrained into the rotator chair, positioned in yaw and pitch chair orientations, respectively. For each optokinetic stimulus run, three speeds of OKS-rotation were presented in succession (20, 60 and 40 degrees per second) in one direction for 15 seconds each. Immediately after the last image, the optokinetic nystagmus was recorded in darkness for 15 seconds. The same stimulus sequence was then presented with OKS-rotations in the opposite direction. Later during the IML-1 mission, the protocol was repeated while the test subjects were free-floating inside the Spacelab module.

(6) Sensory perception and motion sickness reports. The IML-1 crewmembers were asked to report their perceptions of particular motions while in microgravity and define if those motions were (1) different than on earth and (2) more or less confusing (or disturbing) than on Earth. The subjects were also asked to describe, quantify, and record any changes in space motion sickness symptoms during the space flight. The occurrence of motion sickness and the nature and degree of symptoms were important to the interpretation of the collected data, as was the intake of anti-motion sickness medication. Motion sickness symptoms were reported using a special score (0=no symptoms to 20=vomiting) during other MVI experiments. To do so, the astronauts used a voice recorder during the experiments and a checklist for evaluations performed at the end of each test and at the end of their work shift.

(7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Positional or spontaneous nystagmus occurs when the vestibular receptors indicate that the head is accelerating. In microgravity, the presence of spontaneous nystagmus (positional nystagmus has no meaning in 0-g) suggests that the CNS is receiving a head acceleration signal and is forwarding motor signals to the eye muscles. During baseline data collection, eye movements to detect spontaneous nystagmus were recorded during the following tests: (1) gaze nystagmus test (at + 10 and 20 degrees), (2) sinusoidal pursuit tracking test, using a swinging pendulum over + 30 degrees, (3) Benign Paroxysmal nystagmus test (test for positional nystagmus), and (4) positional nystagmus testing with eyes open and occluded vision and with eyes closed using the following sequence: sitting, supine with head hanging, supine with head straight up, supine with head turned to the right, and then to the left, and finally with the right ear to the floor and repeated with the left ear to the floor. The subject was returned to an upright (sitting) position between each test position. Eye movements were recorded with electro-oculography (EOG). During the space flight, eye movements were recorded during all test sessions to enable observations of transient spontaneous nystagmus before and after each rotational test.

(8) Changes in dynamic posture. Many astronauts returning from space exhibit some degree of postural dysfunction. To quantify these dysfunctions, a posture platform system (used for clinical diagnosis of disorders in balance control) was modified for postflight testing of movement coordination and sensory organization. For movement coordination tests, the foot plate was rapidly translated (maximum translation + 7 cm) or rotated (maximum tilt + 10 degrees) to provide stimuli to the subject’s posture control system. The postural responses to the sudden perturbations were monitored and recorded for a period of 2.5 seconds each. Sensory organization tests required the subjects to attempt a stable upright stance under different sensory input conditions. The conditions could be altered by a tilting foot-plate and a skipping visual surround which could be changed individually or both at the same time. The postural reaction to each sensory input was recorded for 20 seconds after each input.

Preflight, the MVI testing was completed in six single test sessions which were conducted on L-130 (130 days prior to launch), L-68, L-30 and L-15. The inflight test schedule included tests on seven flight days of the 8-day IML-1 mission for the MVI. Each of the four test subjects followed an individual test schedule. Postflight sessions were conducted on landing day, and 1, 2, 5, 8, and 30 days after landing.

RESULTS:
(2) Vestibulo-ocular reflexes. There was a consistent increase in the VOR gain observed at the mid-to-high frequencies (0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz) of chair rotation towards the end of the space flight. And the observed changes were greater in pitch than in yaw position of the chair.

(5) Optokinetic nystagmus. Although not statistically different, there was a trend for the gain of the optokinetic nystagmus to be increased during the space flight and during early postflight testing.

(6) Motion Sickness and perceptual reports. All four subjects reported some form of motion sickness symptoms. One subject reported severe malaise through most of the flight; the other three crewmembers reported significantly subsided symptoms by the third flight day prior to the majority of most MVI measurements. Three of the four crewmembers reported an increase in motion sickness symptoms while performing the MVI experiments. Reports from two subjects indicated that sensations of rotation, induced by both oscillatory and ramp stimuli, were somewhat more intense in orbit than on Earth. Also, during the pitch ramp stimuli, three of the four subjects tested inflight indicated that they felt they were tumbling “head-over-heals” rather than rotating in pitch (laying on their side).

(7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Before the flight, positional nystagmus was observed in all four subjects. During the inflight performance of the MVI experiments, transient spontaneous nystagmus was observed: all four subjects displayed some form of nystagmus, and one subject displayed vertical downbeat nystagmus, a form of nystagmus which exhibits all the characteristics of vestibular origin.

(8) Changes in dynamic posture. Two subjects participated in postural equilibrium tests on landing day and several times during the recovery period. The other two subjects were tested for the first time at R+1 and several times during the slower, secondary phase of recovery. The two subjects tested for the first time on R+1 displayed signs of disturbed postural equilibrium control 24 and 27 hours after landing, recovered to preflight levels by 47 and 48.5 hours after landing, and overshot preflight levels by 120 and 122.5 hours post landing. The two subjects tested on landing day (R+0) showed little or no improvement in recovery on R+1 and R+2. At about 120 hours after landing, both subjects had recovered to preflight levels and by 190 hours after landing one subjects displayed hyperstability. This led to the conclusion, that some postflight tests (most likely the pitch axis rotation test) interfered with the readaptation process.

experiment_title: Microgravity Effects on Bone Cell Gene Expression
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Astronauts on long-term missions suffer continuous calcium loss and degradation of skeletal weight-bearing bone mass. Bone loss has been attributed to a decrease in the rate of bone formation, which is possibly caused by both direct and indirect effects of microgravity. Systemic or hormonal changes in body chemistry or the cellular response to a lack of stress due to gravity could contribute to this condition. Osteoblastic cells must properly attach to the extracellular matrix (ECM) in order to grow normally. Fibronectin (FN), a cell surface adhesion protein, mediates the attachment of various cell types to other components of the ECM and is a known factor in cell shape and growth regulation. This experiment addressed whether the FN message, protein synthesis, and matrix organization affect bone formation.

Approach:

About 120,000 to 200,000 cells of an osteoblast cell line, clonally derived from embryonic mouse calvaria (MC3T3-E1), were plated for flight experiments. These plates were grown in 10% serum containing alpha minimal essential medium (a-MEM) and then the plunger units were held in the shuttle middeck for 17 hours before launch. A modified guanidinium thicyanate method was used to extract the cultured osteoblast cells. Agarose gel electrophoresis was used to identify polymerase chain reaction bands. The bands were then photographed and scanned at 400 dpi (dots per inch) for quantification.

Results:

Analysis of transcriptional and translational control of FN (fibronectin) suggest that aberrations in the FN portion of the ECM (extracellular matrix) due to microgravity do not cause cell morphology changes. Further extrapolation indicates that loss of osteoblast growth in space flight is not due to changes in FN. However, other alterations may be related to FN binding and receptor-mediated signaling changes in microgravity. Samples fixed for immunofluorescence localization studies showed that microgravity did not affect FN synthesis, that FN protein had been exported out of the cell, and that the cell matrix was organized normally. Furthermore, 1-G on-controls, ground controls, and samples activated in microgravity had indistinguishable regulation of FN. Overall, these data suggest that changes in FN regulation do not directly changes in cell shape, bone matrix formation, and loss of bone growth in microgravity.

experiment_title: The Role of the p21/p53 Pathway in Spaceflight-Induced Tissue Degeneration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In this study we hypothesized that following spaceflight and upon reloading of mice 1g, the gene expression changes related to tissue degeneration and unloading observed in STS-131 immediately after flight, might be reversed and that markers of bone formation and progenitor cell differentiation would gradually reappear.

APPROACH:
For STS-133 BSP we received mouse tissues 1, 5, and 7 days post-landing and recovered bone from the pelvis and femur as well as bone marrow. Bone samples were from juvenile mice exposed to RSV infection shortly after landing and therefore may reflect responses to infection over the course of 7 days in addition to the effects of spaceflight and subsequent reloading at 1g. Sham infected mice were available but the low n=2 selected by the BSP, does not allow their inclusion in statistically significant this study. Our studies included microCT analysis of bone loss during spaceflight and subsequent recovery over 7 days as well as patterns of gene expression in bone tissue and bone marrow progenitor lineages.

RESULTS:
We are currently conducting gene expression data collection for bone and bone marrow and conducting data analysis, however preliminary results suggest that some markers of gene expression associated with tissue degeneration and cell cycle arrest in space such may still show elevation following reloading for 1-7 days, suggesting at least some cell cycle arrest effects of microgravity may persist upon reloading, with the caveat, of course, that these studies are conducted in a RSV infection background and in skeletally immature, growing mice.

experiment_title: Magnetically Agitated Photocatalytic Reactor for Water Recovery
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Magnetically Agitated Photocatalytic Reactor (MAPR) under development at the University of Florida is well suited for many water purification applications including recovering water during missions in space, removing contaminants from water in the home, providing drinking water onboard ocean vessels, supplying troops with drinking water during military operations, and providing safe water for disaster response when water is desperately required but not available. Additionally, the technology has homeland security applications for decontamination of intentionally poisoned water supplies and a safe method disposal of the chemical weapons arsenal. As sunlight can be used as the light source, this technique offers a unique and affordable solution to water quality problems that face developing countries. In addition to water applications, the MAPR could be designed for air purification applications including use in the airline industry, underground mining, or automobiles. Traditionally water has been purified of harmful contaminants by activated carbon adsorption or photocatalytic oxidation. Although both are effective, activated carbon has a finite adsorption capacity and requires replacement or regeneration. Photocatalytic slurries may encounter problems such as separation of photocatalysts from recovered water. The advantage of using magnetic substrates is that they can be agitated by an external magnetic field to provide enhanced mixing of the photocatalyst particles with pollutants, and to enhance exposure to UV light. In addition, because the magnetic substrates are controlled by a magnetic field, the recovered water will be free of the composite particles. Faster destruction rates allow for compact treatment devices, which are critical to the applications listed above. Furthermore, this innovative technology is attractive because of its compactness and ability to function reliably without the extensive use of consumables (i.e., very infrequent replacement of UV lamps and media).

NASA has identified a number of water treatment options that have shown promise in space. The water recovery system on any particular mission will be a collection of individual treatment units, with each treatment unit focusing on a select group of contaminants. The goal of this research was to develop a post processor for the destruction of organic compounds and microbes that may not be removed in water subsystems prior to the MAPR. The overall objective was to develop a microgravity-compatible, compact reactor that is safe and reliable that provides product water that meets or exceeds NASA’s potable water quality requirements. Furthermore, this innovative technology has a reduced ESM because of its compactness and ability to function reliably without the extensive use of consumables (i.e., infrequent replacement of the UV lamps or use of solar UV). The technology proposed herein is applicable for implementation on board the International Space Station (ISS), in-flight, or for planetary (e.g., Lunar, Mars, etc.) missions. The assessment phase of the project will quantify the reactor removal efficiency with respect to pH, conductivity, total organic carbon (TOC), and trace organics. Optimize the MAPR with respect to particle design and loading, number of UV lamps, and UV wavelength. Post processing of water from prior subsystems is crucial to ensure crew health.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The catalyst synthesis process has been improved. A barium ferrite core that is commercially available rather than ball milled lead to a greater consistency in the catalyst performance. Double coatings of silica and titania respectively produced further improvements in performance such that a 10 mg/L phenol solution can be mineralized without photolysis in 7 hours with 3-365 nm lamps and 100 mg of catalyst.

The magnetic field of the MAPR has been improved to increase the UV exposure of the catalyst. To accomplish this, a permanent magnet has been added above the reactor to counteract the force of gravity, which tends to cause the catalyst to remain near the bottom of the reactor. The result of this modification is that the reaction rate of mineralization is more than double that without the permanent magnet. In the context of long-term space missions, this is a highly advantageous modification as the field can be adapted to the gravitational requirements of the environment by using a DC electromagnet or changing permanent magnets. If a permanent magnet is used it will not contribute to increases in the power requirements for equivalent system mass calculation.

The MAPR with the permanent magnet addition was optimized for catalyst mass, solenoid operating frequency and current using phenol as a model pollutant. The optimal catalyst mass was 400 mg with steep declines in performance if the mass is either increased or decreased. The phenol mineralization was relatively consistent for solenoid frequencies between 20 and 80 Hz above which performance declined significantly. Phenol mineralization increased linearly with current up to 1 A. Further increases in current did not improve performance, but increased the heat and power requirements.

experiment_title: Simulated Microgravity and Radiation-Induced Bone Degeneration: Oxidative Stress- and p53-Dependent Mechanisms
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

To determine the risks and mechanisms of tissue degeneration in the spaceflight environment, we will examine the combined effects of radiation and simulated weightlessness on bone. We will focus our studies on two important pathways, p53 and oxidative and nitrative stress-related species, in bone marrow progenitor populations because there is abundant evidence that the biological effects of weightlessness and those of radiation share these mechanism. Experiments will be conducted using the rodent hindlimb unloading model, the best validated animal model for simulating weightlessness, followed by irradiation. In Aim 1, we will test the hypothesis that simulated weightlessness of mice modulates the response of bone and bone marrow to radiation, both acutely and during tissue regeneration. In Aim 2 we will identify the target marrow-derived stem, progenitor and differentiated cell populations sensitive to the combined stimuli of simulated weightlessness and radiation. In Aim 3, we will explore the relevance of specific ROS/RNS and p53-dependent mechanisms for mediating cellular responses to combined simulated weightlessness and radiation. The results of these studies are expected to provide important information for the development of countermeasures both to help prevent degeneration of connective tissues such as bone during spaceflight and to improve subsequent tissue regeneration.

APPROACH:

Experiments will be conducted using the rodent hindlimb unloading model, the best validated animal model for simulating weightlessness, followed by irradiation. In Aim 1, we will test the hypothesis that simulated weightlessness of mice modulates the response of bone and bone marrow to radiation, both acutely and during tissue regeneration. In Aim 2 we will identify the target marrow-derived stem, progenitor and differentiated cell populations sensitive to the combined stimuli of simulated weightlessness and radiation. In Aim 3, we will explore the relevance of specific ROS/RNS and p53-dependent mechanisms for mediating cellular responses to combined simulated weightlessness and radiation.

RESULTS:

We were the first to report in the scientific literature on the influence of simulated weightlessness and radiation on mineralized tissue. Our published results show that total body irradiation of adult male mice with doses of iron as low as 0.10 Gy and doses of photons (Cesium-137) as low as 1.0 Gy can cause significant loss of mineralized tissue within the spongy areas of bone. This bone loss is very rapid (within 3 to 7 days), and appears to be caused by an increase in the activity of bone resorbing osteoclasts. The importance of the osteoclasts for radiation-induced bone loss is further supported by our findings that radiation can increase the number of osteoclasts in cultured cells.

One of our surprising findings is that radiation-induced bone loss is restricted to high turnover rate cancellous tissue, in contrast to unloading-induced bone loss, which manifests in both cortical bone tissue (outer shell) as well as cancellous tissue. As a consequence, the mechanical properties of the spine are largely preserved after low dose, total body irradiation alone and are likely to be preserved for most bones, at least in the short term.

Simulated weightlessness at the time of radiation exposure appears to impair skeletal remodeling even during a prolonged period of recovery. Furthermore, relatively low doses of space radiation can exert system-wide and persistent change. All of our experiments have been conducted using adult, male mice of a single strain (C57Bl/6J). Differences in biological responses to treatments can occur simply due to age, gender, strain, as well as species, and therefore further studies are needed to help assess human risk. Nonetheless, our findings suggest space radiation, alone and combined with musculoskeletal disuse, may pose a long-term risk to the skeletal health of astronauts.

experiment_title: Ground Based Measurement of Bone Loss in Astronauts Using AMPDXA GCS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory and the School of Medicine were building a Ground-based Clinical System using Advanced Multiple Projection Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (AMPDXA) principles to go beyond bone densitometry to measure the structural mechanics of bones and muscles. Exposure to microgravity during long-duration space flight decreases bone and muscle mass but the implications for injury differ from similar losses on earth and cannot be discerned by densitometry.

The goal of the Advanced Multiple Projection Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry Ground-Based Clinical System (AMPDXA-GCS) was to produce an operational instrument that could be transferred to the NASA-Johnson Spaceflight center for use in the pre-and post-flight bone mineral density (BMD) and bone structure measurements on astronauts.

The original aims of the project include:
1. Design, fabrication, and testing of AMPDXA-GCS.
2. Validate the utility, radiation safety, and method of operation of the AMPDXA-GCS configuration.
3. Address key technical challenges necessary to migrate the AMPDXA-GCS from ground-based studies to space flight.
4. Transfer AMPDXA-GCS technology into commercial clinical uses.

The AMPDXA-GCS will be able to detect 1% changes in bone mass and geometry and 2% changes in muscle mass and it will permit biomechanical assessments with similar accuracy. It will also decompose soft tissue into fat and muscle. Its accuracy and broad measurement capability make the AMPDXA-GCS superior to any conventional means for assessing bone health and strength.

An imaging system with AMPDXA-GCS qualities in space would be an unrivaled tool for rapid, high-precision testing of the effects of countermeasures on the musculoskeletal system. Thus, AMPDXA-GCS technology is highly likely to result in new tests for countermeasures efficacy and it promises to make a significant contribution to NASA Critical Path Roadmap (CPR) risk reduction. AMPDXA-GCS monitoring techniques could also benefit millions of people suffering from osteoporosis and other bone disorders. Research and clinical medicine will both benefit from increased ability to more precisely monitor bone health and the efficacy of treatments. Plus, the design principles will allow the development of a compact less expensive version for limb imaging that could be conveniently used in a variety of remote settings such as rural clinics and nursing homes.

The AMPDXA-GCS builds on the successes demonstrated in previous NSBRI funded collaborations between the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (SOM) which resulted in an AMPDXA Laboratory Test Bed (LTB) and a Human Test Bed (HTB). Since the AMPDXA-GSC will operate on slightly different principles (three X-ray beams at fixed angles) than the previous system design it was necessary to demonstrate the new concept using a test system-the AMPDXA-GCS Test Bed (ATB). The ATB was constructed and initial operating tests verified the new single scan with three fixed beams principles. The original 4-year project was terminated in its second year due to lack of future funding by the NSBRI. With the realization that because of the lack of funding the AMPDXA-GCS would not be built, the investigators turned their attention and remaining funding (with permission of the NSBRI) towards demonstration of the AMPDXA-GCS principles on a commercial DEXA scanner with the goal of commercializing the new technology invented under NSBRI funding.

APPROACH:
To this end the JHU team began working with the latest Hologic DEXA scanner and was able to modify text based scan protocols available in the system to allow multiple projection imaging. Multiple projection images were obtained from a sample bone at a constant distance by properly rotating the C arm and translating the patient table. We were then able to convert the Hologic data files into x ray attenuation files using a visual basic program. Software operations on these files resulted in bone mineral decomposition files. Several scans were made on phantoms and various bone samples such as a pig femur. At this point investigators were able to use their previous software to calculate bone cross sectional properties and compare the results to previous scans of the same bone using CT. A good comparison resulted between the Hologic derived properties, CT scan (used as reference), and their previous AMPDXA scanner (HTB). This proved that a commercial system could be modified to provide improved bone analysis embracing AMPDXA-GCS principles. Because of lack of source code, the scanning protocols developed were slow and would need to be improved before human testing could begin. The JHU Team was in discussions with Hologic about source code and funding future efforts when the project terminated due to lack of funding.

RESULTS:
A bench-top version (ATB) of the AMPDXA-GCS system has been fabricated to test out the physical principals of the new AMPDXA system. The ATB system is operational and images of cadaver bones and phantoms have been made. A new higher accurate phantom for new geometry has been designed and is in use. The x-ray tube produces a beam that is parallel to the plane of the table and detected by 3 detectors positioned at zero, minus 15, and plus 15 degrees apart. Lead collimators are used to limit the beam to just the area of the detectors. A linear motion stage is used to move a test sample through the beam which simulates the motion of the C-arm relative to the patient in the final AMPDXA-GCS design. The bench-top also allows adjustment of tube to sample ("patient") distance in order to optimize the final design. The tube to detector distance can also be varied on the bench-top as part of this optimization.

The x ray beam intensity was monitored by a scintillating detector diode located near the x ray source. This detector diode is referred to as the beam monitor. Beam intensity information allows the system to monitor patient dose and can be used to correct detector data for intensity variation and drift. It was decided to make the beam monitor a separate USB device. The microcomputer and analog board designs were merged onto one board and connectors for the scintillation detector were added. Although the electronics of this USB device are not placed in an aluminum enclosure, the beam monitor is completely enclosed by a black Kapton enclosure. The beam monitor and respective electronics have been manufactured and fully tested. With the hardware and software components of the test bed integrated, the next phase of the project was to evaluate the detector performance. A series of tests were developed and executed that measured the linearity response, dynamic range, and signal to noise ratio (SNR) properties of the detector.

While the dynamic range and linearity tests were straight forward, the SNR tests and analysis were much more complex. The reason for this complexity involves patient size variability. Theoretically, the SNR is a function of the difference between the two kilovoltages used. Because attenuation is always much greater at the low kVp for thicker patients, the optimal combination of kVp and beam filter is not readily apparent for thicker patients. In order to quantify the detector SNR a stepped phantom was built using various thicknesses of plastic and aluminum. The optimization experiments used four different thicknesses of plastic to simulate different patient thicknesses and examined the SNR produced in a nominal thickness of aluminum. The upper kVp was fixed at 140 kVp and the lower was varied from 70 to 110 kVp in 5 kVp increments. Investigators concluded that with the current detector configuration a low kVp of 110 would provide a reasonable SNR with thicker patients.

experiment_title: Risk of Intervertebral Disc Damage after Prolonged Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this research is to comprehensively characterize space-flight induced changes in disc morphology, biochemistry, metabolism, and kinematics. These data will be correlated with measures of back pain intensity and disability. The hypothesis is that spontaneous space-flight back pain and disc herniation are due to biomechanical and biological pathomechanisms. First, microgravity leads to higher than normal physiologic disc swelling and increased disc height that may stiffen the lumbar motion segment and cause abnormal segmental movement patterns. These biomechanical changes increase risk for annular rupture, vertebral endplate microfracture, and facet joint capsule strain. Second, increased disc swelling may alter nuclear matrix osmotic pressure and nutrient transport from endplate capillaries in adjacent vertebra. These biological changes adversely affect disc cell metabolism, causing pain and inducing disc matrix degradation.

APPROACH:
This investigation uses state-of-the-art imaging technologies to quantify morphology, biochemistry, metabolism, and kinematics for lumbar discs of crew members before and after prolonged space flight. These data will be correlated with low back pain that spontaneously arises in space in order to establish pain and disc damage mechanisms that will serve as basis for future countermeasure development. Successful completion of the investigation will include a comprehensive database of microgravity-induced intervertebral disc and vertebral changes (type and magnitude), as well as a prioritization of these changes regarding their deleterious effects and risks for crew member injury based on clinical findings.

Crewmembers will be imaged twice pre-flight (over a one-month time frame) to establish baseline data and to characterize measurement repeatability. After long-term microgravity exposure (180 days on ISS), crewmembers will be studied while maintaining supine posture as soon as possible after return to 1-G in order to quantify the acute effects of prolonged space flight. Also, pre- and post-flight, they will don a compression device so that MR images are obtained before and after 50% axial body weight load. This compression device loads the spine and simulates 50% body weight load (not including loads from muscles) on the lumbar spine in upright posture. Subsequently, crewmembers will be tested after 3 and 6 months of re-adaptation to 1-G in order to distinguish immediate and longer-term recoveries. The proposed measures represent a comprehensive set of tests that evaluate exposure severity, potential injury mechanisms, and pain generator localization.

RESULTS:
At the conclusion of the experiment, results will be posted when data becomes available.

experiment_title: Optimization of the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System Post-Processing System
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A Post Processing Subsystem (PPS) was previously tested as part of the Integrated Advanced Water Processing System (IAWRS). The PPS, which processed reverse osmosis, permeate and air evaporation condensate, performed final treatment of an International Space Station (ISS) -equivalent wastewater stream, and produced NASA-potable water during 180 days of testing. Processes utilized by the PPS include ion exchange, photo-oxidation, photo-sterilization, microfiltration, and residual biocide addition, and a modular design allows for the replacement of all subassemblies. The subsystem’s technology readiness level is 6 (tested in a relevant environment), and follow-on testing is intended to evaluate functional improvements to the integrated subsystem. The proposed work focuses on optimizing the organic and inorganic contaminant removal subassemblies.

Organic contaminants are destroyed using ultraviolet (UV) photo-oxidation. IAWRS testing demonstrated that a single 40-W, 185-nm photo-reactor was sufficient to maintain effluent organic carbon < 50 ppb, an order of magnitude less that the NASA requirement. However, sufficient data was not collected during the IAWRS test to determine the minimum acceptable size of the UV photolytic subassembly. Commercially available mixed media ion exchange (IX) resins are used for the removal of inorganic contaminants such as ammonium, and chloride. However, IAWRS test results showed that more than 30% of the IX bed capacity was consumed by the removal of bicarbonate, which has no effect on water potability.

The overall objective of this work was to collect sufficient data to accurately size a minimum mass, power, and volume Post Processing Subsystem (PPS). Two tasks were addressed: 1) determining the minimum power required by the UV photolytic subassembly, and 2) evaluating methods to increase IX bed life by reducing bicarbonate loading.

APPROACH:
To fulfill the objectives of the TDP, testing was divided into three phases: Phase I was intended to evaluate an alternative separate cation/anion (SC/A) IX configuration designed to increase bed life by reducing bicarbonate loading. In this configuration, a SAC (strong acid cation) IX resin and a vacuum MC function to extend downstream bed life by reducing bicarbonate loading on the SBA (strong base anion) IX resin. The performance and bed life of the new configuration was evaluated against the standard mixed-media IX (MIX) bed configuration. Phase II focused on testing the UV photolytic subassembly. Two 14-W UV photo-reactors were tested in place of the original 40-W units at flow rates sufficient to identify organic contaminant breakthrough. ROP and AES condensate ersatz was used as the feed streams. Phase III evaluated the performance of the optimized PPS and verified that the targeted reductions in IX resin and electrical power were achieved while processing ersatz solutions.

RESULTS:
Phase I: The SC/A and MIX bed PPS configurations were evaluated using ersatz solutions representing ROP and AES condensate. For the SC/A configuration, total inorganic carbon (TIC) removal averaged 70 and 82% for the ROP and AES feeds, respectively. No apparent variation or degradation in TIC removal was observed over the seven month testing cycle. The SC/A configuration reduced ROP and AES anion loading on the SBA bed by 35% and 85%, respectively. Overall, the SC/A test configuration exhausted an average of 44% less SBA resin when processing ROP than the standard MIX bed configuration. For AES feed, even greater SBA savings (upwards of 77%) were observed for the SC/A configuration compared to the MIX configuration. The calculated SBA resin capacity averaged across test runs was 1.1 + 0.1 meq/ml-resin, a value that is in agreement with the manufacturer’s specification of 1.1 meq/ml for UP4000.

Average water loss due to vapor diffusion across the vacuum MC was 24.9 ml/day. Although this mass loss must be counted against the SC/A configuration, it is noted that there was no attempt to optimize (i.e. minimize) the size of the MC, which was considered to be oversized for the current application. To mitigate this water loss, future designs of this PPS configuration could include both proper scaling of MC size and recovery of water from the vacuum line.

Neglecting water loss, the SC/A operating at 64 mL/min exhibited a mass savings of 28 and 53% for the ROP and AES feeds, respectively. For a typical 9:1 ROP to AES feed solution, the SC/A mass savings was improved by 30% when compared to the MIX configuration. In the final test configuration, SC/A with UV lamps, 75% of the samples tested exhibited total organic carbon (TOC) levels below the prescribed detection limit of the TOC analyzer (< 0.5 ppm). The specific power consumption calculated for two runs of SC/A-UV test stand processing AES feed at 64 mL/min were 7.8 and 5.6 W-hr/(mg TOC removed). Continued testing of the SC/A-UV configuration is planned for Phase II of the PPS TDP.

Phase II: Results aren’t available.

Phase III: Results aren’t available.

experiment_title: Biochemical Status of Humans in Long Duration Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objectives was to perform a systematic and integrated biochemical exmination of the human state in microgravity conditions to study metabolic adaptation to long-duration space flight conditions.

APPROACH:
Blood samples were drawn to study the biochemical regulation of the body's homeostasis during adaptation to a weightless environment. The role of hormonal mechanisms in the variations in the water-salt, lipid, and protein exchange were studied.

RESULTS:
To better understand how humans adapt to microgravity, researchers measured hormonal, metabolic, and biochemical indicators on the ground and the final stages of long-term space flight. They found no changes in some types of hormones, such as those secreted by the adrenal cortex, which controls stress response. They did find changes in hormones that reflect an individual’s metabolism and activity, such as thyroid hormones. Some of the indicators varied depending on flight duration and crewmember age. The data will be used to assess the physical state of crew members on long-duration space flights and help develop and improve diagnostic tools and preventive measures.

experiment_title: Structural Changes and Cell Turnover in the Rat's Small Intestine Induced by Spaceflight.
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this project was to test the hypothesis that the generalized, whole- body decrease in synthetic activity due to microgravity conditions encountered during space flight would be demonstrable in cells and tissue characterized by a rapid rate of turnover. Jejunal mucosal cells were chosen as a model since these cells are among the most proliferative in the body.

Approach:

Sections 1 µm thick were cut from each of the five sample segments from each of the three jejunal regions per animal and stained with toluidine blue. To accurately determine the mitotic index for each respective region, at least 2,000 cells per region per animal were examined. To determine villus length and crypt depth, at least twenty villi and crypts were measured per region per animal using a computerized image analysis system coupled to a bright field microscope equipped with a 4x objective and video camera. All data were statistically analyzed by analysis of variance and differences between means were detected.

Results:

The percentage of mitotic cells present on the crypts of Lieberkuhn in the proximal, middle, and distal regions of flight rats did not differ significantly from controls. Although the ability of jejunal cells to divide by mitosis was not impaired in the flight group, there was, however, a reduction in the length of villi and depth of crypts. Since villi in flight rats were lined by normal mucosal cells, the concomitant reduction in villi height and crypt depth probably reflects changes (e.g. shrinkage) in the connective tissue core of villi and is not due to an impairment in the migration of newly proliferated cells needed to replace those desquamated.

experiment_title: Synergistic Effect of Zero-g and Radiation on White Blood Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biological effects, such as genetic mutation, chromosome aberrations and cell lysis, were seen in both ballistic and orbital space flights that occurred before Gemini 3. In some cases, these effects were of magnitudes many times greater than would have been predicted from the expected radiation exposure received during flight. These magnitudes were thought to occur for two reasons: (1) it was thought that the components (particles) of radiation above the Earth’s atmosphere might have unexpected biological effects that could not be predicted in Earth-based laboratories and (2) it was thought that radiation and zero-g acted synergistically to produce unexpectedly large effects. This experiment was conducted to test these two possibilities.

APPROACH:
A series of human whole blood samples was irradiated during the mission with radioactive phosphorus (32P) beta-rays, with a known quantity and quality of radiation. Inflight control samples were also used, and were not irradiated with the experiment source, but just flew to encounter the normal radiation of the space flight. An identical series of blood samples was irradiated on the ground and used as a control. Increased aberrations in the inflight samples, including the control, would be evidence of an effect of some space flight parameter. Any effect not seen in the inflight control would be attributed to a synergism between radiation and some space flight parameter.

Because induction of chromosome aberrations is a non-linear function of radiation dose, a graded series of four different radiation exposures was used. Two complete sets of blood samples were flown to protect against loss of data; each sample set was from a different blood donor. In total, ten 3 ml blood samples were flown; eight were irradiated with each of the four doses, and two were not irradiated and served as the inflight controls. The simultaneous ground control experiment consisted of ten 3 ml samples drawn from the same donors at the same time as the inflight samples. As an additional control, blood samples were obtained from the flight crew before and after the flight, and short-term leukocyte cultures were prepared. Preflight, on Gemini 3, the samples were obtained as close to the mission as possible (2 days prior to launch) from both the flight and backup crews, so that the samples would remain viable. On Gemini 11, the samples were obtained 9 days prior to launch. On both flights, the leukocyte cultures were prepared and incubated at 37 degrees C, treated with colchicine, fixed and then chromosome preparations were made.

Irradiation was accomplished by identical experimental devices, one on the ground at the launch site, and the other on the righthand hatch of the Gemini 3 spacecraft. Each device contained 22 fluoroglass dosimeters. Approximately 9 hours before launch the two identical experiment devices were assembled and tested, then at 210 minutes before launch (for Gemini 3) and 150 minutes before launch (for Gemini 11), the flight unit was mounted into the spacecraft. On Gemini 3, the ground-control unit was placed inside a temperature-controlled cabinet, in which the temperature was periodically adjusted to correspond to the temperature readout from the spacecraft. The longer duration of Gemini 11 meant that the samples were in the weightless period much longer before they were irradiated. Samples were refrigerated inflight to ensure the survival of the leukocytes. Therefore, the ground control unit was placed inside a refrigerator that matched the refrigerator temperature of the inflight samples (2 to 4 degrees Celsius). Furthermore, the device provided a telemetry signal for monitoring the temperature on the ground, an improvement over the Gemini 3 mission.

Irradiation was initiated by the pilot 50 minutes and 18 seconds after launch, and continued for 20 minutes. Correspondingly, the ground unit was activated and deactivated at 52 and 72 minutes, respectively. Except for minor accelerations caused by maneuvering “burns” of the spacecraft, the flight device remained weightless for nearly 3.5 hours.

Ideally, the team wanted to use X- or gamma-rays to irradiate the blood samples, but could not for two reasons: (1) the small mass allotted to them for the experiment excluded it and (2) too much shielding would have been required to protect the flight crew. Therefore, beta-rays were chosen. Radioactive phosphorus (32P) was chosen as the radiation source for three reasons: (1)it emits only a single beta-particle, (2) the particle energy was suitable and (3) it had been used extensively in radiobiology studies to date. On Gemini 11, the amount of 32P in the device was decreased, since the samples would be subjected to increased beta-ray leakage and Bremsstrahlung radiation within the device.

After the mission, blood samples were obtained as soon as possible from the flight crew (6.5 hours after landing). By 10 hours after launch, all blood samples had been put into culture, and all cultures were fixed between 72 and 77 hours after launch. A cytogenetic analysis was made of each sample; the frequencies of chromosome aberrations were determined. Yields of both single-break and multiple-break aberrations were calculated, both for the flight samples as well as the ground samples.

Production of chromosomal aberrations is one of the best known effects of radiation, so it was selected as the parameter to measure for this study. Human leukocytes were chosen as the cell to be studied, since the cells would all be in a uniformly sensitive stage in the cell cycle and because the investigator team had extensive experience working with leukoctyes.

RESULTS:
Gemini 3 postflight analysis of the fluoroglass dosimeters in the experiment device showed that the doses, start/stop times of irradiation, and temperatures for the ground and flight units all agreed well. For Gemini 3, the flight device temperature stayed between 14 and 38 degrees Celsius, whereas the ground device stayed within a 2 to 29 degree Celsius range. For Gemini 11, the temperature of the flight device increased, starting at approximately 14 minutes after launch, to between 6 to 10 degrees Celsius and remained in that range for the first 24 hours of the mission. The device temperature decreased when the spacecraft was depressurized for the first extravehicular activity (EVA). The device operated within the normal 2 to 4 degree range until switched off simultaneously with the ground unit after approximately 65 hours inflight. The ground unit always remained within the normal temperature range. Later, it was discovered that an unusually high hatch temperature caused the inflight high refrigerator temperature. The higher temperatures did not affect the blood samples nor the results.

The dosimeters also confirmed that the radiation exposures were of the required duration. The inflight readings of the 22 dosimeters in the flight device compared well with the readings of the 22 dosimeters in the ground device. Doses were estimated for preflight and postflight by means of fluoroglass or Fricke-solution dosimetry. As a result, there was a 2 rad dose on the ground samples, with a large portion (about one-third) of that being Bremsstrahlung with a peak energy of about 65 keV. The inflight package registered somewhat higher exposures than 2 rad.

All of the blood sample cultures were successful and yielded satisfactory chromosome preparations. Very little hemolysis was noted. A total of 4600 cells were analyzed.

Results showed that the occurrence of single-break aberrations was much higher in the flight samples. There was no significant difference between the yields of multiple-break aberrations in the flight and ground control samples. The flight crew chromosome aberration analyses showed no increase in aberration frequency due to space flight. However, the small positive effect seen in the differences of single-break aberrations did stimulate further scientific interest in this topic. It appeared that some space flight factor did interact synergistically with radiation to affect the chromosome rejoining system (i.e. the cell’s ability to repair damage), thus producing the single breaks.

On Gemini 11, a parallel test was also conducted on the bread mold Neurospora crassa. Those results are reported in another experiment record in this archive.
