experiment_title: Analysis of Volatile Organic Compounds on Mir Station
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
With long-term space habitation quickly becoming a reality, the need for development of more advanced life support systems has become a priority. One drawback of current life support systems is the lack of real-time, on-site monitoring of the changing concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) present in the living environment. Applications of this technology extend far beyond life support systems; they have a number of ground-based uses as well. These include engine exhaust analysis, human breath analysis, stack monitoring, and fence-post monitoring. Technological advances in this field are vital to ensure human health and will have to be thoroughly researched before long-term space habitation is possible.

The Mir station environment is one example where this type of real-time, on-site, monitoring of VOCs would be very useful. The types and concentrations of VOCs in the Mir station atmosphere are not well characterized. Detailed information regarding the types and concentrations of VOCs present in the Mir environment would be very useful in assessing the long term health risks associated with living in such an environment. Present methods of monitoring VOCs using cartridge and grab methods of sampling and GC/MS for analysis are both proven and cost-effective, but have several drawbacks including the lack of on-site, real-time monitoring. Newly developed direct sampling ion trap mass spectrometry (DSITMS) shows excellent promise in both real-time monitoring of VOCs and space portability.

The following were objectives of this experiment:

  • Characterize the Mir station environment using proven sampling and analysis methods

  • Demonstrate the use DSITMS for direct monitoring of VOCs in air samples collected from Mir station

  • Document the types and concentrations of VOCs present on the Mir station

  • analyze the results in collaboration with other investigators in order to further the goals of the NASA research announcement.

    APPROACH:
    During the NASA (2-6)/ Mir (21-24) missions, air samples were taken from various locations on the Mir space station. Twenty-four hour time averaged air samples were obtained using Solid Sorbent Air Samplers (SSASs) and instantaneous air samples were obtained using Grab Sample Canisters (GSCs). The air samples collected from the Mir station were returned to the JSC toxicology lab; a subset of these was transferred to Dr. Belisle's lab for analysis (the 1st subset of Mir-21 samples were analyzed at Dr. Palmer's laboratory). Both GSC and SSAS samples were analyzed by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) and direct sampling ion trap mass spectrometry (DSITMS). Samples were analyzed via GC/MS using a modified version of the EPA TO-14 method. The VOCs were first concentrated and then isolated from the bulk of the air sample. A GC/MS data system was then used to separate and detect individual VOCs. Once separated from one another, both retention time matches and library searching of mass spectral data were used to identify individual VOCs. Calculating the actual concentrations of the VOCs was very complex due to the fact that the Mir samples had been repressurized, and therefore diluted, during analysis at the JSC toxicology lab. Taking this into account, many correction factors and proportional relationships between intensities of samples and standards were used when calculating actual concentrations of VOCs present in the Mir environment.

    DSITMS analysis was performed on samples from Mir 22, 23, and 24. Air samples from Mir-24 were reserved for DSITMS analyses only. Air samples were introduced into an ion trap mass spectrometer (ITMS) by a prototype sample introduction system known as a Real-Time Air Monitor (RTAM). The ITMS then analyzed the samples in MS scan mode in order to detect as many VOCs as possible in a single pass. MS/MS analysis would have provided better selective deduction of individual VOCs but due to limited sample volume this was not a viable option. VOCs were tentatively identified by the presence of characteristic ions. This data was then compared to intermediate and working gas standards prepared on the same day.

    RESULTS:
    Analysis of air samples taken from the Mir station showed the air to be nominal, if not better, than that of most indoor environments on earth. Space maximum allowable concentrations (SMACs) were not available for all VOCs identified, but most fell between 0.1 and 1000 mg/m3. Nearly all VOCs measured were less than 1mg/m3 and were well within SMACs.

    The target compounds for the GC/MS analysis included VOCs in the TO-14 standard plus additional VOCs identified in samples from prior Mir missions. Several fluorocarbons and chlorofluorocarbons were identified in Mir samples. These compounds are highly volatile and were shown to be not very well trapped by the SSAS devices. Several aromatic hydrocarbons were identified, including benzene, which is thought to have been a product of incomplete combustion from the solid fuel oxygen generator fire (SFOG). Biogenic hydrocarbons identified on Mir most likely came from plant growth experiments. Similar to the fluorocarbons, these compounds were better identified by the GSCs. Two siloxane compounds were identified in Mir samples and are thought to have come from either silicone-based sealants or anti-perspirants, both of which are common on Mir.

    Although the DSITMS analysis was more qualitative than quantitative, it was proven effective and reliable. The DSITMS analysis was effective because it identified all VOCs present above the 10-50 ppb detection limit. The DSITMS was proven reliable in that it did not indicate any false positive (identifying a VOC that was not present in GC/MS analysis). Although DSITMS is still under development it's selectivity, speed, and simplicity make it a viable option for future earth and space applications.

experiment_title: Morphological and Biochemical Examination of Heart Tissue: III. Cyclic AMP Receptor Protein Distribution in Heart Muscle of Rats Flown on Cosmos 2044
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The effect of space travel on the cardiovascular system has been investigated to determine if measurable changes could be noted, and if such changes might influence the health of the individual. The present study was undertaken in order to gain insight into a specific biochemical mechanism which may be associated with cardiac changes that experimental animals undergo as a consequence of travel in space, the mechanism in question being cyclic AMP-receptor reactions in the cell particulate fraction.

Approach:

Tissue homogenates in addition to the subcellular fractions were aziado-labeled and analyzed for total cyclic AMP-binding analysis. Photoaffinity labeling of regulatory subunits (RI and RII) of cyclic AMP dependent protein kinase was carried out to measure cyclic AMP binding protein activities. Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, in the presence of sodium dodecyl sulfate, was carried out using a conventional size as well as a mini-gel apparatus.

Results:

Cyclic AMP binding protein activities were decreased in heart tissue of flight rats. Densitometric analyses showed a significant decrease of RII in the particulate cell fraction extract. The photoaffinity labeling of soluble fraction was unaffected, as previously observed on Cosmos 1887. A negative correlation resulted when incorporation of total counts of aziado-labeling was based on body weights, while no changes were seen when total label was calculated on the basis of adrenal gland weights. Factors which influence body weight changes therefore may alter hormone response, while changes in a relatively minor aspect of cyclic AMP mediated reactions may have a metabolic affect on an organismic level.

experiment_title: Effect of Spaceflight on Microbial Gene Expression and Virulence (Microbe)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Determine the effects of spaceflight, and nutritional status, on gene expression and virulence of three microbrial pathogens: Salmonella typhimurium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Candida albicans.

APPROACH:
Three Group Activation Packs (GAPS) were assigned to each of 4 microbial projects: (1) S. typhimurium in rich media (2) S. typhimurium in minimal media (3) P. aeruginosa in rich media, and (4) C. albicans in rich media. The thermal and radiation profiles of the flight samples were collected by two temperature loggers and two radiation area monitors (RAMs), respectively. Synchronous ground controls (12 GAPs) were loaded at the same time and in the same configuration as the flight samples. Asynchronous ground controls, using the recorded temperature flight data were performed at the PI lab post-flight utilizing a Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV). FPAs were loaded with flight reagents (terminators an growth media) and static cultures and installed into the GAPs at approximately launch minus (L-5) days. The loaded GAPs were handed over for a late load into the orbiter to ensure that the healthiest static cultures in stasis medium were utilized for the space flight experiment.

RESULTS:
Data showed that Salmonella typhimurium grown in rich LB media in spaceflight displayed increased virulence, biofilm-like formation, and global alterations in global gene expression, as compared to synchronous ground controls. It was hypothesized that media ion concentrations could be manipulated to prevent/turn off the enhanced Salmonella virulence imparted during spaceflight (tested on STS-123). A total of 167 genes in the flight S. typhimurium were expressed differently to those in the ground controls. Sixty-four of these genes are involved in the expression of Hfq (a protein that binds to mRNA) suggesting that Hfq is involved in regulating some of the Salmonella responses to space flight.

experiment_title: Epidemiologic Analyses of Risk Factors for Bone Loss and Recovery Related to Long Duration Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss is estimated to occur at a rate of one percent per month in space, particularly in weight-bearing bones in the legs and spine. This rate of loss is equivalent to what a human might lose in a year with advancing age on Earth. It remains unknown what this loss signifies for future fracture risk in crewmembers. While unloading of the skeleton in the weightless environment of space is considered the key factor contributing to bone loss, there are likely other factors that also play a role. Current prevention strategies have not been effective at preventing this bone loss. Improved understanding on the risk for fracture following long-duration space flight, as well as the factors contributing to bone loss in microgravity, and its recovery, are needed in order to develop better prevention strategies for the benefit of crew health, both during and after long-duration space exploration, and mission success.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Investigate the risk of microgravity exposure on long-term changes in bone health and fracture risk.
  2. Provide a summary of the current evidence available on potential risk factors for bone loss, recovery and fracture following long-duration space exploration.

APPROACH:
Data assembly at NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) on risk factors known to be related to bone loss and fracture risk was completed in early 2012. The investigators performed analyses on these available data to help better understand the variability in hip bone mineral density (BMD) loss and recovery, postflight. Risk factor data included, medication use, bone turnover markers, and surrogates of exercise status inflight, such as changes in strength measures, and lean muscle mass. Data assembly and data cleaning were completed. The investigators noted that there were limited data on risk factors available beyond the initial return post long-duration flights, so analyses were restricted to the immediate post-flight period.

RESULTS:
Following review of all the different measures available for analyses, the investigators identified several different risk factors which may help identify those at greatest risk for bone loss during long-duration missions. These included pre-flight measures of elevated bone resorption, as well as surrogate markers of better muscle strength and greater aerobic capacity preflight. Results suggest that individuals with high bone resorption markers preflight may benefit most from anti-resorptive therapy before a long-duration mission. Findings also suggest that those who are the most physically fit preflight may have bones that have adapted to greater than average loading stimuli and therefore may be more susceptible to enhanced bone resorption once unloaded in microgravity, reinforcing the importance of maintaining adequate physical conditioning during long-duration space flight. Of note, the results are from data largely prior to US crewmembers having access to the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED), which may have helped overcome this important risk factor.

The data from this study is medical and thus is housed with the Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH). A final report was archived in the LSDA.

experiment_title: Factors Modulating Radiation-Induced G2 Delays
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The progression of cells through the cell cycle is maintained by control mechanisms that operate through the activation of checkpoints at defined positions. Feedback controls detect any failure to complete DNA replication, DNA repair, or spindle assembly, and arrest further progression of cells through the cell cycle until proper completion of the event occurs. Delays in the cycle often occur following exposure to ionizing radiation and correspond to activation of specific checkpoints in the phases of G1, S, and G2. The delays may reduce adverse effects of radiation by allowing repairs to occur. Since delays in G1 and G2 are longer than those of S, G1 and G2 are suitable targets in development of strategies to modulate cell sensitivity to radiation.

Compounds such as caffeine can reduce radiation-induced delay in G2, but, to date, no compounds can increase the duration of the G2 delay. Increasing this delay may protect against radiation by allowing cells to repair. Since hypothetical compounds that increase delay may act by enhancing repair, they could be useful when administered after radiation exposure, because repair requires hours for completion.

Biological cells produce many compounds that affect their own function and the function of surrounding cells. Some of these compounds are secreted into the extracellular environment, and when cells are grown in culture, the compounds are secreted into the growth medium creating conditioned medium. Some mammalian cells have been found to produce factors with G2-Arrest Modulating Activity (GAMA). The goal of this study was to characterize and define the effects of these factors. The hypothesis was that GAMA acts as a radioprotector by promoting repair in irradiated cells and could be applied as radiation protection for humans in space. The aims of the study were to demonstrate the production and excretion of GAMA by mammalian cells, standardize production conditions, and characterize the biological properties of GAMA.

The method by which cells produce GAMA, and the characterization of its genes and receptors are worthy of study. The effects of GAMA on cell survival and mutation induction are also of interest. GAMA and other substances with similar action could be developed for use against not only the early and late effects of radiation, but also cancer development and damage to the central nervous system.

APPROACH:
Two main cell lines were used to demonstrate the production of GAMA and its properties. The A1-5 cell line consisted of rat embryo fibroblasts containing a mouse p53 mutant and activated ras oncogene. The p53 protein was temperature sensitive and had an altered shape at 39.5°C. An antibody that could bind normal p53 was able to bind the mutant at 32.5°C but not at 39.5°C. The cells containing the p53 mutant grew at 37°C but stopped replication and arrested at the G1 checkpoint in the cell cycle when subjected to 32.5°C. The cells were subcloned to obtain a cell line displaying a single G1 peak in flow cytometry.

The T101-4 cell line was made from primary rat embryo fibroblasts with a different mutation of mouse p53 and the same ras oncogene. This mutation of p53 did not bind to the same antibody used to bind the temperature-sensitive p53.

Cells were grown under standard conditions in large volumes to prepare material for testing the presence and effects of GAMA. One million cells were grown for four days in twenty milliliters of complete growth medium. The distribution of cells in the various phases of the cell cycle was monitored by flow cytometry. Other cell lines, in addition to A1-5 and T101-4, were also used to test the effects of GAMA and their ability to produce GAMA.

A Siemens therapeutic X-ray machine operated at 250 kV, 15 mA with a 2mm Al filter was used for irradiations. The dose rate at a 50 cm irradiation distance was 2 Gray per minute and the effective photon energy about 70 keV. Dosimetry was performed with a Victoreen dosimeter.

Three different filters with pores that retained molecules larger than 10 kilodaltons (kD), 5 kD, and 1 kD were used to investigate the size of GAMA. To test whether GAMA was a peptide, proteases were incubated with aliquots of the 10kD ultrafiltrate containing GAMA. This medium was incubated with 0.25% trypsin for two hours at 37°C, then neutralized with serum. The medium was also incubated overnight at 37°C with Proteinase K, a protease with less specificity than trypsin. The first attempts for the purification of GAMA used a Biocad station. Western blotting was used for further protein analysis.

Induction and rejoining of radiation-induced DNA double strand breaks were measured using asymmetric field inversion gel electrophoresis. Such double strand breaks are thought to be severe lesions that, if unrepaired or misrepaired, would lead to cell death.

To show that a G2 delay was not a result of a lethal accumulation of cells in G2, the effect of caffeine was observed. Caffeine sensitizes cells to radiation and reduces the duration of G2. If an accumulation of cells in G2 was due to a genuine G2 arrest, caffeine should reduce the duration. If the accumulation of cells was due to non-specific, cell-line-related artifacts, caffeine should only have a minimal effect. Staurosporine, also known to affect cell radiosensitivity and G2 arrest, was used to bolster findings obtained from the caffeine test.

Experiments with heavy ions as the radiation source were conducted because high Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation effects are important to NASA. Exponentially growing A1-5 and T101-4 cells were exposed to various doses of 1 GeV/A Fe ions and growth was followed for 36 hours by cell counting. Cells were collected and fixed in ethanol to study progression through the cell cycle by flow cytometry. The role of caffeine and staurosporine was also investigated.

RESULTS:
A1-5 cells were more radioresistant than the control T101-4 cells. The difference was among the largest observed with cell lines generated after transfection of primary rat embryo fibroblasts with oncogenes or anti-oncogenes of different families. Both cell lines demonstrated similar yields of radiation-induced DNA double strand breaks, severe damage that could lead to cell death. Rejoining was also similar in the two cell lines suggesting a similar capacity in repairing this type of damage. The incidence of misrepair was not a factor in the discrepancy since progression from G1 into S after radiation was similar between both cell lines.

A moderate increase of radiation-induced inhibition of DNA replication in A1-5 cells compared to T101-4 cells was observed. However, dramatic differences in radiation-induced delay in G2 between the two cell lines were observed. T101-4 cells showed a modest accumulation of cells in G2 that increased with increased radiation dose. However, A1-5 cells were found to give a much longer delay in G2 with more than 70% of cells accumulated in G2 after exposure to 6 Gray. Cell division did not occur for up to thirty hours after irradiation. A two millimolar solution of caffeine caused a substantial reduction in the accumulation of A1-5 cells in G2, suggesting a genuine G2 arrest and not a lethal accumulation of cells in G2. A reduction was also observed in the duration of G2 arrest in T101-4 cells but was modest when compared to that of A1-5 cells. Staurosporine confirmed the findings observed from caffeine. There is strong indication that A1-5 cells undergo a genuine long, radiation-induced G2 arrest.

Observations from varied experiments indicated that G2 arrest was modulated in A1-5 cells by a factor produced by the cells and excreted into the growth medium. Duration of the G2 arrest was shorter when cells were at a lower density before radiation and a growth medium change a few hours before irradiation significantly reduced the duration of the delay. A change of medium after irradiaton also reduced the duration of the G2 arrest. Radiation caused the accumulation of cells in G2 that persisted for over forty hours but cells that underwent a medium change at the peak of the G2 accumulation started dividing a few hours later. Thus, GAMA was present in the conditioned medium of non-irradiated cells. The G2 arrest could be reverted by transferring the cells to fresh medium, thus removing GAMA. GAMA was present in the conditioned medium of cultures grown for four days starting at a concentration of one million cells per dish. The concentration of GAMA in cultures of A1-5 cells grown for thirty hours starting from 100,000 cells per dish was not high enough to modulate G2 arrest, unlike what was observed with cells grown for 30 hours starting from 250,000 cells per dish.

GAMA was estimated to have a molecular weight of 1 kD after conditioned medium was filtered through 10 kD, 3 kD and 1 kD filters. Cells that were incubated in fresh medium supplemented with the material left in the 10 kD and 3 kD filters displayed G2 accumulation kinetics similar to that with only fresh medium. Cells transferred to the filtrate displayed a G2 arrest similar to that of cells kept in conditioned medium. GAMA passed through the 10 kD and 3 kD filters and was present in the ultrafiltrate and, thus, was smaller than 3 kD. A reduced effect was observed with the 1 kD molecular weight cutoff suggesting that GAMA is partially retained by this filter. Dialysis experiments produced similar results and confirmed that GAMA is of a low molecular weight.

Further testing indicated that GAMA is stable in heat. When the conditioned medium was exposed to 56°C for an hour, its ability to arrest cells in G2 was not altered. GAMA was proven to be a peptide when exposure to the protease trypsin resulted in a shorter G2 delay. Researchers expected that a less specific protease would have a more dramatic effect on GAMA activity, and, indeed, the Proteinase K experiment showed a dramatically reduced ability to arrest cells in G2.

GAMA was produced in a variety of cell lines other than A1-5. Conditioned medium from these other cells showed a significant ability to retain the irradiated A1-5 cells in G2. Not all cell lines can utilize GAMA to arrest in G2 after irradiation. Conditioned medium from cell lines that produce GAMA was unable to arrest irradiated T101-4 and other cells in G2. An intermediate response was found from cells containing a defect in a protein that causes a defect in the rejoining of DNA double strand breaks. Thus, GAMA must act via a receptor that must also be present for GAMA to exert its G2 arrest modulating activity.

Some conclusions stemmed from the experiments with irradiated cells. Several cell lines produced low molecular weight stable peptides, which had the potential of modulating radiation-induced cell cycle checkpoints. Response to the factors likely required the presence of appropriate receptors in the cells; more cells produced the factors than responded to them. The factors were likely to be active after exposure to low as well as to high LET radiation. Characterization of a compound that prolonged G2-arrest and possibly protected cells from radiation defined a new class of radioprotectors with direct application in radiation protection. Since the compound was made by cells, it was expected to be of limited toxicity in the normal range of concentrations. There may be application in radiation protection during space exploration. Because the compound was expected to act by modulating repair, it could be taken shortly after radiation exposure, as soon as radiation monitors in space register increased cosmic ray activity.

Results from this study indicate the possibility of developing countermeasures to unwanted exposures of radiation by promoting repair processes. Compounds like GAMA may mitigate early or acute radiation exposure and mitigate the carcinogenic effects of radiation. They may also help mitigate damage to the central nervous system from radiation.

experiment_title: Pharmaceutical Countermeasure Effects on Tissue-Level Quality of Immobilized Bone
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reduced mechanical loading during bed rest or space flight produces rapid and severe bone loss. Recovery of this bone loss requires re-loading for at least twice the reduced loading period. One strategy for enhancing recovery with re-loading is to mitigate the initial osteopenia with a bisphosphonate treatment that suppresses bone resorption in postmenopausal osteoporosis. However, bisphosphonates also suppress bone tissue repair. This can lead to microdamage accumulation and degrade the tissue-level mechanical properties important to fatigue and fracture resistance. This project investigated whether the bisphosphonate risedronate (RIS) administered during long-term limb immobilization (IM) in an animal model would slow cortical bone loss, allowing enhanced recovery and maintenance of tissue-level mechanical properties upon remobilization (RM).

APPROACH:
This investigation measured changes in tissue-level mechanical properties of IM bone treated with RIS and subsequent RM. The benefit of RIS is in slowing bone loss during long-term IM. There are potential benefits over long-duration space flights. However, reduction in tissue-level mechanical properties with RIS treatment followed by RM, point to an increase in susceptibility towards crack propagation. This is a concern, and should be considered in the optimization of bone loss mitigation and post-flight recovery regimens.

RESULTS:
Tissue-level mechanical properties were measured on machined specimens under static and dynamic loads. Tissue-level mechanical properties were decreased and the sensitivity to fatigue crack propagation increased, compared to control. Toughness was positively correlated with post-yield, i.e. plastic strain to failure. The apparent decrease in tissue-level toughness was substantiated by observations of relatively smooth fracture surfaces and increased microcrack density in the IM bones versus control. RIS treatment during IM was effective in partially preserving bone mass by suppressing turnover. At the tissue-level, RIS completely preserved toughness, fatigue life and sensitivity to fatigue crack propagation at control levels. Combined, these results suggested that RIS given during long-term IM slowed bone loss and maintained tissue-level mechanical properties. Twelve-months of RM did not recover cortical bone morphology in the non-drug treated group. At the tissue-level, RM did not recover fatigue-life and partially recovered toughness, mainly due to increased post-yield strain to failure. In comparison, RM in the previously RIS-treated group completely recovered cortical area and width, primarily by endosteal infilling of the marrow space. However, RM of previously drug-treated bone dramatically affected the tissue-level mechanical properties. Reduced toughness and fatigue life, and increased sensitivity to fatigue crack propagation, were all significant versus control.

experiment_title: Ultrasonic Assessment of Anisotropic Mechanical Properties of Cancellous Bone after Disuse with and without Anti-Resorptive Therapy (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Currently, the approach most widely used to examine bone loss is bone densitometry, which cannot show the microarchitectural aspects of cancellous bone that are key to estimate bone’s mechanical integrity. Recently, a novel architecture-density based approach for acoustic wave propagation in a poroelastic media was developed. This approach provides the potential to use ultrasound measurements in bone to examine tissue architecture in addition to bone mass. Initial studies show that this approach significantly improves prediction of mechanical properties of bovine and human cancellous bone when compared to density-based approaches. Better estimation of bone mechanical properties is expected to result in enhanced discrimination of osteoporotic and non-osteoporotic bone. The Aim of the study was to investigate the ability of this microstructural-based approach to discriminate quantitatively the changes on density, microstructure and mechanical properties of bone in the real-world situations of a rapidly evolving osteoporosis (disuse), both with and without antiresorptive treatment, and after recovery. The present research builds on the ongoing NSBRI studies. From these studies, canine cancellous bone samples were obtained and split into four groups: Immobilized (Im), Immobilized and treated with antiresorptive therapy (ImTx), Non-immobilized control bones (Cn), and non-immobilized control bones treated with bisphononate (CnTx). Ultrasound wave velocities were measured in three anatomical directions (SI, ML and AP). The values of ultrasound velocities and the bone density were used to directly compute the directional anisotropic mechanical properties of cancellous bones in the four analyzed groups. In particular, from these measurements it was found a noticeably change in mechanical properties when comparing control and immobilized cancellous bone samples. The group of bones immobilized and treated with antiresorptive therapy has shown an intermediate level of mechanical properties when compared against the control and immobilized bone samples. These results were found in close agreement with previous results from Dr. Schaffler’s research project, which have shown that anti-resorptive treatment with bisphosphonate reduced bone loss in disuse but did not completely inhibit it. Dr. Schaffler data suggest that disuse osteoporosis differs from other osteoporoses in its sensitivity to antiresorptive treatment.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
The results from the project support this suggestion and demonstrate the ability of ultrasound procedure to assess differences between normal, disuse-induced osteoporotic and normal bone. Moreover, the analysis of the data for the three anatomical directions have shown that beside changes in bone density, the ratio of anisotropy in healthy bone is highly modified during disuse. However, this ratio of anisotropy can be preserved in disuse-induced osteoporotic bone when using the antiresorptive therapy. Observations of directional (anatomical) changes of bone loss undergoing disuse and treated with anti-resorptive therapy were effectively assessed through changes in mechanical properties from ultrasound measurements. Furthermore, mechanical properties obtained from ultrasound measurements were compared against mechanical properties computed from a poroelastic model using measurements from 3D images of the trabecular bone samples from microCT images. In particular, it was found a high correlation between mechanical properties derived from ultrasound measurements and obtained from direct measurement of the microstructure in samples. Finally, using the poroelastic model, the directional information of the microstructure was extracted from each ultrasound measurement and compared to direct measurements from microCT images. The correlation between the bone density obtained from ultrasound and microCT images was moderated, but highly improved when the bone density was directionally modulated with this structural information. The structural information derived from ultrasound measurements were then shown relevant to improve the assessment of mechanical properties when analyzing anisotropic cancellous bone. The results obtained during the first year of the present project suggest that the ultrasound measurements and/or the use of the new poroelastic model can effectively distinguish directional and global changes in trabecular bone undergoing disuse and treated with antiresorptive therapy. The effectiveness of the ultrasound measurements to determine anisotropic changes in mechanical properties of bone was demonstrated against direct analysis of 3D images obtained from microCT. The Aim of the proposed research for the coming year consist in determine microstructure and mechanical properties of bone that has been allowed to recover from long-term disuse (restoration of mechanical loading + bone anabolic agent). In these experiments, anisotropic mechanical and structural properties of cancellous bone will be analyzed from a newly initiated series of experiments (NSBRI grant, Bone recovery after bisphosphonate and PTH treatment of disuse osteoporosis BL00406) that examines recovery potential for disuse and bisphosphonate treated bone, once mechanical loading has been restored. Data suggest that once trabeculae are lost, recovery can only occur through thickening of the remaining trabeculae. These studies will determine whether our acoustical anisotropy approach remains a good predictor of anisotropic mechanical properties in “restored” as well as normal and osteoporotic bone. Anisotropic mechanical properties of bone in which recovery was augmented using a bone anabolic agent (PTH) will be also examined.

experiment_title: Quantifying and Predicting Operationally-Relevant Performance in a Long-Duration Spaceflight Analog
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-duration exploration missions (LDEMs) will expose crewmembers to many risks that could adversely affect mission outcomes. Minimizing such risks will require identifying and validating objective indicators of behavioral health and performance, understanding the contribution of sleep loss on individual behavioral health, and identifying countermeasures that can reduce these risks. Cognitive tests can help identify deficits in specific brain systems, but the results are not easily converted to a metric of operational performance. Currently, the Robotic On-Board Trainer (ROBoT) is used operationally by astronauts, on the ground and in the International Space Station, to practice Canada Arm activities. The investigators are modifying ROBoT for research and for quantitative performance assessment. They are also developing and testing NINscan-SE: a multi-use system for measuring brain and physiological function. Both ROBoT and NINscan-SE are being characterized, validated, and will undergo analog feasibility testing in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility. This study has the following specific aims:
  1. Characterize operational task performance changes during 45-day HERA missions, including the roles of time-in-mission, workload, sleep debt, and operational emergencies.
  2. Characterize brain and systemic physiology changes during 45-day HERA missions, including the roles of time-in-mission, workload, sleep debt, and operational emergencies.
  3. Identify physiological or behavioral variables that predict operational performance.
  4. Quantify the influence of behavioral health countermeasures on both operational performance and (neuro) physiological measures.

APPROACH:
Thirty-two crewmembers will be recruited by NASA for the eight 45-day simulated LDEM HERA studies, and 32 control subjects will be recruited by the investigator. Data collections will be will be scheduled 1 – 2 weeks prior to each mission, during the 45-day mission itself, and one week post-mission. The crewmembers will be in the HERA facility to simulate the long duration and the control subjects will be tested in an off-site laboratory. The control subjects will not be sequestered and will only be required to participate in operational tasks relevant to this study. They will be trained and tested on the same schedule as HERA participants to provide as close a temporal match in training and testing as possible.

HERA and control participants will perform ROBoT tasks and undergo physiological monitoring two times a week on matching schedules. The controls will enable the investigators to differentiate changes in operational performance due to task repetition from any changes due to HERA sequestration. In addition, two emergency events will be introduced in the first and last weeks of each mission period. These will consist of an unexpected need to capture a wayward satellite traveling near the limits of Canada Arm capabilities. Investigators will work with other HERA investigators to coordinate ROBoT and physiological data collection before, during, and after one or more countermeasure (CM) deployments during the HERA missions. The CM(s) may include a lighting intervention, a Virtual Space Station-based behavioral intervention, diet, exercise, or other intervention. The precise experimental design will depend on the nature of the CM, but investigators will test hypotheses that the CM(s) generate detectable changes in ROBoT performance and/or in rest and task-related (neuro) physiological recordings.

RESULTS:
This study is in progress. Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: Reduction in Density and Expression of Vasopressin Receptors in the Kidneys of Rats Following Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

A number of studies have demonstrated that renal function is altered during and immediately following space flight. It has been suggested there is a decreased renal responsiveness to vasopressin following space flight and that this may be the mechanism for the increased urine flow that is observed following return to normal gravity. This experiment measured vasopressin receptor expression and activity in kidneys taken from rats 1 and 14 days following space flight of 15 days duration.

Approach:

Twelve male Fischer 344 rats were individually housed in the RAHF during space flight. Ground controls consisted of rats similarly kept in the RAHF and another 12 rats maintained in standard vivarium cages. Flight animals were killed within 5 hours of landing and real-time quantitative RT-PCR was used to determine mRNA levels for the vasopressin V2 and V1a receptors. The proportion of V2 and V1a receptors was determined by measuring 3H-labeled arginine vasopressin binding to kidney membranes.

Results:

Measurements of renal vasopressin V2 and V1a receptor mRNA expression by quantitative RT-PCR demonstrated little difference at either 1 day or at 14 days following return from space. Evaluation of 3 H-labeled arginine vasopressin binding to membranes prepared from kidneys indicated that the majority of the vasopressin receptors were V2 receptors. Furthermore, the data suggested that binding to vasopressin V2 or V1a receptors was unaltered at 1 day and 14 days following space flight. Similarly, the ability of vasopressin to stimulate adenylate cyclase suggested no change in vasopressin V2 receptor activity in these animals. These data suggest that, whatever changes in fluid and electrolyte metabolism are observed following space flight, they are not mediated by changes in vasopressin receptor number or vasopressin-induced stimulation of adenylate cyclase.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Effects on the Mouse Retina: Histological, Gene Expression and Epigenetic Changes After Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

This project aims at testing the overall hypothesis that cephalad fluid shifts elicited by either microgravity or hindlimb suspension (HS) represent a stress factor that induces optic disc neuroanatomical changes, as well as retinal cell deterioration and loss via oxidative stress. To date, there have been limited flight animal studies aimed at studying the effects of microgravity on the retina (Tombran-Tink, Adv Exp Med Biol, 2006; Grigoryan, Adv Space Res, 2002). The study will provide data for the new Visual Impairment and Intracranial Pressure risk. The second objective is to investigate the effects of HS in the retina of rats and to identify relevant genes that are significantly modulated by the mechanical stress imparted by the fluid shifts. This is a principal step towards the validation of HS as a model for the study of ocular alterations induced by simulated microgravity.

APPROACH:

The first specific aim of this pilot project is to perform histological and gene expression analysis of retinas collected from mice flown in STS-133 and STS-135 and from their ground control counterparts. The second specific aim is to perform similar analysis in retinas from hindlimb suspended rats, focusing on pathways consistent with cellular and oxidative stress, thus validating this ground analog animal model for the study of retinal stress in microgravity. The third specific aim will explore the potential efficacy of reversatrol and EGCG as a nutritional countermeasures to mitigate the risks or retinal oxidative stress and degeneration in conditions of simulated microgravity.

RESULTS:

Upon completion of this task, we have expanded the immunohistopathologic analysis of the rodent retina as far as the effects of and responses to spaceflight observed in the eyes of mice aboard shuttle mission STS-133 and STS-135, focusing, for the first time, on molecular and cellular processes. While the results reported here represent pilot data due to the small sample size, these data provide for the first time, direct evidence suggesting that oxidative stress, neuronal damage, and mechanical injury take place in the retina and optic nerve of rodents flown in low-Earth orbit for a period under 2 weeks. Our work gives a first insight into the impact of space-associated factors on biological processes like cell death, oxidative stress, and probable mechanical injury in the rodent eye.

Moreover, comparative results obtained with two different mouse strains (albino versus pigmented mice) suggest that susceptibility to stress factors is determinant of the extent of the stressors effects. While individual variability is not regularly encountered with genetically homogenous mouse strains, we observed some individual susceptibility variation, which may be ascribed to a particular stress impact in spaceflight, part of which is stochastic in nature (radiation).

The present work also investigated the contribution of cephalad fluid shift alone in the rat retina by using the well-characterized hindlimb suspension (HS) model, and identified, for the first time, a gene expression response suggestive of mechanical stress imposed by cephalad fluid shift on the eye. In addition, an antioxidant nutritional countermeasure based on a green-tea enriched diet resulted in a decreased stress response, suggesting an association between the possible mechanical stress and oxidative stress genetic circuits.

experiment_title: Systems Impacts of Waste Processing
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Solid waste processing has potential and unavoidable impacts on all life support sub-systems. Either waste is produced that must be disposed of, waste processing has impacts on other sub-systems that must be considered, or waste is usable to reduce the cost of supporting the mission. The crew produce both trash and metabolic waste, food crops produce large quantities of inedible biomass, all systems produce used spares and consumables, and processing of the various kinds of waste typically produce particulate and trace gas contaminants, as well as producing or using quantities of water. Investigators proposed to identify life-support-related solid waste streams, options for processing the waste, costs and benefits, and recommend particular approaches for particular near-term missions.

APPROACH:
The approach for this experiment continued to be built around equivalent system mass (ESM), as has previous life-support work that has done over the past decade. Expected waste streams for long-duration missions based on historical and current data were defined. This involved working closely with Kennedy Space Center (KSC), Shuttle Transportation System (STS), and International Space Station (ISS) personnel, as there is no waste monitoring program currently in place for these programs. Data from earlier programs was also investigated. Based on these data, waste stream models were developed for the missions defined in the Safety and Mission Assurance Panel (SMAP) Reference Missions Document. This involved extrapolation to longer missions and for different environments. Waste processing scenarios ranging from simple dumping to complete destruction of waste were developed. ESM impacts of the various technologies were determined, and assessed mission ESM impacts based on generally agreed assumptions about infrastructure.

RESULTS:
Waste processing was compared for terrestrial and space applications. Typical quantities of terrestrial domestic municipal waste were about 0.6 kg/person per day, with sewage being collected separately and gaseous emissions typically not considered at all. The standard waste production models for space missions that were developed previously were expanded to include new exploration missions and non-metabolic wastes. Typical rates varied from 1.8 to 3.5 kg/md. Potential life support contingencies and probable consequences for the waste system were identified. In general, contingencies would increase waste loads, sometimes by orders of magnitude. New types of wastes could be created that would be challenging to deal with.

For the Mars transit, surface, and base waste models, each of the types of waste was classified by proportion of five categories: ash, equipment, organic materials (biodegradable), plastic (non-biodegradable organics), and water content. This data was used to determine sizing of equipment in calculating ESM.

Missions were tracked, including the new exploration missions, and appropriate equivalencies were determined for trade studies. Technology drivers were identified and their impacts on waste processing considered. Equivalencies are anticipated to fall due to development of infrastructure technologies over the next several decades as exploration missions take individuals further from Earth.

Waste processing technologies were identified for Skylab, STS, and ISS missions, and from recent Advanced Life Support (ALS) projects. Waste technology interfaces were identified. Specific performances were calculated for the different technologies. Results varied from 1.7 kg processed per kg ESM for lyophilization on a transit mission to 7,000 for compacting on a Mars base. However, interface impacts could not be considered on a technology basis. Pre- and post- processing was in some cases as large an impact as the primary processing technology.

Waste approaches were optimized using ESM as the primary metric. Interfaces were a driver in trade studies especially where oxidative processes were considered. Water balance was a major factor in determining the optimum life support system. Water balance varied depending on the technologies used, from a loss of about five kg per crewperson per day for an open loop system, to a gain of about 0.7 kg with the maximum water recovery from waste. Extravehicular Activity (EVA) could result in a loss of about 0.4 kg/md with current EVA technologies and a Mars surface EVA model. Bioregeneration reduces the amount of waste and supply needed, but can have an unfavorable effect on water balance as less water is imported in food. Thus, any losses such as for EVA become more important. Some improvements in ALS reference missions were identified.

experiment_title: SL-3 Project Data
experiment_description:
Objectives
The understanding of space biology and the biomedical problems of space requires that animals be carried into space and that the crew have access to them.  In order to provide valid data on the biological effects of microgravity, it is mandatory that the Research Animal Holding Facility (RAHF) adequately maintain the animals.  This study was to provide common, Project-Office-collected data to other investigations having need of that common data.

Approach
A total of twelve large rats (400 g) and twelve small rats (200 g), all specific pathogen free, were flown in the RAHF for seven days.  About three weeks before flight, biotelemetry transmitters for measurement of EKG, deep-body temperature and heart rate were implanted into seventeen large rats, five of which were selected for flight.  Three to five days after surgery, implanted rats were placed in flight-type cages and the signals from their transmitters monitored to establish preflight diurnal rhythms.  About thirteen days before launch, the remaining animals were also placed in flight-type cages where the rats could learn to use the flight feeders and lixits.  Body, food, and water weights were colected preflight and postflight.  EKG's, activity, food and water consumption, and film were collected during flight.  The 24 flight animals were inspected and weighed at recovery at the landing site in California, then flown to Kennedy Space Center for further inspection, microbiological sampling, and sacrifice.  Organs and tissues were weighed and preserved for biosample distribution for further analyses.

Results
All data were successfully collected.

experiment_title: Morphological and Biochemical Examination of Heart Tissue: IV. Altered Myosin Expression in Rat Ventricular Muscle
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Microgravity is known to produce cardiovascular deconditioning, changes which may result in part from a regulation of cardiac muscle gene expression at the level of translation. However, little is known about the possible role of transcriptional regulation in the control of the heart during space flight. The purpose of the study was to examine the potential role of transcriptional regulation of myosin expression experienced by rats flown in space.

Approach:

Total RNA was extracted from the frozen, powdered muscle with the guanidinium isothiocyanate-cesium chloride method. Varying amounts of total RNA from each sample were electrophoresed on an RNA denaturing gel, probed with a 32P- labeled oligonucleotide probe specific for the beta-myosin heavy chain mRNA, and exposed to x-ray film which was subsequently scanned densitometrically. Statistical differences between the flight and control groups were determined by analysis of covariance for the heavy-chain mRNA expression and mapping of composite densitometric scans.

Results:

No differences between the flight and control groups were observed in the myosin protein isoform profile of the cardiac muscle samples. Beta-myosin heavy-chain mRNA expression was also not statistically different. In part, this lack of difference may be artifactual, because on a relative basis, many other species of contractile protein and RNA may also be changing in content, as demonstrated by the covariance mapping, where there were clearly differences identified by the probe between flight and control hearts. Therefore, the cardiovascular deconditioning that is observed may begin early during exposure as a change in transcriptional regulation of gene expression.

experiment_title: The effect of weightlessness on the tendon-to-bone insertion
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The overall objective of this proposal is to examine the effect of prolonged weightlessness on the biology of tendons and their insertions into bone. Samples from STS135 will allow us to verify our results from STS131. These specimens will also allow us to perform additional assays to verify our hypotheses. Raman microprobe spectroscopy will be performed at the tendon-to-bone insertion to determine the mineral gradient across the insertion.

APPROACH:

Experiment animals: 15 mice flew on this mission and 30 mice were housed at KSC to serve as ground controls. Left and right shoulders (humerus-rotator cuff-scapula units) and ankles (Achilles tendon-calcaneous bone) were removed from each mouse approximately two hours after landing, processed, and shipped to our laboratory. Ongoing studies analyzing specimens from this mission include: biochemistry and proteomics on rotator cuff mouse muscles, micro-computed tomography on the humeral head bone, biomechanics on the supraspinatus tendon-to-bone insertion, and histology on supraspinatus tendon-humeral head and Achilles tendon-calcaneous samples.

RESULTS:

The effect of microgravity on the rotator cuff tendons and their bony insertions: Microgravity led to significant increases in MMP-3 and MMP-13 mRNA expression and significant decreases in tendon cross-sectional area. These changes led to a surprising increase in the modulus and strength of the tendon-to-bone insertion. The stiffer tendon-to-bone insertion may be indicative of early tissue pathology.

The effect of microgravity on the humeral head bone: Preliminary data from STS-131 and STS-135 demonstrate that bone resorption is increased (as indicated by increases in the ratio of RANK-L to OPG gene expression) and osteoblast differentiation is decreased (as indicated by decreases in osterix and Runx-2 gene expression). Bone mineral density (BMD) and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th.) were decreased due to microgravity.

The effect of microgravity on the rotator cuff muscles: Microgravity significantly downregulated the expression of myogenic genes indicating atrophy/degeneration of the muscles due to microgravity. Downregulation of adipogenic genes indicated that degeneration due to microgravity may occur through different pathways than degeneration due to tendon and/or nerve injury in gravity conditions. An increase in collagen type III indicates muscle fibrosis. Preliminary proteomics results indicated that the expression of a large number of proteins was changed due to microgravity conditions. These changes included proteins related to muscle metabolism, muscle type, and fatty acid/glucose metabolism.

experiment_title: Demonstration of JEM Water Recovery System (JWRS)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Efficient use of resources is especially important when considering space flight beyond low earth orbit. Onboard storage of sufficient potable water for long-duration, exploration class space missions is not feasible. Therefore recovery and recycling of potential water sources, such as condensation and crew urine, is essential. This objective of this investigation is to demonstrate the use of the JEM Water Recovery System (JWRS) to recover potable water that meets NASA’s quality standard from urine.

APPROACH:
Urine will be collected from crew using the onboard Urine Collection Device and transferred into the JWRS. Urine collections from one or more crew members will continue until at least one liter of urine has been collected. In addition, ten cc of urine will be placed in a sample tube and frozen for later return to Earth. When sufficient urine has been collected, the JWRS will be commanded from the ground to begin processing. The processed water will be analyzed using analytical instruments onboard. Samples of processed water will also be placed in sample bags and frozen for return to Earth.

In addition to crew samples, simulated urine will be processed four times.

All returned samples will be analyzed in detail.

RESULTS:
Results for this investigation are unavailable. This is an international experiment. NASA does not currently have an agreement with international space partners to archive their data in the LSDA.

experiment_title: Evaluation of vestibular dysfunction induced by a long-term stay in the ISS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The vestibular system is situated in the inner ear and comprises two components: the otolith organs, which perceive linear accelerations (gravity) and the semicircular canals, which perceive angular accelerations (rotational movements). The vestibular system sends neural signals to the central nervous system, and regulates posture, eye movements, arterial pressure, and muscle-bone relationship. However, it is known that the vestibular system is highly plastic.

Spaceflight may differentially affect gravity and rotation sensors, given the input to the gravity sensor becomes zero but input to the rotation sensor is preserved in space. To examine this, gravity and rotation sensor function will be separately evaluated before and after the ISS mission, and these functions will be correlated to body balance impairment.

These studies are important, because the impaired vestibular system may relate spaceflight-induced medical problems such as gravity sickness, impaired body balance, orthostatic hypotension, and muscle and bone atrophy. To examine mechanisms of spaceflight-induced medical problems, investigators separately evaluate otolith and canal functions, and test whether weak galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) can ameliorate an impaired vestibular function. The purpose of the research is to evaluate otolith and canal functions separately and to correlate those functions to body balance impairment. Additionally, the effect of weak-noise-GVS on body balance will be examined.

APPROACH:
To test this hypothesis, the otolith function and the semicircular function will be separately examined before and after the ISS stay. Furthermore, this study will also test the hypothesis that a weak GVS might ameliorate the impaired vestibular function. Ten astronauts will be required for this study. Participants as subjects from ISS crews who stay for six months (more than four months).

Baseline data collection will be conducted 4 times: once preflight and three times postflight. All procedures are noninvasive and finished in one hour. To evaluate otolith function, ocular vestibular evoked myogenic potential (oVEMP) and cervical VEMP (cVEMP) will be measured. In these tests, myogenic potentials are measured from the eyelid muscle and the cervical muscle evoked by sound or vibration. To evaluate canal function, air caloric tests will be performed. During this test, eye movements will be recorded, while air of 50ºC and 24ºC are injected from the external auditory canal. To evaluate balance ability, the subject will stand on a balance board for 60 seconds, with or without the eyes open and with or without weak GVS.

Additionally, a Crew Questionnaire related to motion sickness and instability will be completed. Subjective symptoms of motion sickness, dizziness, nausea status, unusual motion and medication usage within 24 hours of each data collection session will be documented.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Histological Studies on the Tibial Bone of Rats in the 1975 Cosmos 782 Flight: I. Endochondral Osteogenesis; Medullary Bone Turnover
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment concerns the histological evaluation of endochondral ontogenesis in rats subjected to weightlessness in Earth-orbit for nineteen days. Balances between cartilage formation and resorption, and medullary bone formation and resorption were analyzed in the proximal segment of the tibia.

Approach:

Tibial lengths, appearance of the proximal tibial epiphysis and metaphysis, and measurements of the bony spongiosa in the latter, were determined for flight rats and compared to ground controls. Fixated samples were stained with hematoxylin and eosin, and Mallory's triple stain (aniline blue, orange G, and acid fuchsin), and studied histologically. Measurements were made whenever possible to provide quantitative support for the qualitative histological evaluations.

Results:

Growth retardation was not marked, falling between a negligible level and 25%. Bone formation was slightly impaired in synchronous controls, and to an appreciably greater extent in flight animals. Bone resorption was moderately accelerated in synchronous controls, markedly more so in the flight animals, to an extent under which virtually all preflight medullary bone was removed and in addition a substantial fraction (1/4 -1/2) of that formed during flight was also resorbed. Although the results suggest that disuse atrophy and other restrictions during the experiment account for part of the imbalance, the condition of weightlessness added a considerable further imbalance.

experiment_title: Modeling and Control of Bio-systems
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In 1964, NASA discovered that sufficient cooling of an astronaut could not be accomplished via air convection in the suit due to ventilation. Thus, NASA upgraded to the liquid cooling garment (LCG) to provide better thermal comfort. The astronaut controls the temperature of the water flowing through the LCG by manually adjusting the temperature control valve (TCV) located on the front of the space suit. However, manually manipulating the TCV setting can dramatically reduce the productivity of the astronaut, distracting them from the extra-vehicular activity (EVA) mission at hand. In general, humans are poor judges of their thermal state and since an astronaut’s attention is focused on other things during EVA, there are time lags in the application of temperature control. This can cause overheating or overcooling; placing unneeded thermal stress on the astronaut, and possibly degrading EVA performance. An attractive solution to this problem is the use of automatic control for thermal comfort. Before an automatic controller can be designed, human thermal models are needed to accurately describe the transient heat transfer processes and predict the thermal response within an acceptable band of accuracy. Such human thermal models can also be extended to predict thermal stress for various applications involving fire fighters, combat pilots, hazardous waste workers, and other relevant industries.

Hysterical paralysis is a conversion disorder characterized by some lack of motor functioning brought about by psychological mechanisms without the presence of organic injury in the central nervous system. In conversion disorders, it is assumed that the victim when presented with distressing mental conflict, which seem insurmountable, converts this anxiety into a somatic symptom to resolve or alleviate the tension. It is important to note that these physical symptoms are not intentionally produced to malinger. In many instances, the victim is unaware of the stressor that might have caused the symptoms. An assumption can be made that there must be some neurobiological dysfunction that can explain hysterical paralysis. So, mathematical modeling could be the first step to elucidate the neurobiology involved with conversion motor paralysis. In turn, identifying the specific location of brain lesions that produce hysterical paralysis can aid in the diagnosis of this disorder.

The first goal of this research was to develop a more complete model of the human's thermoregulation to handle various applications involving astronauts in space, warfighters, fire fighters, combat pilots, hazardous waste workers, and other industries where comfort in thermally stressful environments needs to be insured. Specifically, the model includes: the arteriovenous anastomoses (AVAs), an accurate model of the human digits, and cold induced vasodilation (CIVD). Future work will be needed to 'individualize' the model to investigate the effect of physiological variations (gender, age, race, body composition, body type, etc.). In addition, the effect of microgravity on human thermal physiology will need to be quantified.

The second part of this research was to develop a preliminary computational model for hysterical paralysis using neuro-circuitry information and systems biology principles. The model captures the salient features of the neuro-psychiatric disorder reported in the literature. Studies are on-going to model in more detail both the intra-cellular and extra-cellular features of the model, within the framework proposed.

The third part of this research was to develop a computational model of a pyramidal cell in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to better understand its role in the reinstatement of cocaine-seeking behavior. Studies have shown that the BLA and nucleus accumbens (NAcc) play a key role in cue-primed reinstatement. Therefore, once the BLA model is complete, a network level model involving the BLA and NAcc will be developed.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
In the human thermal modeling front, a comparison in cold-induced vasoilation response (CIVD) response between predicted and measured finger temperatures was conducted and it was shown that there is a fairly good agreement, indicating that the model is capable of showing CIVD responses in the fingers. As anticipated, the predicted response of finger temperature without CIVD is lower than the finger temperature response with CIVD during the oscillatory stage. The obvious conclusion is that the CIVD mechanism reduces extremity discomfort and prevents injuries due to cold exposure.

A study was conducted by the author and colleagues for the purpose of determining tolerance limits for subjects experiencing extreme heat stress. Participants (7 males, 7 females, 19 – 26 years old) exercised (200 and 425 W) at three different environments (normal – 23.9ºC, 45% RH; jungle – 35ºC, 75% RH; and desert – 43.3ºC, 20% RH) while wearing heavy clothing. A neural network predictive model based on the experimental data was developed. In addition, another objective was to determine whether previously developed heat strain models like the Givoni-Goldman prediction can accurately predict tolerance limits in comparison to experimental data obtained by the author and colleagues. Both models predict the response of the ‘average’ individual, thus correction factors based on individual characteristics (i.e. fitness, body type, acclimation status, etc) were incorporated to improve the prediction of heat strain. In addition, past heat strain predictive models and individual characteristics that effect tolerance limits were extensively reviewed by the author.

experiment_title: Behavioral Issues Associated with Long Duration Space Missions:  Review of Astronaut Journals
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
(2003 - 2010): The Journals experiment was a focused study of human factors, behavior, and performance issues during expeditions to the International Space Station (ISS). The investigator has studied conditions analogous to space craft in previous projects, including a two-year study (conducted for NASA with the cooperation of the European Space Agency and the French Polar Institute) in which content analyses were performed of diaries maintained by the station leaders and physicians at the Antarctic and South Indian Ocean remote duty stations. That study provided the first rank-ordering of the behavioral issues in terms of importance associated with isolation and confinement, based on quantitative data. This experiment used the same content evaluation techniques on journals kept by ISS crew personnel during ISS expeditions.

The experiment tested the hypothesis that the analogous conditions could provide an acceptable model for space craft (i.e., to validate or refute the results of the previous study). Specifically, the study was designed to 1)evaluate how isolation and confinement on long duration space missions can affect crew health and morale, which are important factors that can influence mission success, 2) convert behavioral and human factors data contained in journal entries into quantitative data on the importance of the various behavioral issues involved in long-duration isolation and confinement, and 3) systematically analyze the content of astronaut journals in order to enhance the design of procedures and equipment to support human performance during exploration of the moon and Mars.

(2011 - forward): The original study period of the Journals experiment (2003-2010) tested the hypothesis that the analog conditions provided an acceptable model for space operations. Substantial support for the hypothesis was found, but ISS crew size has increased since then. The Journals experiment is being continued to collect data from members of larger crews to determine if there are differences in behavioral issues that could be attributed to crew size.

The objective of the study extension is to obtain behavioral and human factors data relevant to the design of equipment and procedures to support adjustment and sustained human performance during extended duration isolation and confinement.

For the continuation of the experiment with 10 additional subjects, the specific objectives of the proposed study are to 1) collect data concerning the relevant behavioral factors from 10 additional astronauts while serving as members of 6-person crews onboard the ISS; 2) compare the experiences reported by members of larger crews to those of the two and three-person crews who participated in the original journals study; 3) assess the effects of other changes that have been implemented since the journals study concluded (e.g., cupola, sleep chambers, procedures); 4) further test the third quarter phenomenon; and 5) provide a safe and constructive outlet for the frustration and irritation that usually accompany isolated and confined living. The ultimate objective of the study is to provide data-driven recommendations to inform decisions concerning the priorities that should be placed on the various behavioral issues to prepare for and manage future space expeditions. Study results can be applied to improve selection, training, support, scheduling, and the design of equipment and procedures.

APPROACH:
Approximately seven days before launch (L-7), the participating crewmembers complete a very brief questionnaire. While on orbit, crewmembers made journal entries at least three times per week in a personal journal. The journal was either electronic (e.g. using a laptop) or paper. In addition to the journal entries, participating crewmembers also complete a brief questionnaire at the mid-point of their respective expeditions. Approximately 4-6 days after landing (R+4 to R+6), the crewmembers complete a questionnaire identical to the mid-point questionnaire.

RESULTS:
(2003 - 2010): Personal journals that were provided by ten subjects during ISS expeditions were analyzed to obtain information concerning a wide range of behavioral and human factors issues. Astronauts wrote most about their work, followed by outside communications (with mission control, family and friends), adjustment to the conditions, interactions with crew mates, recreation/leisure, equipment (installation, maintenance), events (launches, docking, hurricanes, etc.), organization/management, sleep, and food.

The results were presented in a final report that was published in July 2010 by NASA as NASA/TM-2010-216130. The study found evidence of a decline in morale during the third quarters of the missions and identified key factors that contribute to sustained adjustment and optimal performance during long-duration space expeditions. Astronauts reported that they benefited personally from writing in their journals because it helped maintain perspective on their work and relations with others. Responses to questions asked before, during, and after the expeditions show that living and working onboard the ISS is not as difficult as the astronauts anticipated before starting their six-month tours of duty. Recommendations included application of study results and continuation of the experiment to obtain additional data as crew size increases and operations evolve. Astronauts have reported that participating in the Journals Experiment has helped them adapt to the isolation, confinement, and other special conditions of the ISS.

(2011 - forward): At the conclusion of the experiment, results will be posted when data becomes available.

experiment_title: PowerCell Spaceflight Project
experiment_description:
Overview:
The German Aerospace Center (DLR) invited NASA Ames to participate in the DLR’s first CompactSat mission, Eu:CROPIS. DLR made provisions for Ames to fly a secondary payload known as Payload 2 on the Eu:CROPIS S/C. DLR invited Ames to develop and deliver a science payload that compliments the science objectives of Eu:CROPIS primary payload. The vision for the mission was to develop enabling technologies required to sustain long-term human life support systems, particularly in reduced gravity environments such as those on the moon and on Mars.

Mission ConOps:
1. The Eu:CROPIS satellite will establish artificial gravity levels by controlling the rate of rotation about its axis
2. Science experiments will be repeated at different gravity levels
3. One year mission lifetime
4. 6 month duration at each of two gravity levels: Lunar & Martian
5. Orbit: ~600 km, Sun Synchronous Orbit
6. DLR is providing the NASA PL2 system unregulated power from the spacecraft bus and an RS-422 communication interface with the Eu:CROPIS S/C C&DH
7. Downlink of PL2 science data will be performed as a regular part of spacecraft operations by DLR, and the raw data will be provided to the science team

Instrument Description:
The PowerCell Payload System includes a pair of independent air-tight enclosures. Each measures 15 inches x 3.16 inches x 10.6 inches (38 centimeters x 8 centimeters x 27 centimeters), weighs 15 pounds (6.8 kilograms), consumes 10 watts when active, and houses two of the 48-well microfluidic cards plus fluidic, thermal, optical, electronic, and control subsystems. One microfluidic card carrying its full complement of microbes will be filled and measured at each artificial gravity level. In each gravity regime a payload fluidic system will deliver nutrients to 48 microwells integrated into a microfluidic carrier or “card”. Each microwell houses a PowerCell mini-ecology in dried form suitable for many months of stasis. The temperature is stabilized as the dried organisms hydrate and 4 miniature LEDs provide white light to initiate photosynthesis. Periodically, a sequence of optical measurements is made by the other 3 LEDs—violet, cyan, and red— plus a dedicated photo-detector to monitor the growth and composition of each well’s ecosystem.

OBJECTIVES:
In its first test flight, the PowerCell Payload will investigate the performance of microbial mini-ecologies containing both photosynthetic microbes and consumer organisms. Cyanobacteria will produce the carbohydrate sucrose (table sugar), which will feed Bacillus subtilis, a robust bacterium commonly found in soil and the gut, which has already proven that it can withstand the rigors of space while in the spore form.

A second objective of the PowerCell Payload is to conduct synthetic biology remotely in outer space. The basic technique for introducing genetic material into a living cell, “transformation”, involves the transfer across a cell’s encasing membrane of molecules carrying genetic information. The PowerCell Payload will examine if and how reduced gravity levels affect transformation processes.

The third objective is to test protein production under different gravity regimes. Using the tools of synthetic biology, B. subtilis was engineered to produce several proteins which will be produced at the three different space gravity regimes. The ability to make proteins in space will be fundamental for human exploration, as proteins will be used to produce a range of critical substances, from on-demand food and vaccines to building materials.

APPROACH:
As its mini-ecologies are exposed to several levels of artificially generated gravity, the PowerCell concept will be evaluated for effectiveness under non-terrestrial gravity environments. A rotating spacecraft will provide gravity similar to that of the International Space Station (ISS) for a few weeks, and then the Moon for six months, and Mars for an additional six months. The results will be compared to a series of identical experiments on Earth.

At each gravity regime, a payload fluidic system will deliver nutrients to the 48 microwells integrated into a microfluidic carrier or “card”. Each microwell houses one of the three experiments in dried form suitable for two years of stasis. The temperature will be stabilized as the dried organisms hydrate. Periodically, a sequence of optical measurements is made by the 3 LEDs—violet, cyan, and red— plus a dedicated photo-detector to monitor the growth and composition of each well.

RESULTS:
This investigation is currently in progress.  Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.
