experiment_title: Geology, Geochemistry and Lithology Science Support Activities
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Lunar Airborne Dust Toxicity Assessment Group (LADTAG) has been assigned the task of evaluating dust hazards to humans, and recommending exposure standards for lunar dust suspended in breathing air. Over the 40 years that have transpired since the last Apollo crew left the lunar surface, much has been learned about the toxicity of small particles. Based on experience with industrial minerals such as sandblasting quartz, investigators know that even if a dust is not hazardous due to a three-day exposure, it may nonetheless be quite toxic when the exposure covers a longer duration. The Lunar Airborne Dust Toxicity Assessment Group (LADTAG) was chartered by NASA to set an exposure standard for six months of episodic exposure to lunar dust. In order to accomplish this, it is necessary to learn how lunar dust toxicity compares to both toxic and non-toxic terrestrial dusts.

Dust exposure standards, similar to those established for quartz and asbestos on Earth, will determine the design, mass, power, and cost of airlocks, ports, and dust control systems that are incorporated into lunar habitats and shirtsleeve rovers. The Lunar Airborne Dust Toxicity Advisory Group (LADTAG) Geology team, led by JSC senior scientist David S. McKay, encompasses expertise in geology, geochemistry, and geophysics, with a combined total of over 100 years of lunar research. This team provides three major research thrusts for the LADTAG research effort: (1) Evaluation and Recommendations; (2) Isolating the respirable fraction of lunar dust for inhalation toxicology studies, and (3) Lunar soil simulant development.

APPROACH:
(1) Evaluation and Recommendations: Lunar dust in situ is subjected to processes that likely cause grain surfaces to become chemically reactive, potentially increasing the toxicity of the dust. Moreover, lunar dust contains metallic iron in spheroids of 30 nanometers and smaller diameter. The effect of this nanophase iron on human tissue and cells is yet to be determined; such material does not occur on Earth and it is thus unknown whether humans have any specific evolutionary ability to deal with it. The detailed characteristics of sub-micrometer lunar dust are only poorly known, and this is the size range of particles that are of greatest concern for our toxicology studies.

In addition to being potentially hazardous to humans, lunar dust is detrimental to equipment. Electrostatic charging of the dust due to UV irradiation and solar-wind-proton implantation must be characterized in order to design methods of mitigating these effects. Our team will provide high-fidelity simulants by continuing our research in the effects of radiation, proton bombardment, and triboelectric charging. One of the most unusual features of actual lunar dust is the presence of minute iron spheres, up to 30 nanometers in diameter, which often cover the surface of the grain. The investigating team has simulated these iron spheres in a silicate matrix for use in toxicology studies. Their activities in support of Evaluations and Recommendations include basic research on chemical activation, passivation, size and shape analysis, and simulating the unique qualities of the surfaces of lunar dust grains as it will be found on the lunar surface.

In addition to providing knowledge about past research on lunar dust, the team will be conducting new experiments to address unknowns that have not previously been considered. For example, we plan dissolution studies, both with dust simulant and with actual lunar dust, to learn more about how dust particles behave when ingested. This provides critical background information for toxicology studies.

(2) Isolating the respirable fraction of lunar dust for inhalation toxicology studies: Inhalation toxicology studies using lunar dust will be used to determine the allowable exposure limits. These experiments must be performed in a standardized manner so that the results obtained can be realistically compared to the results of experiments using other substances (such as silica dust). Consequently it is necessary to separate the respirable particles from a lunar sample, because the typical laboratory equipment for inhalation studies depends on having particles in the proper size range at the start of the experiment. The investigating team efforts focus on dust in the respirable range and include the particle size distribution, mineralogical and morphological habits of the dust in lunar-habitat conditions, dust reactivity and passivation in applicable conditions, and direct cell interactions with nano-scale-iron-rich minerals and glasses. This allows LADTAG to define risks and establish appropriate standards for manned lunar missions. These analyses allow them to prepare lunar soils with the targeted size distributions and properties for use by the toxicology groups for inhalation and cell reaction studies. An additional by-product is the development of improved techniques for separating and handling nano-scale particles for Scanning Eletron Microscope (SEM), Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM), and elemental analysis.

RESULTS:
These requirements have inspired the team to develop a method of separating the respirable fraction of lunar dust from a bulk soil sample, without using sieves, which allows maximum recovery of the available dust in the sample. The total amount of lunar sample available for this study is less than 300 grams. The developed method uses pneumatic transport with ultrapure nitrogen as the carrier gas; thus the lunar material is not exposed to water or other liquids. The separation method incorporates a small fluidized bed as well as gas impactor size separation steps and a cyclonic separator. Analysis of the separated material with a Microtrac™ laser diffraction system has been used to validate the process. Lunar soil simulant development: The geology team is developing new methods to simulate the chemically active surface of dust grains. Specifically, the areas of concern for LADTAG are the physical and chemical properties of the finest fraction (less than 3 µm) of lunar soil (“dust”), and the interaction of lunar dust with biological as well as mechanical systems. Before the hazards of lunar dust can be managed, they must be understood. The path to understanding the hazards includes both experimental and analytical work. The experimental work cannot be performed on actual lunar samples without first validating the proposed techniques using an appropriate simulant material. By developing an appropriate dust simulant, the Geology Team provides the basis for all other areas of research within LADTAG.

All aims have been realized. Bulk samples of lunar dust were obtained from CAPTEM and respirable size particles of native lunar dust were separated using a new pneumatic technique developed by the Geology Team. This technique was used to separate additional respirable particles from coarse lunar dust, which had been reduced by grinding. Mass median aerodynamic diameter of separated particles were measured with particle sizers and confirmed to be in the respirable range. Respirable particles were utilized in studies with rodents that assessed the toxicity of the lunar dusts.

experiment_title: Thioaptamer Diagnostic System
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
AM Biotechnologies in partnership with Sandia National Laboratories developed a Thioaptamer Diagnostic System (TDS) to quickly quantify clinically relevant biomarkers inflight using only microliters of virtually any complex sample. The system combines ambient-stable, long-shelf-life affinity agent assays with a handheld microfluidic gel electrophoresis affinity assay quantification technology. The system is easy to use, compatible with operation in microgravity, and designed to permit simultaneous quantification of 32 or more biomarkers from a single astronaut sample.

APPROACH:
Phase 1 of this project demonstrated that a thioaptamer assay used in the microfluidic instrument can quantify a specific biomarker in serum in the low nanomolar range. AM also successfully identified novel affinity agents to bone specific alkaline phosphatase (BAP) and demonstrated their use to detect BAP using the microfluidic instrument. Phase 2 will expand the number of ambient stable affinity agents and demonstrate a TDS prototype to NASA. AM anticipates that the TDS at the end of Phase 2 will be at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 or 5. In Phase 3, AM and Sandia will produce flight units for NASA research use on the International Space Station (ISS) as well as for diagnostic use on future long duration missions.

experiment_title: Evaluating the Spaceflight Infectious Disease Risk Potential of Pathogenic and Commensal microorganisms using Caenorhabditis elegans as a Human Surrogate Model for Infection
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Understanding the impact of the spaceflight environment on the disease-causing potential of a wide variety of pathogenic and commensal microbes is critical for ensuring crew health, safety and performance. Changes that occur to both the immune system of astronauts and pathogenesis of microbes during spaceflight could represent a formidable challenge to the successful transition from short-to-long duration missions. This is a critical issue to address since a) the crew’s immune system is dysfunctional during flight, and b) results from our collaborative team and others have demonstrated that spaceflight and/or spaceflight-analogue culture globally alters the virulence, gene expression and/or pathogenesis-related phenotypes of several microbial pathogens. This proposal aims to further improve infectious disease risk assessment for astronauts by investigating the likelihood that a variety of microorganisms may exhibit alterations in virulence in response to the microgravity environment.

APPROACH:
This will be accomplished by profiling changes in virulence, persistence in the host, and targeted changes in gene expression of a select panel of pathogenic and commensal microorganisms exposed to spaceflight-analogue culture using the Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV) bioreactor. Microbes proposed for this study include 1) Salmonella Typhimurium, 2) Staphylococcus aureus, 3) a Space Shuttle environmental isolate of Burkholderia cepacia, and 4) Lactobacillus acidophilus, a commensal microorganism. The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) will be used as a human surrogate model of infection to evaluate changes in microbial virulence in response to RWV culture and will also be profiled for targeted changes in the expression of genes important for host immunity. Moreover, as astronauts have dysfunctional immune systems during spaceflight, the susceptibility of an immunocomprised C. elegans mutant to infection with these same microbes will also be evaluated. Results from this work hold potential to provide deeper insight into the likelihood, consequence and respective uncertainties of this HRP risk.

The design of this study was such that only the bacteria were cultured in the RWV, while the C. elegans hosts (wild type and an immunocompromised mutant) were grown prior to infection on standard nematode growth media (NGM) agar plates on their normal laboratory diet of Escherichia coli OP50. The infections then took place in liquid medium using a variety of exposure times (1-18 hours) in order to minimize any reversion of the low-shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG)-associated phenotypes (i.e., changes in virulence and pathogenesis-related stress resistance) during the infection.

RESULTS:
Under the conditions of this study, we found that transient exposure of the RWV-cultured microbes to C. elegans in a static dish was not sufficient for establishing a lethal infection in the nematode relative to the uninfected control nematodes fed on OP50. The outcomes of the infection process in liquid were quite different from what was previously reported for these pathogens using a solid agar medium. This indicates the need for further study design optimization. Persistence studies with S. Typhimurium did however indicate an early difference in the bacterial colonization numbers within the nematode intestine infected with LSMMG versus control cultures. We also observed an interesting phenotype following S. aureus infection, in which the bacterium appeared to form a biofilm-like structure around the anterior of the worm in liquid. Studies are ongoing to further investigate these findings.

experiment_title: Impact of Space-Radiation Induced Alterations on Toxic Protein Accumulation Associated with Neurodegenerative Disease
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In addition to the risk of cancer, there is concern that prolonged exposure of astronauts to deep space radiation will lead to degenerative changes in different organ systems, including the brain. Indeed we previously demonstrated that space radiation impaired cognitive performance and exacerbated Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology in a widely used mouse model of AD. Accumulation of the toxic peptide amyloid-ß occurs in AD and has been clearly established as an inherited cause of the disease. Space radiation at relatively modest doses elicits chronic inflammation and oxidative stress responses that alter normal brain function and may contribute to amyloid-ß accumulation by inhibiting normal clearance mechanisms. Recent data from our laboratory shows reduced clearance of amyloid-ß in mouse brain many months after exposure to space radiation. Thus, we hypothesize that radiation exacerbates Alzheimer’s disease pathology by altering the ability of the brain to remove amyloid-ß. To address this hypothesis we propose experiments that explore three possible cellular mechanisms linking radiation-induced neuroinflammation to reduced amyloid-ß clearance. We also propose to determine whether a drug that reduces brain inflammation and enhances amyloid-ß clearance can mitigate radiation-induced changes in Alzheimer’s pathology and cognitive decline in a mouse model of the disease. Taken together, these studies will lead to a better understanding of the biological mechanisms underlying risks for neurodegenerative disease after space radiation exposure.

Specific Aim 1: We will assess the role of LRP1 at the BBB on Aß clearance at different radiation doses and post-exposure durations in WT mice using established tracer techniques. LRP1 expression levels in brain microvessels and parenchyma will be determined and correlated with Aß clearance.

Specific Aim 2: We will evaluate the role of the glymphatic system in radiationinduced accumulation of brain Aß, and inulin, an ISF flow marker, at different radiation doses and post-exposure durations in wild-type (WT) mice. Alterations in ISF flow will be correlated with measures of astrocyte activation and neuroinflammation.

Specific Aim 3: We will determine the effects of radiation on the proliferative capacity of microglia during normal response to injury in WT mice, and for the ability of microglia to phagocytize Aß in vivo using APP/PS1 mice. Alterations will be correlated with measures of neuroinflammation and evidence of microglial phenotypic changes, including senescence.

Specific Aim 4: To more firmly establish mechanisms linking cellular changes to Aß accumulation, we will attempt to reduce radiation-associated effects on AD pathology and cognition using a radio-protective and anti-inflammatory drug that also enhances Aß clearance from the brain.

APPROACH:
For Aims 1, 2, and 3, dose and time-course studies will be carried out with 8-10 month old male C57BL/6 wild-type mice using whole body, awake irradiation at the NSRL with HZE particles (Iron, 600 MeV/µ and Silicon or Oxygen, 300 MeV/µ) and protons (150 MeV/µ); note that final ion selections will be discussed with NASA space radiation element program directors. Doses will be 50 cGy and lower for HZE and 100 cGy and lower for protons; time points will be 3, 6 and 12 months after irradiation. In consultation with NASA program leaders we will also endeavor to examine effects of GCR simulation as capabilities come online. For selected doses and time points, experiments will be replicated with both male and female mice. In addition to wild-type mice, the studies proposed in Aim 3 will also employ transgenic APP/PS1 mice, which represent a preferred approach for measuring in vivo phagocytosis of Aß by microglia. Aim 4 will employ both male and female APP/PS1 mice on the C57BL/6 background as a means to model the effects of radiation on chronic Aß accumulation in vivo.

This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Recovery of IGF-1 Signaling in Bone by Skeletal Reloading (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prolonged space flight causes osteopenia due to decreased bone formation secondary to impaired osteoblast proliferation and increased osteoblast apoptosis. Hindlimb unloading by tail suspension, a model for skeletal unloading of space flight, causes osteoblast precursor and skeletal tissue resistance to the effects of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). The nature of this resistance is characterized by decreased activation of the IGF-1 receptor and downstream signaling pathways. Osteoblast precursors isolated from unloaded bones demonstrate decreased expression of integrins, putative mechanosensors that bind extracellular matrix proteins, and in vitro treatment of normal osteoblasts with echistatin, an integrin antagonist, recreates the phenomena of unloading-induced IGF-1 resistance. Additionally, mechanical stimulation of human osteoblasts activates the IGF-1 receptor and augments the receptor response to IGF-1. These effects are abrogated by echistatin treatment. These findings suggest that integrin receptors have a role in mechanical regulation of IGF-1 receptor in osteoblasts.

Investigators hypothesized is that interaction of integrin and IGF-1 receptor signaling cascades is required for IGF-1 activation of its receptor and intact IGF-1 signaling in osteoblasts. Mechanical loading stimulates the formation of an integrin/IGF-1 receptor complex, thus, enhancing IGF-1 signaling and enabling mechanically induced osteoblast proliferation and bone formation. To test the hypothesis, investigators proposed the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the means by which skeletal reloading regulates skeletal response to IGF-1. Tail suspended rats treated with IGF-1 will be skeletally reloaded to preserve bone mass and osteoblast IGF-1 signaling. Integrity of IGF-1 signaling will be correlated with the interaction between integrins and the IGF-1 receptor.
  2. Determine the mechanism for regulation of the osteoblast IGF-1 receptor by integrins in response to mechanical loading by pulsatile fluid flow. Formation of the integrin and IGF-1 receptor complex in human osteoblasts will be stimulated by fluid flow loading in order to determine the components within the complex and their function.

    APPROACH:
    The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

    RESULTS:
    At the completion of this project investigatores established the critical regulatory role of integrins in IGF-1 signaling of osteoblasts. Mechanical stimulation of human osteosarcoma (HOS) cells activates the IGF-1R including the proliferative MAPK signal pathway and the anti-apoptotic Akt signal pathway in a ligand independent manner. The sensitivity of HOS cells and its IGF-1R to mechanical stimulation requires and is influenced by integrin receptor signaling. This is illustrated impaired activation of IGF-1R induced by echistatin and augmented activation of IGF-1R by stimulation of integrin receptors with exposure to their ligands. The results of siRNA knockdown experiments indicate that both integrin beta1 and beta3 are required for normal activation of the IGF-1R by treatment with either ligand or mechanical stimulation. The integrin regulation of IGF-1 signaling in osteoblasts allows osteoblasts to sense and respond to mechanical load, providing a link between mechanical loading, bone formation, and skeletal integrity.

    The feasibility of intermittent cyclic skeletal loading and IGF-1 infusion to prevent unloading-induced bone loss was evaluated. Tail suspended rats treated with intermittent short duration cyclic loading totaling only 42 minutes over 2 weeks had significantly blunted unloading induced trabecular bone loss. The mechanism of the enhanced response of the unloaded bones to cyclic loading is due to augmentation of bone formation rather than reduction in osteoclast activity and these responses were not affected by IGF-1 treatment. However, within the cortical bone compartment, the intermittent loading induced stimulation of periosteal bone formation was further augmented by treatment with IGF-1. These findings demonstrate the complex nature of the skeletal response to mechanical loading in that in cancellous bone, the threshold for mechanical stimulation induced bone formation in the unloaded state is lower than that required to prevent unloading induced osteoclast mediated bone loss and IGF-1 has a limited role in modulating the response of cancellous bone to mechanical loading but works synergistically with mechanical loading in cortical bone at the periosteal bone surface. The complexity of these differing skeletal responses to mechanical and pharmacologic treatments and the interactions between the integrin and IGF-1 signaling cascades in osteoblasts will need to be considered in the design of potential targets for countermeasure treatments to preserve the effects of mechanical loading and prevent the bone loss of space flight.

experiment_title: Light Flash Observations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the Apollo missions 12-17 and Skylab missions 2-4, the crews observed and recorded the frequency and character of light flashes through their eyes. After approximately 17 minutes of dark adaptation, tiny dots and thin streaks of white light were seen at frequencies of approximately three events per minute by crewmembers when on translunar coast (TLC) or transearth coast (TEC) or over the polar part of Skylab orbits. When near the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), where the proton flux was over 1000 times greater than in other parts of the orbit, the frequency increased to approximately nine events per minute for Skylab altitudes of 443 km.

Nearly 20 years ago, it was hypothesized that astronauts were likely to see flashes of light from cosmic ray particles when they were outside the shielding provided by the Earth’s magnetic field. The site of action of these particles, and whether cosmic particles actually caused the light flash phenomenon, were topics of conjecture in 1970, when this phenomenon was first reported. The causes for luminous phosphenes included ionizing radiation, mechanical pressure, electrical currents, magnetic fields, stimulation of the cerebral cortex, or pathological conditions of the Central Nervous System (CNS). In 1970, these phenomena were believed to be caused by ionizing heavy nuclei such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, which transversed the spacecraft and the body when outside the Earth’s magnetic shielding. The conjecture that the major mechanism for these visual phenomena was Cerenkov radiation was controversial.

Simulation studies were used to determine whether carbon, nitrogen, oxygen or other ions with equivalent ionizing characteristics could cause the same phenomena seen by astronauts. The exact mechanism in which the retina was stimulated by ionizing particles traveling at velocities below those necessary for emission of Cerenkov light was unclear. Experiments in which nitrogen ions were stopped in the cerebral cortex showed that the brain and optic nerve were not stimulated. Several mechanisms existed by which cosmic particles could produce visual sensations. They were: 1) electrical excitation resulting in near-ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the vicinity of the retina, 2) ionization by cosmic ray particles through the retina, 3) local ionization by the products from a nonelastic collision of the high-velocity proton and carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen, or 4) a shock wave phenomenon from charged particles passing through the tissue matrix.

The purpose of the experiment was to ascertain quantitatively the frequency, character, latitudinal dependence, and identity of cosmic particles that caused the light flash phenomenon during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. The ultimate objective was the assessment of radiation hazards of long-term Earth-orbiting and interplanetary missions.

APPROACH:
Special features of the experiment included measurement of the characteristics of the cosmic-particle environment in the vicinity of the eye, measurement of dark adaptation, and continuous onboard accumulation of the light flash observations from astronauts and particle detectors throughout one complete 90-minute orbit.

Two revolutions of the Earth were devoted to this experiment. During revolution 110, the silicon telescope-spectrometer was deployed to measure the trajectory, atomic charge Z, and velocity of cosmic particles with a stopping power of 10 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater. During revolution 111, two crewmembers donned special masks in order to become completely dark-adapted. After approximately 10 minutes, the two observers reached dark adaptation and made continuous observations of visual sensations. At each event, a push-button signal from the observing astronaut was recorded on the digital tape and the verbal description was recorded on the onboard tape recorder. The third crewmember operated the experiment control unit, which received data from silicon detectors and silver chloride AgCl(Cd) crystals. The crystals were used to register particle tracks in four sectors of orbit, those corresponding to the northern latitudes, equatorial latitudes, the SAA, and the southern latitudes. After the flight, the digital tapes, voice tapes, detector boxes, and masks were returned to the investigators.

The digital tapes were transcribed, and each event was related to the orbital position of the spacecraft. Events from the silicon detectors, pushbuttons and control unit were read from the digital tape by a specially constructed microprocessor. The push-button events and time marks were related to the verbal reports. The energy and trajectory information were inadequate because of a paucity of recorded events.

The AgCl(Cd) crystals were transported to the University of Frankfurt, Germany, where they had been produced and calibrated. The crystals were analyzed for the abundance of tracks produced by protons, alpha particles, or heavier ions.

The characteristics of the cosmic particle environment inside the spacecraft were determined by converting the spectrum and abundance of particles outside the spacecraft to the number of particles with various stopping powers and residual ranges, using aluminum shielding data for 512 sectors of solid angle around the spacecraft.

RESULTS:
There were 82 visual events reported by two crewmembers during a 90-minute orbit at an altitude of 225 kilometers (km).

The results of the light flash experiment indicated that the abundance of ions that caused the light flash phenomena was minimal between latitudes 30° N and 30° S. The frequency of light flashes between latitudes 30° N/50° N and 30° S/50° S was 25 times higher than noted in the equatorial latitudes. Increased flash phenomena were not reported through the SAA, as was expected after reviewing a Skylab 4 report of increased activity through the SAA. However, at the 225-km altitude of Apollo-Soyuz, the proton flux was much less than that of the Skylab 4 altitude of 443 kilometers. Also, the shielding of the Apollo spacecraft was greater than that of Skylab. This distribution of flashes was correlated with the distribution of cosmic particles with stopping power greater that 15 kilo-electron volts per micrometer in the eye.

The frequency of reported light flash events was strongly dependent on latitude. At the points of closest approach to the geomagnetic poles, the observed events occurred at one to two per minute; however no events occurred near the equator. These observations were consistent with the change in abundance of cosmic particles with latitude that was also noted during the Skylab 4 mission. The increased rate of visual events near the south geomagnetic pole can be explained by increased dark adaptation of the crewmembers. The observed event rate correlated with a cosmic particle abundance for heavy particles with energy losses > 5 kilo-electron volts per micrometer.

The AgCl(Cd) detector results suggested that 60 events of 15 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater would be observed during three-minute intervals in the northernmost portions of the orbit. The highest observed event rate at high latitudes was only 14 events per three minutes near the south magnetic pole. This rate implied a 23-percent efficiency for the detector. However, near the equator, where only a few events were observed, the detectors recorded the equivalent average of 73 events per four cm2/minute. An explanation of this inconsistency was that the fading time from the heavy ions was long relative to the orbit sectors. Thus, identification of the heavy particle environment in each sector could not be expected. Also, particles interacting in the crystals hours before the experiment might have been included in the event.

Assuming the complete retina target area of four cm2, the efficiency of visualizing the events was 36 percent for the northernmost sector. In the SAA sector, the detector efficiency diminished to eight percent. Thus, the AgCl(Cd) detector data did not correlate well with either the observed event rate or the calculated abundances.

There were no reports of high frequency throughout the SAA, as was expected from a previous Skylab 4 report of markedly increased flash activity. At the 225-km altitude of Apollo-Soyuz, the proton flux of particles was 14 times less than at the 443-km altitude of Skylab 4. Also, the aluminum shielding of the Apollo command module was much greater than that of Skylab.

The more favored hypothesis for the events seen in the SAA, particularly at higher altitudes, was the mechanism of proton nonelastic nuclear collision with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in tissues of the retina. This mechanism was similar to that proposed for neutron interactions, which also cause discrete flashes. If the average cross-section for interactions such as (p, p’, 3a) on carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen was assumed to be approximately 450 millibars in the proton energy range of 175 million electron volts (MeV) or less, only one event per three minutes would occur during Apollo-Soyuz altitude of 225 km. Under the reduced shielding conditions of Skylab 4, 51 times more protons would interact with the eye tissues of one observer, or 26 events might be observed during a three-minute interval. The average rate was 28 events per three minutes on Skylab 4. Thus, the nuclear collision hypothesis for the origin of light flashes in the SAA had some validity.

experiment_title: Quantitative Analysis of Selected Bone Parameters
experiment_description:
Objectives:

According to previous space flight research, differential effects are noted not only between weight bearing and non-weight bearing bones, but also are seen within different regions of the same bone. Therefore, one of the objectives of this study was to determine growth at the periosteum in different regions both in weight bearing (tibia) and non-weight bearing (rib) bones. Following both Cosmos 782 and 936, an arrest line was found in all flight rats and was both more distinct and more extensive than in controls. Another objective of this study was to obtain more precise measurements and further define this arrest line.

Approach:

The Merz grid was used to quantify the rate of periosteal bone formation in the tibial and humeral diaphysis, and to aid in quantification of the fractional area of trabecular bone and the fractional area of fat in the bone marrow of the proximal tibial metaphysis. Additional cross-sections of the tibial diaphysis were used for chemical characterization of the arrest lines.

Results:

The skeletal alterations induced by space flight were determined to be: a reduced rate of periosteal bone formation in the tibial and humeral diaphyses; and a decreased trabecular bone volume and an increased fat content of bone marrow in the proximal tibial metaphysis. Inhibition of periosteal bone formation in the humerus was not as dramatic as in the tibia, probably due to the lower rate of periosteal bone formation in the humerus relative to the tibia. An increased incidence of arrest lines was seen in flight animals. The staining properties of these arrest lines and the demonstration that osteocyte canaliculi rarely pass through them, suggest that they represent a cessation of bone matrix formation followed by reinitiation of bone formation at a later time. The rate of periosteal bone formation in the rib was not significantly decreased during space flight, possibly due to its non-weight bearing nature; periosteal bone formation rate in the rib may be too low to exhibit a significant change during a relatively short flight. Endosteal bone resorption was not affected markedly by space flight.

experiment_title: Bone Formation through Biomineralization and Bioengineering (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Earth has its own host of problems concerning bone repair. Although bone is unique in the body in its capacity to repair without scar formation, there are events due to trauma, surgery, degeneration or diseases that require surgical intervention and the gold standard for treatment is bone grafting. In the United States alone, over 6.3 million fractures occur annually, and of those 550,000 require bone grafting. Autografts are osteoconductive in that they provide a scaffold through which host bone can infiltrate, osteoinductive in that they induce stem cell proliferation or differentiation into osteogenic cells and osteogenic in that they contain osteogenic cells capable of forming bone. Therefore, autologous cancellous bone grafts continue to be the bone repair treatment of choice despite drawbacks such as donor site morbidity and the finite quantity available. Allograft bone does not suffer these drawbacks but will induce varying degrees of immunogenic responses from the host and has the potential for pathogen transfer. There remains an overwhelming need for a bone graft material that reproduces the four desired properties of the autograft: bio-resorbability, osteoconductivity, osteoinductivity and osteogenicity.

Understanding the signals that direct biomineralization is paramount for successful synthesis of self-assembled artificial bone and dentin biomimetic materials. Bone and seashell are biominerals shown to undergo both whole cell and single protein directed biomineralization. Furthermore, mammalian osteoblasts have been shown to produce shell-like structures in the presence of shells. Bone and nacre chips with no growth factors incubated with osteoblasts demonstrated biomineralization in the intervening gap: new bone near the bone chip and new nacre near the nacre chip. Understanding the concomitant changes in the microenvironment and their impact on osteoblast function and differentiation will enable the design of biomaterials that can create or direct specific functions. The hypothesis of this project is that water soluble proteins from seashell mother of pearl (nacre) cause osteoblasts to build bone and nacre. Nacre-initiated osteogenesis occurs in vivo, but not the production of new nacre. Despite its osteogenicity, nacre is not widely used as an implant material due to its limited dimensions and in vivo results that vary with preparation procedures. Regardless, nacre's presence changes the cellular microenvironment and causes functional changes in mammalian osteoblasts that direct them to build mollusk shell material. This behavior does not occur with the geological or synthetic mineral comprising nacre (aragonite), supporting our hypothesis that soluble factors are responsible. Nacre provides a model for engineering such factors into biomaterials.

The specific aims of this proposal were: 1) to determine the differences in gene expression of osteoblasts producing bone and osteoblasts producing nacre; 2) to determine the different proteins in the microenvironment of osteoblasts producing nacre vs. those producing bone; and 3) to pattern hydrogels with DMP1 and N40 (Dentin Matrix Protein 1, a hydroxyapatite nucleation protein in bone and dentin; and Nacre 40, an aragonite nucleation protein in nacre) to direct biomineralization in desired patterns.

APPROACH:
Twenty 8 week experiments were performed in which osteoblasts were cultured with chips of nacre from abalone or pinctada maxima, and/or chips of bone. Each experiment consisted of 6 cases: osteoblasts alone, bone-bone, bone-pinctada, bone-abalone, pinctada-pinctada, or abalone-pinctada. These experiments were observed weekly for mineralization and photographed. Media were collected and frozen for MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and SDS-PAGE. Three 8 week experiments were performed in which the conditions were repeated as above, except with the goal of patterning the mineralization in poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) hydrogels. PEGDA was polymerized with PEG-RGDS and with appropriate bone or nacre chips, and these were seeded with osteoblasts. Media were collected and frozen for MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and SDS-PAGE.

RESULTS:
Key findings:
1) When osteoblasts are in the presence of nacre, they are induced to form bone more rapidly than without nacre present.
2) When osteoblasts are in the presence of nacre, they will produce altered mineralization, including mineralization that looks like nacre and mineralization that looks like highly rectangular bone formation, rather than the typical spheroid bone nodules. Yet when osteoblasts form this altered mineralization due to the presence of nacre, the effect is spontaneous rather than predictable. Out of 100 experiments, the altered mineralization occurred only once.
3) In the 99 experiments where there was no altered mineralization, there was a protein at 868.368 Da. When there was altered mineralization, this protein peak was absent.
4) Nacre proteins can be patterned into hydrogels in a specific pattern.
5) Osteoblasts will lay down bone on patterned hydrogels in the pattern defined.

Impact of key findings:
The fact that the "nacregenesis" by osteoblasts was spontaneous rather than repeatable resulted in too few samples to perform gene analysis (specific aim 1). The protein identified at 868.368 Da that is absent when altered mineralization occurs may be a critical regulatory protein (specific aim 2). In future experiments, antibodies to this protein could be constructed to determine whether altered mineralization would occur with an antibody to the protein. This work was the first to ever demonstrate the capacity to pattern bone formation (specific aim 3). This is critical because many orthopedic biomaterials and agents can induce bone formation, but none have spatial control over where that bone will form. This is the first work that may provide such control, which is crucial in bone repair near the brain or spine.

experiment_title: Computational Model Prediction and Biological Validation using Simplified Mixed Field Exposures for the Development of a GCR Reference Field
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project addresses the need to develop and utilize mixed field irradiation protocols that approximately
represent the shielded tissue environment in space and that can be combined with single-beam studies to validate
and further improve cancer risk models. Extensive studies have been carried out on the induction of chromosomal
aberrations by low- and high- linear energy transfer (LET) radiation in human lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and
epithelial cells exposed in vitro. The results, which are consistent with computational modeling predictions,
establish chromosome aberration models as an LET-sensitive tool for predicting damage from single ion
exposures. However, there is a lack of data on chromosome aberrations induced by low dose rate chronic
exposure and mixed field beams such as those expected in space.

This investigation will define a simplified mixed field and make model predictions of the effects of dose rate,
mixed fields, and shielding on expected biological damage. Chromosome aberration studies at NASA’s Space
Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) will provide the biological validation needed to extend the computational models
over a broader range of experimental conditions leading up to the galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) simulator,
which will help to reduce uncertainties in radiation quality effects and dose-rate dependence in cancer risk
models. These models can then be used to answer some of the open questions regarding requirements for a full
GCR reference field, including particle type and number, energy, dose rate, and delivery order.
This study has the following specific aims:

1) Evaluate the effects of dose rate on biological damage using acute and chronic exposures with single ion
and mixed field beams to irradiate normal human fibroblasts and to measure chromosome aberrations.
2) Compare the external field versus local tissue field approach by measuring chromosome aberrations in
normal human fibroblasts using shielded and unshielded.

APPROACH:
hTERT-immortalized human normal skin fibroblast cells 82-6 were grown as monolayers at under typical culture
conditions supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), antibiotic antimycotic and L-glutamine. Cells were
irradiated in a confluent state. The premature chromosome condensation (PCC) technique will be used to collect
G2/M-phase chromosomes. After irradiation, fibroblast were allowed to repair for 16 hours, and then subcultured
at low density. After 10-18 hours of incubation, cells were arrested in mitosis by adding colcemid to a final
concentration of 0.1 ug/ml in the culture media and then cells were incubated for an additional six hours.

Approximately 30 minutes before collection, 50 nM of calyculin were added to the culture media to condense the
chromosomes in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.

Whole blood was collected from healthy volunteers and irradiated with accelerated heavy ions. Immediately after
exposure, whole blood cultures containing RPMI 1640 media supplemented with 20% calf serum, and 1% were
incubated at 37 degrees Celsius.

Chromosomes were analyzed using the 3-color whole-chromosome fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)
technique during the first cell division after irradiation, and chromosome aberrations will be identified as either
simple exchanges (translocations and dicentrics) or complex exchanges (involving at least two chromosomes and
at least three double strand breaks).

RESULTS:
Chromosome analysis of 150 samples (human fibroblasts, epithelial cells and lymphocytes) collected during the
first three years were completed. Chromosome samples collected from mouse bone marrow 16 months after
exposure to single or mixed beams were analyzed. Both 4 beam mix and 6 beam mixed exposure shows less than
additive effects in chromosome aberration frequency both in human fibroblasts and blood lymphocytes. In
addition, 4 beam mix and 6 beam mix showed similar frequency of chromosome aberrations.

experiment_title: Nutritional Modulation of Pancreatic Endocrine Function in Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ground-based and in-flight investigations illustrate changes in insulin, glucose, and amino acid metabolism in space flight. These observations may relate to altered pancreatic endocrine function, which is insufficient to meet the needs of microgravity-induced insulin resistance, and altered amino acid metabolism. The changes observed include decreased glucose tolerance, increased circulating insulin, and increased reliance upon glucose in muscles. The metabolic milieu resembles an insulin resistant syndrome, accompanied by a compensatory increase in pancreatic insulin secretion. However, the increase in insulin secretion is insufficient to ameliorate muscle atrophy. The increased insulin secretion is well correlated to muscle atrophy in space flight. The influence of these changes upon the loss of muscle mass and general endocrine metabolic state are not well established, however. Countermeasures which could modulate insulin and glucagon secretion in a compensatory manner to overcome insulin resistance and promote amino acid uptake by peripheral musculature might decrease muscle atrophy and reduce injury following re-adaptation to unit gravity.

It is hypothesized that human pancreatic islets of Langerhans have an increased requirement for amino acids in microgravity. It is also hypothesized, that supplementation with specific additional amino acids will augment, enhance and normalize insulin secretion, when space flight paradigm stressors known to decrease insulin secretion, are applied. The specific aims in this study are to:

1) assess the effect of a microgravity model cell culture on basal amino acid requirements and endocrine secretory function in human islets of Langerhans, and
2) determine human islet endocrine function while testing amino acid countermeasures in the microgravity model.

RESULTS:
It is anticipated that these studies will further refine our understanding of human pancreatic amino acid requirements and endocrine regulation: phenomenon which may be limiting to extended-duration space flight missions. These studies will test countermeasures to augment pancreatic endocrine function, while considering both insulin and glucagon production in a way that will involve supplementation of diet with additional amino acids. These measures are ultimately aimed at improving space flight induced muscle atrophy, and ameliorating current re-adaptation constraints.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Habitability Acceptability Questionnaire (SHAQ) Development and Validation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The primary objective of this study was to develop and validate a Space Flight Habitability and Acceptability Questionnaire (SHAQ), to assess the behavioral health and performance impacts of volume, layout, and other design features of vehicles and habitats for long-duration exploration missions and other operational environments. A secondary objective was to characterize the behavioral health and performance risks associated with reduced volume and the lack of individual crew quarters in missions of shorter duration (up to 45 days). SHAQ responses served as the primary outcome metric to study the behavioral health and performance effects of habitat area layouts.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Empirically assess the initial sensitivity, construct validity, divergent validity, and concurrent validity of SHAQ over eight 45-day Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) missions.
  2. Refine SHAQ based on the results of the HERA validation study.
  3. Draft a NASA Technical Report and/or manuscript for publication that (a) provides the results of SHAQ research and development efforts and (b) offers habitability recommendations for future deep space exploration missions.
  4. Author a SHAQ User Guide for public dissemination providing details on administration, scoring, and data management and interpretation.

APPROACH:

Investigators evaluated the quantitative responses to SHAQ as the primary measure. For concurrent validity, habitability-related items from the System Usability Scale (SUS) were administered during SHAQ sessions. Construct and divergent validity was assessed through measures of individual and team behavioral health and performance from complementary HERA investigations such as BHP Standard Measures in HERA. Operational acceptability was assessed during post-mission debrief interviews. Using a within-subjects repeated-measures design, the researchers collected SHAQ data from HERA 16 crewmembers in reference to the Sleep/Bedroom, Hygiene/Bathroom, Work/Office/Workshop, and Food Preparation/Kitchen/Galley habitat areas in the HERA operational environment, private hotel rooms, and individual home habitats.

RESULTS:

SHAQ has high construct validity, internal consistency and reliability, concurrent validity, and discriminant validity (e.g., significantly higher facilitation of group activities in HERA Work/Office/Workshop and Food Preparation/Kitchen/Galley areas versus. Hygiene/Bathroom and Sleep/Bedroom areas; significantly lower ratings of privacy, comfort, and convenience in HERA versus. hotel). The resulting data and validated SHAQ instrument can be used to inform recommendations and thresholds on habitat size, layout, and design options to support individual and team behavioral health and performance in operational environments.

experiment_title: Protecting Scientific Integrity through Disclosure of Conflicts of Interest
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project was designed to help institutions develop ethically justified conflict of interest policies which also are acceptable to the various stakeholders. It has three phases: (1) analyze currently existing policies; (2) survey the stakeholders (subjects, researchers, administrators, bioethicists); (3) with the help of a panel of experts, develop a set of recommended policies.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Key findings:
Investigators analyzed 235 existing institutional policies and discovered major differences in six sets of issues: (1) the conflicts to be disclosed; (2) the people whose conflicts must be disclosed; (3) to whom the conflicts must be disclosed; (4) when the conflicts must be disclosed; (5) how the conflicts should be managed; (6) what should be done when unreported conflicts are discovered. The conclusion of the paper was that the current regulatory schemes underdefine how institutions should deal with the reporting and management of conflicts of interest.

Investigators surveyed the attitudes of many stakeholders about these differences. These included 158 senior researchers, 297 senior research officials, 195 ethicists, 17 journal editors, 7 agency officials, and 253 research subjects. The major findings were that: (1) all respondents supported wider disclosure, especially to subjects; (2) researchers, while supportive, were less supportive than any of the other groups; (3) subjects and research officials were more supportive, but not as supportive as bioethicists; (4) there was much unclarity about the function of this wider disclosure, even among those supporting it.

In the development of the policy document, investigators used the results of the surveys from part two, a content analysis of a wide variety of proposed standards, and the advice of an expert panel. The main conclusion was that the current PHS regulations need to be supplemented in the following ways: (1) finder fees should be disclosed; (2) all equity interests, regardless of value, should be disclosed; (3) disclosures should be made for trusts controlled by investigators; (4) disclosures should be made to subjects; (5) management strategies going beyond disclosure should be employed when the risks to the subjects and the extent of the conflict are greater; (6) severe penalties are inappropriate except in cases of intentional or repeated failures to disclose.

experiment_title: Recovery of Musculoskeletal Quantity and Quality upon Multiple Microgravity Exposure
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As space missions become longer, it is apparent that long-term risks of multiple, or even single, exposures to microgravity on crew musculoskeletal health need to be defined and addressed. Even though the magnitude of the long-term deterioration in morphology and strength is largely unknown, it is clear that such risks will be heavily influenced by the genetic make-up of an individual. Investigators recently identified and characterized a genetically diverse mouse population that, similar to astronauts, includes a diverse range of responses to hindlimb unloading and reambulation. Using this population, investigators addressed the consequences of multiple exposures to simulated weightlessness on long-term quantity and quality of trabecular and cortical bone as well as muscle, and investigated how recovery periods between periods of weightlessness can be optimized. Changes in tissue morphology, density, and mechanical properties were assessed longitudinally in each genetically distinct mouse by in vivo micro CT and finite-element modeling, allowing for the identification of skeletal baseline indices that modulate changes in tissue morphology and strength during altered levels of loading. Detailed mechanical tests were performed at the endpoints to assess the long-term quality of the tissue. Together, the proposed studies provided a unique opportunity to establish the range of responses of genetically diverse individuals to multiple unloading and reambulation phases. Optimizing the length and distribution of recovery periods between disuse exposures may ultimately help to maintain long-term musculoskeletal morphology and strength.

Specific Aims:
1. To determine whether the total exposure time to weightlessness conditions or the number of repetitive exposures is the primary determinant of skeletal morphology and strength.
2. To determine the musculoskeletal consequences of altering the length and distribution of the recovery periods between multiple exposures to weightlessness.

APPROACH:
Ninety adult (16week) female F2 (BALB/cByJ x C3H/HeJ) mice were divided into three groups (n=30/group) – two groups subject to disuse and an age-matched ambulatory control. The experimental disuse groups were exposed to a total of 9 weeks of HLU and 42weeks of RA. In contrast to SA1, all disuse groups were subjected to three 3 week HLU cycles. However, the RA period following each HLU period was either 3 week or 9 week. The physical activity of each mouse was monitored using a three-dimensional activity monitoring cages for 24 hours at baseline, before and after each HLU cycle, and before sacrifice. Animals were single-housed and given free access to food and water during ambulation, HLU, and RA. Animals were weighed and randomly distributed into the different experimental groups. The well-characterized Morey-Holten hindlimb unloading model was used to simulate microgravity in all studies. All animals were sacrificed at 14months of age, about 6 months after the completion of the final HLU cycle. All mice have completed the HLU periods and are currently in the final RA period prior to sacrifice.

RESULTS:
Activity Patterns: Throughout the experimental duration, total activity counts were almost identical between the two experimental groups and not significantly from the control group.

Abdominal Fat: Consistent with changes observed in astronauts, the temporal changes in abdominal fat consistently exhibited a reduction during HLU and an increase during RA. The 9 week recovery period was sufficient to normalize the loss in adiposity experienced during the first unloading period. In contrast, the 3week recovery period was too short for fat levels to return to control levels. In this group, the decrease in fat volume during the second and third HLU period were much smaller than during the initial unloading phase, giving rise to almost identical total fat levels as in the 9 week recovery group at week 31 of age. Here, only total adipose tissue (TAT) volume is reported but the temporal patterns were indistinguishable from the changes in subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) volume.

Spinal Bone Density: The in vivo µCT scans of the abdomen facilitated the analysis of apparent volumetric density of the lumbar spine. In normally ambulating controls, bone density slightly increased until 40 weeks of age. In contrast, 3weeks of HLU greatly reduced bone density. Similar to changes in adipose tissue, the 9 week but not the 3week reambulation period restored bone density to control levels. In the 3week recovery group, the magnitude of bone’s response to unloading lessened with the second and third unloading period, rendering a spinal bone density by 31weeks of age that was similar to that of the 9 week recovery group in which the effect of the second unloading period was similar to the first one.

Distal Metaphysis of the Femur: Trabecular bone volume fraction (BV/TV) in normally ambulating control mice was relatively stable over the experimental period. As expected, both experimental groups experienced a large drop in bone volume fraction over the first unloading period. They also both started to recover some of these losses during the initial reambulation phase. The degree of recovery was almost three times as great in the 9 week recovery group than in the 3week recovery group. Three interesting phenomena were observed. First, the drop in bone volume fraction was greatly reduced during the second and third unloading phase in the 3week recovery group but not in the 9 week recovery group. Second, after the second unloading phase, the 3week group did not recover any bone during the subsequent reambulation phase. And thirdly, the total amount of bone loss was almost identical between the two experimental groups by week 31 and significantly different from normal controls. Bone’s susceptibility to unloading and reambulation was not only reflected by changes in the quantity of trabecular bone, but also by its micro-architecture. As revealed by changes in normally ambulating mice, aging caused a steady decrease in the number of trabeculae which concomitantly became thicker. Unloading caused significant decreases in these two architectural parameters. During reambulation, trabecular thickness increased while trabecular number continued to decrease. Similar to all other outcome measures presented above, the values for trabecular number were similar between the 3week and 9week recovery groups at the end of the second (third) HLU period (week 31 of age). Trabecular thickness was the only variable that was different between the 3week and 9 week recovery groups. Interestingly, including a 3week recovery period after unloading was more beneficial than the 9 week recovery period. Trabecular tissue mineral density, while sensitive to HLU and RA, only showed very small changes during the loss and regain or weightbearing.

Cortical bone was also sensitive to unloading, however to a much lesser degree. Even though the magnitude of the response of cortical bone was less, the patterns were remarkably similar to trabecular bone; at 31weeks of age, the total amount of cortical bone loss was almost identical between the two experimental groups.

Mechanical Modeling of the Femoral Distal Metaphysis: In vivo microcomputed tomography accurately tracks changes in trabcular and cortical bone quantity and micro-architecture but does not directly provide any data on bone’s mechanical stiffness. To this end, the investigators employed finite lement modeling (FEM) to convert the µCT scans into mechanical models. Qualitative preliminary results emphasize the devastating mechanical impact that alterations in trabecular and cortical bone morphology can have. In control bones, the relatively small, age-related decrease in bone volume did not significantly raise stress values between baseline and 31weeks of age. In contrast, a significant increase in Von Mises stresses were observed in bones that underwent consecutive unloading/reambulation cycles, regardless of whether the recovery period was 3 week or 9 week. Quantitatively, as a function of age, peak von Mises stresses closely tracked the changes in trabecular bone volume fraction.

Correlations between Activity Patterns and Changes in Morphologic Indices: One of the motivations for expanding the scope of this grant proposal and to add activity monitoring was to address the question whether the differential capability of individual mice to recover tissue during reambulation is related to their level of activity. Investigators found that the amount of activity only plays a minor role in explaining the differences in regaining tissue after unloading (as reflected by R2 values that are all below 0.3).

experiment_title: Evaluation of Space Radiation-induced Myocardial and BM-derived EPC Damage and Assessment of Associated Long-term Degenerative Cardiovascular Risks
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The main objectives of this study were to determine space radiation-dependent short- and long-term degenerative cardiovascular (CV) risks on the molecular, cellular, and tissue levels in the heart as the primary organ and bone marrow (BM)-derived endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) first, as a primary space radiation target and second, as a possible significant contributor to degenerative CV risks, later on in life. The central hypothesis is that low-dose space radiation-induced DNA damage repair is inefficient in BM-derived EPC and this may lead to increased mutagenesis with subsequent long-term loss of endothelial function of BM-derived EPCs. This may then pose significant degenerative CV risk on physiologic homeostasis in the aging heart and on the regeneration and neovascularization processes in the heart under pathologic conditions such as acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

This study addressed two high-priority research topics of this specific solicitation and NASA research interests for degenerative risks to the heart -- (1) development of murine models to estimate risks for degenerative heart diseases; (2) determine the progression rates and latency periods for space radiation-related degenerative CV risks as a function of radiation type (proton versus heavy ion), exposure frequency (single versus fractionated), age, and age plus adverse CV event.

APPROACH:
Comparisons were made between two types of low-dose radiation - proton versus iron and single versus fractionated exposures. In short-term in vitro studies (minutes, hours, and up to 30 days after exposure) investigators evaluated ex-vivo expanded EPCs and cardiomyocytes DNA damage and repair as well as radiation-induced bystander effects (irradiated cells emit signals to "un-hit" cells), angiogenic gene expression in EPCs. In short-term in vivo studies in the heart investigators evaluated acute damage (inflammation and cell death), DNA damage, and repair kinetics. In the long-term studies (3, 6, 9, and 12 months after exposure) investigators evaluated oxidative stress and antioxidant defense in BM-derived EPCs, alterations in several EPC endothelial functions, number of circulating peripheral blood EPCs, and cardiomyocyte contractility. In the last part of the studies investigators assessed CV risks as a result of low-dose radiation plus aging and CV risks under pathological condition -- radiation plus aging plus adverse CV event (i.e., AMI). Here they evaluated post-AMI survival, alterations in cardiac physiology (echocardiography), infarct size, inflammation, cardiac regeneration, neovascularization, and mobilization of EPCs from BM.

SUB-PROJECT 1:
Title: Delayed Cardiomyocyte Response to Total Body Heavy Ion Particle Radiation Exposure Identification of Regulatory Gene Networks. Background: Understanding the effects of low dose ionizing radiation (IR) for ions of high atomic number (Z) and energy (HZE) on cardiovascular (CV) tissue is important for characterizing the risk of human space exploration. Cardiomyocytes (CM) are the basic contractile cells within the heart, whose contractile function directly influences the pathogenesis of heart disease. Understanding of complex processes that take place in CMs after insults caused by IR, such as proton and HZE particles, is paramount to our understanding of CV system function during and after exploration-type space missions.

Methodology: Adult (8-9 months old) male C57Bl/6NT mice were exposed to single full-body IR of proton (90 cGy, 1 GeV) or 56Fe, iron particles (15 cGy, 1 GeV/nucleon); 0.15 Gy was delivered using 1 GeV/nucleon iron ions (linear energy transfer-LET ~151 keV per µm) or 0.9 Gy at 1 GeV energy protons (LET ~0.22 keV per µm). Primary left ventricular (LV) CMs were isolated using standard preparation protocol that includes cannulation of the aorta and collagenase digestion followed by a Ca2+ gradient selection, yielding >90% of Ca2+ tolerant CMs. Investigators looked at molecular responses using transcriptome profiling in isolated LV murine CMs to 1H- and 56Fe-IR at 1, 3, 7, 14, and 28 days post-IR using Ingenuity IPA and NIH DAVID programs.

Main Findings: Unsupervised clustering analysis of gene expression segregated samples according to the IR response, and time after exposure with iron IR showing the greatest level of gene modulation. Little differential transcript modulation was seen in response to whole body proton IR. There were two notable types of upstream regulators – cytokines and transcriptional regulators. Individual transcription factors were inferred to be active at 1, 3, 7, 14, and 28 days after exposure. The activation of several developmental transcription factors, such as TBX5, GATA-4, MEF2C two weeks after 56Fe-IR, strongly suggest initiation of cardio-protective and regeneration responses in 56Fe-IR hearts. To identify time independent changes in biological pathways, investigators also analyzed differences between iron and proton arrays. The top five significant pathways identified were Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s, oxidative phosphorylation, cardiac muscle contraction, and Huntington’s disease, followed by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy. These top five significant pathways shared the majority of transcripts that were involved in mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation function illustrating the inter-relationship between the same oxidative phosphorylation genes that play a role in neurodegenerative and cardiovascular disorders/diseases.

Summary: These data suggest that the molecular response to 15 cGy, 1 GeV/n of iron is unique and shows long-lasting gene expression in cardiomyocytes, up to 28 days after exposure. In addition, proteins involved in signal transduction and transcriptional activation via DNA binding play a role in the response to HZE particles. This study may have implications for NASA’s efforts to develop more accurate heart risk estimates for astronaut safety via identification of specific to HZE IR molecular markers as well as for patients receiving conventional and particle radiotherapy.

SUB-PROJECT 2:
Title: Different Sequence of Fractionated Proton and Single Low Dose Iron Radiation Induce Divergent Biological Responses in the Heart. Background: Astronauts are exposed to IR composed of a spectrum of low-fluence protons (1H) and high charge and energy (HZE) nuclei iron (i.e., 56Fe). During GCR each cell in an astronaut’s body is traversed by a 1H about every three days and HZE nuclei about every few months. Hence, the traversal sequence of cells with an ion in space could be random. Therefore, a scenario that a cell in human body may be hit first with several 1H particles then with HZE or an HZE then several 1H should be equally probable. The effect of cosmic IR during and after space flights on cardiovascular (CV) system is unknown.

Methodology: Investigators evaluated the effect of low-dose fractioned and sequential IR dose regimens in 8-9 month old C57BL/6NT male mice in the following groups: Group 1- control; Group 2 - 1H 17 cGy once every 2 days for a total of 3 doses (fractionated proton); Group 3 – Fractionated 1H 17 cGy once every 2 days for a total of 3 doses followed by a single dose of 56Fe 15 cGy 2 days after the last dose of proton; Group 4 – a single dose of 56Fe 15 cGy/followed by fractionated 1H 17 cGy once every 2 days for a total of 3 doses 2 days after a single 56Fe-IR. The energy for both ions was 1 GeV. Cardiac function was assessed by echocardiography and hemodynamic measurements. To determine the effect of fractionated/sequential regimens of 1H and 56Fe-IR on recovery after an ischemic event, acute myocardial infarct (AMI) was induced by ligation of left anterior descending coronary artery 1 and 3 months post-IR.

Main Findings: In IR + Aging group, at 1 and 3 months post-IR, fractionated 1H-IR alone or fractionated 1H-IR followed by a single 56Fe-IR did not induce negative effect on post-IR mice survival and cardiac function, and cardiac fibrosis was decreased in mice of these IR groups. However, when a single 56Fe-IR was followed by a fractionated 1H-IR, there were several negative and CV degenerative developments. In this group post-IR survival was decreased by >20% at 1 and 3 months, left ventricular (LV) end diastolic pressure (LVEDP) was increased at 3 months, and LV maximum pressure change (dP/dtmax) was decreased at 1 month; both of which are indicative of negative hemodynamic developments in the heart of the surviving fraction of mice in 56Fe-IR/1H+1H+1H radiation regimen - Group 4.

In IR + Aging + AMI group, fractionated 1H-IR alone or 56Fe-IR followed by fractionated 1H-IR did not have significant negative effect on post-AMI survival and cardiac function at 1 month post-IR. However, when fractionated 1H-IR was followed by a single 56Fe-IR, there were several negative developments. In this group, at 1 month, there was a 24% decrease in post-AMI survival and a substantial increase in post-AMI cardiac fibrosis. These findings are indicative of significant negative effects for post-AMI recovery after 1H+1H+1H/56Fe-IR regimen in the surviving fraction of mice in Group 3.

Summary: Taken together, the findings in mixed ion fractionated/sequential IR groups strongly suggest dramatically different biological responses due to diverse sequence and fractionation of 1H versus a single 56Fe-IR. These findings emphasize the necessity to determine underlying molecular mechanisms responsible for this significant mix ion fractionation and sequence-dependent divergent responses in the heart during aging and in case of a possible ischemic cardiovascular event.

SUB-PROJECT 3:
Title: Particle Radiation Induced Long-lasting Cyclical Decreases in the Number of Bone Marrow Pregenitor Cells is Associated with Upregulation of Several Pluripotent Stem Cell Markers Over Ten Months Post-IR. Background: Radiation-induced decreases in the number of bone marrow (BM)-derived endothelial progenitor cell (BM-EPCs) and their lineage precursors which include Early- and Late-Multi-Potent Progenitor cells (E-MPPs and L-MPPs) could contribute to the pathogenesis of ischemic and vascular diseases. Investigators examined the effect of full-body single dose of proton (1H) at 0.5 Gy, 1 GeV, and 0.15 Gy, 1 GeV/nucleon of iron (56Fe) ionizing radiation (IR) on survival of multipotent progenitor cell populations. The survival of E-MPPs and L-MPPs in the BM after particle IR in C57BL/6NT mice were determined at 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 28, and 40 weeks post-IR.

Methodology: Total BM-derived mononuclear cells were triple-stained with FITC-labeled RAM34 antibody (that consists of CD34, c-kit, and Sca1 antibodies), PE-Cy7-AC133, and PE-hematopoietic lineage cocktail, then sorted by Fluorescence Associated Cell Sorting (FACS) analysis for Early-MPPs and Late-MPPs.

Main Findings: Compared to control mice, 1H-IR increased the number of both E-MPPs (665%) and L-MPPs (203%) by 1 week, whereas 56Fe-IR decreased E-MPP (74%) and L-MPPs (65%) at 1 week post-IR, suggesting an initial stimulation by 1H and “a hefty” damage by 56Fe in the BM milieu. In 56Fe-IR mice, E-MPPs were partially recovered between 4 and 12 weeks but declined again below ~55-70% of control levels between 28-40 weeks. In 1H-IR mice, E-MPPs were close to control levels up to 4 weeks, but declined >50% at 8 and 28 weeks. These long-lasting cyclical effects on the number of BM-derived E-MPPs and L-MPPs suggest the presence of prolonged non-targeted effects in BM milieu. Total RNA isolated from L-MMP cell pellets up to 10 months post-IR to determine the expression of three pluripotent stem cell markers - Sox-2, Nanog and Oct-4. Our targeted gene expression results reveal long-lasting and cyclical (2 and 10 months) upregulation of these Sox-2, Nanog and Oct-4 in Late-MPPs. Without a significant preconceived notion, the decrease in the number of Early- and L-MPPs associated with upregulation of three pluripotent stem cell factors in BM may indicate a significant depletion/loss of stem and progenitor cells in the BM and an activation of endogenous re-programing signaling. The specific mechanism(s) of this phenomenon is not known.

Summary: These long-lasting and cyclical effects of IR on the BM E-MPPs and L-MPPs after a single 1H or 56Fe IR dose suggest the presence of prolonged and non-targeted effects in BM milieu, particularly in cells that were not traversed by IR directly. The function of the surviving fraction of E-MPPs and L-MPPs and, more importantly, their impact on cardiac homeostasis, cardiac repair, and regeneration, remain unknown. These findings warrant inquiry into the mechanistic studies of the stem cell functions such as, pluripotency and self-renewal, in surviving fraction of BM progenitor cell populations. In addition, future longitudinal studies are necessary to determine whether BM progenitor cell populations may be affected in astronauts after deep space missions as well as after low dose terrestrial IR exposure, such as full body CT and PET scans.

SUB-PROJECT 4:
Title: Ionizing Particle Radiation Induce Cyclical Increase in Bone Marrow-derived Endothelial Progenitor Cell Apoptosis. Background: Long-lasting radiation (IR)-induced chromosomal instability has been demonstrated in the bone-marrow (BM) after full body IR with either X-rays or neutrons. It has been shown that after space flights, the numbers of myeloid and lymphoid BM-derived stem and progenitor cells are reduced to just one-half of their normal levels. This result suggests that endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) may be similarly reduced in the bone marrow milieu. During future exploration-type space missions, astronauts will be exposed to space IR composed of a spectrum of low-fluence protons (1H) and high charge and energy (HZE) nuclei (e.g., 56Fe) for extended time. BM-derived EPCs are critical to endothelial cell (EC) maintenance and repair. The data on the effects of low-dose ionizing space-type particle IR on survival and proliferation of BM-EPCs are limited.

Methodology: Investigators studied the effects of low dose proton and 56Fe (iron) IR on BM-EPCs in mice and cultured BM-derived EPCs. Adult (8-9 months old) male C57Bl/6NT mice were exposed to a single full-body IR of proton (90 cGy, 1 GeV) or 56Fe particles (15 cGy, 1 GeV/nucleon). Mononuclear fraction of BM cells (MNCs) were isolated from full-body IR mice at 2, 5, 24 hours and 7, 14, and 28 days. The ex-vivo expanded BM-EPCs were obtained by culturing the BM-MNCs for 72 hours in EPC selective culture media. After 72 hours in culture they assessed apoptosis and proliferation of BM-derived EPCs. In the second part of the study, BM-EPCs were obtained from non-irradiated (non-IR) mice and subjected to IR. After 2, 5, and 24 hours, IR conditioned medium (IR-CM) was collected and transferred to non-IR BM-EPCs to test the non-targeted effects in the naïve non-irradiated BM-EPCs. Twenty four hours after incubation with non-IR, control and IR-CM media, the formation and decay of DNA double strand breaks were assessed by p-H2AX staining. The production and accumulation of inflammatory cytokines was measured by enzyme-linked immunesorbent assay (ELISA).

Main Findings: The results showed that there was a cyclical (early 2-5 hour and delayed 28 days) increase in BM-EPC apoptosis and decreased proliferation after a single, full body, low dose 1H- or 56Fe-IR in mice. In both 1H- and 56Fe IR-CM treated naïve BM-EPCs, the number of p-H2AX foci was significantly increased between 2-24 hours after co-culture, which was associated with 2-15-fold increases in the concentration of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1 alpha, IL-1 beta, MCP-1, and MIP-1 alpha, in IR conditioned media.

Summary: The data indicate that early, within hours, increase in BM-EPC apoptosis may be the effect of direct IR exposure, whereas late increase in apoptosis and decrease in proliferation could be a result of non-targeted effects in the cells that were not traversed by IR directly. Further, identifying the role of specific cytokines responsible for IR-induced non-targeted effects in BM milieu may allow development of mitigating factors to reduced long-term effects of ionizing particle IR.
