experiment_title: Microgravity Changes in Heart Structure and Cyclic-AMP Metabolism
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Physiological changes which are the consequence of altered gravity conditions were studied in order to evaluate their effect on manned travel in space. Cardiac deconditioning has been found in astronauts, in humans after prolonged bed rest, in monkeys exposed to hypokinesia, and rodents exposed to increased gravity or weightlessness. Altered gravity has been shown to induce morphologically observable changes associated with myocardial degeneration (accumulation of lipid droplets, increased glycogen storage, alterations in microtubule distribution). In this experiment, cardiac ultrastructure and cyclic AMP metabolism were studied in tissues of space-flown rats.

Approach:

Tissues were post-fixed and processed for electron microscopy. Adenylate cyclase activities were monitored by following the conversion of 3H-ATP to 3H-cAMP, and cAMP was removed by column chromatography. Low Km and high Km cAMP-PDE activities were determined, and the reaction product (3H-5 AMP) was elutriated from a polyacrylamide boronate affinity gel chromatographic column. cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity was measured as the incorporation of P-ATP into protein. Assays were carried out with protamine as the exogenous phosphoacceptor protein and in either the absence or presence of exogenous (10-6M) cAMP, as was phosphorylation of endogenous substrate proteins without the addition of protamine. Compartmental subunits distribution of regulatory cA-PK subunits was determined using a photoaffinity labeling method with [32P]-8- azido cyclic AMP, and type I and type II cA-PK were separated on SDS-gradient gels and identified by autoradiography of Western blots.

Results:

Changes in ultrastructure and biochemistry were found in the heart tissue of flown rats. An accumulation of lipid droplets and changes in glycogen deposits and microtubules were observed at the electron microscope level as a result of space flight. Adenylate cyclase and low Km PDE activities were not altered, but a decrease in high Km phosphodiesterase was seen in flight homogenates. Protein kinase activity decreased, while activity ratios increased, indicating that the holoenzyme was more extensively dissociated and inactivated during space flight. Together with other studies of responses to catecholamines, results show that ß-adrenergic responses were affected during space flight. While events at the cell surface level were within the range of homeostatic control, intracellular signal processing of the receptor interactions was modified. Results suggest that heart muscle energy metabolism may be altered in microgravity.

experiment_title: The Evaluation and Selection of Catalyst to Mineralize Organic Impurities in Reclaimed Water
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
New technologies in wastewater reclamation are beneficial to all water purification processes in any environment.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Current results are most promising. Testing began on September 21, 2003. The synthetic carbon substrate catalyst developed by Environmental Life Support Technologies (ELS) is effectively oxidizing International Space Station (ISS) ersatz feed to TOC levels less that analyzer detection limits (less than 50 ppb TOC) at 90 degrees C. Feed ersatz was 11 ppm TOC at 25 ml/min (43 minutes residence time). The ELS catalyst is a ‘synthetic carbon’ based catalyst loaded with five percent Platinum and Ruthenium. The substrate is 30 mesh resin bead that has been ‘fired’ at a high temperature. ELS technologies is the manufacturer and previous testing in a 10cc reactor by Cliff Jolly at ELS labs has shown good activity and lifetime. JSC’s new alloy20 reactors are 1.9 liters so flow ranges will hopefully be widespread enough for good kinetic data.

The Engelhard catalyst evaluation was promising but loss of activity was observed after a few weeks of testing. Early data indicates the catalyst ESCAT 226 will oxidize a 10 ppm TOC Ersatz feed stream to levels below the 500ppb standard using air with temperatures ranging from 95 C to 130 C, but catalyst slowly becomes leass active with time until the target TOC cannot be reached. This conclusion was based on repetitive runs with identical test conditions. Inspection of the catalyst beads showed erosion of the alumina beads and therefore loss of Platinum. Catalyst surface scans show a high load of iron coming off the reactor walls onto the catalyst. New reactors were fabricated from alloy20 for future runs.

The second catalyst tested showed no visible degradation probably due to its monolithic design. The ceramic honeycomb cylinders are coated with platinum but the surface area and adsorption characteristics are not as high as a metal oxide bead. Best TOC reduction observed was 65 percent at minimum flow and 130 degrees C on feeds ranging from 2 ppm to 20 ppm TOC.

experiment_title: Effects of Low Dose Radiation and Radiation Countermeasures on Infection by Spaceflight Analogue Cultured Salmonella using 3-D Biomimetic Human Tissue Models
experiment_description:
Objectives
Microgravity and radiation are major biological stressors associated with the spaceflight environment. Their cumulative impact on host-pathogen interactions and infectious disease risks are rarely considered. Since the cumulative effects of these stressors during spaceflight may result in unexpected negative impacts on crew health and performance that neither condition alone would predict, the ability to develop effective countermeasures is limited. Spaceflight and spaceflight analog culture have shown increased virulence and pathogenesis-related characteristics of the foodborne pathogen, Salmonella Typhimurium. S. Typhimurium is responsible for disqualification of food destined for the International Space Station and has been found aboard NASA spacecraft. Spaceflight-analogue cultures of S. Typhimurium have been shown to possess increased ability to infect 3-D biomimetic human intestinal tissue models.
S. Typhimurium is a major cause of foodborne illness causing intestinal inflammation and diarrhea. It was selected as the model microorganism for this study due to its response to culture in both spaceflight and Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV) spaceflight analog environments and due it’s potential for causing disease in flight, eliciting an intense inflammatory response during infection of human cells. The primary objective of this proposal is to evaluate the possibility that low dose radiation will exacerbate the already increased bacterial pathogenicity of S. Typhimurium observed following spaceflight analog culture. The impact of a radiation countermeasure to provide protection against both radiation and pathogen-induced tissue damage and inflammation will also be determined in this study. This study will address the following aims:
1. Characterize the impact of spaceflight- analogue culture on the ability of S. Typhimurium to infect 3-D biomimetic intestinal tissue models before and after exposure to low dose radiation.
2. Evaluate the ability of the radioprotective compound, EC-18, to protect 3-D intestinal models from low dose radiation, S. Typhimurium infection, and the cumulative impact of these stressors. Microbial responses to spaceflight and spaceflight analog culture have been profiled for decades and there is extensive evidence from this collective body of work to suggest that bacterial pathogens are ‘’hardwired’’ to respond to the presence (or absence) of environmental stimuli under these conditions.

Approach
This study will employ the use of the NASA Rotating Wall Vessel which is a rotating bioreactor in which cells are maintained in suspension in a gentle fluid orbit, creating a sustained low fluid shear and low turbulence environment for cell growth. The bioreactor will be used as a spaceflight analog culture system for S.Typhimurium and will also be used to establish 3-D biomimetic intestinal tissue models. All studies will be done in triplicate. Virulent S. Typhimurium strain will grown in Lennox Broth (LB) as shaking overnight cultures at 37°C and then inoculated into fresh LB media, which will be grown in RWV at 37°C until late log phase under Low Shear Modeled Microgravity (LSMMG) and control orientations. 3-D cultures will be harvested from the RWV for use at 15-16 days. For all the studies, 3D models will be seeded evenly into multi-well plates for treatment. EC-18 will be provided as its active ingredient in a lipid-based liquid. Adherence, invasion and intracellular survival assays will be performed using a standard gentamicin exclusion assay. Percent colonization will be calculated by normalizing Colony Forming Units at each time point to initial bacterial inoculum for LSMMG and control cultures. Samples will be processed and read on a Bio-Plex 200.

Results

The PI team observed little-to-no differences in viability of the 3D co-culture model following exposure to X-ray radiation up to 2 Gy. These findings differ from earlier observations using the same models with exposure to gamma irradiation, which showed signs of significant cell damage.
Infection of the models using S. Typhimurium cultured under LSMMG and control orientations in the absence of X-ray radiation were significantly different, matching the previous findings showing that LSMMG-cultured S. Typhimurium invaded better than the 1xg cultures. Infection of the models following low dose radiation (0.1, 0.5 Gy) did not alter this trend significantly. EC-18 treatments under these conditions also did not show significant differences.
Overall, based on prior findings using gamma irradiation, the PI team believes that if these studies were repeated with a different type of radiation, there would likely be more of an impact to the viability of colonization phenotypes.

experiment_title: A Simple and Compact Countermeasure for Maintenance and Enhancement of Neuromuscular Control During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Sensorimotor control is vital for successful execution of mission-critical tasks in microgravity, and on planetary and lunar surfaces. However, exposure to microgravity results in disruptions in sensorimotor, cardiovascular, and neuromuscular systems that can present as balance and gait disturbances, cardiovascular deconditioning, and loss of muscle mass, muscle coordination, and strength. Astronauts regularly participate in strength and conditioning programs to mitigate cardiovascular and strength decrements associated with space flight; however, recent research suggests sensorimotor-based countermeasures may be necessary to maintain functional performance following spaceflight. Neuromuscular control enables dynamic interactions with the environment via fast subcortical responses.
Through this study, the researchers seek to examine the patented Leg Dexterity System (the leg version of the Valero Dexterity Test™ from Neuromuscular Dynamics, LLC) to enhance neuromuscular control and complement and amplify the efficacy of exercise as a countermeasure to neuromuscular performance decrements during and after space flight.
This experiment will address two hypotheses:
(1) Supplementing an eight-week strength and conditioning regimen with the Leg Dexterity System increases dynamic stabilization and neuromuscular control abilities.
(2) Despite the sex differences in dexterity levels reported in past research, there will be no sex difference in the amount of improvement in dynamic stabilization and neuromuscular control abilities.

APPROACH:
This study will recruit 30 subjects (15 males, 15 females) between 40-60 years of age to complete eight consecutive weeks of small group circuit training classes (three one-hour duration classes per week for 24 total sessions). Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two cohorts: with Leg Dexterity System training and without Leg Dexterity System training. Subjects enrolled in the study will participate in small group circuit training classes using high-intensity aerobics to target strength building and muscular and cardiovascular endurance.
Participants undergoing Leg Dexterity System training will apply compression force to a platform affixed to a spring on a single-axis force sensor while partially seated on a bicycle saddle and holding on to handlebars. While in this position, participants will be instructed to support their weight equally using the bicycle saddle and nontest limb in order to unload the test leg. A tablet will provide real-time visual feedback of the compression force to encourage a steady maximal sustained compression for 10 seconds. Support for the hypotheses of this study will be quantified by improvements in dynamic and static stability via pre- and post-training outcome measures, including a single limb balance test, single limb hop and balance test, and phase portrait analysis.

RESULTS:
The results of this ground experiment will inform the utility of the simple and compact Leg Dexterity System to mitigate neuromuscular control decrements and justify space flight analog studies to further refine the development of this sensorimotor-based countermeasure.

experiment_title: Microgravitational Effects on Chromosome Behavior (Yeast)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The principal objectives of this flight experiment were to determine the effects of the space-flight environment on cell yield, survival and ability to undergo meiosis, and to monitor mitotic chromosome segregation and recombination in the space-flight environment. Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a model unicellular eukaryote, was used in the experiment. Two types of yeast cultures were flown: mitotic cell cultures, in which yeast cell populations are established by budding and mitosis, and meiotic cell cultures, in which yeast cells undergo meiosis and ascospore formation. The mitotic cell cultures are microbial analogs of human somatic mitotic cell division while the meiotic cell cultures are microbial analogs of human meiosis and gamete formation.

APPROACH:
Two yeast diploid hybrids were prepared. STS42-1 is a Rec+, Rad+, Spo+ strain capable of mitosis or meiosis at both 22 and 36 degrees C. STS42-2 is a temperature conditional strain that exhibits Rec+, Rad+, Spo+ at 22 degrees, but Rec-, Rad-, and Spo- at 36 degrees and grows mitotically at either temperature. Two cultures of each strain were incubated during flight under four conditions: in microgravity at 22 degrees, in a 1-g centrifuge at 22 degrees, in microgravity at 36 degrees, and in a 1-g centrifuge at 36 degrees. The ground cultures were incubated under similar conditions, static at 22 degrees, in a 1-g centrifuge at 22 degrees, static at 36 degrees, and in a 1 g centrifuge at 36 degrees. All cell cultures were analyzed with respect to 1) the total number of cells and buds produced during growth, 2) the percent survival of the cells following plating on nutrient synthetic complete growth medium, 3) frequencies of the cells having phenotypes indicative of mitotic gene conversion, intergenic recombination, and/or mitotic chromosome segregation anomalies, and 4) presence of cells that entered meiosis during the stationary phase following cessation of mitotic cell division.

RESULTS:
There was no marked enhancement or reduction in total cell yield due to microgravity conditions. The incubation temperature appears to be the principle factor in the total cell yield; cell densities of cultures incubated at 22 degrees were greater by a factor of 2 or less than the densities of those incubated at 36 degrees. The average survival of the STS42-1 flight culture cells ranged from 51 percent to 75 percent, with the 22 degree cultures being the highest. The average survival rate of the STS42-2 flight cell cultures ranged from 24 percent to 72 percent with the 22 degree cultures being the highest. The most striking discovery was the higher than expected recovery of Rec- intergenic mitotic recombinants from the 36 degree flight cultures. Rec- is recombinant deficient at 36 degrees in ground controls. STS42-2 also preserved its Rec- phenotype during flight at 36 degrees with respect to resistant segregants due to gene conversion, events that result in mitotic segregants and failure to initiate meiosis. One hypothesis for this behavior is a difference in the nature of the lesion that initiates mitotic recombination in flight as opposed to ground.

experiment_title: Functional Immune Alterations, Latent Herpesvirus Reactivation, Physiological Stress and Clinical Incidence Onboard the International Space Station
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Some aspects of adaptive cellular immunity have been characterized during space flight, while many other areas of immunity (humoral, innate, cell specific functional, etc.) have not. The objective of this project is to characterize multiple diverse facets of immunoregulation during long-duration space flight. Investigators hypothesize that while aspects of adaptive immune function are depressed during space flight, aspects of humoral or innate immune function may be unaltered or even sensitized. This would explain the observed reactivation of latent herpesviruses in astronauts, and also the elevated incidence of skin rashes and hypersensitivity reactions during International Space Station (ISS) missions. If the hypothesis is validated, it would be an important consideration for any future immunology countermeasures. For example, one would not give an immune ‘booster’ to address T cell function in a crewmember if it might potentially worsen on-orbit skin rashes or allergy symptoms. Investigators further hypothesize that there is a widely disparate post-landing recovery for various aspects of immune dysregulation following flight. Previous data have demonstrated that ISS astronauts maintain shedding of latent herpesviruses at least to R+30. This study will fully characterize all relevant immune dysregulation through a post-mission recovery.
The specific scientific aims are as follows:
  1. Longitudinally examine the effect of space flight on previously uninvestigated aspects of immunobiology including leukocyte distribution and various aspects of innate cellular function. Several previously validated assays of adaptive cellular distribution and function will be examined concurrently to correlate both innate and adaptive immune dysregulation within crewmembers.
  2. Determine the effect of space flight on various soluble markers of in-vivo immune-physiological status, including plasma, salivary and urinary markers of stress, inflammation, cytokine profiles, antimicrobial activity, and latent viral reactivation. Several solicited parameters are also planned to augment this specific aim, including proteomics and/or genomics.
  3. Correlate findings of immune status with astronaut environmental, human, and stress factors such as sleep/wake data, crew work schedules, surveys of in-flight symptomology and/or medication use (voluntary), vehicle docking/undocking, extravehicular activity (EVA), etc. This correlative work should help to inform NASA’s scientific and operational communities about the influence of spaceflight-specific environmental factors on immunity, factors which may potentially be modulated in accordance with countermeasures development.
APPROACH:
The primary purpose of the study is to determine both acute and chronic alterations in crewmember immunobiology (both innate and adaptive parameters) in conjunction with relevant parameters from other disciplines (nutritional, radiation, virology, host-pathogen, stress, etc.). Parameters will be examined longitudinally in astronauts before, during, and following space flight. Postflight assessments will be extended to determine the time course for full recovery of any dysregulated parameters

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: 3D Tissue Analogues For The Study Of Varicella-Zoster Virulence And Infectivity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV), present in 93% of the population here on Earth, remains largely inactive the human body after the initial immune response at normal gravity (1G). When a VZV infected human leaves 1G for space flight, the normally inactive virus begins to re-express, presenting a potential health and safety problem. VZV may assume increased virulence and/or live virus numbers in microgravity. This could, in combination with a general diminished immune competency, lead to heighten states of infection for in flight astronaut populations and present a risk for associates of returning crews. This study will demonstrate the sensitivity of the model and provide an operational deliverable in the form of a reliable test for live quantifiable virus. Specific goals of this study were to establish and validate Normal Human Neural Progenitor (NHNP) as viable target for VZV infection, establish 3-D NHNP as a ground-based analog for study of VZV in modeled microgravity, and use 3-D NHNP as an operational analog for VZV in microgravity.

APPROACH:
As samples of activated VZV from astronauts are difficult to obtain and work with, this study utilized a laboratory strain of VZV, appropriate ground patient samples, 3-D recapitulated lung (MeWo) and neural (NHNP) tissue analogs that mimic aspects of the human physiology. This allowed a further exploration of the native and in-flight virus replication and virulence, while also validating the 3-D Neural Model. Currently laboratory work with VZV is done with 2-D malignant melanoma lung fibroblast cells (MeWo). This experiment developed 3-D Normal Human Neural Progenitor (NHNP) model with VZV and compare the results to the 2-D MeWo model. Uninfected and infected 2-D MeWo cells were expanded and conditioned in a media designed to support the rigorous nutritional needs of 3-D cultures. This media is called GTSF2. Thereafter all MeWo and NHNP cells, (2-D and 3-D) were maintained in GTSF2 in order to adequately support cells in the bioreactor and to eliminate the variable of having multiple media used in a single experiment. Three dimensional models are proving to be excellent predictive models of physiologic response to disease and infection. It is anticipated that VZV will infect this three dimensional model. If it does so, this in itself will be an accomplishment as VZV is not regularly cultured in neural cells but rather lung tumor cells, the wrong anatomical target. Furthermore, having a nuerotrope like VZV infect the correct target tissue rather than lung will undoubtedly allow for study of the virus in a more in vivo like environment and will likely yield new, more accurate information as to the growth and replication of the virus. This approach planned to establish and validate 3-D NHNP as a viable target for VZV infection. Comparing the results of VZV grown in modeled microgravity to VZV collected from the saliva of ground based patients or returning astronauts can determine similarities and differences in DNA sequenced between the actual and analog virus samples.

RESULTS:
NHNP cells were cultured in 3D on a scaffold of Cultispher beads in a rotating wall vessel (RWV) bioreactor and analyzed by multicolor fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH), flow cytometry, confocal microscopy and RT-PCR to assess their genetic stability as compared with 2D NHNP cell cultures. Comparison of 2D and 3D cultured NHNP cells by mFISH respectively showed no chromosomal rearrangements or breaks, indicating genetic stability of NHNP TLAs for at least a six month period in culture. Flow cytometry analysis confirmed that after 180 days in culture, NHNP TLAs expressed neuronal progenitor markers CXCR4, CD133, CD105-Endoglin, CD 90-Thy-1 and CD49f-a6 Integrin at levels comparable to the parental NHNP (2D) cell population. Markers of hematopoietic differentiation, CD38+ and CD45+ were not detected in either culture. An example of the tissue-like complexity of the NHNP TLA constructs is shown by environmental scanning electron micrographs (ESEM), which illustrate the relative size, density, and indistinguishable nature of the individual neural cells in the tissue assembly. In addition, confocal microscopy confirmed that NHNP TLAs expressed mature neuronal markers: neuron-specific nuclear protein (NeuN), ß-Tubulin-III, microtubule associated protein A&B (MAP 2 A&B), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). TLA microcarrier substrates alone did not show autofluorescence. Similarly, progenitor (Nestin) and mature (ß-Tubulin-III) neuronal markers were detected by immunohistochemistry in human TG removed at autopsy. Quantitative analysis of mRNA expression revealed higher levels of the early progenitor markers CXCR4 and CD133 in NHNP TLAs than in human TG even though only few NHNP cells expressed the two proteins. Later stage developmental markers, CD105, CD90 and CD49f, were expressed to a lesser extent in NHNP TLAs than in human TG, suggesting that NHNP TLAs are less differentiated than primary TGs. Neuronal markers Nestin and ß-Tubulin-III were expressed at comparable levels in TG and NHNP TLAs. Lower expression levels in the NHNP TLAs than in human TG were observed for the neuronal marker neurofilament 200 (NF-200), again indicating NHNP TLAs are generally less differentiated than human TG. Taken together, the data indicated that NHNP TLAs, which had undergone 18–20 fold expansion over the three-month time period, share some similarities but are less differentiated when compared to mature human TGs removed at autopsy.

experiment_title: HZE-induced Mammary Cancer Development Processes in Murine and Humanized Models and Their Influence on Radiation Quality Functions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This work was designed to provide insight into the cancer risks arising from exposure to space radiation. It asked questions about how cancer is started by radiation exposure, how cancer progresses, and how these processes might be the same and different after exposure to radiation encountered in space, and the more common gamma-rays encountered on Earth. Since breast cancer is one of the most common cancers associated with radiation exposure, this is an important model system. Understanding the progression of breast cancer after exposure to space radiation will help NASA to make better risk estimates for their long-term exploration missions. A better understanding of the factors that control breast cancer progression in general can also have a large impact on Earth, by suggesting better intervention or treatment strategies for this very common disease.

APPROACH:
The proposed research used a model of breast cancer development in which mouse or human mammary stem cells are used to grow mammary glands in mouse mammary fat pads. When the stem cells used are irradiated prior to transplant, progression from very early stages of cancer (ductal dysplasias) can be monitored. Investigators used this model to compare the development of cancer from cells exposed to gamma-rays versus cells exposed to HZE particles that are found in galactic cosmic rays. The histological progression of pre-cancerous lesions was monitored using markers of cell growth, senescence, apoptosis, proliferation, and angiogenesis. This information was to be correlated with global gene expression profiling of non-persistent and persisting dysplasias to gain further insight into the molecular mechanisms driving progress towards cancer after exposure to the different types of radiation. Studying the cancers that are initiated by radiation in both mouse and human mammary cells allows a direct comparison of cancer processes that may differ between species as well as between radiation types. This is important, as most assessments of human space radiation risk are based on experiments in rodents. In summary, this work was to assess the standard approach for generating HZE risk estimates in humans, which is to use gamma-ray to HZE quality functions that have been derived from rodent studies, and then to apply them to gamma-ray-based human epidemiological data.

RESULTS:
The goal of Specific Aim 1 is “to quantitatively compare early tumor initiating events induced by HZE vs. gamma rays in murine mammary epithelial stem cells using the well-established ductal dysplasia model as well as a 3D in vitro model.” The experiments were designed to both quantify and characterize potential differences.

Investigators have also used mammosphere cultures to examine effects of irradiation on the survival of stem cells in the irradiated mammary gland as measured by the frequency of mammospheres obtained from control and irradiated mice. Mammary cells were obtained one week post irradiation. They observed an approximately 50% reduction in the number of mammospheres obtained following gamma irradiation, which did not appear to be dose dependent over the 0 to 4 Gy dose range. A comparison of the effects of 1 Gy of gamma rays, protons, or iron showed a similar decrease that was not dependent on radiation type.

Work on this aim initially used the classic ductal dysplasia model to quantify initiated cells as measured by the frequency of persistent dysplasias in cleared mammary fat pads 16 weeks after injection of mammary epithelial cells. The mammary cells were obtained from 12 week old female BALB/c mice 16 weeks after irradiation with Cs-137 gamma rays, SPE 1972 protons, or 1 GeV/n Fe-56 ions. Following injection of cells, the frequency of persistent dysplasias was quantified 16 weeks later. This model was heavily dependent upon the ability to obtain a consistent number of mammary outgrowths from experiment to experiment in order to quantify dysplasias. Unfortunately, investigators found a wide variation in the ability to obtain fully developed mammary glands using this model. In some studies more than 90% of the mammary fat pads injected had outgrowths while in others as few as 50% yielded evaluable mammary outgrowths. As a result, data were quite variable and thus required us to perform many more experiments to obtain reliable results. The mice from these experiments also had a high rate of infection, necessitating more repeated experiments. During this time, they also devoted considerable effort to optimizing all steps of mammosphere shipping, RNA recovery, amplification and labeling.

Because of the variability encountered in the classic assay emerged, investigators compared three approaches for quantification of initiated cells and development of lesions in the murine transplantation model, and found that an intraductal transplantation model based on a recent paper by Behbod et al. (Breast Cancer Res, 11(5): R66, 2009), proved much more efficient than the initial cleared fat pad approach. They found that intraductal injection of murine mammary epithelial cells provides similar data to that previously obtained using the cleared fat pad dysplasia model (Adams et al. Cancer Res 47(16): 4425-4431, 1987) but requires less time, is more reproducible, and provides more tissue for analysis. Furthermore, based on Behbod et al. 2009, this approach should enable direct comparison of radiation effects in murine versus human breast epithelial cells.

This approach is not dependent upon the development of mammary glands in order to quantify the dysplastic nature of injected cells. The frequency of dysplastic outgrowths scored in the intraductal injection model tracked well with the frequency in the cleared fat pad approach in studies in which greater than 90% of mammary fat pads injected produced mammary outgrowths. Histological characterization of the outgrowths with respect to their dysplastic nature was performed, and approximately 90% of the outgrowths were classified as dysplastic while 10% could be classified as ductal carcinoma in situ. Both classifications support the interpretation that the cells from which the outgrowths were derived were preneoplastic in nature. This approach also provided a greater number of dysplastic cells for analysis than the classic approach, as the outgrowths were confined in a well-defined area.

Investigators found that the number of persistent dysplastic growths (fully initiated cells) is higher in mice transplanted with mammospheres derived from mice irradiated with Fe particles compared to those irradiated with gamma rays. This supports their hypothesis, that in comparison to low LET gamma-rays, HZE particle exposure would produce more efficient conversion of mammary cells to a pre-neoplastic state, similar to the response previously seen for high LET neutron exposures. Once the new approach had been worked out, mammary epithelial tissue was harvested after exposure of Balb/c mice to SPE1972 Protons, 1 GeV/n 56Fe, 350 MeV/n 28Si, gamma rays, or from controls. Cells from the tissue were dissociated and grown in attachment-free and non-differentiating conditions to allow mammosphere formation. Mammospheres were collected, dissociated into individual cells, and cultured as secondary mammospheres, which were then collected and injected into recipient mice for the formation of dysplastic lesions. Samples of both the primary and secondary mammosphere cultures were retained for gene expression studies.

While the first set of mice sacrificed (4 weeks) showed similar lesion frequencies to those that had been seen previously, at the second set of sacrifices (12 weeks) investigators found that all of the initial outgrowths had regressed when allowed to remain in situ. The reason for this discrepancy from previous results is not known, and when the entire experiment was repeated, no lesions were observed, so the unexpected regression issue could not be resolved.

The goal of Specific Aim 2 was “to assay both phenotypic progression and molecular profiles using the mammary ductal dysplasia and 3D stem cell models to determine whether HZE irradiation results in qualitatively different processes, compared with gamma-ray irradiation, that point to different mechanisms of carcinogenesis.” Investigators compared expression of genes considered putative stem cell markers (Klf4, Nanog, Wnt1) and epithelial cell markers (cytokeratin 14 - basal myoepithelial, cytokeratin 18 - luminal) in the primary and secondary mammospheres used for injection. They found that the stem cell markers Klf4 and Wnt1, as well as the basal myoepithelial marker cytokeratin 14 were expressed at higher levels in secondary compared to primary mammospheres, suggesting a shift in cell types and a possible enrichment for stem cells with the second round of culture. They also looked at the potential effect of radiation exposure to the donor mice on expression of these genes in primary and secondary mammospheres. All the genes examined were up-regulated in primary mammospheres from irradiated mice, but in the secondary mammospheres expression levels were beginning to return to the levels in unexposed controls. This may be a function of the additional ten days between irradiation of the animals and the measurement of gene expression in the secondary mammospheres, reflecting a gradual reduction in the radiation effect as time progresses. It may be that gene expression is not the most appropriate method for assessing relative stem cell enrichment, however.

RNA was harvested from lesions from mice sacrificed at 4 weeks. As noted above, for unknown reasons no lesions were identified in mice sacrificed at 12 weeks. Unfortunately, the RNA from the early lesions was of lower than expected quality, with RIN values between 4 and 6, indicative of degradation. In light of the low quality and missing late lesion samples, array hybridization was not undertaken.

Due to the persistent technical difficulties encountered with the mouse lesions, investigators extended their work to include studies of human cancer stem cells in support of their aims. Cancer stem cells (CSC) can be identified in several different tumors based on the presence or absence of specific cell surface markers. Breast CSCs have been identified by the surface marker expression of CD44+/CD24low. CD44 is expressed on the surface of cancer stem cells from a variety of tumor types and high CD44 expression is associated with increased risk of metastasis and poor overall patient prognosis. CD44 positive breast cancer stem cells have been shown to be highly refractory to radiation and chemotherapeutics and are enriched following radiation treatment. Investigators exposed exponentially growing cultures of breast cancer cell lines (MDA-231, MDA-468, and MCF-7) to gamma radiation and analyzed CD44 expression 24 and 5 days post-exposure using flow cytometry. The standard CD44 form (CD44s) was measured and a change in CD44s intensity was observed in the cell lines 24 and 5 days after exposure to gamma radiation. In MDA-231 the pattern of CD44s intensity was decreased at a dose as low as 0.1 Gy and increased following 10 Gy radiation exposure as early as 24 hours and persisted after 5 days. MDA-231 and MDA-468 displayed similar CD44s patterns 5 days post-exposure. Interestingly, MCF7 showed decreased CD44s levels for each radiation dose at 24 hours but no change at 5 days post-exposure. The patterns of CD44s expression were stable for at least two weeks in progeny of irradiated cells at all doses studied. Taken together these data show that radiation alters CD44 signaling in breast cancer cells in a dose dependent manner.

Mammalian tissues generally experience oxygen (O2) concentrations in the range of 2 to 8%, far lower than the standard atmospheric O2 environment (20%) in which most cells are cultured in the laboratory. When grown under atmospheric O2 many human cell lines have been shown to accumulate oxidative damage and undergo premature senescence. To test the effect of O2 culture conditions on the intensity of CD44s staining investigators cultured MDA-231, MDA-468, and MCF7 at 3% O2. The results at 24 hours post exposure revealed a different pattern of CD44s intensity compared to 20% O2 in each cell line. Radiation dose dependent differences were not observed in MDA-231 or MCF7. In MDA-468 increased CD44s intensity was observed after exposure to 10 Gy. At 5 days after radiation exposure the pattern of CD44s in MDA-231 was similar when grown under 3% or 20%. In MDA-468 cells grown at 3% O2 CD44s intensity decreased (relative to control) for both the 0.1 and 1.0 Gy samples. Although no radiation effect on CD44s intensity was observed in MCF7 cells grown at 20% O2, under 3% O2 they showed a CD44s pattern similar to MDA-231 and MDA-468. The data confirm the initial finding that low dose exposures seemed to decrease the “stemness” of cancer cell populations as defined by CD44 expression, while high doses increase the tendency to “stemness.” It also indicates that O2 tension influences cancer stem cell physiology and radiation response, and should be considered when using in vivo models.

experiment_title: Vestibular Experiments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Vestibular Experiments were planned by a team of researchers from the US and Canada to study the causes of space motion sickness (SMS) and associated sensory-motor adaptations to weightlessness. SMS symptoms have been consistently reported in the Soviet space program and were also seen in the Apollo and Skylab crews. In addition, incidence among Shuttle crews has exceeded 50 percent. Space motion sickness is now recognized as a significant problem affecting astronaut performance, safety, and well-being. Symptoms generally appear soon after insertion into orbit and range from malaise and irritability to nausea and severe vomiting.

Many hypotheses attempt to explain the underlying causes of SMS and the majority of them focus on how the vestibular system is affected by microgravity. The vestibular system is responsible for our ability to sense changes in the speed and direction of bodily movement, even when our eyes are closed. We use information from the vestibular organs to walk, maintain an upright posture, and to see clearly as our head moves. The vestibular system consists of two similar vestibular organs located on either side of the head in the inner ear and it functions to maintain the body's balance by detecting the position and motion of the head. Each organ is made up of three semicircular canals and two otolithic organs which detect angular and linear accelerations, respectively. The otolithic organs depend on gravity to function properly; therefore, they are especially sensitive to microgravity conditions. The vestibular organs and the eyes work in conjunction to send signals to the brain, which then activates the appropriate muscles to keep the body balanced. According to the sensory-motor conflict theory, motion sickness results when incoming sensory signals to the brain no longer match expected patterns learned during previous sensory/motor experience. Exposure to microgravity affects the function of vestibular organs causing a mismatch in visual and vestibular signals which results in a sensory-motor conflict in the central nervous system (CNS). A good example of this occurs when a crewmember is floating weightless and upright in reference to the Shuttle's floor, but in reality he or she may be completely upside down due to microgravity. Accordingly, visual inputs in this situation would indicate the correct "up" and "down" orientation but the vestibular organs would not sense the correct orientation because they rely on gravity to function properly. Researchers believe that this sensory-motor conflict is the underlying mechanism responsible for SMS, illusions of motion, and spatial-orientation disturbances.

These investigations were aimed at assessing human vestibular function and visual responses in space during the 10 day Spacelab 1 mission. Each experiment examined a different motor output to reveal some aspect of the way the CNS adapts to the altered vestibular inputs resulting from exposure to microgravity. The sensory reinterpretation hypothesis which served as a basis for all the experiments was divided into three working hypotheses as follows: (1) that as a result of sensory-motor experience in microgravity, otolith afferent signals are centrally inhibited or reinterpreted as indicating head translation rather than tilt, (2) that longitudinal (z-axis) reflex sensitivity to "falling" is decreased, (3) that visual and tactile cues should play an increasing role in spatial orientation.

APPROACH:
Visual-Vestibular Interaction: The "Rotating Dome" experiment was designed to test the hypothesis that with increasing adaptation to weightlessness, crewmembers become increasingly dependent on visual and tactile cues as opposed to vestibular cues. The experiment hardware consists of a motor-driven rotating "dome" (drum) into which the subject’s head is placed. The visible surface of the dome was white and covered with randomly positioned colored dots. When the drum rotates, a sensation of self rotation in the direction opposite to that of drum rotation is felt. This tilting sensation causes a muscle reflex which attempts to turn the head back to a vertical position. Since the head is actually held stationary by a biteboard assembly, the neck torque produces counter rotation forces in the body. On Earth, the onset and strength of this sensation are thought to be inhibited by the lack of confirming motion signals from the vestibular organs. In microgravity, this inhibition should be reduced and thus researchers expected the crewmembers to feel a stronger sensation of self rotation.

Each experimental run consisted of a series of six trials. For each trial, the dome rotated at a constant angular velocity of 30, 45, or 60 deg/s clockwise or counterclockwise for a period of 50 seconds (s) followed by a 10 s stationary pause separating the trials. Two separate sequences of trials, each with randomized speed and direction, were utilized in the study. Crewmembers were instructed to deflect a rotary knob "joystick" to indicate the speed and direction of their own perceived self-motion. Ocular torsion was measured with a video camera installed in the center of the rotating dome. Body sway data was recorded using a video camera with a back view of the subject and the rotating dome. Inflight, the above experiment procedure was also performed with the crewmember constrained in a bungee-cord harness. The harness was employed to produce tactile and proprioceptive forces on the legs, trunk and feet that the subject would feel in a 1-G environment.

The "Rod and Frame" experiments also investigated visual-vestibular interaction by measuring static visual field dependence. The experiment tested the subject's ability to indicate the direction of the vertical as influenced by a tilted visual framework. The experiment was only performed pre- and postflight, since it's purpose was to determine if the increased dependence on static visual cues for orientation in space would carry over after flight. Subjects were seated in a chair in a dark room and viewed a dimly lit frame with sides 107 cm long by 2.5 cm wide surrounding a rod 99 cm long and 2.5 cm wide, located 180 cm from the subject. This frame was tilted to 28 degrees in either direction from the upright position. The subject told the experimenter to rotate the rod about a central axis until the subject judged it to be vertical. Angular deviation of the rod was measured by a potentiometer, and constituted the determination of field dependence. During each experimental session, four measurements were taken in each direction, as well as two control measurements without the frame.

Otolith-Spinal Reflex: These experiments focused on the neural link between the otolith organs and the motor neurons of the spinal cord which control limb muscle activity. These neural pathways control the otolith-spinal reflex which is responsible for preparing the leg muscles for a landing from a fall. The experiments were set up to assess changes in the otolith-spinal system during and after prolonged exposure to microgravity. Researchers wanted to investigate how the otolith-spinal system adapts to a new sensory-motor environment, and how it readapts to gravity after landing. The protocol for the "Hop and Drop" experiments was designed to examine calf muscle responses during unexpected "falls" to see if the otolith contribution is altered and determine if the time course of this alteration correlates with other otolith response measures.

Pre- and postflight falls were produced as the subject grasped a handle above his head, raised his feet, and then dropped to the floor as the handle was released. In the absence of gravity, the downward acceleration toward the Spacelab floor was provided by adjustable elastic cords which connected a torso harness to the Spacelab floor. A total of nine cords, grouped into 3 sets of 3, ran from the harness attachment points to the floor. When properly adjusted, they provided a downward force approximately equal to the subject's weight as he hung by his arms from the handle. By removing one elastic cord from each set the acceleration was reduced to 0.67 g, and by removing another from each set it was reduced further to 0.33 g. All data were collected in the first 150 milliseconds (ms) after release. The electromyographic (EMG) response was recorded from 2 surface electrodes located over the lower ends of the lateral and medial heads of the gastrocnemius of the left leg. A ground electrode was placed on the midline over the soleus 5-10 cm below the others. During inflight testing, head longitudinal acceleration was recorded using an accelerometer strapped to the subject's head and an electronics package worn at the waist. This signal was used to confirm both the times of onset of fall and of landing, and the magnitude of acceleration stimulus. Contact with the floor was detected by means of a ribbon switch attached under the subject's left foot. During pre- and postflight testing sessions, the onset of fall was detected by a microswitch located in the releasing device. Contact with the ground was determined using a series of ribbon switches located under a section of carpet upon which the subject landed. All test sessions included 45 falls, with a stimulus of 0.2 g for the first 15, 0.5 g for the next 15 and 1.0 g for the final 15. To achieve stimuli of less than 1.0 g during pre- and postflight testing, the subject wore a parachute harness which was attached to counterweights via a cable and pulley system.

Awareness of Orientation and Limb Position: Many astronauts have reported that they lose their sense of "up" and "down" orientation with respect to the vehicle when their eyes are closed or when the lights are turned off. Researchers wanted to investigate this problem further by examining the role of limb position awareness in this orientation disturbance. On Earth, the central nervous system uses tactile and proprioceptive cues from the limbs to factor in the effect of gravity on the "up" and "down" orientation process. However, in microgravity the tactile and proprioceptive cues from the limbs may be altered, and researchers wanted to investigate the origins of the loss of spatial orientation. More specifically, they examined whether the disorientation occurs immediately after closing the eyes or whether it requires some time for the memory of orientation to "wash out". They also examined whether the loss of limb position awareness is caused by microgravity or sleep periods. Experiments were conducted in the Spacelab module in both a loosely and tightly tethered condition to control for the effects of tactile forces. Experiments were also conducted in the Orbiter middeck bunk area in order to make observations after sleep. Subjects were instructed to view the location of several different target objects placed on nearby walls, were blindfolded, and were then asked to describe the position of their limbs and to point accurately to the targets. Different intervals of time were measured between the time of blindfolding and the time of describing the position of their limbs.

Posture Control: Researchers have found that exposure to microgravity causes postural difficulties both during microgravity and for several days postflight. The difficulties may be due to the changes in central processing of vestibular information that occur during prolonged exposure to microgravity. This study was designed to identify changes in electromyographic (EMG) latency and amplitudes that might explain the postural instabilities observed postflight. These experiments were only conducted before and after the 10 day Spacelab 1 mission. The "Posture Platform" experiments used a pneumatically driven platform to initiate changes in standing posture. Subjects wore hard soled shoes and were instructed to stand on the platform with their eyes open (or closed) facing a wall with head erect and legs straight. As the platform is suddenly tilted proprioceptive reflexes that normally stabilize posture are inappropriate to maintain stability. Therefore, the body relies on other sensory systems such as the vestibular organs to compensate for the disturbance in posture. Prior to testing, surface electrodes were placed over the tibialis anterior (TA) and the gastrocnemius-soleus (G-S) muscles of the left leg. The raw EMG signals from the ankle flexors (TA) and ankle extensors (G-S) were sampled for 10 s at 200 samples per second by a microcomputer that also controlled the movement of the platform. Six trials were performed consisting of a randomized set of three up and three down tilts of the platform with the eyes open, followed by a different randomized set of six trials with eyes closed. The EMG signals were later analyzed for latency, amplitude, and frequency of oscillation of the late, post 500 millisecond, response.

The "Sharpened Romberg" test is a standardized procedure for measuring standing stability and posture. This test was also used as a method of evaluating the postflight postural instabilities of the Spacelab 1 crew. The experiments used two long rails (one narrow and one wide) mounted on wooden beams to conduct four different tests. (1) Narrow rail walking: The subject walked with arms folded in front, heel to toe, along the narrow rail for a maximum of six steps. (2) Narrow rail standing: The subject stood, eyes open, with arms folded, in the heel to toe position on the narrow rail for a maximum of 60 s per trial. (3) Wide rail standing/eyes closed: The subject stood heel to toe on the wide rail and when stable, closed his eyes. The position was maintained for a maximum of 60 s. (4) Wide rail standing/eyes open: The subject stood heel to toe on the wide rail for a maximum of 60 s with eyes open. All trials were terminated if the subject unfolded his arms or placed a foot on the floor. The operator measured the duration of the test or, in the case of the narrow rail walking test, the number of steps. Individual scores for each subject were the sum of the best three out of five trials for that test.

Motion Sickness Susceptibility: The motion sickness susceptibility investigation involved a head movement/symptom monitoring experiment and pre- and postflight susceptibility tests which were designed to systematically collect data on the origins, prediction, symptoms, and prevention of the disorder. The design of the experiments placed emphasis on resolving the issue: is space sickness another form of motion sickness? In order to document the relationship between head movement and symptom intensity two subjects wore the Acceleration Recording Unit (ARU). The system consisted of 3 angular and 3 linear miniature accelerometers mounted on a rectangular metal case. The package was held on the back of the head by a velcro cloth brow band so that it moved with the head during all movements. Subjects were asked to don the ARU as soon as possible after reaching orbit and to wear it as much as possible during their waking hours. To obtain frequent reports for correlation with head movement data, subjects were asked to make brief reports consisting of Mission Elapsed Time and a numerical estimate of "overall discomfort". The overall discomfort scale was based on a midrange value of 10 which was chosen as the marker for the symptoms felt when one was halfway to vomiting. Subjects also used pocket voice recorders and a multi-item symptom checklist to record observations on symptoms as they were noticed and as time permitted. In addition to symptom monitoring, two subjects were scheduled to make provocative head movements to explore the influence of eye closure and axis of head movement. The protocol consisted of a "Susceptibility Test" and a "Symptom Comparison Test" which were scheduled for the end of the working day on Mission Days 0, 3, and 8. If the subject was asymptomatic to start the test, the subject would strap into a seat and make 7 forehead to knee head movements, then rest for 10 s while making a checklist symptom report, and then repeat until the first symptom occurred or 5 min elapsed. If symptoms were present at the start, the Susceptibility Test would be skipped, and the subject performed only the Symptom Comparison Test. This approach was used because the Comparison Test protocol required a slightly symptomatic subject so that the stimulus/response relationship would be immediately obvious. Subjects first made up to 7 forehead to knee movements with eyes closed, and then repeated this with eyes open, and ranked the two conditions in terms of provocativeness. After a pause for recovery, subjects were then to make 90 degree head movements (eyes open) for 20 s periods successively in pitch, yaw, and roll, and then rank these movements also.

Vestibular Reactions to Lateral Acceleration: Linear acceleration is a stimulus of prime importance in the investigation of the effects of microgravity on vestibular function. Researchers have found that exposure to microgravity alters otolith function during and after space flight. These pre- and postflight experiments were designed to assess otolith adaptation after space flight by exposing the subjects to transient linear acceleration. Preflight tests established a baseline for each test subject and each test. Sled test sessions were conducted 120, 64, 43, and 10 days before the mission. Postflight measurements were made during the period of readaptation following landing. Postflight testing sessions were conducted on landing day three to five hours after landing for two of the crewmen and on all four crewmen 1, 2, 4, and 6 days after landing.

The subject was restrained in a cushioned aluminum chair by a five-strap harness. The head was restrained with an instrumented foam lined helmet. The helmet provided a means for measuring acceleration at the subject's head, eye movement by electro-oculography (EOG), and attachment of a Nikon F-3 camera to take pictures of both eyes. A biteboard carrying a fixed reference in the view of the camera enabled measurement of and correction for any residual head movement within the helmet. Four tests with the U.S. Laboratory Sled were performed using lateral upright (y-axis) acceleration: (1) perception of motion, (2) closed loop otolith assessment test (CLOAT), (3) dynamic ocular torsion, and (4) horizontal eye deviations.

(1) Perception of linear motion: This test measured a subject's ability to detect the presence and direction of small linear accelerations. The cart was positioned at the center or end of the track and a step acceleration was then applied to the cart. A step deceleration was applied after the cart had traveled one quarter of the track. Thirteen step accelerations ranging from 0.001 g to 0.08 g were presented in a random order, once in each direction for each acceleration level. When the subject detected his direction of acceleration, he indicated this by displacing the hand-held joystick in the direction of subjective acceleration. For a given trial of thirteen levels presented randomly, the threshold was defined to be the lowest acceleration level for which the subject correctly detects three out of four runs at that level and above.

(2) CLOAT: This test measured the subject's ability to use linear acceleration cues to perform a manual control task. During CLOAT the subject made use of otolith sensory information in a closed loop sensorimotor nulling task where the motor function (hand manipulation of a joystick) was presumed relatively unaffected by exposure to microgravity. The subject was in control of sled velocity using a joystick. A disturbance motion was generated by the computer and combined with the subject's control. The disturbance consisted of a random appearing velocity profile made up of 12 logarithmically spaced sinusoids added together lasting 82 s. The subject's task was to try to nullify the disturbance motion by holding the cart still, thereby closing the loop. CLOAT was performed once in the light and three times in the dark for each test session. The resultant sled velocity profiles in the dark were averaged in the frequency domain before further analysis was performed.

(3) Dynamic ocular torsion: This test isolated the gravitoinertial contribution to dynamic ocular counterrolling. The inability to distinguish between gravitational and inertial forces results in an ocular torsion response to lateral acceleration with the head upright. In this case, the gravitoinertial force vector, rather than the pure gravitational force vector, is rotated with respect to the head. The orientation of the head remains fixed and no rotational accelerations impinge on the head. Sinusoidal oscillation of amplitude 0.61 g was used at two frequencies, 0.42 Hz and 0.83 Hz, for 12 and 15 cycles, respectively. Torsional eye position was obtained by correlation and trigonometric analysis of eye and head position in photographs obtained with a camera. Photographs were taken at a rate of 2.5 frames per second. Eye torsional position was derived from two landmarks obtained from either naturally occurring landmarks in the iris or marked contact lenses adhered to the eye by a drop of distilled water. Head roll position was obtained from fiducial marks on extensions of a dental biteboard which appeared in the field of view of the film frame.

(4) Lateral eye deviations: This experiment complemented the ocular torsion study and involved measurement of the vertical and horizontal axes of eye movement during linear acceleration along all three body axes. Eye movements were recorded via electro-oculography (EOG) using surface electrodes placed around the eyes and preamplifiers built in to the sled helmet. Horizontal eye deviation and ocular torsion tests were performed with the subject facing sideways to the direction of the motion stimulus and fixating on an imaginary point on the laboratory wall. Vertical eye movement and nystagmus tests were performed with the subject seated and pointed in the direction of motion or lying down with his face to the ceiling. The subject was asked to indicate the direction of illusory subjective rotation, if any, verbally and with the Sled joystick.

Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR) and Nystagmus Dumping: These experiments were designed to test how the semicircular canals and otoliths function to control compensatory eye movements and nystagmus during body rotation about the vertical axis. Specifically, the researchers wanted to investigate how otolith signals possibly override semicircular canal signals to create postrotational nystagmus "dumping" in subjects who are rotated about the vertical axis and suddenly stopped. Investigators predicted that the dumping effect would be absent in microgravity due to altered otolith function. The subject was seated in the tubular frame seat which was mounted to the Spacelab floor on a pivot, and manually rotated by a second crewmember . Horizontal and vertical eye movements and head angular acceleration were measured and recorded by a belt mounted data recording system worn by the subject. Eye movements were measured with bitemporal EOG electrodes. The subjects eyes were covered but remained open. They were instructed to look straight ahead. In each session, the subject was rotated clockwise about a vertical axis for 1 min at 120 deg/sec, stopped, and postrotational VOR was recorded for 1 min. This procedure was repeated 3 times, alternating rotation directions. In the first two tests the subject maintained the head erect position throughout. In tests 3 and 4 (dumping tests), the subject pitched his head forward 90 degrees 5 seconds after chair rotation stopped, maintained this position for 5 seconds, and then resumed the head upright position. Nystagmus slow phase velocity (SPV) was then calculated. Preflight tests were conducted 151, 120, 65, 43, and 10 days prior to launch. Postflight data was obtained on days 1 and 2 after landing.

RESULTS:
Visual-Vestibular Interaction (Rotating Dome): Subjective Reports and Vection (Visually Induced Motion Sensation) indications: All subjects' comments indicated an increased visual dependence for orientation during flight, with an enhanced effect late in flight. Large individual differences in preflight sensations were also reflected during the inflight tests. Localized tactile cues reduced the visual effect in various ways early in the flight, but had less of an effect late in flight. All subjects reported stronger and more rapidly occurring vection when they experimented free of the biteboard in front of the rotating dome.

Visual-Vestibular Interaction (Rotating Dome)- Vection Indications: To measure the effects of weightlessness on the sensation of vection, statistical tests of the time from the start of dome rotation to onset of vection were performed. For each subject, each preflight dome run was compared with each inflight free-floating dome run. Despite the uniform comments that the bungee-cord-induced localized tactile cues inhibited vection in flight, neither average vection intensity nor average onset latency supported the subjective reports with statistically significant results. For seven of the eleven inflight comparisons, the average onset latency for a six trial dome run was longer when tactile cues were applied. Only 27 of the 47 individual trial comparisons produced weaker average vection intensity with tactile cues than for the free-floating conditions. When all trials were combined for each subject in a given test run, the variability in vection onset time became too large to permit statistically significant conclusions. However, the inflight mean onset times were generally lower than preflight, as were the postflight onset times.

Visual-Vestibular Interaction (Rotating Dome)- Body Sway: Rear-view video images of the subjects during all the flight experiments revealed considerable body sway only for one subject during the free-float dome run on the seventh day of flight.

Visual-Vestibular Interaction (Rod and Frame): Three of the subjects were field independent, with average deviations of the rod toward the frame of less than six degrees. The raw rod and frame data show high variability, but there is a trend toward increased field dependence which lasts for several days postflight. Each of the four subjects showed an increase in visual field dependence following the flight.

Otolith-Spinal Reflex - Response to Sudden Falls: All four crewmembers were tested before and after flight, but only two subjects were able to participate during flight and on landing day. One subject was tested on mission days (MD) 0, 1, and 6, and the other subject on MD 0, 1, 6, and 7. EMG responses were recorded in 200 ms increments, with 25 ms shown before the moment of release and 175 ms after. The early EMG burst actually consisted of two sub-components. The latency which marked the dividing line between the first and second sub-components varied between subjects, but was somewhat constant for individual subjects.

Otolith-Spinal Reflex - Two Subjects Tested Pre-, In-, and Postflight: Sub-component 1 showed similar results for both subjects. In nearly every case, the size of the response increased with the strength of the acceleration stimulus. There was no apparent change of the response postflight relative to preflight. Sub-component 1 decreased significantly immediately upon reaching orbit, and declined further during the flight, with most of the latter reduction occurring between MD 0 and 1. After MD 0, stimuli of 0.33 g and 0.67 g were close to or below threshold for eliciting a response to sudden falls. Sub-component 2 showed a different pattern of behavior. Except for inflight, the response did not usually increase with the acceleration stimulus. Postflight, a stimulus of 0.2 g tended to elicit a smaller response than the same stimulus preflight. Inflight, each subject seemed to adopt a different strategy. Sub-component 2 in subject A decreased upon entering weightlessness, and then changed little for the remainder of the flight. In subject B, however, sub-component 2 resulting from a 1-g stimulus increased dramatically, whereas those resulting from 0.33 g and 0.67 g stimuli were decreased on MD 0. All three continued to decline throughout the flight.

Otolith-Spinal Reflex - Four Subjects Tested Pre- and Postflight: The results from subjects A and B were combined with results from subjects C and D to extend the data analysis to four subjects. However, because of extreme variability of sub-component 2 between subjects, only sub-component 1 results are presented. No significant trends were noted in the data pre- or postflight, nor was there a significant difference postflight compared to preflight. This indicates that readaptation of the otolith-spinal system under study is a very rapid process, occurring much quicker than the original adaptation to microgravity.

Awareness of Orientation and Limb Position: In the absence of usable graviceptor information regarding body orientation in weightlessness, the nervous system must pay increased attention to the remaining sensory orientation signals. Subjective reports from crewmembers indicate large variations in individual styles, but never a prolonged sense of absence of a reference frame or disorientation.

Posture Control: Due to the variability of the responses, a better understanding of the relationship between pre- and postflight EMG activity was achieved by examining individual responses rather than averaged data. EMG activity of subject B during the first tilt up trials with eyes open on test days L-10, R+0, R+1, and R+6 was analyzed. The eyes open (EO) tilt up responses of the TA muscle showed small changes between the responses on the last preflight test, L-10, and postflight R+6. On R+0 and R+1, the first response to a tilt up had a larger initial response. However, no consistent pattern of change in the initial response amplitudes within or across the subjects was found. The G-S responses were markedly different than the TA response pattern. The late responses had generally the same shape, being characterized by one or two peaks following the initial peak with most of the response remaining flat for the remainder of the period. The eyes closed (EC) tilt up trials qualitatively showed postflight changes primarily in the late response. The initial peak changed very little from the preflight level. The late response on R+0 and R+1 showed several large and prolonged periods of EMG activity in the TA and G-S muscles as the subject fought to maintain balance. Successive EC tilt up responses from subject A on L-10, R+0, and R+1 show clear changes between preflight and R+0 data with less distinction on R+1. The increased amplitudes throughout the recording session clearly separated preflight from R+0 EMG responses in subjects A and B. The tilt down trial responses changed from preflight to postflight. The EO and EC responses on L-10 and R+6 showed a similar pattern of TA and G-S activity. The postflight data on R+0 and R+1 showed higher TA activity than that found preflight or on R+6.

Motion Sickness Susceptibility: Three of the four crewmembers reported persistent symptoms which were proportional to activity level. These three crewmen also vomited during the first or second day of the mission. Head movements on all axes were provocative, particularly in pitch and roll. ARU amplitude distributions of head angular and linear acceleration were computed over successive 15-minute intervals. These data showed that both crewmen who wore the ARU were compelled to limit their head movements when symptoms appeared after several hours of physical activity in orbit. However, after several days in orbit symptoms subsided, and head accelerations increased in magnitude and variability. Static visual cues were identified as a second major stimulus in space sickness. Difficulties in identifying the subjective floor, walls, and ceiling using static visual information were noted. Sudden changes in subjective self-orientation were occasionally experienced due to reinterpretation of available visual cues. The inflight symptom pattern was generally the same as the preflight pattern, except that facial pallor and cold sweating were usually not seen. Medication (0.5 mg scopolamine/2.5 mg dexedrine or 25 mg promethazine/25 mg ephedrine) was taken by all crewmembers and was judged helpful, with minimal side effects.

Vestibular Reactions to Lateral Acceleration: Perception of Linear Motion: The three parameters measured were threshold acceleration, velocity constant, and a regression coefficient associated with determining the velocity constant. Eight preflight trials were conducted with subject A and six trials with each of subjects B, C, and D. In general, preflight measures showed fairly stable measures of velocity constant. Preflight measures of threshold were more variable than velocity constants on a trial by trial basis. The lowest threshold obtained from among the trials in a particular session was used as the indicator of threshold for that day. Preflight thresholds were in the range of 0.002 g to 0.004 g. Postflight, measures of both velocity constant and threshold tended to be more variable than the preflight baseline.

Vestibular Reactions to Lateral Acceleration - CLOAT: Each of the four crewmen tended to have his own control strategy which developed in the early preflight sessions. Performance was determined by the scalar performance measure (SPM), a single parameter value derived in the frequency domain. Performance stabilized in the late preflight sessions for subjects A and B. For each crewmember, performance in the dark and in the light improved over the first three preflight sessions. For CLOAT in the light, little change was exhibited between pre- and postflight.

Vestibular Reactions to Lateral Acceleration: Dynamic Ocular Torsion: Only pre- and postflight data are available from subjects A and B due to inflight equipment failure. At each test session the folded torsion measurements were correlated to the sinusoidal stimulus frequency. However, the fitted sinusoidal amplitude showed high variance from one preflight session to the next in the same subject. In each case, the first measurement postflight had an amplitude smaller than or equal to three of the four preflight measurements in the same subject at the same frequency. Subsequent amplitude measurements postflight increased for both subjects at both frequencies.

Vestibular reactions to Lateral Acceleration - Lateral Eye Deviations: No results available.

Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex Nystagmus Dumping: Head erect post-rotatory VOR gain was unchanged in the pre- and postflight measurements. A shortening of the apparent time constant of post-rotatory slow phase velocity decay was observed in 3 of the 4 subjects. Increased decay was statistically significant 6-20 seconds after chair stop. Four days postflight, the group time constant had recovered to preflight norms.

experiment_title: BRIC: Plant Mechanical Signaling During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Plants are exquisitely sensitive to mechanical stimulation which triggers changes ranging from widespread alteration in patterns of gene expression to profound shifts in development. Indeed, so pervasive is the mechanical stimulation from internal and external forces, such as the weight of tissues and organs, to a biology that has evolved under a constant 1xG, that the resultant signaling is thought to provide a required regulatory background to control a wide range of plant developmental and physiological processes. Despite this acknowledged role in plant morphogenesis, the overall contribution of such mechanical cues to plant function remains poorly defined, largely due to the difficulties in removing the pervasive 1xG-driven mechanical signal when conducting experiments on Earth. The microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS) therefore provides a unique tool to both directly address this hypothesis of mechanical load-driven morphogenesis, as well as to ask what features of plant growth in space reflect disruption of this mechano-signaling regulatory network. We have therefore grown seedlings of Arabidopsis thaliana on board the ISS using the Biological Research in Canisters-Petri Dish Fixation Units (BRIC-PDFU) hardware. We are comparing their patterns of growth and gene expression to ground-based controls to ask how the well-defined "fingerprints" of mechanical response are altered in space. In addition, we are characterizing plants grown in space whose mechanical signaling has been artificially activated or inhibited by mutations in a gene (TCH2) which has an established role in the mechanical signaling system of plants. Results from such analyses will address the fundamental question of the role of mechanical loading on plant growth and development on Earth as well as probing how manipulating this system through targeting specific mechanoresponse genes might be used to tailor plant growth to thrive in the unique environment of spaceflight. This experiment has also been supplemented with a parallel geneLAB experiment to monitor the growth, development, and gene expression patterns of a series of natural variants of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana in space. These variants (ecotypes) have been chosen to span the range of likely ecotypes to be used in future spaceflight experimentation and so will provide key baseline comparisons to help understand the impact of ecotypic makeup on responses to spaceflight.

APPROACH:
Flight: Preflight testing (Science and Payload Verification Tests) was successfully completed in 2014 and the payload of 4 BRIC canisters containing a total of 20 60 mm Petri dishes of seeds launched on September 21, 2014 on board SpaceX-CRS4. All on orbit operations were successfully completed and the frozen samples were returned via SpaceX's Dragon capsule, splashing down on October 25, 2014. Samples were transported to Kennedy Space Center where they were de-integrated on November 4, 2014. Analysis at this point indicated ~ 100% seed germination in all BRIC19 and geneLAB samples. The samples were shipped to The University of Wisconsin-Madison for subsequent analysis.

Parallel ground-based analysis: In parallel to the flight experiments, the ecotypes from geneLAB and the cml24 touch mutants have been monitored for their responses to touch and gravitropic stimulation on Earth. Plants expressing the GFP-based 'Yellow Cameleon Nano-65' Ca2+ sensor were generated and Ca2+ changes in response to touch and gravitropic stimulation (90° rotation) monitored by confocal ratio imaging. cml24 mutants show altered touch-induced growth and effects on Ca2+ signals. In addition, alterations in gravitropic growth between wild type, the cml24 mutants, and geneLAB lines have been quantified and are being correlated with the gene expression changes seen during spaceflight.

RESULTS: Between November 2014 and February 2015, samples were thawed, growth parameters measured, and RNA extracted for subsequent analysis of gene expression. The RNA samples were then submitted to the University of Wisconsin-Madison Biotech Center where they underwent RNA sequencing for RNAseq analysis (measurement of the level of gene expression of all genes in each sample plant's genome). RNAseq data is currently being analyzed to detect patterns of gene expression changes in both the BRIC19 and geneLAB samples associated with spaceflight. These changes are being verified in duplicate samples by the independent technique of quantitative PCR.
