experiment_title: Preventing Desynchronization of the Circadian System in Long-Term Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Many biochemical, physiological, and behavioral parameters exhibited by organisms show daily fluctuations and most of these daily rhythms persist in constant conditions, thus, demonstrating that they are driven by endogenous oscillators. The rhythms that persist in constant conditions with a period close to 24 hours are called circadian rhythms. One the most important aspects of space flight is the absence of geophysical 24-hour cycles, which, of course, affects the overall temporal organization of the organisms. In the case of long-duration manned space flight, it is crucial to understand how the whole circadian system would react and behave in such circumstances. The investigators discovered that exposing rats to constant dim light for 60 days may induce spontaneous internal desynchronization in a few animals. In the present research proposal they further examined this phenomenon by investigating the physiological consequences of spontaneous internal desynchronization and to develop countermeasures to obviate the occurrence of internal desynchronization in animals exposed to constant dim light. Spontaneous internal desynchronization has profound effects on the capability of the organisms to perform (mentally and physically) and to remain healthy.

Recent studies have shown that a subset of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) innervating the SCN are directly photosensitive and able to convert electromagnetic radiation into neural signals. Melanopsin, a photopigment based on vitamin A, was found in these RGCs and is the strongest candidate for the circadian photopigment within these cells. The spectral sensitivity of these RGC peak around 474 nm. It is now believed that these RGCs provide the main light input to the circadian clock.

APPROACH:
This project has provided important data on the physiological mechanisms that are involved in the maintenance of the synchronization among the different circadian oscillators. The data generated by this project is expected to allow the design of specific treatments (pharmacological or environmental) that will prevent the desynchronization of the circadian system. Such treatments will then be employed in the treatment of circadian dysfunctions due to a pathological (or environmental) condition that may affect some individuals. Furthermore, the LEDs that were developed may be useful in the treatment of several pathologies such as seasonal affective disorders and sleep disorders.

RESULTS:
Investigators tested the efficacy of their new blue narrow-band light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Their data indicate that these LEDs are very effective in modulating some circadian parameters (melatonin suppression and phase-shift of the locomotor activity). Preliminary data support the safety of these LEDs.

experiment_title: Effect of Microgravity on Adipose Tissue Remodeling and Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In this study, we will develop a 3D in vitro model of adipose tissue for culture under microgravity conditions to mimic spaceflight. Rotating wall vessels allow us to generate a weightlessness condition and these will be compared to standard (Earth gravity) dynamic cultures. By first evaluating the effect microgravity has on 3D adipocytes alone, we can isolate the metabolic effects independent of vascular flow. Upon characterization on the effect on adipocytes alone, we can begin to add complexity by co-culturing with endothelial cells to provide a vascular network. This allows us to study how vascular remodeling due to changes in flow and/or pressure can impact metabolic function.

Upon conclusion of this one year period, this project will generate a fundamental knowledge base and working model of (vascular) adipose tissue function under microgravity conditions. These findings will have major implications on space travel and human health on Earth. This will provide preliminary data for several larger scope grants as these models can be probed in more detail for mechanistic understanding of the effects of gravity on human metabolic function. The studies can also be expanded to determine how nutrients are stored and metabolized in adipose tissue differently in space and on Earth by supplementing the media with various fatty acids (unsaturated versus saturated) and glucose levels (low versus high). Future directions would also include how obese adipose tissue behaves differently as a result of microgravity exposure and how microgravity may inhibit or enhance browning (thermogenic capacity) of white adipose tissue.

experiment_title: Vision and Aging in the Astronaut Population
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Aging causes changes that may weaken your eyes, and affect your vision. Probably the most common aging effect of the eye is presbyopia, which affects more than 60 million Americans. This condition is caused by the loss of lens elasticity, resulting in the loss of the ability to focus on near objects or small print. Other aging-related conditions are less benign and can lead to irreversible blindness when left untreated. These diseases tend to begin painlessly and without symptoms in their earliest stages. Risk factors for these diseases include being over the age of 60, having a family history of the disease, or having the predisposing condition (e.g., diabetes). These eye diseases are described below.

Cataracts are cloudy areas or opacities in the lens, which may be caused by aging, or trauma. Cataracts, which form slowly and painlessly, may stay small and not interfere with vision. Fortunately, surgical treatment for advanced cataracts has a higher than 90% success rate. Cataracts affect almost 20.5 million people in the U.S. age 40 and older. The corresponding figures for the astronaut and comparison participants are 29 and 37, respectively.

Glaucoma is a buildup of pressure in the eye caused by an imbalance in fluid production and drainage. This increased pressure can damage the optic nerve, retina, or other parts of the eye. In some cases, elevated intraocular pressure is a clue to the condition, but in most instances glaucoma is only detected through a dilated eye examination. Glaucoma is controlled by medication, and surgery if necessary. More than 2.2 million people in the U.S. age 40 and older have glaucoma. Three astronauts and ten comparison participants age 40 and older have been diagnosed with glaucoma.

Retinal disorders: the two most relevant retinal disorders are age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic retinopathy. In AMD, vision deteriorates when the macular cells in the retina break down for reasons that are yet unknown. AMD rarely leads to complete blindness; however, it will lead to loss of central vision function, thereby potentially effecting one's ability to perform discriminating tasks such as reading, driving or watching television. Its effects can range from mild to profound. AMD cannot be cured, but it may be slowed by laser treatment, or medication and nutritional supplementation with antioxidants. Vision loss can be improved by low-vision aids. More than 1.6 million people in the U.S. age 50 and older have AMD. This condition affects one astronaut and five comparison participants age 50 and older.

In diabetic retinopathy, chronic high glucose levels lead to damage in retinal blood vessels. This condition is the most common vision complication that diabetics suffer, and is the leading cause of new blindness. Controlling the underlying disease, diabetes, is the best prevention. Diabetic retinopathy may be slowed or stopped through surgery, when it is diagnosed in its early stages. This disease affects more than 5.3 million people in the U.S. age 18 and older. No Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participant has reported being diagnosed with diabetic retinopathy.

APPROACH:
The data represents the prevalence of these diseases in the LSAH participants as compared to that of the general U.S. population, as estimated by the National Eye Institute.

RESULTS:
In general, both astronauts and comparison participants show lower prevalence of these eye conditions than the U.S. population, which may be a result of the healthy worker effect. For all of the diseases except cataracts, astronauts also have a lower prevalence than comparison participants.

Cataracts, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy have silent onset, and when left untreated can lead to irreversible blindness. Therefore, regular and thorough eye examinations, including dilated pupil examination, every one to two years are essential for early detection and prevention of these diseases.

experiment_title: Comparative Packaging Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Advanced Food Technology (AFT) is currently working to design a stable, palatable, and nutritious food supply, to support long-duration missions beyond Low-Earth Orbit (LEO). Identifying high-barrier food packaging is integral to this work, as food quality is greatly reduced upon interaction with environmental moisture and oxygen. This research project evaluated the long-term performance of three packaging materials: a low barrier material, a clear high barrier material, and an opaque high barrier material. One ingredient and two food products, all extremely vulnerable to oxygen- and moisture-induced spoilage, were packaged in the three materials. The quality of these food items with long-term storage at relevant temperature and humidity parameters was examined regularly by instrumental analysis and sensory evaluation. Quality of these food items over time has indicated the relative longevity of each packaging material. Data obtained have suggested the continued need of a metalized overwrap material to ensure the quality and shelf life of foods packaged in clear materials for ISS and long duration spaceflight applications. Critical limits of quality for evaluated food products and recommendations for packaging of NASA food items in long duration missions were identified based on the findings of this study.

APPROACH:
The Comparative Packaging Study research project evaluated the long-term performance of three packaging materials: a low barrier transparent material, a high-barrier transparent material, and a high barrier opaque material. One ingredient and two food products, all extremely vulnerable to oxygen and moisture induced spoilage, were packaged in the three test materials. The quality of these food items with long term storage at relevant temperature (21-23oC) and humidity (25%RH – 75%RH) parameters was examined regularly for 36 months. During this time, the foods were evaluated for any increases in moisture content, increases in staling aroma compounds, and changes in other food quality indicators. Sensory testing (or taste testing) was also used to assess the quality of the foods over storage time, by having volunteers compare the aging items to control samples.

RESULTS:
The assessment of the packaged food items over time has indicated the relative longevity of each of the three packaging materials. The opaque material preserved the food quality the longest of the three materials (>36 months), and its success appeared to be unaffected by the different storage conditions studied. After considering all results, AFT researchers were able to establish minimum limits for food quality indicators, which will likely simplify food storage studies for NASA missions in the future. AFT researchers also used the results of this study to make recommendations on the use of the three materials to support current and future NASA missions. Among these recommendations, AFT researchers encouraged the use of the high barrier opaque material to ensure the quality of food for storage on ISS.

experiment_title: Simulated Space Radiation Studies for the Assessment of Chromosomal Damage: An Integrated Experimental and Theoretical Approach
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Outside of the protection of Earth's atmosphere humans are exposed to increased radiation, even inside the shielded walls of their spacecraft. Significant aberrations in the chromosomes of humans who stay in space for long-durations have been measured. The blood cells of several Mir crewmembers showed such abnormalities. This is of great concern since these aberrations lead to the death of cells, mutation of genes and, eventually, cancer. This study investigated the frequency of several classes of chromosomal aberrations (lethal, non-lethal, carcinogenic and complex) that occur in human cells irradiated by protons and high-energy HZE particles through various types of shielding. p> As high-energy radioactive particles penetrate the hull of a spacecraft, some of them are fragmented into a mixture of component particles. Understanding what comprises this mixed beam of radiation is imperative for predicting the overall effect on chromosomes. The experimental portion of this study was complemented by the development of an effective theoretical model to predict radiation-induced aberrations. This research will help design future spacecraft shielding so that radiation risks are minimized. The ultimate goal is to lower the radiation risk to astronauts during long-duration missions.

APPROACH:
Cultured human fibroblasts and epithelial cells were irradiated within realistic shielding types. The studies were conducted using proton beams, and later, heavy nuclei and protons, including energetic protons, neon and iron particles. Shielding material will vary in material and thickness. These measurements were designed to lead to development of a chromosome model and calculation of the frequency of radiation-caused aberrations.

It is not feasible or cost-effective to lab-test all variations or types of shielding. The product of this research study was an algorithm made into a user-friendly software that allows NASA to predict shielding effectiveness before designing and building spacecraft. In addition, the orientation of cells during irradiation were altered randomly to test the hypothesis that, to be realistic to actual conditions of the body during space flight, cell orientation needs to be altered during radiation exposure.

RESULTS:
The theoretical model developed in this project can be used to predict biological effects such as chromosome aberrations for incident mixed beam combined with mixed beam due to nuclear disintegration caused by shielding materials. The effectiveness of the HZE iron ions for induction of acentric fragment producing chromosome-type aberrations at the first mitosis after irradiation of human GM2149 cells in G0 was not measurably different for incident iron ion energies of 0.3, 0.6, or 1GeV/n. Furthermore, the filtration of 1 GeV/n or 0.6 GeV/n Fe ions with 1.8cm or 5.4 cm of aluminum or 5.5cm or 11.0cm of polyethylene did not measurably alter the effectiveness of the emerging beam. One of the most important conclusions derived from the successful completion of this study is that, based on the current estimate of thicknesses of shielding materials, the biological effects of a mixed beam due to fragmentation processes will not be much different than the un-fragmented and pure beam.

experiment_title: Core Temperature and Circadian Rhythms in Humans During Long-Term Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The circadian timing system (CTS) has been shown to be involved in the coordinated daily variation of almost every physiological and psychological system evaluated thus far. Maintaining synchronized circadian rhythms is important to health and well-being. The investigators hypothesize that long-term space flights significantly affect the synchronization of the circadian rhythm in humans due to changes in body composition, reduced physical activity, and/or changes of heat transfer, thermoregulation, and non-24-hour light-dark cycle in space. Therefore, the investigators aim to investigate the changes of core temperature profiles in humans during long-term space flight. Typically, 36 hour rectal temperature profiles are used to determine any changes associated with the CTS. However, such long-lasting continuous rectal temperature recordings are quite inconvenient for the subjects being investigated, especially during daily exercise and hygiene activities. Therefore, we recently introduced the double sensor, a new non-invasive heatflux method for determining body core temperature. The double sensor is located at the forehead and at the sternum/chest and allows continuous body core temperature measurements for extended periods of time.

Data on circadian rhythm obtained with the double sensor pre- in-, and post-flight shall be correlated with melatonin, which is one of the best-studied hormones following a classical circadian pattern. The results derived from the study might be useful to:

  1. understand the time course and basic principles of the adaptations of the human autonomic nervous system in space,
  2. adjust more adequately physical exercise as well as rest- and work shifts, and
  3. foster adequate workplace illumination in the sense of occupational healthcare to humans in space.

APPROACH:
Pre- and post-flight data collections for circadian rhythms will include 36-hour body temperature monitoring sessions on L-180, L-60, L-30 and postflight on R+7, R+30, R+60. Temperature sensors will be placed on the head and chest and skin surface temperatures will be recorded continuously during 36-hour periods, starting in the evening on Day 1 until the morning of Day 3. Once preflight and once postflight a 24-hour urine collection is planned together with the last preflight and first postflight data recording. Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) measurements is planned once preflight (as close to launch as possible) and once postflight (as close to landing as possible).

Inflight temperature recordings are proposed for FD 15, FD 30, and every 30 days after that until the end of mission (FD 60, FD 90, FD 120, FD 150). During each inflight session, the crewmember will be instrumented with the double-sensors (Thermolab hardware) during the pre-sleep period of Day 1, and body temperature will be recorded continuously for 36 hours until the morning of Day 3.

experiment_title: In-Flight Holter Monitoring
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Cardiac rhythm disturbances have been noted in some crewmembers during space flight. This occurs more frequently in crewmembers on long-duration missions. This experiment investigated whether heart rate exhibited less variability in microgravity than on Earth, if electrocardiographic (ECG) changes occurred during flight, and if changes in ECG related to age occurred during flight.

APPROACH:
Preflight:
The crewmember was trained to don and doff the holter monitor and to complete the Activity Log. Twice preflight, the crewmember donned the holter monitor and wore it for 24 hours. Food, exercise, medications, and sleep were logged during the 24 hour period that the equipment was worn.

In-flight: On a single flight day, the crewmember donned the holter monitor, applied five electrodes to the chest, and attached the lead wires to the electrodes. Food, exercise, medication, and sleep were logged during the 24 hours the equipment was worn. At the end of the 24 hour period, the crewmember doffed the hardware and stowed the holter monitor and activity log.

Postflight: On R+3 days, the crewmember donned the holter monitor and wore it for 24 hours. Food, exercise, medication, and sleep were logged during the 24 hour period the equipment was worn.

experiment_title: Inflight Salivary Pharmacokinetics of Scopolamine and Dextroamphetamine
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Pharmacologic studies of therapeutic agents used by astronauts during space flight need to be performed to compare drug bioavailability and effectiveness during weightlessness with those characteristics under 1-g conditions. To determine the applicability of noninvasive salivary drug monitoring for pharmacokinetic evaluation of therapeutic agents during space flight, three drugs that are frequently used by crewmembers have been selected for in flight study - acetaminophen, a relatively innocuous, common pain relief medication whose disposition characteristics have been well established, and a scopolamine/dextroamphetamine combination, an operational medication used for the treatment of space motion sickness during missions. The feasibility of such an application for salivary drug monitoring depends upon the distribution of detectable levels of the drug into saliva and the establishment of a consistent saliva/plasma (S/P) ratio over the entire disposition profile of the drug.

Ground-based investigations to establish the S/P ratios of scopolamine have been conducted in normal subjects. Following intravenous and oral administration, scopolamine readily distributes into saliva with consistent S/P ratios over the entire disposition profile. In this investigation, the pharmacokinetics of scopolamine/dextroamphetamine following oral administration to crewmembers before and during space flight were evaluated using salivary concentrations to estimate the disposition parameter changes of anti-motion sickness agents during missions.

APPROACH:
Participating crewmembers received an oral dose of 0.4 mg scopolamine and 5 mg dextroamphetamine in combination as a capsule (SMS medication) twice on separate occasions during ground-based studies and once during space flight. Saliva samples were collected at designated time periods for 36 hours using the cotton ball saliva collection kit designed and developed by investigators at the Johnson Space Center (JSC). The saliva samples collected during the first 12 hours post-dosing were divided into two aliquots. Scopolamine concentrations were determined using the RPLC-receptor binding assay in one set of the 12-hour sample aliquots. The remainder of the samples for the entire 36 hour duration of the study was frozen for later analysis to determine dextroamphetamine concentrations.

RESULTS:
Evaluation of the salivary concentration-time profiles indicated that large deviations in the concentration-time profiles of scopolamine in crewmembers occur during space flight when compared to their ground-based control profiles. In one crewmember, a significant decrease in the peak concentration and an increase in the time to reach peak concentration were observed, while opposite results were obtained for another crewmember.

The third crewmember repeated the study twice during the mission, and the changes in both instances were relatively small when compared to the results from the other crewmembers. Large intersubject variability, inadequate sample volumes, and insufficient data make it very difficult to reliably assess the pharmacokinetic behavior of scopolamine in crewmembers during space flight. The use of scopolamine was subsequently discontinued due to its unreliable effectiveness and a reported rebound effect after discontinuing it.

experiment_title: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations:  Sensory-Motor Investigations (SMI)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During space flight, space motion sickness (SMS) and perceptual disturbances have led to reductions in performance efficiency and sense of well-being. During entry and immediately after landing, such disturbances could have a serious impact on the ability of the commander to land the Orbiter, as well as on the abilities of all crewmembers to egress from the Orbiter, particularly in a non-nominal condition or following extended stays in microgravity. An understanding of spatial orientation and motion perception is essential for developing countermeasures for SMS and perceptual disturbances during space flight and upon return to Earth. Countermeasures for optimal performance in-flight and a successful return to Earth require the development of preflight and in-flight training to help astronauts acquire and maintain a dual adaptive state.

This study was intended to enhance the understanding of adaptation to space flight and readaptation after flight on various aspects of human spatial orientation, neurosensory, sensory-motor, physiological, and perceptual functions and on autonomic gastric functions associated with space motion sickness (SMS). This experiment correlated the postflight recovery of postural equilibrium control, head and gaze stability, readaptation changes in vestibular function, and examined the relationship between voluntary oculomotor performance and passive vestibulo-ocular responses following space flight. Changes in stomach nerve response to food consumption over the first few days of flight were to be observed and analyzed, and evaluated when SMS symptoms occurred. The investigators were also interested in how nerve activity correlated with the symptoms before, during, and after their occurrence.

APPROACH:
Protocol A
Voluntary Head Movement (VHM)
Standard electro-oculography (EOG) techniques recorded horizontal and vertical eye position. A head mounted tri-axial rate sensor measured head velocity in the pitch, yaw and roll planes. The BOG and rate sensor signals were collected with the Superpocket physiological monitoring system and recorded on a TEAC cassette recorder. A goggle assembly controlled visual conditions via an electronic shutter, changing instantly from a clear state to an opaque state according to the experiment protocol. A cruciform target and four additional visual targets were mounted on the middeck locker for on-orbit data collection and on a screen during baseline data collection. A microcassette recorder delivered a sinusoidally-modulated audio tone during one portion of the VHM protocol. Tasks performed in-flight were tested pre- and postflight as well. Subjects were asked to report perceptual sensations associated with each stimulus.

VHM Inflight - Four of the six inflight experiments were designed to investigate voluntary oculomotor function. Two additional experiments were performed pre- and postflight only investigated this function. The protocols involved a combination of eye and/or head movements to acquire targets along a visual display. Calibrations of eye and head signals were performed. Each task was repeated three times in both the horizontal and vertical planes. The tasks are described below:

  • Head Calibration - the subject directed a head-mounted laser spot to the central target and moved their head to pre-selected targets in both the horizontal and vertical planes.
  • Eye Calibration - with head fixed, subject acquired a successive sequence of target positions in the horizontal and vertical planes, visually fixating on each target for two seconds.
  • Target Acquisition - a cruciform target arrangement, located 34 inches from the subject's eyes was used to display a series of targets in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Subjects acquired each target with both a head and eye movement.
  • Gaze Stabilization - the subject first visually fixated on a wall-fixed target with the head in a central position. When the goggles became opaque and vision was occluded the subject rotated the head while maintaining ocular fixation on the just-seen wall-fixed target. When the goggles became clear the subject refixated the target with the eyes only. The subject then rotated the head back to center, keeping eyes on the target.
  • Spontaneous/Gaze Nystagmus - was measured with the crewmember fixating on a wall target, and then imagining the same wall-fixed target with vision occluded, and then with the eyes closed. Gaze nystagmus, or the effect of a change in eye position was evaluated by having the crewmember fixate on imaginary 40 degree targets (vision occluded) in both the vertical and horizontal planes for 20 seconds per imaginary target. Measurement of eye movements continued for an additional 20 seconds when the eye position was returned to straight ahead gaze.
  • Sinusoidal Head Oscillations -
    With Vision: Subjects attempted to maintain visual fixation on a wall-fixed target while smoothly oscillating his/her head in yaw or pitch in cadence with an audio tone that is sinusoidally modulated to sweep over the bandwidth of interest (chirp).
    Without Vision: Subject repeated the chirp with vision occluded while attempting to maintain ocular fixation on the remembered location of the target. The subject repeated this entire procedure in each plane for each condition.

    VHM Pre/Postflight

  • Non-Predictable Target Tracking - for these trials, the target was initially stationary in the center of the field of view. At an unpredictable time, the target began to move at constant velocity, either rightward, leftward, upward, or downward. The onset time of target motion, direction of motion, target velocity, and final target displacement was randomized.
    Predictable Target Tracking - the target oscillated at 0.3 Hz. For each trial, tracking was performed for at least six cycles.
  • Positional Nystagmus - spontaneous eye movements were collected with the crewmember in seven different static positions:
    1. Seated upright
    2. Supine
    3. Supine with head turned to the right
    4. Supine with head turned to the left
    5. Supine with head and neck extended over the edge of the examination table (head and neck will be supported by test operator)
    6. Body and head turned to the right side
    7. Body and head turned to the left side

    Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN)
    A binocular Optokinetic Stimulator provided a full visual field optokinetic stimulus during the OKN protocol. Standard electro-oculography (EOG) techniques recorded horizontal and vertical eye position. The EOG signals were collected with the Superpocket physiological monitoring system and recorded on a TEAC cassette recorder. Tasks performed inflight were tested pre and postflight as well. Subjects were asked to report perceptual sensations associated with each stimulus.

    Postural Equilibrium (pre/postflight)
    Measurements pertaining to postural equilibrium were collected using standard electromyography (EMG) techniques on the upper thigh and lower calf segments of the subject's left leg, sway-bars situated at the shoulders and hips, and force transducers situated in the foot plate of the posture platform. In addition, overhead and full field video was recorded through the entire test session. The subject's primary task was to maintain a normal upright stance.

    Head and Gaze Stability During Locomotion (pre/postflight)
    Whole body movement during locomotion on a treadmill and during a jump task was videotaped and the locations of retroreflective markers placed on specific locations on the body were analyzed with the aid of a computerized motion analysis system. In addition, eye movement and leg muscle activity during these tasks were recorded using standard electro-oculography (EOG) and electromyography (EMG), respectively.

    Path Integration ((pre/postflight)
    To examine the cognitive processing of spatial orientation information, whole body movement during locomotion along a previously memorized path (parallelogram or square) were videotaped and the locations of retroreflective markers placed on specific locations on the body were analyzed with the aid of a computerized motion analysis system.

    Protocol B
    This experiment marked the first attempt to obtain measurements of the stomach muscle activity in humans during space flight. In this study, myoelectric activity of the stomach was examined following a meal. Gastric activity associated with space motion sickness was measured using EGG in which electrical impulses associated with stomach secretion and movements were recorded. To perform this EGG, three electrodes were situated on the abdomen.

    Each subject participated in two preflight training sessions which occurred at 12 months prior to launch (L-12) and at 10 months prior to launch (L-10). To compare subject inflight EGG data that were associated with eating to eating under normal ground conditions, there were two baseline data collection sessions. These sessions occurred after both preflight training sessions. During one baseline data collection session, subjects were given fluids and during the other session, they were given a small meal. Subjects fasted for 6.5 hours before a data collection session. When the small meal was consumed, data collection began 20 minutes before the 5 to 10-minute meal and continued for three hours following the meal. To ensure proper and consistent placement of EGG electrodes on the abdomen inflight, a permanent marker was used to mark the correct locations after a meal had been consumed within eight days prior to flight.

    The EGG data were collected using a portable recording instrument designed for space flight. The electrodes amplified the signal at its source and the main part of the recording instrument amplified it further. A one Mb RAM card held twenty-four hours of data. The hardware was lightweight and worn on a belt. It was capable of registering input from the crewmember regarding food or water consumption and SMS symptoms. There were five events that were coded by number: eating, drinking, stomach awareness/discomfort, nausea and vomiting. When a crewmember experienced one of these events, he pressed the event marker with the correct code number and the event with its corresponding Mission Elapsed Time (MET) was recorded. Insertion of event markers did not disrupt data collection or logging.

    The EGG equipment was donned as early as possible in the flight. Continuous data collection occurred for at least the first three flight days. The electrodes, RAM card and battery were replaced every 24 hours.

    RESULTS:
    Protocol A
    Results for this portion of the experiment aren’t available at this time.

    Protocol B
    Crewmembers responded normally to ingestion of a meal preflight, showing an increase in the amplitude and power of the normal three gastric cycles per minute. An abnormal decrease in the dominant power occurred on Flight Day (FD) 1 for all subjects but the response returned to normal on FD3. Individual differences were observed and one crewmember actually showed a slight abnormal preflight response to the meal. All three crewmembers experienced moderate to severe loss of appetite on FD1 and two of them showed mild loss of appetite on FD3. When appetite returned and SMS symptoms resolved, the gastric responses after a meal returned to normal.

    Two nausea events were recorded by one crewmember and one vomiting event was recorded by another crewmember. Percent spectral power was assessed to determine the regularity of normal gastric slow waves. The percent of time that normal waves are recorded by the EGG and the percent of time that abnormal (faster or slower) waves are recorded is the percent spectral power. EGG data showed that in the first episode of nausea 60% of spectral power was associated with deviations in normal contraction cycles before nausea was reported. Forty percent of the power was associated with fewer contractions per minute and 20% was associated with higher contractions per minute. The percent of spectral power associated with these alterations of rhythmic contractions increased to approximately 75% for 15 minutes following the report of nausea, then decreased to about 45%, which was noted at 45 minutes following the nausea report.

    In the second report of nausea, the percent spectral power associated with altered stomach contractions was high (75-80%) throughout the entire period of EGG recording. The researchers speculated that the data indicated that this second report of nausea lasted longer than the first. Also of note was that the first nausea report data corresponded to slower gastric contractions two to three times more than faster ones throughout the entire recording period. In the second episode, data was associated with faster frequency contractions during the time following the nausea report. Other studies have shown that faster frequency contractions are associated with motion sickness as compared to slower frequency contractions.

    Similar to the nausea, the EGG data showed altered stomach contraction rhythms before and up to 30 minutes following the vomiting episode. For this entire time, 75 to 80% of the spectral power was associated with abnormal rhythms. Forty-five minutes after the report the gastric activity was normal. One interesting point is that this crewmember specifically stated that he had no symptoms prior to vomiting, which is a fairly common characteristic of SMS. For both nausea and the vomiting episodes, crewmembers had altered rhythmic gastric contractions at least 30 minutes prior to reporting the symptom.

    The abnormally fast neural myoelectric waves that are detected by EGG have been associated in other studies with decreased spontaneous movement of the stomach and the absence of stomach contractions. Findings in this study indicate that spontaneous stomach movement may be decreased during both mild and severe symptoms of SMS, which occur during the first few days of space flight. The perturbations of this movement may affect absorption of nutrients and oral medications for both astronauts and motion sickness victims on Earth. Since astronauts must treat several physiologic abnormalities that occur in space, it is important that drug absorption and bioavailability be preserved for pharmaceutical effectiveness. Also, crewmembers must maintain adequate nutrition for physically and mentally demanding work, much of which is critical to safety of the crew or the vehicle.

    This investigation utilized a noninvasive technique to successfully record human stomach myoelectric activity in space over a long period. Future work should involve confirmation of these findings and further characterization of the altered stomach rhythms in relation to the presence of nausea and vomiting, especially in regards to the precise timing of the EGG data and the subjective reports of the SMS symptoms. This technique could potentially be utilized for monitoring stomach muscle and nerve conditions as an early warning before SMS symptoms appear. It could also potentially assist flight surgeons in making decisions regarding medication administration and timing. However, in order to function in such a manner, the data would have to be available real-time or near real-time.

experiment_title: A Gene Expression and Histologic Approach to the Study of Cerebrospinal Fluid Production and Outflow in Hindlimb Suspended Rats
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The etiology of the Visual Impairment and Intracranial Pressure (VIIP) syndrome is unknown. It is hypothesized that weightlessness-induced cephalad fluid shift, possibly associated with elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), may play a critical role. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics changes may be involved in the ICP increase. Leveraging on an existing hindlimb suspension (HS) analog in rats, we propose to study the molecular aspects of CSF production and outflow modulation as a result of HS in the tissues involved in these two processes of CSF dynamics, namely choroid plexus (CP) and arachnoid granulations (AG), respectively. On available tissue shared from the parent animal experiment (cohorts 3 and 4), we will perform differential gene expression profiling in the CP and AG of rats subjected to HS and their normal posture controls. In addition, we will compare the ultrastructure of the CP and AG and the histologic localization and distribution of putative targets implicated in CSF dynamics (aquaporins and cellular junction proteins) of the CP and the endothelial cell layer of the venous sinuses, in normal posture and in HR rats within each cohort. The research groups involved in this proposal have the necessary resources and techniques in place at their laboratories in order to maximize the likelihood of success in this project. An anticipated product of this study is the reduction of the uncertainty in the likelihood or consequence of the visual impairment risk by gaining a study tool (validated animal model) and knowledge on the molecular basis of the biological processes involved in CSF dynamics changes generated by HS.

APPROACH:
One of the responses to exposure to the microgravity spaceflight environment is a pronounced cephalic fluid shift. This project tests the hypothesis that this fluid shift is a causative factor in the ocular changes seen in astronauts during and following long-duration spaceflight. The study uses the well-documented rat hindlimb suspension (HLS) model to examine the relationship between cephalic fluid shifts and the regulation of intracranial (ICP) and intraocular (IOP) pressures as well as visual system structure and function. The experimental protocol uses HLS durations of 7, 14, 28, and 90 days. Subgroups of the 90-day animals are studied for recovery periods of 7, 14, 28, or 90 days. All HLS animals have age-matched cage controls. All animals have ad lib access to food and water. A 12:12 LD cycle is present. Eyes are collected at baseline, 7, 14, 28, and 90 days of HLS, and at 7, 14, 28, and 90 days of recovery, for histologic and gene expression evaluations. The study has started with the young adult male, young adult female, and old males cohorts. Comparing data between these cohorts will allow to determine if there is a gender and age difference in the responses. Following completion of these two groups, there will be one additional cohort exposed to elevated CO2 levels similar to those experienced on ISS (International Space Station). This last group will allow to determine if a mild (~1%) hypercapnic environment plays a role in the cephalic shift response and possible development of VIIP (Vision Impairment and Intracranial Pressure).

The continuation of this project entitled "A Gene Expression and Histologic Approach to the Study of Cerebrospinal Fluid Production and Outflow in Hindlimb Suspended Rats" addresses the mechanisms of production and resorption of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain at the molecular and histologic levels, and how these processes are affected by the fluid shift imposed by hindlimb suspension as a model of microgravity.

This study depends on the availability of tissue samples from collaborators at University of California (UC) Davis.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Crew Activities / Maintenance Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA spacecraft utilized prior to the Skylab Orbital Workshop (OWS) contained a habitable volume of 15 cubic meters or less. Within this volume, the crew interfaced with approximately 1,300 controls and displays and 800 stowage items. The Skylab OWS increased the habitable volume to over 340 cubic meters, and the man/machine interfaces to approximately 3,000 controls and displays and over 10,000 stowage items. The ability to operate this complex array of hardware on a daily basis and to produce meaningful scientific results were some of the prime areas for investigation during the Skylab missions.

The Crew Activities/Maintenance Study involved manual dexterity, locomotion, logistics management, maintenance, and various planning functions necessary for creating a favorable daily working routine. The objectives were:

1. To evaluate man/machine relationships by gathering data concerning the crew's ability to perform work in 0-G.
2. To systematically document man's performance.
3. To evaluate the data obtained relative to the design criteria for Skylab missions.
4. To report the evaluations and conclusions in terms useful to the designers of future manned spacecraft and to the planners of future manned missions.

APPROACH:
Because the crew's daily activities limited the opportunities for data collection, the spectrum of daily tasks was carefully evaluated to identify suitable candidates for providing the desired data. Data were obtained via crew comments, 16-mm motion-picture film, and television transmissions.

Film was apportioned and distributed throughout each mission to observe technique changes, as a function of time, to as many different activities as possible by selecting the lowest possible frame rates. Scheduled and unscheduled television transmissions provided near real-time visual cues to assess the ease or difficulty of performing onboard activities. Crew comments were solicited through structured questions and evaluation forms contained in onboard checklists. Ad hoc crew commentary during the missions added to the data bank, and structured postflight debriefings completed the collection and clarification of information.

Logistics Management: To categorize the inventory of re-locatable items onboard Skylab, groupings based on the mass of the item were established. Items weighing less than 5 kilograms (kg) were considered small, items weighing between 5 and 50 kg were considered medium, and items weighing more than 50 kg were considered large. The hypothesis was that subjective crew impressions of the ease or difficulty of handling these items, combined with photographic and television coverage, would lead to a definition of boundaries for mass and dimensions of hardware.

Maintenance: Planning for the Skylab Program, as in previous NASA manned programs, did not include detailed recommendations for the possibility of inflight maintenance. Design reliability and redundancy were supposed to eliminate the need for inflight maintenance. However, a committee was established during the design and production phases to study inflight maintenance, recommend a set of tools, and provide a list of candidate tasks for the missions. A standard set of mechanical tools was recommended, with specific deletions of certain items in a continuous set when no particular task could be identified that required that individual tool. Obvious debris generators (saws, drills, etc.) and all types of test equipment were excluded from the inventory of maintenance equipment to be launched initially. Tasks selected for the experiment involved predominantly simple replacement chores (changing lightbulbs and filters) and numerous remove-and-replace tasks for failed items.

RESULTS:
Mass: The largest mass requiring manual relocation on board Skylab was the food container. Six of these containers were bolted to the grid floor of the forward compartment of the Orbital Workshop (OWS) at launch. Each container had a mass of approximately 100 kg and dimensions of approximately 0.6 by 0.6 by 1.0 meter. During the first day of activation, the Skylab-2 crew moved these containers from their launch location to a permanent stowage rack approximately 6 meters away. The relocation presented no difficulty; even without handles on the containers, the mounting flange served as a natural handle. Numerous other items classified in the large and medium categories were transferred by each crewmember with exceeding ease and efficiency across distances varying from 1 to 20 meters.

Techniques for moving objects varied among crewmembers. A common method for moving items in the medium and large categories involved the crewmember moving the item along the desired path, accelerating himself past the item, and then reorienting himself at the terminal point to catch the item as it arrived.

Items that fell into the lower end of the small category (less than 5 kg) were the ones that presented logistics management problems to the crewmembers. Individual items with masses from a few grams to 1 kg were easily perturbed in 0-G and were extremely difficult to release with no residual motion. Airflow created by the ventilation system was sufficient to move these small objects about quite readily. Also, when several such items were stowed in a common location without means of retention, it was difficult to retrieve one item without upsetting the others. Quite often, the entire inventory would be extracted. The time lost in retrieving and re-stowing such inadvertently freed objects became an irritating perturbation to the timeline.

Size: The limiting factor for handling large objects in 0-G was the cross-sectional area of the item rather than its mass. If a crewmember could see where he and the item being transported were going, he could effect the maneuver very readily. The cross-sectional dimensions of the food containers approached the upper limit of visual obstruction that could be tolerated. The food containers presented a visual obstruction because they had to be aligned and slipped into a rack over the full 1-meter length.

Large items that did not present a visual obstruction were handled very effectively. Several of the Skylab experiment containers were quite massive but had a rather long and narrow configuration. One experiment container slightly less than 2 meters in length with a cross section of approximately 25 by 25 centimeters was transferred from the command module to the forward compartment of the OWS (a distance of approximately 20 meters) without incident. Five hatchways and a short tunnel of less than 1-meter in diameter presented no problems during the transfer.

Very small objects were just as troublesome because of size as they were because of mass. They were easily misplaced, hard to contain in multiple quantity, and not amenable to individual restraint. Clothing pockets were the most efficient transport containers for such objects.

Handling Provisions: Small objects and the majority of the medium objects could be handled as whole objects. When attitude control of the item during transfer became a concern, specific handles (preferably as close to the center of gravity as possible) were needed. In those instances in which one handle resulted in awkward handling characteristics, two handles in opposing positions were deemed appropriate.

Logistics management in a weightless environment required thought in both the design of items to be handled and the actual inflight management of these items. Large masses could be easily unstowed, transported, and restowed, provided they did not obstruct the crewmember's view of the translational path or the stowage interface, and provided the crew had sufficient grasp for easy motion initiation, termination, and attitude control.

Maintenance: Because the need for repair-type tasks seemed unlikely, demonstration tasks were proposed to ensure that representative disassembly, changeout, and reassembly-type tasks would be performed in weightlessness. Less than halfway through Skylab-2, the need for creating these demonstration tasks were conclusively removed. Without the inflight maintenance accomplished by each crew, the Skylab Program would have ended.

The most important lesson learned in the area of inflight maintenance was that man could perform maintenance tasks as readily in 0-G as he could on Earth with proper tools, worksites, restraints, accessibility, procedures, and illumination.

Although various unscheduled repair tasks were distributed among all three manned Skylab missions, each mission had a distinct maintenance character of its own. The anomalies associated with the unmanned launch of the OWS left the Skylab-2 crew with the job of repairing the workshop and rendering it habitable. Consequently, much of the Skylab-2 mission was devoted to effecting major spacecraft repairs and putting the ship into proper order for follow-on use. The Skylab-3 crew was then confronted with the majority of the system and experimental "bugs" that required many man-hours of troubleshooting to locate, isolate, and either correct or recommend corrective action. Thus, the Skylab-4 crew inherited numerous servicing and corrective action tasks.

Tools: For man to be as effective as possible in conducting space flight operation and inflight maintenance, the proper tools and test equipment should be included for performing the required tasks. Skylab crewmembers found a use for virtually every tool they had on board and, in some cases, used ingenuity to fabricate a needed part or tool when it was not available. When a screw broke off the bicycle ergometer pedal during the second mission, the sawtooth and file blades of the Swiss Army knife were used to pry and gouge the fractured remains from the hole. An ensuing scavenger hunt eventually located a suitable replacement item from a mounting bracket on one of the spare urine separators. Thus, not only were the tools important but an appropriate inventory of repair consumables was also necessary.

Two primary complaints were voiced by Skylab crewmembers regarding tools. First, all the necessary tools were not included. Second, if a tool was available, it sometimes did not perform well because of safety requirements that had been imposed to render the tools ready for flight. Most tools were stripped of their original finish and replated with safety-acceptable exterior coatings. This resulted in some instances of poor fits between interconnecting elements such as handles, drivers, extensions, and end fittings.

In categorizing items, tools were considered small and, as such, were subject to the handling problems previously discussed for those objects. The prime nuisance was in transporting tools and repair parts from their stowage location to their use location. The tool caddy used was ineffectual for this job, and tools and parts were usually transported in pants pockets.

Worksite: A manned spacecraft should have a dedicated worksite where inflight maintenance tasks could be performed. A workstation could be permanent or portable and should provide restraints for the item being repaired, the tools used, and the loose pieces resulting from disassembly. Skylab had no such workstation; therefore, the crewmembers had to improvise when performing off-line maintenance tasks.

Numerous sites were chosen as temporary workbenches at different times by different Skylab crewmembers. The eating table in the wardroom was a favorite place as a workstation but the compartment was a high-traffic area and the table was not well suited for the restraint of loose items.

During the Skylab-2 mission, docking probe troubleshooting, verification, and checkout tasks required the services of all three crewmembers; one to hold the probe, one to read the procedures, and one to perform the work (which required both hands). A worksite capable of restraining the object of interest, retaining the tools, and holding the checklist would have freed two crewmembers for other activities.

The Skylab-3 crew sometimes chose to work on the top surface of the ventilation cover that housed the ventilator fan and filter for the Waste Management Compartment (WMC). This unit protruded approximately 1 meter above the surface of the grid floor in the forward compartment and was located approximately 1 meter from the front of the rack of food containers, thus presenting a nearby surface for use as an interim stowage area. Pieces of tape were looped to form an adhesive outer surface when affixed to the food containers, thus providing retention of small parts such as screws, nuts, and bolts.

The most effective worksite was improvised by the Skylab-4 crew. They took many of the small off-line repairs and servicing tasks to the air mixing chamber return-air vent screens in the dome of the OWS. The 60 mesh screens had an air velocity of approximately 1.5 meters per second across the surface and were approximately 0.3 square meters in area. This combination of aerodynamic retention and available useable surface area provided for a suitable workbench. A small bin was created by taping cardboard sides approximately 10 centimeters in height to the screen, thus reducing the tendency of small loose items to be dislodged from the screen by either airflow turbulence or an inadvertent bump by the working crewmember. This principle of aerodynamic retention should find application in the design of a workbench for future vehicles.

Accessibility: Some maintenance tasks had to be performed while systems remained on-line because of the nature of the task or the inability to remove the suspect element for off-line inspection and repair. Particularly for these types of tasks, as well as for those in which the necessary component could be removed, it is important that the crewmember have free access to the task. This aspect of maintainability engineering should be addressed during the design of subsystems to ensure the crewmember can get to the job during flight. Accessibility was of interest both inside and outside the spacecraft because some of the most significant maintenance tasks were performed during periods of extravehicular activity (EVA).

The jammed solar array wing was easily freed by the Skylab-2 crew after they gained access to it. Two of the crewmembers spent the major part of an EVA period trying to position one of them to cut the strap that was holding the wing. An access path to the area would have made the task routine.

During another EVA period, the Skylab-4 crew came across the same situation when trying to position themselves to troubleshoot and repair a malfunctioning antenna within the Earth resources array of experiment equipment. They finally accomplished the task but only after expending considerable time and energy. A path to the worksite and proper restraints in the area of the task also would have rendered this task routine.

The discovery of a malfunctioning coolant loop during the Skylab-3 mission led to a time-consuming and complicated troubleshooting activity in search of the leak that was causing the problem. A multitude of high-torque screws had to be removed to open the access panels and to expose the portion of the system in question. The time and effort required to perform this preliminary activity almost resulted in the cancellation of the actual troubleshooting task. With the access route cleared by the Skylab-3 crew, the Skylab-4 crew was able to repair the coolant loop with replacement coolant in a very routine manner, thus not only rendering the subsystem usable again but also demonstrating the feasibility of such servicing operations in weightlessness.

The Skylab-4 crew performed several activities related to accessibility that resulted in marked improvements in the daily living and working routine. By unbolting and removing three sections of flat metal plate from the wardroom floor, they exposed considerably more grid floor for use as a restraint interface, which improved the efficiency of the activities within that compartment. The crew also cut cardboard sections from checklist covers and used them to construct modules within drawers and close-outs between drawers in the film vault. This action solved the problem caused by loosely stowed components in one drawer floating into a position that jammed the operation of the drawer.

As demonstrated repeatedly throughout the Skylab Program, with proper tools, restraints, accessibility, procedures, and an adequate worksite, man can conduct inflight maintenance tasks as effectively on orbit as he can on Earth. This capability should be incorporated into the planning of future programs from the initial design stages to ensure the most effective use of a crewmember's time. If inflight maintenance could be accepted as a nominal activity, perhaps more cost-effective measures could be taken in designing systems, experiments, and equipment.

experiment_title: Impact of Spaceflight on Primary and Secondary Antibody Responses (Ground study); Tetanus Antibody Response by B cells in Space (TARBIS) (Flight study)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
The spaceflight environment influences immune cell distribution, ex vivo responses to antigen, and cytokine expression. However, few studies have characterized the impact of the spaceflight environment on the host immune response following an in vivo immune challenge, particularly those involving B cells and antibody production. The International Space Station (ISS) provides an ideal laboratory within which investigators can explore this unique environment and its impact on the host response. Through the use of a mouse model (with an immune system that closely parallels that of humans), we will establish a link between exposure to the spaceflight environment and decrements in immune system activation. This study is significant because it will directly test the hypothesis that host immunological health will be compromised in space.

APPROACH:
On-orbit Flight Activities, Procedures, and Timeline
Mice will receive health checks upon unloading and transfer from the Transporter to the Habitat after capsule docking no later than 24 hrs after hatch opening. Animal health will then be monitored daily via continuous video recording from one camera at a time from all of the Habitats on-orbit (including other investigations which may be running concurrently) and down-linked to Ames science staff. Ground personnel shall have the option of programming or manually controlling which camera is being down-linked and recorded at any given time. Water levels will be checked every 3-4 days. After a minimum of 14 days after animal transfer from the Transporter to the Habitat, all 20 mice will be moved to the MSG and receive intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of vehicle, tetanus toxoid (TT), CpG, or CpG + TT (n=5/group).

Ground Activities
Ground controls will be run following spaceflight environmental parameters in orbital environmental simulator(s) (OES) chambers at KSC ACF. Delay between launch and start of environmental controls may be up to 8 days, depending on the logistics and capability of the telemetry system. Mice will be housed in flight Habitats with RFB diet and lixit water to match on-orbit groups. The operations done on ground will be conducted to match the same relative time points during the day/night cycle of the animals on-orbit, so that procedures on ground control mice are conducted at the same points in the animals’ circadian rhythm.

Each experimental group for ground controls will be doubled to improve the statistical significance of the experiment with a total of 40 mice (4 groups of 10). Therefore, 2 Transporters will be required for the flight in orbital environmental simulator(s) (OES) that have been programmed with telemetry data from the flight. At the same relative time point (accounting for delay in starting ground controls after flight) the mice are transferred from the Transporter to the Habitat, the 40 ground control mice will be transferred from the 2 Transporters into 4 Habitats, and maintained in OES programmed with telemetry data from the ISS. OES shall be programmed to mimic the following conditions experienced by the Transport and then the Habitat: CO2, O2, temperature, and humidity.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: MiniCog: A Portable and Fast Assessment of Cognitive Functions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts work in a dangerous and noisy environment, and have extraordinarily compressed work schedules. In addition, they are isolated from friends and family for long periods of time. Thus they may be fatigued, depressed, or anxious. Such stressors conspire to make individual performance and that of the team as a whole, particularly vulnerable to cognitive decrements. It is crucial to assess cognitive ability at regular intervals while astronauts work. In a project funded by the NSBRI, the investigators implemented a portable system, the MiniCog Rapid Assessment Battery (MRAB), which assesses nine different cognitive functions. This system is intended to provide an "early warning alert," indicating when an astronaut or worker is suffering from stress-related deficits, such as fatigue, that may affect performance. One strength of the system is that the assessment is quick. The information can be used by the astronauts or workers themselves, either alone or as part of a team, or by a supervisor. In all cases, users can be warned to pay additional attention and take extra care, or better yet, take a break, consume food or caffeine, or even take a nap.

In this phase of the research, investigators proposed two major goals: First, they wished to extend the MiniCog system by a) programming the software to run on additional operating systems, b) allowing users to predict their performance before and after taking a test (but before seeing their scores, which would be compared with their predictions), c) adding wireless relay capability, and d) by including an additional initial screening test. Second, investigators planned validation studies of the MRAB tests, partly in collaboration with NSBRI team members David Dinges, Philip Lieberman, and Judith Orasanu. In their own lab, they planned to conduct three kinds of studies: 1) correlating scores on MRAB with scores on assessment batteries currently used by NASA; 2) examining the effects on cognitive performance of four factors (anxiety, noise, circadian rhythm, and time-pressure); examining the mitigating effects of three potential countermeasures (a pre-learned short relaxation procedure, vigorous exercise, and caffeine).

APPROACH:
During the second year of the study, investigators initiated a study to address the following question: Is the MRAB capable of detecting the effects of induced anxiety on very specific aspects of performance? Thirty-one participants came to the lab for three one-hour practice sessions within a two-week period. During this time they practiced the tasks eight times. At the end of the two-week period participants returned to the lab for a final session, during which they completed the MRAB tests and a series of mood and cognitive state questionnaires before and after receiving instructions about a stressful public-speaking task they would perform, and then again after they had performed this task.

RESULTS:
Mean state anxiety scores on the Spielberger State Anxiety Inventory (SA) changed significantly only in females, from 38 at the beginning of the session to 47 upon learning that there would be a public-speaking task (and 46 at the end of the session, which was not a significant decrease); in males the scores were 31 and 34 (and 33 at the end), respectively. In contrast, Spielberger reports increases to 50 and 61 (males and females) during a stressful movie. Investigators were hoping the task would induce stress levels similar to the movie condition, but this did not occur, and with the funding shortage, there was no opportunity to redesign the protocol and administer it to more participants. In looking at the MRAB scores of just the female participants during the final session, investigators found an increase from baseline (at the beginning of the session) in ERs on the "cognitive set switching" task (from 1.85% to 4.63% [p<.01] upon learning about the public speaking task) and on the "filtering" task (from 2.91% to 5.49% [p<.01] at the end of the session). However, RTs decreased on other tasks: MR, SWM, and VWM (all tasks for which there were non-significant increases in ERs).

experiment_title: Leg Plethysmography
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Signs and symptoms secondary to fluid shifts in weightlessness were among the first physiologic effects noted in the manned space flight program. These effects included puffy faces, nasal congestion, in-flight and postflight weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiovascular changes. The headward shift of body fluids, both intravascular and extravascular, results from the absence of the 1-g hydrostatic gradient. The purpose of this study was to measure leg volume changes during space flight.

APPROACH:
The stocking plethysmograph, first used on STS-5, 7 and 8, continued to be used for determination of direct girth-length measurements. From a series of circumferential measurements, volume was calculated under the assumption that a truncated cone represents a reasonable approximation of a leg volume segment.

On these later Shuttle flights, the original leg volume protocol was modified to study the time course of leg volume changes; a sequence of measurements were made as early as possible in flight. Furthermore, leg volumes were obtained pre- and postflight during the routine medical stand tests.

RESULTS:
Time course of the fluid shift was determined to be exponential with a time constant of 6-8 hours. A second result seen was the relatively small amount of fluid which is pooled in the legs postflight and the disproportionately large signs of orthostatic stress this induced. Either the blood volume remains small or there is a large pooling elsewhere in the body. There was also a suggestion that a blunting of normal heart rate response may have occurred.

The volume change and percentage change were all compared with the preflight volume determinations. The landing measurements were made within 1.5 hours of touchdown. The postflight measurements were made during the first week post-landing. It should be noted that the 1-g leg volume measurements for Skylab and ASTP were made with the crewmembers in the supine position, whereas the measurements in the Shuttle program were made with the crewmembers standing. When going from standing to supine, there is a shift of approximately 300ml of blood out of the legs.

The in-flight volume changes found in the 11 subjects from the Shuttle program demonstrated a mean volume change of 1026 ml or 11.6% with a range from 1790 ml or 16.9% to 685 ml or 8.3%. The majority of the subjects had a 10% to 12% volume change. This compares with the 12.2% from Skylab and 10.0% from ASTP. The source of this leg volume change is a relatively rapid shift of blood followed by interstitial fluid and probably intercellular fluid, with some tissue loss secondary to muscle atrophy.

experiment_title: Sleep and Wake States in Biosatellite III Monkey: Visual and Computer Analyses of Telemetered Electroencephalographic Data
experiment_description:
Objectives:

It is well established that the different sleep states are necessary in sufficient quantity for the continuance of physiological and psychological well-being. This circadian rhythm, as well as others, can be perturbed by a variety of factors such as unfamiliar surroundings, selective deprivation, rapid travel across time zones, etc. This study was to investigate the effects of the weightless environment on the sleep and wake states in system of the nonhuman primate.

Approach:

Ten EEG, two EOG, and two EMG channels were among the 33 channels of physiological data monitored on Biosatellite III. EEG electrodes were stereotaxically positioned bilaterally in the parietal and visual cortex, the hippocampus, and the amygdala. EOG leads were placed at the right and left outer canthi, and EMG sensors were implanted in posterior cervical and lower scapular sites. Data were telemetered to Earth-based tracking stations at the rate of 22.4 kilobits per second, collected every 97 minutes, and length of capture varied with elevation of spacecraft above the horizon, typically five to seven minutes. The monkey was acclimated to twelve-hour day/twelve-hour night cycle in the capsule.

Results:

The sleep of the Biosatellite III primate in orbital flight was abnormal in amount and bizarre in its distribution. It was characterized by rapid transitions in sleep state, brevity of state, and unusual transitions from one state to another. The monkey never achieved its normal terrestrial cycle, and the remarkable fragmentation of consciousness required meticulous and virtually microscopic scoring of EEG records. A dramatic reduction was noted in REM and stage four sleep. Eye movements, normally only seen in REM, were observed during stage two and stage four sleep. The changes began concurrently with the onset of the weightlessness and were not secondary to altered fluid balance or body temperature. There was a complex response to the independent variable of weightlessness, with a sudden decline on day eight attributable to fluid loss and redistribution of blood in the thorax consequent to zero gravity state. The observed fragmentation of consciousness appeared similar to the sleep of medical patients with high cervical cord transections.

experiment_title: Bacteria and Spores
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Cells are the fundamental building block for all living organisms. The word cells was first coined by physicist Robert Hooke during his examination of a cork slice under a microscope. Complex organisms such as plants and animals are made of many cells that work together. Microorganisms are single cell organisms that are too small to see with the naked eye. Microorganisms were first discovered with the invention of a microscope by the Dutch scientist Anton van Leeuwenhoek. Leeuwenhoek, who made microscopes to count threads in drapery material for his shop in Holland, first described microorganisms as animalcules or little animals. Improvements in microscopes have greatly increased the knowledge of microorganisms and have led to many advances in medicine. However, much is still to be learned about the biological processes of microorganisms. The objective of this experiment was to determine the effects of microgravity on the survival, growth rates, and mutations of certain bacteria and spores.

APPROACH:
Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli were selected from a group of eleven non-pathogenic bacteria species that were screened before the Skylab 2 flight for experiment suitability. Originally planned for one flight on Skylab 2, this experiment was performed a second time on Skylab 4 to collect additional data. B. subtilis and E. coli were grown from broth culture and added to a water solution containing polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). PVA kept the bacteria alive but dormant until the experiment was started. The PVA solution containing bacteria was transferred to a circular disk of filter paper. The PVA suspension polymerized, holding the bacteria forms suspended on the filter paper in a viable state. Each disk was covered with aluminum foil for storage until inoculation. Bacterial growth was initiated by the insertion of the filter disk into agar-filled Petri dishes. Nine of the Petri dishes were placed in an incubator at approximately 95 degrees F and six were incubated at ambient temperature of approximately 77 degrees F. The cultures were periodically observed and photographed by crew members. Bacteria Petri dishes were placed in a food chiller to stop colony growth and preserve the cells for postflight analysis. However, the loss of the Skylab heat shield during launch resulted in a 10 day period where the maximum ambient temperature that the bacteria inoculum discs were exposed to was approximately 120 degrees F. This high temperature may have affected the viability of the bacteria. Inoculation of the Petri dishes with the bacterial disc was performed, however, and the total incubation time was extended from 48 hours to 69 hours. On Skylab 4, Bacillus mycoides was substituted for E. coli because of the failure of E. coli to grow on Skylab 2.

RESULTS:
During Skylab 2, colonies of E. coli did not develop and 75 colonies of B. subtilis developed following inflight inoculation. Bacteria growth rate was slower than expected for the flight cultures, therefore, the incubation time was extended from 48 hours to 69 hours. In addition, the ground control colonies also experienced a slower than expected growth rate. This experiment was repeated on Skylab 4 with B. mycoides substituted for E. coli. However, B. mycoides, like E. coli, failed to grow colonies on Skylab 4. The slower-than-planned growth rate of both flight and ground control colonies was also observed on Skylab 4. In addition, it was observed that there was contamination in the Petri dishes. Overall, bacterial control cultures grew more colonies compared to the Skylab cultures. However, the colonies that grew on Skylab were larger, grew faster, and were more irregular than control colonies. On Skylab 2, B. subtilis colonies were 50 percent larger than control colonies. Individual cells grew larger in diameter, but did not significantly increase in number. In addition, Skylab grown bacteria appeared to be more sensitive to postflight antibiotic treatment.
