experiment_title: Psychosocial Performance Factors in Space Dwelling Groups
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The original aims of this project focused upon the development of an experimental test bed for modeling performance effectiveness and psychosocial adaptation in support of exploratory space flight missions beyond Earth's atmosphere. The research methodology adopted to accomplish these objectives provided for distributed interactive multi-person simulations in computer-generated environments focused upon psychosocial performance interactions within and between space-dwelling flight crews and Earth-based control center groups. The experimental setting provided the automated means for setting the context for the analysis of space crew performance as well as monitoring electronically the interactive effects of simulated communication modality constraints and other environmentally stressful conditions. Distributed interactive simulation experiments characterized the extent to which variations in the structure and function of communication channels within and between space-dwelling and Earth-based groups affect the ability to accurately discern and respond to the realities and requirements of mission operations. The effects of environmentally stressful time constraints as well as the appetitive and aversive characteristics of programmed incentive conditions have been analyzed in the context of spaceflight simulations.

APPROACH:
Newly-initiated studies on management system variations consisted of developing methodologies for assessing crew performance effectiveness under rigid schedule-based management of crew activities by Mission Control versus more flexible, contingency-based, autonomous management of crew activities by themselves. Autonomous management consisted of having a crew arranging all aspects of their exploratory activities. Schedule-based management was simulated by Mission Control-defined performance requirements with regard to ordering and time spent in each geographic region and surface vehicle task assignments, and requiring that this schedule be strictly adhered to. Tests of this methodology have shown clear adverse effects of mission control-defined schedule limitations that resulted in both decrements in crew performance effectiveness and increases in negative psychosocial adaptation self-report measures.

RESULTS:
Newly-initiated studies on workload condition variations were designed to assess crew performance and psychosocial adaptation under longer-duration, 12-hour mission simulations conducted during different parts of a 24-hour circadian cycle (either ‘Early’: 9am–9pm, or ‘Late’: 9pm–9am). ‘Late’ workloads produced significant decrements in individual performances that included reaction time deficits, attentional lapses, psychosocial communication reductions, failures to properly report rule solutions, and inadvertent discarding of high-valued geologic samples. Significant changes occurred in the patterns of positive, negative, and physical self-report ratings following ‘Late’ workload Missions such that positive self-reports decreased while negative and physical self-reports markedly increased. Importantly, in spite of these numerous decrements, crew performance efficiency remained at normal levels. Lapses in individual crewmember performances thus appeared to be compensated for in the overall crew performance, indicating the utility of multi-person crews as countermeasures to failures or reductions in individual performances under adverse workload conditions. Nevertheless, the dramatic decrease in psychosocial communication during late missions could be an early warning sign of crew desynchronization that could hinder crew cohesion and adaptability to malfunctions, environmental disruptions, or schedule demands.

The results of these distributed interactive simulation studies showed clearly that cooperative and productive interactions were maintained between individually isolated and dispersed crewmembers in a task-driven environment. All experimental flight crews actively engaged in communicating and effective problem-solving over extended time intervals without benefit of one another’s physical presence. In addition, investigations of communication modality constraints indicated that there was a high degree of interchangeability between available communication modes as well as use of ‘indexical’ features of the simulation display as countermeasures to maintain effective crew performance. Further, variations in crew configurations (crewmates reassigned to vehicles other than those normally operated) showed clearly that performance effectiveness levels were significantly reduced during missions in which crew assignment changes resulted in inexperienced, or “Weak” crew configurations, as contrasted with highly-experienced, or “Strong” crew configurations. Crew composition variations were also shown to have effects upon group dynamics that were not necessarily reflected by the crew performance measures. Finally, studies of positive and negative incentive conditions on crew performance effectiveness have shown increased performance effectiveness under both positive and negative incentive conditions, but an adverse change in psychosocial adaptation – i.e., negative incentive conditions characterized by a pronounced increase in negative self-report ratings accompanied by decreased positive self-report ratings, and positive incentive conditions characterized by positive self-report ratings only. Thus incentive conditions associated with simulated spaceflight missions can significantly affect psychosocial adaptation without compromising task performance effectiveness in trained and experienced volunteer crews.

experiment_title: Magnifying Lens Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to observe changes in the relationship between head and eye movements due to wearing 2.2x magnifying telescopic lenses. This study was conducted in the late 1980’s. Pre-studies were conducted with in-house subjects prior to the Magnifying Lenses Study which was composed of 10 subjects.

APPROACH:
Study 1, Magnifying Lenses Study: 5 in-house subjects participated in this study. Each subject had electrodes placed above and below the right eye. Dark adaptation was accomplished by the subject wearing red goggles for 20 minutes prior to data collection. The subject was placed approximately 26 inches from a center target with 1 LED 3.25 inches above and below it.

After a pre-test eye calibration (tracking LEDs with eyes), rectangular head calibration (moving head up and down and pausing at limits) and a sinusoidal head calibration (moving head back and forth between limits as directed by a tone @0.5 hz and +/- 7.5 deg displacement), an initial baseline was collected for fixation of an actual target condition and fixation of an imaginary target condition. At this point, the subjects donned the magnifying goggles. Red plastic was placed behind the lenses to maintain dark adaptation. Data was collected immediately for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. Hereafter, data was collected every 8 minutes for both target conditions. After 40 minutes the magnifying goggles were removed and the red goggles were immediately donned. Data was immediately collected at 0, 8 and 16 minutes for both target conditions. Each test concluded with post-test and eye calibrations.

This protocol is unique in that it requires the subject to focus on a center target while making voluntary pitching head movements as directed by a tone. A “beep” at each limit helped the subject match the head movement with the tone. The head movements and the fixation on the center target were continuous throughout the entire test. During the data collection, which lasted 55 seconds, the subjects were asked to fixate an actual or imagined target without blinking. Blinking was acceptable during times data was not collected.

Study 2, Shorter Duration Magnifying Lenses Study: This protocol was modified from the earlier one. The duration of the test protocol was approximately 35 mins. Five in-house subjects participated in this study. Each subject had electrodes placed above and below the right eye. Dark adaptation was accomplished by the subject wearing red goggles for 20 minutes prior to data collection. The subject was placed approximately 26 inches from a center target with 1 LED 3.25 inches above and below it.

After a pre-test eye calibration (tracking LEDs with eyes) and a sinusoidal head calibration (moving head back and forth between limits as directed by a tone@ 0.5 hz and +/- 7.5 deg displacement), an initial baseline was collected for fixation of an actual target condition and fixation of an imaginary target condition. At this point the subjects donned the magnifying goggles. (Red plastic was placed behind the lenses to maintain dark adaptation.) Data was collected immediately for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. After 2 mins, data was again collected for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. At this point, the magnifying lenses were donned and data was collected for both fixation conditions at 0, 5, and 10 mins (after donning the magnifying lenses). After 10 mins, the magnifying lenses were removed, and the subjects donned the original dark adaptation goggles. Data was collected for both fixation conditions 0 and 3 mins after removing the magnifying lenses. Each test concluded with post-test head and eye calibrations.

This protocol is unique in that it required the subject to focus on a center target while making voluntary pitching head movements as directed by a tone. A “beep” at each limit helped the subject match the head movement with the tone. The head movements and the fixation o the center target were continuous throughout the entire test. During the data collections, which lasted 55 seconds, the subjects were asked to fixate an actual or imagined target without blinking. Blinking was acceptable during times data was not collected.

Study 3, Magnifying Lenses Study After Wearing Lenses During 1 Hour of Normal Routine Activities: Two in-house subjects participated in this study. Each subject had electrodes placed above and below the right eye. Dark adaptation was accomplished by the subject wearing red goggles for 20 minutes prior to data collection. The subject was placed approximately 26 inches from a center target with 1 LED 3.25 inches above and below it.

Data was collected in two separate sessions on the same day. Eye and head calibrations were performed in each session. During Session 1 data was collected at 0, 5, and 10 mins after initiating pitching head movements for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. After completing data collection in Session 1, the subject was disconnected from the head and eye movement monitoring system and donned the magnifying lenses. The subject wore the magnifying lenses for 1 hour, performing normal routine activities at work (walking, reaching for objects, etc.). After the 1 hour of wearing the lenses, the subject was reconnected to the head and eye movement monitoring system. Data was collected at 0, 4, and 10 mins after initiating pitching head movements for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. The magnifying goggles were then removed and replaced by the original dark adaptation goggles. Data collection for both fixation conditions was collected at 0, 5, and 10 mins after removal of the magnifying goggles.

This protocol required the subject to focus on a center (actual or imagined) target while making voluntary pitching head movements as directed by a tone. A “beep” at each limit helped the subject match the head movement with the tone. The head movements and the fixation on the center target were continuous only during the two separate test sessions. During the data collections, which lasted 55 seconds, the subjects were asked to fixate an actual or imaged target without blinking. Blinking was acceptable during times data was not collected.

Passive Pitch Magnifying Lens Study

Method: Test subjects were recruited for two 1-hour (approximate) test sessions. During one test session the subjects wore the magnifying lenses. During the other test session, the subject wore dark adaptation goggles. The subjects wore electrodes by placing infant EKG electrodes (silver/silver-chloride) above and below each left eye after scrubbing the surface of the skin around the eye with an alcohol swab.

After electroding, the subjects dark adapted for 20 minutes, using the standard red goggles. Each subject was then restrained in a comfortable position in the prototype Mode C PAT chair. At this time the LEDS were attached. The subject either continued to wear the red goggles or exchanged them for the magnifying lens goggles. (The starting condition of wearing the magnifying lenses or the dark adaptation goggles was alternated between subjects. The subjects never wore the magnifying lenses until they were seated in the Mode C. The dark adaptation is maintained throughout the test as red plastic is placed in front of the magnifying lenses.) A Velcro foam-padded strap secured the subject’s head to the chair rest.

An eye calibration system consisting of two leads and a center target were placed in the center of the subject’s field of view. The subjects directed which way the system should be moved (up, down, left, right,) so that both LEDs could be seen and the center target was in their straight-ahead gaze. The magnifying lenses established the viewing constraints due to the limited field of view (approximately 15 degs). The LEDS were placed vertically approximately 2.5 inches apart and approximately 32 inches from the subject.

Data was not ready to be collected. The subjects were instructed to gaze at the center target while the amplifier was reset. When the LEDs lit, the subjects were instructed to track the lights, trying to make clean, smooth, and sharp eye movements. The subjects were instructed to fixate on the particular LED that was lit at the time until the next one came on, trying not to anticipate the lighting of the other LED. The subjects were instructed that they should not move their head in any way during the 30 minute test.

During each test, data (eye calibrations) was collected 6 times over 30 minutes. The duration of each data collection was 30 seconds. Between data collections, the subjects were passively pitched for 5 minutes in the Mode C at a frequency of 0.5 hz and an amplitude of +/- 7.5 degs. During the passive tilt, the subjects fixated on the center target.

RESULTS:
Although not clear in all cases, it appears that there is a much greater decrease in amplitude across time when the subjects wear the magnifying lenses than when they wear the standard dark adaptation goggles.

experiment_title: Self-guided Depression Treatment on Long-duration Space Flights: A Continuation Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Depression could present a threat to the success and safety of long-duration space missions, and crews need the ability to manage it effectively. The primary objective of this study was to develop a self-guided interactive multimedia program that is capable of facilitating clinical improvement in persons with depression, when used in an entirely self-help format. Software developed through this study enables evidence-based treatment for depression to be made available to astronauts at any time in any location. It could be used autonomously or in combination with other medical resources.

Specific Aims:
1. Complete the development of a training module to recognize and prevent depression.
2. Develop a module to implement computer-based Problem-Solving Treatment (PST), an evidence-based treatment for depression.
3. Evaluate the efficacy of the computer-delivered PST module for depression in a randomized controlled trial.

APPROACH:
The methodologies for this study are embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
To address Aim 1, investigators produced a brief training video, in which Dr. Mark Hegel discusses the signs and symptoms of depression, how it can affect performance, and how it can be treated. A self-assessment of depression was created in a previous study, and already exists in the system. There is evidence from other studies that going through a course of PST can help prevent the future onset of depression in at-risk populations. Therefore, Aim 1 was addressed via the training video and the PST program, itself.

Addressing Aim 2 was the most challenging and time-consuming part of this project: designing and producing a fully-automated self-treatment program for depression. The end product was a six-session interactive media program in which users are guided step-by-step through a full course of PST, an evidence-based treatment for depression. Each session involves a coach (Dr. Mark Hegel, a psychologist who is an expert in PST) who appears in numerous video and audio clips to help users/patients proceed through the stages of the treatment. The program was designed to exercise a form of "clinical judgment," by helping users/patients troubleshoot ways to improve their work on particular problems. The program also tracks 9 variables which are utilized to analyze the user's/patient's work across sessions and problems, and give suggestions on how to improve their problem-solving success, in general. This work has resulted in what appears to be the most sophisticated self-help program ever developed, in terms of media usage and data handling. It includes 247 audio and 160 video files to tailor the PST session to the individual.

Aim 3 was addressed via a randomized clinical trial pilot study, comparing the PST program to a seven-week waitlist control condition. Investigators had originally planned to include 68 persons with minor depression in the study; however, the time required to complete development of the PST intervention program precluded enrolling this number. Therefore, they enrolled 14 persons in a pilot study (7 in the experimental group and 7 in the control group). The mean age of participants was 50 years, and all had completed at least 4 years of college, making them somewhat analogous to the astronaut population. The primary outcome was depression, as measured via the Hamilton Depression Inventory (HDI). No differences were found between groups on the HDI at pre-test.

The investigators partnered with another NSBRI study (PI: Dr. Gary Strangman), by sharing some participants. Participants were to be evaluated via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and near-infrared spectroscopy at three points: pre-treatment, mid-treatment (between sessions 3 and 4) and post-treatment. Unfortunately, MRI malfunctions and scheduling problems caused two of the seven participants assigned to the experimental group to have a four- and a nine-week lapse between sessions three and four. Because their a-priori study procedures called for participants who lapse for more than three weeks between sessions to be removed from the study, data from these two participants were not included in the final analysis. Investigators did, however, allow them to complete the final three sessions, since they wished to continue and had not caused the lapse of time. Also, one control group participant dropped out, leaving six in that group.

Percent change was compared using Kruskal-Wallis Chi Square at pre- and post-treatment for the experimental group and pre- and post- a no-treatment period of seven weeks for the control group. A 52.65% reduction in depression was found for the five experimental group participants, whereas an 11.12% reduction was found for the control group. The difference in percent change was significant (p<.04), and an extremely high effect size was found (Cohen's d=1.73).

It is notable that if data from the two persons who lapsed longer than two weeks is included, the percent change is not significant, which suggests that if the treatment is used as recommended (i.e., with no more than a three-week lapse between sessions), it is likely to help, but if not used as recommended, it is unlikely to help. It is also notable that no subjects ever "no-showed" for a scheduled PST session with the software.

experiment_title: Optimization of Root Zone Substrates (ORZS) for Reduced-Gravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Many long-term space flight life-support scenarios assume the use of regenerating green plants to provide food supplies for crewmembers, as well as to recycle waste products. To date, Brassica rapa (turnip), Apogee wheat, and four species of salad plants have grown in microgravity throughout their useful life cycles, with wheat and Brassica producing viable seeds in nearly normal amounts and quality. These successes came at the end of nearly a decade of repeated efforts using the same equipment to arrive at the optimal settings for substrate moisture and oxygen. The Optimization of Root Zone Substrates (ORZS) for Reduced Gravity Experiments program, an NASA Research Announcement project managed at the Space Dynamics Laboratory (SDL) as part of SDL's Space Plant Technology program, was developed to provide direct measurements and models for plant rooting media that will be used in future Advanced Life Support (ALS) plant growth experiments. The goal of this program is to develop and optimize hardware and procedures to allow optimal plant growth to occur in microgravity. Key to this effort is validating wet substrate oxygen diffusion calculations. While the measurements appear simple and well studied in agricultural soils on earth, collecting repeatable results at high water contents in the coarse-textured growth media required for microgravity requires a modified approach. Collecting accurate data under both 1-G and microgravity conditions and correctly interpreting these data at reasonable cost requires careful management and organization, and expert technical microgravity experience. Only a few microgravity substrate water management experiments have been conducted. ORZS will be the first experiment to directly measure oxygenation parameters in wet substrates. ORZS is a joint venture between the Space Dynamics Laboratory (SDL) at Utah State University and the Institute of Biomedical Problems (IBMP) in Moscow, Russia. SDL has designed, fabricated, assembled, and partially tested the hardware and software. IBMP completed the testing and certification of the hardware. IBMP also assisted in training the Russian crewmembers on this hardware, which will be launched on a Progress flight and housed in the Russian module on the International Space Station (ISS). SDL has a cooperative agreement with IBMP to conduct a joint experimental effort to satisfy the ORZS scientific and modeling requirements. This combined program is developing a new hardware module, the Lada Module for the Investigation of Substrates (LADA-MIS), to conduct the experiment.

The objectives of the ORZS program are to:
1. Determine optimum conditions for plant growth with each substrate type through side-by-side gas exchange and moisture-level controllability experiments in microgravity. These comparisons include substrates that have been adapted by the Photosynthesis Experiment and System Testing and Operation (PESTO) and Microgravity Plant Nutrient Experiment (MPNE)-02 experiments, along with more theoretically describable substrates. These substrates are likely to be used in future NASA payloads. The wetting and water level control will be managed using the best available management protocols.
2. Develop mathematical relationships to model microgravity gas diffusion, and compare results to ground measurable substrate properties. Tools will be provided that will allow experiment designers to extend results to new substrates to achieve conditions not available with current media and management protocols.
3. Organize the relationships developed into an extended, validated substrate design and management procedure and publish it to support future experiment and ALS system designs.

APPROACH:
After the hardware is delivered to ISS and set up, the system runs autonomously, performing repeated cycles of wetting and drying the diffusion cells. Data is collected during all experiment phases. Russian crew participation includes the initial set up, periodic photo sessions, and oversight of regular data downlinks.

RESULTS:
Samples from the ORZS investigation were returned to Earth for analysis by the experiment team. Data from the flight system of gas diffusion cells with different substrates will be compared with results from similar ground control gas diffusion cells to describe gas diffusion in microgravity.

experiment_title: Particle Radiation-Induced Dysregulation of Protein Homeostasis in the Brain
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The space atmosphere is comprised of wide spectrum of highly energetic and charged particle radiation. Exposure to this type of radiation in the galacto-cosmic environment or unplanned solar particle events (SPE) may pose a potential health hazard to humans in long-term manned space explorations. In this project, investigators aim to conduct in-depth investigations of those cellular pathways that regulate the removal of damaged proteins, repair of DNA damage, and response to conditions of oxidative stress through protein modifications in the brain. Protein modification by ubiquitin is a highly regulated process that is catalyzed by specific enzyme families that are capable of modifying the correct protein in the correct cellular location at the correct time in order to control important processes such as the maintenance of genomic stability, cell cycle progression, removal of damaged or misfolded proteins, impaired autophagy, apoptosis, and gene transcription. Depending on the radiation dose and beam quality, particle radiation may cause significant damage to proteins and oxidative stress in the cells in the central nervous system, leading to dysfunction of the cellular ubiquitin-related pathways, an increase in the levels of extracellular ubiquitin, and persistent subsequent downstream effects on regulation of stress-associated signaling pathways in many different cell types within the central nervous system (CNS), precipitating neurodegenerative disease.

Investigators hypothesize that quantitative changes in cellular ubiquitin pools occur when neuronal cells are exposed to particle radiation and aim to study the impact of protein degradation after particle radiation using both in vitro and in vivo model systems. Information gathered from this research will aid in reducing the uncertainties associated with predicting risks both in the estimation of risk to astronaut health and the design of appropriate countermeasures to ameliorate any potential negative effects in space flights.

APPROACH:
Brain tissues from different regions of the brain, including the hippocampus, cerebellum, cortex of C57Bl6 mice were harvested at 1 and 8 weeks post proton irradiation. Investigators also analyzed archived brain tissues from C57Bl6 mice that were irradiated with 1 GeV/u Iron ions and maintained for 11 weeks post irradiation. These tissues were derived from their previous NASA-funded work.

Three primary mouse neuronal stem cells in suspension and one Human Neural Stem Cells in monolayer were used in these studies. Cells were thawed and cultured using vendor-recommended protocols 1 week prior to proton irradiation.

Animals and cell cultures were irradiated with a single dose of 50 or 100 cGy of 250 MeV protons. Proton beam dosimetry was conducted on the day of the exposure. Average dose rate was approximately 30 cGy/minute.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. However, preliminary results are available.

Archived brain tissues from the hippocampus of C57Bl6 mice that had been irradiated with 100 cGy of 1 GeV/n Iron ions and harvested at 11 weeks post irradiation were analyzed. Tissue sections were digested and processed using the methodology that investigators have developed previously for accurate quantitative analysis of ubiquitin-related pathways and networks employing liquid-chromatography coupled to a hybrid, high resolution linear ion-trap/Orbitrap tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) system. Results show significant increases in polyubiquitin (pUb) chains linked through Lys-48, Lys-63, and Lys-11 in hippocampal tissue of both male and female mice after Fe-irradiation relative to the sham irradiated controls. In particular, Lys-63-linked chains relative to controls for the hippocampus from irradiated mice were 2.69-fold higher (p=0.017, n=3) for males and 2.62-fold higher (p=0.0077, n=3) for females. Such increases in pUb chain linkages are common hallmarks to most neurodegenerative diseases.

Approximately 1100 proteins were identified in the samples and comparisons of relative changes among these will yield more detailed information on which specific pathways are most affected. Among these, a number of proteins known to play significant roles in neurodegenerative diseases were differentially expressed in the Fe-irradiated hippocampus tissue. Neurogenic differentiation factor 2 (NDRF) (p=0.01) is one such candidate protein.

Primary mouse neuronal stem cells in suspension and one Human Neural Stem Cells in monolayer were irradiated with 0.5 and 1 Gy 250 MeV protons. Cellular proteins were harvested from these cells at 24 hours post irradiation.

Quantitative results for Lys48-linked polyubiquitin in human cultured neuronal stem cells showed that a single 1 Gy exposure of protons resulted in a significant increase in polyubiquitin-linked peptides (p=0.04) in the human neural stem cells at 24 hours post irradiation. However, there was no difference in the level of polyubiquitin-linked proteins in the three different mouse neuronal stem cell types. These results point to differences in protein processing between the human and mouse-derived neuronal cells. Investigators intend to repeat this study with different time points to better understand the kinetics of protein degradation as a function of radiation dose and beam quality.

In conclusion, results show that long-term changes in protein turnover pathways related to the ubiquitin proteasome system can occur in specific brain regions as a result of exposure to particle radiation.

experiment_title: Morphometric and EM Analysis of Tibial Epiphyseal Plates From Cosmos 1887 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Studies have shown that bone formation ceases during space flight, that the matrix formed during flight does not mature normally, and consequently cannot mineralize normally. The cartilaginous epiphyses of the long bones of space rats have received less attention, even though some of the changes that are seen in bone (e.g. decreased length and decreased trabecular mass) must originate in the epiphyseal region. The objectives of the present study were to look for differences in plate parameters and cell and matrix ultrastructure, in proximal tibial epiphyseal plates of space-flown rats.

Approach:

Light and electron microscopy studies were carried out on decalcified tibial epiphyseal plates. Height and cell number per zone and plate, shape of plates, and size of collagen fibrils were determined. A series of micrographs were taken in each zone, and measurements of collagen fibril length and width were made using a digitizing tablet. Means per section were averaged to obtain means per animal and statistical analysis was performed.

Results:

Flight animals had more cells than synchronous controls in the proliferative zone, and less in the hypertrophic/calcification region. The total number of cells, however, was significantly higher in flight animals. No differences were found for perimeter or shape factor of growth plates, but area was significantly lower in flight animals in comparison to synchronous controls. Collagen fibrils in flight animals were shorter and wider than in synchronous controls. The time required for a cell to cycle through the growth plate is 2-3 days, so most of the cells and matrix present were formed after the animals had returned to 1 g, and probably represent stages of recovery from microgravity exposure.

experiment_title: Evaluation of Thermoregulation During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Impaired thermoregulation may have significant impact during space flight operations such as extravehicular activities (EVA), entry, landing and egress. Impaired thermoregulation, as represented by an increase in core (intestinal) temperature in response to a given thermal load, has been consistently observed in subjects confined to bed rest or immersed in water (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Further, these changes were observed during exercise following these simulated microgravity exposures (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Similar changes were expected to occur during space flight.

This impairment of temperature regulation may be manifested as decreased exercise capacity and increased orthostatic intolerance; it may also be manifested as higher levels of core body temperature for a given level of work (oxygen consumption, Vo2) both during and after space flight. The higher core temperatures may be due to altered cutaneous vasodilatory reflex (delayed onset of vasodilatation and decreased skin perfusion for a given level of core temperature), increased sweating threshold, and decreased sweating sensitivity, while heat production might not be altered. The purpose of this preliminary experiment was to assess human core (intestinal) temperature and thermoregulatory responses to exercise after adaptation to long-duration spaceflight. Specific objectives of this experiment were to:

1) Determine whether overall thermoregulation is impaired during space flight by comparing core temperature (Tin) during two submaximal levels of aerobic exercise preflight, inflight, and postflight;

2) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by altered heat production, as calculated by indirect calorimetry;

3) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by impaired heat loss, as assessed by the skin blood flow/core temperature relationship (where changes in skin blood flow are measured pre- and postflight by laser Doppler flowmetry, and estimated during all tests by calculations of tissue conductance) and by the sweating response. Local sweat response/core temperature relationship was measured pre- and postflight using a dew point hygrometer, and total body sweat loss is estimated during all tests by measuring body weight loss.

It was anticipated that, for a given absolute level of work, body temperatures would increase to a greater degree due to (1) a smaller production and/or decreased efficiency of evaporation of sweat, and (2) decreased convective heat loss from the surface of the skin.

APPROACH:
This investigation examined body temperatures (skin and core), heat production (indirect calorimetry), and evaporative heat loss during 2 standard levels of exercise (40% and 65% of preflight VO2peak).

Submaximal Cycle Exercise Test (before and after flight) - Graded maximal cycle exercise testing was first conducted to volitional fatigue on 2 crewmembers in the supine position. These sessions occurred 2-3 days before the preflight submaximal exercise tests, repeated during the last 5 days of the mission, and 6 days after landing (R+6). The graded maximal cycle exercise test protocol consisted of:

  • 5 minutes of supine rest on the ergometer
  • 2 minutes of warm-up at 50 Watts (W)
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 100 W
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 125 W
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 150 W

    After the 150-W segment of the protocol, exercise intensity was increased by 25 W-per-minute until the subject could no longer maintain the 75-rpm pedaling frequency. Cool down was conducted at 50 W for 3-5 minutes after maximal exercise. During each maximal test, oxygen (O2) uptake and carbon dioxide (CO2) production were measured and averaged over 30-s intervals using a gas analysis system. Heart rate was continuously monitored with a standard electrocardiogram (ECG). Blood pressure was measured during the last 30 seconds of each exercise level using manual sphygmomanometry. The highest level of O2 uptake, averaged over a 60-s period, was designated peak oxygen consumption (VO2peak). Exercise intensities requiring 40% and 65% of the preflight peak value were used during the submaximal tests.

    The supine submaximal cycle tests were conducted 145-146 days before flight (L-145) and on R+5. All testing was performed at room temperature (22.6-23.3°C; 56-64% humidity) and at the same time of day to mitigate circadian effects. Postflight sessions occurred during the summer (July, 1995), but the crewmembers were almost exclusively confined to air-conditioned buildings. The submaximal exercise tests consisted of a continuous protocol of the following:

  • 20 minutes of quiet rest
  • 20 minutes of exercise at 40% preflight VO2peak (50 or 60 W)
  • 20 minutes of exercise at 65% preflight VO2peak (100 or 110 W)
  • 10 minutes of quiet resting recovery

    Heart rates during submaximal exercise were monitored with a heart watch. Blood pressure was measured twice before exercise and every 10 minutes during exercise with a manual sphygmomanometer. Skin temperatures were measured continuously with four external skin thermistors (forearm, calf, thigh, chest) and recorded with a data logger. Core temperature was measured using a small ingestible telemetry thermal sensor pill that was ingested 6 hours before exercise. Temperature data was sampled every 30 seconds and stored in a receiver.

    Skin blood flow velocity was measured continuously with a laser Doppler skin blood flow monitor using an integrated probe attached to the forearm with a local skin-heating (38°C) collar. Local sweating rate at the upper quadrant of the chest was measured continuously with a dew point hygrometer sweat system. The dew point sensor was ventilated (500-800 ml· min-1) with ambient air from the room. Subjects towel dried after each exercise session and were weighed in the same dry gym shorts before and after exercise. All measurement devices were calibrated before each exercise session.

    Submaximal Exercise Test (during flight): No submaximal data was collected during flight due to the late arrival of the Spektr module and scheduling problems after the module arrived.

    RESULTS:
    These results should be viewed as preliminary results only, since the low number of subjects did not allow for statistical analysis of the data. However, the results do suggest that thermoregulation was impaired following long-duration space flight.

    Maximal Exercise: The preflight maximal exercise supine cycle VO2peak values for the subjects were 32.6 and 29.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. Due to the limited active muscle mass with this form of exercise, these supine cycle values were each approximately 20% lower than the measured upright treadmill VO2peak values. During flight, Subject 1 was reported to have performed approximately 70% of the standard prescribed Russian countermeasure program (which consists of approximately 2 hours each day of aerobic and resistive exercises), while Subject 2 was reported to have performed less than 70% of the prescribed countermeasures. Near the end of the mission, on flight day 112, Subject 1 had a cycle VO2peak of 27.2 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 17% from preflight); for Subject 2, the value was 20.8 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 29%). After flight, neither crewmember could complete the exercise protocol, stopping after 28-29 minutes. Postflight, cycle VO2peak on R+6 was further reduced to 23.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subject 1 (reduced 28% from preflight). For Subject 2, no value was obtained because the medical monitor would not allow the postflight maximal exercise test to be performed because of the subject's delayed recovery from the mission.

    Submaximal Exercise: Both crewmembers were able to complete the preflight submaximal exercise protocol; final exercise heart rates were only 137 and 123 bpm for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. On R+5, Subjects 1 and 2 could not complete 11 and 12 minutes of the 65% VO2peak level, respectively. In both cases, the medical monitor terminated the test shortly after the exercise heart rate exceeded the preflight response. In each case, the subject appeared fatigued and was having difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency.

    Blood pressure responses to exercise were similar before and after flight. Oxygen uptake on R+5 was similar to preflight values, except at the last sampling time for Subject 1, where the lower value was most likely due to his difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency. The Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) value was higher at most sampling times on R+5.

    A consistent difference was not seen between pre- and postflight supine resting skin temperatures at any measurement site. Resting intestinal temperature was similar preflight and at R+5. During postflight exercise, the core temperature, (Tin, ingestible telemetry pill) at test termination was similar (37.8 degrees C for both subjects despite a 29% shorter exercise time and a 40% reduction in the total cumulative work (W• min-1).

    The sweating and skin blood flow responses for the two subjects were altered postflight. The slope of the sweating/Tin relationship (mg• min-1• cm-2• °C-1) was reduced from 4.5 preflight to 2.1 postflight for Subject 1 and from 11 to 3.6 for Subject 2. The slope of the skin blood flow/Tin relationship (percent change Perfusion Unit• °C-1) was also reduced from 346 preflight to 214 postflight for Subject 1 and from 214 to 143 for Subject 2. Tin thresholds for the onset of sweating and vasodilation were not altered in a consistent manner after flight. For sweating, Tin thresholds (°C) were 37.4 preflight and 37.6 postflight for Subject 1 and 36.6 and 36.6 for Subject 2. For skin blood flow, Tin thresholds were 37.3 preflight and 37.5 postflight for Subject 1 and 37.6 preflight and 37.7 postflight for Subject 2. Total body sweat (weight) loss during preflight exercise was 636 g vs. 272 g postflight for Subject 1 and 455 g vs. 45 g postflight for Subject 2. Subject 2 had just reached the sweating threshold postflight when the session was terminated. Body weight on R+5 was reduced in both crewmembers from the preflight value--for Subject 1 by 0.8 kg and for Subject 2 by 2.3 kg.

    In conclusion, these preliminary findings suggest alteration of heat loss responses in two crewmembers following a 115-day space flight. The sensitivity of the heat loss responses was reduced after long-duration space flight, resulting in a faster rate of increase in core temperature.

experiment_title: Assessment of Human Factors: Effects of Vibration on Visual Performance During Launch
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Short Duration Bioastronautics Investigation (SDBI) 1904 is an operational assessment of visual performance during the concomitant vibration and g-loading that is experienced during space craft launch. The goal of the visual performance SDBI is to provide supplementary data that is collected by the seat vibration Detailed Technical Objective 695 (DTO 695). While the DTO 695 data alone are important in terms of providing a measure of vibration and g-loading, human performance data are required to fully interpret the impact of the vibration values collected as part of the DTO 695.

The primary objective of human factors SDBI 1904 is to determine visual performance limits during operational vibration and g-loads, specifically through the determination of minimal useable font size using planned Orion display formats. Data will be collected during the ascent phase of three shuttle missions.

The Constellation Program (CxP) Thrust Oscillation Focus Team (TOFT) has requested assistance in development of CxP unimpeded crew performance specifications. Testing was done during the Gemini program to determine vibration amplitude and frequency acceptability for crew performance under increased g-loads. These studies were never systematically validated with flight data, and were performed using Gemini era displays and controls, as opposed to the glass cockpit concepts currently planned for future exploration vehicles. This SDBI will qualitatively measure middeck crew visual performance, and will be conducted in conjunction with DTO 695 that will gather vibration and linear acceleration data on crewmember seats during launch. The results of the DTO and SDBI will give the CxP TOFT and the Human Systems Integration Group (HSIG) flight data on which requirements will be based, and can be further validated during ground testing. Both SDBI 1904 and DTO 695 are low impact with respect to flight resources, and combined they represent an efficient and focused problem solving approach.

APPROACH:
The collection of human visual performance limits and Orbiter seat vibration data will allow the CxP to develop unimpeded crew performance specifications. These data are requested to be collected on three flights, with three middeck crewmembers per flight (targeting crewmembers in seats 5, 6, and 7). Operationally relevant data is required to mitigate thrust oscillation problems with Ares 1/Orion, including appropriate display and control design.

Prior to flight, Astronaut Support Personnel (ASP) will mount the three placards (approximately 22” X 28”) on the desired middeck locker locations. During ascent, data will be recorded via a video camera mounted on the middeck with a view of the crew’s hand signals that will indicate the number of the readable quadrant. The crew will be trained to scan the quadrants at short time intervals such that the minimal readable display format is continuously located throughout the solid rocket booster (SRB) burn. Zero through four fingers will be held up to indicate format readability. This video information will then be correlated with the accelerometer data taken as part of DTO 695 in order to assess crew vibration response during the ascent phase of flight.

Prior to main engine cutoff (MECO), a short questionnaire attached to the crewmember’s kneeboard will be used to collect supplemental, subjective data. This survey will be stored in the Return-to-Houston bag for later return to Earth. A detailed debrief will occur once participating crewmember return to the Johnson Space Center (JSC).

RESULTS:
The visual performance data collected by this SDBI (i.e., font size for proposed Orion display formats), coupled with subjective comments, will lead to a better understanding of visual performance under the varied vibration and g-loads in an operational setting. These results will be directly applied to future Constellation display format designs in order to mitigate the risks associated with thrust oscillation and human performance.

experiment_title: Stress, Cognition and Physiological Response During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES: The experiment consists in cognitive testing by means of using Stroop tests. The Stroop-effect is a demonstration of interference in the reaction time of a task. For example, when the name of a color (red) is printed in a different color (green), naming the color of the word takes longer and is more prone to errors than when the color of the ink matches the name of the color. The experiment will be repeated on different days with different emotional stimuli (life related and mission related) and a memory workload.

The goal is to investigate which aspects of the complex set of cognitive abilities involved in such tasks are affected by stress, and more specifically by drawing a distinction between automatic and controlled processes. In addition, the stress and emotional states of astronauts have been behaviourally estimated only through subjective rating scales. This experiment plans to assess those more objectively by physiological measures of autonomic activation and by cognitive processing through the strength of the emotional Stroop-effect.

The main object of the present research is to evaluate, through both cognitive performance and physiological indicators, the impact of anxiety on complex cognitive processes in both in-flight and ground conditions.

APPROACH:
Anxiety level will be measured using a well-known Stroop-like effect, the emotional Stroop, where the response time should be lengthened by provoking the negative emotional content of verbal stimuli (e.g., CANCER; ACCIDENT), which has been shown to be greater for stimuli that relate to the subjects individual anxieties. The cognitive tasks to be used will distinguish between automatic and controlled processes and to test the hypothesis that the increase of anxiety (as it may occur in space) affects controlled processes to a greater extent than automatic ones. Evidence for controlled processes will be obtained through the efficiency of inhibition necessary to avoid the irrelevant dimension in the Stroop situation, the between-trials interference effect (negative priming) observed when an item appears in the color that had been the ignored word for the previous stimulus (e.g. GREEN printed in red, respond red, followed by YELLOW printed in green, respond green). Furthermore, failure of control will be indexed by the observation of intrusion errors in a memory task requiring the participant to exclude the items of a given list. The latter memory task will be combined with the Stroop in a dual-task design. In addition, after each testing period a very short Stroop-test will be performed during a 70 seconds hyperventilation period to allow correlation with ground data on cerebral blood flow following a similar protocol. The physiological activation related to the anxiety level will be measured from the analysis of heart rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Additional stress indicators, such as galvanic skin response and salivary or urinary cortisol measures will be collected. The protocol includes twelve testing sessions of maximum 30 minutes each: 4 preflight (Launch day-90, L-88, L-60, L-58), 4 in-flight (L+3, L+4, L+5, L+6), and 4 post-flight (Return day+58, R+60, R+88, R+90).

experiment_title: Quantitative Analysis of Selected Bone Parameters
experiment_description:
Objectives:

If bones are formed in relation to gravitational stresses, one would anticipate that prolonged recumbency and/or prolonged weightlessness would be associated with hypercalciuria, bone demineralization, and osteoporosis. To better understand the effect of space flight on bone, parameters including formation and mineralization, resorption, length, density and pore size distribution, and bone mechanical properties were studied in rats both immediately postflight and at 25 days post- flight.

Approach:

Bone density and pore size distribution were measured by mercury porosimetry in the left humerus, while humerus mechanical properties were evaluated with a standard torsion test machine. Bone formation, mineralization, and resorption rates were determined by quantitative histological techniques using the left tibia, while osteoblastic and osteoclastic cell populations were determined from the right. Length measurements were made with calipers, and correlation, regression, and covariance analyses were made by means of computer programs based on standard statistical methods.

Results:

Space flight had little effect on the bone porosity parameters measured, while the flight and synchronous animals (compared to vivarium controls) did show a significant decrease in bone density immediately postflight. The most striking effects were those on bone formation; all parameters investigated in the flight animals immediately after flight were significantly decreased from both vivarium and synchronous controls. An arrest line was found at both the endosteum and the periosteum of flight animals suggesting that a complete cessation of bone growth occurred during the flight. By 25 days postflight, flight animals showed a significant increase in formation, suggesting that a rebound in bone formation had occurred following flight.

experiment_title: Rotating Membrane Water Purification for Long-Term Human Presence in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The recovery of potable water from wastewater is critical for life support and the environmental health of crewmembers during long-term space missions. The wastewater stream is contaminated with particulates, microorganisms, detergents, salts, and organic compounds, all of which must be removed before the water is suitable for reuse. Standard terrestrial techniques for water treatment and recovery are not suitable for aboard spacecraft. However, rotating reverse osmosis (RO) systems, the focus of this research, show promise for water treatment and recovery. Rotating membrane systems in which a cylindrical filter rotates in a cylindrical shell setting up internal fluid flows have potential to greatly reduce the rate at which the filter loads with membrane foulants. This can substantially extend the life of water filtration systems requiring far less frequent change out of expendable components than standard filtration. Furthermore, because of their anti-fouling characteristics rotating membrane systems are applicable to ultrafiltration (UF) and RO to generate pure water. In their previous NASA-funded research, investigators studied the potential for combining rotating membrane filtration with RO to remove dissolved chemical species. Their initial measurements of rejection and flux for rotating RO membranes and their theoretical model indicate that rotating RO has higher flux and rejection than standard RO systems while simultaneously achieving a greater recovery. Their previous work established the concept of a low-pressure rotating RO membrane system. A mathematical model based on the film theory and the solution-diffusion model agreed well with the experimental results obtained using this first generation prototype. Based on the model, the filtrate flux and contaminant rejection depend more strongly on the transmembrane pressure than on the rotational speed. The first generation apparatus was built to provide proof of the concept for rotating RO and was not capable of operating at high pressures or for long time periods. Therefore, the goal of the current work has been to improve the flux of the device by increasing the transmembrane pressure up to 500 psi and enabling long term testing (7 to 60 days) of the device. To accomplish this, a second generation prototype of a rotating reverse osmosis filter and the accompanying flow circuit was designed and fabricated. The solution diffusion thin film modeling of the system was also continued. Due to the need for long-term testing with high pressures, the operational mode of the second generation apparatus was altered. The theoretical model was used to determine the optimal design geometry of the second generation prototype.

A separate supplemental study was conducted using ion exchange textiles as organic supports for urease immobilization with the aim of developing reactive fibrous materials able to promote urea removal. Investigators have shown that urease can be successfully immobilized on cation exchange textiles using various coupling agents. The urease immobilized onto cation exchange textile offers various advantages. First, the textile (nonwoven fabric) form offers high surface-to-volume ratio and packing density. Furthermore, ion exchange resins in the form of beads move around resulting in abrasion which produces fine particles and degrades the surface. Using an ion exchange textile can prevent such abrasion maintaining the active surface area and preventing plugging downstream. Second, the immobilization procedure used here is simple to carry out without the need for complicated immobilization methods or the use of electron beam or gamma irradiation. Third, the activation energy of the urease immobilized is nearly as low as that of free urease, suggesting that the enzymatic reaction of the immobilized urease is nearly as good as that of the free urease. Fourth, although the kinetic parameters are slightly less favorable than those of free urease, the good storage stability and operational stability of the immobilized enzyme suggest superior potential of the immobilized enzyme for practical application. Finally, a preliminary study of the performance of the biotextile in a continuous flow reactor indicates that the biotextile can convert over 80 % of the urea over a period of several days.

The objective of this project was to advance rotating membrane technology for practical application in wastewater recovery and water purification for long-term human space flight. The effective recovery of wastewater during long-term space missions is critical for life support and the environmental health of crewmembers. Standard terrestrial techniques for wastewater treatment are not suitable because of microgravity or limitations related to mass, volume, and power. Except for the problem of fouling, membrane technologies are quite promising because of their compactness, reliability, and energy-efficiency. The use of rotating membrane technology seems likely to overcome the problem of fouling. Rotating filters offer the potential for smaller size than comparable cartridge filters because of their anti-fouling character. As a result, the mass and volume penalties for rotating membrane systems are most likely less than for standard membrane systems. The results of this research will make available the design tools and technology that along with the understanding of the pertinent physical processes gained in previous research should allow rotating membrane technology to provide a significant, long-term impact in wastewater recovery and many spin-off applications.

APPROACH:
To further enhance the second generation prototype, the performance of commercially available reverse osmosis membranes was evaluated using a laboratory scale batch filtration method. The permeate flux and rejection of ionic solutes and dissolved organic carbon were measured experimentally to select best performing membranes among seven types of membranes (five RO and two nanofiltration) with three different ersatz wastewater solutions simulating transit mission wastewater, early planetary base wastewater, and biological water process effluent.

RESULTS:
Task 1 – Development of a Second Generation Prototype: A new rotating reverse osmosis filtration system was developed to accommodate an operating pressure of 500 psi for long-term tests.

experiment_title: Role of Growth Hormone Secretagogues and Exercise on Muscle Homeostasis Under Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The investigators proposed to test the hypothesis that increased systemic levels of growth hormone (GH) through stimulated growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH) action on the anterior pituitary in concert with resistive exercises may provide a long-term solution for muscle homeostasis under conditions of prolonged weightlessness. As a key hormone replacement therapy, induced secretion of GH, by GH secretagogues were studied for its potential on muscle mass in small mammals under simulated microgravity. Induction of GH provided a chronic pulsatile source of a growth-promoting protein whose biosynthesis or secretion is reduced in long-term space flight. Mice were used in hind-limb suspension models to determine the role of a novel drug MK-0677 on maintenance of muscle mass and whether concentric exercises might act in synergy with hormone treatment. As a means to engineer and ensure long-term protein production that would be workable in humans, gene therapy technology was also employed to monitor muscle mass preservation during hindlimb suspension, after direct intramuscular injection of a genetically engineered muscle-specific vectors expressing GHRH. Effects of this gene-based therapy were assessed in both fast twitch (medial gastrocnemius) and slow twitch muscle (soleus). End-points included muscle size, ultrastructure, fiber type, and contractile function, in normal animals, hind limb suspension, and reambulation. A goal of the NASA-HEDS2 was to develop countermeasures that allow humans to live and work in microgravity for duration over a year and to minimize readapting to Earth’s gravity, and optimize crew safety, well-being, and performance. The investigators proposed to test the hypothesis that the GH/IGF-I axis through autocrine/paracrine mechanisms may provide long-term muscle homeostasis under conditions of prolonged weightlessness.

Specific Aim I: To determine the role of overexpression of hGH in transgenic mice on muscle mass accretion under condition of hindlimb under loading.

Specific Aim II: Does Growth hormone secretagogue, MK-0677, provide signaling for muscle mass homeostasis in response to unloading?

Specific Aim III: Does ectopic expression of GHRH via injectable muscle expression vectors and MK- 0677 act in synergy to potentiate the secretion of GH?

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Enhancement in muscle mass could occur by GHRH secretagogue activity increasing the systemic levels of growth hormone, which then elicits increased level of systemic or local IGF-I production in muscle. It is very important to note that space flight conditions induce stress to some degree by heavy workloads, lack of sleep, impaired circadian daylight cycles, and nutrition. Hormones secreted in greater amounts as part of the stress response include ACTH and cortisol which increased greater than 100% during Skylab missions. Cortisol is one of the primary muscle catabolic factors that rapidly elicits muscle protein break down and impairs GH secretion and reduces IGF-I levels, increases bone loss, and damages the immune system. Also, when adult rats were treated with dexamethasone, IGF-I was still able to stimulate protein synthesis in the epitrochlearis muscle, but only by 41.9 percent of the increase found in a pair-fed control group.

experiment_title: Cognitive/Behavioral, Sensory, and Motor Changes Induced by Solar Particle Event (SPE) and Galactic Cosmic Ray (GCR) Irradiations
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Assessing the biological consequences of living in the space radiation environment represents one of the highest priority areas of NASA research. Of critical importance is the need for an assessment of the vulnerabilities of the central nervous system (CNS) leading to functional neurobehavioral changes during long-term space missions, and the development of effective countermeasures to such risks. The present research addressed this need via the application of a comprehensive animal model to determine the effects of radiation exposure on neurobehavioral tests of vigilance and impulsivity.

APPROACH:
The 1-year project focused on the use of an animal model that employs neurobehavioral tests identical or homologous to those currently in use in human models of risk assessment by U.S. agencies such as the Department of Defense and Federal Aviation and Federal Railroad Administrations for monitoring performance and estimating accident risks associated with such variables as fatigue and/or alcohol or drug abuse. As a first approximation for establishing human risk assessments due to exposure to space radiation, the present work provided animal performance data obtained with the rat Psychomotor Vigilance Test (rPVT), an animal analog of the human PVT that is currently employed for human risk assessments via quantification of sustained attention (e.g., ‘vigilance’ or ‘readiness to perform’ tasks). Ground-based studies indicate that radiation can induce neurobehavioral changes in rodents, including impaired performance on motor tasks and deficits in spatial learning and memory. The present study tested the hypothesis that radiation exposure impairs motor function, performance accuracy, vigilance, motivation, and memory in adult male rats.

RESULTS:
The psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) was originally developed as a human cognitive neurobehavioral assay for tracking the temporally dynamic changes in sustained attention, and has also been used to track changes in circadian rhythm. In humans the test requires responding to a small, bright-red-light stimulus (LED-digital counter) as soon as the stimulus appears, which stops the stimulus counter and displays the reaction time for each trial in milliseconds for a 1-second period. Simple to perform, the PVT has only very minor learning effects, is widely used in human risk assessments in operational environments, and has been recently developed and adopted for use on the International Space Station (ISS) for astronauts as a “self-test” to provide performance feedback, detect changes in alertness, prevent errors, and manage fatigue from sleep loss, circadian disruption, and high workload requirements. A rodent version of the PVT, the rPVT, has been developed and demonstrated to track the same types of performance variables as the human PVT – i.e., general motor function and speed, fine motor control, inhibitory control (“impulsivity”), timing, selective attention, motivation, and basic sensory function. Five cohorts of 16 rats each (total N = 80) were trained on the rPVT, exported to Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) for head-only radiation exposure (0, 25, 50, 100, and 200 cGy protons @ 150 MeV/n), then returned to Johns Hopkins for follow-up testing.

For this project, an automated, computerized training and testing facility was developed for measuring long-term effects of radiation exposure on cognitive/behavioral functions involving vigilance and impulsivity in rodents at the Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions. Establishment of the test facility included 10 experimental testing chambers and associated equipment for assessing neurobehavioral function in rodents as well as for the daily automated, computerized training and testing of behavioral functions in test subjects. The facility supported both the exportation of groups of well-trained subjects to radiation exposure facilities such as BNL and the Department of Radiation Oncology of the Johns Hopkins Hospital, as well as the importation of radiation-exposed rodents from such facilities for detailed, long-term neurobehavioral risk assessments at the investigator’s facility.

Results of the study demonstrated that the rPVT was readily learned by all rats and required as little as 5-7 days of training to acquire baseline performance levels. Validation data were also obtained to compare the performances on the PVT between humans and rodents; these data demonstrated that comparable performances were observed across species in terms of speed and distribution of response latencies, and the relative frequencies of performance lapses and errors of commission (i.e., premature responding). Following irradiation, performances in the rPVT were disrupted at exposure levels of 50, 100, and 200 cGy, showing a consistent, significant increase (i.e., slowing) in reaction times and increased lapses in responding, both indicative of a decrease in sustained attention. Additionally, premature responses showed consistent increases at the higher radiation levels. None of these changes were observed in the non-exposed control animals. Over this same time period, no significant changes were observed in discrimination accuracy, motivation (as indicated by trials completed), or food intake. Additional analyses also demonstrated a division within the exposure groups such that approximately 45-50% of exposed animals evidenced neurobehavioral deficits following radiation (“responders”), while the remainder of exposed animals were unaffected (“non-responders”). When analyzed separately, the responder groups showed distinct deficits in accuracy rates, lapses in attention, and in response speed, with these effects being independent of dose. That is, responder animals in the 25, 50, 100, and 200 cGy groups all evidenced similar degrees of disruption in sustained attention. Additionally, the changes in sustained attention were tracked over time for up to 1 year post-exposure and found to persist over this extended time period.

These results demonstrated the sensitivity of tests such as the rPVT for assessing the effects of head-only space radiation on cognitive neurobehavioral function. Exposure to protons at relatively low doses (e.g., 25 and 50 cGy) produced highly specific effects on vigilance that included impaired attention and motor function (i.e., slowed reaction times, increased lapses in attention, and increased premature responding). Such deficits could significantly impact routine performances in operational environments during lunar and Mars missions, and also negatively affect post-mission adjustment upon return to Earth. These findings support the likely continued success of the rodent model for studying the cognitive, neurobehavioral, and CNS risks associated with living in the space radiation environment while providing an innovative experimental platform for exploring the bases of individual vulnerability to radiation-induced impairments and evaluating potential prophylactics, countermeasures, and treatments.

experiment_title: Brain Pituitary Axis Development in the CEBAS Minimodule
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Using the (CEBAS), which could lead to an aquatic CELSS to provide plant and animal biomass for nutrition on long duration flight, this study focused on the reproductive biology of animals in space. Information was gathered on microgravity-induced changes to the brain-pituitary axis and in the organs that receive information from the environment. Space flight conditions may affect the development and functioning of the neuroendocrine system that regulates the reproductive system.

Approach:

Xiphorous helleri, a freshwater teleost, was used to study the brain-pituitary axis in embryos, neonates, immature, and mature specimens. Two hundred juveniles and four gravid females were flown in the CEBAS. Histology, cytology, immunohistochemistry, morphometry, and in situ histochemistry were used to evaluate the synthesis, storage and release of neurotransmitters, neuroregulatory peptides, neurohormones, pituitary hormones, and the structure of the specimen's cells and organs. The olfactory system and the pineal organ were also studied in a similar fashion. Four living specimens were kept to monitor post flight growth and development.

Results:

The distributions of (Neuropeptide Y)NPY, (Neurotensin)NT, Androgen Receptor)AR, and (Dynorphin)DYN were found to be identical in both Flight specimens and ground-based laboratory module. Intense distribution of Immunoreactiv-Galanin (ir-GAL) in the cell bodies of the NOR was observed in all flight specimen while ir-GAL was absent in the laboratory module. The distribution of FMRF-amide fibers in the brains of the flight specimen appeared sparse and less intense when compared to laboratory controls. There was no significant difference in growth rate and maturity in both flight animals and laboratory control groups.

experiment_title: Maturing Technology for Major Reductions in Energy, Mass, and Crew Time for Plant Lighting in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To develop and demonstrate proof of concept for two novel technologies that together will greatly advance the potential for growing food crops in space for crew life support at distant space destinations.

APPROACH:
The first technology is a “smart” LED-based sole-source lighting system for saving considerable energy for many reasons. The second technology is a crop-stand gas-exchange system consisting of a large cuvette, an open gas-exchange system, and computer controls for CO2, temperature, and atmosphere flow rate. Lighting parameters are controlled by a second computer. Using the smart lighting system in conjunction with the crop gas-exchange system will give real-time crop response of hydroponically grown crops to light (PPF, R/B ratio), temperature, and CO2 at all stages of crop production, which will define additional opportunities for significant energy savings during controlled-environment crop production.

RESULTS:
Due to the complex multiple components of the gas-exchange / cuvette / hydroponics / lighting system, plus the restrictions of a modest budget, it has been necessary to design, fabricate, build, test, troubleshoot, and refurbish components of the integrated plant-monitoring system using local resources and student projects rather than the services of a professional engineering corporation, which we wouldn’t have been able to afford. Other than HELIAC, which was developed in collaboration with ORBITEC, a (then) small business with strong interests in the space program, the rest of the crop-monitoring system has been developed locally. A design-build local engineer developed cuvette as a side job, and has been through several iterations of retrofit and refurbishment as our integration tests indicated. Purdue University Engineering and Engineering Technology students, both undergraduate as well as graduate, have contributed to development of the open air-flow system, to programming for control of CO2 concentration and air flow, data logging, calculating, and reporting of gas-exchange parameters, and to development of a uniform airflow and thermal-control environment within the cuvette per se. Life science undergraduates collaborate with engineering students to develop protocols for growing test crops hydroponically, to measure gas exchange, manage data, and perform routine system maintenance. At the end of the extended project all development tasks still were not completed because of limited student time, turnover, graduations, etc., but the effort to develop a fully integrated, operational crop-growth / multi-plant gas-exchange system continues using other funding sources. It is planned for a leak-free, thermally stabilized open gas-exchange system to be completed by the end of 2014, and for proof-of-concept crop-growth / gas-exchange studies to be conducted during the spring semester of 2015. That study will establish interactive dose-response curves for Pn vs. PPF at several different CO2 levels at each important phase of a crop-production cycle, and for those experiments to be replicated statistically. A key objective of that study will be to identify precisely when during the time course of a crop-production cycle that optimizing environments are needed, what the minimum inputs are, and when they no longer are needed. The outcome of that study is expected to identify additional times and ways in which significant resources (e.g., CO2) and energy (e.g., light, electricity) can be saved during crop production, and that is expected to additionally reduce costs of growing food in space. The current plan is to complete the proof-of-concept study by May, 2015, write up and internally review a manuscript for publication, and submit an article for publication to a peer-reviewed journal by fall, 2015. An army of past and present engineering, engineering technology, and life science students will be co-authors on that proof-of-concept article that will come out of this technology-development effort enabled by NASA grant NNX09AL99G. This NASA grant will be acknowledged as the main funding source supporting the new research technology proof-of-concept work. Once published and operational, this tool will be proposed for data gathering and further upgrade in future grant proposals. It is anticipated to provide incentive for future fund raising because of it’s powerful analytical capabilities.

experiment_title: Sleep, Physical Inactivity, Circadian Rhythms, and Cardiovascular Vulnerability
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Round-the-clock work schedules aboard spaceships and in most industries on Earth leave people with an increased risk for developing cardiovascular diseases (CVD), in part due to the disruption of endogenous human clocks. Endogenous circadian rhythms, generated by these clocks form the basic framework of human physiology. In order to improve the understanding of the mechanisms leading to increased CVD, it is essential to understand the endogenous circadian rhythm in vascular endothelial function, which is an early and a robust marker of CVD. It will be determined if an endogenous circadian rhythm in endothelial function exists using a five day forced desynchrony protocol, and if standardized activities performed during the night shift impair endothelial function.

APPROACH:
Twelve healthy participants will live on four artificial 18 hour days consisting of six hour sleep and 12 hour wake periods. Participants will be isolated from all time cues and will remain in dim light during the wake periods and complete darkness during sleep. The dim light allows the human pacemaker to freely run. All behaviors including food and activity will be identical across all wake periods such that the effects of the behaviors and the endogenous circadian clocks can be separated out. Endothelial function will be measured as flow mediated dilation (FMD) every four hours during the wake periods. To understand mechanisms, blood will be drawn to measure physiological markers such as epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cytokines. Biomarkers inform us about the mechanisms modulating vascular function at various circadian phases. Identification of a rhythm in endothelial function along with the mechanisms that control it will set the stage for developing chronotherapeutic countermeasures against vascular function impairment (such as timing antioxidants and exercise) in space and on Earth.
