experiment_title: Influence of Exercise on Human Single Muscle Fiber Function with Long-Term Bedrest
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this investigation was to extend the previous space flight and ground-based studies that have examined the cellular mechanisms related to the loss of muscle mass and function with long-duration unloading. Investigators measured the contractile properties of individual slow- and fast-twitch muscle fibers from lower limb skeletal muscles and the concentration of the two main contractile proteins, myosin and actin, from single muscle fibers. These cellular physiology and molecular muscle studies were conducted on subjects before and after 90-days of bed rest with and without countermeasure activities (aerobic and resistance training). These studies will provide further insight into the mechanisms of muscle wasting associated with space flight and provide information on effective countermeasures to maintain skeletal muscle mass and function in male and female space travelers.

APPROACH:
Vastus lateralis and soleus muscle biopsies were analyzed for global protein fractions (mixed, sarcoplasmic, myofibrillar) and force-specific proteins (myosin, actin, collagen).

RESULTS:
Significant Findings:
1. Upper Leg – Complete and viable exercise countermeasures for whole muscle and single muscle fiber contractile function/structure. The resistance plus aerobic exercise program was complimentary for unloaded skeletal muscle.
2. Lower Leg – Incomplete exercise prescription. The resistance plus aerobic exercise program was better than resistance exercise alone.
3. Nutrition – The nutrition countermeasure provided no benefit for the protection of skeletal muscle during long-term unloading. In fact, the nutrition intervention led to greater loss in thigh muscle mass as compared to control.
4. Potential gender-related issues for skeletal muscle. Women appear to loss more muscle mass in a shorter period of time compared to men.
5. The WISE 2005 exercise prescription protocol and hardware were as good as or better than what investigators have reported with the International Space Station (ISS) regimen.
6. The last decade of exercise countermeasure research has significantly reduced the time necessary to protect most muscle groups (<2% total time in the unloaded state) for crewmembers.

Vastus Lateralis
This study shows that the concurrent training program of resistance (2-3 days per week) and aerobic (3-4 days per week) exercise was protective of the thigh muscle during 60-days of bed rest in women. This finding is supported by the maintenance of whole muscle and single muscle fiber parameters (MHC I and IIa) during the bed rest period. These data indicate that in light of the difficulty in protecting slow-twitch muscle fibers by resistance training alone during prolonged unloading, concurrent resistance and aerobic training protocols should be considered as a viable countermeasure for the upper leg of crewmembers during long-duration space travel. The nutrition countermeasure did not provide an ergogentic benefit for whole muscle or single muscle fiber size and function during bed rest. This information should be useful to the international space community and health care industry working with patients stricken with extended bed rest.

Soleus
While the addition of aerobic exercise to resistance exercise proved complimentary and completely protective for the vastus lateralis, whole muscle and single muscle fiber properties for the soleus, in particular the MHC I fibers, did not achieve the same level of protection. The fact that MHC I fibers from the vastus lateralis and soleus muscle atrophy to a similar extent with long-duration unloading, but respond differently to the same exercise loading program, was an interesting and novel finding. These data suggest that unique and specific exercise regimens for the upper (vastus lateralis) and lower leg (soleus) may be necessary to protect human skeletal muscle during extended unloading periods. The difference in the vastus lateralis and soleus muscle response to the concurrent exercise program is not a volume of exercise issue per se, but more related to the type of muscle contractions performed. All of the muscle contractions performed as part of this investigation (>100,000 per muscle group over 60-days) were dynamic in nature. However, given that the soleus is suited for postural support; static type contractions of longer duration to more closely mimic the typical load on Earth in a 1-g environment may be required. It is not recommended that static load contractions be performed in lieu of dynamic contractions. Rather, it is likely that a proper combination of static and dynamic contractions will be necessary to protect the quantitative (size) and qualitative (intrinsic speed and power) properties of the soleus muscle fibers.

experiment_title: Stability of Pharmacotherapeutic Compounds
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Analysis of certain medications returned from the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have indicated that some pharmaceuticals are significantly degraded in space, and this may compromise treatments and the health of crews on future exploration missions. Data gathered from past Space Shuttle missions suggest that some of the medications packed in the Shuttle's medical pack degrade even after relatively brief periods (less than 20 days) of space flight. The observed degradation included both physical and chemical characteristics of medicine formulations. Physical and chemical instability of medications could render treatments ineffective for assurance of optimal crew health during long duration space exploration missions. An evaluation of subjective data on medications used by crewmembers during space flight indicated that 8% of all treatments administered in the Space Shuttle program were reported ineffective. Pharmaceutical instability may modify effectiveness and safety, and is one possible cause of the ineffectiveness of treatments.

The objective of this project was to identify the pharmaceuticals that degrade in space by collecting data on the magnitude and time course of degradation of select pharmaceuticals. This investigation studied the effects of radiation in space on complex organic molecules, such as vitamins and other compounds in food and medicine. This could help researchers develop more stable and reliable pharmaceutical and nutritional countermeasures suitable for future long-duration missions to the moon and Mars.

APPROACH:
The pharmaceutical kits contained 35 types of pharmaceutical drugs, including tablets, ointments, suppositories, and injectable solutions. In addition to the food and drug items, the kits were equipped with two temperature loggers and a dosimeter to measure radiation.

RESULTS:
There was no crew interaction with the contents of the kits, which were configured to prevent them from being inadvertently opened. One of the kits was immediately returned on STS-122 after 13 days, while the other three remained aboard ISS for 353, 596, and 880 days of spaceflight. Each kit was returned on subsequent Shuttle flights. The flight kits were analyzed in parallel with the eight ground control kits, identical to those flown.

Results from this investigation designed to examine changes in chemical content and physical attributes of dosage forms stored aboard space missions suggest that there may be differences with respect to potency and rate of degradation of formulations stored in space compared to those on the ground. Some APIs and formulations may be more sensitive than others, and specific chemical and formulation characteristics may influence the stability of medications in space. Cumulative low dose radiation and dispensers used for solid dosages in space appear to influence stability of pharmaceuticals in space.

experiment_title: Suited Contingency Ops Food
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Advanced Food Technology (AFT) project aims to provide astronauts with a food system that will maintain safety and ensure performance throughout NASA exploration missions. Part of this task has involved the development of a nutrition delivery system for use in suited survival operations. In addition to the constraints of mass, volume, and crew resources that influence design of all spaceflight systems, design of a contingency food system is also affected by other constraints. A contingency food system must have adequate interface with mission pressure suits and relevant vehicle hardware, and must function in a hypobaric and microgravity contingency environment. Proposed in FY2009, the Suited Contingency Ops directed research project has sought to define the requirements for and facilitate the development of such a contingency food system. Although the need for NASA to develop a food system to support contingency events is no longer immediate, the tasks conducted to date for this project offer valuable insight into hardware design for nutrition delivery to suited crewmembers, and are likely to have relevance to NASA in the future. These tasks and the corresponding findings are summarized within this report.

APPROACH:
The methodology is not available.

RESULTS:
To ensure that the NASA food system promotes crew safety and performance in all mission phases, AFT has worked to develop a nutrition system that would feed astronauts in pressurized spacesuits. In addition to the constraints of mass, volume, and crew resources that influence the development of all spaceflight systems, design of a contingency food system is also affected by other constraints. The designed delivery system hardware must interface with pressurized spacesuits and vehicle hardware, and must function in the absence of pressure and gravity. Additionally, the beverage for use in this system must meet a variety of requirements related to crew health and nutrition in contingency events.

Due to changes in agency direction, the direct need for a contingency food system is no longer present. This project has, therefore, been concluded prematurely. Still, the work conducted to date on this project is likely to be relevant to NASA needs in the future. In the event that there becomes an interest in pursuing this type of development in the future, researchers have made a diligent effort to summarize project methods, task findings, and specific recommendations for future work.

experiment_title: Software Enabled Therapeutics for Psychiatry, Neurology, and Pain
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
On exploration missions, astronauts will not have access to comprehensive health care services for periods of two years, and possibly longer. This exposes the astronauts to several risks: 1) Risk of adverse behavioral conditions and psychiatric disorders. 2) Risk of performance decrements due to inadequate cooperation, coordination, communication, and psychological adaptation within a team. 3) Risk of acute and late Central Nervous System (CNS) effects from radiation exposure. This includes CNS damage leading to acute and/or late changes in motor function, behavior, or neurological disorders. 4) Risk of performance errors due to fatigue resulting from sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, extended wakefulness, and work overload.

APPROACH:
The overarching goal of this study was to design and develop the PEAR eFormulation System – a suite of digital eHealth applications connected to a predictive analytics platform, designed to work in combination with psychoactive medications to address anxiety, depression, cognitive function, as well as other CNS indications such as sleep disorders. The combination of eHealth and pharmaceutical interventions provides the ability to impact both brain chemistry and cognitive experience simultaneously, providing a synergistic approach to addressing CNS problems, and a means to dynamically adjust interventions to better match an individual’s response to medication and to eHealth interventions.

RESULTS:
The main results of the project are as follows: 1) Five eHealth apps were developed to address problems identified as risks during extended space flight, including anxiety, depression, diminished cognitive function, and sleep dysfunction. 2) A server-based platform was developed to coordinate and manage the eHealth apps, and to provide the predictive analytics required to manage digital health therapy used in combination with pharmaceutical intervention. 3) In addition to providing effective interventions, the apps and platform support the collection and analysis of real-time behavioral and biometric data. This information is to dynamically adjust interventions. 4) The system provides an extended analysis and reporting capability, and can support all aspects of intervention management and basic research.

experiment_title: Alterations in Postural Equilibrium Control Associated with Long Duration Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The sensorimotor systems of humans have evolved phylogenetically and ontogenetically to optimize body movements and posture control in the terrestrial gravitational field. The central nervous system (CNS) has developed neurosensory systems that monitor and process sensory inputs from visual, vestibular, somatosensory, and proprioceptive receptors to assess the biomechanical state of the body (spatial orientation), and neuromotor systems that create, select, and employ motor command strategies and synergies to adjust the biomechanical state toward the desired equilibrium point. Adaptation to microgravity alters neurosensory systems by eliminating, reinterpreting, or modifying the weighting of sensory information used to assess spatial orientation in response to the sudden loss of tonic gravitational otolith stimulation. Adaptation to microgravity also alters neuromotor systems by modifying the repertoire of motor command strategies and synergies used for movement control in response to the sudden redistribution of forces along the body, reductions in the biomechanical support reactions, and alteration of relationships between motor command and body movement. These inflight sensorimotor adaptations disrupt postflight postural equilibrium control. The long-term objective of this experiment was to determine the role of central adaptive mechanisms in reorganizing postural equilibrium control in humans subjected to long-duration space flight. Ultimately, these data, when coupled with similar data obtained from short-duration missions, will lead to development of return-to-duty criteria for returning crewmembers, to development effective countermeasures to the untoward effects of sensorimotor adaptation to space flight, and to improving our understanding of the adaptive processes required to compensate for clinical deficits in sensory-motor function.

Hypotheses:
(1) The effectiveness of reflexive (open loop) responses to stability-threatening external disturbances, which is known to be reduced after space flight, presumably because of inflight neuromotor adaptation, will be further reduced by concomitant neurosensory adaptation.

(2) The effectiveness of the closed loop control of quiet stance, which is known to be reduced after space flight, presumably because of inflight neurosensory adaptation, will be further reduced by concomitant neuromotor adaptation, and the magnitude and recovery time course of this ataxia will increase with mission duration because of the increased time for sensory-motor adaptation to microgravity.

APPROACH:
The Equilibrium investigation used two test paradigms: (1) neuromotor control tests and (2) neurosensory control tests. Only pre- and postflight data collection sessions were scheduled.

NeuroMotor Control Tests:
Graded perturbations were used to challenge the posture control system by suddenly moving the center of mass close to the backward limit of stability. Two types of perturbations were used: support surface translations and chest pushes.

Base-of-support perturbations were administered at two displacement levels by automatically translating the posture platform force plate (support surface) in the forward direction using a computer-controlled DC motor. The lower displacement level (1.25 cm over 250 msec) was used to assess response thresholds, while the higher displacement, level (5.70 cm over 400 msec) was used to assess the subject's ability to scale the motor response appropriately. Data from the eyes open support surface translation trials can be compared directly to the large existing set of U.S. postflight data currently being collected. Chest pushes were administered manually at two force levels by one of the investigators using a push stick with integral force transducer. The lower force level (2-5 Kg peak) was used to assess response thresholds, while the higher force level (10-20 Kg peak) was used to assess the subject's ability to scale the motor response appropriately. Data from the eyes open chest push trials can be compared directly to the large existing set of Russian postflight data collected by the Institute of Biomedical Problems (IBMP) group.

Changes in the roles of sensory inputs in selecting and issuing motor commands can be inferred from the data collected during the reduced sensory input trials. The role of vision can be inferred from comparisons between eyes-closed trials and eyes-open trials, and the combined roles of ankle proprioception and plantar somatosensation can be inferred from comparisons between trials with the subject standing directly on the force platform and trials with the subject standing on thick (10 cm) foam rubber atop the force platform.

The primary dependent measures in this experimental paradigm are derived from electromyographic (EMG) activity observed in the anti-gravity muscles of the leg and trunk. In particular, latencies of the initial EMG responses are used to assess the subject's ability to detect the perturbation and to select and issue a motor response. EMG sequencing, strength, and duration, coupled with biomechanical measurements of segmental and center of mass body movements are used to assess the strategy, synergy, and scaling of the motor response. Times to recovery of biomechanical equilibrium are used to assess the effectiveness of the motor response, and total integrated EMG activity is used to assess the efficiency of the response.

Neurosensory Control Tests:
Eliminating vision, decorrelating ankle proprioceptive inputs from Earth-vertical, and/or decorrelating visual inputs from Earth-vertical challenged the posture control system. These conditions altered the set of accurate sensory inputs available to the CNS for detection of sway errors and development of compensatory closed loop motor output adjustments.

Sets of six sensory organization tests were administered automatically using a modified clinical dynamic posturography system. To decorrelate the ankle proprioceptive and visual inputs from Earth-vertical, the pitch orientations of the support surface and visual surround with respect to the subject's ankle joint were servo-controlled to follow the subject's center of mass sway. This process, which is referred to as sway referencing, eliminated changes in ankle angle and visual flow during low frequency body sway. The six sensory organization test (SOT) conditions used were:

SOT 1. Eyes open - this is a control condition; all available sensory feedback systems are intact; tests the overall effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system;

SOT 2. Eyes closed - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system without visual feedback;

SOT 3. Sway-referenced vision - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate visual feedback; examines how well the system resolves visual-proprioceptive and/or visual-vestibular conflicts;

SOT 4. Sway-referenced support surface - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate proprioceptive feedback; examines how well the system resolves proprioceptive-visual and/or proprioceptive-vestibular conflicts;

SOT 5. Sway-referenced support surface with eyes closed - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate proprioceptive feedback and absent visual feedback; only vestibular feedback is accurate; examines how well the system resolves proprioceptive-vestibular conflicts and/or how well the system controls posture with only vestibular feedback;

SOT 6. Sway-referenced support surface with sway-referenced vision - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate visual and proprioceptive feedback; only vestibular feedback is accurate; examines how well the system resolves simultaneous visual-vestibular and proprioceptive-vestibular conflicts and/or how well the system controls posture with only vestibular feedback.

During each test session, three trials of each of the six sensory organization test conditions were presented to the subject. Each trial lasted for 20 seconds, and the order of presentation of the 18 trials was randomized.

The primary dependent measures in this experimental paradigm are derived from biomechanical measurements of segmental and center of mass body movements. In particular, peak-to-peak sway amplitudes, equilibrium scores, and center of pressure (COP) under each condition were used to determine the degree to which the posture control system used visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive feedback to maintain closed loop control of postural equilibrium.

Protocol for Pre- and Postflight Studies:
Upon arrival at the test facility for each test session, the subject completed a pretest questionnaire designed to identify any uncontrolled factors that could potentially influence the test results. The subject's height was then measured (first pre- and postflight sessions only). Before posture testing, the subject donned a loose-fitting pair of 'gym' shorts to facilitate EMG electrode placement and joint position monitoring. The skin surface at each EMG electrode site was then prepared for electrode placement by scrubbing the region with an abrasive skin cleanser (Omni-Prep). Once each site was prepared, a pre-gelled, disposable, silver/silver chloride surface electrode was applied. The impedance between each electrode and a single ground reference electrode was then measured. The following EMG electrode sites were used: tibialis anterior, soleus, quadriceps (primarily rectus femoris), hamstrings (primarily biceps femoris), paraspinals (at approximately the L-4 level), abdominals (lateral to the midline, just below the umbilicus).

Before the subject stepped onto the posture platform, the operator powered-up the EquiTest system and zeroed any sensor offsets. The subject then donned a safety harness and mounted the platform. Next, the operator fastened the safety harness to the safety bar that loops over the platform, positioned the subject on the platform, and attached the body segment position measuring devices (sway bars) and breast plate. The subject then donned a set of headphones used to provide a masking noise input that would eliminate external auditory cues from the posture platform and environment, and the operator adjusted the video camera for a clear field of view.

Each test session began with the neuro-sensory control tests, during which the subject attempted to maintain upright postural equilibrium control under the following sensory conditions:

(1) Eyes Open, Fixed Support Surface
(2) Eyes Closed, Fixed Support Surface
(3) Sway-referenced Vision, Fixed Support Surface
(4) Eyes Open, Sway-referenced Support Surface
(5) Eyes Closed, Sway-referenced Support Surface
(6) Sway-referenced Vision, Sway-referenced Support Surface

Each of these conditions was repeated three times during the test in randomized order for 18 trials. The duration of each trial was 20 seconds, and the time between trials was less than 5 seconds.

The motor control tests followed immediately. During the sensory tests, the subject attempted to recover upright postural equilibrium control as quickly as possible after the following postural perturbations:

(a) Small amplitude chest pushes (2-5 Kg)
(b) Large amplitude chest pushes (10-20 Kg)
(c) Small amplitude support surface forward translations (1.2 cm during 250 msec)
(d) Large amplitude support surface forward translations (5.7 cm during 400 msec)

Each of these conditions was repeated twice under each of the following sensory feedback conditions:

(a) Eyes Open
(b) Eyes Closed
(c) Eyes Open, standing on thick (10 cm) foam rubber
(d) Eyes Closed, standing on thick (10 cm) foam rubber

The 16 trials without foam were presented first in randomized order. The 16 trials with foam were presented immediately after, also in randomized order (except for R+1 and R+5 when time constraints did not allow for "foam" trials). The duration of each trial was approximately 6-10 seconds, and the time between trials was less than 5 seconds. Chest pushes were applied manually by one of the investigators using a pushing device with integral force transducer. Support surface translations were applied automatically under computer control using the EquiTest system.

Throughout the test period, the operator controlled the execution of the test protocols at the EquiTest system computer rack, while standing near enough to the platform to steady the subject when the subject lost balance. The operator depressed a foot switch to execute the test procedures. When the EquiTest system detected that the subject had lost balance, it automatically interrupted the test procedure and waited for operator's command to abort or continue the test. The overall testing equipment utilized during this experiment included safety harness, hip/shoulder sway bars w/potentiometers, overhead camera, white noise generator, calibrated subject push stick, subject breastplate, dual-axis rate sensors, and a VCR. Others to be described in more detail include the dynamic posturography system, camcorder/tripod, macintosh data acquisition system, and an EMG monitoring system.

RESULTS:
Overall, the test procedures worked quite well. The motor control procedure was somewhat tedious at times and should probably be shortened for future experiments. In addition, the custom computer interface software was sensitive at times to the speed with which the operator selected test trials. It occasionally selected the wrong test, distorted or lost the real-time center of pressure display, or "locked up" the two experiment control computers. This software should be improved before using the system for future experiments.

Mir 18
Balance control deficits following long-duration space flight appear to be far more profound than those following short-duration space flight: two of the three Mir 18 subjects were too ataxic to attempt the balance control testing on R+0, while only 4 of 45 short-duration crewmembers were that severely affected. The nature of postflight balance disturbances appears to be the same following long- and short-duration space flight missions: returning crewmembers are unable to adequately use vestibular system inputs immediately after flight.

Neuromotor disturbances persist for a much longer period following long-duration flight than following short-duration flight. Furthermore, they appear to be affected by changes in available sensory information. Complete recovery is substantially delayed following long-duration missions; the slow phase of the recovery process appeared to progress much more slowly than with short-duration subjects.

Mir 19
Two Mir 19 crewmembers participated in this experiment, partially fulfilling the postflight data collection requirements. Balance control performances on R+1 were among the lowest ever recorded. Balance control deficits appear to be far more profound, but similar in some aspects to those observed after 5-15 day Shuttle missions:

(1) Contribution from vestibular system information is decreased early after flight
(2) Reliance on visual system information is highly increased early after flight
(3) Head-on-trunk locking strategy has emerged early after flight

Complete recovery is substantially delayed following long-duration missions; the slow phase of the recovery process appeared to progress much more slowly than with short-duration subjects. New motor control strategies (co-contraction strategies) seem to emerge early after flight and persist for many days. These strategies were previously unobserved in the short-duration subjects, but, following reanalysis, appear in some subjects. The new strategies may reflect structural changes in the brain stem or the spinal cord. Further study of this observation is warranted.

CONCLUSION:
The primary goal of these investigations was to extend the understanding of the central adaptive mechanisms responsible for the appearance and amelioration of postflight postural ataxia. Building on the substantial neuromotor information base that the Russian IBMP group has amassed from primarily long-duration missions, and the similarly substantial neurosensory information base that the U.S. investigators have amassed from primarily short-duration missions, a set of combined studies on the joint US/Russian Shuttle-Mir Science Program was planned. To that end, a joint protocol was developed; employing key elements of both the standard IBMP test procedures and standard JSC test procedures, to which crewmembers were subjected before and after flight.

Results from the Mir 18 and 19 subjects have been quantitatively disappointing because so much early postflight data were lost. The limited data obtained have allowed the investigators to begin making direct comparisons of the independent techniques used in the two space programs, but are not likely to be sufficient to lead to new insights into how data from the Russian and U.S. information bases can be combined.

experiment_title: Cellular Immune Response
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The functional capacity of lymphocytes (phytohemagglutinin (PHA) responsiveness only) was found to be depressed for studies conducted during Apollo missions 7 through 13 and Skylab missions 3 and 4. T-lymphocyte numbers were also suppressed in Skylab. The objective of this study was to examine the effects of space flight on the cellular immune response in Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) crewmembers.

APPROACH:
Samples of heparinized peripheral venous blood (10cc) were obtained preflight and postflight on days L-30 (30 days before liftoff), L-15, L-5, R+0 (day of recovery), R+1 (recovery +1 day), R+8 and R+13. Samples were processed within 1 to 24 hours of collection. Parameters measured for this study included: 1) white blood cell concentrations, 2) lymphocyte numbers, 3) B-lymphocyte and T-lymphocyte distributions in peripheral blood and 4) lymphocyte responsiveness to PHA, pokeweed mitogen (PWM), Concanavalin A (Con A) and influenza virus antigen. Before separation, total leukocyte counts were performed using a hemacytometer and/or a Coulter Counter. Differential counts were determined using slide preparations stained with Wright’s stain.

Lymphocytes were separated by Ficoll-Hypaque centrifugation, which uses a special liquid that provides a density gradient. Higher density blood cells are pulled far down into the liquid by centrifugal action, while the more buoyant lymphocytes remain near the center. The supernatant was removed by pipette, and the resulting mononuclear cells were washed three times in minimum essential medium (MEM).

B-lymphocyte distributions were determined by calculating the percentage of 200 mononuclear cells with surface immunoglobulins, which were detected by the immunofluorescent antibody technique. The presence of E-rosette-forming lymphocytes (T-cells) was determined using a concentration of one million lymphocytes in 0.25 ml of 0.5% sheep red blood cell (SRBC) suspension. After mixing, the tubes were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes, and then placed in ice water for 2 hours. Approximately half of the supernatant was removed, and the top cell layer was gently resuspended. Two hundred lymphocytes were counted with 3 or more adhering SRBC’s, which were used as criteria for E-rosetted lymphocytes.

Purified lymphocytes (one million cells) in MEM containing 40% fetal calf serum were placed in culture plates. The antigens were diluted in MEM (containing Pen-Strep and L-glutamine) in the following concentrations: 0.01 ml PHA/ml MEM; 0.01 and 0.05 ml PWM/ml MEM; and 25 and 50 micrograms Con A/ml MEM. These diluted antigens were placed in the appropriate wells of the tissue culture plates in 0.1 ml aliquots (in duplicate). The cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide atmosphere at 37 degrees Celsius (3 days for PHA and 5 days for Con A and PWM). On the day of harvest, samples were treated as described in the following section for influenza virus antigen cultures.

An inactivated monovalent type A influenza virus vaccine containing 1600 chick cell agglutinating units/ml of a Hong Kong strain was dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline and stored at -70 degrees Celsius until used for tests. Separated lymphocytes were added in 0.1 ml aliquots for each influenza antigen dilution, and the cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide incubator at 37 degrees Celsius for periods of either 2 or 3 days. On the day of harvest, cells were pulsed for 2 hours with 1 microcurie of methyl(tritium)-thymidine, a radioactive marker. Cells were then harvested with an automated harvester onto glass-fiber filter strips and counted in a liquid scintillation counter. Data were expressed as counts per minute (CPM)/one million lymphocytes, and the stimulation index (SI) was calculated by dividing the mean result for stimulated cultures by that for unstimulated cultures. Allantoic fluid was used separately as a control of each crewman’s reactivity to chick embryo proteins.

RESULTS:
Preflight (L-30) white blood cell (WBC) counts for ASTP and Skylab were 6640±1830 WBC/mm3 and 6013±254 WBC/ mm3, respectively. The ASTP crew had significant increases in WBC numbers noted on R+0 (11,110±4210 WBC/mm3) and R+1 (13,530±610 WBC/mm3). Individual variation in WBC values was noted among the three Skylab crewmembers at R+0 (8980±5560 WBC/mm3), which is reflected in the large standard deviation. However, all values were within clinically normal ranges (7110±2400 WBC/mm3). Less variation overall was noted for total lymphocyte values; however, values at R+0 for ASTP (1950±490 lymphocyte count/mm3) and Skylab 4 (1177±381 lymphocyte count/mm3) were decreased below their previous baseline values (ASTP L-30=2820±480 lymphocyte count/mm3 and Skylab L-30=1940±670 lymphocyte count/mm3). Fluctuations in the individual values of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and nonreactive lymphocytes of ASTP crewmembers were indicated, but values remain within one standard deviation for normal laboratory values. T-cell values ranged from 1.29 million +/- 490,000 to 2.53 million +/- 440,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=1.59 million +/- 630,000 lymphocytes/ml), B-lymphocytes from 470,000 +/- 20,000 to 710,000 +/- 40,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=510,000 +/- 300,000 lymphocytes/ml) and nonreactive lymphocytes from 120,000 +/- 120,000 to 710,000 +/- 370,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=850,000 +/- 560,000 lymphocytes/ml). In contrast, highly significant changes were noted in B and T cell distributions of the Skylab 4 crewmen.

Results from culture studies show a definite decrease in the ability of lymphocytes to react with PHA at R+0 (SI=20±15) and R+1 (SI=12±8) for all three Apollo astronauts. Baseline SI mean at L-30 was 36±4. By R+8, all were back within normal ranges (SI range=10 to 282). Crewmembers began and remained at low-level SI ranges for Con A (3 to 49) throughout the preflight and postflight periods, except for one subject, who had a strengthened Con A stimulation of 151 at splashdown. Considerable individual variation was noted in the PWM data and no consistent trend was obtained. Variation of antigen stimulation indexes may be expected, due to the rapid exchange of cells between different compartments in the body. The entire Apollo crew responded to influenza virus England strain preflight in cultures, and one of the three astronauts responded postflight to influenza virus Hong Kong strain. Total lack of reactivity may reflect influenza susceptibility.

ASTP crewmembers experienced contact with toxic gases upon splashdown. Depressions observed at R+0 were caused by either space flight or gas exposure a few hours prior to sample analysis. Similar depressions in lymphocytic responsiveness were observed in Skylab 3 and 4 data, although both of these missions were of much longer duration than ASTP. However, in comparable missions of similar lengths (i.e., the Apollo series) no changes in lymphocytic responsiveness were reported. The toxic gas exposure was severe enough to create concern for lung inflammation, which resulted in a corticosteroid treatment on R+1. Most cortisone preparations are known to cause a lymphocytic reaction. Consequently, it is likely that the increased immunosuppressions noted by cultural responses on R+1 for all mitogens and on R+8 for Con A were attributable to the steroid therapy.

experiment_title: Mechanical and Gravitational Countermeasures to Ocular Changes during Strict Head-down Tilt Bedrest
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is associated with structural and functional ocular and cerebral changes, including optic disc edema, and develops in approximately two-thirds of astronauts during long-duration space flight. Due to the potential of irreversible functional vision changes during exploration-class space flight missions, a countermeasure capable of preventing SANS is needed. Currently, the mechanisms underlying the development of SANS are unknown, however, exposure to a constant headward fluid shift during extended spaceflight is hypothesized to play a major role. Exposure to strict 6° head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest, a spaceflight analog, has been previously shown to induce optic disc edema in two-thirds of subjects. This study will implement 30 days of strict 6° HDT bed rest in healthy subjects to investigate various countermeasures to the development of optic disc edema and SANS.

This study has the following specific aims:

1. Determine if daily exposure to actual upright posture and simulated LBNP hydrostatic pressure gradients prevents ocular and cerebral structural changes during 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest.

2. Determine if daily exposure to actual upright posture and simulated LBNP hydrostatic pressure gradients prevents ocular functional changes during 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest.

3. Determine if daily exposure to actual upright posture and simulated LBNP hydrostatic pressure gradients prevents vascular and cerebrospinal fluid changes during 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest.

APPROACH

This study will include 72 human subjects separated into 6 groups (12 subjects per group): two control groups defined by NASA and four countermeasure treatment groups. Control group 1 will be upright seated during the day (16 h) and supine at night (8 h). Control group 2 will remain in strict 6° HDT bedrest with no countermeasures (Group 2). Of the four countermeasure treatment groups, two will include countermeasures NASA previously selected to investigate: daily exposure to exercise with veno-occlusive thigh cuffs during HDT bedrest (Group 3) and daily B-vitamin supplement intake during HDT bedrest (Group 4). The remaining two treatment groups include strict HDT bed rest with six hours of 25 mmHg LBNP, daily, during strict HDT bedrest (Group 5), and six hours of upright (seated) posture, daily, during the strict HDT bedrest portion of the study (Group 6).

The six-hour exposures (Group 5 and Group 6) will be split into two sessions of three-hour exposures, once in the morning and once in the afternoon. All subjects will undergo baseline data collection for 14 days before the bedrest study (ambulatory), 30 days of bedrest, and 14 days of post-bedrest recovery data collection (ambulatory). This PI is responsible for groups 1, 2, 5 and 6. :

RESULTS:

This study will lay the groundwork to determine future countermeasure strategies that can prevent SANS during space flight. It is critical to determine if optic disc edema can be prevented or attenuated utilizing the most effective, currently available fluid shift countermeasures: LBNP and gravity. Overall, the quantification and comparison of physiological changes within the six groups included in this study will help to determine the necessary magnitude and duration of countermeasure needed to prevent SANS.

experiment_title: Reactivation of Latent Viruses During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reactivation of latent viruses may pose an important health risk for people living and working in extreme environments, such as space and Antarctica. Risks associated with many infectious agents are reduced by the preventative measures of the health stabilization program before each mission. However, reactivation of latent viruses is unaffected by such actions. A variety of stess factors may cause reactivation of these viruses, such as psychosocial stress, trauma, sunlight, resiratory infection, and fever. Stress-induced changes in immune function under such conditions may also increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a DNA virus that infects more than 90% of the adult population worldwide and is the etiologic agent of infectious mononucleosis, is highly infectious. Normally, primary infection is a self-limiting disease leading to a lifelong persistence of EBV in the B-lymphocytes or epithelial cells of the oropharynx of infected individuals. EBV can be found in saliva after reactivation, which can be triggered by a variety of factors, perhaps including space flight. The physical and psychological stresses associated with the launch and landing of spacecraft, and living and working in the crowded, closed environment in microgravity, may result in viral reactivation and shedding.

The limited access to space requires the use of ground-based analogs of space flight. Environmental chambers have been used since the Skylab program (1973-1974) to simulate specific aspects of space flight. In the present study, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was used to identify EBV DNA in saliva and CMV DNA in urine as a measure of viral shedding in response to 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
Viral shedding and reactivation patterns were studied for eight subjects (five male and three female) participating in the 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center. Saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects before, during, and after chamber isolation. Blood and urine samples were collected once before entry and once after exit.

Samples from 11 healthy age-matched adults were collected as controls (ten males and one female). Saliva, urine, and blood samples (one of each) were collected from each of these subjects on day 1, day 7, and day 22 of the tests. This collection schedule closely approximates the pre- and postflight collection schedule of a 12-day Shuttle flight. One-time urine samples were also collected from 30 additional healthy age-matched subjects for CMV analysis.

Saliva samples were collected with Salivette kits, which consist of a cotton roll in a polypropylene vial. Subjects placed the roll in their mouth until it became saturated, and then returned the roll to the vial. Saliva samples were centrifuged immediately after collection and stored frozen at -70ºC. All samples collected from a given subject were analyzed simultaneously. Using a polymerase chain reaction assay, saliva samples were processed for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA and urine samples were analyzed for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA detection. Saliva (2 to 3 ml) and urine (3 ml) specimens were concentrated with a 100-KD filtration unit. DNA was extracted by a nonorganic extraction method, and EBV DNA was detected as described here briefly. The PCR primers were directed at the EBV polymerase accessory protein gene (BMRF1): P1, 5-GTC CAA GAG CCACCACAC CTG and P2, 5-biotin CCC AGA AGT ATA CGT GGT GAC GTA GA. These primers were used at a concentrationof 200 µM with 10 µM deoxynucleic acid triphosphates. PCR was optimized using buffer II with 2.5 mM MgCl2. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was added to a final concentration of 5%. AmpliGold (2.5 units per 100 µl reaction mixture) was added, and 5 µl of the purified DNA was added to 20 µl of the reaction mixture. The cycle parameters were 95ºC for 9 min, followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 15 sec, 61ºC for 15 sec, and 72ºC for 15 sec, with a final extension step at 72ºC for 5 min.

CMV DNA was detected using primers that target the major immediate early gene (P1, 5-TGT CCT CCC GCT CCT C and P2, biotin 5-ATG AAG GTC TTT GCC CAG TA). All reactions were carried out using a Perkin-Elmer GenAmp system 9600. An initial denaturation step of 94ºC for 9 min was followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 30 sec, 69ºC for 15 sec, 72ºC for 30 sec, 72ºC for 7 min, and a 4ºC hold. The amplified product was analyzed for the presence of EBV or CMV using the Digene Sharp Signal System according to the manufacturer's instructions.

EBV and CMV antibody titers from blood samples were determined by indirect immunofluorescence assay. Commercially prepared substrate slides and control sera were used for determining antibody (IgG) titers for viral capsid antigen (VCA) and early antigen (EA) of EBV, CMV, and measles (Bion Enterprises, Park Ridge, IL). Four-fold dilutions of plasma were prepared with phosphate-buffered saline. The endpoint titer was determined as the highest dilution of serum in which immunofluorescent-positive cells could be detected. All specimens were batch analyzed and read blind-coded.

The frequency of viral shedding in saliva and viral antibody titers in plasma from chamber study subjects and controls were tested for normality. One-way analysis of variance was performed to study significant differences across different times during the study.

The method of generalized estimating equations with a logit link was used to find significant difference between the phases (pre-, in-, and postchamber). The differences between sampling periods were considered significant if P < 0.05.

RESULTS:
A total of 418 saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects participating in the two chamber studies. Overall, EBV DNA was detected in 35% of the 418 total saliva samples collected from these subjects. The subjects in the 60-day chamber study had EBV DNA in 13% (range 0 to 31%) of their samples, and the subjects in the 91-day study had EBV DNA in 51% (range 33 to 81%) of their samples. During both studies, all but one subject (in the 60-day chamber study) shed EBV.

Sixteen urine samples collected from the subjects of both chamber studies before and after the in-chamber phase were analyzed for CMV DNA. Interestingly, not a single sample showed evidence of CMV DNA. The presence of CMV DNA in urine from the control group was also rare (1/81 samples).

Viral antibody titers for EBV and CMV measured in samples from all 8 subjects before and after the study were not significantly different. Therefore, the data were pooled for further analysis. No significant differences in EBV VCA, EBV EA, or CMV IgG antibody titers were observed before and after either of the studies. Interestingly, EBV antibody titers did not differ significantly from the controls. However, CMV antibody titers of subjects were greater than those of the control group before and after the study.

Our current finding of increased viral reactivation in closed chamber study subjects agrees with our previous Space Shuttle and Antarctic data. These results support and extend our previous observations that latent viral reactivation increases during space flight, which is consistent with a stress-induced decrease in immune function.

experiment_title: Thermoregulation in Humans during Long-Term Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment investigated the circadian rhythm of core temperature and the thermoregulatory and cardiovascular adaptations during rest and exercise in the course of a long-term microgravity exposure on the International Space Station (ISS). The data derived might be important not only to understand human adaptation in space in view of the thermoregulatory and cardiovascular system, but as well as associated to problems dealing with body weight loss and de-synchronization of internal rhythms which affect the overall health and performance of astronauts/cosmonauts.

Measuring core body temperature is not straightforward because a thermometer must be placed close to the heart for best results. Many types of thermometers exist, from the type that goes under the tongue to the type that goes into the ear, but unfortunately the most accurate way of reading a core temperature is inserting a thermometer in the rectum. Body temperature tends to be lower in the feet and lowest in the early morning hours between four and six.

APPROACH:
As part of this experiment, a total of 11 astronauts took their temperatures using Thermolab, an instrument developed by Dr. Hanns-Christian Gunga, of the Center for Space Medicine and Extreme Environments in Germany. The Thermolab sensor is non-invasive, and can be read from a distance, making it a valuable tool for astronauts working in space. It makes use of two sensors — one attached to an astronaut's head, the other to his or her chest. Mission controllers on the ground were able to monitor the astronauts' temperatures as they continued working on the ISS. This experiment was performed in conjunction with the NASA sponsored VO2max study. Astronauts wore the Thermolab hardware while performing the VO2max study protocol.

RESULTS:
This experiment shows that an astronaut's temperature rises by one degree Celsius during the first two months on the ISS and remains there until it drops back to normal on return to Earth. Comparing data to other studies shows a correlation with Interleukin-1, a hormone that causes fever when sick. Raising body temperature by a degree requires 20% more energy, derived from food, so mission planners need to know more about this phenomenon in order to estimate the required food supplies for long-duration missions.

experiment_title: Study of Muscarinic and GABA (Benzodiazepine) Receptors in the Sensory-Motor Cortex, Hippocampus, and Spinal Cord
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In this experiment, frontal lobe samples from brains of space-flown rats were processed for the study of muscarinic (cholinergic) and GABA (benzodiazepine) receptors, and for immunocytochemical localization of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). The aim was to explore the feasibility of investigating neurotransmitters and their receptors in space flight experiments.

Approach:

For receptor binding studies, slides with 20 micrometers frontal lobe sections were incubated with 3H-ligand, washed, and later placed in an x-ray cassette. Tritium sensitive film was placed over the slides and later developed. For GABA and GFAP immunocytochemistry, slide-mounted tissue sections were fixated with appropriate solutions and rinsed in cold phosphate buffer saline.

Results:

Although radioactive labeling of both muscarinic cholinergic and GABA receptors proved to be successful with the techniques employed, distinct receptor localization of individual laminae of the frontal neocortex was not possible since the sampling area was different in the various groups of animals. In spite of efforts made for proper orientation and regional identification of laminae, it was found that a densitometric (quantitation of autoradiograms) analysis of tissue did not contribute to the final interpretation of the effects of weightlessness on these receptors. As to the immunocytochemical studies, the use of both markers, GFAP and GABA antiserum, confirmed the suitability of the techniques for frozen material. Similar problems to those encountered in the receptor studies prevented an adequate interpretation of the effects of microgravity exposure on the localization and distribution of GABA and GFAP.

experiment_title: Differentiation of Bone Marrow Macrophages in Space (BONEMAC)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The goal of the BoneMac spaceflight experiment was to determine how C57BL/6J mouse macrophage differentiation was suppressed during space flight by: 1) testing the hypothesis that CSF-1 receptor expression in progenitor cells was decreased, 2) assessing effects of the space flight environment on differentiation mechanisms; this involved studying cell phenotypes, mRNA expression, and cytokine expression during progenitor cell differentiation, and 3) determining which differentiation processes are affected by examining cell surface phenotypes and gene expression.

APPROACH:

Primary murine bone marrow cells from the humeri, femor and tibia of adult C57BL/6J mice were used for this experiment. The collected cells were suspended in growth medium supplemented with macrophage colony stimulating factor (CSF-1) and loaded into the primary chambers of 48 FPAs. Formalin was loaded into the secondary chambers of 32 FPAs; 6.0 M guanidinium isothiocyanate (GITC) was loaded into the secondary chambers of 8 FPAs, and growth medium plus CSF-1 (nonpreserved) was loaded into the secondary chambers of 8 FPAs. A total of 6 GAPs were loaded with 8 FPAs each. After loading, the cells were placed into the CGBA (37 degrees C) to start incubation, pre-launch. In flight, one set of BONEMAC GAPs were operated on FD6, and a second set of GAPs were operated on FD15 to allow the bone cells to differentiate for different time durations. Post-flight, the FPAs were processed and analyzed. A ground control maintained at SLS Lab followed the same protocols and timeline as the flight samples.

RESULTS:

We differentiated mouse bone marrow cells in the presence of recombinant macrophage colony stimulating (rM-CSF) factor for 14 days during the flight of space shuttle Space Transportation System (STS)-126. We tested the hypothesis that the receptor expression for M-CSF, c-Fms was reduced. We used flow cytometry to assess molecules on cells that were preserved during flight to define the differentiation state of the developing bone marrow macrophages; including CD11b, CD31, CD44, Ly6C, Ly6G, F4/80, Mac2, c-Fos as well as c-Fms. In addition, RNA was preserved during the flight and was used to perform a gene microarray. We found that there were significant differences in the number of macrophages that developed in space compared to controls maintained on Earth. We found that there were significant changes in the distribution of cells that expressed CD11b, CD31, F4/80, Mac2, Ly6C and c-Fos. However, there were no changes in c-Fms expression and no consistent pattern of advanced or retarded differentiation during space flight. We also found a pattern of transcript levels that would be consistent with a relatively normal differentiation outcome but increased proliferation by the bone marrow macrophages that were assayed after 14 days of space flight. There also was a surprising pattern of space flight influence on genes of the coagulation pathway. These data confirm that a space flight can have an impact on the in vitro development of macrophages from mouse bone marrow cells of mice.

experiment_title: Suited Contingency Ops Food - 2
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In a contingency cabin depressurization event, it is expected that crewmembers would be in a pressurized suit for up to 144 hours, requiring nutrition to be safely delivered against a pressure differential of 4 psi. The Advanced Food Technology (AFT) group sought to develop both a prototype fluid delivery system that would overcome the pressure differential and guidelines for a nutritional beverage compatible with the delivery system. Two prototypes were developed and analyzed. The bag-in-bag (BiB) prototype, designed to equalize the suit pressure with the beverage pouch and enable a crewmember to drink normally, was operated successfully in both vacuum chamber and suited subject tests. The Boa restrainer pouch, designed to provide mechanical leverage to overcome the pressure differential, was not successful, and recommendations for improved performance have been offered. Guidelines for developing contingency beverage prototypes, including viscosity and rehydration properties, were compiled based on their compatibility with the delivery hardware. Contingency beverage shelf life predictions were calculated based on generated vapor sorption isotherm curves. Evaluation results and food product parameters have the potential to be used to improve future prototype designs and develop complete nutritional beverages for contingency events and extended EVAs.

The objectives of this experiment are to develop food product parameters to meet nutritional, acceptability, stability, and suit interface criteria, and to test several concepts for dispensing liquid through a feed port into a pressurized suit.

AFT will receive energy requirements and nutritional requirements from HHC (Nutritional Biochemistry Laboratory). The food parameters that enable compatibility with the in-suit feeding system will be defined by interfacing with Crew Survival Systems (CSS).

APPROACH:
An approach for this experiment is currently not available.

RESULTS:
The BiB prototype was successful to allow the crewmember to drink nominally. Additional work will be done to improve this protoype. The Boa was not successful, and a decision was made not to continue work on this prototype.

experiment_title: Effect of Load levels of Subject Loading Device on Gait, Ground Reaction Force, and Kinematics during Human Treadmill Locomotion in a Weightless Environment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this experiment was to determine the influence of Subject Loading Device (SLD) external load (EL) magnitudes on the ground reaction force (GRF) and kinematics during locomotion in microgravity. The SLD is currently used by crewmembers while they are exercising on the Treadmill with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization (TVIS) onboard the International Space Station (ISS). The TVIS with integrated SLD is intended as a countermeasure to bone loss and neuromuscular deconditioning. A crewmember exercising on the treadmill receives an external load by means of an upper-body harness that attaches to the SLD via extender straps or bungees. GRF is imparted as the SLD pulls the crew member toward the treadmill surface during locomotion. The SLD utilizes a mechanical spring-loaded cable and pulley system to transfer specific loads to the crew member via an upper-body harness. It is not known how this type of loading affects the gait, GRF, and kinematics during locomotion on the ISS.

The primary objective of this investigation was to determine if gait kinematics and GRF during locomotion at 0-G, using a simulated ISS treadmill and SLD, were significantly different from those found during locomotion at 1-G. The secondary objective of this investigation was to quantify the load magnitude, variability, and stiffness of the external load (EL) applied.

APPROACH:
Four subjects (3 men, 1 woman, 28.0 ± 5.6 years, 170.8 ± 9.1 cm, 75.1 ± 11.2 kg) walked at 3 mph (4.8 km/h) and ran at 5, and 7 mph (8.0 and 11.2 km/h) during microgravity (0-G) on the KC-135 aircraft and on the ground (1-G). The KC-135 creates microgravitational conditions by flying a "roller-coaster" parabolic-shaped path. Before the study began, all subjects passed a modified Air Force Class III physical exam and signed an informed consent document. This study was approved by the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS).

A treadmill instrumented with force plates (Kistler Gaitway, Amherst, NY) was used to measure vertical ground reaction forces. A ¼-inch-thick aluminum plate with a cutout equal in size to the TVIS running surface was placed over the treadmill running surface. The two bilateral SLD units were mounted on either side of the treadmill in a configuration similar to that used during actual space flight. Two harnesses were used: a Russian-designed harness and the U.S.-designed harness currently in use on the ISS. Both harnesses were tested because it was anticipated that either will be used with the ISS treadmill. Each harness was attached to the SLD in two manners: relatively non-compliant extender straps and compliant bungees.

RESULTS:
The mean EL provided to subjects during dynamic locomotion was smaller than that predicted from static measurements. When extender straps were used, the EL decreased by 4 to 10% as locomotion speed increased from 3 to 7 mph. Furthermore, as the EL setting was increased from low (70% BW) to full (100% BW) loading, EL decreased approximately 2-3% at each speed. When bungees were used in series with the SLD, the dynamic EL decreased 14% for walking and 4-8% for running. The mean EL stiffness with extender straps was 3.55 kg/cm, and 0.71 kg/cm with bungees. Thus, the bungees decreased load stiffness by a factor of approximately 5. This greatly reduced the variation in EL during locomotion. Bungees also reduced asymmetries in EL. Both the reduced stiffness and reduced asymmetry should improve crewmember comfort.

The similarity of kinematic parameters obtained at 0-G and 1-G suggests that locomotion patterns in microgravity are similar to that occurring in 1-G, especially when EL levels approach full body weight loading. However, a more extensive kinematic analysis is required to further support this conclusion.

The ability of the SLD to reproduce 1-G-like GRFs was more limited. The SLD was able to reproduce 1-G-like peak impact force, and at higher load levels also reproduced 1-G-like impulse magnitudes. However, even at EL levels close to full body weight, locomotion with the SLD device does not reproduce the peak active force or loading rate experienced at 1-G.

A limitation of this study was that the treadmill used was not the actual TVIS. Although the tread area replicated the TVIS, the test treadmill was bolted to the floor of the aircraft. The TVIS on the ISS floats in a pit in the service module and is connected to the structure only by soft springs, which provide vibration isolation from the ISS structure. TVIS is equipped with gyroscopes to maintain stability of the device during exercise. It is possible that the vibration isolation system associated with the TVIS may result in decreased resistance of the treadmill surface to any applied forces, thereby dampening ground reaction forces. Therefore gait timing patterns, kinematics, and ground reaction force parameters may be different on the TVIS. For these findings to be confidently applied to the TVIS, an experiment needs to be conducted in microgravity on a device that reproduces the vibration isolation system used for TVIS.

Because peak active force and loading rate are considered to be important factors for maintenance of bone mineral density, the development of next-generation subject loading devices should strive to replicate 1-G levels of these parameters. In addition, more research should be conducted; possibly including long-term training and bed rest studies, to determine how the alterations in GRF that would be expected to occur at 0-G might affect neuromuscular conditioning and bone mineral density.

experiment_title: Combined Effects of Nutritional and Exercise Countermeasures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Muscular inactivity contributes to the loss of strength and muscle mass and is inherent in space flight. The decrease in rate of muscle protein synthesis with inactivity results in a loss of lean body mass (LBM) and muscle function. Supplementation with Essential Amino Acids (EAA) during bedrest stimulates muscle protein synthesis and preserves LBM. The loss of muscle function with inactivity is partially ameliorated by EAA supplementation and resistive exercise preserves muscle protein synthesis and function during bed rest.

This investigation was designed to evaluate multiple countermeasures to reduce the loss of muscle strength and mass and has the following objectives:

  • Determine if the anabolic stimulus provided by EAA ingestion is capable of ameliorating the catabolic effects of a 90 day 6o head-down bed rest by stimulating mixed muscle fractional synthesis rates during bed rest.
  • Determine the ability of resistive exercise (RE) alone to stimulate muscle protein synthesis during 90 days of bed rest at 6 degree head-down tilt, resulting in the partial preservation of lean muscle mass and the preservation of muscle strength by the neuromuscular stimulus provided by RE. In addition, the use of RE will reduce the development of insulin resistance, maintain skeletal muscle perfusion and muscle oxidative capacity and reduce tissue fat accumulation.
  • Determine if a combined countermeasure incorporating both EAA and RE can provide an additive anabolic stimulus greater than either intervention alone and if this stimulus will maintain muscle protein synthesis thus preserving lean muscle mass and function, maintain glucose tolerance and skeletal muscle perfusion and ameliorate the loss of muscle oxidative capacity.

    • APPROACH:
    Campaign 3A represented the Control Group for this investigation which served as a control for EAA supplementation and exercise as countermeasures against changes in muscle protein synthesis, insulin resistance, and changes in lean body and fat body mass.

    DXA data were collected to determine the effect of bed rest on lean and fat body mass of the whole body and leg. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used as a noninvasive means for measuring muscle oxidative capacity and lipid content. Glucose and insulin levels were measured during the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Resting energy expenditure was measured to predict total caloric requirements and nitrogen balance was calculated from 24-hour urine collection. Muscle biopsies of the vastus lateralis were obtained to calculate muscle fractional synthetic rate (FSR).

    RESULTS:
    This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during Bed Rest Campaigns 3A, 3B, and 3C Studies. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study.

experiment_title: A Systems-Biology Approach to Assessing the Impact of a Centrifugation Model of Spaceflight on Cross-System Communication
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
We hypothesize that hypergravity-induced changes in gut microbiome, SNS function, and inflammatory activity lead to a breakdown in the communication between distinct physiological systems (as measured by changes in cardiopulmonary control); and that these responses depend on the gravitational environment. Furthermore, we propose that these gravity-dependent deficits can be countered by a combination of prebiotic nutritional supplements that are known to preferentially expand stress protective bacterial species.

APPROACH:
Specific Aim 1. Confirm that centrifugation results in detectable changes in gut microbiome, as well as in sympathetic and inflammatory activity, indicative of increased health risk. Mice will be placed on the 8 ft diameter centrifuge at Ames Research Center and exposed to 1.5 or 2 G for 4 weeks. After centrifugation, adrenal glands, blood, liver, spleen, and intestines will be collected and assessed for changes in sympathetic and inflammatory activity as well as for changes in microbiome as compared to matched 1G controls.

Specific Aim 2. Confirm that prolonged exposure to hypergravity leads to a breakdown in communication between distinct physiological systems, causing decrements in function. The same mice used in Aim 1 will be used here. Our model focuses on brainstem control of cardiopulmonary function, driven primarily by sympathetic/vagal innervation. The brainstem, spinal cord, heart and lungs will be collected. Analysis will focus specifically on the nucleus tractus solitarii (NTS), the first-order integrative site for vagal afferents projecting from the gut, heart, and lungs to the central nervous system. The NTS coordinates efferent output to targets that are critical for the control of breathing, heart/vasculature, and gut. In vivo and in vitro electrophysiology will be used to quantify changes in sympathetic tone and confirm that synaptic activity within the NTS is altered by changes in microbiome. Immunohistochemistry and RNAseq will be used to assess changes in inflammation and stress-related message, allowing us to determine the role cytokines and downstream effectors play in modulating NTS neuronal activity correlated with cardiorespiratory control.

Specific Aim 3. Determine that centrifugation-induced changes in health status signaling are linked to changes in microbiome. Based on our previous findings, we hypothesize that ingestion of a prebiotic supplement blend [galactooligosaccharides (GOS)+polydextrose (PDX)+lactoferrin + milk fat globule membrane protein (MFGMP)] will both prevent gut microbial dysbiosis produced by centrifugation and increase selective stress protective gut bacteria (i.e., lactobacillus and bifidobacteria). Prebiotic-enriched chow or calorically matched chow will be available ad libitum throughout the experiment, starting 1 week prior to centrifugation. Mice will be placed on the 8 ft diameter centrifuge at Ames Research Center and exposed to 2 G for 4 weeks. Parameters described in Aims 1 & 2 will be assessed as described.

Year 1: Experiment Overview Male and Female, C57BL/6 mice (10/group) were ordered from Jackson Laboratories and shipped to the Ames Research Center Animal Care Facility (ACF). After a 1-week acclimation period, the mice were moved to the 8 ft. diameter centrifuge facility for an additional 1-week acclimation period. During this time, we collected baseline ECG measurements and fecal samples. Thereafter, the mice were placed on the centrifuge and exposed to 2 G for 4 weeks. Controls were kept in the same room in similar lighting, temperature and noise conditions. The centrifuge was stopped briefly twice a week to change bedding, food, hydrogel packs and to perform health checks. Two weeks into the run, we collected fecal pellets from all mice and measured ECG activity on a subset of mice. After centrifugation, we again took ECG measurements on all mice prior to tissue collection. Adrenals, blood and spleen were collected to assess changes in sympathetic and inflammatory activity via flow cytometry, multiplexed cytokine arrays and ELISAs. Fecal pellets and intestines were collected to evaluate changes in the adherent commensal bacteria of the gut microbiome. Assays include 16S rRNA sequencing, taxonomic analyses, and selective bacterial culture.

Year 2: Experiment Overview For part two of the study, female C57BL/6 mice (10/group) will be used. All experiment details will remain the same as in year one except for the addition of a vivarium control group and the prebiotic diet (specific aim 3). The vivarium control group will be housed at the Animal Care Facility for the entire experiment duration and shall serve as the unexposed condition. Additionally, all mice will be provided either a prebiotic or control diet to evaluate the responses from changes in the gravitational environment.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Development of a Nitrifying Packed Bed Bioreactor for use in an Advanced Water Recovery System for Microgravity Environments
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study addressed two challenges in microgravity wastewater reclamation for bacterial processes: nitrification and aeration. Biological wastewater processing requires sufficient nitrification, which in turn requires adequate oxygenation through aeration. This project constructed, analyzed, and modeled a gravity independent nitrification (GIN) reactor. The results of this work will be used to develop an aerobic nitrification reactor that will be coupled with an anaerobic bioreactor currently in development at the Advanced Water Recovery System Development Facility at Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
Performance was measured as conversion of ammonium to nitrate as a function of residence time and ammonia load. The conversion of ammonium to nitrate is critical in maintaining the anoxic bioreactor TOC reduction efficiency. The ammonium effluent from the first stage anoxic bioreactor is fed to the second stage nitrifying reactor where the ammonium is oxidized to nitrate and then returned to the anoxic reactor as a nitrate reactant necessary for organics reduction by the anaerobic bacteria.

RESULTS:
A material balance on the system predicts that only 50 mg/L of ammonium can be theoretically oxidized to nitrate given the maximum solubility of oxygen at current conditions. Given that the system is currently oxidizing 300 mg/L of ammonium the membrane oxygenator must be doubling as a bioreactor where the bacteria are consuming oxygen within the oxygenator and hence increasing the transfer of oxygen across the membrane at a rate much higher than that given by equilibrium saturation of air and water with no reaction.

The Stevens reactor operated with pure oxygen at 25 psig and yet could not achieve good conversions of ammonium to nitrate at ammonium levels higher than 50 mg/L. This is probably due to poor transfer of oxygen in the silastic tubing oxygenator. A major conclusion of the results is that the cross flow hollow fiber medical oxygenator provides an excellent environment for the nitrifying bacteria to thrive as well as excellent transfer of oxygen from air to the wastewater stream.
